en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā* on the *Vinayapiṭaka* (First Part).
Prologue to the Book:
Having bowed down to the Sugata, whose heart is full of compassion and who bestows welfare,
and to the stainless Dhamma and the Saṅgha endowed with perfect virtues.
Many commentaries on the meaning of the Vinaya,
composed by various predecessors, were intricate and filled with diverse methods.
Among them, some were very extensive and difficult to penetrate due to their textual complexity.
In some places they are inconsistent both in meaning and in wording;
some are incomplete, and some cause confusion. Therefore, having extracted the essence from those [texts] in a concise form, [this work is composed].
Illuminating the hidden meaning, purifying what has been misunderstood, and clarifying the underlying principles wherever they appear—
in order to sever the doubts of the monks who live with lightness of heart regarding the Vinaya— [he composed this work].
I shall write a brief commentary on its hidden meaning.
Regarding the commentary on the introduction to the work:
at the beginning of the commentary on the Vinaya, wishing to pay homage to the Triple Gem, [the author] intends to demonstrate its possession of distinguished qualities.

He said, "Even for ten million eons," and so forth. For it is through the possession of distinguished qualities that one becomes worthy of veneration, and veneration performed toward those worthy of veneration accomplishes the intended purpose.

Regarding this, the teachers elaborate in many ways in various places on the purpose of performing the homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the commentary; however, we shall show here only the purpose intended in this context.
Therefore, it should be understood that the performance of homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the commentary is for the purpose of completing the commentary as promised without obstacle.

For it has been said: "By its power, obstacles are destroyed. Indeed, by performing homage to the Triple Gem, through the departure of defilements such as lust, through the sharpening of qualities such as wisdom, through the increase of longevity and so forth, and through the state of possessing preeminent merit, [obstacles are removed].
The completion of the commentary exactly as promised, without any obstacles, follows immediately after this.
In that regard, wishing first to pay homage to the Blessed One, he said: "He who, even in ten million eons... and so forth.
Furthermore, because this teaching of the Vinaya has arisen from knowledge dominated by compassion (*karuṇā*), it is itself dominated by compassion.
The praise has begun. For this is the nature of a teacher: namely, that his praise corresponds to the undertaking [of the task].

And here, by the mention of "compassion" (karuṇā), it should be understood that all the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha are included by way of implication, because all other qualities of a Buddha are rooted in that [compassion].
In this context, the word *yo* (who), being an indefinite term, is connected with the word *nātho* (protector). Even for ten million eons (*kappakoṭīhi*)...

"Immeasurable time" (*appameyyaṃ kālaṃ*) means a period of time that cannot be measured even by counting in terms of tens of millions of eons (*kappakoṭi*), such that one could not say, "there are this many tens of millions of eons.
By the word *api* ("even"), it is shown that it is all the more impossible to measure by counting in terms of years.

Furthermore, the phrase "immeasurable time" is used in the accusative case to express continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*); thus, it refers to a duration that cannot be delimited even by counting in terms of tens of millions of eons, let alone by way of incalculable units (*asaṅkhyeyya*).

However, because it must be delimited, he shows that [the Buddha] reached physical exhaustion and fatigue while performing extremely difficult tasks, such as the five great renunciations, for an immeasurable period of four *asaṅkhyeya* eons, continuously and without interruption.

"For the welfare of the world" means for the benefit of the world of sentient beings. He is called a "Protector" (*nātha*) because he protects; that is, he aspires for the welfare and happiness of those to be trained.
The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, he is called *nātha* because he "torments" (*nāthati*) the defilements residing in those to be trained;

or, he is called *nātha* because he "entreats" (*nāthati*) those to be trained, urging them on even by requesting them to perform what is for their own benefit. Thus, it is said that he is the refuge of the world, the lord of the world, and the leader of the world.

Regarding the phrase "of the Greatly Compassionate One" (*mahākāruṇikassa*): it refers to one whose heart is shaken by compassion and who, for the sake of the welfare of the world, [engages] in extremely difficult deeds.
The meaning is: "of that Greatly Compassionate One who has come after having experienced such suffering in manifold ways.

In this context, *karoti* means compassion (*karuṇā*); the meaning is that it scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it is extended or directed toward those who are suffering.
Or else, it is called *karuṇā* because it "strikes" (*kiṇāti*); for when there is suffering in others, it strikes, afflicts, and destroys [the heart of] the compassionate one.
Or, the meaning is "the suffering of another. Or, it is *karuṇā* because when there is suffering in another, it causes a trembling and heartache for the virtuous.

Alternatively, *ka* means happiness; it obstructs that, thus it is *karuṇā*. For this [compassion], characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others, obstructs and hinders the happiness of compassionate ones due to their lack of regard for their own happiness. One who is devoted to compassion is a compassionate one (*kāruṇika*).
"Great, compassionate, the Great Compassionate One; let there be homage to him"—this is the remainder of the reading.
Thus, having praised the Blessed One in brief by way of his compassion and all his qualities of omniscience, he now spoke the verse beginning with "asambudhaṃ" in order to praise the True Dhamma.
Therein, that which is unawakened (*asambudhaṃ*) by the world of living beings, yet has been resorted to by the Buddha...

The connection is: "He goes to existence; homage to that excellent Dhamma. Therein, *asambudhaṃ* means "not awakening," which is to say, "not penetrating according to its true nature. Here, the suffix *-anta* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
*Yaṃ* refers, in an indefinite sense, to the nine supramundane states together with the scriptures, indicated here as the object of action (*kamma-bhāva*). *Buddhanisevitaṃ* means...

This is its specific qualification: it has been "practiced" (*nisevita*) by the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), or by the Pacceka Buddhas and Disciple-Buddhas (*sāvakabuddha*), according to their respective capacities, through the practice of the field of activity (*gocarāsevana*) and the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanāsevana*);

the meaning is that it has not been abandoned. In this context, the fruit of the scriptures (*pariyatti-phala*) and Nibbāna are practiced solely by way of the practice of the field of activity, whereas the Path (*magga*) is practiced both by way of the practice of cultivation and by way of the practice of the field of activity, such as through the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
It is practiced. They become from existence to existence. Alternatively, the meaning is that they become small and great by way of being inferior, superior, and so forth;
for the vowel *a* is seen to have the sense of "growth," as in such expressions as "the qualities of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*).

Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*) means growth, and "non-existence" (*abhava*) means decline. Or else, "existence" refers to the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), and "non-existence" refers to the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

"Becoming and non-becoming" (*bhavābhava*) refers to the aforementioned states of existence and non-existence; "that becoming and non-becoming" (*taṃ bhavābhavaṃ*). "Goes" (*gacchati*) means approaches.

"The world of the living" (*jīvaloka*) is the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "Destroyer of the net of defilements beginning with ignorance" (*avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsino*) is an epithet qualifying the Dhamma.

In this context, "ignorance" (*avijjā*) is nescience (*aññāṇa*), because one does not know, that is, does not understand the true nature of phenomena as they are. "Of which [defilements] it is the first" refers to craving and the others.
They are called *kilesā* (defilements) because beings are defiled by them; and they are called a *jāla* (net) because they are like a net in the sense that they entangle beings.
He destroys—that is, he utterly annihilates—that net of defilements such as ignorance by means of his virtue (*sīla*), thus he is "the destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance.
Now, is it not the case that here the nine supramundane states together with the scriptures (*pariyatti*) are intended? And therein, is it not the Path alone that [destroys] the defilements?

Is it not the case that it destroys [defilements] and does not lead [to them]? It is said: because the Path also destroys defilements by means of reaching Nibbāna, Nibbāna is also said to "destroy defilements.
Furthermore, since the function of the Path in destroying defilements is completed by its fruit (phala), the fruit is also called a "destroyer of defilements.
And the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhamma) is also [so called] because it serves as the decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the destruction of defilements.

There is no fault in saying that he is "worthy of being called the destroyer of defilements. Regarding the phrase "of that excellent Dhamma": this is a specifying statement for that which was previously unspecified.
In this context, it is called "Dhamma" because it sustains one who practices according to the instruction, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery or the suffering of saṃsāra.
That very Dhamma, described in the manner stated, is "excellent" (vara) by virtue of having nothing superior to itself.
"Exalted and unsurpassed" refers to the supreme Dhamma; the meaning is: "May there be homage to that supreme Dhamma.
Having thus praised the True Dhamma by way of its qualities as a whole through this brief method, he now speaks the words beginning with "by qualities" in order to praise the Noble Saṅgha.
Therein, the connection is: "I bow to that Noble Saṅgha which is endowed with qualities. [The qualities are] virtue and so forth.

And here, "qualities" (guṇā) are intended as both mundane and supramundane. Although one should say "knowledge of liberation and liberation" (*vimutti-vimuttiñāṇa*), it is stated as "knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) by way of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (retaining only one member of a similar group).
Alternatively, the inclusion of "liberation" should be understood through the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), which functions as a synonym for "etcetera" (*pabhuti*).

In this context, "liberation" refers to the fruit (*phala*). "Knowledge of liberation" refers to the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). By the word "etcetera," the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*), and so on, are included.

The qualities should be understood as being comprised [within it]. Because it is like a field for the increase of the preeminent merit of people who seek the wholesome, he says, "the field for people who seek the wholesome.
For a field (*khetta*) is so called because it protects (*tāyati*) the sown seed by causing it to yield great fruit. Regarding the term "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*):
here, they are "noble" (*ariya*) because they have gone far away from defilements (*ārakattā kilesehi*) and because they do not proceed toward what is not the goal (*anaye na iriyanato*).

And because they are worthy of being approached by the world together with its devas as a refuge through their noble conduct, and because they are to be approached for that reason, and because the purpose of those who have approached them is accomplished, they are the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
The eight types of noble persons are the Noble Ones; the assembly or collection of Noble Ones is the Noble Saṅgha (*ariyasaṅgha*); [he pays homage] to that Noble Saṅgha.
Now, having directed the flow of merit produced by this prostration to the Triple Gem toward the intended purpose, he himself—

In order to show that the composition of this commentary on the Vinaya—which is being praised—is itself rooted in the Dispensation (Sāsana) by way of demonstrating that the Vinaya is the root of the entire Dispensation, he spoke these two verses beginning with "iccevaṃ.
"Puññābhisanda" means a flood of merit, a stream of merit, or a mass of merit; "tassānubhāvena" means by the power of that aforementioned stream of merit.
The connection is that they will praise the Vinaya once their obstacles have been destroyed by power.
It should be construed thus: "In whom standing, the well-established teaching of the Blessed One—the one who is firmly established—becomes established.
Therein, "in whom" means in which Vinaya Piṭaka. "Standing" means being complete both in text and in meaning among persons possessed of a sense of shame.
"In the sense of being established" means in the sense of being set in motion. "The Teaching" (sāsana) refers to the teaching comprised within the three trainings.

"Of one not established" means of one not established in the two extremes characterized by devotion to sensual pleasures and devotion to self-mortification; some also say this refers to "even though the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna.
"Well-established" means well-established in the Middle Way, which is free from those two extremes. "Unmixed" is a neuter noun indicating the state of being unmixed with the tenets of other schools.
It means that they will explain [the text] without mixing it up and without confusion.

"Relying on the power of the ancient teachers" (nissāya pubbācariyānubhāvaṃ) means relying on the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) as expounded by the ancient teachers, not by one's own power; this is the intended meaning.
Now, since the ancient commentaries already exist, what is the purpose of this new exposition of the Vinaya? To this he says: "Granted, however," and so forth.
In this context, "entirely" (*kāmaṃ*) means "according to one's wish" or "in every respect"; thus it is said [to be] "complete.
Its connection is with the phrase "this Vinaya has been praised. "By the bull-like former teachers" (*pubbācariyāsabhehi*):

the Elder Mahākassapa and others are indeed "former teachers" (*pubbācariya*), and they are "bulls" (*āsabha*) in the sense of being unshakable and supreme; thus it is meant "by those excellent former teachers."
But who were those former teachers? He says: "By those whose stains and taints were washed away by the water of knowledge," and so forth.

Those by whom the three stains of passion and the rest, as well as the four taints beginning with the taint of sensual desire, have been washed away—cleansed and purified by the water, that is, the fluid known as the knowledge of the supreme path, through the production of the state of non-arising in the future—are "those whose stains and taints were washed away by the water of knowledge"; [the text refers] to them as "those whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava).
The meaning is as follows: although they were those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), they were not merely dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*);

therefore, he said, "by means of purified clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and analytical insight (*paṭisambhidā*). In this context, "clear knowledge" refers to either the threefold clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) or the eightfold clear knowledge (*aṭṭha vijjā*).

Furthermore, because [the compilers] selected and included such individuals as the Elder Mahākassapa and others—despite their having attained analytical insight—it is shown that their capacity for describing the true Dharma (*saddhamma-saṃvaṇṇanā*) was preeminent; thus he said.
“By those skilled in praising the true Dhamma.
*Sallekha* means that which scrapes away (*sallikhati*), makes thin, or diminishes the mass of defilements or the abundance of requisites; it is the collection of qualities such as fewness of wishes.

However, here, because the subject matter concerns those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), the meaning should be understood specifically in the sense of scraping away the abundance of requisites.
"Sallekhika" means produced by effacement (*sallekha*); "in that which is effacement" refers to the attainment of effacement such as the observance of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

"By those for whom similes are not easily found" means those for whom there is no easily available simile such as "it is like this or that" regarding their practice of effacement; by them. By the phrase "of the Mahāvihāra," he excludes other schools (*nikāyantara*).
Here, by the term "Vihārasīsa," one should understand the inclusion of all the monks residing there as well as those who received their alms together with them.

Therefore, because the Elder Mahākassapa and the other compilers of the Dhamma were the source of the purification of view and conduct for those Mahāvihāravāsins and served as their standard of recognition, they are called "the banners of the Mahāvihāra."
"By them this Vinaya was expounded," meaning it was correctly and fully described by them. How so? He says:

"by various methods. This means by various methods following the excellent lineage of the Fully Enlightened One—that is, by methods that follow the intention of the Blessed One, which are in accordance with the Supreme Omniscient Buddha.

Having thus demonstrated that the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) is complete and lacking nothing, he now states "the commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) and so forth, in order to show the specific purpose and the request for his own work. In this context, "because it is composed" (*saṅkhatattā*) means because it has been written.
"It does not accomplish any purpose" (*na kañci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇāti*) means it does not achieve any goal.
By the words "That commentary... and so forth, he shows the manner in which he composed his own commentary.

Therein, beginning the commentary that is now being spoken of, and because the entire Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) must be included here, he takes the Great Commentary as the body for this commentary now being spoken of, and [takes] the *Mahāpaccarī*...

The connection between the words should be understood as follows: "Whatever exposition has been stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*], and whatever exposition has been stated in the well-known commentaries such as the *Kurundi*, from those expositions as well, without abandoning the most appropriate meaning and by incorporating the Theravāda tradition, they will properly commence the commentary. And here, the meaning is being explained.
*Etāyāti* is formed by changing the *ttha*-sound to the *ṭṭha*-sound. *Mahāpaccariyaṃ* means that which is named the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Here, *paccarī* refers to a raft; because it was composed while sitting upon one, it received that very name.
They say: "There is a monastery called Kurundīvallivihāra; because it was composed there, it received the name ‘Kurundī’."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā*.
"The meaning that is appropriate" means the meaning that is consistent with the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, or the meaning that is consistent with the fourfold logic of the Vinaya.

When it is said, "I shall compose the commentary by taking only the *aṭṭhakathās*," this refers to the fact that the doctrines of the Elders (*Theravāda*) stated in those *aṭṭhakathās* are external [to other traditions].
Thinking that they too were included therein, he said, "the Theravāda is included," meaning that they were included within the Theravāda as well.
With the verse beginning "That [teaching] of mine," he shows the manner in which the listeners should practice. In that context, "Dhammapadīpassa" means:
because it dispels the darkness of delusion, the Dhamma itself is like a lamp; thus, the Blessed One is the "Lamp of the Dhamma."
"Of him. "Honoring" means worshipping and respecting with the mind; they should attend and listen.

By the words beginning with "By the Buddha," he demonstrates that [this work] is authoritative by way of showing the purity of its origin through his own self-praise, and thereby shows that it should be followed.
In this regard, just as the Dhamma and Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha, so too...

The connection should be understood as follows: "Because the masters of the Sinhalese commentaries—who were learned in the minds of those sons of the Buddha, such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others, by whom that [Dhamma] was likewise known—composed the commentaries in former times.
In this context, "Dhamma" comprises the Sutta and Abhidhamma; "Vinaya" refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka; and "Vutta" (spoken) [refers to the word of the Buddha].
It has been spoken by the Blessed Buddha both according to the letter and according to the meaning. For there is no sūtra passage (*tantipada*) called "unexplained" (*abyākata*) by the Blessed One;
rather, the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) consist precisely of those miscellaneous teachings (*pakiṇṇakadesanā*) delivered by the Blessed One here and there.
"Known in that very same way" means that just as it was spoken by the Buddha, so too—without destroying even a single word or a single syllable—and [preserving] the intended meaning...

"Without disturbing" means being known and understood. "Not abandoning their wisdom" means not forsaking the entire determination of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā-vinicchaya*)—which consists of the tradition of the Elders received and brought down by the lineage of elders, designated as "wisdom"—and which proceeds both as an exposition of the Canon (*pāḷi-vaṇṇanā*) and as material independent of the Canon (*pāḷi-mutta*), among those sons of the Buddha.
"They composed commentaries" refers to the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Mahā-paccarī*, and so forth.
They composed the Sinhalese commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāyo*). There is also a reading, "They composed the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathāmakaṃsu*), where the meaning is the same.
Therefore—because they previously composed the commentaries without distorting the intention of those sons of the Buddha—therefore.
The construction is: "Whatever was stated in the commentaries, all that is authoritative. *Hi* is merely a particle.
Because the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is already indicated by the word "therefore" (*tasmā*), or else it has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), namely: "only the authoritative [texts].
If everything stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) were authoritative (*pamāṇa*), then in that case even errors due to negligence (*pamāda-lekhā*) would have to be authoritative;
therefore he said, "having excluded errors due to negligence," referring to those who, while writing from one stage to another, fail to maintain mindfulness through negligence.
"Errors of omission" (*pamādalekhā*) refers to instances where what should have been written in one place is instead written in another, or due to similar lapses;

these will be clarified by themselves in various places within the *Samantapāsādikā*. Furthermore, the following is the construction of the meaning (*atthayojanā*) by way of showing the connection for the word "since" (*yasmā*):
since it is stated in the commentaries that here, in this Dispensation, for those who possess reverence for the trainings...

The wise alone are the authority; and since this commentary, even with its distinction consisting merely of the abandonment of other languages and so forth, is not different in meaning [from the original], it will therefore indeed be authoritative.
Thus, it should be studied accordingly. "From those" means from those commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"Having abandoned the other language itself" means having removed the Sinhalese language itself. And the "path of detail" (*vitthāramagga*)...
"Having summarized" means that, having abandoned such a path of prolixity— which, although it should have been stated in its proper place according to the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*),
was instead explained through an excessively extensive sequence of words, including the analysis of word-meanings and so forth,
and by repeating the same method of meaning with only slight variations— [the author] proceeds by means of a wholesome explanation of the meaning.

The intention is this: having indicated by way of reference that what remains should be stated in the same manner as already explained in due order, we shall now explain it by way of summary. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the Vinaya, it is said:

"Having brought forward even what is stated further on in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), and having elaborated upon it here and there, [one who is ordained] by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*)... is one who has received full ordination; he is a bhikkhu."
Regarding the statement, “Having condensed such a detailed path— just like the detailed exposition of the four types of formal acts (kamma) beginning with the act of seeking permission (apalokana)—
it was said,” it would be more appropriate to say, “without deviating from the sequence of the text (tantikkama).
For to state what ought to be stated in one part of the Canon (pāḷi) in another place is indeed called "speaking by deviating from the sequence of the text."

For it has been said: "Having abandoned the textual sequence that had come down in due order—which was suitable to be explained exactly as it stood—and because it explains what was explained in the Sinhalese commentaries in inappropriate places by explaining it in its proper place, it is said: 'without deviating from the sequence of the text in any way.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
But how is it that when the detailed path is condensed, the exposition (*vinicchaya*) does not diminish? He says: "without leaving out any of the exposition at all.
Even while condensing, he does so by repeating [the points], yet he condenses only these [specific elements];
as for the exposition, however, he leaves out none of what is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), omitting not even the slightest portion.
This is what is meant. "Without deviating from any sequence of the thread" means without overstepping any sequence of the Canon;
the sense is: "We shall explain the Canon in its proper order.
"The meaning of the words of the Suttantas" refers to the discourses on meditation and so forth found in the Verañjakaṇḍa and other sections of the Suttanta.
In the Sinhalese commentaries (*Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā*), having stated, "It is the burden of those who specialize in the Suttas," the intention is:
"We shall fully elucidate the meaning of the points that ought not to be disparaged, in accordance with each respective Sutta. "Hessati" means "will be" or "will be performed.
And here, in the first interpretation of the meaning, [the sense is: "having accomplished the fourfold task, beginning with the relinquishing of other languages..."
The grammatical identity of the agent (*samānakattukatā*) should be understood in the sense of commentary as follows:
"This commentary will be composed by me, elucidating the meaning of the words of the Suttanta masters. However, in the latter interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood as:
"Having first performed the relinquishing of other languages and so forth as mentioned above, this commentary will be made by us, elucidating the meaning of the words of the Suttanta masters."
Thus, the state of having a common agent should be understood by way of the teacher.
The method of explaining the introductory discourse for the commencement of the book is finished.
The Discourse on the External Introduction.

Now, among the many types of discipline such as the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*), he says "therein," etc., showing the discipline that was promised by him as something to be explained with the words, "I shall explain that discipline.
Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) means in the verses already mentioned. The word "first" (*tāva*) should be understood in the sense of "initially"; thus, first—
This indicates that after having established the Vinaya, one will subsequently provide its commentary. "To be established" means to be determined.
"Therefore this is said" means that because it is to be established, for that reason the defining statement beginning with "this is called Vinaya" and so forth is spoken;
such is the meaning. "Of it" refers to the Vinaya. "Mātikā" means a summary or table of contents, for it is the basis for the explanatory passages.
Because it stands in the place of a mother, it is called a "matrix" (*mātikā*), as it is like a mother.
Now, having established the matrix for the subject matter that is to be commented upon, he says, "It was said by whom," and so forth.
This is what is meant: this [work] is adorned with the introductory narrative (nidāna), beginning with the words, "At one time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā."
Having stated the aforementioned details regarding the person by whom the Vinaya Piṭaka was spoken, the time at which it was spoken,
the reason for which it was spoken, by whom it was preserved, by whom it was brought [to this land], and in whom it is established,
I shall now provide a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya, demonstrating in many ways the meaning of the passage beginning with "At that time" (tena samayena).

And here, regarding the statement "by whom, when, and because of what," although one might wish to state it separately, it is not stated apart from the introductory formula beginning with "At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is because, according to the statement, "It is excellent in the beginning by way of the introduction,
and excellent in the end by way of the conclusion [‘this he said’],” both the introduction and the conclusion are included within the Teacher’s teaching itself, as they conform to it.
Since the *nidāna* (introduction) is also included within the Vinaya-pāḷi itself, it is stated: "by whom, when, and for what reason.

This too establishes the *mātikā* (matrix) by making it related specifically to the Vinaya Piṭaka. For that which is called "this" in the *mātikā* relates generally to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka everywhere.
Now, however, extracting that [phrase] separately and demonstrating it, he says "tattha vuttaṃ yena" and so forth.

"Tattha" means in those words of the matrix (mātikā). "Idaṃ" refers to the introductory statement beginning with "tena samayena. The word "hi" should be understood in the sense of "yasmā" (because); thus, what is meant is:
because the speech of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is not a statement based on his own personal perception (*attapaccakkha*), therefore [this introduction is used]. "Attapaccakkhavacanaṃ" means...

"It does not exist" means that the statement spoken [by others] is not something established by one's own direct experience. Alternatively, it means that the statement spoken at the time of one's own direct experience—that is, at the time when one is living—is not [true].
By both of these senses, the meaning is that the word spoken by the Blessed One does not fail to exist.
Commentary on the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā)
Regarding the phrase "and what is called the First Great Council" (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma cesā*):

here, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of including what is yet to be said, or it has the sense of an introduction (*upaññāsa*). An "introduction" (*upaññāsa*) is said to be the commencement of a sentence. This is indeed the habit of authors:
when, having said something, they begin to say another thing, they employ the word *ca*. This occurs in various places according to the requirements.
"Recitation" (*saṅgīti*) means the singing or speaking together of the scattered teachings and discipline (*dhamma-vinaya*) by way of grouping them according to their common purpose.
It is called a "Great Recitation" (*mahāsaṅgīti*) because of its vast scope and its venerable nature. And this is called the "First Great Recitation" with reference to the second and subsequent ones.
It "establishes" (*nidadāti*) the teaching by making known what was previously unknown through the factors of place, time, and so forth.

It is called the *nidāna* because it shows what has been done; for the sake of proficiency therein, he says, "beginning with the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma," since the activity that serves as the cause for the arising of the paths and fruits in those to be trained is, in the primary sense, the Buddha’s work.
Therein, the Dhamma itself—consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth—is the "Wheel" (*cakra*) in the sense of being set in motion; thus it is the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*).

"Wheel" (*cakkam*) means command; because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is the "Dhamma-wheel" (*dhammacakka*). Alternatively, it is the "Dhamma-wheel" because it is a wheel according to the Dhamma—that is, by way of the proper method.
"When the Buddha’s task was completed" (*katabuddhakicce*) connects with "the Blessed One, the Protector of the World," meaning when the Blessed One had finished his duties as a Buddha.
"At Kusinārā" is a locative expression used in the sense of proximity. "In the Mallas’ Sal Grove at Upavattana" refers to that [location].
He shows the Sālavana grove belonging to the Malla kings, which serves as the suburb of the city.
There, because those entering the city approach it from the garden and proceed along it, it is called "Upavattana";
thus, the Sālavana grove situated between the garden and the city is so named. For that garden was located to the south-west of Kusinārā.
From that park, a road adorned with rows of *sāla* groves proceeded facing east, then turned northward toward the southern gate of the city;
by that road people entered the city, and for that reason it was called "Upavattana.
There, it is said, in the midst of rows of *sāla* trees with interlacing branches and abundant shade—
The couch for the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One was prepared; it is with reference to that that it is said, "between the twin sāla trees.

That which is grasped by means of kamma and defilements is *upādi*; this refers to the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandhā*) and the matter produced by past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). Because these remain due to the fact that kamma and defilements have not been completely abandoned, they are called *upādisesa*.
The state where there is no such remainder is *anupādisesa*, which is the element of Nibbāna (*nibbānadhātu*); [the phrase refers to] by means of that.

This is a designation of the instrument (*karaṇaniddesa*) in the sense of a characteristic of being thus (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). In the term *parinibbāne*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimittatthe*);
the meaning is: "for the sake of the final nibbāna, they have gathered together in that place. *Saṅghatthero* means the Elder who is the senior of the Saṅgha.
And here, even though the word *saṅgha* depends on the word *bhikkhusatasahassa* (one hundred thousand monks), a compound is formed with the word *thera* because it is elliptical (*gamakatta*).
"Just as Devadatta’s family home [is well-known]"—this is the connection: the Venerable Mahākassapa inspired the bhikkhus for the purpose of the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
He stated the reason for generating such inspiration with the words "seven days after his final passing," and so forth. Seven days combined together...

"Sattāhaparinibbuto" means one who has been *parinibbūta* for seven days; the connection is that [Subhadda] was recollecting the words spoken by Subhadda, an elder who had gone forth late in life, regarding one who had been *parinibbūta* for seven days.
With the words "Enough, friend," etc., he shows the speech uttered by him. Therein, "alaṃ" is a word of refusal.
"By that Great Ascetic" (*tena mahāsamaṇena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative.
The meaning is: "We are well liberated from that Great Recluse"; the intention is, "and we were afflicted by it. Alternatively, *homā* is a present tense verb used in the sense of the past;
the meaning is *ahumhā* ("we were"). Regarding the phrase *ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati*:
it is called a *ṭhāna* (basis) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein, as its existence is dependent upon it; thus, it is a cause. *Kho* is used for emphasis; *etaṃ* refers to this reason.
"It exists indeed; it does not not exist"—this is the meaning. "What is that reason? he says: "Because of those evil bhikkhus," and so forth.
Here, *yaṃ* is a mere particle, or it is a designation of the reason; the meaning is: "That reason by which they might cause [the teaching] to disappear—that reason exists.

"With the Teacher passed away" (*atītasatthuka*) means: the Teacher has passed beyond this [world], or it belongs to him; thus it is the "dispensation with the Teacher passed away. (*Pāvacanaṃ*) means the dispensation.
"Padhāna" means speech; "pāvacana" refers to the Dhamma and Vinaya. "Having gained a faction" means having gained a faction of those who are shameless.
"Before long" means not for long at all. "As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure" means for as long a time as the Dhamma and the Vinaya remain among persons who possess a sense of shame.
"Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā" (this was spoken by the Blessed One) means that it was spoken by the Blessed One while reclining on his deathbed.

"Desito paññatto" (taught and laid down) refers to the teaching (*desanā*), which is the bestowing and awakening to both the Dhamma comprised within the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas and the Vinaya comprised within the Vinaya Piṭaka;
it is the making known of that very [Dhamma] according to its various modes and the establishing of it without confusion.
"Proclamation. "After my passing away, this Dhamma-Vinaya shall be your teacher":

after I have attained final Nibbāna, this Dhamma-Vinaya will fulfill the role of a teacher for you. "The Dispensation" (*sāsana*) is threefold by way of the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*paṭivedha*);
but in its ultimate sense, it consists of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*). "Enduring" (*addhaniya*)...
The connection is: "May it be capable of enduring the journey and may it remain for a long time.
Now, explaining the particular favor bestowed upon himself by the Perfectly Enlightened One, he said: "And that which I [received] from the Blessed One," and so forth.
Therein, the connection of the phrase "and that which I" (*yañcāhaṃ*) is with the word "favored" (*anuggahito*). Therein, "since" (*yaṃ*) means "because" or "for which reason."
This has been said. Or rather, this is a grasping at action; thus, in the phrase "supported by that," it grasps the support.
The words beginning with "Will you wear [them]? were spoken by the Blessed One when he desired to exchange robes with the Elder Mahākassapa.
As for "But will you wear mine, Kassapa?", [it means]: "Kassapa, you [will wear] these [robes] worn out through use..."
When he says, "Will you be able to wear rag-robes? this is not said with reference to physical strength;
rather, he speaks thus with reference to the fulfillment of the practice.

"Rag-robes made of hemp" refers to robes made of hemp-fiber rags that have been discarded after wrapping a corpse, which were taken up after brushing away the maggots as large as a water-jar. [From] streets and so forth...
Because it stands upon dust in any place whatsoever, it is called *paṃsukūla* in the sense of being "protruding" (*abbhuggata*), like a bank (*kūla*) among them.
Alternatively, the meaning of the word *paṃsukūla* should be understood as: that which goes to (*ulati*) or attains a state of worthlessness (*kucchita-bhāva*) like dust (*paṃsu*).
*Nibbasanāni* means those whose function as clothing has been finished; the meaning is "worn out through use. *Ekameva*...

The plural form is used for that robe because it consists of many parts. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "by means of common use" (*sādhāraṇaparibhoga*) means by means of using it together with oneself;
thus, he was assisted by both common use and by being established on an equal footing.

Now, for the purpose of establishing himself on an equal footing with others regarding the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), which are distinguished by the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*):

The Blessed One spoke thus, beginning with the words "Bhikkhus, I... and so forth, showing a summary of the text found in the *Kassapa-saṃyutta* by means of an elliptical formula (*peyyālamukha*) and by mentioning the opening term.
Therein, "as far as I wish" (*yāvade ākaṅkhāmīti*) means "just as far as I wish," that is, for as long a time as I desire;
the reading "yāvadevā" is also found. [This refers to] the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

Herein, the "nine successive dwellings" (navānupubbavihāra) refers to the eight attainments of the fine-material and immaterial spheres together with the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), so designated because they are to be entered into in successive order.
The "six direct knowledges" (chaḷabhiññā) refers to the five direct knowledges together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa).

Regarding the phrase "by establishing oneself as equal to oneself": "I [will remain] for as long a time and in as many dwellings of attainment as [the Buddhas possess] regarding the direct knowledges..."

"I employ [these powers], and so too did Kassapa"—thus, by establishing himself as equal to the aforementioned superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*), this was said merely as praise for the Elder on account of his commonality with those superhuman qualities;
it does not imply total equality with the Blessed One. For, taking into account the excellence of the Blessed One's virtues, the disciples and the Paccekabuddhas...
They do not approach even a fraction, even a minute part [of it]. The intention is: "What other debtlessness could there be for him, other than the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya?
In this context, "for him" (tassa) should be understood as "for that favor" (tassa anuggahassa) or "for me" (tassa me);
for in some manuscripts the reading "tassa me" is seen. "Debtlessness" (āṇaṇyaṃ) means the state of being free from debt. [This is] by the granting of his own armor and sovereignty.

In this context, while referring to the robe (*cīvara*), the mention is made specifically of the armor (*kavaca*); and while referring to the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), sovereignty (*issariya*) is taken as the illustration.
Now, explaining the aforementioned meaning by means of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he says "As it is said," and so forth.

Therein, in the phrase "on one occasion" (*ekamidāhaṃ*), the word *idaṃ* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). "On one occasion" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) means at one time. "From Pāvā" (*pāvāyā*) means from the city of Pāvā.
"One who has set out on a journey" means one who has set out on a long road; for here the word *addhāna* is a synonym for "long.
"The entire Subhadda Chapter should be understood in detail" means that the Subhadda Chapter as it appears in the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka should be brought here and explained in detail.
“After that” means after the Subhadda chapter.

By the phrase “the entire Subhadda chapter should be understood in detail,” having shown the extent of the Subhadda chapter’s text with the words “whatever we do not wish, that we shall not do,” he now shows the remaining text itself, which proceeds by way of generating enthusiasm, saying: “Come now, we...”

He said, "Venerable sir," and so forth. Regarding that, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that "unrighteousness (*adhamma*) means unrighteousness consisting of the opposites of the ten courses of wholesome action.

However, because there arises a multitude of faults as causes for the failure to compile the Dhamma and Vinaya—due to the necessity of generating enthusiasm for the purpose of compiling the Dhamma—it is precisely this [neglect] that is referred to here as "unrighteousness shines forth."
And it should be said that the Dhamma which is the opposite of that [unrighteousness] is what is being excluded.

Furthermore, because it is stated that "those who speak unrighteously are powerful, while those who speak according to the Dhamma are weak," one must understand by what unrighteousness those such as Subhadda and the Vajjiputtakas become speakers of unrighteousness, and by what Dhamma the others remain speakers of the Dhamma. It is precisely these [latter] that are referred to here as "unrighteousness" (adhamma).

And it should be called "Dhamma. Therefore, one should understand that the collection of faults such as evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), which has the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and so forth as its cause, is *adhamma*;
whereas the multitude of qualities such as fewness of desires (*appicchatā*), which has the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and so forth as its cause, is *dhamma*.
It "shines forth" (*dippati*) even before; or rather, as long as *adhamma* is not capable of obstructing *dhamma*.

The meaning is: "it exists even prior to that. "Dippati" means "it will shine" (*dippissati*). For, by connection with the word *pura*, this present tense usage refers to the future sense, just as in the expression "the god rains before [it is time].
"Avinaya" refers to non-discipline, which is the opposite of the discipline of abandonment (*pahānavinaya*) and so forth.
"Tena hi" is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. "In those who uphold the entire teaching of the Teacher consisting of the ninefold *sāsana*"—entire...
The Teacher’s Dispensation (*satthusāsana*) consists of the ninefold division (*navanga*), such as the discourses (*sutta*) and verses (*geyya*).

Because it is to be mastered by those desiring the goal, and because it constitutes the mastery of human aims pertaining to the present life and so forth, the three baskets (*piṭaka*) are called "the teaching" (*pariyatti*).
Those who uphold this teaching—comprising the ninefold division and the Teacher’s Dispensation—are called "upholders of the teaching of the ninefold division and the Teacher’s Dispensation."

"Of such a kind" is the meaning. They are "dry-insight practitioners" (sukkha-vipassaka) because insight is dry, coarse, and unsmeared due to the absence of the moisture of serenity-meditation (samatha-bhāvanā).
Regarding the phrase "those who bear all the various divisions of the Three Pitakas": the collection of the three Pitakas is the "Tipiṭaka";
they are so called because they bear all the various divisions of the scriptures (pariyatti), which are divided into many categories such as the ninefold division (navaṅga) and so forth.
"Those who have mastered all the divisions of the entire Pāḷi of the Tipiṭaka.
But why? That is to say, for what reason? "A trainee" (*sekkha*) is one who trains. He is called "one who has duties to perform" (*sakaraṇīya*).

The meaning is that he has duties remaining because the function of the three higher paths has not yet been completed. "Of him" (*assa*) means by him. "Because of being of great assistance" means because of being of great benefit. "Of him" (*assa*)...
It would be so. "Excessively trusting" means being overly confident. "Him"—the connection is that he was admonishing the Elder Ānanda.

The Elder Mahākassapa [admonished him] on account of the Elder Ānanda’s occasional wandering through the countryside with a community of junior co-residents who were unrestrained, and because those co-residents had all renounced the training at one and the same time.
Restraining him, he said, "This boy does not know his own measure. Here, the word *vā* is used as a filler;
he spoke thus to challenge the Elder, implying that this boy does not acknowledge his own limits.

In that case—meaning, such being the situation—"although he is still a learner" (*sekkho*) is not stated because learners are capable of falling into wrong courses of conduct; rather, it refers specifically to those who are beyond training (*asekkhā*).

It should be understood as meaning "because he was chosen [by being] selected. Therefore, the connection here should be understood as: "Even though he is a trainee (sekha), nevertheless let the Elder select even the Venerable Ānanda";

it is not, however, to be construed as: "Even though he is a trainee, nevertheless he is incapable of going on a wrong course. The phrase "incapable," etc., is a statement of his inherent nature. In that regard:
"By desire" means by longing or affection. "To go to a wrong course" means to do what ought not to be done.
"Mastery" means studied and learned. Regarding the phrase "Rājagaha is indeed a great resort": here, that in which cattle graze is a *gocara*, meaning a place for cattle to graze.
Like a grazing ground (*gocara*), it is a *gocara*—a place for wandering for alms. Since that is great, it is a "great resort" (*mahāgocara*), namely Rājagaha.
"Should obstruct" means should prevent.

"On the seven days of the *sādhukīḷana* festival": here, because one plays with great care (*sādhuka*) by way of worship after repeatedly proclaiming the basis for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), it is called the *sādhukīḷana*.
"Drawn near" means close at hand. "Brings the rains" means approaches [the rainy season].
"Herein" (*ettha*) means during the period of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*).
"There indeed" (*tatra sudaṃ*) means in that Sāvatthī; *sudaṃ* is merely an expletive particle. "With aggravated humors" (*ussannadhātukaṃ*) means having accumulated humors such as bile and phlegm.
"To comfort" (*samassāsituṃ*) means to satisfy. "On the second day" means on the day following the day he entered the Jetavana monastery.
They say: it is called *virecana* because one is purged by means of it. Milk that has been infused with medicinal herbs is itself the purgative; thus it is "milk-purgative" (*khīravirecana*).
"With reference to which" means with reference to which drink of medicine it was said. "A small amount of medicine" (*bhesajjamattā*) means a trifling amount of medicine.
For this word *matta* has the sense of "little," as in such expressions as "a small amount of happiness" (*sukhamattā*) or "the giving up of a small amount" (*pariccāgamattā*).
"Repairing what is broken and dilapidated": here, "broken" (*khaṇḍa*) means cut, and "dilapidated" (*phulla*) means cracked; their "repairing" (*paṭisaṅkharaṇa*) means making them new again.

It is called a "pariveṇa" because it is perceived and seen as a delimited area. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the connection with "repairing what is broken and dilapidated" among those monasteries (*vihāra*).
"The first month" (*paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ*) means the first month of the rainy season; this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*).

It is said, "by the Blessed One... praised," because many rules concerning lodgings have been laid down, and because many formal acts (kamma) related to lodgings have been prescribed in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
"On the second day" means on the day following the day when [the monks] had thought, "Let us carry out the repair of what is broken and dilapidated."
On the very day of the commencement of the rains retreat, they thought thus: "Like a dwelling place for glory" means like a residence for glory.
"And like a watering-place where birds gather from all sides" means that the eyes of all people fell upon the pavilion alone;
thus it is said, "like a watering-place where the birds of the eyes of gods and men alight. "The world’s delight" means...
*Lokarāmaṇeyyakaṃ* means that which is worthy of being enjoyed (*ramaṇaṃ*) or which brings delight (*rāmaṇīyabhāvaṃ*) in the world.
*Daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍaṃ* means the essence (*sāraṃ*) among things to be seen (*daṭṭhabbesu*); it is "clearly serene" (*vippasannaṃ*) because of that essence, hence *daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍaṃ*.

Alternatively, it is *daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍo* because its ornament (*maṇḍo*), its embellishment (*maṇḍanaṃ*), its decoration (*alaṅkāro*), is the most excellent and essential (*sārabhūto*) thing to be seen.
*Maṇḍapa*: It is called a *maṇḍapa* because it protects (*pāti*) or wards off the heat of the sun’s rays (*maṇḍa*).

"Possessing a beautiful canopy from which various flower garlands and pearl pendants are streaming forth" means that there is a lovely and splendid canopy (*vitāna*) here from which various flower garlands and pearl pendants are streaming out, as if being vomited or ejected.
This is because the ground-work has been perfectly completed and made variegated with offerings of various flowers.
Thus it is said: “like a floor paved with various jewels and gems.
Here, “a floor paved with jewels” (*maṇikoṭṭimatala*) refers to a surface made by grinding and setting jewels; “like that” is what is meant. “Worthy of a seat” means worthy of sitting upon.

“Inlaid with ivory” means inlaid with ivory. “He offered” means he presented it. “Without clinging” means without grasping at any phenomenon through craving or views. “Fault in speech” means there is no untruth in the discourse.
"According to seniority" means without overstepping the order of seniority. "Some" refers to some among the Majjhima-bhāṇakas themselves;
for it should be understood that all that was stated previously is indeed what the Majjhima-bhāṇakas say.
However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say, "The Elder came to the assembly on foot. Among them, some say "by way of the air," and "all of them [came] in such and such a manner..."
They say: "Because they remained for as many days as had passed since their arrival, they spoke in such and such a manner, taking each [day] in turn.

"Making whom the leader? means making whom the eldest. "Taking up a fan" here refers to the natural habit (dhammatā) of those preaching the Dhamma to the assembly, intended to dispel nervousness from the hands and to conceal facial expressions.

It should be understood as "habitual practice" (*āciṇṇa*). For it is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of things (*dhammatā*) to those who preach the Dhamma—whether they be Buddhas or disciples—who have attained ultimate self-restraint, that they take up the fan for fanning the mind.

Regarding the question, "Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense laid down?", how is its status as being "first" established prior to the Council (*saṅgīti*)? It is established by means of the sequence of the recitation of the Pātimokkha and so forth.

Because the initial occurrence [of the teaching] was established previously. For it should be understood that, for the most part, all three Piṭakas were recited by this very sequence during the Blessed One’s own lifetime, and were subsequently chanted in that same order—specifically the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
"In what matter" (kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ) uses the locative case in the sense of a cause or occasion. "And between, venerable sir, Rājagaha... [and so forth].
"Between Nāḷandā and Rājagaha" means in the middle of the space between Nāḷandā and Rājagaha. Because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case is employed.
"In the royal pavilion" (*rājāgārake*) means in a small house built for the king's recreation.
"At Ambalaṭṭhikā" refers to a royal park of that name. Why is it asked here, "With whom?"?
However, since this was not spoken by the Blessed One alone, but something was also spoken by the king, it should be understood that it was stated thus without specifying "starting from whom.
As for the term "Vedehiputto," he is the son of the daughter of the King of Kosala, not the daughter of the King of Videha.
But because his mother was wise, she "strives" (īhati) by means of "veda"—that is, by means of knowledge.
Because she "struggled" (*ghaṭati*) and "exerted herself" (*vāyamati*), it should be understood that she was born with the well-known name "Vedehī.
Thus, having shown the First Great Council by way of its sign, purpose, time, place, teacher, agent, instrument, and manner,
[the text now proceeds] to the various classifications, such as the singlefold and so forth, for the sake of proficiency in the Dhamma and Vinaya as they were established therein.
To demonstrate this, he said, "All this," and so forth. Therein, regarding the phrase "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ*):

path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) has unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause; this is what is called "perfect enlightenment.

By the phrase "by one who reviews," he refers to the phenomena that arise by way of spontaneous utterances (*udāna*) and so forth. "The flavor of liberation" (*vimuttirasa*) is the relish of the fruit of arhatship.
Or it is "the attainment of liberation" because it produces the highest fruit; or it is "the function of liberation" because it brings about the absolute liberation from the defilements.

Regarding the statement that the remainder of the Buddha’s word is "Dhamma": although the Vinaya is indeed Dhamma because it possesses the nature of the teachings (*pariyatti*) and so forth, nevertheless, the word *dhamma* used here in a distinct grammatical relation (*bhinnādhikaraṇa-bhāva*) in proximity to the word *vinaya* refers to that which is devoid of the Vinaya system.
He illuminates the tradition, such as the "accumulation of merit and knowledge" (*puññañāṇasambhāra*) and the "ox-yoke" (*gobalibadda*), and so forth. This is the summary meaning of this verse:

"Seeking the builder of this house of selfhood, the carpenter that is craving (*taṇhāvaḍḍhaki*), I have not found that wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhiñāṇa*) by which it is possible to see him. Through many births in *saṃsāra*... [and so on].

Not having obtained it, from the time of my initial resolve onwards, I have wandered and transmigrated through this cycle of existence for as long as this period numbering many hundreds of thousands of births;
because this thing called birth— being mixed with old age, sickness, and death—
is painful to undergo again and again, and because that [cessation] does not turn back so long as it is not seen, I was seeking it.
"They will run on for the sake of their goal. "You have been seen" means: now, by me while penetrating the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), you have been seen.
"Again to the house" means: again to this house of mine, which is designated as this personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"You shall not do" means: you will not do it. He states the reason with the words "All of yours," and so forth: all the remaining comforts of your defilements (*kilesa*) have been broken by me. By you, of this...
The peak, the pinnacle, and the dome of the house of the self—which is comprised of ignorance—has been dismantled and destroyed.

My mind has gone toward Nibbāna, which is the absence of formations, by way of making it its object. And I have attained, reached, the fruit of the path of Arhatship, which is the destruction of craving;
this is the meaning. However, some [interpret] "the mind itself having gone to the absence of formations" [as follows]:...
They have attained the destruction of craving”—thus they also explain the meaning.

“Some” refers to the reciters of the Khandhaka. Regarding the phrase “on the day of the first quarter of the moon,” this should be connected with the words “arose as he was reflecting,” and not with the words “having attained omniscience.
“By knowledge consisting of joy” means by knowledge associated with joy (*somanassa*).
"I announce" means I inform; the meaning is "I awaken. "In the interval" means in the intermediate space; the meaning is "in the middle. Regarding the *Suttantapiṭaka*:
just as "action" (*kamma*) is the same as "course of action" (*kammanta*), so too "discourse" (*sutta*) is to be understood as "discourse-text" (*suttanta*).
"Not included in the recitation" refers to such works as the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka* and the *Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa*. [It is so called] because it is characterized by sixteen recitations.
“It has sixteen sections,” it is said. For indeed, in the Parivāra-pāḷi, it is stated regarding the first Pārājika: “Where was it laid down?

and so forth. These eight sections—the Section on Laying Down (Paññattivāra), the Section on the Occurrence of an Offense (Kathāpattivāra), the Section on Falling Away (Vipattivāra), the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāra), the Section on Origination (Samuṭṭhānavāra), the Section on Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇavāra), the Section on Settlement (Samathavāra), and the Section on Synthesis (Samuccayavāra)—followed by which [the text continues]: “On account of engaging in sexual intercourse...”

It should be understood that the Parivāra is said to be "characterized by sixteen sections" because it is presented through sixteen sections— namely, those same eight sections repeated again due to the distinction of specific conditions, such as "Where was the *pārājika* laid down?"—
thus making sixteen sections in total for both the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga.

"Having the purpose of making firm tasks loose": this should be applied respectively to those offenses that are wrong by worldly convention (*lokavajja*) and those that are wrong by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
"Transgression" (*ajjhācāra*) is conduct that proceeds by overcoming the boundary of restraint; it is a violation. "By that" means by reason of its manifold methods and so forth.
"This" refers to the words of the verse beginning with "because of its manifold specific methods. "Of this" refers to the Vinaya.

"But the other," however, refers to the Sutta. Regarding the phrase "in the division of one's own welfare, another's welfare, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes matters pertaining to the present life and the future life, as well as mundane and supramundane matters.

"Because it was spoken in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained" means that, unlike the Vinaya which is taught by establishing commands through a position of authority, this was taught in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, conforming to their individual temperaments.

Because it has been so stated. Without teaching by way of the gradual training (anupubbasikkhā) and so forth, he said, “like the fruit of a crop,” showing the subsequent manifestation for those to be trained at a later time.
Showing that [the result] arises only for those possessed of the proper means, he said, “like milk from a cow”;
for one milking a cow on its horns and the like, or at the wrong time, or when it has not yet calved, does not obtain milk.

Because they go [to it]. "In this" means in the Abhidhamma. Regarding the term "Abhidhamma": although there is no offense for the emission of semen during sleep, unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) is still found therein;
thus, it refers to those phenomena (*dhammā*) that are free from confusion with the formulations of the Vinaya.

Some also say it refers to "phenomena free from confusion because of the absence of contradiction between what precedes and what follows. "By way of object and so forth" means by way of object, association, kamma-door, path of practice, and so on.

"Lakkhaṇīyattā" means "because it is to be recognized. Regarding the phrase "yaṃ panettha avisiṭṭhaṃ," the meaning is that among these three terms beginning with "Vinayapiṭaka," that which is undifferentiated—that is, common to them all—is the word "piṭaka.
"Mā piṭakasampadānena" means "do not take [it] by way of the transmission of the Pāḷi text. "Yathāvuttena" means "in the manner already stated," such as "in this twofold sense," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction of teaching, the distinction of the dispensation, and the distinction of discourse": here, the word *bheda* (distinction) should be applied individually to each term—namely, *desanābheda*, *sāsanabheda*, and *kathābheda*.

Furthermore, *bheda* means diversity (*nānatta*). Regarding the words "among those" (*tesu*): it refers to among the Piṭakas. "Training, abandonments, and profundity" (*sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāva*) is a compound;
the meaning is that he elucidates these, as appropriate, according to their respective contexts.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "expound the distinctions of the scriptures" (*pariyattibheda*), meaning expound the distinctions of their mastery. Furthermore, the connection is:

"expound all of that as well"—namely, in which [scripture], such as the Vinaya and so forth, and in what manner one encounters both success (*sampatti*) and failure (*vipatti*). Alternatively, the connection is:
"expound all of that as well"—namely, the distinctions of the scriptures, the success, and the failure, in which [scripture] and in what manner one encounters them.
It should be applied. The terms "elucidation" (*paridīpanā*) and "explanation" (*vibhāvanā*) are stated here in accordance with what was said in the preceding verses;

however, in meaning they are one and the same. "Worthy of command" (*āṇāraho*): one who is worthy of issuing a command is "worthy of command," namely the Blessed One, because he is the Perfectly Enlightened One.

For he, due to his great compassion and because he is the teacher who teaches without error, is worthy of issuing a command, as his words are authoritative. [This applies] to both the conventional and the ultimate levels.

He says "due to the abundance of commands" (*āṇābāhullato*) because it is possible [that this was the case]. This same method applies to the following cases as well. "The first" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Those with frequent offenses" refers to the Elder Seyyasaka and others. Indeed, they are called "those with frequent offenses" because of the abundance of their faults;
that is, those for whom there are many, numerous, and abundant offenses, faults, and transgressions. Regarding the phrases "those with manifold underlying tendencies" (*anekajjhāsayā*), and so forth:

*Āsayo* (the underlying disposition) is the same as *ajjhāsayo* (inclination); in its essential meaning, it consists of both view (*diṭṭhi*) and knowledge (*ñāṇa*). *Cariyā* refers to the six root temperaments, beginning with the temperament of lust (*rāgacariyā*).
Alternatively, *cariyā* means conduct (*carita*), which is twofold by way of good conduct (*sucarita*) and bad conduct (*duccarita*).

*Adhimutti* (resolve) is the inclination of beings based on their past associations; it is twofold, distinguished as inferior (*hīna*) and sublime (*paṇīta*). *Yathānulomaṃ* (in accordance with) refers to [the suitability] of the inclinations and so forth.
"Appropriate. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means in conformity with the intrinsic nature of the Dhamma.
Regarding "restraint and non-restraint," here the meaning is both minor and major restraint; the vowel *a* here has the sense of "increase.

"The unraveling of views" means the liberation from views. Because the Sutta-piṭaka contains a great abundance of teachings on concentration, beginning with the words "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," etc.
In the Suttanta Piṭaka, it is called the "training in higher consciousness" (adhicittasikkhā).

It is the abandoning of transgression regarding the defilements—that is, the phenomena of corruption—or regarding the defilements of karma; specifically, it is the abandoning of that transgression which occurs through the doors of body and speech.

Defilements that persist within the continuum by way of latent tendencies (*anusaya*) are unable to transgress by way of breaking the virtue (*sīla*), even when they are active (*pariyuṭṭhita*); therefore, he said: "Because it is the opposite of transgression..."

"Of virtue. "Abandonment of the obsessions" (*pariyuṭṭhānappahāna*) means the abandoning of that which is called an obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), because it occupies a position by way of arising after having exhausted the occurrence of the wholesome in the mind by way of providing an opportunity.

"Abandonment of the underlying tendencies" (*anusayappahāna*) refers to the seven defilements, such as sensual lust and so forth, which are firmly rooted and capable of arising in the continuum when they obtain their causes, due to not having been abandoned by the Noble Path.
They are called *anusayas* because they lie down (*sayana*) repeatedly within the continuum (*santāna*); their abandonment is [the subject].

"Abandonment by way of a factor" (*tadaṅgappahāna*) means the abandonment of each respective unwholesome factor by means of its corresponding wholesome factor, such as generosity, virtue, and so forth.
"Abandonment of the defilement of misconduct" refers to the very misconduct of body and speech wherever it arises.
It is called *saṃkileso* because it thoroughly defiles and afflicts that continuity; its abandonment occurs by way of "abandonment through the factor itself" (*tadaṅgavasena*).

Because concentration is the direct opposite of sensual desire, the abandonment of the defilement of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkilesa*) is taught in the Sutta Piṭaka. Because it reveals the nature of phenomena as empty of a self and so forth, the abandonment of the defilement of views (*diṭṭhisaṃkilesa*) is taught in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
"In each one of these" means: here, in each one of these three Piṭakas. Regarding "the Dhamma is the Pāḷi":

here, because the Dhamma possesses distinguished meanings such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, and because it is the natural expression of the Buddhas, the "Pāḷi"—meaning a row or series—is a succession of words that are preeminent and exalted; thus, it is the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti).

The Pāḷi Dhamma is the continuous series of name-designations (*nāmapaññatti*) that have been definitively established by the Blessed One through his mind among ultimate terms, by virtue of being expressive words corresponding to meanings distinguished as conventional or ultimate. If it is asked, "What is the distinction between the teaching (*desanā*) and the Dhamma?
[the answer is: It is because of its quality of awakening others to the Dhamma that has been mentally established in the manner already described.
The manifestation of speech by the most excellent persons should be understood as “teaching. Therefore it was said: “Teaching is the teaching of that text which has been determined by the mind.
Furthermore, both of these are, in the ultimate sense, merely sound, because there is no conventional designation (sammuti) that is divorced from the ultimate reality (paramattha).
Adopting this very method, some teachers [state]: “Both the Dhamma and the teaching, in the ultimate sense...”

They say, "It is just sound," and they too are indeed blameless. This should be understood as being analogous to how it is said that "the rebirth-linking resultants of the sense-sphere have limited objects.

For it cannot be said that "the rebirth-linking resultants of the sense-sphere have only produced ultimate realities as their objects," because unwholesome states such as lust and so forth—and wholesome states such as loving-kindness and so forth—are preceded by conceptualizations of the forms of men, women, and the like.

Because it arises even after having apprehended an object (*ārammaṇa*). Furthermore, since this conceptualization is rooted in ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), its status as having the ultimate as its domain can be established;
it should be understood that the same applies here as well. And in all three of these, the connection is that "these—phenomena, meaning, teaching, and penetration—are profound.
And herein, the profundity of the phenomena and so forth, which are components of the Piṭakas, is being stated.
It should be understood that this [definition] has already been stated for both the collection [of the Dhamma] and the Piṭaka itself.

They are "difficult to penetrate" (*dukkhogāhā*) because they are plunged into with difficulty, or because their penetration—the act of plunging or entering within—is difficult. "In these" (*ettha*) refers to these Piṭakas;
this locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
"Result of a cause" (*hetuphala*) means the fruit of a cause. "Expression of the Dhamma" refers to an expression of both meaning and phrasing that is non-perverted.
The phrase "from the perspective of the object and from the perspective of non-delusion" is a demonstration of the modes of comprehension for mundane and supramundane [Dhammas] respectively;

it connects with the term "comprehension of this. For the mundane [comprehension] is called "comprehension from the perspective of the object," because it proceeds by taking the meaning of the Dhamma and so forth as its objective support.

It is so called. However, the supramundane [wisdom], although not taking that [name-and-form] as its object because it has Nibbāna as its object, is called "understanding through non-delusion" because it proceeds toward the phenomena (dhammas) and so forth by destroying the delusion regarding them.

"In accordance with the meaning, among the phenomena" means "in accordance with the effect, among the causes. "In accordance with the path of designation, among designations" refers to the path of the sixfold designation by name (*nāma-paññatti*).
The path of designation; the meaning is "designations corresponding to that.
*Dhammajāta* means a variety of causes, or the cause itself. *Atthajāta* means a variety of effects, or the effect itself.
This is to be connected with the phrase "and this teaching. "And whatever penetration there is herein" refers to the penetration found within these [categories of] phenomena, meanings, and teachings.
The meaning [is as follows]. "In this" means in these three Piṭakas.
Regarding the phrase "like a water-snake," here the word *alagadda* refers to the seizing of a water-snake, just as in expressions such as "the playing of the lute" is called "the lute";
furthermore, "seizing" here should be understood as a "bad seizing," because there is no contradiction in the case of other types of seizing.
Therefore, because this [discourse] has the seizing of a water-snake as its simile, it is called the "Alagaddūpama" (The Simile of the Water-Snake). Here, "alagadda" refers to a venomous snake.
For it is "alaṃ" (sufficient) or "pariyatta" (adequate), or it possesses a "gada" (disease) consisting of poison that is capable of taking away life;
thus, what should be called "alaṃgada" is referred to as "alagadda."
“Having the goal of escape from the round” means that its purpose or function is the escape from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). “Like a storekeeper” means he is a storekeeper;
one who guards the treasure of the Dhamma, yet for whom the study of the scriptures is devoid of purpose—that is the “storekeeper’s study.
“Ill-grasped” means wrongly grasped. Therefore it was said: “memorized for the sake of criticism and so forth. And here, “criticism” (*upārambha*) refers to [the study of] the scriptures...
“Relying on [the Dhamma] for the sake of disparaging others. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), one includes such things as the desire for debate, gain, honor, and so forth.
“With reference to which” means with reference to that faulty grasping of the scripture (*pariyatti*). “It was said” means it was said in the *Alagaddūpama Sutta*.
“And they do not experience its meaning” means that these people who grasp it wrongly do not experience the meaning of that Dhamma, which consists in the fulfillment of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
"They do not experience" means they do not find [it]. "One who has penetrated the imperturbable" means one who has penetrated the fruit of arahantship.
Now, having determined and demonstrated the attainments and failures as appropriate within the three Piṭakas, he says: "But in the Vinaya," and so forth.
Therein, the restrictive particle "of those very same" [is used] because there is no detailed explanation of the six direct knowledges and the four analytical insights in the Vinaya.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For in the *Verañjakaṇḍa*, only the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) are analyzed.

In the second [section], the restriction "of those very same" is made in view of the four analytical knowledges (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), because even the three types of higher knowledge are included within the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*).
In the phrase "and of those," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the remaining [qualities] are also present therein. [In the] *Abhidhammapiṭaka*...
For the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā), the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), and the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā) have already been mentioned.

The restrictive term "there itself" (tattheva) is employed to indicate that the analytical insights are thoroughly classified in that very same place. "Upādinnaphassa" refers to the contact associated with the path that brings about the practice of the path.
"Tesaṃ" means of those Piṭakas. "Etaṃ" refers to this word of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
Regarding the verse beginning "Thirty-four suttantas," this is the construction of the meaning:

that collection (*saṅgaha*) which, by way of counting the suttas of that *nikāya*, consists of exactly thirty-four suttantas and is comprised of three sections (*vaggas*), is the "three-sectioned collection" (*tivaggo saṅgaho*).
This first *nikāya* is here called the Dīgha Nikāya. "Anulomiko" means not contrary; it is a name according to its meaning (*anvatthanāmo*) because it conforms to the purpose.
It has been said. "Even a single collection" (*ekanikāyam-pi*) means even a single group. "Thus variegated" (*evaṃ cittaṃ*) means thus diverse.

"Just as these" (*yathayidaṃ*) means just as these [are]. The Kṣatriyas who dwell in Poṇika and Cikkhallika are called the "Poṇika group" (*poṇikanikāyo*) and the "Cikkhallika group" (*cikkhallikanikāyo*).
"Comprising fifteen chapters" (*pañcadasavaggapariggaho*) means encompassed by fifteen chapters. "Thousands of discourses" (*suttantānaṃ sahassāni*).
Regarding the reading "seven hundred suttas," it should be construed as "seven thousand suttas and seven hundred suttas.
However, in some places the reading is "seven thousand suttas and seven hundred suttas.
"Shown previously" means shown in the exposition of the Suttanta Piṭaka.
