"Vedanti" means knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Tuṭṭhiṃ" means joy (*pīti*). "By way of the aggregates of Dhamma" means by way of the heaps of Dhamma.

The connection is: "I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha. "Two thousand from the monks" means that I received two thousand [teachings] taught by those very monks, such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and others. "In me" means in my heart; thus spoke the Elder Ānanda.
He points to himself. The construction is: "Those teachings that proceeded within my heart were eighty-four thousand.
And this is stated with reference to the masses of Dhamma mastered during the Blessed One’s lifetime;
however, after the Blessed One had attained *parinibbāna*, regarding the *Subha-sutta* and *Gopakamoggallāna-sutta* taught by the Elder Ānanda at the Third Council—
Furthermore, it should be understood that the aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*) exceed even eighty-four thousand by way of the *Kathāvatthu* treatise spoken by the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa.

A discourse with a single sequence of connection (*ekānusandhika-sutta*) refers to such texts as the *Satipaṭṭhāna*; one with multiple sequences of connection (*anekānusandhika*) refers to such texts as the *Parinibbāna-sutta*. For indeed...

It occurs by way of various teachings on various doctrines in different places. The *Tikadukabhājana* (Analysis of Triplets and Couplets) is to be understood according to the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* and the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
The "Analysis of Mind-Occasions" (*Cittavārabhājana*) is stated by way of the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "There is a basis" (*Atthi vatthu*), "basis" (*vatthu*) refers to the *Sudinnakaṇḍa* and so forth. "Matrix" (*mātikā*) refers to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Intermediate offense" (*antarāpatti*) refers to...

An offense prescribed on account of a different matter among the intervals between the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "The triad-cut" (*tikacchedo*) refers to the delimitation of triads such as the three *pācittiya* offenses.

The connection is that "the word of the Buddha was compiled. "Of it" (*assa*) refers to the word of the Buddha. The connection is "as if giving a cry of 'well done' at the conclusion of the recitation.
"Marvels" (*acchariyāni*) are those worthy of clapping one's hands, such as the raining of flowers, the tossing of robes, and so forth.
The connection is that she who is called both “the five hundred” and “the Elder Nun” is what is known as the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
Thus ends the method of commentary on the narrative of the First Great Council within the *Vimativinodanī*, the sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā.
Commentary on the Second Council Discussion:
Having thus shown the First Great Council, the author says "of this" and so forth, pointing out the purpose for which it was presented here by way of conclusion.
In that regard, "this lineage of teachers" refers to this succession of masters in Jambudīpa.
The sequence: "Vijitāvino" means those who have conquered because they have overcome all defilements that are their adversaries.
"Jambusirivhaye" means in that island whose name is "Jambusiri"—that which is called Jambudīpa;
for the island itself is called "Jambu" because it is distinguished by a great jambu tree. [It was] being unceasingly...
Having made it indestructible. By the three terms beginning with *vinayavaṃsa*, only the Vinaya Piṭaka itself is meant, because they are synonymous expressions.
*Pakataññutaṃ* means proficiency; what is meant is "state of being clever. *Dhuraggāhī* means one who takes up the primary burden;
what is meant is that he took [the responsibility] as the leader of all. *Bhikkhusamudāyo* is a collection or assembly of monks.
The connection is: "they have gone out (nibbāyiṃsu). And having illuminated everywhere—that very True Dhamma—having made it manifest in all places.
"Radiant" means endowed with the radiance of wisdom (*paññā-juti*), or possessing splendor; the meaning is that they were of great majesty.
"They have gone out" means they have attained *nibbāna* through the element of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa*). "Without attachment" means free from clinging.
"Athāti pacchā" means "afterwards," that is, after they had attained final nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "siṅgīloṇakappo kappati," here the word *kappa* has the sense of "option";
thus, even the option of *siṅgīloṇa* (horn-salt) is permissible. The meaning is that this alternative view is also permissible;
the same applies in all cases. In that context, having carried salt in a horn, [one may eat] alms-food that is otherwise saltless.
It is permissible to eat together; the intention is that one does not store food.
"The two-finger-breadth allowance" (dvaṅgulakappa) means it is permissible to eat at an improper time when the shadow has passed the length of two finger-breadths.

"The village-to-village allowance" (gāmantarakappa) means that for one who has been invited with the thought, "I will go to another village," it is permissible to eat food that is not considered leftover (anatiritta).

The meaning is "it is allowable. "The residence-allowable" (āvāsakappa) means it is permissible to perform sangha formal acts, such as the Uposatha, separately in various dwellings within a single boundary.

"The consent-allowable" (anumatikappa) means that while those [monks] have not yet arrived, the sangha performs the formal act in a quorum with the intention, "We shall obtain their consent when they arrive," and subsequently obtains their consent.

The intention is that it is allowable to take [the medicine], and thus it does not constitute a *vaggakamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly). It is allowable as an *āciṇṇakappa* (the practice of the elders); the meaning is that what has been practiced by teachers and preceptors is allowable.
Furthermore, it should be understood that some such practices are allowable and legitimate (*dhammika*), while others are not allowable and illegitimate (*adhammika*).
It is allowable as an *amathitakappa* (the practice of unchurned milk): that which is milk having abandoned its state as milk but not yet reached the state of curds.
The meaning is that it is permissible for one who has finished eating and refused further food to eat what is not left over (*anatiritta*).

Regarding the phrase "it is permissible to drink *jaḷogi*," here *jaḷogi* refers to fresh liquor; the intention is that it is allowable to drink that which consists of fermented ingredients but has not yet reached the state of being actual intoxicant (*majja*).
Regarding "gold and silver" (*jātarūparajata*), here [it refers to that which] has not undergone transformation from its natural state.
“Always gold indeed”: it is called *jātarūpa* because its form (*rūpa*) has been born (*jāta*); thus, it is gold (*suvaṇṇa*). It shines (*rajati*) due to its white nature;
thus, it is silver (*rajata*), that is, *rūpiya*. “Son of Susunāga” means the son of Susunāga.
“Son of Kākaṇḍaka” means the son of the brahmin Kākaṇḍaka. “Among the Vajjīs”: the plural is used because it is the name of a country (*janapada*).
Regarding the phrase *tadahuposathe*: here, *tadahū* means "on that day. It is called *uposatha* because they "dwell near" (*upavasanti*) it;
"they dwell near" means they live having become endowed with the undertaking of virtue or by fasting and so forth. *Kaṃsapātiṃ* means a golden bowl.
*Māsakarūpaṃ* means simply a *māsaka* coin. By the words "all this should be told," [it refers to] what has come down in the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka.
This shows that the entire Pāḷi must be brought here and recited. The connection is: "They recited it exactly as it had been chanted.
And the connection is: "This, moreover, is the rehearsal (saṅgīti). "Among them" means among those elders who were the rehearsers.
The connection is: "These co-residents are to be known as renowned. "Sāṇasambhūta" refers to the Elder Sambhūta, a resident of the region of Sāṇa. This is the second [section].
It should be connected as "saṅgaho" (a gathering). "Pannabhārā" means those who have laid down the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*).
"Abbudam" they say is a calamity. Some say: "Because they distort the word of the Blessed One and thereby illustrate their own words, 'abbuda' is a criminal act.
"Idam" is a demonstrative reference to what is about to be spoken. "Sandissamānā mukhā" means appearing face-to-face.
"Bhāvitamaggaṃ" means one who has produced jhāna. Regarding "sādhu sappurisa": here "sādhu" is a particle used in the sense of a request;
the meaning is "I entreat you. "Haṭṭhapahaṭṭho" means repeatedly delighted. "Udaggudaggo" refers to being uplifted by the joy that produces physical transformations;
for a person possessed of joy is called "udaggudaggo" because of the exaltation of body and mind.
"At that time" means at the time when they held the second council; the sense is: "at that time.
"They did not reach that legal issue" means they did not arrive, nor did they come, to adjudicate that legal issue raised by the Vajjiputtakas.
This is to be connected with "they were no more. Having remained for as long as their lifespan lasted...
The connection is with the word “parinibbūta” (fully extinguished). But having done what did the elders attain parinibbāna? He says:
“Having performed the second compilation,” and so forth. “Aniccatāvasaṃ” means dependence upon impermanence. “Jammaṃ” means wretched.
“Durabhisambhavaṃ” means unassailable, impossible to overcome; the connection is: “having thus understood impermanence.”
The method of commentary on the account of the Second Council is finished.
Commentary on the account of the Third Council:
"For seven years" (*satta vassāni*) is the accusative case used to denote continuous duration. "Aticchatha" means "passing by," [that is,] "desire to pass beyond."
The meaning is: "Go elsewhere from here and seek alms. "For the purpose of dismissing the meal" means for the purpose of the function of swallowing the food;

the meaning is, "for the purpose of eating. Regarding "one who is sixteen years old": he has the description (*uddesa*)—that is, the statement—of being sixteen years old, thus he is "one whose description is sixteen years," which means "one who is sixteen years old."
"In the three Vedas," and so forth: in the three Vedas known as the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda.
It is said that these very three Vedas were composed by righteous seers (isī) such as Aṭṭhaka and others for the purpose of revealing the path to heaven to the world;
for this reason, they are called by those names. However, the Atharvaveda was later [composed] by unrighteous brahmins for the purpose of killing living beings and so forth.

It was done. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the three earlier Vedas, having removed the righteous branches (*dhammasākhā*), the unrighteous branches such as the *yāga-vadha* (sacrificial slaughter) and so forth were inserted.
*Nighaṇḍu* refers to the science that elucidates synonyms and corresponding alternative names for trees and other things;
for in the world, it is called "nighaṇḍu. *Keṭubha* means that which "keṭati" (expounds), namely, that which sets forth the classification of ritual actions and so forth.
*Keṭubha* is a treatise on poetic embellishment (*kavīnam upakārasattha*) consisting of various modes of composition (*kiriyākappavikappa*).
Herein, "mode of composition" (*kiriyākappa*) refers to that by which action—characterized by the differentiation of speech and so forth—is fashioned (*kappīyati*) and varied (*vikappīyati).

Furthermore, because it possesses many variations through the analysis of phonemes, word-connections, word-meanings, and so forth, it is called "the manifold mode of composition" (*kiriyākappavikappa*). This [definition] is stated with reference to the *Mūlakiriyākappa* text.

It has been stated. Together with the *nighaṇḍu* and the *keṭubha*, they are "with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*" (*sanighaṇḍukeṭubhā*); [this refers to] the three Vedas. Within those [Vedas] that are "with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*":

that by which letters (*akkhara*) are analyzed according to the division of places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and so forth, and according to the division of etymological derivation (*nibbacana*), is "the analysis of letters" (*akkharappabheda*), namely, phonology (*sikkhā*) and grammar (*nirutti*).
Together with the analysis of letters, they are "with the analysis of letters" (*sākkharappabhedā*); within those [Vedas] that are "with the analysis of letters."

Making the *Āthabbaṇa-veda* the fourth, those for whom there is a fifth consisting of ancient tales (*itihāsa*) connected with such expressions as "Thus it was" (*itiha āsa*) and "Thus it was" (*itiha āsā*) are called "those for whom the fifth is *itihāsa*" (*itihāsapañcamā*).
These are the three Vedas; [the phrase] "in these, with *itihāsa* as the fifth" refers to them. The two questions beginning with "Whose mind...
and so forth are stated with reference to the moment of arising of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
In that regard, concerning the first question: "It arises" means it arises by virtue of being possessed of the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
"It does not cease" means it does not cease because it has not yet reached the moment of cessation (*nirodhakkhaṇa*). "His mind"—this is the question:
"Will that mind of that person cease and will it not arise again in the future? And because this [question] is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīya*), [it is set aside].
The answer here should be understood in this way: At the moment of arising of the final consciousness of an Arahant, that consciousness arises but does not cease;

it will not arise again in the future, for it will certainly cease upon reaching the moment of its own cessation, and because there is no further rebirth-linking, another consciousness will not arise. However, setting aside one who possesses the final consciousness...
In one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), the consciousness of others that possesses the moment of arising arises by way of possessing the moment of arising;
because it has not yet reached the moment of dissolution, it does not cease, but having reached dissolution, it will certainly cease.
Furthermore, another [consciousness] will arise and will also cease either in that same personal existence (*attabhāva*) or in another. "Or for whom... and so forth.

Regarding the second question, "Will it cease and will it not arise?"—this refers to one whose consciousness, by virtue of being in the moment of arising, reaches the moment of dissolution and will cease, yet will not arise again due to the absence of rebirth-linking; for such a person whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), the question is:
"Does that consciousness arise and not cease? Since this is to be answered categorically, the reply is: "Yes."
The answer should be understood as follows: "Unable to carry it upward or downward" means being unable to take the upper word with the lower word,
or the lower word with the upper word, in terms of their meaning— being unable to apply them together,
join what precedes with what follows, and thereby determine the sense.
Because there is no falling away from the virtue undertaken through the state of fulfilling the precepts for stream-enterers, he said, "Now he is incapable of turning back from the Dispensation.
"Having increased" means having expanded the meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths.
It is called a *dantapona* because by it one cleanses or purifies the teeth; thus, it refers to a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*). Of those that are new or incoming...
Having thoroughly examined for several days his modest nature and his possession of qualities such as patience and loving-kindness,

the Elder— though he already knew through direct higher knowledge (abhiññā) that the novice was worthy— swept the floor and performed other services once more. He did so because it was appropriate to accept manual labor and provide assistance, and to inform the novice as well as other monks who were following his example that such conduct was fitting.
Some also say it was "for the purpose of taming his mind. "He established the Buddha’s word" means he began to have him learn the Buddha’s word.
Since the practice of the entire Vinaya conduct is prescribed only for those who are fully ordained (upasampadā), its mastery is likewise appropriate only for them;
thus he said, "setting aside the Vinaya Piṭaka. Even though the Buddha’s word had been established in his mind...
The phrase "having placed it in his hand" is said to show that it was handed over for the purpose of being kept safe.
"The consecration to sole sovereignty" refers to the consecration performed by way of supreme lordship over the entire Jambudīpa.
"Royal powers" means majesties accompanied by royal majesty. "From which" means from that sixteen-jar [consecration]. "Deities themselves brought [it] day after day."

"Connection" (*sambandho*). "Daily" (*devasikaṃ*) means day by day. "Medicine and myrobalan" (*agadāmalakaṃ*) refers to medicinal myrobalan that is capable of cleansing the body and removing all defects with only a small amount.
"From the Chaddanta Lake" (*chaddantadahato*) means from a celestial mansion situated near the Chaddanta Lake, or from a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*);
the meaning is that such special wish-fulfilling trees exist there, or that they are brought from there.
*Asuttamayikaṃ* means a cloth made of *sumana* flowers, not woven from threads, but fashioned solely from celestial *sumana* blossoms.
*Uṭṭhitassa sāliyo* refers to self-growing rice; here the singular number is used with reference to the collective whole, meaning "of the rice. *Nava vāhasahassāni*:
in this context, four handfuls make one *kuḍuva*; four *kuḍuvas* make one *pattha*; four... [the text continues].
One *āḷhaka* makes one *pattha*; four *āḷhakas* make one *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make one *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make one *khārī*;
twenty *khārikās* make one *vāha*, which is described as "one cart" (*ekaṃ sakaṭaṃ*) in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and other works.
"Making it free from husks and chaff" means making it devoid of husks and broken grains. A Buddha-image fashioned from that [material].
"Passing by" is the connection. The mention of "produced by the radiance of merit" is made because they resemble those produced by the radiance of merit created by the Nāga kings.

Regarding the phrase "the garland of spotless banners," they say that what is called a "banner-garland" (ketumāla) is a mass of rays seen emerging from the head and forming a cluster upon the crown of the head.
"Heretical sect" (*bāhirakapāsaṇḍa*) means a doctrine proclaimed by outsiders. "He took up" means he examined it while investigating. "On fine seats" (*bhaddapīṭhakesu*) means on seats made of cane.

"Essence" (*sāra*) means the essence of virtue. "In the lion-cage" (*sīhapañjara*) means near the great window. It is "tamed" (*danta*) because of the state of a mind free from the agitation of defilements;
it is "guarded" (*gutta*) because of the protection of constant mindfulness ever-present.
"Khuraggeyeva" means at the conclusion of the hair-cutting ceremony. "He shines exceedingly" is the connection [of the sentence].
"He was a merchant" means he was a honey-merchant. "By reason of former association" means by reason of living together either in the past or in a previous birth.
"Or by reason of present benefit" means by reason of practicing what is beneficial in the present existence. Thus, by these two causes, that which is termed affection—

Love arises. What is it like? He says: “Just as a lotus in water. In the phrase “just as a lotus,” the particle *vā* is used in its short form with the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
The word *yathā* is used in the sense of a simile. This is what is meant:
just as the lotus and other water-born flowers such as the *paduma* arise depending upon two causes—namely, water and mud—so too does love.
“Dhuvabhattāni” means regular meals. “Vajjāvajjaṃ” refers to both minor and major offenses.

Regarding the phrase “he made the burden [of the Saṅgha] fall upon the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa,” it should be understood that the Saṅgha made him the bearer of this burden in order to inform the king of the Elder’s great power and his status as the leader of the Saṅgha at that time through his role as the guide for the duties of the Dispensation; it was not because others were unaware of it. Of the Dispensation...

"An heir" means: "Am I or am I not an internal kinsman of the Dispensation? Those sons and daughters who renounce [their children] in order to go forth in the Dispensation are called "blood-relations" (*sālohita-ñātaka*) within the Buddha's Dispensation;

for they have renounced their own legitimate children (*orasaputta*) who are capable of upholding the entire Dispensation, rather than merely being givers of requisites—it was with reference to this meaning that the Elder [spoke].
“Great King, one does not become an heir to the Dispensation merely by this much,” he said. Regarding the phrase *kathañcarahi*:
here, *carahi* is a particle indicating impatience (or indignation). *Tissakumārassa* refers to the king’s younger brother, who shared the same mother.

*Sakkhasī* means “you will be able. *Sikkhāya patiṭṭhāpesun* means they established him in the training, beginning with the abstention from taking life and ending with the abstention from eating at improper times.

By means of formal undertaking, according to the formula beginning with, "For two years, I undertake the training precept of abstaining from taking life among the six precepts," they established him in the training immediately after granting the authorization for the training.
One who possesses an anointment lasting for six years is called a *chavassābhiseka*.
"Entirely the Theravāda" refers to the Pāḷi as it was recorded in the two councils.

It is called "the Theravāda" because it was set apart from those who held divergent views, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas and others. Indeed, this Vibhajjavāda is called "the Theravāda" because it was preserved without confusion and brought forth by the Elder Mahākassapa and others;
some also write it as "satheravādaṃ. In that regard, [as stated] in the commentaries...
One should apply [the text] by bringing forward the words: “the word of the Buddha, comprised within the Three Piṭakas, together with the commentaries and the Theravāda.
“Having attained the fire element” means having attained the jhāna that has the fire-kasiṇa as its object.
“In the assembly” means in the hall of justice in the center of the city. “Views” (diṭṭhigatāni) refers to the views themselves. “But this is not so...”
"Can they be pacified by one living among them? For one living among them, because of being included within their very midst, does not have words that are accepted;
therefore, he thought thus. "Ahogaṅgapabbata" refers to a mountain of that name.
They also write it as "Adhogaṅgāpabbata," but that is not correct. "Pañcātapena tappenti" means [tormenting] by the five heats. In the four...
Having kindled fires in various places and standing in their midst, they heat themselves by gazing up at the solar disk and basking in the sun's rays.
"They revolve around the sun" means that from the time of sunrise until sunset, they keep looking toward the sun and continue revolving while facing the sun.
"They exerted themselves, thinking 'We shall pierce through it'" means they made an effort, thinking "We shall destroy it."
"Confident" (*vissaṭṭho*) means free from the apprehension of death; the meaning is "fearless. "Having gone out for the hunt" (*migavaṃ nikkhamitvā*):
"hunt" (*migavaṃ*) is the sport of killing deer while wandering in the forest; having gone out for that purpose, the meaning is "having gone out for the sake of killing deer.

It is said "by the elephant-king" (*hatthināgena*) for the purpose of distinguishing him from [other] snakes, *nāgas*, and so forth. "Even as he was looking on" (*tassa passantasseva*): this is used in the sense of disregard.
The word *sāmivacanaṃ* means "while he was looking right there. Regarding the phrase "having flown up into the air," this is not a power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*);
rather, he demonstrated this power even to a householder because the power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is not prohibited.
For the power of transformation consists in abandoning one's natural form and displaying the form of a nāga or other such beings. *Chaṇavesaṃ* means a festive costume. *Padhānagharaṃ* means...
A secluded dwelling suitable for the exertion of energy by way of application to meditation. "He too" refers to the king's nephew.
"With a wholesome intention" means having a pleasant disposition. "Fallen into doubt" means having become uncertain.

Regarding the phrase "each with a retinue of a thousand bhikkhus," although it was stated in the form of a command—"Go and take them along"—the elder bhikkhus went because of their concern for the welfare of the Sasana.
For this is a permissible message (*kappiya-sāsana*), not one connected with householders' worldly affairs.

Although it is appropriate for the Elder to come even when told "the king summons you" for the sake of a Dhamma-duty, he did not come even after being sent twice, thinking, "This is an improper request.
[He thought: "The Elder is of great power; he practices according to the instructions and is an authoritative standard."
Desiring the successful completion of the duties to be performed for the king and for both factions by inspiring great respect within himself, he did not come under the guise of improper speech.
"A boat joined together on one side" means a boat-coupling (*nāvā-saṅghāṭa*).
He said, "having arranged for protection," because of the great number of the enemies of the Dispensation. "Yaṃ" means "because. "Abbāhiṃsu" means they dragged [him] away. "From the outside" means...
"From outside the garden": this was said with reference to the appearance [of the earth] as exceedingly difficult for those who were watching;
thus he said, "The shaking of a portion of the earth is difficult. However, in this case, there is no such thing as a separate difficulty regarding the act of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"A wild cat of the island": this refers to one that has been raised and trained by fowlers for the purpose of catching birds of its own kind, and placed in a snare-trap location.
The quail who remained still. Regarding the verse, "One does not touch the result of karma through dependence":
if your mind does not become corrupted by an evil deed, then even a sinful act committed by a hunter in reliance upon you will not touch you.
For that evil does not defile you, who are noble, free from concern for such deeds, and devoid of worldly attachment; it does not defile your mind.
The meaning is "he does not adhere. What does he profess by way of virtue?

He is a "proponent of what" (*kiṃvādī*). Alternatively, what kind of doctrine (*vāda*) is his? That is "the doctrine of what" (*kiṃvāda*); since he possesses that, he is a "proponent of what" (*kiṃvādī*).

Those for whom there is a doctrine that both the self and the world are eternal are "eternalists" (*sassatavādino*). [They hold this regarding] either sentient beings or formations (*saṅkhāra*), or a portion thereof.
The doctrine that proceeds as "eternal" is *ekaccasassata* (partial-eternalism); those intent upon that are the *ekaccasassatikā* (partial-eternalists).
The four doctrines that proceed with reference to the finite and infinite—namely, "finite," "infinite," "both finite and infinite," and "neither finite nor infinite"—are the *antānanta*;
those intent upon them are the *antānantikā* (finitist-infinists). That which does not die and is not cut off is *amarā*; thus it is not for me, nor is it "so" for me.
They are "Eternalists" (*amarāvikkhepikā*) because their views and speech proceed by means of such [positions] as "I do not know," and they possess a wavering [of mind] regarding these.
Alternatively, there is a species of fish called *amara* that is difficult to catch; they are "Eternalists" because their wavering is like that of this *amara* fish.
A self that has arisen spontaneously, without depending on any cause whatsoever, according to its own whim.

Those engaged in the doctrine that "the world and [the self] exist" are the proponents of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannika*). Those whose doctrine is that "the self possesses perception" are the proponents of perception (*saññīvāda*).
The same applies here to the proponents of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*) and the proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*).

They are called annihilationists (*ucchedavāda*) because they assert annihilation thus: "With the breakup of the body, the being is annihilated. "The present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to one's own individual existence (*attabhāva*) as it is directly perceived.

They are called "proponents of Nibbāna in this very life" because they claim that Nibbāna, the stilling of suffering, is attained through the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure right here according to one's desire.
One who speaks by way of analysis is an *Vibhajjavādī*; this refers to the Blessed One.

He does not state everything in a single uniform manner, but analyzes it according to the nature of things (*yathādhamma*), making it free from tangles and thicket-like obscurities so that views, doubts, and the like may vanish—distinguishing between conventional and ultimate truth.
When phenomena appear without confusion in this way, it is said that he is "one whose nature is to analyze exclusively.
"Crushing the doctrines of others" means that he crushes all doctrines of others— both those arisen at that time and those yet to arise—
by means of explaining the matrices (*mātikā*) and the bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*).
The method of explaining the account of the Third Council is finished.
Regarding the explanation of the account of the lineage of teachers,
while answering the question "By whom was it brought?", [the author] first demonstrates what occurred in Jambudīpa up until the Third Council.

Now, in order to show the succession of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*) in the island of Siṃhala, the passage beginning with "But from the Third Council onwards" (*tatiyasaṅgahato pana uddhaṃ*) is commenced.
"This island" (*imaṃ dīpaṃ*) refers to Tambapaṇṇidīpa. It is called "this island" because the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) was composed by the teacher while residing on that island.
"For some time" (*kañci kālaṃ*) is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasamyoga*); [it means] "at some time."
The meaning is as follows: "Ancient" (*porāṇā*) refers to those who composed the Sinhalese commentaries on the island of Siṃhala. "Named Bhadda" (*bhaddanāmo*) refers to the Elder Bhaddasāla.

"They came, not committing evil" (*āguṃ pāpaṃ na karonti*)—thus they are *nāgas*. "They recited the Vinaya Piṭaka"—this is the grammatical connection. "Those of Tambapaṇṇi" (*tambapaṇṇiyā*) is a locative expression.
"The five Nikāyas"—this is because the Vinaya and Abhidhamma have been taken separately; thus, [the remaining] five are distinct from those two.
The Nikāyas are to be taken up. Regarding the phrase "in the treatises," the construction is:

"they were made to recite the Abhidhamma treatises. One who possesses the three Piṭakas is called "one who has the Tipiṭaka"; however, it is stated as "Tipeṭako" instead of "Teipiṭako" for the purpose of preserving the meter.
"Tārakarāja" refers to the moon. Regarding the "name of a flower," both Mahāpaduma Thera and Sumana Thera are to be understood here; thus it is mentioned twice.
“Named Puppha” is what was said.
“Vanavāsī” means the kingdom of Vanavāsī. “Karakavassa” means a rain that causes the falling of snow, or a rain resembling a torrent of hailstones.
“Having carried away” means having carried away by a flood of water. “Wearing torn and tattered robes” means [robes] cut with a knife.

A *dhāraṇaka* is one who wears a cloth dyed with various colors. A *bhaṇḍu* is one who is shaven-headed. "Unable to endure his arrogance" means being unable to endure the arrogance characterized by the disparagement of others' virtues that arose within himself due to the Elder's spiritual power, as well as the anger occurring in that manner.
"Lightning bolts are falling" means they fall while thundering. [He thought: "It is not capable of producing fear and terror in me."
"Na assa na bhaveyya" (he would not be, he would not exist) is the construction. "Aññadatthu" means "absolutely. "Kasmīragandhārā" refers to the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kasmīra-Gandhāra.
"Isivātapaṭivātā" means they were fanning [the Buddha] on all sides and from every direction with the breezes generated by the movement of the robes and bodies of the bhikkhus.
"Dhammacakkhu" is the knowledge regarding the three lower paths. "Anamataggiya" refers to the *Anamatagga Saṃyutta*.
“Exceeding” (*sāmadhikāni*) means exceeding [the number]. “Five kingdoms” (*pañca raṭṭhāni*) refers to the five Cīna kingdoms. “Swiftly” (*vegasā*) means with speed.
“He established a protection on all sides” means he established a protection by way of a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the purpose of preventing their entry.
“Three thousand four hundred and fifty” (*aḍḍhuḍḍhāni sahassāni*) means three thousand plus a half of a fourth; that is to say, three thousand five hundred and fifty.
"Diyaḍḍhasahassaṃ" means "one thousand and a half"; that is, one thousand with an additional half, meaning more than five hundred and fifty.
"Niddhametvāna" means having expelled.
"Rājagahanagaraparivattakena" means having circled around the city of Rājagaha, keeping it to the right from outside.
"Having gone by the path already traveled," or "by way of going. "He caused to ascend" means he set it upon [the mountain]. "They flew into the sky" means they leapt up into the air.
"The best of mountains" refers to Cetiyagiri. "In front" means in the eastern direction. "Of the best city" refers to the excellent city of Anurādhapura.
"On the peak named Silakūṭa" refers to the mountain summit of that name. "The son of Prince Sīha"—here [refers to] the daughter of the King of Kaliṅga...
They say, "A lion cub was born in the womb of the lion. On the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha, either the Jeṭṭha constellation or the Mūla constellation occurs;
thus he says, "It is called the Jeṭṭha-Mūla constellation.
Because it involves the chasing, harming, and afflicting of deer, it is called *migava*, the sport of shooting deer. The form of a red deer means appearing in the guise of a *gokaṇṇa* deer.
"Of the size of a chariot-pole" means of the size of a chariot-goad. "One called a creeper-pole" means it received that name because it was adorned with a golden creeper made of silver.
On the flower-pole, blue and other flowers [are depicted];
on the bird-pole, various kinds of wild animals and birds appear as if they were fashioned by diverse craftsmanship. "The royal insignia" means...
"Objects worthy of a king": these are the finest articles. "Conch" refers to the right-spiraling conch used for consecration (*abhiseka*).
"Increasing powder" (*vaḍḍhamāna*) refers to cosmetic powder; some say it means "bath powder. "Ear-ornament" (*vaṭaṃsaka*): what is called an ear-ornament is meant by "vaṭaṃsaka.
"Nandiyāvaṭṭa" is something made of gold in the shape of a *nandiyāvaṭṭa* flower for the sake of auspiciousness. "Maiden" (*kaññā*) refers to a daughter of the noble class (*khattiya*).

"Hand-wiping cloth" (*hatthapuñchana*) refers to a costly yellow-colored cloth for wiping the hands. "Mud the color of dawn" (*aruṇavaṇṇamattika*) is that which originates from the abode of the *nāgas*.
"A pair of cloths" (*vatthakoṭika*) means simply a set of two garments. "Brought by the *nāgas*" (*nāgamāhaṭa*) means brought by the *nāgas*.

"The ambrosial medicine" (*amatosadha*) is a type of medicinal pill with that name; it is called thus because its function is similar to that of ambrosia (*amata*). "By way of a summary of floor-coverings" (*bhūmattharaṇasaṅkhepena*)...

In the manner of a ground-covering. "Fortune-tellers" means readers of omens. "Enough, let us go" was said by him while declining [the invitation], thinking, "Because it is too close to the city, it is not appropriate.

"Of eight thousand and nine hundred living beings" means of eight thousand five hundred living beings. "The Appamāda Sutta" refers to the Mahā-appamāda Sutta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya; it is stated that this is the Rājovāda Sutta.
*Mahaccā* means *mahatā* (with great). *Upasaṅkamanto* means that he approached while appearing exceedingly exhausted; this is the meaning.
The connection is with the phrase *tumhe jānanatthaṃ* (for the purpose of making you know). Regarding *pañcapaṇṇāsāya*, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"In this context, 'catupaññāsāya' (forty-five) should be said. For if that were the case, it would accord with the statement made later regarding 'sixty-two arahants.'"
“Crowded with the Ten Brothers” means filled with the ten brothers, beginning with Devānampiyatissa, who were the sons of Muṭasīva.
“The Perfectly Enlightened One has not been seen for a long time” is said with reference to the relics.

“All musical instruments” refers to all types of musical equipment, or the musicians associated with them. “Having caused to be presented” means having assembled them by way of commissioning offerings.
"During the increasing shadow" means after the meal. "A rain like lotus leaves" refers to a rain that falls without wetting those who do not wish to be wetted, as if upon lotus leaves.
"The Great Hero" refers to the relics themselves by way of a designation for the Teacher.
"Having turned toward the western direction and stepped back" means that while standing facing the east, by stepping backward, he [faced] the western direction.
It is said that he was "facing the western direction" with reference to his approaching such a place.
They say that "Mahejavatthu" is the name of a certain abode of deities.
"By pajjaraka" means by the disease called *pajjaraka* produced by non-human beings (*amanussa*). "Deva" means a cloud. "Anuppavecchī" means...
"He was liberated. Regarding the phrase "there was a dispute," one should understand this as a present tense usage (*vattamānappayoga*) in view of the time of the action.
This applies in all such cases. "That very place stands"—this is the connection.
One must supply the words "and rays connected with the six colors" and "and streams of water of the six colors"; in this way, the connection is established here.
They say: even after the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, such a miracle occurred through his power;
in order to show this, he spoke the verse beginning with "Thus inconceivable.

"Providing protection" means performing a *paritta* (protective chant) so that the *yakkhas*, who had been driven away by his own skillful means, would not enter again. "*Āvijji*" means he went around.
"King’s brother" means the king’s younger brother. "Queen Anulā" was the wife of the king’s elder brother.
"By one who emits a web of rays" means by one emitting a web of rays that are glossy, flavorful, and full of nutritive essence (*ojas*).
The connection is: "he went in a single day. "He sent" means he dispatched a written message. "He looked toward" means he gazed upon or longed for. "Heavy" means...
"Weighty" means that which is not to be transgressed. "He honors me" means he looks up to me.
"The color of a smith" refers to the color of the king’s ordinary goldsmith. "Three fathoms in height" means three fathoms in width. Regarding the phrase "by the sovereignty over all Jambudīpa":
here, "sovereignty" (*rajja*) is what belongs to a king; it consists of both the revenue arising from all of Jambudīpa as well as his commands and so forth. By that...

The meaning is "I worship. It is not appropriate to give by setting a temporal limit—such as "I give this to him for seven days"—using an object like the entire earth or a palace, because giving is characterized by the relinquishment of the object (*vatthu*). Indeed, one who gives in such a manner is said to give only for a limited time;

and since giving consists in the relinquishment of the object, it is improper to take back that which has already been relinquished, such as the earth and so forth. However, when [the duration] is fixed...
Since [the suffixes] *āya* and so forth have been abandoned [in the preceding cases], it is appropriate to include them hereafter because they have not been abandoned.
Therefore, according to the method already stated, the "giving of sovereignty" (*rajjadāna*) from this point onward should also be understood as occurring by way of the giving of *āya* and so forth.
"Becoming water-bubbles" means having the form of water-bubbles, like the sprouts of a *ketakī* creeper. "Like a lattice-window" is a neuter noun; [it refers to] windows.

The meaning is that it resembles a wooden board placed in the form of a lattice; or alternatively, the meaning is that it resembles a window and a net made of thread and so forth. Regarding the term *devadundubhi*: here, "deva" means a cloud;

the thundering of that cloud—which, due to its clear and white nature, appears as if it were empty space—is called *devadundubhi*, which some also call "the drum of the sky. *Phaliṃsu* means they thundered.
“By the dances of the mountains” means by the dancing of the mountains as they whirl here and there due to an earthquake.
“By the *hiṅkāra* sounds of the *yakkhas*” is said because the *yakkhas*, filled with wonder, uttered the sound “hiṃ.
“By their respective skills” means by their own individual proficiency in the arts. “Having given the consecration” means having given the consecration with the water from Lake Anotatta.
“Families of deities” (*devatākulāni*) refers to the families of nāgas, yakṣas, and other deities who stand surrounding the Great Bodhi tree; this is the grammatical connection.
Regarding King Gopaka, they likewise call him “Taraccha. “By this retinue” is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment;
the meaning is “together with this retinue. “Tāmalitti” is a seaport of that name on the shore of the ocean. This is its [description].
The third [time] is said with reference to the bestowal of sovereignty over the Bodhi tree whose branches were established in the golden basin.
Prior to that, however, the bestowal of sovereignty was once performed by the Great Bodhi itself from an uncut branch;
thus, including that, the King honored it with sovereignty on four occasions. On the days when it was honored with sovereignty, it is said that from the entire island...
Having taken the revenue that had arisen, he offered it specifically to the Great Bodhi tree.
"On the first day of the *pāṭipada*" means on the first day of the bright fortnight (*sukkapaṭipadadivasa*).
For this is called "the first day of the *pāṭipada*" in relation to the first day of the dark fortnight (*kaṇhapakka-pāṭipadadivasa*); and this is the conventional usage in that island of Tambapaṇṇi.

It was stated [previously] having taken [the period from one full moon to the next]; however, here, the conventional designation "one month" refers to the interval from one full moon until the following full moon.
Therefore, according to this convention, it should be said "on the second *pāṭipada* day," because here the *pāṭipada* of the dark fortnight (*kaṇhapakkha*) is treated as the first *pāṭipada*.
In the phrase "it goes down" (*gacchati vatare*), the word *areti* means exhaustion. In "a league all around" (*samantāyojanaṃ*), the suffix indicates continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
"Upayogavacanaṃ" means "in every place within a distance of one *yojana*.

"In the form of a *supaṇṇa*" means that the royal families of the *nāgas*, desiring to seize the Great Bodhi tree by force and carry it off to the *nāga* realm, were terrified by the *garuḷa* form assumed through supernormal power (*iddhi*).
"Having seen that splendor" refers to the greatness of the worship being performed by the deities and others for the Great Bodhi tree.

The construction is as follows: having seen the greatness of her spiritual power (*ānubhāva*), she herself, desiring to worship in that same manner, requested the Elder Nun (*therī*). Regarding the phrase "in the site of the Samuddasāla":
it refers to the place where the King, standing there, saw the Bodhi tree approaching across the ocean through the Elder’s power;
and because they later built a hall named Samuddasāla to mark the spot where the ocean was seen, it is called the Samuddasāla site. In that [place].
On the site that had become the Samuddasālā. "Of the Elder" means of the Elder Mahāmahinda.
"Flower-offerings" (puppha-agghiyanī) refers to flower-stūpas resembling gabled halls (kūṭāgāra). "Āgato vatare" means he came here; "are" signifies joy.
"With eight families of ministers and eight families of brahmins"—that is, with sixteen families of noble birth. "He governed the kingdom" means he ruled the kingdom.
He sent [him] away to investigate. "At the gate-tower of the royal grounds" means at the gate-tower of the royal park.
"Successive insight" (*anupubbavipassanā*) refers to successive insight beginning with arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*).

Regarding the phrase "simultaneously with the establishment of enlightenment," although it should have been expressed using an instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*), the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) "from the establishment of enlightenment" (*saha bodhipatiṭṭhānā*) was used by changing the grammatical case. Mindfulness (*sati*).
Indeed, when used with the word *sahasa*, it must be expressed in the instrumental case. "They appeared" means they became manifest.
"In the place of the great seat" means in the location established by the great stone seat on the eastern side. "Having honored, he paid homage" means he paid homage to the future Mahācetiya.
However, because only mere worship was performed at the former site of the Mahāvihāra, the Saṅgha will also be junior [in seniority] in the future.

It should be understood that the state of not being worthy of salutation has thus been made manifest. However, in the future, Buddhas such as Metteyya and the Paccekabuddhas must indeed be saluted with reference to the moment of their Buddhahood, for they are persons distinguished by their intrinsic nature;
this is how it should be grasped. "Mahāariṭṭha" refers to him who went forth at Cetiya-giri together with fifty-five kinsmen.
It was said: "In the site of the pariveṇa of the minister Meghavaṇṇābhaya" means in the place that served as the ground for the pariveṇa to be constructed by the minister of King Meghavaṇṇābhaya.
Because it arose in the sky as an auspicious omen, its charming sound was like the roar of the sky itself; thus it is said, "the sky resounded with a great roar. For indeed...

There is no such thing as a phenomenon called "space" that would produce sound; rather, that sound should be understood as being produced by a particular variation in temperature occurring within space.
On the day of the first Kattika invitation ceremony... [etc. ...he proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka:
this was said with reference to the day he began reciting the Vinaya. *Anusiṭṭhikarānaṃ* means "of those who provide instruction."
*Rājinā* is a genitive case used in the sense of the dative; the meaning is "by King Devānaṃpiyatissa.
*Aññepi* (others also) refers to others besides the sixty-eight great elders beginning with Mahinda. Showing their specific identities, he says:
*tesaṃ therānaṃ*, etc. Therein, *antevāsikā tesaṃ therānaṃ* means the disciples of those sixty-eight great elders beginning with Thera Mahinda, such as Ariṭṭha and the rest.
And it should be connected thus: "the pupils" refers to the pupils of the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha, namely Tissa-Datta, Kālasumana, and others.
"The pupils of the pupils" means the succession of pupils belonging to those pupils mentioned in both instances.
"Of the kind previously described" refers to the lineage of teachers revealed by the verses beginning with "Mahinda, Iṭṭiya, Uttiya," and so forth.
“Does not leak” means it does not flow out; the meaning is that it does not forget. Regarding the phrase “in those possessing mindfulness, understanding, and fortitude”:

here, *sati* (mindfulness) refers to the state of having grasped and retained [the teaching]. *Gati* (understanding) refers to the knowledge that grasps the distinctions between the meanings of words.

*Dhiti* (fortitude) refers to the energy applied in retaining what has been grasped and so forth. Regarding “among those who are anxious about wrongdoing,” this refers to those who investigate whether something is permissible or impermissible. “Those who stand in the place of mother and father” means...

Having stated this, he said "for they are dependent on that," and so forth, in order to support that very point. "In dependence upon the mastery of the Vinaya" means in dependence upon the thorough mastery of the Vinaya Piṭaka.

"One's own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded" means that because one who possesses shame and upholds the Vinaya does not incur an offense through the six modes such as ignorance and lack of shame, their own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded, being free from defects such as breach or fracture.

He is well-guarded. For those who are "plagued by remorse" (*kukkuccapakatānaṃ*)—meaning those who are afflicted, troubled, and overcome by remorse arising on account of what is allowable and what is unallowable—he is a refuge by dispelling their remorse according to the Vinaya and establishing them in purity.
One who is "without timidity" (*visārado*) is so called because his fear has departed. "When speaking thus, there is no fault... [and so forth].
Knowing that "there is no fault," he speaks fearlessly in the midst of the Saṅgha. Regarding "enemies":
both personal enemies and those who are enemies of the Dispensation, such as the Vajjiputtakas. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means by means of reasoned speech;

having shown the training rule (sikkhāpada), he refutes them so effectively that they are unable to establish what is contrary to the Dhamma (asaddhamma). Thus, having thoroughly subdued them, he speaks.

He restrains. "For the sake of the endurance of the true Dhamma" means for the sake of the persistence, that is, the continued existence, of the threefold true Dhamma consisting of the scriptures (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha).
In such passages as "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," the mastery of the Vinaya—or the Vinaya-prescription itself—is for the sake of restraining the doors of body and speech.

"Non-remorse" (*avippaṭisāra*) is the absence of remorse and the absence of distress regarding what has been done and what has not been done. "Gladness" (*pāmojja*) is tender joy (*taruṇapīti*). "Rapture" (*pīti*) is intense joy.
"Tranquility" (*passaddhi*) is tranquility of body and mind. "Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is the discernment of name-and-form together with their conditions.

"Disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) is insight (*vipassanā*). "Dispassion" (*virāga*) is the Noble Path. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) is the supreme fruit. "Knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*)...

The knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "Without clinging" (*anupādā*) means without clinging to any phenomenon, having relinquished them. "For the sake of final Nibbāna" (*parinibbānatthāya*):

because there is no final Nibbāna in the interval before the knowledge of reviewing has arisen, it is stated as a condition for that final Nibbāna by way of being an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*), etc.
"This talk is for this purpose": this talk on the Vinaya is for the sake of this final Nibbāna without clinging.
*Atthāya* means for the purpose. *Mantana* refers specifically to the counsel of the Vinaya—the counsel related to the Vinaya by which monks determine, "We shall do it thus; we shall not do it thus.
*Upanisā* means that which lies near (*upanisīdati*) and bears fruit; it is the cause.
The meaning is that even this succession of causes, beginning with "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," has this same purpose. *Sotāvadhānaṃ* (attentive listening).
Attention to the ear for the purpose of reflecting upon oneself regarding this discourse on the chain of conditions (*paccaya*) has that same purpose.

*Yadidaṃ* is a particle. That which is liberation—consisting either of the path to arahantship or its fruit—of the mind which, by not clinging through the four kinds of clinging, exists for this purpose, namely for final nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*). Alternatively:

It is also appropriate to apply this by way of conclusion, as follows: "Whatever this Dhamma may be, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging, its being liberated, its disappearance, its parinibbāna—for that purpose is this talk.
This is because the liberation of the path and fruit has already been discussed previously.
"Application" (āyoga) means repeated exertion by way of grasping and so forth.
The method of commentary on the account of the succession of teachers is finished.
Thus ends the method of commentary on the external introductory narrative (*bāhiranidānakathā*) within the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā.
The commentary on the Verañja section:
*Seyyathidaṃ* means "what is that? or "how is that? It is a term used for an indefinite description;

a "definite description" (*niyamaniddesa*) is one that describes its own meaning by specifying it according to its own form, whereas an "indefinite description" (*aniyamaniddesa*) is not such a definite description.
"Speech" (*vacana*) is so called because one speaks by means of it; it refers to speech that is an unrestricted or general description. "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the word *tena*.
"Reflection" (*parivitakka*) is that which proceeds [in such questions] as: "Of which Blessed Buddhas was the holy life (*brahmacariya*) not long-lasting?
"Either before or after" refers to the passage spoken prior to that word *tena*, or the passage yet to be spoken below.
The meaning is "it blows. "By what is established by its own meaning" means by what is established through its inherent capacity (*sāmatthiya*).

"In this regard, this is merely an indication of the entrance" means that this is an indication of the mere means for illustrating the aforementioned reasoning. For "entrance," "door," and "means" are identical in meaning.
The connection is: "the word *samaya* is seen [in this sense]. The connection is: "of this word *samaya*, 'assemblage' (*samavāya*) is the meaning."

"Depending on the time and the occasion": here, "time" (kāla) refers to the appropriate time for approaching; "occasion" (samaya) refers to the convergence of causes such as physical strength and so forth;

the meaning is "depending upon" or "in reliance upon" these. "Moment" (khaṇa) means opportunity. For the arising of a Buddha and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path (brahmacariya).
That itself is the occasion. For this very reason it is said, "or else alone. "The great occasion" (mahāsamaya): [is explained as follows].

"A great multitude. "In the woods" means in a forest thicket. Regarding the phrase "And the occasion for you, Bhaddāli," here "occasion" (*samaya*) refers to the cause for transgressing the training rules.
What is that? It is the Blessed One’s knowledge of one's own misconduct; the meaning is that the cause designated as "occasion" was not penetrated by him.
The passage beginning with "The Blessed One" and so forth shows the manner in which he did penetrate it. "While learning" means something...
Because he was capable of learning something, he was called "Uggaha" (the Learner); this is the name of the wanderer Sumanaparibbājaka.
They call it *samaya* because it is there that views (*diṭṭhi*) are proclaimed; thus it is the *Samayappavādaka*, Mallikā’s park.

That very place is also called "Tindukācīra" because it is surrounded by a row of *timbaru* trees known as *tindukācīra*; and it is also called "Ekasālā" because there is only one hall (*sālā*) for residence there.

It is also called “having a single hall. “The realization of the goal” (atthābhisamaya) is because of the attainment of the aforementioned goal—benefit—pertaining to both the present life and future lives.

“The realization of conceit” (mānābhisamaya) is through the abandoning of conceit. “The sense of oppression” (pīḷanaṭṭha): oppression is the harming of one who possesses it; it is the making of one non-expansive.
The sense of oppression is simply the state of being oppressed. “Torment” (santāpa) is by way of the suffering of suffering and so forth.
"Tormenting. "Transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) refers to the state of being subject to transformation in two ways—by aging and by death;

it is that which is to be fully understood and penetrated, thus it is "full comprehension" (*abhisamaya*). That itself is the meaning of full comprehension, as are "affliction" (*pīḷana*) and the others.
And here, because prefixes are merely indicators, even when the word *samaya* is extracted for its meaning, the word *abhisamaya* remains with its prefix.

Uddhaṭo (extracted). Therein, *samaya* means a collection (*samavāya*), because it is that wherein there is a coming together (*ekato pavatti*) of conditions for the production of a result by way of their conjunction.

Alternatively, *samaya* means a moment (*khaṇa*), because when there is a conjunction of supporting conditions for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), beings come and proceed therein.
Or, *samaya* refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhamma*), because they "come together" (*sameti*) therein, or because they themselves "go" (*eti*)—that is, they arrive and pass away.
*Samaya* means time. It is a *samaya* because the parts come together (*samenti*) in it, or because it comes together in them; thus, it is a collection (*samūha*).

It is a *samaya* (cause) because from it the fruit arises when there is a conjunction of other conditions (*paccayantara-saṅgame eti āgacchati phalanti*). It is a *samaya* (view) because, through the perversion of perception, one approaches and adheres to phenomena (*saññā-vasena vipallāsato dhammesu eti abhinivisati*).
It is a *samaya* (attainment) because it is an approaching, a coming near, or an acquisition (*samīpaṃ ayanaṃ upagamanaṃ*). It is "just right" (*sammadeva*).
"Samaya" is the going away (*ayana*) or departure of combined words; it means abandoning. Or, "samaya" is the going toward (*ayana*) or knowing of combined truths in a truly right way;
it means penetration. In this manner, the application of the word *samaya* to various meanings should be understood.
And here, the multiplicity of meanings for the word *samaya* has been stated in its general sense; for it does not apply to only one specific meaning.

The word *tadanya* (other than that) also applies here. Therefore, it should be understood that just as the meanings are distinct, so too the conventional terms (*samaya-sadda*) expressing those respective meanings are themselves distinct.
This applies everywhere in the enumeration of meanings.
In this context, *tathā* refers to those [works] of Sutta and Abhidhamma by means of the instrumental and locative cases; *idha* refers to the Vinaya; and *aññathā* [refers to...].

By the expression "by means of the instrument" (*karaṇavacanena*). "Entirely" (*accantameva*) means without interruption (*nirantara*). "State" (*bhāva*) is indeed action (*kiriyā*); the definition of one state by another state through action is "the characterization of a state by a state" (*bhāvena-bhāvalakkhaṇa*), such as:
"When the moon has risen, the prince was born. As for the passage beginning with "For the locus...
(*adhikaraṇañhi*), in the Abhidhamma, the word *samaya* functions in five senses: time, collection, moment, assembly, and cause.

It is not as in the *Vinaya*, where only the sense of "time" (*kāla*) applies; rather, among those [three meanings], the two—time and collection—are suitable for describing the state of being a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa-bhāva*) of the phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) mentioned therein.

However, all three—including the senses of moment (*khaṇa*), coincidence (*samavāya*), and cause (*hetu*)—are suitable for describing the existence of contact and so forth by way of their own nature and by way of characterizing their existence. Thus, the aforementioned meaning is demonstrated through the method of analysis.

It is stated [in this way] in order to establish [the meaning]. In that context, the application of the locative sense (*adhikaraṇattha*) is as follows: at whatever time, or within whatever collection of phenomena (*dhammasamūha*), or during whatever occasion (*samaya*) serving as the locus, wholesome [states] have arisen, at that very same time, or within that very same collection of phenomena, or during that very same occasion, contact (*phassa*) and the other [mental factors] exist.
However, when there is a moment (*khaṇa*), a concurrence (*samavāya*), or a cause (*hetu*)—that is, when such an occasion (*samaya*) exists—[then they arise].

When wholesome [states] have arisen, contact and the other factors exist even at that very moment and time; thus, the application of the sense of "characterization by existence" (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa) should be understood.

Regarding the phrase *hoti c'ettha*: there is a summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*) here concerning the subject matter as previously stated. Regarding *aññatra*: in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma. "Difference in mere expression" means that due to the elegance of the teaching, there is a difference in the sound alone, but not in the meaning. "In general" means by way of commonality.
In the passage beginning with *iriya-patho*, "posture" (*iriya-patho*) is the path—that is, the locus of occurrence—of posture, which consists of activity pertaining to all the doors.
Because there is an absence of karma that is not based on the [four] postures, the postures themselves—standing and so forth—are the "abidings" (*vihāra*).

Being "become sublime" (*brahmabhūta*), meaning having become excellent through the manifestation of a mind intent on the welfare of others and so forth, loving-kindness and the rest are called the "sublime abidings" (*brahmavihāra*).

However, the remaining exalted states, by virtue of their illumination and other qualities established through the removal of all hindrances and so forth, are called "divine abidings" (*dibbavihāra*). By way of being sublime abidings...

Because they are apprehended separately, loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others are not included here. The "dwelling of the noble ones" (*ariya-vihāra*) refers to the attainments of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*).

To show that the word "root" (*mūla*) is conventionally established specifically for the roots of trees and so forth, the term is qualified by another word for root, thus it is said "root-of-roots" (*mūlamūla*), just as one says "suffering-of-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
This is because greed and the other [defilements] are not common to the minds of those who have abandoned the roots of fault.
“It was stated: ‘because of the uncommon cause.

In that context, ‘it might occur’ means that a certain objection might arise regarding those locations such as Verañjā and so forth. But what is the purpose of stating the causal background in both ways?
He says: ‘for the purpose of indicating the village of the alms-round,’ and so on. In that regard, ‘his’ refers to the Blessed One.”
*Kilama* is exhaustion; *attakilamatha* is the exhaustion of one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*).
*Attakilamathānuyoga* is the repeated application, that is, the recurring engagement, in that [exhaustion].

Sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) is "attached" (*līnā*)—meaning joined—by way of association with the pleasure found in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*). It functions by being "clinging" (*allīnā*) to those sensual desires or pleasures that coexist with it and serve as its objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
"Sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukhallikā*) is craving; "devotion to sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*) is the repeated application to that sensual pleasure.
"Having grown up in the world" means having been nurtured by the enjoyment of material things. The construction is: "When arising, he arises solely for the sake of the welfare of many people, etc.
To clarify the meaning of "Saṅgha" as being a collection due to the commonality of view and virtue, he said "view," and so forth. Here...
And [he dwells] with the view described as: “This is the noble view that leads out, leading the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering;
he dwells having attained conformity of view with such a view”; and with the virtues described as: “Those virtues which are unbroken...
[and so on] ...conducive to concentration; he dwells having attained conformity of virtue with such virtues.”

The meaning is: by that group of recluses (*samaṇagaṇa*) which is a collection (*saṅghāta*), i.e., joined together (*saṅghaṭita*), by what is reckoned as the commonality (*sāmañña*) of virtues. Or rather, there should be the reading here:

*“diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅkhātasaṅghātenā”* (by that which is a collection reckoned as the commonality of view and virtue). The meaning of that is: by that collection of recluses which is a joining (*saṃhanana*) consisting of the commonality of view and virtue.
For with such a reading, the meaning is more logically consistent from the standpoint of grammar. *Assa* means: of the great community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).
In the phrase "he recites the *brahma*," the word *brahma* refers here to the Veda; that [Veda] is threefold, according to the divisions of *mantra*, *brahmana*, and *kalpa*.
Among these, the three Vedas beginning with the *Iruveda* are the *mantras*, and they are primary; the others, however, are dependent upon them. Therefore, only the primary ones are included.
"He recites the *mantras*" means he recites the *mantra*-treatises beginning with the *Iruveda*. The *Iruveda* and so forth...

Because they must be guarded and spoken, they are called "mantras. To clarify the two previously mentioned meanings—namely, that one is a *brāhmaṇa* because of having cast out evil and a *samaṇa* because of having stilled evil—the passage beginning with "for this has been said" was stated, providing two examples.
Indeed, taking up this statement, "He is called a *samaṇa* because of having stilled evils," [it continues]: "because of having stilled evil..."
It is said, “He is called a *samaṇa*”; however, the phrase “one who has banished evil” (*bāhitapāpa*) is a statement found in another metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).

“Attained through qualities as they truly are” means attained through qualities according to reality (*yathābhūta*). “Possessing something” (*sakiñcana*) means having defilement (*sadosa*). Regarding the term “by way of lineage” (*gottavasena*):
here, lineage (*gotra*) is that which protects (*tāyati*) one from going (*gam*); and by the word *go*, both expression and cognition are meant.
"By some kind of loss" means by some loss such as the loss of relatives and so forth; the meaning is "by way of decline.
"Beyond that" refers to the words beginning with "at Verañjā. Regarding the term "the accusative case in the sense of describing one who has become thus":

one who has become or reached this particular state is "one who has become thus" (*itthambhūta*); the description of such a person is "describing one who has become thus" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*), and that is precisely the meaning here.

The meaning is "stating one who has become thus. Alternatively, the meaning of "stating one who has become thus" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*) is the sense of describing someone as having "become" (*bhūta*) or "arisen" (*jāta*) in such a manner (*itthaṃ*, *evaṃpakāra*);
the meaning is that the accusative case is used for that [description].
And here, in the word *abbhuggato*, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the sense of stating one who has become thus, because it illustrates the manner of rising after having overcome [something].

Regarding the phrase "tena yogato taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ," although this accusative case (*upayogavacana*) shares the same referent as the genitive (*sāmivattha*), it is stated as being "in the sense of describing a particular state" (*itthambhūtākhyānatthe*) because it serves to indicate such a description; for this very reason, he says:
"The meaning is 'of that venerable Gotama.'"

This is what is meant: just as in the expression “Devadatta is good toward his mother” (*sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi*), where the accusative case is used to express a state of being characterized by something due to its connection with the prefix *abhi*, so too here—in the phrase “Now, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama’s fame has arisen toward him” (*taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ abhi evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo uggato*)—the accusative case is used to express a state of being characterized by something due to its connection with the prefix *abhi*. [The example continues: “Devadatta is good.”

In the phrase *mātaram abhi*, here—given that there is an occasion for either the locative case (in the sense of a locus) or the genitive case (in the sense of possession), as in "Devadatta is intent upon his mother," or "toward his mother," or "with respect to his mother"—the accusative case is employed in connection with the word *abhi*, which indicates the sense of "thus-described" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*).
This is just as in this example: Devadatta is one who is oriented toward his mother or related to his mother.

Just as the meaning "he has reached the state described" is understood there, so too here the meaning "the Master Gotama’s kinsman, the sound of his fame, has risen up, having overcome [all others] and reached the manner of rising" is understood.
For in that case, the mention of Devadatta is like the mention of "fame" here; and the word "mother" used there is like... [the rest of the sentence].
Furthermore, just as the word *sādhu* was included in the phrase "that venerable Gotama," so here the inclusion of the word *uggata* (arisen) should be understood.

He said "kitti evā" (merely fame) to show that it is not merely sound, but rather sound that has become fame (*kittibhūto saddo*). Thus, *kittī* means praise; the sound that makes that [praise] known is *kittisaddo*.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "or the sound of praise.
Regarding the phrase "He, the Blessed One" (*so bhagavā*): here, *so* (he) indicates well-known renown;

he is that one who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) and shattered all defilements (*kilesa*), shook the ten-thousandfold world system and awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*).
Because he is so well-known in the world, it is said, "That Blessed One" (*so bhagavā*). This term "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) is a mention of the Teacher's name, not a mention of his qualities.
However, later on, "Blessed One" is indeed a mention of his qualities.
By the phrase "by this and by that," he shows that each of the terms beginning with "Worthy One" (*arahant*) occurs in dependence upon a multitude of various qualities.
By the two words *suvidūra* and *vidūra*, he shows that it is exceedingly far away; for "far-ness" (*vidūratā*) is indeed the state of being very far (*suvidūratā*).

By the phrase "because of the destruction of the defilements together with their latent tendencies" (*savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattā*), he shows that the Arahantship of the Blessed One is not shared with the Paccekabuddhas and others, because their latent tendencies have not been abandoned.

And what is called "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*) is the cause of the impairment of the three applications of the door, such as the non-comprehension of the entire range of the knowable (*sakalañeyyānavabodha*), even in one who is free from defilement.

The mode established by defilements is like the mode established by shackles for those whose feet have been bound for a long time: it is the cause of their remaining cramped even when the shackles are released.
That by which Pilindavaccha and others possess such defects as being addressed with the term "outcaste" (vasala) should be understood as "habitual tendency" (vāsanā).
Regarding the word *āraka*, the vowel *ā* is shortened, the letter *ka* is changed to *ha* with a nasalization (*sānussara*), according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).

The derivation of the word “arahant” should be understood. In the same way, the derivations of the subsequent terms should be understood according to their respective etymological methods (*niruttinaya*).

And the connection is with this phrase: “the wheel of saṃsāra. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in “merit, etc.,” one includes non-meritorious formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) and imperturbable formations (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
Because the taints (*āsava*) themselves are the cause of ignorance and the rest, they are the origin; thus he said, “consisting of the origin of the taints.”

For it is said: “With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance. The threefold existence (tibhava)—comprising the various types of resultant form, kamma-formations, and non-percipient form—is itself the chariot;
[the phrase] “in that chariot of the threefold existence” refers to this. The “wheel of saṃsāra” is the aforementioned arising of defilements (kilesa), kamma, and resultants.
“And the succession of the aggregates, Of the elements and the sense bases...”
“The continuity of existence, proceeding without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
Thus, that which is called *saṃsāra* is a “wheel” (*cakra*) because it revolves like a wheel;
the connection is that all its spokes have been destroyed by this [Buddha]. By “this one” is meant the Blessed One. “Awakening” (*bodhi*) is knowledge; that has arisen here as the clear essence.
The seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). The "wisdom-axe that brings about the destruction of karma" refers to the knowledge of the path of arahantship;

it should be understood that this is stated as being distinguished by the specific qualification "bringing about the destruction of karma" in order to show that it cuts through the karma known as volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra).

Thus, having demonstrated by means of several factors the wheel of saṃsāra, as well as the chariot of the three realms of existence consisting of the remaining factors— the phenomena of name-and-form which have become the fruit—
and the manner in which those who ride that chariot are slain by the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; now, by means of all twelve factors of dependent origination,
[the text] demonstrates the wheel of saṃsāra alone, divested of the chariot, and the various ways in which its spokes do not strike.
The phrase "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth was stated in order to demonstrate this. In that context, *anamatagga* means "having a limit that is not known" (*anu-anu-amata-agga*);
the sense is that its beginning is unknown even by those who follow it in every way.

The statement "because it has ignorance as its root and ends with aging-and-death" is said by superimposing a unity upon the ten factors beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), for they do not each individually have ignorance as their root.
Furthermore, there is the fact that aging and death constitute the conclusion [of the dependent origination], because this is not stated in the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-pāḷi*.

Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said with reference to the fact that even those [factors] have ignorance as their root according to their respective natures, and that they have aging and death as their conclusion by way of the momentary aging and death that constitutes their own specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). In this way, their individual status as "links" (*aṅga*) is established.
Having thus shown the entire wheel of saṃsāra in all its aspects, [the author now addresses] the knowledge by which the Blessed One’s severing of the spokes of this wheel of saṃsāra was accomplished.

Since the summary heading for that "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) is stated as "wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena," [it follows that] because ignorance and the other factors that are components of the wheel of existence are related as condition and conditionally arisen, [this knowledge is established].

Having shown the mode of occurrence by way of grasping, [the author] next demonstrates, by means of the text from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* beginning with "Thus this ignorance is the cause," which is stated as a conclusion to that same meaning,
the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) in its own form;
and having shown the analysis of its occurrence in those very factors such as ignorance by way of the four summaries (*catusaṅkhepa*), and so forth, thereafter—

By the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the Blessed One," the Blessed One’s state of having fully penetrated dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in all its aspects through that knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) is shown; then, by the passage beginning with "Again,

by this knowledge of the stability of phenomena," in order to show how the Blessed One’s wheel of saṃsāra was shattered by that knowledge, [the text addresses] therein the ignorance regarding suffering and the other truths.
"Ignorance and so forth" has been stated. Therein, "of the three bases" refers to the three bases of the eye, the ear, and the mind.
This same method applies to "of the three contacts" and so forth. The six groups of craving are to be understood by way of craving for forms and the rest.

"Attainment of heaven" means attainment within the happy realms of sense-sphere existence. "In the same way" means precisely through the condition of clinging to sense-pleasures. "Attainment of the Brahma-world" means...

[He develops loving-kindness] for the attainment of the fine-material Brahma-world. Since all lust (*rāga*) whose object consists of the phenomena belonging to the three planes is a state of defilement-lust (*kilesakāma*), even lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) is simply clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*);
thus it is said: "One develops loving-kindness precisely with clinging to sense-pleasures as its condition.

Regarding the phrase "in the remaining applications rooted in clinging," this refers to the applications rooted in clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). In that regard, the method of application is as follows:
— Here, someone adopts the view: "There is no other world; the self is annihilated.
