On account of that clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), he engages in misconduct with the body, and so forth. Furthermore, another adopts the view:

"In such-and-such a state of existence the self is annihilated," and for the sake of rebirth in the realms of sense-desire, form, or formlessness, he performs various wholesome deeds; thus [this] is rooted in clinging to views.
The application [of this principle] should be understood in this very manner for the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*).

Furthermore, another person, misapprehending an impure path as "a pure path" by thinking, "Purification comes through virtue, purification comes through observances," engages in misconduct with the body and so forth due to the condition of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*);
in this way, the application rooted in clinging to rules and observances should be understood across all states of existence.

Now, in order to show the manner in which ignorance and the other conditions grasp their respective objects for that knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*)— which is capable of destroying the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra—

it has been shown by the passage beginning "In the sensual existence, ignorance is a condition for volitional formations in the sensual existence" how ignorance and the others function as conditions and conditionally arisen states;
and that very same knowledge, together with the mode of their occurrence within ignorance and the rest, [is now further explained].
Having brought forward the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text, he says "evamayaṃ" and so forth, showing it by way of conclusion. In the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*, however, it is said:

"Now, that which was shown by the expositor of the wheel of saṃsāra—namely, that in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is the condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) in the realm of sense-desire, and so on—demonstrates the state of being a condition for ignorance and the rest, and the state of being the arisen-from-conditions for volitional formations and the rest."
It is said: "Bringing forth that very *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text, he spoke beginning with 'Thus indeed' (*evam-ayaṃ*) as a conclusion.

This same reading is also recorded in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the commentary on the Vinaya. And therein, by means of the passage beginning with "Ignorance (*avijjā*) in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth," the state of being condition and conditioned—presenting the wheel of saṃsāra—is stated.

Ignorance is not its hub, because this has already been shown previously by the passage beginning with "the root-cause," and because there is no concluding summary here as there was for the wheel-form above, since that was presented as an application.
Furthermore, it is said: "Moreover, he shows that very relationship of condition and conditioned state by way of a conclusion.
And yet, in this case, the relationship of condition and conditioned state is not the primary focus by way of a conclusion.

Rather, it is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), which proceeds by way of discerning conditions, that is shown here as a conclusion to the aforementioned mode of discerning conditions.

For it is said: "In this way, ignorance is the cause, formations are cause-born, and both these phenomena are cause-born—this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. In the past... [and so on].

In the passage, “Ignorance is the cause for the past time... [and so on] ...for the future time... [and so on] ...knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa),” it is specifically knowledge of the stability of phenomena that is shown as the primary factor.

However, because the wisdom that discerns conditions—such as “ignorance is the cause, volitional formations are produced by a cause,” and so forth—is called “knowledge of the stability of phenomena,” the aforementioned statement is intended to illustrate the manner in which that knowledge discerns conditions.
It is stated by way of being the object, not by way of being the primary factor.

This is the meaning here: "In this way"—that is, by the method just described—this ignorance is the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), and the volitional formations have arisen through that cause.
"Both of these" means that since this ignorance is distinct from the primordial nature (*pakati*), the Lord (*issara*), and so forth as imagined by others...

Like [the eye], it is not causeless, permanent, or stable; rather, because of the statement, "With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance," it too is caused, conditioned, and indeed impermanent.
Therefore, both these—ignorance and formations—are produced solely from causes.
"Thus" (iti) means: the wisdom that, in the manner just described, grasps the conditions—that [wisdom] regarding the stability of phenomena...
It is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) because it occurs in accordance with reality regarding causes.
For here, the status of ignorance and the other factors as conditions and so forth is stated merely by way of elucidating the object of knowledge, not by way of their being primary;
rather, it is knowledge itself that is stated here as the primary factor. Therefore, this is for the purpose of showing the mode of discerning conditions for this very knowledge.
Below, in the section on the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), the status of ignorance and the other factors as conditions and so forth was already stated;
here, too, it is summarized by way of conclusion, and not for the purpose of demonstrating the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
This is my own opinion on this point. Furthermore, if the phenomena arising from conditions have not been seen, it is impossible to see the causal status of the conditions themselves.

In the description of the knowledge that discerns conditions, it should be understood that the phrase “volitional formations are arisen from a cause” includes the phenomena that have arisen from conditions as well.

By this method—in accordance with the method stated for ignorance—one should expand all the terms ending with birth, such as: “volitional formations are the cause; consciousness is arisen from a cause,” and so forth.

Thus, having shown the mode of occurrence of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) regarding ignorance and the other factors according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text, it is now said, beginning with "Therein," in order to show the mode of its occurrence in those conditions by way of other modes as well.
Therein, "therein" refers to those factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Ignorance and the rest are subsumed therein by virtue of their commonality as causes.
"By way of similarity of fruit" is the concise statement; "group," "collection," "portion," or "heap" is the meaning.
That [group], though twofold by way of its nature (jāti), becomes fourfold by way of the distinction of time. The term "present time" (paccuppanna-addhā) follows [from the context].

Craving, clinging, and existence are included because they share the commonality of defilement and karma, and because they are inseparable from them. Even the cycle of defilements beginning with ignorance is included due to their similarity in being phenomena subject to ripening (vipākadhammadhammatā).

Regarding the phrase "here it is the kamma-process itself," he says, "these five factors," and so forth. In expressions such as "resultant states" (*vipākā dhammā*), although only the immaterial aggregates born of kamma are denoted by the term "resultant" (*vipāka*), the pentad of results—including both the mental and the material—is referred to as the "resultant process" (*vipākavaṭṭa*) in contexts such as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
This is because the immaterial is predominant and because of its abundance therein; that is, the process is dominated by the resultant and is replete with the resultant.
Or rather, the meaning is that they are suitable [to be spoken of]. Alternatively, the word *vipāka* (result) should be understood here as a synonym for *kammaja* (born of karma).
"By way of birth, aging, and death" means that since there is no such thing as birth, aging, and death apart from ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), it refers to them by way of those [terms];

the meaning is: by means of them, through their medium. They are "modes" (*ākāra*) because they are manifested or made known; thus, they are the specific forms of ignorance and so forth, and therefore [it is said] "by way of the mode of conditions."

The meaning is as follows. It should be understood that "one connection" refers to the connection between cause and fruit (*hetuphalasandhi*) which serves as the cause for uninterrupted occurrence; the second is the connection of fruit and cause (*phalahetusandhi*);
and the third is the connection of cause and fruit (*hetuphalasandhi*).
Having thus shown the manner in which the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) occurs with respect to ignorance and the other factors in many ways, now—

In order to show—according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*—that the Blessed One had penetrated dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in all its aspects even before they were spoken by those [disciples], and that this knowledge is the basis for the application of the term "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), the passage beginning with "Thus the Blessed One" was stated as a conclusion.
Therein, "thus" (*iti*) is a reference to the manner already described; therefore he said:

"Fourfold summary," and so forth. "In all aspects" means that he penetrates [this] by way of all modes—both those explicitly stated here, such as "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations in the sensual existence," and those not explicitly stated here but found in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* and other texts.
"That" refers to the knowledge by which the Blessed One knows thus; it is knowledge in the sense of having been known. "In the sense of what is known" means...
"In the sense of knowing" means "in the sense of fully understanding," which is to say, in the sense of penetrating.

Now, in order to demonstrate the utility of this knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*)—which has been explained at length along with the various modes of discerning conditions—the passage beginning with "By means of this knowledge of the stability of phenomena... was stated.
In this context, the connection is: "One should strike down with the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*). How so? He says:

"Those phenomena," and so forth. Having understood those phenomena, beginning with ignorance, as they truly are by means of that knowledge of the stability of phenomena—which is like the weapon of the great thunderbolt-knowledge—one becomes disenchanted by means of the weapon of powerful insight (*vipassanā*), becomes dispassionate by means of the weapon of the Noble Path, and is liberated. One should strike down [the defilements].

The construction is: "he destroys. For even the knowledge of the Noble Path (ariyamaggañāṇa) is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) by way of its function, because it awakens to the truth of the origin of suffering and so forth.

Although the worship performed by establishing a dwelling is directed toward a single aggregate of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha), it is nevertheless the worship of the Blessed One himself, because it proceeds solely out of love for the Blessed One and because [the dwelling] is adorned with shrines containing his relics and so forth.

He said to the Blessed One, beginning with "having dedicated [this]... and so forth. Regarding the phrase *kilesārīnaṃ so muni* ("that sage is the enemy of the defilements"), there is an elision of the nasalized vowel (*niggahīta-lopa*);

the meaning is "because the enemies of the defilements have been slain. In the phrase *paccayādīnaṃ cārahō* ("one who is worthy of requisites, etc."), an elision of the nasalized vowel is likewise to be understood.
Regarding the term *sammāsambuddho*, he says "it is *sāma*" because the word *sam-* occurs here in the sense of "they lie down" (*sayanti*); thus, he is "not to be led by others" (*aparaneyyo*).
The meaning is "having sacrificed. Regarding the phrase *sabbadhammānaṃ* ("of all phenomena"), this is established because no specific object has been grasped [to limit it].

For when there is no mention of a partial [scope], the absence of limitation (*nippadesatā*) regarding what is to be grasped is understood, just as in the expression "the initiated one does not give" [which implies he gives nothing at all].

And having established it thus, it should be understood that the word *buddha* is established in the sense of the agent (*kattar*) itself, regardless of any particular meaning, due to the desire for it to function as an accusative.
"Because of non-existence. For here, from the perspective of the word, only this much is obtained: "He is a Perfectly Enlightened One because he has rightly and personally awakened.
However, the phrase "of all phenomena" is stated by taking what is obtained from the perspective of the meaning;

for an act of awakening is not logically possible without an object. "To be directly known" means by means of mundane and supramundane knowledge that is preeminent in its characteristics and so forth, and in its aspects such as impermanence and so forth.

Regarding "the dhammas of the four truths that are to be known": he says that the Noble Truth of Suffering is that which is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*), meaning it is to be known by delimiting it through its aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
"That which is to be abandoned" (*pahātabba*) refers to the Truth of the Origin. "That which is to be realized" (*sacchikātabba*) refers to the Truth of Cessation.
Furthermore, the use of the plural number here is made with reference to the distinctions established by way of synonyms, such as "with remainder" (*sopādisesa*) and so on.

In the verse beginning with "To be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*), by the very inclusion of the causal phenomena—the truths of origin and the path which are to be abandoned and developed—the results thereof, namely the truths of suffering and cessation, are also established as being "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) and "fully understood" (*pariññāta*), and "to be realized" (*sacchikātabba*) and "realized" (*sacchikata*).
Thus, it should be understood that these too are included herein. Therefore, he said: "Therefore..."
“I am a Buddha. Because all four truths have been awakened to by me, therefore I am a Buddha with respect to the entire field of the knowable (*ñeyya*);
the meaning is that I have fully understood them.
He said this because craving, through its occurrence in the form of a longing for various objects, is the primary cause for the diversity of suffering.
“By way of being the root cause”: this refers to both the eye and its origination. “Non-occurrence” means the cause for non-occurrence, not mere non-existence.
Because it possesses states and is conditioned by factors, it includes all its various classifications.

“Understanding of cessation” is the penetration of cessation by way of the clear realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*). “Even by extracting each individual term” refers to the eye.

The intention is that [the classification] is by way of isolating each individual category—beginning with "the origin of the eye"—and not merely by way of their commonality as the truth of suffering and so forth.

Since craving is also to be fully understood because it is included within the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), the phrase "six groups of craving" is stated in order to show its status as the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, regarding the personal existence (*attabhāva*) in which that [craving] arises, [it is shown] by way of being its fundamental cause.
The craving established in previous existences that gives rise [to suffering] should be understood as the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).

"Kasiṇas" refers to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) having the kasiṇas as their object. "The thirty-two aspects" refers to the hair and so forth, as well as the meditative absorptions that have them as objects. "The nine existences" refers to the nine existences:

the three beginning with sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), the three beginning with perception-existence (*saññībhava*), and the three beginning with one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*). "The four meditative absorptions" refers to...
The four jhānas have been described in their general sense without regard for specific objects.
It should be understood that the inclusion of resultant and functional states is appropriate in all instances as the case may be.

Furthermore, in this context, craving should be understood as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for wholesome states, while for functional states, it is the cause of that particular individual existence (*attabhāva*).

Craving (*taṇhā*). Regarding the phrase "in accordance with" (*anulomato*): here, ignorance (*avijjā*) is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), and the preceding craving and taints (*āsava*) that give rise to it should be connected as the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*).

However, in the case of the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth, ignorance and the rest themselves should be connected as being the truth of origin. "Therefore" (*tena*) means for that reason. "True knowledge" (*vijjā*):
it is called true knowledge because it makes its own object known (*vidita*). "Because of being accomplished" (*sampadannattā*): because of being endowed with, or because of being fulfilled.
Or [it may be understood] thus. Therein, in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, regarding "mind-made psychic power" (*manomayiddhi*):

because it is stated here, "In this case, a bhikkhu manifests another body from this body," mind-made psychic power is that which occurs by way of producing another body through the jhāna-mind within the body;
in its actual meaning, it is simply wisdom (*paññā*) associated with jhāna. The seven true qualities (*saddhamma*).
They are: faith, moral shame, moral dread, erudition, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom.
It "goes to the deathless direction" because it proceeds toward the direction of Nibbāna—the deathless—since that must be seen by those seeking to cross over suffering.

Furthermore, this indicates that because these bases of conduct constitute the Noble Path comprised within the Three Trainings, they must be sought with absolute certainty by those who desire Nibbāna.
[The Blessed One] shows this. Now, in order to show that this perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*) is not shared with disciples and others, it was said:
"In that regard, the perfection of true knowledge... and so forth. Therein, omniscience is accomplished by way of the true knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayavijjā*);

and great compassion is accomplished by way of the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*), which is included within the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) that constitute the factors of conduct. Thus he said: "True knowledge... [and so forth]."
"Because of his great compassion. Regarding the phrase "just as" (*yathā*): here, *tanti* is merely a particle;

the meaning is that just as any other Buddha endowed with clear vision and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*) would direct [beings], so too does this one. "By that" means by the avoidance of what is harmful and the directing toward what is beneficial.
"Those who torment themselves, etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), those who torment others and those who torment both are included. "Not clinging to states of existence, not returning" means...
"Because they do not arise again for those who have abandoned them, he does not approach them again.
In this context, the locative case is used because it is to be established by means of speaking appropriate words. "Untrue" (*abhūta*) means having an unreal meaning.

"Not so" (*atacca*) is a synonym for that same term. "Not connected with the good" (*anatthasaṃhita*) means associated with faults such as slander and the like. "Well-spoken" (*sammāgadattā*) is because of its being beautiful speech.

*Gada* means speaking; the meaning is "to speak. Since his speech (*gada*) is beautiful (*sundara*), one should say "Sugada"; however, by applying the rules of phonetic transformation (*niruttinaya*), the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, and thus it is called "Sugata.
"By way of its intrinsic nature" means by way of the nature of suffering (*dukkha*).
"The world" refers to the world of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. He states the aforementioned point by means of a sutta.
"Where," and so forth. Therein, "where" means in that Nibbāna known as the end of the world. "That" refers to the end of the world; the construction is:
"I do not say that it is to be known or reached by bodily movement within the world of space.

This was stated because the devaputta Rohita had asked about reaching the end of the world by way of bodily motion. "Without reaching the end of the world" is said with reference to the world of the aggregates and so forth.

Thinking, "I shall show it to those who travel only through limited places by means of the movement of knowledge, rather than to those who wander through the world of space on foot," he said, "But furthermore," and so forth.
Therein, "in the fathom-long carcass" refers to the body; by that, he shows the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

"In that which is percipient" indicates the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) under the heading of perception (*saññā*). "In this very life" indicates the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*).

“World” (*loka*) means the world of aggregates and so forth; the meaning is “suffering. “Cessation of the world” (*lokanirodha*) refers either to the cessation of the world by means of Nibbāna, or to Nibbāna itself.
For although Nibbāna is not a location, it is the cause for the cessation of those [aggregates], and thus, by way of metaphorical designation, it is as if it were dependent upon them.
Therefore it was said: “I also proclaim the cessation of the world within this fathom-long carcass,” and: “The eye in the world...”
[This is] like [in the passages] beginning with: "In regard to what is agreeable in form, what is pleasant in form, it is here that this craving ceasing ceases.

*Kudācanaṃ* means "even at any time. *Appattvā* means "without having attained" by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). *Tasmā* means "because," because it is not possible to attain that by going; therefore.
*Hava* is merely a particle, or it has the sense of emphasis (*ekamsatthe*). *Lokavidū* means one who knows the aggregates and so forth according to their true nature and other aspects.

He is "one who has attained peace" (*samitāvī*) because he has realized the Dhamma of the Four Truths; or the meaning is that his defilements have been stilled. He "does not long for" or "does not crave," because he is free from rebirth-linking.
Having thus shown the world in brief, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, there are three worlds" was spoken in order to show it in detail.
Therein, the "world of beings" (*sattaloka*) is the collection and continuity of the aggregates bound by the sense-faculties. For that [world] consists of form and so forth...

It is called a "being" (*satta*) because it is bound by the fetters; and it is called the "world" (*loka*) because kamma, defilements, and their results are "found" (*lokiyanti*) therein. The world of space is a collection and continuity of temperature-born matter not bound to the faculties.
For that is called "space" (*okāsa*) because it is the support for beings and formations, and it is called the "world" (*loka*) because beings and their supports—the supported—are found therein.

Furthermore, all the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), whether bound by faculties (indriya) or non-faculties, are called the "world of formations" (saṅkhāraloka) in the sense of being conditioned by causes and in the sense of breaking down and falling apart.
That which brings its own fruit is "nutriment" (āhāra); it is a condition.

Those things whose nature is to persist by means of that [nutriment], having arisen until their dissolution, and whose nature is to proceed, are "sustained by nutriment" (āhāraṭṭhitika); these are all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhatadhamma). All...

By the word "beings" (*satta*) as well, it is the formative forces (*saṅkhārā*) themselves that are grasped, because the teaching is based on individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) according to the needs of those to be trained.
"As far as the moon and sun revolve" means as far as the place where the moon and sun turn and move about.
"Because of their shining" (*virocana*)—that is, because of their radiance or illumination—is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). "The quarters of space are pervaded."
All directions, as far as they extend, are perceived free from darkness. Alternatively, *disā* is the plural form of the accusative case. Therefore, the meaning is:
"as many directions as shine and illuminate by means of the radiant moon and sun.

"A world-system of a thousandfold" (*sahassadhā loka*) means a spatial world of that same measure consisting of a thousandfold variety; the meaning is "a thousand world-spheres" (*sahassacakkavāḷāni*). "In this" (*ettha*)...
"In a thousandfold world-system. "Power" (*vasa*) means that power, which is reckoned as psychic potency (*iddhi*), operates; this is the meaning.
"That too" refers to the threefold world. "By him" connects to the Blessed One, meaning that by this Blessed One even the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*) is known in every respect.
"One world" refers to this [world] which, according to the method stated below, exists in dependence upon conditions for all conditioned things.
By that commonality, the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*) is one and of a single kind; this same method applies to the others as well.

In all cases, only mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhammā*) are intended by the term "world" (*loka*), because supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara*) lack the quality of being fully understood (*pariññeyyatā*). The aggregates that have become objects of clinging are the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*).
The seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) refer specifically to beings born in such-and-such ways.
Those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; those with diverse bodies and unified perceptions; those with unified bodies and diverse perceptions;

those with unified bodies and unified perceptions; and the three lower formless realms—these seven classes of beings are called "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) because consciousness stands there.
In this context, they are called "those with diverse bodies" because diversity of body exists in them.

"Those who have diversity of perception" means those for whom there is diversity of perception. Here, rebirth-linking consciousness is included by way of its perception; this same method applies to the others as well.
Among these, all human beings and the six classes of sense-sphere devas are called "diverse in body and diverse in perception.
For their bodies are diverse due to their mutual dissimilarity, and their rebirth-linking perceptions are diverse due to their ninefold variety. Regarding the three planes of the first jhāna:
The beings of the Brahmakāyika realm and those in the four woeful states (apāya) are called "those with diverse bodies and a single perception.

For among them, although the bodies of all three—the Brahmā’s Retinue (Brahmapārisajja) and the others—are mutually dissimilar, their rebirth-linking perception is one and the same, being the result of the first jhāna;
likewise for those in the woeful states, though for all of them it is exclusively the result of unwholesome, rootless (ahetuka) kamma.

The rebirth-perception (*paṭisandhisaññā*). Those belonging to the plane of the second jhāna are the Limited Radiance (*parittābha*), Immeasurable Radiance (*appamāṇābha*), and Streaming Radiance (*ābhassara*) gods, who are called "unified in body but diverse in perception.
For all of them, the body is of one and the same measure, but their rebirth-perception is diverse due to the fruition of the second and third jhānas.

On the plane of the third jhāna there are three classes beginning with the Limited Beauty (*parittasubha*); on the plane of the fourth jhāna there are [the remaining classes], excluding the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*).
In the nine planes—the Vehapphala realm and the five Suddhāvāsa realms—beings are said to have "unity of body and unity of perception.
However, because there is no diversity of light, diversity of body is not apprehended anywhere; it is apprehended only through diversity of shape.
Non-percipient beings do not enter into the reckoning of stations of consciousness due to the absence of consciousness. [The station of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception...

However, just as with perception, because consciousness is also subtle, it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; therefore, it is not included among the stations of consciousness that possess the manifest functions of consciousness.
Consequently, only the remaining three—the base of infinite space and so forth—are taken up.
Together with those, these seven should be understood as the stations of consciousness.
The eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhammā*) are gain, loss, fame, infamy, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain;

these are called "worldly conditions" because they are the inherent nature of the world. Furthermore, it should be understood that the attachment and aversion arising from the conditions of gain, loss, and so forth, are expressed here by the very terms "gain" and so on.
The nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsā*) are the seven stations of consciousness mentioned above.

Thus, together with the four immaterial realms (ārūpa) having non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) as the fourth, they are called the "nine abodes of beings" (sattāvāsa). They are called "abodes of beings" because beings dwell therein;

that is, the category of beings. In terms of meaning, it should be understood that here it is precisely the generation proceeding in such a manner that is taken as the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka).
"Ten bases" (dasāyatana) refers to the ten [bases] excluding the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the base of the mind (manāyatana).
And here, among the three realms of existence (bhava), the three feelings alone are spoken of as the "world-state" by way of seeing gratification;
likewise, the four nutriments (āhāra) are so stated by way of seeing conditions. By way of seeing the signs for grasping at a self, the six internal bases (āyatana) alone are so stated.
By way of seeing the state of being one who perceives grossness, the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) alone are so stated; and by way of seeing attachment and aversion...

Alternatively, the eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhammā*) are included; indeed, by way of showing the gross bases (*thūlāyatana*), the ten bases themselves are stated as being of the nature of the world.

By the inclusion of these, all name-and-form phenomena (*nāmarūpa-dhammā*) belonging to the three planes—which are dependent upon them, bound to them, and have them as their object—are included by their very meaning.
It should be understood, however, that the remaining categories, beginning with the singlefold, are included in their own specific forms.
Regarding the passage beginning with "He knows the disposition" (*āsaya*): that wherein the mind lies down is the "disposition" (*āsaya*).
Although the mind may operate upon other objects, that wherein it enters and remains by its own inherent tendency is the disposition; this is twofold:

the disposition toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭāsayo*) and the disposition toward the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭāsayo*). Therein, the disposition toward the round is also twofold, by way of the views of eternalism and annihilationism. However, the disposition toward the cessation of the round is that which is termed insight (*vipassanā*).
It is twofold: conformable patience and knowledge of things as they really are, which is termed the path. As it is said:
"The views of eternalism and annihilationism, conformable patience, and that knowledge which is of the nature of things as they really are—this is what is called 'inclination'."
The Blessed One knows both of these dispositions (*āsaya*) of beings in every respect at the very moment they do not arise.

"Latent tendencies" (*anusaya*) refers to the sevenfold latent tendencies, such as the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). "Conduct" (*carita*) is what is stated in the *Niddesa* as "good conduct and bad conduct.
Alternatively, "conduct" means "disposition" (*cariyā*); these are the six root dispositions, beginning with lust, according to their association (*saṃsagga*) and combination (*sannipāta*).
They are of many kinds. *Adhimutti* means the element of inclination; it is the state of being bent toward this or that according to the mind’s liking. That is twofold:
inferior inclination (*hīnādhimutti*) and sublime inclination (*paṇītādhimutti*). That by which one associates with those of inferior inclination, such as the immoral, is inferior inclination.
That by which one associates with those of sublime inclination is sublime inclination. Both of these [types]...
The Blessed One knows their disposition in every aspect. Those who have little dust of passion and so forth are "few-dusted" (*apparajakkhā*), meaning they possess no excessive faults such as lust.
Those with excessive faults such as lust are "greatly dusty" (*mahārajakkhā*).

Those endowed with the faculties of faith and so forth—whether sharp or dull, acting as decisive supports—are "of keen faculties" (*tikkhindriyā*) and "of dull faculties" (*mudindriyā*). [He knows them] by means of the beautiful or unbeautiful dispositions and so forth mentioned above.

They should be understood as being endowed with good qualities and bad qualities; they are easy to instruct and easy to understand when they are fixed in the rightness of the path, but difficult to instruct when they are perverted.
Those who possess the necessary supporting conditions for the penetration of the paths and fruits are capable, while those who lack them are incapable.
Thus, by knowing the specific qualities within the mental continuum of beings, the world of beings is also known, [for there is no being] apart from the Dhamma.
It should be understood as "the absence of a being.
Regarding the phrase "one world-system... fifty yojanas," the word "is" (*hoti*) is to be supplied. "The measurement by circumference is stated"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"The entire circumference of the world-system is three million six hundred thousand... hundreds [of yojanas]."
And it should be connected with the words "and they exist. "Therein" means in the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The interpretation is that this earth, known as *vasundharā*, is reckoned to have a thickness of two hundred thousand and forty million (*nahuta*) *yojanas*; such is its extent.
In this context, "such" (*ettakaṃ*) should be understood as an adverbial modifier of the action. The supporting water is also of such an extent, of such a measure.
The construction is: "having offered [the sacrifice], it was established. "Therein" means in the Cakkavāḷa (world-system). "Plunged deep and risen up" means both deeply submerged and elevated.
"Vast" means great. "The Himavat is five hundred yojanas high" means its height or elevation is five hundred yojanas.
"With trunks and circumference of three to five yojanas" means the measurement of the girth of their trunks is fifteen yojanas.
“Nagavhayā” means “Jambū,” which is a designation for a tree; this is the construction [of the compound].

“On all sides” means by way of its complete beauty; the meaning is that it is one hundred *yojanas* in extent both in length and in breadth. “By whose power” means by whose majesty, in the form of its greatness, its endurance for an eon (*kappa*), and so forth.
“Having encompassed all of that, it stands as consisting of the world-system”—this refers to everything mentioned below.

The mountain range of the world-sphere (*cakkavāḷasiluccaya*) stands surrounding that; the meaning is that "this is what is called a single world-system" (*ekā lokadhātu*), where the letter *m* is used for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
Alternatively, it should be construed thus: "This mountain range of the world-sphere stands surrounding all that world-system. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that world-system.
"The abode of the Thirty-three" (*tāvatiṃsabhavana*) is the city of the Thirty-three (*tidasapura*). "The abode of the asuras" (*asurabhavana*) is the city of the asuras (*asurapura*).
The Great Niraya of Avīci is likewise ten thousand *yojanas* in extent;

however, it should be understood that although it measures one hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth between its four walls of iron, it is said to be ten thousand *yojanas* when including the sixteen surrounding *ussada-nirayas*.
"In the intervals between those" means in the spaces between those world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). Of worlds—that is, of world-systems.
The intermediate spaces that exist between them are the "world-intervals" (*lokantarikā*).

Indeed, in the intervals between each of the three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), which are like the space between three cart wheels or three footprints placed close together, there arises—due to the unwholesome karmic ripening of sentient beings—an individual cold hell called a "world-interval hell," measuring eight thousand *yojanas*.
"Infinite" means [extending] horizontally in the eight directions.
The world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) are infinite like space; however, there are indeed limits above and below.

Regarding the phrase "by the infinite Buddha-knowledge," it should be understood that knowledge is called "infinite" precisely because of its association with the capacity to penetrate an infinite range of knowable objects (*ñeyya*).
"Of himself" (*attanō*) is a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "from himself. [It refers to] one who is more distinguished than himself by his qualities.

The connection here, and the inclusion of the word "tarat" (crossing over), is made by way of explaining the meaning of the term "anuttara" (unsurpassed), not because of the existence of anyone who is distinguished [in that regard].
For in the world with its devas, there is no one even equal to the Tathāgata, much less his equal;
therefore he said, "unequal even in the quality of virtue," and so forth. In that context, "equal to the peerless Fully Enlightened Ones" means...
"Unequaled" (asamasama). "Without a counterpart" (appaṭima) means there is no match for him. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

In this context, a "counterpart" (paṭimā) is a mere comparison; a "counter-part" (paṭibhāga) is a similar comparison. A "counter-person" (paṭima-puggala) should be understood as one who stands in a state of rivalry.

"By himself" (attanā) means from himself. In phrases such as "persons to be tamed" (purisadamma), those who are to be tamed are "dammā"; although one should say "tameable persons" (dammapurisā), [the word order is inverted] because of the qualifier.
Having placed the word at the end [of the compound], it is said “tameable persons” (*purisadamma*);
and here, the inclusion of the term “persons” is by way of excellence, since women too are to be tamed. “Made free from craving” means made free through the removal of the poison of hatred.

“Meaningful word” (*atthapada*) means a word that makes the meaning manifest; this is the sense of the term *vākya*. And by virtue of being a single word, the Teacher’s status as the charioteer of tameable persons is unique, not shared by others.
It has been demonstrated; therefore, the Blessed One said "hi" and so forth. "The eight directions" refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Unattached" means moving without attachment due to having attained mastery.

"Visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to one's own manifest personal existence; that which is connected to this is "pertaining to visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhammika*), meaning the welfare of this world.
*Samparāya* means that which is to be reached or encountered through the influence of kamma and defilements; it refers to the world beyond (*paraloka*).

That which pertains to this is *samparāyika*, meaning for the sake of the world beyond. *Paramattha* means the supreme or highest goal, which is Nibbāna. *Sattha* means that which exists together with a purpose;
it refers to a multitude of people traveling to another region for trade with merchandise as capital. This [is] his...

“Teacher” (*satthā*) means one who leads; according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), he is like a caravan leader (*satthavāha*). Thus it is said: “The Teacher, the Blessed One, is the caravan leader.
Now, in order to demonstrate this meaning by way of the explanatory text (*niddesapāḷi*), the passage beginning with “Just as a caravan leader” was spoken.
In that context, “caravan” (*sattha*) refers to a group of merchants. A “wilderness” (*kantāra*) is a waterless region of the forest where they cross over water.
Even forest regions inhabited by robbers and the like are designated as "deserts" (*kantāra*) precisely because they are similar to them in the sense of being difficult to traverse.
Having stated this in general terms as "he crosses a desert," he explains it specifically by saying "a desert of robbers," and so forth.

In the phrase "from the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One. As in the expression "from the preceptor" (*upajjhāyato*).

"He consumed [it]" means, in the presence of the Blessed One. "He grasped the sign in the sound" means that through his familiarity with hearing the True Dhamma during the appearances of previous Buddhas, he grasped the form [of the word] in the sound, thinking, "This is what is called 'Dhamma'.
For it is precisely through former application that such animals as bats and others develop confidence in hearing the Dhamma and so forth.
Otherwise, it would follow that even all animals could likewise produce such faith.

For if it were to arise [in them], since the Blessed One is capable of proclaiming the Dhamma with its miracles to all beings simultaneously across infinite world-systems, it would follow that all beings had already attained liberation prior to this [event]. As for those gods, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth—

It should be understood that those who, by their very nature, possess knowledge of the ownership of kamma and so forth, are alone capable—despite lacking prior decisive support (*upanissaya*)—of first generating the confidence that serves as the decisive support for turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya-pasāda*) through hearing the Blessed One’s true Dhamma and other means; others are not. Regarding the phrase "Am I indeed one of those?":
here, [the thought] arises, "Having looked back, 'From where was I reborn here? [one realizes], 'From the state of a frog.'"
Regarding the word “knowing”: this much is already established by the expression of astonishment, “O, even I am such a one!”, and thus it should be understood that it is not explicitly stated.
“Shining” means blazing and radiating light. In the verse beginning with “A frog...”, the phrase “in the water” indicates the place where he was born;
by this, the possibility of being a land-frog is excluded. Furthermore, although turtles and others are born in the water, they may also have their range on land.

The phrase "one who ranges in water" (*vārigocaro*) is stated in order to exclude [the possibility that he might be] "one who exists" (*atthi*); the meaning is "one who moves in water. Regarding the expression "by way of knowledge pertaining to the end of liberation" (*vimokkhantikañāṇavasena*):
here, "liberation" (*vimokkho*) is that by which one is completely liberated from defilements;

it is the supreme path (*aggamaggo*). "The end of that" (*tassa anto*) is the fruit of the summit (*aggaphalaṃ*). That which exists therein is "pertaining to the end of liberation" (*vimokkhantikaṃ*). This includes everything together with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

"Buddha-knowledge. Now, in order to show the distinction between the term "Buddha" (*buddha-pada*) and the term "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddha-pada*), the passage beginning with "Because...

was stated. For by the term *sammāsambuddha*, the power of the Teacher’s knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is expressed; however, by this term *buddha*, the power of his knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*) is also included.
Therefore, he said: "He awakened other beings as well," and so forth.

"Guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanaṃ" means that this term "Bhagavā" is a designation spoken out of reverence for one who is distinguished by all qualities such as virtue (sīla) and is therefore the highest and most venerable among all beings.
"Seṭṭhaṃ" refers to a word expressing excellence, because it is accompanied by excellent qualities. Alternatively, "vacanaṃ" means that which is expressed; it refers to the meaning.
"Best" (*seṭṭha*) is the meaning. "Supreme" (*uttama*): here too, the method is the same. Regarding "one who is fit for weight and reverence" (*garugāravayutta*):
here, "weight" (*garu*) is reverence (*gārava*). Or, reverence is the act of honoring because of his connection with weighty qualities.

Thus, he is "fit for weight and reverence" because he is endowed with great and weighty reverence that is not shared by disciples and others. Alternatively, he is "weighty" (*garu*) because he is the teacher of the entire world.
The phrase "also associated with that very respect" (*teneva gāravayutto cāpi*) should likewise be applied.

That which is known by way of its state is "pertaining to the state" (*āvatthika*). Likewise for the "pertaining to the characteristic" (*liṅgika*). That which has come from a sign is "pertaining to a sign" (*nemittika*).
That which occurs by chance, without regard for any sign through the influence of a designation, is "fortuitously arisen" (*adhiccasamuppanna*); thus he said.
“Without regard for the meaning of the words”: this refers to that which has come about by whim, or whatever is desired.

Herein, it should be understood that an external mark (*liṅga*) is such as a staff and so forth, while an internal sign (*nimitta*) is such as the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) and so forth. Alternatively, a mark is that which is visible to ordinary people, whereas a sign is its opposite.
“Description by way of realization” (*sacchikāpaññatti*) is a description based on the cause of the realization of all phenomena.

Alternatively, "manifest designation" (*sacchikāpaññatti*) means a designation established through direct perception. For whatever qualities are the cause for that [designation], those qualities have become directly perceived by the Teacher;
thus, like those qualities, it too is indeed called "manifested. The intention is that it is not merely a conventional expression (*vohāramatta*) for others.
"That which is caused by such qualities" means that this name is caused (*nemittika*) by those qualities which serve as its cause (*nimitta*).

"Jātaṃ. He says "they say" (*vadanti*) using the plural number out of respect for the General of the Dhamma (*dhammasenāpati*), or with reference to the restatement made by the compilers of the Council (*saṅgītikāra*).

One who possesses fortune (*bhaga*)—which is distinguished by sovereignty and so forth—is "the Fortunate One" (*bhagī*). One who, by habit, frequents (*bhaji*) or cultivates the noble qualities such as the paths and fruits, as well as secluded places such as forests, is "the Frequenter" (*bhajī*).
One who possesses a share (*bhāgī*) in the requisites such as robes, in the essence of the meaning and so forth, and in the qualities of virtue and so on, is [the Fortunate One].

The meaning is "heir. He is called *vibhattavā* because he has analyzed—that is, he has analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma through various modes such as enumeration (*uddesa*) and detailed exposition (*niddesa*).
He is called *bhagavā* because he has broken (*bhagga*) evil states such as lust; this construction applies throughout.

He says "the venerable ones" (*garū*), for even in the world those who are venerable are called *bhagavā*; thus, the meaning is that because he is venerable, he is therefore *bhagavā*. [He is also so called] because of what is reckoned as the perfections (*pāramitā*).

One who possesses fortune (*bhagya*) is "fortunate" (*bhagyavā*). "By many methods" means by numerous stages of cultivation (*bhāvanā-krama*), such as the cultivation of the body (*kāya-bhāvanā*) and so forth.
"Of one whose self is well-cultivated" (*subhāvitattano*): this is a genitive case used in the sense of identity; thus, the meaning is "one whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is well-cultivated.

One who has gone to the end of existence (*bhava*), which is Nibbāna, is "one who has reached the end of becoming" (*bhavantago*). In each of these instances, the derivation of the word *Bhagavā* should be understood according to the method of etymological analysis (*niruttinaya*).

Now, in order to show the word-derivation (*padasiddhi*) together with the distinctions in the methods of connecting the meaning, by summarizing the meaning demonstrated by the nine phrases of the explanatory verse (*niddesagāthā*)—namely, "Idāni bhagī bhajī"—into the six phrases of the verse beginning with "Bhagyavā," it is said:

"But this is another method," and so forth. In that context, regarding the phrase "change of phonemes" (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*), the word "iti" has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*); for that very reason...
It comprises these three types of characteristics: modification of a syllable, elision of a syllable, and application according to the meaning of the verbal root.
"By the method of grammar" means by the method of grammatical rules (*saddalakkhaṇa*). Because words such as *piśodara* belong to the class of "formative groups" (*ākatigaṇa*), it is said:
"having taken the characteristic for inclusion in the *piśodara*-class and so forth. The very act of including is the characteristic; for it is the making of something included within that [class].
Inclusion. "Bhagga" means wholesome (*kusala*).
The four faults, beginning with greed (*lobha*), are taken as single units. Those beginning with shamelessness (*ahirika*) are taken as pairs.

"Upanāha" is simply anger (*kodha*) that obstructs the mind by way of repeated resentment, expressed through such phrases as "I have reviled him. It has the characteristic of [obstructing] the recognition of past favors rendered by others.
Sycophancy (*makkha*) is the rubbing away of another’s virtues. Flattery (*palāsa*) is the grasping of equality with those who are learned and so forth, thereby making oneself their equal.
Deceit (*māyā*) is the concealing of one’s existing faults. Crookedness (*sāṭheyya*) is the proclaiming of non-existent virtues.
Stubbornness (*thambha*) is rigidity and lack of deference even toward teachers. Aggression (*sārambha*) is characterized by the impulse to do something even more than that. Birth and so forth...

Conceit (*māna*) has the characteristic of loftiness based on [birth, etc.]. Excessive conceit (*atimāna*) has the characteristic of haughtiness. Pride (*mada*) is simply conceit that has reached the mode of intoxication based on birth and so forth;
it is twenty-sevenfold. Heedlessness (*pamāda*) is the mind’s relinquishment toward the strands of sensual pleasure. The three kinds of misconduct are bodily misconduct and so forth.
The three kinds of corruption are through the corruption of craving, views, and misconduct. The stains are greed, hatred, and delusion.

Those same three types of misconduct, such as bodily misconduct and so forth, are the threefold unwholesome states. The perceptions of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty are called the threefold perceptions.

Those same [perceptions] are the thoughts (vitakkas). Craving, views, and conceit are the proliferations (papañcas). The inversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self are the fourfold inversions. Desire and so forth are the wrong courses (agatis).
Greed for the requisites such as robes and so on are the four types of craving-clinging (taṇhūpādāna). [Regarding] the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training...
Doubt, and anger toward fellow practitioners of the holy life—these are the five heart-fetters (*cetokhila*). Lack of dispassion regarding sensual pleasures, the body, and forms;

indulging in the pleasure of sleep and so forth after eating as much as one desires; and practicing the holy life with the aspiration for some class of deities—these are the five bondages of the mind (*cetanāvinibandha*).

The five kinds of delight (*abhinandanā*) consist of delighting in forms and so forth. Anger, spite, insolence, craftiness, desire for gain, and adherence to one's own views—these are the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

The six roots of dispute; the six groups of craving beginning with craving for form; the eight types of wrongness beginning with wrong view, which are the opposites of the factors of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Dependent on craving comes seeking; dependent on seeking comes gain; dependent on gain comes decision-making;
dependent on that comes desire-and-lust; dependent on that comes attachment; dependent on that comes possessiveness; dependent on that...
Avarice, the guarding based upon it, and the multitude of various unwholesome states beginning with the taking up of the rod caused by such guarding—these are the nine phenomena rooted in craving.
There are the ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with the destruction of life.

There are the four eternalist views, likewise the partial-eternalist views, the views concerning the finite and infinite, the eel-wrigglers, the two views of fortuitous origination, and the sixteen [views].

The sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) consist of: eight theories of perception (*saññīvāda*), eight theories of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*), seven theories of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*), five theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and five theories of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).

The six types of craving—craving for form and so forth—become eighteen each when divided into craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
These become thirty-six according to their occurrence with respect to internal and external forms and other objects, and further, by way of the three periods of time.

There are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering. By connecting the word “division” (*pabheda*) with each term individually, it should be applied as "the divisions of greed," and so forth.

"All the hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause distress and fever" means all the many hundreds of thousands of defilements that produce the distress known as fever for sentient beings, according to their classification by object and their classification by mode of occurrence.
The analysis should be understood in this way. The connection is: "He shattered the five Māras. Regarding "of perils" (*parissayānaṃ*), it means of calamities.

Having thus analyzed the meaning of the two words "fortunate" (*bhagyavā*) and "one who has shattered" (*bhaggavā*), he now states "And because of his fortunateness," etc., in order to show the meaning conveyed by those two.
In that context, [the phrase] "of one who bears the marks born of a hundred merits" (*satapuññajalakkhaṇadharassa*)...
[This refers to] the Blessed One, who bears the marks of a Great Man produced by many hundreds of merits.

"Sovereignty over one’s own mind" means precisely the attainment of mastery over one’s own mind through the application of the perception of the non-repulsive toward things that are repulsive and so forth, as well as by way of mental concentration (*cetosamādhi*).
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "the powers such as *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, etc.," [the following are included]: *mahimā*, *patti*, and *pākamma*.
These six are also included: lordship (*īsitā*), mastery (*vasitā*), and the ability to resolve according to one’s wish (*yatthakāmāvasāyitā*).
Among these: *aṇimā* is the making of the body minute; *laghimā* is lightness by virtue of being capable of traveling through space on foot and so forth;

*mahimā* is the production of greatness in the body; *patti* is the reaching of a desired place; and *pākamma* is the accomplishment of a desired object through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and other means.
*Vasitā* (mastery) is the state of being a lord, the quality of sovereignty (*issarabhāva*). It is mastery (*vasībhāva*) over the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).

It is the attainment of confidence (*vosānappatti*) wherever one goes—whether traveling through the air or performing some other act—and the ability to settle according to one’s desire (*yatthakāmāvasāyitā*).
Some also say it refers to "the manifestation of forms such as a youth. *Sabbangapaccaṅgasirī* is the beauty of all the major and minor limbs. The word *atthi* follows [as a copula].

The *lahusādhana* (easy method of derivation) is intended for the respective [temporary] periods, while the *garusādhana* (difficult method of derivation) pertains to the long term and is intended for the attainment of Buddhahood and so forth.

That he "possesses the *bhagas*" is thus *bhagavā*; this is established according to the rules of grammar (*saddasatthanaya*), whereas all the remainder should be understood as established according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*).

In the expressions "in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, tormenting, and changeability," and so forth, the word *attha* (meaning) should be applied to each term individually as "the meaning of oppression" (*pīḷanaṭṭha*), "the meaning of being conditioned" (*saṅkhataṭṭha*), and so on.
Therein, suffering has the characteristic of oppressing by its own intrinsic nature;
that which is the very fact of oppressing—the "meaning of oppression"—is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Furthermore, because it is conditioned by its origination, therefore...

The meaning of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) is manifested through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*). And because the Path (*magga*) is very cool since it removes the burning of the defilements, therefore its meaning of "coolness" is manifested through the vision of the Path, owing to its being the opposite of that [burning].

Furthermore, the meaning of "change" (*vipariṇāma*) is manifested through the vision of Cessation (*nirodha*), which is by nature unchanging. [This is] from the perspective of the intrinsic nature of a single dharma possessing its own individual essence.
Because they must be conceptually distinguished from the other three truths, four meanings are stated.

However, for the truth of the origin (*samudaya*), its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is the meaning of accumulation (*āyūhana*), due to its function of heaping things together. By seeing that very same [truth] as suffering, its meaning as a source (*nidāna*) is revealed.

By seeing cessation (*nirodha*), which is disjunction (*visaṃyoga*), its meaning as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is revealed. By seeing the path (*magga*), which is the outlet (*niyyāna*), its meaning as an impediment (*palibodha*) is revealed.
Furthermore, the essential nature (*sabhāva*) of cessation (*nirodha*) is the sense of escape; its sense of seclusion is manifested by the vision of its origin (*samudaya*).

Through the vision of the conditioned path, it has the sense of the unconditioned; or, through the vision of suffering—the state of being subject to death which constitutes its objective domain—it has the sense of the deathless (*amata*).
The essential nature of the path (*magga*), however, is the sense of outlet (*niyyāna*); its [sense of] seclusion is manifested by the vision of its origin.
The sense of cause (*hetvattha*) is that this [suffering] alone is the cause of suffering, while this very same thing is the cause for attaining Nibbāna.

The sense of seeing (*dassanattha*) is that by showing the extremely subtle cessation, it is precisely here that seeing occurs. The sense of the pre-eminent (*adhipateyyattha*) is manifested through the seeing of the pre-eminent suffering.
These very factors, beginning with oppression (*pīḷanā*), are called the sixteen aspects (*soḷasa ākārā*).

Physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is the state of having the body withdrawn from sensual pleasures (*kāmehi*). Mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) that are secluded from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth.

Seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*) is called *nibbāna*, which is secluded from those four types of acquisitions (*upadhi*); for "acquisitions" are so called because fruits are acquired therein—namely, the aggregate of sensual pleasure consisting of the five strands of sense-pleasure, the defilements (*kilesa*), and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).

The Noble Path—attained through the contemplation of non-self (anattā) and attained through the contemplations of suffering (dukkha) and impermanence (anicca)—attains, in due order according to its approach, the designations of the void (suññata), the desireless (appaṇihita), and the signless (animitta) liberations. For it is called "liberation" because it is liberated from the defilements (kilesa).
The meaning is that just as in the world one might take a single syllable from each word and say "mekhalā," so it is here as well. "Mehana" refers to the private parts; "kha" refers to the opening.
Regarding the phrase "together with the devas" (*saha devehi*) and so forth: it is called the world "with devas" (*sadevako loko*) because it exists together with the devas.

The construction should be understood as "that which is with devas" (*taṃ sadevakaṃ*), and so on. By the expression "with devas" (*sadevakavacanena*), it is meant by the word "devas" standing as a qualifier for the term "with devas.
Since that [word "devas"] is also included within the compound word "with devas," this usage is made by applying the designation of the whole to its constituent part. Otherwise, by that...
Because of the inclusion of the world specifically distinguished as "devas," there would be no inclusion of the deities of the five sense-sphere realms; the same applies to what follows.

By the term *samāraka* (together with Māra), all the deities of the Controlling Power (*vasavatti*) who are associated with that word "Māra" are included; thus he says, "the inclusion of the deities of the sixth sense-sphere realm.
Those called *brahmakāyika* (of the Brahma-body) belong to the plane of the first jhāna. They are the beginning...
The inclusion of those Brahmās whose limit is the formless realm (ārūppapariyanta) constitutes the inclusion of the Brahmās of the Brahmakāyika and other such classes.
Because the word *loka* is common to the world as space and so forth, the inclusion of the "world of beings" (*sattaloka*) alone was made by means of the term "generation" (*pajā*);

thus he said, "by the word 'generation,' there is the inclusion of the world of beings. By the expression "together with devas," the devas of rebirth are included; by the expression "together with recluses"...

Because the pure deities (*visuddhideva*) have already been included, it is said: "By the expression 'together with gods and humans' (*sadevamanussa*), there is the inclusion of conventional deities (*sammutideva*) and the remaining humans.
In this context, "conventional deities" refers to kings; "the remaining humans" refers to those left over from the category of conventional deities, namely recluses and brahmins.

Since the word *pajā* (people) is used as a term exclusive to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), the inclusion of the word *loka* (world) in the phrase "the world together with its gods" (*sadevakaṃ lokaṃ*) serves to include the physical world (*okāsaloka*).
It is said that "the world of space is determined by three terms" because it restricts [the scope] to the world of space alone.
This is stated with reference to the primary meaning expressed by the triad of terms beginning with "together with the devas.

However, it should be understood that the qualification "world of space" here also includes the world of sentient beings, such as devas and Māras, because they are implied by the force of the context, just as in expressions such as "he has come with his son," where the son and others are included.

And in this method, the word "and" (*ca*) should be supplied and connected as follows: "this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and the generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.

Here, by the inclusion of the world of space and the world of beings, it should be understood that the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), which serves as the sign for the conventional designation of both those worlds, is also included because it is inseparable from them. Others, however, [interpret] "with its devas," etc.,...
They say: "By means of five terms, the world of beings (*sattaloka*) itself is grasped by way of its specific constituents, such as the devas;

by grasping that, the world of space (*okāsaloka*), which is the support for those beings, and the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), which is the objective domain of the designation for both, are also necessarily included.
And having applied this as a qualification of the word "world" (*loka*), they say: "the generation together with its devas (*sadevakaṃ pajaṃ*)."
The world... [and so on]... together with its devas and humans, its generation—this is how it should be construed.
The immaterial-sphere world (arūpāvacaraloka) is included by way of elimination (pārisesanayena), since the others have already been included by the intervening terms.
By the mention of "Māra," the gods of rebirth who are dominated by him and resemble him are also comprised; thus he says, "the sixfold sense-sphere deva-world."
Regarding these eight assemblies— the assembly of khattiyas, brahmins, householders, ascetics, the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa gods, Māra, and the Brahmās—
since the four assemblies beginning with those of the Four Great Kings are included by the terms "together with the devas" and so forth,
they are here covered by the phrase "together with ascetics and brahmins"; and by the phrase "together with devas and humans," [the remaining four are included].
Since the assembly of kṣatriyas and the assembly of householders have been mentioned by this [term], he said, "by way of the four assemblies.

This is connected with the phrase, "the human world (manussaloka) is included therein. In that context, "human world" means a collection of humans; therefore he said, "or else, the world of all remaining beings.
Showing another alternative, he said, "or the human world together with conventional deities (sammutideva). By the word "deities," conventional deities are meant.

Since the remaining humans are included by the terms *samaṇa*, *brāhmaṇa*, and *manussa*, even in these two alternative interpretations, one qualifies the word *pajā* (progeny) with the word *manussa*—referring to human beings—as "human progeny," and that [progeny] is further described as being together with the gods; thus it is "together with the gods" (*sadevā*).
Being both "together with the gods" and "humans," it is "together with gods and humans" (*sadevamanussā*); that is "together with gods and humans. (*taṃ sadevamanussaṃ*)

"Beings. Furthermore, as for the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins," the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) should be made in such a way that the word "beings" (*pajā*) refers exclusively to human beings;
otherwise, the reference would not be restricted to humans alone, because [the phrase] would include some other category of being as a qualifier for all human beings.
[The phrase] "the non-existence" [is used]. Now, desiring to show that this includes the remaining beings such as nāgas and so forth, he says:

"or the entire world of all remaining beings. Here too, it should be construed either as "the entire world of all remaining beings by way of the four assemblies," or as "the entire world of all remaining beings together with conventional gods and humans."
Having thus far shown a *yojana* by taking the world part by part, he now says "And here too," and so forth,
in order to show the fruitfulness of each respective qualification even in the alternative of grasping the entire world without dividing it into parts.
"By way of the highest limit" means by way of knowing [the world] through the delimitation of those included in the celestial realms (*devagati*), which constitute the highest limit.

The construction is as follows: the sound of fame (*kittisaddo*), having arisen, makes itself heard by those listening through the word "together with the devas" (*sadevaka*), which is a constituent part of itself.
"Order of connection" (*anusandhikkamo*) means the sequence of connecting both meanings and words; its sense is "the order of knowing.

Regarding "by direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*), he says "by direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya*) because it is a designation [of *abhiññā*] with the elision of the letter *ya*. "By way of being all-auspicious" (*samantabhadrakattā*) means by way of all aspects.
Because of its beauty. "The Dhamma of the Dispensation" refers to the textual Dhamma (*pariyatti-dhamma*) that elucidates the Dispensation of practice and realization (*paṭipatti-paṭivedha-sāsana*).

"Because it was well-awakened by the Buddha"—this triad is stated with respect to the cause, the nature, and the fruit of the Dhamma; likewise for the triad concerning its origin from the Protector (*nātha*).
It should be understood that the two middle triads are stated solely with respect to the fruit. "Because of the purity of duty": having heard the Dhamma...
This is for the sake of the purity of purpose known as "right practice" for those who act according to what they have heard.

Now, while teaching the Dhamma that is excellent in its beginning and so forth, the Blessed One elucidates the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—both the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path.
Regarding the term *brahmacariya* used to elucidate that, [the Blessed One teaches] the phrases "it has meaning," and so forth.

The words have been stated as qualifiers, not as [qualifiers] of the "Dhamma-word" (*dhammapada*). Desiring to explain the meaning in its various aspects by way of this perspective, he said, "But in such cases as 'with meaning' (*sāttha*) and 'with phrasing' (*sabyañjana*)," and so forth.
Therein, the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*) and the entire body of the doctrine (*tantidhamma*) are called the "holy life of the Dispensation" (*sāsanabrahmacariya*).
For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, [he does so] just as he does with regard to virtue (*sīla*) and the rest...
It also reveals the Dhamma of the discourses that elucidate that [Dhamma], because the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) is a collection of words and meanings.

"Accordingly" means as is appropriate. For the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya), which is comprised within the three trainings, and the holy life of the path (maggabrahmacariya), possess a fulfilled meaning through the attainment of the goal (atthasampatti);
that is, through the attainment of the goal consisting of the successive distinctions to be realized.
And because it exists together with its meaning and purpose, it is "meaningful" (sāttha) indeed, but not merely "well-phrased" (sabyañjana).
The holy life of the Dispensation, known as the "Dharma of the Thread" (tantidhamma), is both meaningful and well-phrased by virtue of the aforementioned meaning.

Although the speech of the Kirātas and other Mlecchas is likewise meaningful and well-phrased, [the Buddha] said, "Devadatta is equal in status," referring to the possession of distinguished meaning and phrasing.

Just as in the passage beginning with "Sāvitti," it is said to be "possessing meaning and possessing phrasing"; thus he says: "It possesses meaning through the perfection of its meaning, and it possesses phrasing through the perfection of its phrasing.

In that context, the perfection of such a kind of meaning—by hearing which and practicing accordingly one attains the destruction of all suffering—is called the "perfection of meaning" (*atthasampatti*); the sense is "the state of having perfected meaning. As for the perfection of phrasing:

The meaning of "perfection of phrasing" (*saṃpannavyañjanatā*) is the capacity to make even a profound meaning clear by means of the Magadhi language, which is naturally endowed with phonemes such as the soft and the hard consonants.
Now, in order to demonstrate the meaning according to the method of the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Netti 4, twelve terms), [the text] begins with "proclaiming" (*saṅkāsanā*), and so forth.

It has been stated. Therein, in brief, "manifestation" (*saṅkāsanam*) means that which is manifested (*saṅkāsīyati*) or explained (*dīpīyati*); this meaning should be understood according to the objective case (*kamma-sādhana*).

The same applies to the remaining terms. First, "manifestation" (*kāsana*) and "clear manifestation" (*pakāsana*)—both of these refer to the detailed explanation of what is termed a statement of the summary (*uddesa-attha-vacana*).
Furthermore, "repetition of what was once said," as well as "explication" (*vivaraṇa*) and "analysis" (*vibhajana*)—both of these [refer to the same].

This is the statement regarding the meaning of exposition (*niddesa*). "Detailed explanation" (*vivaṭa*) refers to a more extensive description, and "analysis" (*vibhatta*) refers to making known through various modes;
these two are the detailed statements comprised within what is termed the "statement regarding the meaning of further exposition" (*paṭiniddesa*).

"The conjunction of words and meanings" (*atthapadasamāyoga*): the six aforementioned words themselves are "words of meaning" (*atthapada*) because they constitute the analysis of the meaning of the scriptures.
The meaning is: "Because it is connected to eight divisions by virtue of being accompanied by them. A syllable (*akkhara*) is a phoneme occurring at the beginning or middle of an unfinished word;
alternatively, a single syllable or a word is a syllable. A word (*pada*) is that which ends in a grammatical case-suffix (*vibhatti*).

A phrase (*byañjana*) is a sentence (*vākya*), so called because it manifests the meaning expressed by the words. A mode (*ākāra*) is the differentiation of that very same spoken meaning in various ways.
Name (*nāma*). Etymology (*nirutti*) is the derivation of what has been stated by way of its mode (*ākāra*). Exposition (*niddesa*) is the expansion of the meaning of that derivation.

Alternatively, according to the statement: “He makes known by means of syllables (*akkhara*), he reveals by means of phrases (*pada*), he opens up by means of phonemes (*byañjana*), he analyzes by means of modes (*ākāra*), he clarifies by means of etymologies (*nirutti*), and he makes manifest by means of expositions (*niddesa*),” these [terms] denote the sense of a summary (*uddesa*) consisting of making known and revealing.

"Words" refers to syllables and phrases. "Phrasing" refers to words that express the meaning of a detailed exposition (*niddesa*), which consists of explanation (*vivaraṇa*) and analysis (*vibhajana*).

"Etymological exposition" (*niruttiniddesa*) refers to words that express the meaning of a further exposition (*paṭiniddesa*), which consists of making [the meaning] clear (*uttānīkaraṇa*) and presentation (*paññatti*);
the sense of "with phrasing" is due to the presence of these two.

Regarding "depth of meaning" and so forth: "meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the textual tradition (*tanti*), or else to cause and fruit (*hetuphala*). "Dharma" refers to the textual tradition, or else to the cause.
"Teaching" (*desanā*) is the verbal expression of the Dharma in accordance with its nature. "Realization" (*paṭivedha*) is the unerring comprehension of the aforementioned meaning and other factors.
Now, these—meaning and the rest—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, just as the great ocean is for fish and the like.
And therefore, they are profound. Among these, because penetration (*paṭivedha*) is dependent upon the meaning (*attha*) and shares the same nature as the meaning, it is said:

"It is 'possessing the meaning' (*sāttha*) by way of profundity of meaning and profundity of penetration. Although the teachings of the Dharma (*dhamma*) are also dependent upon the meaning, because they themselves consist of the form of the phrasing (*byañjana*), it is said:
"It is 'possessing the phrasing' (*sabyañjana*) by way of profundity of Dharma and profundity of teaching."

The knowledges categorized under the meanings and so forth as previously stated are the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) and the others. Therein, "nirutti" means the utterance of words by extracting [their etymological components]; the sense is "etymology" (nibbacana). Among the three analytical knowledges, the knowledge is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Worldly people gain confidence in meanings solely through the medium of credible speech, not through the medium of the meaning itself; therefore, he said, "because it is credible," and so forth.
The word *kevala* is a designation for "entirety," hence he said, "by way of its being complete and perfect.
The word *brahmacariya* here indicates the entire Dispensation comprised of the three trainings; thus he said, "because it is encompassed by the three trainings," and so forth.
To show this same meaning by another method, he said, "Moreover," and so on. In that context, *sanidāna* means...
It is "with its source" (*sanidāna*) because it possesses an introductory statement (*nidānavacana*) that illuminates the place, time, and other such details.

It is "with its origin" (*sauppattika*) because it is connected with the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and other such factors. In this regard, the sequence for connecting the text is as follows:
