"The Brahmin Verañjaka [said]: 'Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama... dwells,' and 'That venerable Gotama has such a beautiful reputation: "Thus indeed he is... and so forth, up to "...he proclaims. " Thus.
And he heard: "He has emerged," and "He teaches the Dhamma... [and so on] ...which is beautiful in its conclusion;
and while teaching, he proclaims the holy life (brahmacariya) endowed with qualities such as being meaningful and well-phrased," and "It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Having heard this, the Brahmin of Verañjā then approached the Blessed One.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, although it is stated that the passage beginning with "It would indeed be good" expresses the Brahmin’s reflection—namely, "Even a mere sight [of him] would be good; having formed this intention, he then approached...
[etc.]"—nevertheless, the word "he heard" (*assosi*) must be connected immediately after the phrase "he proclaimed the holy life" (*brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti*).

Although it appears as such, nevertheless, because it is stated by delimiting it with the word *iti*— in the sense of the aforementioned indication, namely, "It is indeed good to see such Arahants"— and because the word *iti* is not seen elsewhere [in that context],
there is a different mode of presentation in the text by way of showing what ought to be stated in between, beginning with "Then, at Verañjā... and so forth.

And the connection [of the narrative] is appropriate by supplying the word "he heard" immediately after the statement, "It is indeed good to see such Arahants," according to the manner already described.
For the Master of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya) shows the reason for the Brahmin’s approach by way of demonstrating that his aspiration arose solely from what he himself had heard.
It should be understood that the passage beginning with "Even a mere sight is good" was spoken having formed such an aspiration.
As for the phrase "like cold water by means of hot water," this is stated according to the sequence [of the simile] as it entered the mouth;

however, the meaning should be taken as "like hot water by means of cold water" because of the Brahmin’s own unappeased nature. Or else, it is because the Blessed One possesses the brilliance of knowledge.
Having understood that [the Buddha] is like warm water, and having understood that the brahmin, being free from that [suffering], is like cool water, it should be taken as it was thus spoken.

Regarding "oneness" (*ekībhāva*), it refers to the state of being of one form through the act of mutual greeting. In the passage beginning with "by which," the construction is: "that conversation by which the brahmin greeted him was a conversation conducive to greeting.
In that context, "endurable" (*khamanīya*) means that this body is full of suffering.
"May I be able to endure it. "Sustaining" means being able to sustain oneself through that which is called long-term continuity.
"Free from illness" (*appābādha*) is due to the absence of disease. "Free from affliction" (*appātaṅka*) is due to the absence of a miserable life.
"Lightness" (*lahuṭṭhāna*) is the fitness for rising quickly and without difficulty for the sake of performing various duties. "Strength" (*bala*) is the body's capacity to endure all tasks.
He asks, "Is there strength? *Phāsuvihāro* means a dwelling in comfort (*sukhavihāro*).
He says, "It is called 'sāraṇīya' by lengthening the vowel *i* in *saraṇīya*," because it is "to be remembered" (*saritabbabhāvato*). *Pariyāyehi* means by reasons (*kāraṇehi*).
*Bhāvo* is an action (*kiriyā*); the neuter word occurring in that sense is called a "neuter abstract noun" (*bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso*), meaning a word that qualifies an action.
The meaning [of *ekamante*] is: in one corner, in a suitable place. "The state of being broken-toothed and so forth" means the condition of having broken teeth, grey hair, and the like.
"In the rotation of kings" means the succession of kings; that is, in turn.

He says, "in a lineage that has existed for a long time," to show that his old age is due to being born into an ancient and noble family, and not merely due to years. It acquires (*lāti*) the greatness of riches.
"He is called 'old' because he grasps," thus it was said: "endowed with greatness in worldly existence" (*vibhava-mahattatā*).

"In the matter of manifestation" means in the matter designated as the manifestation of intrinsic nature (*pakati-vibhāvana*). "Or does not salute" means he does not perceive that [the person] is one who should be saluted;
what is meant is that his nature is such that he does not perceive [this]. "Whether form is permanent or impermanent"—here too, [it refers to] one whose nature is [to perceive it as] permanent.
The meaning is: "having the nature of impermanence. In the phrase "or impermanent," the word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
"Just born" means born for a mere moment; the meaning is "immediately upon being born. Regarding the passage "after walking seven steps...
he looked back," the looking back—though performed prior to the walking—is [included here] just as in such expressions as "he went out after closing the door."
It should be understood that this was spoken as if it were said later.

"He looked" means that when the miracle of the opening of the world had occurred, he looked with the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*). "Best" means more highly praised. "He honored" means he worshipped. "Supreme" means most excellent.
"That speech" refers to the speech beginning with "I am not that, O brahmin. "One should stand firm through higher knowledge" means one should be established in *arahatta* (the state of an Arhat).
"By way of birth" means by way of birth as a kṣatriya and so forth. "By way of rebirth" means by way of rebirth among the devas. "Drawing toward" means dragging [toward oneself].
The brahmin, perceiving an absence in the Blessed One of that essence of harmony consisting in acts such as salutation, said, "He is devoid of essence";
for he meant the absence of that very essence of harmony—such as craving for form—which is the opposite of those qualities.

The Blessed One, in order to show that [the mind] is "devoid of the taste of flavor" (arasarūpa), spoke the words beginning with "bases, objects, and so forth," demonstrating how the word *sāmaggirasa* (the essence of harmony) functions in relation to the taste of form (*rūparasā*) and the like.

"Made like the stump of a palmyra tree" (*tālāvatthukatā*) means that their mental continuum— the basis for those tastes of form and so forth— is like the ground of palmyra trees whose roots have been severed.

Regarding the phrase "katam" (made), it is stated that in this sense the middle word is elided and the vowel is lengthened in the grammatical exposition (*niddesa*). Thus, in the expression "tālavatthu viya," and so forth:

those for whom the base (*vatthu*) has been made like the base of a palmyra palm (*tāla*) are called "tālavatthukata. This should be understood as an instance where the qualifying term is placed last (*paranipāta*);

the meaning is "those for whom the palmyra-base has been made. A palmyra tree with its top cut off is itself a "non-base" (*avatthu*) because it no longer serves as a support for leaves, fruit, and so on.
The "palmyra-stand" (*tālāvatthu*): those things for which it serves as a stand—namely, visible forms, tastes, and so forth—are "made into a palmyra-stand.

This apprehension of the meaning by way of a different referent (*aññapadatthavasena*) is easy to understand according to the method explained below; thus, in order to show the specific meaning, he says, "made like a palmyra tree with its top cut off.
And in this way, even when the attachments to visible forms, tastes, and so forth—which resemble the top [of the tree]—are severed, that which constitutes their basis...
The continuum of consciousness, which resembles the base of a palm tree, remains present right up until the place of final Nibbāna.

However, if the meaning is taken according to the literal expression by means of a descriptive compound (*visesanasa-māsa*), it would follow that visible forms, tastes, and so forth, would occupy the same position as the base of the palm tree.
As for the fact that in the *Sāratthadīpanī* this fault is avoided by [stating] that visible forms, tastes, and so forth are wholesome or unwholesome...

That which was stated [in the Sutta]—namely, "these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata," etc.—does not accord with the Pāli text, nor does it accord with the commentary which speaks of "the flavors of form" consisting in the relish for sensual pleasure.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), as long as they have not attained final Nibbāna, the arising of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome deeds continues;
therefore, their state cannot be compared to a palmyra tree with its crown cut off. Alternatively, regarding the palmyra tree with its crown cut off...

Even when the meaning is grasped through a descriptive compound (*visesanasa-māsa*)—taking "that which has been made like the site of a palmyra tree" as a simile for the state of being subject to non-arising again, while disregarding both what remains and what does not remain—there is no fault whatsoever.

Since the prefix *anu-* functions in the sense of "afterwards," he said, "there is no subsequent existence," and so forth. [The phrase] "they have gone to non-existence after" means by way of the state of being subject to non-arising afterwards.
"It has gone to non-existence. "Not wonderful" means that it is not marvelous in each successive instance.
"And as for what you say" means that the reason you cite—namely, the absence of the essence of harmony such as prostration and so forth—is a reason characterized by a lack of flavor;
the meaning is that such a reason does not exist.

4. "The meaning spoken with intentional reference" (*sandhāya bhāsita-attha*) refers to the meaning with which the brahmin spoke the words, "Venerable Gotama, you are one who enjoys no pleasures," and so forth; and it refers to that meaning with which the Blessed One allows for his own state of non-enjoyment and so on.

5. "Family custom and practice" (*kula-samudācāra-kamma*) means family tradition and conduct. "Bodily misconduct" (*kāya-duccarita*) is misconduct occurring from the body, that is, from the bodily door. "Of many kinds" (*aneka-vihitā*) means of various modes. 6.

"Of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañca-kāmaguṇika-rāga*) refers to that which is attached by way of excessive clinging to the five objects of sense-desire, beginning with visible forms.

Regarding *kāmarāga*: by this, he shows the absence of the nature of sensual lust (*kāmarāgatā*) in the case of the sensual lust that arises for non-returners (*anāgāmin*) through attachment to clothing, ornaments, and so forth, because that [lust] is included within the category of lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and so on. Regarding the phrase "the remainder":

here he states that personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) are eradicated by the first path, while the rest are eradicated by all four paths; therefore, he says "according to their respective order."

7. “He feels disgust” means he feels as if he were disgusted, or I perceive him as “feeling disgust. “In the sense of being produced by lack of skill” means in the sense of being produced by ignorance (*aññāṇa*).

8–10. “Therein” refers to the two alternative meanings previously stated. Since the word “womb” (*gabbha*) is used here as a synonym for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he says, “for the sake of obtaining rebirth-linking in the world of the gods.
“Becoming non-rebirth” refers to those [phenomena] that arise moment by moment.
The manifestation of phenomena. 11.
The "dharma-element" (*dhammadhātu*) is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For that indeed holds and examines phenomena as they truly are;
thus it is called the "dharma-element. "Attained to skill in teaching" means being able to teach by way of rearranging [the material] according to one's own preference.
"Skillfulness" (*samatthatā*) refers to the grace of teaching; he has attained that. "The expansion of compassion" (*karuṇā-vipphāra*) means the pervading of all beings with great compassion.

Manifesting through a simile the very characteristic of such qualities, he said: "A mind equal to the earth. Precisely because of that, due to its nature of not being provoked to anger, it is the state of being unshakeable (*akuppa-dhammatā*).
"Followed by birth" (*jāti-anugata*) means bound to birth. "Pervaded by old age" (*jarā-anusaṭa*) means enveloped by old age.
"Like a stump in the round" means it has become like a stump standing motionless within the cycle of existence because it is impossible to extract it from that round.
Regarding the fear of constant death for those born, he said, "Having died today," and so forth.
"Peerless state of being born first" means the incomparable state of being the first-born of the noble birth; the meaning is the state of being the eldest of all.
By saying “*pī*” instead of “*apī*,” he shows that the particle *pi* exists as a separate indeclinable (*nipāta*).
“Properly laid upon” means they were properly placed on top by one who did not cause injury with her feet or other limbs;

although the root *sayati* is intransitive, it should be understood as transitive here because of its prefix *adhi*. “Nail-tips” refers to the tips of the nails. The wings of birds serve as substitutes for hands and feet.
He said: "With hands and feet drawn together. "There" means in the place of light. "Of those emerging" means among those emerging;
this is a genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*).

"Egg-shell" means the shell of the egg. "The world itself is the world-dwelling. It is called a "Bodhi tree" because one awakens (*abujjhi*) there; or it is that which awakens by itself, or that by which others awaken.
"Tenā" (by that) refers to both the Path and omniscient knowledge as "bodhi. That which is awakened to is Nibbāna, which is "bodhi.
The phrase "and between the bodhi" is a second illustration intended to show that the word "bodhi" can apply to a tree even without the word "tree" being explicitly used.
"Varabhūrimedhaso" means one whose wisdom is spread out like the great earth. "Tisso vijjā" refers to the path of Arahantship.

The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*), designated as right view, which occurs together with oneself, along with the other two higher knowledges (*mahaggata-vijjā*), is called the "three knowledges" (*tisso vijjā*) because they arise by way of destroying the defilements that are their obstacles.

The same principle applies here to the "six direct knowledges" (*cha abhiññā*). The "knowledge of the disciple's perfection" (*sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa*) refers to everything that is to be attained by the foremost disciples.
"Worldly and supramundane knowledge. Regarding "the knowledge of paccekabodhi," the same principle applies here as well.
"Applying the simile" means the establishing of the meaning of the simile as being equal to the object of the simile (*upameyya*).

"By way of the meaning" means by way of the meaning of the object of the simile. By the phrase "sharpness, pungency, clarity, and brilliance," he shows that insight has reached the state of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
By the phrase "the time of transformation," the attainment of the state of leading to emergence is indicated. And at that time, she is as if carrying the embryo of path-knowledge;
thus it is said, "the time of conceiving the embryo. By "attained in successive order" is meant attained through the sequence of the first path and so forth.
"Endowed with four factors" refers to: "Granted, let only skin, sinews, and bone remain..."
Energy endowed with the four factors as described thus: "Let my flesh and blood dry up in this body.
In such passages as "desire is lust," etc., desire (*chanda*) is weak greed proceeding in the mode of aspiration in the sense of wishing;

stronger than that is lust (*rāga*) in the sense of being colored by passion; and even stronger than that is desire-and-lust (*chandarāga*). By way of the perception of signs and secondary characteristics...
There is the thought that has arisen; even stronger than that is the lust that arises by way of a powerful thought; even stronger than that is the lustful thought.
This distinction is stated according to the different modes of manifestation and the different stages of a single state of greed (*lobha*).
Commentary on the First Jhāna Discourse.
“Seyyathidaṃ” means “how is that?”—this is the sense. “Etaṃ” is a restrictive particle applied specifically to the preceding word, meaning “this class of things.
“Tannissaraṇato” means because of the escape from those sensual pleasures. “Esa” is the particle *eva* (indeed). “Kāmadhātu” refers to sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).

“Nekkhamma” refers to the first jhāna. “Esa” indicates a restriction. [The kinds of seclusion are] seclusion by way of its factors (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*).
"Those beginning with the seclusion of its factors" refers to the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites, such as bodily seclusion and so forth;

these three alone are relevant here in the discussion of *jhāna*, because seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*) and the others are impossible in this context. "In the Exposition" means in the *Mahāniddesa*. "In that very place" means in the *Mahāniddesa* itself.
"In the Analysis" means in the *Jhānavibhaṅga*. "This being so" means when there is an inclusion of both kinds of sensual desires (*kāma*).
"By the former" means by physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). "In this" means in these two types of seclusion, namely of body and mind. "By the second" means by mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*).

"Of these" refers to the words "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*) and "secluded from unwholesome states" (*vivicca akusalehi*), which, according to the method already stated, express the twofold seclusion from sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and from defilements (*kilesakāma*); and here the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Of the state of foolishness...

The phrase "abandoning the cause" follows. For unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) are the cause of foolishness (*bālabhāva*). "Nourishing the underlying tendency" (*āsaya-posana*) refers to both the purification and the increase of that underlying tendency.
The connection is that only the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga*. Regarding this, he states the reason:

"because it shows their state as being opposed to and counteractive of the factors of higher jhāna. In that context, [the passage] beginning with "with applied thought" (*savitakka*)... [etc. is used.
The meaning is: "because of showing that the jhāna factors being mentioned are the opposites of their respective adversaries.
There is also a reading: "because of showing the state of being the opposite of the adversaries of the higher jhāna factors.

In that context, [it means] "because of showing the state of being the opposite of the higher jhāna factors being mentioned by way of their direct adversaries," and [it refers to] "the hindrances themselves as they were stated in the Vibhaṅga."
They speak of the meaning. *Peṭaka* refers to the work composed by the Elder Mahākaccāyana that follows the method of the *Nettippakaraṇa*;
it is called "peṭaka" because it is a commentary on the Piṭakas—this is the sense of "in that.
He says "conjecturing" (*ūhana*) because "thinking" (*vitakkana*) is the conceptualization of an object. Regarding the object [as] "form, form," and so forth...
For one who strikes [the object], the striking of the occurrence of the sense-object should be understood as "striking above.
The "leading of the mind toward the object" means making it face the object. "Wandering along" (anusañcaraṇa) means revolving around;
and that is simply the arising of the subsequent moment in that same manner, for in the ultimate sense there is no wandering of a single entity. The same applies elsewhere.

"In such cases": "anumajjana" means rubbing or stroking. "Therein" refers to the object (*ārammaṇa*). "Application together with the co-nascent" is by way of performing [the function] in accordance with its own specific activity.
"In some instances" means in all minds accompanied by sustained thought (*savicāra*) that are devoid of the second jhāna; this is the meaning.

Although initial application (*vitakka*) arises together with sustained thought (*vicāra*), it is called "the first impact" with reference to its mode of proceeding by directing the mind onto the object.
It is said: "Vipphāravā" means possessing momentum because its nature has not yet subsided; for that very reason, it becomes a factor of abandonment (*pahānaṅga*) in the second jhāna.
The phrase "in the first and second jhānas" is stated with reference to the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*).
To demonstrate the non-existence of a jhāna devoid of factors, he says, "like a tree," and so forth.
In the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhanapaksa*), the word *viveka* is used as "from seclusion" (*tasmā vivekā*); in the other sense, it is used as "in that seclusion" (*tasmiṃ viveke*).
"It gladdens" (*pinayati*) means it satisfies or increases. "Pervasive flavor" (*pharaṇarasā*) means its function is to pervade the body with sublime forms.

"Characterized by refreshment" (*sātalakkhaṇaṃ*) means having a desirable nature; the meaning is "sweet. Without causing oppression or indifference toward associated states, [it flows] along, along...
"Taking hold" or "being helpful" is assistance (*anuggaha*). "The forest itself is the forest-limit; water itself is the water-limit.
By the phrase "because it is manifest at that particular time," it is shown that even though pleasure exists at the time of obtaining desirable objects and so forth, it is not manifest;
rather, it is joy (*pīti*) alone that is manifest there. And at the time of experiencing the flavor of what has been obtained, even though pleasure exists, [it is joy that is manifest].

This shows that pleasure (*sukha*) alone is more manifest. And here, the experience of the flavor obtained should be understood by way of mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*) alone, not by way of bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*), because the latter is not intended here due to its lack of association with joy (*pīti*).

The phrase "And this joy" (*ayañca pītī*) and so forth is a demonstration of a *samāsa* compound where the referent is distinct (*aññapadattha-samāsa*); in the view that it is a possessive suffix (*taddhita-paccaya*), it is a demonstration of a secondary derivative.

Or: according to the second alternative, by means of a *aññapadattha* compound, he shows that "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*) is a single word and that there is no elision of the case-ending.
"Succession in numbering" is said with reference to the order of teaching. "He attains first" is stated from the perspective of a beginner.
It has been stated that for yogis who have attained mastery (*ciṇṇavasī*), jhāna indeed arises even out of sequence. "It burns" means it consumes.

To the question, "How can there be an intense contemplation (*upanijjhāyana*) by insight (*vipassanā*), which has the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as its object, for the Path (*magga*) which has Nibbāna as its object? he says: "By insight," and so on.
In that context, "it is accomplished by the Path" means by that which abandons the perversions (*vipallāsa*) such as permanence and the rest.

That contemplation of the characteristics is accomplished for oneself through non-delusion by means of the path itself. Alternatively, "by means of the path" means by the function of the path, that is, by the abandoning of the perversions.

"Another" refers to a sentient being. "Because it was not stated" means because it was not stated in the Jhāna Sutta as "one-pointedness of mind. "Because it was stated" means because it was stated in the Vibhaṅga of that same Jhāna Sutta.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Second Jhāna:
Regarding the term "internal" (*ajjhatta*), it is stated that "here, one's own internal [state] is intended," because this qualifies the jhāna.

For jhāna itself is not "internal-internal," since that status belongs only to the six sense-faculties. "Small waves" refers to ripples (*vīci*); "large" refers to billows (*taraṅga*). "Calm" (*santa*)...
"Are calmed," and so forth, are synonyms for one another; the intended meaning is that they have transcended by means of the power of jhāna. "Appitā" means brought to an end, led to destruction.
"Pariyāya" [is used] because the designation "jhāna" applies to the requisites of jhāna, and thus it is not in the ultimate sense.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the third jhāna.

"For the attainment of that" means for the attainment of the third path. "He sees by way of arising" means he sees by way of application, such that through familiarity with the companionship of wisdom, it comes to possess the nature of a natural concomitant. "Vast" means having reached the state of the sublime (*mahaggata*).

"Firm" means having reached a state of stability through the disappearance of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*); for this very reason, he will say: "by means of applied thought, sustained thought, and rapture..."

"Because of being unsurpassed," and so forth. Having shown the divisions of equanimity (*upekkhā*), the passage beginning with "But as for equanimity... was stated in order to clarify the specific kind of equanimity intended here.

In that context, it is called "sixfold equanimity" (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) because, for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it looks on with absolute neutrality toward the course of the six desirable and undesirable objects by way of not abandoning its naturally pure state; and [it is called] "equanimity toward beings" (*sattesu...*).
It is called "equanimity as a divine abode" (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) because it proceeds with an attitude of neutrality;

"equanimity as a factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) because it constitutes an attitude of neutrality toward co-arising states; "pure equanimity regarding that" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) when it is absolute;

"equanimity of jhāna" (*jhānupekkhā*) because, even amidst the supreme bliss accompanying the third jhāna, it remains free from partiality; and [it is so called] because, accompanying the fourth jhāna, it is purified of all opposing factors.
And "purity-equanimity" (*pārisuddhupekkhā*) is described as sixfold according to its various distinct states.
However, when energy itself proceeds in the mode of equanimity toward the conascent formations that are neither over-exerted nor too lax, it is called "energy-equanimity" (*vīriyupekkhā*).
This occurs prior to the attainment of the eight meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), both fine-material and immaterial.

Thus, because it is oriented toward the abandoning of the hindrances, applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth, and because it maintains a state of neutrality by remaining inactive even during their abandonment,
there arises— by way of concentration— the eightfold wisdom that functions in the mode of equanimity; and by way of insight,
there arises [the wisdom] that functions in the mode of looking on with equanimity at the formations comprised within the aggregates of clinging, occurring in the preliminary stage of the four paths.

For the attainment of each respective fruit, there are four types of wisdom occurring in the preliminary stage by way of the desireless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) for each of the four fruits, and two types by way of the void and signless liberations (*suññata-animitta-vimokkha*).

Thus, these ten types of wisdom—making eighteen in total—are called equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*). They are indeed the same as the previously mentioned wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).

In the investigation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇavicinana*), there is what is called equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), which is a state of neutrality. There is also equanimity of feeling (*vedanupekkhā*), which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhavedanā*).

Showing that the analysis of these ten kinds of equanimity should be understood according to the method explained in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* as it occurs in various places, he said: "Thus this [equanimity] is tenfold," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "according to the method occurring in various places":
For this too is stated as a separate heading for the matrix (mātikā), like the headings on planes, persons, and so forth, for the purpose of showing their classification;

it is not, however, a reference to the specific places where the classification by way of planes, persons, and so forth has been presented, since those specific places have already been stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and other works. Therefore, regarding what was said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Of these ten... [and so on].
Showing that the classification of equanimities according to plane, person, and so forth is to be understood by the very method stated in various places, he said:
"Thus this is tenfold," and so on. One should understand that [the statement] was made without taking that [classification] into account. "By the method stated in various places" means:
"In this case, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad... and so forth.
By such passages as, "With a mind that is unhappy, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending," the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) is presented;
and by such passages as, "He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity," the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) is presented.
Thus, because the manner in which these ten types of equanimity are taught can be seen in their respective stated contexts, this [equanimity] is tenfold.
The connection is that equanimity (upekkhā) is to be understood according to the method explained in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.

Regarding the "planes" (bhūmi) and so forth: by way of plane, the sixfold equanimity belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while the equanimity of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra-upekkhā) belongs to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and so on.

Furthermore, the sixfold equanimity belongs only to those beyond training (asekkha), whereas the equanimity of the divine abodes belongs to all three types of persons, including worldlings (puthujjana).

By the phrase "of persons" (*puggalānaṃ*), etc., it is shown by way of the person; by the phrase "the sixfold equanimity is associated with a mind accompanied by joy and equanimity," etc., it is shown by way of the mind;

by the phrase "the sixfold equanimity has six objects," etc., it is shown by way of the object; and by the inclusion within the aggregates (*khandhasaṅgaha*), showing that "equanimity as feeling is included in the aggregate of feeling, while the other nine are included in the aggregate of mental formations"; and [by the phrase] "the sixfold equanimity..."

The divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), the jhānas, purity (*pārisuddhi*), and equanimity as specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are identical in meaning.

Therefore, when one of these occurs in a single moment, the others do not arise; the same should be understood for the equanimity of formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and the equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).

However, the equanimity of feeling (*vedanupekkhā*) and the equanimity of energy (*vīriyupekkhā*) may arise in a single moment. Thus, [the text speaks] both in terms of a single moment and regarding the sixfold equanimity.

The equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) is indeterminate; it may be either wholesome or indeterminate, and so too are the others. However, the equanimity of feeling (*vedanupekkhā*) may even be unwholesome.

Thus, this tenfold equanimity should be understood according to the method stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* both by way of the triad of the wholesome and by way of summary—as in the statement: "In brief, there are four states: energy, feeling, mental neutrality, and knowledge. This is the construction [of the meaning].
And here, although these have not been stated in their specific form in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* by way of the planes,

persons, and so forth, nevertheless, their classification according to plane, person, and so on can be understood by extracting it through the methodical approach (*naya*) in the manner described therein;
therefore, having combined together what was stated there in its specific form and what was not, [this is explained] by means of the methods found in various places, and so forth.

The extension [of the application] was made in nine ways; for that very reason, instead of saying "according to what is stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*," it is said "in the manner already stated.
For instance, when it is said, "A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, having seen a form with the eye...

and so forth, the sixfold equanimity—by virtue of having forms and the rest as its objects—is, in terms of plane, of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and in terms of person, belongs only to those who are beyond training (*asekkha*).
It arises from the mind; it is associated with minds of joy and equanimity; it has six objects as its objective support;
and from the triad of the wholesome, it is indeterminate—thus it can be known by the wise.

Likewise, when it is stated that the six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*), the equanimity of jhāna (*jhānupekkhā*), and the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhupekkhā*) are identical in meaning, and so forth.

Since it is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), its non-arising at the same moment as the sublime abodes (brahmavihāra) such as equanimity (upekkhā), and so forth, can be understood.

And just as with the sixfold equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), the method for discerning the classification of its planes and so on for the remaining [equanimities] should be known from the manner explained in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* according to their respective suitability. "Having the flavor of effortlessness" means even toward that refined pleasure...

The meaning is: "having the function of being the opposite of bowing down. "By means of a person" means by way of a person as the basis. It is the protection of those things associated with the defilements.

"Investigation" is the reaching of the further shore of one's task. "Discernment" is inquiry. "This" refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*). Because it is associated with the mental body (*nāmakāya*), [it is so called].
"Sukhan" (pleasure): thus there is a connection with "tasmā etamatthaṃ" and so forth. "Tassa" means of one possessing the jhāna.
"Taṃsamuṭṭhānena" means by that matter which has as its source (samuṭṭhāna) or cause that pleasure associated with the body as previously named; [it is] by that matter which has that as its source.
"Assa" means of the yogi. "Yassa" means of the material body. "Phuṭattā" means because of being pervaded by exceedingly refined matter.

"Showing this meaning" means: while experiencing the bodily pleasure produced by the mind—which is the cause of physical pleasure—one is said to "experience pleasure with the body" through a figurative designation (kāriyopacāra) for the state of possessing the jhāna;

this is the meaning of "showing this meaning. Regarding the word "yaṃ," he says "yaṃjhānahetū" because it is a particle used in the sense of a cause. "In the attainment of the perfection of pleasure."
"Having reached the ultimate limit of pleasure. The connection [of the sentence] is: "In this way, their abandonment is to be understood.
Then, why is cessation stated only in relation to the jhānas? This is the connection.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discussion of the fourth jhāna.
"Where has it arisen?"—here, "where" (*kattha*) is the locative case used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is: "when what cause exists"?

"With a different adverting" (*nānāvajjane*) means: in that access concentration whose adverting in the preceding cognitive series is "different," that is, distinct from the adverting of the absorption path.

"Fatigue arisen from an uneven posture" refers to the affliction caused by an unbalanced seat. The phrase beginning with "or in access" (*upacāre vā*) and so forth is a presentation of an alternative view.

The meaning is: "even in the proximity of a single adverting [consciousness]. By the phrase "by the pervasion of rapture," he shows that even in a single cognitive series (*ekavīthi*), as in the case of the absorption series (*appanāvīthi*), there is an absence of the mere pervasion by sense-sphere rapture (*kāmāvacara-pīti*).

The connection is: "there might be the arising of this faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*). The connection is: "this [faculty of mental grief] arises. [And] "even with the conditions of applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicāra-paccaya*).

The word *pi* is used in the sense of "also. It should be connected with the phrase immediately preceding it, namely "of that which has been abandoned," thus: "even of the faculty of grief that has been abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārabhāve*), the words "the faculty of grief arises" (*uppajjati domanassindriyan*) should be brought over and connected here.
This locative case is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "due to the subsiding of applied and sustained thought."
Regarding the phrase "applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārā*), the word *iti* here should be understood in the sense of "therefore. Consequently,
because this faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) does not arise even when there are conditions for applied and sustained thought— and indeed, wherever it does arise,
it arises only where applied and sustained thought exist— and because it has not yet been abandoned in the vicinity (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna...
"Applied thought and sustained thought (vitakka-vicārā); therefore, their arising might occur there"—this is how the construction should be understood here.
"There" means in the vicinity (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna. "Its" refers to the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*). "Its arising might occur":

this is stated merely as a possibility based on the observation of the mere presence of conditions. For even the possibility of the arising of mental grief can only be established at the very moment of access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*).

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to maintain that the arising [of unwholesome states] is possible at the moment of the second jhāna, which is devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).

Otherwise, since the arising of unwholesome mental distress (*domanassa*) is impossible at the moment of a wholesome consciousness, one could not say, "its arising might occur therein. Alternatively, this locative case (*bhummavacana*) is used in the sense of proximity, meaning "in the cognitive process (*vīthi*) immediately following access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*)."
The meaning [is as follows]. Regarding the phrase "in the second jhāna": here too, the meaning is that it does not arise even in the immediately preceding cognitive processes (*anantaravīthi*);
the same applies to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) in the subsequent sections. This connects with the phrase "the arising of the faculty of mental joy" (*somanassindriya*).

The statement "they are abandoned" is said because it was stated [in the sūtra]: "through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters" (*pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā*). "By the absence of suffering" (*dukkhābhāvena*)...
By way of the state of suffering (*dukkhatā*). The same applies here to the phrase "by way of the absence of pleasure" (*sukhābhāvena*). By this means:

by the statement that negates both suffering and pleasure. "Characterized by the experience of what is contrary to the desirable and the undesirable" means characterized by the experience of a neutral object (*majjhattārammaṇa*), which is the opposite of the excessively desirable and the excessively undesirable;
for even a neutral object is included within the desirable and the undesirable, as there is nothing existing apart from them.
The method of commentary on the exposition of the fourfold jhāna is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the exposition of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa),
[the author] says "for some they are the bases for direct knowledge" and so forth, because even the formless jhānas are included within the fourth jhāna due to the equality of their factors.

For that very reason, he will say: “Having produced the eight attainments,” and so forth. Among those, only the fourth jhāna serves as the basis for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the basis for cessation (*nirodha*);

the others do not. However, with reference to the quality of being distant [from the defilements], it should be understood that the inclusion of all four jhānas together is made by saying “the four jhānas.
The phrase “states of one-pointedness of mind” refers to the dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).

He said, "It was spoken with intentional meaning (sandhāya)," beginning with the words "of those whose taints are exhausted" (*khīṇāsava*). "Accomplisher of all duties" means the accomplisher of all Buddha-activities, such as the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*) and so forth.
By the phrase "bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities," he includes everything mentioned above, such as its being the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka*).
For this jhāna is thus [described] because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the Path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*), which bestows all the Buddha-qualities of the Blessed One.

It should be understood as "it is said. "Yathayidaṃ" means "just as this. "Abhinīhārakkhaman" means fit for being directed toward [the goal] for the purpose of the various supernormal powers (iddhividhā) and so forth.
"Jhānappaṭilābhapaccayānaṃ" means having the attainment of jhāna as their cause—that is, those things that arise depending upon the attainment of jhāna.

"Of evil things" means of base things. "Within the range of desire" refers to pride and so forth that proceed by way of self-exaltation and the like—having entered the domain of desire but not yet reached the state of being a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) or being associated with it—such as [the thought]:
"Oh, would that the Teacher, having questioned me, were to teach such a Dhamma to the bhikkhus! In some manuscripts, however, it is also read as "of those opposed to the attainment of jhāna."

They write the reading as *pamādapāṭho*, but it should be understood as *pamādappāṭho* (a careless reading), because it was already stated earlier in the very phrase "purified by the removal of the hindrances" (*nīvaraṇadūrībhāvena*) as being the absence of the hindrances that are opposed to the attainment of jhāna. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says:

*“iccha-avacarānan”-ti icchāya avacarānaṃ, icchāvasena otiṇṇānaṃ* (“of those within the range of desire” means of those who move within desire, who have descended according to the influence of desire).)
It should be understood that this reading—“of the various kinds of causes for anger that have arisen”—is also untenable.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: “This reading has not been presented in its entirety.
And therein, by the phrase “of the various kinds of causes for anger,” those faults which have reached the state of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are what are referred to.
This reading should be understood as rejected.

In the phrase "of covetousness, etc.," the word *abhijjhā* (covetousness) includes greed (*lobha*)—which indeed has the nature of a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*)—as well as pride (*māna*) and the rest, because the qualifying phrase "conditions for the attainment of jhāna" follows.
"Both" refers to being free from blemish (*anaṅgaṇatta*) and being devoid of defilements (*vigatūpakkilesatta*).
Both of these should be understood according to their respective order by following the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* and the *Vattha Sutta*.

Although in those two suttas gross faults that have reached the nature of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are also mentioned, nevertheless, because they are spoken of here with reference to one who has attained the fourth jhāna, only the subtle ones are taken up.
Furthermore, in this context, the suttas are [grouped] under the commonality of "blemishes" (*aṅgaṇa*) and "corruptions" (*upakkilesa*).
This is a reference [to a source]. For it is said, "in accordance with the Sutta," and not "by means of the Sutta.
By saying "in the recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*), he states the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) as "knowledge of the recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).
Now, in order to show the distinction between the past lives, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge therein, he says "therein," and so forth.

It has been stated. Since the word *pubba* (former) refers to past existence (*atītabhava*) and the word *nivāsa* (abode) functions as a noun denoting the action (*karmasādhana*), he said: "the aggregates (*khandhā*) inhabited in former, past births.
Here, "inhabitedness" (*nivutthatā*) means the state of having occurred within one's own continuum; therefore, he said "experienced," and so forth.
Now, in order to show the meaning of the word *nivāsa* by way of its function as a noun denoting both one's own and others' continua, [he says]: "the phenomena inhabited..."
Having said, “or inhabited,” in order to explain that, it was stated: “by way of resort and dwelling,” and so forth.

For even those phenomena that have become objects of range (*gocara*) are indeed called “inhabited” by knowledge; however, to show that they are twofold because they are the objects of both one’s own and another’s consciousness, it was stated:
“by oneself,” and so forth. Alternatively, the connection is: “even those known by the consciousness of another are inhabited. Here too, the word *paricchinna* (delimited) [is to be understood].

Having brought them [to mind], they should be connected [to the recollection]. For even in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, the aggregates (*khandha*) of beings previously unknown to oneself are called "known by the consciousness of others" because they have been known by certain others;
the recollection of those is difficult from the outset. Those [beings] are called "known by the consciousness of others" precisely because they were known by those others. Of those...

Because it is to be known by following the continuity of the present stream of consciousness. And those [beings] known by another’s consciousness are of two kinds: those who have attained final Nibbāna and those who have not.
Among them, recollection of those who have attained final Nibbāna is difficult to perform because their mental continuity has been completely cut off.

However, in order to show that previous existence which has reached its culmination as being known by another’s consciousness, [the text says]: “In the case of the recollection of those whose rebirth-linking is severed,” and so forth.

It has been stated. In that context, "those who have cut off the round" (*chinnavaṭumaka*) refers to those who have attained final nibbāna in the past and whose taints are exhausted because they have severed the path of saṃsāra.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the recollection—by means of the "lion’s leap" method—even of those who have not yet attained final nibbāna and who were cognized by the consciousness of another, is included.
One should supply and connect the phrase: "That mindfulness by which one recollects former births is 'recollection of former births' (*pubbenivāsānussati*)."

The word *vihita* is a synonym for the word *vidha*; thus he says "of many kinds" (*anekavidha*), meaning manifold by way of the modes of existence (*bhava*), the sources of birth (*yoni*), and so forth.
Alternatively, taking the sense of *vihita* as "employed" or "described," he says "described by many...

praised" (*saṃvaṇṇita*), explaining that this is stated with the middle term elided where it should have been said "described by many modes" (*anekehi pakārehi vihita*). "By modes" (*pakārehi*)... [etc.]
"By way of name, clan, and so forth. "Described" means spoken by the Buddha and others. Since the prefix *anu-* indicates immediate succession, he says, "at the very moment it was directed downward";

by this, he shows that the preliminary work (*parikamma*) has already been undertaken. With the words "for those who have fulfilled the perfections," etc., he shows that success is achieved even without [further] preliminary work.
“In order to show the manner in which it was undertaken” means for the purpose of showing the aggregates (khandhas) in which one formerly dwelt that were undertaken for recollection.

It is called *jāti* because it is born (*jāyati*); it is existence (*bhava*). That continuity of aggregates (*khandhappabandha*), rooted in a single karma and delimited by its taking up and laying down, is what is intended here by the term “birth”;
thus he said, “even a single [existence],” and so forth. An eon (*kappa*) is an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*); as for its meaning:
Time is designated in dependence upon phenomena as they proceed; its decrease and increase should be understood by way of those [phenomena].
That which has contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), that is, destruction, is its nature is "the aeon of contraction" (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*); it is an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).

That which stands with a nature together with contraction—that is, destruction—is "the aeon of subsistence after contraction" (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). The same applies to "the aeon of expansion" (*vivaṭṭa*) and so forth. In this context, expansion (*vivaṭṭana*) is "expansion" (*vivaṭṭa*).

"Arising" (uppatti) or "increase" (vaḍḍhi). Destruction by fire is a "fire-cataclysm" (tejosaṃvaṭṭa). As for the phrase "in detail," there is no distinction in the limits of the cataclysm in terms of breadth;
therefore he said, "always. To show that it is designated as the "field of birth" because it undergoes transformation at the very moment of its arising—like a single city—it is stated:
"it trembles during rebirth-linking and so forth. Its power (ānubhāva) proceeds.
The intention is that the afflictions, such as disease, of all beings included therein are pacified.
Regarding the statement, "Or however far he might wish," this refers to the objective field;
for the Blessed One—who claims to make himself heard by his voice everywhere at a single moment and to show his own material body—said, "As far as... [and so forth].
Or else, it is said: “...or he might desire.

In the phrase “among these,” the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “One who eats fallen fruit” means one whose food consists of fruits that have fallen of their own accord;
this is stated with reference to his time as an ascetic. “For rebirth here” means for rebirth here in his final existence. “Of a single clan” means by way of the Tusita clan.
"Of one clan. "The others" refers to caste and so forth. "Heresics" refers to those who propound the existence of karma and its fruit.
"Resolution" refers to the period of accumulating merit and knowledge, characterized by such a resolution.

"By way of death and rebirth-linking" means that having observed the death of oneself or another in this or that state of existence, one grasps the rebirth-linking itself without touching upon anything in between; it is in this manner [that it is said].

"Knowing is the rising up to the desired place," he said; thus he spoke the words beginning with "for of them... "In both ways" means both according to the sequence of the aggregates and by way of death and rebirth-linking.
"Also by way of the lion’s leap" means also by way of the lion’s descent. Since energy (vīriya) has the sense of burning and tormenting the defilements, it is called "heat" (ātāpa);
thus he said, "by the heat of energy."

Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye (Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 13. Because it exists in the divine realm (*divi*), it is "divine" (*dibba*); it is said that the eye of clarity belonging to the deities is so called. Therefore, he says, "because it resembles the divine.

By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even at a distance," the grasping of even subtle objects is included. [It is so called] because it succeeds by means of the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*).
All development (bhāvanā) is either the development of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) accompanied by the volitional formations of striving, or specifically the development of energy;
thus it is said, "generated by the power of the development of energy. "By way of divine abiding" means by way of the four jhānas based on the kasiṇas and so forth.

By this, he expresses its divine nature in the sense of being remote [from the lower realms]. By the phrase "because it is dependent upon the divine abiding," [he shows] that it is proximate to the foundational jhāna which serves as its cause.

"They arise because they are based on the divine abodes" means that the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), which is associated with oneself and has entered into the divine abodes, serves as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the occurrence of the knowledge of the divine eye; this is also the meaning.
With reference to the root *div*, in the sense of "shining" or "going," it is said: "by the grasping of light," and so forth. Therein, "by the grasping of light" means:
"By way of grasping the light of the kasiṇa. "In the sense of seeing" means by way of the state of seeing forms;

by this, he shows its status as an eye (*cakkhu*) based on the etymological derivation: "it sees form" (*cakkhati rūpaṃ*) or "it makes manifest" (*vibhāveti*). "By performing the function of the eye":

this is a demonstration of a similar characteristic through the simile "this is an eye just like the [physical] eye"; the meaning is: by performing the function of the eye, which consists in seeing what is level and uneven, and so forth.
The phrase "As it is said" indicates a specific passage from the *Upakkilesa Sutta*. Therein, regarding the terms "doubt" (*vicikicchā*) and so forth:

while the Blessed One was still at the foot of the Bodhi tree and had not yet attained full enlightenment, as he was seeing various kinds of forms with his divine eye, doubt arose in him, thinking, "What indeed is this?
What indeed is that? Then, for the purpose of turning back that doubt, those forms [were described].
While he was not attending to [the object], sloth and torpor arose; then, in order to turn away from that, while again attending to all forms, terror arose regarding demons and the like.

Then, by way of dispelling fear through attending with the thought, "What is there here to be afraid of?", there arose—dependent on his skill in attention—a worldly joy characterized as elation, which is a defilement of concentration.
When one slackens the energy of attention in order to suppress what has arisen, there arises coarseness consisting of physical laziness;
when one again exerts energy to suppress that, there arises over-exerted energy;
when one again slackens energy to suppress that, there arises overly lax energy; and when, having suppressed those, one gazes upon divine forms, there arises what is termed longing.

Craving arose; and while he was attending to various forms such as the inferior and so forth in order to suppress that craving, the "perception of diversity"—which consists of distraction toward various objects—arose.
Then, abandoning that and attending to only one [object], there arose "over-contemplation," which is excessive reflection on forms.
He saw the "illumination," meaning the light produced by the preliminary work. And yet, "I do not see the forms."
The meaning should be understood as occurring in the order of its arising: “Because my attention was intent upon the preliminary radiance, I did not see forms with the divine eye.
That which belongs to humans is called *mānusaka*; it refers to gross forms within the range of the human eye.
Because that very same thing is the sphere of human vision, it is called the "human vicinity" (*manussūpacāra*); thus he said, “having passed beyond the human vicinity.”
"By seeing forms" means by seeing forms that are distant, subtle, and so forth.
Since the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) necessarily arises without the preliminary work of adverting to a form-object that exists prior to it,
and since a form that is arising or ceasing cannot be its object because of its weakness, [it does not arise in that way].
The death-consciousness arises precisely at the moment of the dissolution of kamma-born matter, and the rebirth-linking consciousness arises at the moment of conception;

therefore, he says "at the moment of death," and so forth. Here, the term "seeing beings" is used in reference to a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānena*), as in the passage beginning "those who are passing away," and so on, where it refers specifically to the seeing of forms.
The phrase "whether beautiful or ugly" is stated with the intention that the word *vaṇṇa* denotes shape as well.

As in the passages beginning with "having manifested the form of a great king of elephants," and so forth. He said "gone to a good destination" (*sugati*) because they have gone to a beautiful destination;
thus he says "gone to a good destination" (*sugatigate*). But by this phrase—namely, by the phrase "according to their deeds" (*yathākammūpage*)—[the meaning is established].

Having seen the color of the bodies of those in hell, which are split apart by the falling of fire-flames, weapons, and so forth, [this is understood] by the subsequent sense-sphere impulsion-moments (*kāmāvacara-javana*) themselves.
Since even their experience of suffering is dependent upon the fruit of vision, it is said that "it is merely the function of the divine eye.

"He attends in this way" means that, desiring to know those karmas, he enters the foundational jhāna, and having emerged from it, he attends by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*) with the thought, "What indeed... and so forth. Then, taking that karma as his object, [he sees it].

The construction is as follows: that knowledge which arises in conjunction with the fine-material-sphere fourth jhāna, having arisen after the preliminary work (*parikamma*) of adverting (*āvajjana*) and so forth, is called "knowledge of the passing away according to kamma" (*yathākammupaga-ñāṇa*). The same method applies to the seeing of devas.

"A separate preliminary work" means, as in the case of the knowledge of past lives and so on, [it occurs] without the preliminary work for the divine eye-knowledge (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), but separately.
There is no preliminary work (*parikamma*). However, some here say: "There is no need for the preliminary work of entering the foundational jhāna;

rather, immediately after the mental attention [thinking] 'What indeed is this action? and so forth, the action [occurs]. Taking that action and its associated states as the object under the heading of 'action,' the path of absorption arises.
The same applies to knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*); therefore, there is no separate preliminary work."
They say, “There is no separate preliminary work; it is said that these succeed together with the divine eye.

This should not be accepted, because even for those who have attained mastery over the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), these do not arise without the preliminary work consisting of the foundational jhāna and so forth.

Furthermore, since there is no such thing as a “separate preliminary work” apart from the mere foundational jhāna and its like, it should be understood that these knowledges are accomplished by means of the divine eye alone.
Likewise, regarding the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*): when one desires to know the future course of a being seen with the divine eye,
immediately following the foundational jhāna and so forth, in accordance with the power of his knowledge, there arise all mundane and supramundane phenomena—
comprising the five aggregates included within previous personal existences that are destined to arise in many future aeons, as well as those associated with them and having them as their object.

The construction is as follows: even for the knowledge of future states associated with the fourth jhāna, which arises by taking conventional designation (*sammuti*) as its object at a single moment, there is no separate preliminary work (*parikamma*).
However, some here [hold that] "just as in the case of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*), there is indeed the grasping of names, clans, and so forth; and that..."
At the moment of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), it occurs only during the subsequent moments of sense-sphere impulsion (*kāmāvacara-javana*),

because at the time of conceptualizing a name, other conceptualizations are impossible, and because there is no limit to the arising of the mental object through kamma. However, regarding all phenomena that serve as signs for conceptualization—
even if they exist and are seen simultaneously by direct knowledge— one may subsequently designate them "having such-and-such a name" and so forth, according to one's preference.
A conceptualization arises through a sense-sphere consciousness regarding many forms seen with the eye, such as the conceptualization of a pillar, a jar, and so forth.
And whatever has not been conceptually determined in some respect is also fit for conceptualization; thus, everything is indeed conceptually determined by way of name, clan, and so on.
Just as it is here, so too in the case of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*), the text refers even to that which is merely fit for conceptualization.
They say that [the Blessed One] spoke with the inclusion of the specific designation (*apadesa*) by means of the words "of such-and-such a name," and so forth. Others, however, say:
"The entire range of name, clan, and so on is cognized in a single moment; one merely expresses in speech that which is preferred.

Even they are identical in meaning to the former [view], because even at the time of subsequent expression regarding what was previously seen, it must be conceptually constructed; thus, it is simply the perception of a phenomenon that is subject to conceptual construction (*parikappa*).

This has also been approached by them in terms of its meaning. However, some say: "Because of such statements as 'having passed away from there, he reappeared elsewhere,' it is easy to grasp [the past] together with names, clans, and so forth, through the sequential knowledge of past and future phenomena.
That is indeed incorrect, because it would entail the loss of omniscience due to the impossibility even for Buddhas to know everything simultaneously. In the Pāḷi: "These, alas..."
The passage beginning with "bhonto" (they become) is a demonstration of the mode of operation of the knowledge that follows according to karma (*yathākammupagañāṇa*).
Here, "body, speech, etc. refers to bodily and vocal intimation (*kāyavacīviññatti*). It is called "grave" because it is similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya*);
for if there is no seeking of forgiveness, it becomes an immediate offense. "Of that" refers to the censure which is grave by nature. "Elderly" means elderly solely by age, not by wisdom.
"He does not know even the slightest worldly convention;

he is merely a defiler of assemblies because he acts in a way that should cause shame for us"—having spoken thus with this underlying intention, it should be understood that he reviles him by destroying his reputation for virtue.
By addressing him as "Friend" (Āvuso) and so forth, the Elder, desiring the arising of higher paths in him, revealed himself out of compassion. "He became as before" means:

The intention is that there was no obstruction to the path. "One who is older than oneself" means one who is himself advanced in age. Here too, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "sitting in a squatting posture.
Non-returners and arahants would not forgive for the sake of future restraint, while the rest might do so even out of malice; thus he said, "if he does not forgive him."
And those who... [as before] ...encourage others [to do so], they too should be understood as undertaking actions based on wrong view.

Regarding the phrases "endowed with virtue" and so forth, in the primary sense, the one standing at the stage of the supreme path (the Arahant) is intended, because for him alone there is the certainty of attaining final knowledge (*aññā*).

Alternatively, those in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) who are established in virtue and the other qualities are also included, because for them too there is the certainty of the arising of final knowledge. "Final knowledge" (*aññā*) refers to the fruit of Arhatship. "Thus accomplished" means:
Thus it is regarding rebirth. Just as that [rebirth] which is non-detached rebirth, so too this [is the meaning]: "he is reborn in this hell.
To show that which was indicated by the phrase "it is of such a nature," the passage beginning with "that speech" and so forth was spoken. "That speech" refers to the disparagement of the Noble Ones.
"The mind" refers to the mind that disparages the Noble Ones. "The view" refers to the disparagement of the Noble Ones.

The view that sees the absence of fault. Having confessed the transgression with the thought, "I shall abandon all this," yet not having abandoned it nor relinquished it by way of seeking forgiveness;

"just as he was brought and placed in hell" means that just as he was brought and stationed in hell by the hell-wardens, so indeed is he stationed in hell—this being certain for him solely due to his reviling of the Noble Ones.
The intention is that rebirth in hell occurs as a result that comes about through the path, just as a fruit is produced.
Because wrong view is the root of all evil, those faults for which it is supreme—that is, primary—are "faults for which wrong view is supreme.
The meaning is that among all faults, wrong view alone is the supreme fault. [This applies] to one who dies without being free from lust.

"Beyond" (paraṃ) means precisely the grasping for another existence; thus he said, "after death" (paraṃ maraṇā), meaning "immediately thereafter, in the seizing of the aggregates that have been reborn.

"With the breakup of the body" (kāyassa bhedā) refers to the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya); thus he said, "with the breaking [of the body] by the very severance of that by which one stands.
"Ayo" is merit (puñña), because from it one goes (eti) toward happiness. "Of āya" means of arrival, or of the cause. One goes (ayati) by means of desirable objects and so forth.
"It occurs" means arising; it is the gratification. "Like an asura" means like a peta-asura.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (14):
"By penetrating the characteristic through its essential mark" means by penetrating without confusion the characteristic that is designated as the intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

"Nibbattika" means production. "Having reached that state" means having approached that *nibbāna*, which is the state or cause in the sense of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for the path.

"Non-arising" means the cause of non-arising. "By way of defilements" means by way of those defilements—the exhaustion of which through the destruction of these taints (*āsava*) constitutes this knowledge as the "knowledge of the destruction of the taints. By way of those taints...
The meaning is: "by way of another mode" (*pakārantarato*) because all defilements are included therein by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāyato*).

Although the word "he fully understood" (*abbhaññāsi*) is used in the text in the past tense, the description is made in the present tense—"knowing thus, seeing thus"—by taking into account the presentness of each respective act of knowing at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya-kāle*). Precisely through the liberation from the taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the others...
Because of its inseparable connection with that, liberation should also be understood as being seen through the taints (*diṭṭhāsava*).

The knowledge "birth is exhausted" occurs by way of reviewing the destruction of the defilements, while the knowledge "the holy life has been lived," and so forth, occurs by way of reviewing the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna;
thus it is said: "Its plane [is indicated] by 'birth is exhausted,' etc."

In this context, "ground" (*bhūmi*) means the object (*visaya*). Although effort directed toward the destruction of birth is possible even throughout the three periods of time, the passage beginning with "But that which...
was stated in order to show the purposefulness of making such an effort toward that [destruction of birth] and its fruit, which is the non-arising of future aggregates.
For it is by means of the path that defilements are destroyed, as indicated by the phrase "by the non-cultivation of the path," and so forth.
In the future, there will be the birth of the aggregates; however, when those defilements have been destroyed by the Path, the aggregates will not be born.

Because the defilements are simultaneous with their effects, even if they are destroyed by some condition in the manner described regarding birth, their destruction occurs only through the arising of the Noble Path—which is opposed to the defilements—at a moment within the mental continuum, by way of the encounter with a contrary condition.

Because they do not arise in the future—just as the non-arising of seeds in the future due to the falling of a mass of fire upon the continuity of seeds—the very non-arising of the aggregates, which are the fruits of defilements, in the future through the absence of defilements characterized by their arising at the moment of the Path, is what is meant by "the destruction of birth" (*jātikkhaya*).
This is the meaning clarified here; therefore, he said: "Because the Path has been cultivated, [the aggregates] have the nature of non-arising."

"By its attainment, birth is exhausted. Herein, this is the meaning: because the Path—consisting in the absence of defilements—has been cultivated and produced, the birth of the aggregates does not arise due to the absence of conditions.

By means of that attainment of the state of being subject to non-arising—which is defined as non-arising in the future—one says, "Birth is exhausted for me," from the standpoint of conventional usage. For conditioned phenomena do not [cease] by another condition...
Destruction occurs; and if it were to occur, there would follow the consequence of its having other conditions and so forth.
The production of a moment contrary to that [existence] is itself the production of its destruction. "That" is to be connected with "he fully understood one whose birth is exhausted.
"To this state" (*itthattāya*): these modes are *itthaṃ*; the state of being so is *itthattaṃ*; for the sake of that. "Showing": he shows by way of conclusion.
The method of commentary on the Discourse on the Threefold Knowledge is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Declaration of Laymanship: 15. *Aññāṇaṃ* (ignorance):

Due to its connection with the word *dhi*, this is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-attha*). *Pādāni*: [accusative plural] "feet. *Yasasā*: by means of fame, that is, by means of a retinue.
*Kotūhalacchare* means "in wonder and in celestial nymphs (*accharā*). *Ayanti* is the word *abhikkanta*.
To show that this is not a repetition (*āmeḍita*) used twice, but rather refers to two distinct meanings, he says "atha vā" and so forth.

*Abhikkanta* is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka-niddesa*) produced through the commonality of meaning without distinction; it remains the same even when considering distinctions such as the excellence of the teaching (*desanāpasāda*).
He said, "It is excellent... [and so on]... my confidence," because it had already been accomplished previously. [The bowl] was placed face-down by someone;
it turned face-down of its own accord. "By means" (*pariyāyehi*) means by ways, or by the reasons that establish its lack of flavor and so forth.
Because the root *gam* is not transitive, both these words—"Gotama" and "refuge"—are not in the accusative case.
Moreover, while the former [formula] was used, the latter was stated as "I go for refuge to Gotama" in order to show that it is a personal declaration (*paccattavacana*).
By this, he shows that the word *iti* has been elided (*luttaniddiṭṭha*). "From evil" (*aghassa*) means from evil (*aghato*), that is, from sin;
for the word is connected with the ablative case (*nissakka*) because it depends upon the word *tāto*. "One who has attained the path and realized cessation" (*adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe*).
By these two phrases as well, he shows that only those established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*) are indicated, and not those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*);
thus he says, "and for one practicing according to the instruction. By the word "in detail" (*vitthāra*), he includes the passage stated thus:

"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them. "Unshakable" (*aneja*) means free from craving. "Non-repulsive" (*appaṭikūla*)...
It is "unopposed" (*aviruddha*) because it illuminates the meaning through non-contradiction; it is "pure" (*suci*) or "exquisite" (*paṇīta*).

It is "skillful" (*paguṇa*) because it must be made proficient by means of speech, or because it is endowed with the distinguished qualities of words and meanings. "Assembled" (*saṃhata*) means joined together or brought into harmony.

"In which" (*yattha*) is connected to "in which pairs of persons" (*yesu purisayugesu*). And those eight are "seers of the Dhamma" (*dhammadaśā*); they are called seers of the Dhamma because they have seen the Noble Dhamma.
Regarding the words "Saraṇam" and so forth, this is the summary of the meaning: the Triple Gem is called a "refuge" (saraṇa) in the sense of protection from fear, harm, and so on.

Going for refuge (saraṇagamana) is the arising of a state of consciousness that proceeds with the aspect of taking that very Triple Gem as one's protection, shelter, and ultimate resort, by virtue of the qualities of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment and the rest.
One who is endowed with such an arising of consciousness has gone for refuge.
It is called "going" (*gacchati*). This going for refuge is twofold, distinguished as mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).

Among these, the supramundane going for refuge is accomplished at the very moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*) through the total eradication of the defilements (*upakkilesa*) associated with going for refuge. The mundane going for refuge proceeds in four ways:
by the surrendering of oneself, such as "I surrender myself to the Buddha," and so forth; and by being devoted to that which has been thus described.

By entering into the state of a pupil, and by prostration. In all these cases, it should be understood that taking refuge occurs solely by way of [the Buddha being] the most excellent and worthy of offerings, and not by way of kinship, fear, or teacherhood.

Thus, for one who pays homage to a sectarian out of kinship and so forth, the refuge is not broken; but for one who pays homage to another out of [mere] worthiness of offerings, the refuge is broken. This is the worldly [view].
The certainty of attaining Nibbāna is the fruit similar to the going for refuge, because one who has gone for refuge is certain to attain Nibbāna in the future.
Furthermore, the attainment of all mundane success and the transcendence of the suffering of the woeful states and so forth are the fruits of benefit.
Regarding this, defilement consists of doubt, wrong knowledge, and the like, with respect to the three objects. Its breach is also twofold, according to whether it is blameworthy or blameless.
In this regard, the first [type of going for refuge] occurs through such acts as bowing down to non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas), preceded by wrong view;
and because it has undesirable results, it is blameworthy (sāvajja). However, the second [type] occurs at the time of death and is blameless (anavajja).
It should be understood that for the supramundane (lokuttara) going for refuge, there is neither defilement (saṃkilesa) nor breach (bheda) in any way whatsoever.

"Who is a lay follower? and so forth is a question concerning the nature and causes of lay followership. In this context, any householder—whether human or non-human—who has gone for refuge in the Three Jewels according to the method described is a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Furthermore, one is called a "lay follower" because they attend upon (*upāsana*) the Triple Gem through such acts as going for refuge.
Their virtue consists of the five abstinences (*veramaṇī*), and their wrong livelihood includes the five types of evil trade, such as trading in weapons and so forth.
His livelihood is the maintenance of life through the Dhamma and in accordance with justice, having abandoned [unrighteous means].
It should be understood that lack of faith, immorality, and so forth, are failures of the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), while their absence constitutes its perfection.
"By way of the dwelling" means by way of the sections consisting of the places for residing, such as inner rooms and the like. "Occurring on this day" means occurring on this very day.

"Confidence, etc. A "limb of the body" (*kāyaṅga*) is a part of the body caused by bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). A "limb of speech" (*vācaṅga*) consists of the lips, tongue, and so forth, which are caused by vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*).

"Without moving" means without causing to shake. By this it is shown that, prior to the occurrence of speech, there is no separate bodily intimation in the form of a modification of the air element (*vāyodhātu*) that serves as a condition for the movement of the places of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*); therefore, there is no intention to be communicated separately [by such a movement].

Non-existence is included within vocal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*) itself because it assists that [intimation].
