Just as, in cases such as scratching the body with the body, a modification of the earth-element (*pathavī-dhātu*) in form—which serves as the cause for the production of sound—is not considered vocal intimation because it does not separately communicate the intention, so too is this [non-existence].
These are called intimations precisely because they communicate the intention; they do not [arise] otherwise.

It is merely because of the state of being a mere modification of the primary elements that serves as the condition for the arising of movement and sound in air and earth. And thus, it should be understood that the non-intimation (*aviññatti*) of the aforementioned types of modifications—which serve as the conditions for the arising of movement and sound in external things such as trees—is thereby established.
Some [commentators] explain "vocal" (*vācaṅga*) as meaning "a constituent part of speech," such as the words "let it be," "well done," and so forth.
They say that this does not accord with the phrase "without moving him. "Having exercised patience" means having given consent.
There is also a reading, "having maintained patience," which means having held [the intention] by way of not going outside. "Facing toward" means having turned his face back toward the Blessed One;
therefore he said, "without departing."
16. Because the verb *yācati* (to request) is transitive, it is said: "The Blessed One was requested for the rains residence.
To make the meaning already stated more explicit, it is said: "even when there is an abundance of crops. This means:
even at such times when [people] give away something of very little value yet take back a great deal of grain and cooked food. *Bhikkhamānā* means "requesting."
“Vuttasassaṃ” means grain that has been sown. “Tattha” means in Verañjā;

by this, he shows the derivation of the qualifying term through its inversion as “salākāvuttā,” meaning “that wherein only stalks (salākā) remain after the grain has been harvested. Alternatively, the derivation should also be understood as:
“Salākāvuttā” means “that wherein all the grain has been harvested (vutta), produced (nibbatta), and gathered (sampanna), leaving only stalks (salākā).”
Therefore he said, “It is simply by means of the tally-sticks that they succeed.
To show the derivation, “Those whose livelihood is stated by means of the tally-stick are ‘tally-stick-dependent’ (salākāvuttā),” the phrase beginning with “by means of the tally-stick” was spoken.
“In the place for preparing grain” means in the place for threshing grain. “Color-examiner” refers to one who inspects coins.
Regarding the phrase *uñchena paggahena*: here, *paggahena* means "by the bowl" (*patteṇa*); the sense is "having taken that.
For it is called a *paggaha* because monks take hold of it by means of it; thus, it is the bowl. Therefore he said: "the alms-gathering (*uñcha*) which is by means of the *paggaha*," and so forth.
Alternatively, *paggahena* means "by taking" (*gahaṇena*); since it follows that the bowl is what should be taken for the purpose of alms-gathering, he said: "having taken the bowl."
The region to the north of the Ganges is the Northern Path (*uttarāpatha*); those whose dwelling is there, or who have come from there, are the Northerners (*uttarāpathaka*).
Therefore he said, "those dwelling in the Northern Path," and so forth. There is also a reading, "Uttarāhakā," which has the same meaning according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*).
"Mandira" means a rest-house (*assasāla*). They also write "Mandara," but that is not correct. And as for that rest-house, because...
They were made in various ways with a circular shape; therefore, they are called "round bowls" (*assamaṇḍalikāyo*).
The region in the southern direction from the Ganges is the Southern Route (*dakkhiṇāpatha*); the people born there are the people of the Southern Route (*dakkhiṇāpathamanussā*).

They consider the Buddha as their own, having the habit of grasping [him] as "mine," thus they are "those who claim the Buddha as their own" (*buddhamāmakā*); the same applies to the others. Thus [ends] the subsequent [section].
When the meaning is grasped according to the method stated: "They seek a portion" means they seek a part. "Suitable for that" means corresponding to that or sufficient for it.
The connection is: "Having obtained [it], it does not happen. Alternatively, the reading is "laddho" (obtained), meaning that those who are attendants do not obtain it at all.
"Kinsman and best" means one who is both a kinsman and superior due to being endowed with most excellent qualities. In such [persons]...

The intention is that, in such circumstances, this alone is appropriate; therefore, during times when material requisites are difficult to obtain, one should not engage in indirect speech or hints, but rather—

abiding in purity of livelihood through the practice of supreme austerity— one should act only as a noble disciple joined with affection for their kinsmen, while discerning material requisites in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention.

"By the enticement of Māra" means by the mental transformation wrought by Māra, that is, by the delusion of the mind. "He might even entice him" means he might entice him toward Uttarakuru or the city of the Thirty-three (Tidasapura).
[As it is said: "In the dispensation of Phussa, I reviled his disciples:
'Eat barley! Consume it! Do not eat rice-gruel!'"—
Because the unwholesome action described in the *Apadāna* had been provided with an opportunity at that time. "Of regular giving" means of a gift determined by the verbal expression, "I shall give.
"Of practiced conduct" refers even to a thing given after having been brought forward by the body. "Is able" means he is capable.
"In brief" means by way of a summary. "With fathom-wide radiance" means extending eighty cubits all around, below and above.
In those places where it is dense, it is a six-colored radiance from which six-colored rays issue forth like water-channels from a pond and spread through the ten directions;
because it appears to be only a fathom in extent, it is called "fathom-wide radiance" (*byāmappabhā*).
Furthermore, because each of the secondary marks (*anubyañjana*) on the Blessed One’s body is endowed with a perfection of radiance that extends into the sky...
They shine forth clearly like the moon, the sun, and so on; therefore, they are said to be unassailable by anything, even by the fathom-wide radiance [of a Buddha].
In the phrase *anatthasañhite*, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-atthe*) with reference to destruction (*ghāta*); thus he says, "destruction of such speech.
Alternatively, it means that the purpose (*attha*) arises here through the teaching of the Dhamma, or that the purpose consisting of the teaching of the Dhamma and so forth arises therein.
This is the origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the present-day incident (*paccuppannavatthu*).
"Taking one" means taking one of the two reasons for the teaching of the Dhamma, namely, the teaching of the Dhamma itself and the formal laying down of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"Or the breaking of the night" is said with reference to going away on some business for seven days and causing the dawn to rise outside [the monastery].
This is because it is mentioned separately as a reason for interrupting the rains-retreat (*vassaccheda*).

By this, it should be understood that going on a seven-day mission for the sake of interrupting the rains-retreat is permitted. "Not for anything" means they do not think highly of themselves on account of any particular quality.
"We shall later resolve upon virtue" refers to a failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*), namely, the proclamation of one's own existing qualities for the sake of a livelihood.
It has been said. "He will despise" means he will look down upon.

Having stated, "‘Venerable’ (āyasmā) is a term of endearment," in reference to its common usage among both high and low persons, he spoke again, "It is a designation for one who possesses weightiness, reverence, and deference," specifically to show its unique application to high-ranking individuals.
In that context, "together with deference (patissaya)" means together with reliance (nissaya).
"Respectful" (*sappatisso*) means having a support (*sanissayo*); the meaning is that it is a word expressing veneration toward those endowed with venerable qualities.

However, in this context, "designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to the word itself. Regarding "the *pappaṭaka*": in the beginning of the eon, there first arose upon the water a substance in the nature of earth, resembling a lump of fresh butter, which had the property of floating even on water, was non-dissolving, extremely smooth and sweet, and many thousands of yojanas in thickness.

The "earth-nourishment" known as the subterranean realm (rasātala): that which was taken by the humans of the first eon out of craving for taste and consumed, which—by the power of their karma—attained a solid state in its upper portion while remaining in its former mode below;
and by the power of which this great earth, together with its mountains, oceans, and forests, does not sink into the waters below.
Remaining undisturbed like a raft upon [still water], it stands motionless; this is the meaning of "the essence of the earth.
Therefore, he said, "the orb of the earth," and so forth. "Abounding" means endowed with sweet flavor; therefore, he said, "sweet-tasting. "Yielding fruit" means having abundant fruit.
Having said "free from flies," he further said "free from fly-spots" to indicate the absence of even the spots where flies might settle.
He shows this. Regarding the thought, "I shall move those living beings dependent on the earth to that place," one might ask:
"In the case of moving by hand even women among humans, non-humans, or animals, does the fault of 'untouchability' (*anāmāsa*) not occur? It does not occur. Why? Because of the statement:

"There is no offense, monks, for one possessing psychic power (*iddhi*) within the domain of psychic power. For that very reason, the Blessed One, without indicating the fault of untouchability, [spoke of] even the overturning (*vipallāsa*).
He said, “May beings obtain [it]”; this refers to a small village. A *sāpaṇa* is a large market town (*nigama*). "By the placing of the foot" means by the setting down of the foot.
Commentary on the Discussion Requesting the Formulation of the Discipline (Vinaya-paññatti):
"From the very root of the formulation of the Discipline" refers to the heavy rules such as the *pārājikas*, as well as the other training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

This was said with reference to the fact that for the most part [the rules] had not yet been laid down according to the sequence of the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and not because they were entirely unestablished.

For that very reason, the Elder requested of the Blessed One both the laying down of the training rules and the recitation of the Pātimokkha together, saying: "May you lay down and recite the training rules for the disciples.
Indeed, in the Khandhakas, [this was requested by] the Elder Ānanda and others...
Even prior to the going forth of the venerable Rāhula, the training rule was laid down: "Monks, a son must not be given the going forth without the permission of his mother and father;
whoever should give him the going forth incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In this very *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) as well, it says: "Even cooking for oneself... is not permitted," and: "The breaking of the night, the breaking of the rains-retreat..."
And because it is stated, "or has not been made," it is understood that there was already a prohibition against cooking for oneself and so forth.

Thus, although several training rules (*sikkhāpada*) have been laid down, one should understand that the statement, "The Teacher, Sāriputta, has not yet laid down a training rule for his disciples," refers to those *pārājika* offenses and others that have not yet been prescribed. Having turned back from objects of various kinds, correctly...

"One who is mentally absorbed in a single object is said to be ‘withdrawn’ (*paṭisallīna*); thus it says, ‘having attained oneness (*ekībhāva*)’, which means having attained seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*).
‘For a long time’ (*ciram*) is used in the accusative case to express continuous duration.
‘By sixteenfold wisdom’ refers to the teaching in the *Anupada Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*: ‘Bhikkhus, he is one of great wisdom...’"

“Sāriputta is one of broad wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom”—thus there are the six kinds of wisdom mentioned here, as well as the wisdom of the nine successive dwellings in attainment and the wisdom of the path to Arahantship; it is with respect to this sixteenfold wisdom that he is described.
Those Buddhas whose disciples are seen in the Suddhāvāsa heavens are indeed those who are renowned in the world.

Only Vipassī and the others are mentioned here, not the other previous Buddhas. For that very reason, it should be understood that even in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, the deities themselves took up only those who were well-known to them, and not others.
19. "Becoming listless" means they became inactive due to a lack of purpose, not out of laziness; hence he said:
"Not through laziness or weariness," and so forth. "Because of faultlessness" means because of the absence of faults that give rise to transgressions of body and speech.

It was stated, "by way of the seven classes of offenses (*āpatti-kkhandha*) and so forth," because the training precepts (*ovāda-sikkhāpada*) such as "one shall not kill a living being, nor take what is not given," and so on, are actually present.
Since it is said "each time" with reference to the final day of each respective six-year period, this [term] here is used in relation to that.
This is a term of inclusion (*sāmivacana*). The connection is: "The entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus throughout the whole of Jambudīpa observed the Uposatha.

In such passages as "Patience is supreme," *khanti*—which is defined as endurance—is called the "supreme austerity" because it involves the burning away of the defilements that cause one to find fault with the seven conditioned phenomena produced by them.
Nibbāna is supreme among all phenomena because it has emerged from craving, which is defined as "desiring" (*vāna*).
The Buddhas call them "the best. One who, due to the absence of the aforementioned patience, commits the killing of living beings or inflicts such things as mutilation and beating;
one who harms others through seizing the property of others, violating the wives of others, and so forth;

and one who torments another with falsehood, slander, harsh speech, and the like—such a person, by virtue of the absence of having cast out evil (*bāhitapāpatā*) or the absence of having stilled evil (*samitapāpatā*), is not truly gone forth.
The meaning is that one is not even a recluse (*samaṇa*).

The non-arising of all evil through the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), the attainment and accomplishment of the wholesome through mundane concentration and insight (*samādhi-vipassanā*), and the purification and clarification of one’s own mind through all the paths and fruits—this is the instruction and teaching of the Buddhas. Or, "non-reproach" refers to speech.
Not censuring anyone. "Non-injury" means not causing injury to anyone by way of the body, and the restraint of oneself within the remaining precepts known as the Pātimokkha.
The association with virtue dependent on the requisites, characterized as purity of livelihood consisting in moderation in food;

and, by way of that [purity], the restraint of the sense faculties; and, by way of that [restraint], dwelling in the forest, which is designated as a remote lodging. In these things that are thus proclaimed:

The construction is as follows: "That which is the establishment in the Great Noble Lineage—consisting of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation—and the application and devoted practice toward the mundane and supramundane concentration known as *adhicitta* by way of its production, this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
The phrase "as long as the dispensation lasts" is stated because there is no longer a formal *āṇā-pātimokkha* (commandment code) after the Parinibbāna. From that point onward...
There was also no recitation of the *ovāda-pātimokkha*, for only Buddhas recite it, not disciples. Regarding the phrase "during the first enlightenment" (*paṭhamabodhiyaṃ*):
this refers to the period delimited by twenty years from the [date of] enlightenment. However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated:

"Of the forty-five years [following enlightenment], the first fifteen years constitute the 'first enlightenment'"; this is reckoned from the time the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were first promulgated.

"But from that time onwards, they recited only the *āṇā-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha by way of command)"—this was said with reference to the period when the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were being laid down, having completed [the recitation] according to the sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation itself. "An impossibility, an absence of occasion" (*aṭṭhānam anavakāso*) is a negation of the cause by way of negating the respective causes and conditions.
"By which" (*yam*) means "by which cause. "In an impure assembly" (*aparisuddhāya parisāya*) means because of the mixture with shameless individuals (*alajjī-puggala*).
Regarding an impure assembly: it is not only for Buddhas that the recitation of the Pātimokkha is improper in an impure assembly;

rather, this applies to disciples as well. However, the responsibility of purifying the assembly through means such as formal accusation (*codanā*) and reminding (*sāraṇā*), and then conducting the communal life together, rests solely upon the disciples.
The Buddhas, on the other hand, having prescribed the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) and taught the procedures for performing the Uposatha and other rites, leave them to carry out these duties.

They did not perform the acts of admonition, remonstrance, and so forth; for that reason, the Blessed One, without reciting the Pātimokkha before an impure assembly, remained silent throughout the entire night.
And the monks, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, expelled the person of impure character.
Therefore, even for disciples, once they have recognized that the assembly is impure, the performance of formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the Uposatha, [is prohibited].
It should be understood that it is not permissible [to do so] except when it causes an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Of the face-to-face disciples" (*sammukhasāvakānaṃ*) means of all the disciples who went forth during the lifetime of the Buddhas in their presence.
The word *uḷāra* is mentioned again in the phrase "or by way of families possessing abundant and excellent wealth and so forth" for the purpose of indicating an especially high degree of excellence.

It is said. By the word "etc. (ādi), it should be understood that the inclusion of "exalted," "middling," "inferior," and so forth is intended. The connection is: "Those later disciples caused [the tradition] to disappear.
Even if a training rule had not been laid down, if the disciples were of the same caste and so forth, they would [preserve] the texts inherited from their own families.

They would not have lost [the teaching], just like the word of the Blessed One. However, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) had not yet been laid down, and because these monks were not of the same caste and so forth, they caused it to perish. To show this meaning, it was said: "Because they had the same names...
therefore they harassed one another," and so on. But in the section concerning long endurance, regarding the fact that the disciples were of various castes and so forth:

It should be understood that the long duration of the Dispensation (sāsana) is due to its completeness, even though the laying down of the training rules (sikkhāpada-paññatti) is common [to all Buddhas].
If this is so, why do not all Buddhas lay down all the training rules at once? Because the laying down of the training rules is not the sole cause for the long duration of the Dispensation;
rather, it is because disciples, having received the Dhamma and Vinaya for the future, [preserve them].
There is also the occurrence of persons who are to be trained; therefore, when such persons exist, the Buddhas prescribe the training rules (sikkhāpada), and not when they do not.
Thus, it should be understood that even the "complete prescription" is stated as a cause for the long endurance of the Dispensation, because it indicates the existence of those to be trained.
In the Pāḷi, regarding the passage "he exhorted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus numbering one thousand...," here [the term] is delimited by the number one thousand.
It is like [the usage] in such passages as "the Saṅgha of a thousand" or "a thousand world-systems. The construction is: "that thousand is the community of bhikkhus.

Since the word *sahassa* (thousand) is singular in number, one should understand that although it was stated as "of a thousand bhikkhus," the plural designation "being exhorted" (*ovadiyamānānaṃ*) was employed out of regard for its constituent members.
Regarding the phrase "their minds were liberated from the taints without clinging" (*anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu*): here, *āsavehi* is the instrumental case used in the sense of the agent;
*cittāni* is the nominative plural; and *vimucciṃsu* is the passive construction. Therefore, the meaning to be understood here is:
"by means of the taints acting as agents, their minds were liberated without being grasped through the act of making them objects [of clinging]. Thus should the sense be taken.

He said: "For their minds," and so forth. In the phrase "by which taints" (*yehi āsavehi*), the instrumental case is used here in the sense of the agent (*kattuatthe*). "They were liberated" (*vimucciṃsu*) is a passive construction (*kamma-sādhana*).
"Those" (*te*) refers to the taints (*āsava*). "Those" (*tāni*) refers to the minds; this is the plural accusative case (*upayoga-bahuvacana*).

"They were liberated" (*vimucciṃsu*) is an active construction (*kattu-sādhana*); the meaning is "they caused [the minds] to be liberated. "They were liberated without grasping" means that those minds [were liberated] by way of the object (*ārammaṇa-vasena*).

The meaning is that, having not grasped [anything], those taints became released from those minds. Alternatively, "from taints" (*āsavehi*) is an ablative expression, while "were liberated" (*vimucciṃsu*) is an agentive construction. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows:
by not clinging to any conditioned phenomenon through craving and so forth, the minds became liberated. It refers back to the preceding statement in one [text].
The meaning of "regard for the statement spoken as 'in the terrifying forest thicket'" is that it refers back to that preceding statement; thus he said, "that which was spoken," and so forth.
"Terrifying-making" (*bhiṃsanakataṃ*) means the making, the performance, or the action of terror (*bhiṃsana*);
showing the sense of "in that action of terrifying," he said, "by the action of terrifying. "It terrifies" (*bhiṃsayati*)...

“Terrifying” (*bhiṃsana*) means it is indeed terrifying; although it should be called “the state of being terrifying” (*bhiṃsanakatta*), the *ta*-sound has been elided, and thus he says “or else,” etc., to show the meaning by another method.

“Of most beings” (*bahutarānaṃ sattānaṃ*) is an explanation of the phrase “for the most part” (*yebhuyyena*). By that, [he also explains] the phrase “anyone whatsoever” (*yo koci*) as “whosoever enters.”

He shows that the meaning should be understood through various aspects according to the context—that is, because it is possible for the meaning to apply to whichever [Buddhas] enter [parinibbāna], and among them, to the greater number.
"Conclusion" (*nigamana*) refers to the summary of the meaning as it has been stated regarding the subject matter. Herein, this is the sequence of the conclusion:
"For, Sāriputta, regarding the three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī, after their own parinibbāna, by way of the scriptures..."
Due to the absence of individuals who needed to be trained, he was weary and indifferent regarding the detailed formulation of training rules for their sake;
yet, out of compassion for those disciples endowed with the necessary potential, he felt no weariness or lack of enthusiasm when,
even traveling to terrifying forest groves, he would read the minds of others with his own mind and teach the Dhamma to bring about their attainment of the paths and fruits.
"It was not because of the teaching of the Dhamma and Vinaya in detail, Sāriputta;
this is the cause, this is the reason why the holy life of the three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī did not endure for long.
"By way of pairs of persons" means the period during which pairs of persons appear; by way of that, meaning by way of persons. "The very last one":
One who went forth on the day of the Parinibbāna was like Subhadda. Regarding the statement "one hundred and sixty thousand years," this is said starting from the Blessed One’s birth;
however, it should be understood that if calculated from the time of his Enlightenment (Bodhi), the number would be less.
"Only two" means there were exactly two pairs of persons: one while the Blessed One was still living, and one after he had attained Parinibbāna.
20-1. *Asambhuṇantena* means by one who does not attain. *Ko anusandhīti*: what is the connection? The meaning is: what is the relation of this to the preceding discourse?
*Yaṃ vuttanti*: that which was requested; such is the meaning. *Yesūti*: regarding those states of transgression. *Nesanti*: of those taints (*āsava*) pertaining to the present life and so forth.
*Tetīti*: those states of transgression. *Ñātiyeva*: because they revolve around [the self] by way of being grandfather, father, son, and so on, they are called "revolving ones" (*parivaṭṭa*).
The circle of relatives. "Become worldly bait" means that, having become included within the world, it is called "worldly bait" because it is to be grasped by the defilements.

"By way of the summary of going forth" means by way of the portal of going forth, such as the conferring of the ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "This" refers to the non-performance of sexual intercourse and so forth.
"Firmness" is the capacity for the proclamation of the training rules. "Scabrous skin" means pale skin, or natural skin.

"Of beautiful complexion. "The rest" refers to the demonstration of how the remaining words are to be construed. Now, demonstrating the application of the meaning, he says: "Or this [is] below," and so forth.
Therein, the word *vā* (or) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used for what is well-known (*pasiddhiyaṃ*); the meaning is: "For this very thing is below.
He demonstrates the meaning of the phrase "then the Teacher" with the words "Then the Teacher. "Having planted" means in the place where it has been furrowed.
Having increased the raw meat evenly. "In his own teacherhood" means in his status as a teacher or in the duties of a teacher.
"By way of abundance" means by way of being plentiful. "Emerging improperly" means adhering through a wrong method;
the meaning is that they perceive things erroneously. "Mixing essence with essence" means mixing a state that is blameworthy with a state that is blameless.
"Uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ" means that which is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya; the meaning is: "having acted in such a way that the Dhamma and the Vinaya will perish.
"In this matter" (imasmiṃ atthe) means in this context concerning the Saṅgha. "Radiant" (pabhassaro) means having the nature of shining.
"Of such a name and such a clan" (evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto) means that this venerable one is endowed with the name and clan of a stream-enterer; he is called thus.

“Stream-enterer” (sotāpanna) is connected with the preceding term. Regarding the phrase “one whose nature is not to fall into states of woe” (avinipātadhamma), here the word *dhamma* denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
And in terms of meaning, that [nature] is the unwholesome states such as wrong view which cause one to be cast into the states of misery; thus he said, “those states,” and so forth.
Now, in order to show the meaning by way of intrinsic nature alone, he stated, “or falling into states of woe,” and so forth. “Destined” (*niyata*) means within the interval of seven existences.
"One destined for final Nibbāna within the present aggregates. He states the reason for this: "one whose ultimate goal is full enlightenment" (sambodhiparāyaṇo). 22.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" (anudhammatā) means a nature that conforms to the supramundane Dhamma.

"Having granted the inclusion of the invitation ceremony" (pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ datvā) means having given consent by saying, "We shall perform the invitation ceremony on the coming full moon day"; the meaning is that he postponed the invitation ceremony.
By this method, it is shown that it is permissible for anyone to postpone the *pavāraṇā* by some condition or other.
"On the first day of the month of Māgasira" is stated according to the lunar month; the meaning is: on the first day (*pāṭipada*) immediately following the full moon of the latter *Kattika*.
"On the first day of the month of Phussa"—here too the same principle applies. And this is merely an illustration for those to be trained (*veneyya*).

Because he remained in that very place for one, two, three, four, or even five months following the month of Phussa—due to the lack of ripeness [of beings]—and only completed his wandering tour during the remaining months.
As for the phrase "in ten thousand world-systems," this is stated with reference to the devas and brahmas;
however, those among humans who are to be enlightened exist only in this very world-system. As for humans in other world-systems...
In order to inspire the desire for rebirth within this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), she gazes upon infinite world-systems and performs a miracle of instruction suited to them.
Regarding the word "āyāma," he states that the prefix *ā-* has the same meaning as "āgaccha" (come), thus saying, "Come, Yāmā"; [it is like] "ehi gacchāma" (come, let us go).
The meaning [of the passage] is as follows: "Tawny like molten gold" (*suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāhi*) means tawny like liquid molten gold;

the sense is that they are golden-colored. In the canonical text, regarding the phrases "we have been invited" (*nimantitāmhā*) and so forth, the construction is either "we, having completed the rains-retreat, have been invited" or "there are those who, having completed the rains-retreat, have been invited."
"Yanti" means "whatever kind of gift there may be. "No natthīti" means "it does not exist for us";
"no" is an explanation of this, meaning "there is none. "Etthāti" means "in the household life. "Tanti" refers to that reason or that duty. "Kutoti" means "from what cause?
"Yanti" means "by which reason or by which duty. In the second interpretation of the meaning, "etthāti" is explained as "in this."
"Within three months": *taṃ* refers to that gift (*deyyadhamma*). "And therein" (*tattha ca*) means in wholesome states (*kusala*).

"Having thoroughly incited" means by producing a state of sharpness and intensity. "Having showered" means having let fall the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma which pertains to future latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). "On whichever day" means on whatever day.
"In pattuṇṇa and pattapaṭa cloths" means in pattuṇṇa cloth and Chinese silk (*cīnapaṭa*). "Jars" (*tumbāni*) means oil vessels made of leather.

"Having followed up" (*anubandhitvā*) means having pursued [them]. The word *abhirata* is used here as a synonym for "inclination"; thus he says, "according to their inclinations" (*yathājjhāsaya*), and so forth.
*Soreyya* and the others are the cities of Soreyya and so on, which formed the route for the Great Pilgrimage (*mahāmaṇḍalacārikā*).
*Payāgapatiṭṭhāna* is the name both of a particular bathing place (*tittha*) on the Ganges and of the village situated near it. From the *Samantapāsādikā*.
It is called *Samantapāsādikā* because it generates complete confidence on all sides;
it belongs to that [work]. However, those modes with reference to which the term "on all sides" (*samantato*) is used are set forth in detail by the passage beginning with "In this regard...

(*tatthidaṃ*). Therein, regarding what has been called the commentary, namely the *Samantapāsādikā*: [The text continues: "In this regard, 'the Samantapāsādikā' refers to the commentary that has been spoken; therein, in that *Samantapāsādikā*..."
The construction is as follows: "In the state of being entirely pleasing, this is the statement of the verses that will be spoken.

It should be understood that the classification of the *nidāna* (introductions) is shown by way of the external introduction (*bāhiranidāna*), the internal introduction (*abbhantaranidāna*), and the introduction to the training rules (*sikkhāpadanidāna*). Some say: "The elucidation of the Theravāda is the demonstration of the classification of the *vatthu* (bases).

It is also appropriate to say: "It is the demonstration of the classification of the present-day *vatthu* for the training rules. Regarding the "introduction to the training rules" (*sikkhāpadanidāna*):
However, one should understand that specific locations such as Vesālī are the grounds for the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "In this" refers to the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The connection is with the phrase "for the wise who see clearly"; therefore, it should be construed thus: "Therefore, this [work] proceeds precisely as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Thus ends the *Vimativinodanī*, a commentary on the Vinaya-ṭīkā, the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The method of commentary on the Verañja section is finished.
1. The Section on Defeats (Pārājika-khaṇḍa) 1.
The First Defeat (Paṭhama-pārājika).
Commentary on the Section on Sudinna (Sudinnabhāṇavāra-vaṇṇanā) 24.
The sale of merchandise for profit and the lending of goods at interest is called "employing goods.

The effort to recover the principal of such employed goods together with its increase is called "recovery" (uddhāra). [This refers to] that which was forgotten, such as "it was given on such-and-such a day," and so forth.

"Recollection" refers to the arousing of mindfulness and so forth. "Fourfold" means either by way of the four classes—khattiyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and ascetics—or by way of the four types of persons, such as bhikkhus and others.
Regarding the phrase "having seen this, it occurred to him": this word *disvāna* (having seen) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetuatthe*), because the agents are not identical;
just as in the expression, "Having drunk ghee, there is strength," so too in other such instances. "A clansman capable [of attaining the goal]" means...
This was stated by way of the mere nature of the proximate cause (*upanissaya*), not because of being in one's final existence (*pacchimabhavika*).

For that very reason, due to the transgression committed through association with unwholesome friends such as his mother, an obstacle to his attainment arose on account of the remorse that subsequently arose.

It is impossible for anyone to create an obstacle for those in their final existence who have received a prophecy (*byākaraṇa*) regarding previous Buddhas. For this very reason, [the cases of] the Elder Aṅgulimāla and others...
"Even after committing unwholesome deeds, they remained indeed perfected in their attainment. "The final mind" (*carimaka-citta*) refers to the death-moment consciousness (*cuti-citta*).
Regarding the term *saṅkhalikhita*, he says "washed," etc., explaining it as "that which has been written like a conch shell, rubbed, and washed.

Because of its connection with the prefix *adhi-*, the word *agāra* takes the accusative case in the sense of a locative; thus he says, "in the midst of the home" (*agāramajjhe*). [The robes] were dyed with an astringent taste.

Regarding the term *kāsāyāni*, he says: "Because they are yellowed by an astringent taste (*kasāyarasa-pītatāya*). For since it is produced from an astringent substance, the taste itself is also called "astringent taste" (*kasāyaraso*).

26. When the word *jānāti* does not have the sense of "making known," then those learned in the science of grammar maintain that the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental, as in examples such as *sappino jānāti* ("he knows by means of ghee") and *madhuno jānāti* ("he knows by means of honey"). Therefore, he says: "by some suffering... (*kiñci dukkhena*).
"You do not experience. The meaning is "you do not experience by means of any suffering"; for here too, in the word *kiñci*, the locative case ending has been elided in the sense of the instrumental.
For this very reason, he will say later: "In both alternatives, the elision of the case-ending of the first word must be understood as being identical to that of the subsequent word.
However, when the word *jānāti* has the sense of "remembering," then—as in examples such as *mātu sarati* ("he remembers his mother")—it functions accordingly.
Grammarians learned in the science of language state that the genitive case is used in the sense of "utility" (upayoga); thus he says: "Alternatively, the meaning is 'some suffering does not perish'.

The meaning of "does not perish" is that some suffering has not been experienced. "In both alternatives" refers to the second and third alternatives stated by way of the meanings of "experiencing" and "perishing.
"Of the preceding word" refers to the word *kiñci* ("some"). "By the subsequent word" refers to the word *dukkhassa* ("of suffering").

In the case of the genitive case used as a possessive pronoun (*sāmivacana*), where one should have said "of some suffering" (*kassaci dukkhassa*), it should be understood that "something of suffering" (*kiñci dukkhassa*) is used by way of elision (*lopa*).
Regarding the phrase "even by death we [shall reach] you," the word "you" (*te*) is shown to have the sense of accompaniment (*sahattha*);
furthermore, to demonstrate its meaning through the instrumentive case (*karaṇa*), an alternative meaning is stated: "or we shall undergo separation from you."
28. "Gandhabbas" refers to singers. "Naṭas" refers to stage actors. "Nāṭakas" refers to acrobats and the like.

Since one who provides for oneself with pleasant requisites is said to be "sporting" or "playing," therefore, in the second interpretation of the meaning, the words "he sports" and so forth are stated.
Regarding the phrase "giving and bestowing gifts" and so on: here, "giving" (dāna) refers to constant giving, while "bestowing" (padāna) refers to special giving.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes virtue (*sīla*) and the other perfections.

30. "The fourteen types of alms-food" refers to: alms-food for the Sangha (*saṅghabhatta*), designated alms-food (*uddesabhatta*), invited alms-food (*nimantana*), ticket alms-food (*salāka*), fortnightly alms-food (*pakkhika*), Uposatha alms-food (*uposathika*), first-of-the-month alms-food (*pāṭipadika*), alms-food for newcomers (*āgantuka*), alms-food for those departing (*gamika*), alms-food for the sick (*gilāna*), alms-food for those attending the sick (*gilānupaṭṭhāka*), and alms-food for the duty-rotation of the monastery (*vihāra-dhura-vārabhatta*).

These are the fourteen kinds of food. Furthermore, it should be understood that among those dependent on the three requisites such as lodgings, the remaining dhutaṅgas are also included by virtue of the inclusion of the primary factors, such as the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññakaṅga).

"Of the Vajjis" means of the Vajji kings. "Among the Vajjis" is a plural form used with reference to the country; the meaning is "in the country named Vajji. The five strands of sensual pleasure (pañcakāmaguṇa) alone...

"Use and enjoyment" (*upabhogaparibhoga*) refer to things that are to be used and enjoyed; since items such as clothing for women are the requisites for those [enjoyments], he said, "by means of which for them," and so forth.

"Because of being a strict alms-food eater" (*ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikatta*) means because of being endowed with the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of a strict alms-food eater, accompanied by the remaining ascetic practices;
therefore he said, "desiring to go on a sequential alms-round."

31. *Ābhidosika*: "Dosā" means night. That which has been rained upon or stored during that [night] is *ābhidosika*. Alternatively, that which has reached or passed the time of dawn (*abhidosa*) is *ābhidosika*. Therefore, he said: "of that which has passed one night," and so forth. 32.

*Udakakañjiya* refers to both drinking water, water for rinsing, and rice-gruel (*yāgu*). "Tathā" is used in the sense of conjunction. *Anokappanā* is non-acceptance; *amarisana* is intolerance. 34. *Taddhitalopa*:
Regarding what should be called "petāmaha" (grandfather), meaning "come from the grandfather" (*pitāmaha*), there is the elision of the cause for the *taddhita* suffix.
The meaning is: "having elided the letter *e*. Those whose wealth has been taken are the debtors (*iṇāyikā*).

"Obstructed" (*palibuddho*) means one who has been hindered by such injunctions as "Do not go," "Do not eat," and so forth; the sense is that he is oppressed. 35. "By oneself" (*attanā*) means personally.
This belongs to the co-owners (*sapati*), the masters of the wealth; thus it is "property" (*sāpateyya*), which is wealth. That very thing is "fortune" (*vibhavo*).
36. "They break" means that they break even before being grasped. Regarding the phrase "even what is given is the rebirth-linking":
it is said that for a being who has arisen depending upon the semen given by the father, even that rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is called "given" by him.
Alternatively, here the semen itself is called "rebirth-linking" because it is the support for the rebirth-linking; therefore he says, "it quickly establishes itself."
For there is no rule that a being must arise at the very moment of the father's union, because the semen alone has such a rule for its implantation.

However, once the semen is implanted, for as long as seven days or up to half a month, that remains the field for the formation of the embryo, since the mother’s flesh and the trace of blood are always present. This was also the case previously regarding the training rules that were laid down.
"Because it was not laid down as a training rule due to its non-existence" means that, in this first *pārājika* training rule, it is stated that [the offense] was not established.
"Of such a nature" means having such a grave character, that is, being the basis for a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa*;
therefore he said, "He laid down only the remaining five groups of minor offenses. The connection is with the phrase "whatever danger [there might be]."
"From the movement produced by bodily intimation" means from the motion generated by bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
By the restrictive particle "only" (*teneva*), those causes for taking conception that were excluded are also shown; thus, the passage beginning with "But what...
was stated. Therein, bodily contact is mentioned by way of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) on the part of both parties. [In contrast,] it belongs to the woman alone...
The act of clutching the navel is mentioned separately because it occurs through the influence of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).

For when the mother of the wise Sāma, having conceived affection for her son's birth, was clutching his navel, her mind was agitated by sensual lust; otherwise, the birth of a son would have been impossible.
Some also say that Sakka created the signs for the arising of her sensual lust, on account of the specific occasion.
It should be understood that this "grasping at the navel" is mentioned separately from physical contact.
By the grasping of the navel by Maṅgalikā, the birth of Maṇḍabya occurred for the wise Mātaṅga.
A scorpion crawled over the navel of Caṇḍapajjota’s mother and entered it; by that, the birth of Caṇḍapajjota occurred—thus he said, "in this same manner," and so forth.

"Those who come" refers to Sudinna’s former wife. "With reference to which" means with reference to that misconduct. By the phrase "the mother and father are assembled," he indicates the origin of the semen;
by the phrase "and the mother is in her season," he indicates the origin of the blood.
"Gandhabba" refers to a being destined for that state; it means "one who is to go. [This is] because of the *ta*-sound...

And here the letter *dha* has been substituted [for *bba*]. Alternatively, *gandhabbas* are actors and dancers; because he assumes various forms in various states of existence just like them, he too is called a "gandhabba.
Having been reborn there even after the moment of the parents' union, within seven days, he is called "present" (*paccupaṭṭhita*).
"Of the womb" (*gabbhassa*) means of that which is accompanied by the *kalala* stage of physical form.

[This refers] to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). For here, that [consciousness] is intended by the term "womb" (*gabbha*), as in such expressions as "she conceived a womb" (*sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhī*).

The connection is: "his misconduct toward her. In the Canon, immediately after the passage "O, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is indeed free from worms and free from danger," one must supply the words "in that Saṅgha of bhikkhus" and [understand]: "by Sudinna... danger was produced."
The construction should be understood as follows. *Itihā* is a collection of particles whose meaning is "thus" (*evaṃ*).
*Muhuttena* is a synonym for the word *khaṇena*. Even though [the sound] rose up as far as the Brahma-world, it was not within the range of human perception, just as the form of the gods is not;
therefore, it was only when Sudinna spoke afterwards that [it became known].
"May they know" is how it should be understood.

37. "The holy life of the path" (*magga-brahmacariya*) refers metaphorically to the three trainings themselves, which have the path as their foundation, because that very [path] must be practiced for as long as one lives.
"Unfaltering" means not occupied with recitation and so forth. "With broken carriage" means one whose feet are cut off.
"Or with his neck severed. By the word *cintayi* (he thought), he shows that the term *pajjhāyi* (he brooded) is a verb.
Therefore, by bringing in the particle *ca* ("and"), the connection to the canonical text should be made as: "He became emaciated... and he brooded. 38.
*Gaṇasaṅgaṇikā* is the gathering together in a crowd or assembly of people; that itself is *papañca*. Thus, it means "by that *papañca* of socializing in groups."
*Yassa* means *ye assa* (of whomsoever). *Kathāphāsukā* means talk that is comfortable due to a state of trust; the sense is "talk that is easy.
Since derived form (*upādārūpa*) undergoes beautification and nourishment only by way of the primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*), he says "sensitivity," and so forth.
*Dāni* is a particle; here it functions in the sense of the word *pana*, because it is mentioned separately from the word *etarahi*, which expresses the present time.
He said, "But you? The word *no* has the sense of inquiry, just like the word *nu*; thus he said, "I hope that you...

The phrase "that very [state]" refers specifically to the characteristic of longing for the state of a householder. To show that there exists another kind of dissatisfaction (*anabhirati*) distinct from that which is excluded by the particle *eva*, the words "more skilled" (*adhikusalānaṃ*) and so forth were spoken; [this refers to] serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

"Exceedingly skillful" (adhikusalā) means this. "But this," and so forth, is a demonstration of the specific qualities to be explained below. "Mere figurative expression" (pariyāyavacanamattaṃ) means mere verbal explanation of the meaning of the words.

"In that" (tasmiṃ) refers to the Dhamma; the sense is: when it has been taught thus for the sake of dispassion (virāga). "Nāma" is used in the sense of censure. "Supramundane Nibbāna" (lokuttaranibbānaṃ).
This distinguishes [the state] from the Nibbāna that consists in the destruction of defilements, which is described by the passage beginning with "for the sake of dispassion" (*virāgāya*).

Pride (*māna*) arising in dependence on birth is "pride-intoxication" (*mānamada*) in the sense of producing intoxication. "Pride-intoxication of manhood" (*purisamada*) is the pride that proceeds as "I am a man.

According to some, "pride-intoxication of manhood" is either the pride based on the capacity to engage in unwholesome practices, or it is simply lust (*rāga*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes strength-intoxication (*balamada*) and so forth.

The "round of the three planes" (tebhūmakavaṭṭa) refers to the process of karma, defilements, and their results as they proceed within the three planes; it is called a "round" (vaṭṭa) in the sense of its continuous occurrence.

"It fades away" (virajjati) means it disappears. "Wombs" (yoniyo) refers to those such as egg-born and so forth; however, they are called "wombs" because beings, though not actually mixed with one another, are considered mixed by virtue of belonging to the same class of birth.

Regarding the phrase "by way of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning": here, the discernment of conditioned name-and-form by way of its characteristics and so forth is called "full understanding through knowledge" (*ñāta-pariññā*).
Worldly insight proceeding by way of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpa-sammasana*) and so forth is called "full understanding through scrutiny" (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).

The Noble Path is called "full understanding through abandoning" (*pahāna-pariññā*). However, in this context, because the functions of both knowing and scrutinizing are accomplished at the moment of the Path through non-delusion, [they are included].
The three kinds of full understanding are stated with reference specifically to the Noble Path; for that very reason it is said, "only the supramundane path is spoken of.

"Of the thirsts for the state of being drunk in sensual pleasures" means: of those cravings which grasp the aspects such as beauty and so forth—those aspects being reckoned as the state of being drunk—in the case of sensual objects (vatthu-kāma).
Here, by way of the object, the subject is included. "In the three places" refers to [the passage beginning] "for the sake of dispassion..."
Regarding those things spoken thus: “The Dhamma has been taught... [etc. ...not for the sake of grasping.
(39) “For the purpose of attributing the teaching of the Kali age” means for the purpose of attributing fault. *Kali* is a name for anger;

the teaching of that is the *kalisāsana*, which is the censure uttered by way of anger. Transgression (*ajjhācāra*) is indeed violation (*vītikkama*). Of those things that make one a recluse (*samaṇa*)...
“Of the qualities” (dhammānam) means of those qualities such as moral shame (hiri) and dread of blame (ottappa) which constitute the state of a recluse.

In the text, because of its connection with the word *katham* (“how”), the future tense is used in the phrase “you will not be able”; however, some also say it is due to its connection with the word *nāma*.

“With very painful results” means that even an action that is not excessively blameworthy for householders becomes so for those who have gone forth, due both to the transgression of the Blessed One’s command and to the destruction of the three training rules they have undertaken.
And it is said that this is a great offense (*mahāsāvajja*). "Aqueous" (*odaka*) means existing in water;

he says "aqua-duty" (*udakakicca*) and so forth because its function is washing. He says, "it is to be construed with the word 'namely' (*nāma*)," because the future tense "you will enter" (*samāpajjissasi*) has been formed through its connection with the word *nāma*.

Here, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), which is the cause of being difficult to support and so forth, is expressed by the words "difficult to support" and so on, through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause (*kāraṇe kāriyopacārena*).
He said: "Of non-restraint, which is the basis for being difficult to support, and so forth. *Attā* means personal existence (*attabhāva*).

*Dubbharataṃ* means the state of having to be supported with difficulty by oneself and by one's attendants. *Saṅgaṇikā* means the gathering together, the coming together, and the association with beings and with defilements;
thus he said, "by association with crowds," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for the fulfillment of the eight bases of indolence," here [the word] is *kamma*.
"Should be done"—this is one; "he did so"—another; "the path should be gone"—"he went"—another; "I did not obtain a full measure of food"—"I obtained"—another;
"a disease has arisen for me"—"I have recently emerged from illness"—these are the eight things called grounds for indolence (*kusītavatthu*).
And here, indolence (*kosajja*) is expressed by the word *kusīta*; for even without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-jotana-paccaya*), [it conveys the same meaning].
The meaning is understood just as the whiteness of a cloth [is understood].

"For the sake of the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), which consists in the diminution of all defilements" means for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the cause for the diminution of all defilements such as lust; the sense is "for the sake of Nibbāna.

"Connected with restraint and abandonment" means endowed with both the fivefold restraints, beginning with the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), and the fivefold abandonments, beginning with abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*).
"Unbound suttas" (*asuttanta-vinibaddha*) means not arranged according to the suttas classified as *pāḷi* within the three Piṭakas, nor recorded by the compilers of the Councils;
thus he says, "excluded from the *pāḷi*. By this, he shows that such [teachings] have been included in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) as appropriate.
For such miscellaneous teachings (*pakiṇṇaka-desanā*) are the basis for the commentaries. This is what is called "the teaching on the Dhamma by way of penetration" (*okkantika-dhammadesanā*).
The teaching of the Dhamma being expounded through various methods by repeatedly applying it to each respective context—this is why the Blessed One said, "It is said...
and so forth. "With the intention of rejecting" means having a mind that crushes [the offense], thinking, "What is the use of this," even toward a training rule that has been laid down.
"By way of the meaning stated" means by way of the means for attaining stability. In the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, at that time...

In order to show that the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) consists of: (1) the abstinences (*virati*) indicated by such phrases as "abstinence from sexual misconduct" (*kāmesumicchācārā ārati virati*); (2) the volition (*cetana*) indicated by such phrases as "the volition, the act of intending" (*yā tasmiṃ samaye cetanā sañcetanā*);
and (3) the factors beginning with contact (*phassa*) indicated by such phrases as "contact... non-distraction" (*phasso... avikkhepo*) for one who is abstaining from sexual misconduct—it was stated:
"And this meaning [is explained] in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*..."

"It should be understood in the manner already stated," so it is said. "That which therein is the 'body of names' (nāmakāya) and the 'body of phrases' (padakāya)—this is what is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*," they say.
"The 'body of names' is a collection of names, that is, the designation of names itself; the remaining terms are also synonyms for that very thing.
"A division of training" refers to the abstentions and so forth mentioned, as well as the words that elucidate them.

"Because of the benefit" (*atthavasena*) means because of the specific welfare and specific advantages; and since these are the reasons for the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-panñatti*), he said "because of the cause" (*kāraṇavasena*).
Since there is no cohabitation in the absence of dwelling in happiness, "cohabitation" (*sahajīvita*) refers specifically to dwelling in happiness.

"Immoral persons" (*dussīla-puggala*) refers to those who are without virtue and those whose virtue is corrupted. For when the training rule regarding a *pārājika* offense is involved, those without virtue are intended; as for the involvement with the remaining training rules...
Those whose virtue (*sīla*) is defiled by having reached a state of being broken, pierced, and so forth through various transgressions are intended here.
By both [terms], it should be understood that those who are simply shameless (*alajjī*) are called "immoral" (*dussīla*) in this context.
Since all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were prescribed for the sake of ten purposes, the same principle applies here in the phrase "relying on immoral persons," as stated above. Therefore: [ye...]
The meaning has been stated according to what is common to all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) in the phrase “he will cause him to be ashamed,” and so forth.
Therein, “ashamed” (*maṅkutaṃ*) means the loss of brilliance or the state of having a downcast face. Regarding the terms “by the Dhamma” and so on: “Dhamma” is the factual basis;

“Vinaya” is both the formal charge and the reminder; “the Teacher’s instruction” is both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvana*). “While being seen” (*sandissamānā*)—

"Fall into doubt" means being oppressed. For, by relying on a person of immoral character, the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, the formal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed, and there is no concord.

By this, it is shown that it is not permissible to perform any Saṅgha act, such as the Uposatha and so forth, together with those who are shameless, because it would be an enjoyment of what is contrary to the Dhamma.

Because the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies must necessarily be performed due to their fixed timing, they should be understood as being mentioned separately from the formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma).
Disgrace (akitti) means censure; ill-repute (ayaso) means the loss of one’s reputation.

The fourteen duties of the Khandhaka are those stated in the Khandhaka on Duties: the duty of newcomers, the duty of residents, the duty of those going away, the duty of giving thanks, the duty of the meal-distributor, the duty of the alms-collector, the duty of forest-dwellers, the duty of those using the bathhouse, the duty of those using the restroom, the duty of preceptors, the duty of co-residents, the duty of teachers, and the duty of pupils.
These fourteen observances (vatta) must be practiced by all bhikkhus at all times, as appropriate.
However, the eighty-two major observances are to be practiced only at specific times, such as when one has undergone a censure-act (tajjanīya-kamma), and not at all times.
Therefore, they are counted separately. Regarding those [major observances], [the Blessed One said]: "I shall prescribe the observance for bhikkhus who are on probation (pārivāsika)."

Having begun with “One should not grant full ordination… [and so on] … one should not walk the walking-path while another is walking on the ground,” there are sixty-six rules ending with those statements;

following that, [it says]: “Monks, a monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) should not [walk] together with a monk who is senior to him and is also undergoing probation, nor with one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), nor with one who is practicing the penance (mānattacārika), nor with one who deserves the penance (mānattāraha).”

The observances stated in such passages as, “A bhikkhu deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha) should dwell under one roof with another who is deserving of rehabilitation,” are not counted separately because they are identical to those observances practiced by a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu.

Rather, since they must be practiced toward other types of persons—such as those undergoing probation (pārivāsika) or those senior to oneself—they are grouped together and calculated as five; thus, there are seventy-one observances in total.

And in the section on the duties for those who have undergone the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), it is stated: "One should not accept the salutation, the rising to greet, ... [and so forth] ...
nor the rubbing of the back during bathing from a regular (*pakatatta*) monk. This non-acceptance of salutation and so forth constitutes one duty;
and there are ten others, such as "A regular monk must not be accused of failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*)," and so on. Thus, there are eighty-two duties in total.
Furthermore, among these very rules, some are duties such as the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) and so forth, while others are duties for those on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth;

thus, by including what was not previously included, there are exactly eighty-two. However, in another place, according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that "the eighty khandhaka duties" because a slight deficiency or excess does not affect the count.
Alternatively, they are those not subsumed under the fourteen duties mentioned previously.
All the rules (vatta) derived from the Vinaya— whether they be the eighty-two rules or simply the eighty rules— should be understood by grouping them together in that manner.
"Discipline of restraint" (saṃvaravinaya) consists of the restraint of virtue, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy.
The fivefold restraint is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains the bodily misconduct and so forth that are to be restrained and disciplined according to their respective cases;
it is called "discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines them.

As for "discipline as abandoning" (*pahānavinaya*), it consists of abandoning by way of its own nature (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*).

Since all five kinds of abandonment are abandonment in the sense of relinquishing and discipline (*vinaya*) in the sense of training (*vinayana*), it is therefore called "discipline as abandonment" (*pahānavinaya*).

Discipline as settlement (*samathavinaya*) refers to the seven methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*). Discipline as formulation (*paññattivinaya*) is the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself;
for that too is supported by the Blessed One’s formulation of the training rule, since its existence depends solely upon the presence of that formulation.
The connection is: "having formed the chain-method (saṅkhalikanaya) and having formed [the sequence] ten times for each yoke-length (yojana), that which was stated.
In this context, because each preceding word is joined only with the immediately following word, it is called the "chain-method" (saṅkhalikanaya) as it is like an iron chain.
Because each single word among the ten positions is joined with the nine remaining words, it is called "rooted in each single word" (ekekapadamūlika).

Regarding the phrase "one hundred and eight matters": here, in the *Parivāra*, starting from "That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha" and ending with "That which is for the endurance of the True Dhamma is for the assistance of the Vinaya," the *saṅkhalika-naya* (the linked-method) was taught by way of the *khaṇḍacakkavāla* (the wheel-section).
Within that, according to the *baddhacakkavāla-naya* (the bound-wheel-method) found in the *ekamūlaka-naya* (the single-rooted method), that which is for the assistance of the Vinaya—

Having applied this phrase "it is well for the Saṅgha" as well, when the "bound wheel" (baddhacakra) is formed, there are twenty phrases: the first ten being *dhamma*-phrases and the subsequent ten being *attha*-phrases.
However, in the method of the single root (*ekamūlaka*), only nine *attha*-phrases are obtained in a single turn. Thus, across ten turns, there are ninety *attha*-phrases.

There are ninety *dhammapadas*; it should be understood that when these are joined with the ten meaning-terms (*atthapada*) and ten Dhamma-terms (*dhammapada*) as stated in the *saṅkhalikanaya*, they constitute the aforementioned hundred meanings and hundred Dhammas.
Furthermore, regarding this, in the *Sāratthadīpanī* (Commentary on the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, Pārājika-khaṇḍa 2.39), even in the *saṅkhalikanaya*—
Even in the method based on a single root, a gateway for the application of a hundred meanings and a hundred teachings is stated for each;

yet, although that is established in such a way, it does not accord with the verse "a hundred meanings, a hundred teachings," because one must speak of two hundred meanings, two hundred teachings, four hundred etymologies, and eight hundred knowledges. Therefore, according to the method stated here, there are a hundred meanings.
It should be understood that "one hundred dhammas" is what is stated. Regarding "two hundred etymologies":

there is one hundred etymologies by way of etymologies that illuminate the meaning (*attha*), and another hundred etymologies by way of etymologies that are themselves the phenomena (*dhamma*); thus, there are two hundred etymologies.

Regarding "four hundred knowledges": there is one hundred knowledges regarding the hundred meanings, one hundred knowledges regarding the hundred phenomena, and [one hundred each] regarding the two hundred etymologies.
"Two hundred knowledges" means four hundred knowledges. "For the purpose of including more" means for the purpose of collecting what was not explicitly stated.
The method of commentary on the explanation of the first formal presentation is finished.
The commentary on the recitation-section concerning Sudinna is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Monkey’s Cloth (Makkaṭīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā): 40.

Regarding the statement that the present tense is used in the sense of abundance: because there is a desire to engage [in the act] day after day—having engaged at one time and not having desisted thereafter—the present tense is employed here even at a moment when the actual engagement is absent, as in such expressions as "the Mallas are fighting here."
The meaning is that the present tense was used [in the phrase] "he partakes" with reference to the state of being uninterrupted and the mode of living in abundance.
"Wandering about" means moving about. 41.
"Taken together with the goods" means taken along with the merchandise; or this very reading [sahoḍḍhaggahito] is the correct one. That training rule is exactly as before.
It "becomes" [an offense] because it was stated in general terms—without specifying any particular individual such as a human or a non-human—as:

"Whatever bhikkhu should engage in sexual intercourse. Thus, for one who engages in sexual intercourse on any of the thirty kinds of ways among humans, non-humans, or animals—including females, males, eunuchs, and those with both genders—that training rule (sikkhāpada) becomes a cause for the cutting off of the root [of the monastic life].
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). By this, it is shown that [the subsequent rule] serves to clarify the intended meaning of the original rule (*mūlapaññatti*) itself;

for the sake of easy understanding, it functions by way of the object (*vatthu*) to indicate specific details regarding those [acts] that occur [in relation to the body]. "Touching" (*āmasana*) is merely touching.
"Contact" (*phusana*) is a firmer form of contact than that. "Rubbing" (*ghaṭṭana*), however, is even firmer than that, performed with the body against the body.
“Collision” (*saṅghaṭṭana*). “All that” means everything, including seeing and so forth, that occurs through passion.

(42) To show that both the training rules with volition, such as the taking of life, and the training rules without volition, such as drinking fermented liquor, constitute worldly transgression (*lokavajja*) by means of a single definition, [it says]:
“In the case of those with volition, the mind is exclusively unwholesome...”

"Whatever [offense] there is, that is called a worldly offense (*lokavajja*). Regarding this, although the phrase "in the case of the side with consciousness" (*sacittakapakkhe*) is properly stated with reference specifically to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning the absence of consciousness—since it is only in those cases that the side of consciousness can occur—it nevertheless applies to the training rules concerning consciousness as well.

This is because, even in the case of walking and so forth when one acts unintentionally, there arises in the world the conventional designation of "killing a living being"; thus, one may conceptually posit a "side of non-consciousness" for those training rules as well.

The phrase "on the side of those with a conscious mind" (*sacittakapakkhe*) is stated by way of what is common to both types of training rules (*sikkhāpada*), namely those involving a conscious mind and those not involving a conscious mind.
Otherwise, in this statement, the characteristic of worldly fault (*lokavajjatā*) would not have been stated for the training rules involving a conscious mind.

However, when it is said, "On the side of those with a conscious mind, the mind is exclusively unwholesome," then for the training rules involving a conscious mind, the mind is indeed exclusively unwholesome.
For others, the restriction to the unwholesome applies only to the category of those with consciousness, not to the category of those without consciousness.

In that regard, however, it should be understood that the sense—that there may be the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate according to what is possible—is established by implication (*sāmatthiyato*).

Regarding the phrase "in the category of those with consciousness," it should be taken as "with consciousness" by means of a mind that recognizes the transgression of the object (*vatthu*), and not otherwise.

If it were so [that a transgression occurs] by means of a consciousness that understands the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), then it would follow that all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) would be offenses against the world (*lokavajja*).
For even regarding an offense against the formal rule, in one who knows, "It is prohibited;

it is not permissible to do this," a mind of aversion (*paṭighacitta*) arises precisely through the influence of disrespect (*anādariya*). Therefore, the statement that all training rules are offenses against the world would be entirely meaningless.
Because it would follow that one must state [the rule] only to this extent.

And here, since no restriction has been made that "the mind is unwholesome only in the case of the conscious category," it cannot be restricted by saying that "in the case of drinking liquor and so forth, which belong to the unconscious category, the mind is certainly not unwholesome"; rather, it is simply that in the case of the conscious category, the mind...
It is unwholesome (*akusala*) alone, and not wholesome (*kusala*) or otherwise; thus, in this context, the restriction is established.

And in this way, it is justified that even for those drinking without knowing [it is liquor], the drinking occurs with an unwholesome mind alone, and for nuns anointing themselves without knowing [it is] perfume, color, or the like, the anointing occurs even without an unwholesome mind; thus, the possibility of an offense arises in both cases. As for that which...

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "Because of the statement that 'in the case of those with consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome,' it is understood that in the case of those without consciousness, there is no such restriction that 'the mind is exclusively unwholesome' by way of not knowing the object.

This is not correct. For among the thirteen [offenses] excluded from the world that are committed without consciousness, there is a restriction to an unwholesome mind even in the case of those without consciousness, specifically regarding the drinking of intoxicants.

This is because the other twelve [courses of action] can be committed even by unwholesome and other types of consciousness. However, since this restriction is not accepted by anyone and cannot be understood even from the word itself, he shows it as being intended by another [author], saying:

"For if, even in the case of one without consciousness, the consciousness in the category of 'without consciousness' were exclusively unwholesome, then this qualification 'in the category of with consciousness' would be purposeless."
The statement beginning with “it might be” and so forth is entirely pointless, because such a restriction was not intended by anyone.
Indeed, no expert in grammar accepts a restriction that would render the qualification “in the case of the sentient” (sacittakapakkhe) redundant;
rather, in the case of the sentient, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, whereas in the case of the insentient...

However, he maintains that the mind is indeterminate, being either unwholesome or one of the other categories such as wholesome; thus, even the qualification "in the case of those with consciousness" (sacittakapakkhe) would be meaningful.

Furthermore, for the training rules concerning those without consciousness (acittaka-sikkhāpada), their status as offenses against worldly convention (lokavajjatā) is established through the restriction of unwholesomeness to the cases involving consciousness.
And among those [offenses], it is only the drinking of fermented liquor (surāpāna) that constitutes an offense against worldly convention even in the case of those without consciousness.
There is unwholesome mental state (*akusalacittatā*), and as for the others, the view that they exist only on the side of those with a mind (*sacittakapakkhe*) is not contradicted;
thus, there is nothing here that is untenable. As for what is said here:
"For one drinking without knowing [it is liquor]... [etc.]... because an offense can arise even without an unwholesome mental state... [etc.]"

It has been stated: "The drinking of intoxicants and so forth would not constitute a worldly offense (*lokavajja*) for those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) where there is no conscious intent," and so on.

Furthermore, the extensive elaboration found in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, which presents scriptural citations to prove this point, should not be accepted as authoritative, because it contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathās*.
For it is said therein: "And here, the state of being without conscious intent (*acittakatā*) should be understood as the lack of knowledge regarding the object (*vatthu*)."
It is stated: "Because it must be committed by an unwholesome mind alone, it is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*).

As for this statement from the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*)—"In the case where there is a conscious mind, it is a worldly offense because it must be committed by an unwholesome mind alone"—that is not correct.
For in the *Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated generally regarding all worldly offenses that "in the case where there is a conscious mind, the mind is exclusively unwholesome."

For it has been stated in the commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of intoxicants (*surāpāna-sikkhāpada-aṭṭhakathā*) as "because it must be drunk by means of an unwholesome [state of mind] alone," thus distinguishing it even within the category of unintentional offenses by specifying an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacittatā*).

Indeed, one cannot say that "the meaning already stated here in general was stated again in the commentary on the drinking of intoxicants," because there is no purpose in stating again what has already been stated;
this applies to other unintentional offenses as well, excluding those that are violations of worldly convention (*lokavajja*).
Furthermore, because of the possibility of being subject to censure, and because a method stated in one instance is effectively stated for others as well due to their sharing the same characteristic,

it cannot be said that [this method] was "stated only in the training rule on drinking fermented liquor (surāpāna-sikkhāpada)," since it must be stated first of all in the training rule on those engaged in military service (uyyutta-sikkhāpada),
which is a worldly offense committed without intention; or alternatively, having stated it in the training rule on drinking fermented liquor, the same method applies to the remaining rules.
And because it must be extended [by analogy] to those states that are without mind and to those excluded from the world (*lokavajja*).

Furthermore, for one stating the very same point already expressed—namely, that "in the case of those with mind, it is to be incurred by the unwholesome alone"—it should be stated according to the sequence previously mentioned, since the purpose of the repeated statement is to remove doubt and so forth. Regarding the domain of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*):

And [the offense] must be qualified; only after being qualified can it be spoken of, for otherwise the distinction between what constitutes an offense and what does not, and so forth, would be difficult to discern.
For instance, in the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "Because they may be committed even without a conscious intention, they are 'incidental' (*acittaka*);
yet, when there is a mind, because they must be committed with an unwholesome mind, they are both 'worldly offenses' (*lokavajja*) and 'unwholesome minds' (*akusalacitta*)."

In the case of village festivals and the like, both their status as worldly transgressions (*lokavajja*) and their association with unwholesome states of mind (*akusalacitta*) are stated specifically for the category involving a conscious mind (*sacittakapakkha*), but this is not the case for the drinking of fermented liquor (*surāpāna*).

Regarding the latter, however, it is stated in a way that applies to both categories equally—that it "must be drunk only by an unwholesome state of mind"—rather than being specified specifically for the category involving a conscious mind.
Therefore, this drinking of fermented liquor [is an offense] in both categories: whether involving a conscious mind or not.

It is well established that the phrase "because it is to be incurred by unwholesome [mind] alone, it is a world-transgression" (*lokavajjatā*) was stated separately precisely to show both the world-transgression and the unwholesome mind.
By this very fact, one should understand that this [explanation] serves as the fulfillment of the intended meaning of what was stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"In the case of those with minds, it is a world-transgression because it is to be incurred by unwholesome [mind] alone."
