Indeed, with this very intention, in other training rules (sikkhāpada) prohibited by the world which do not involve a conscious state (*acittaka*), it is precisely the presence of an unwholesome mind (*akusalacittatā*) that is stated, and not the presence of three types of minds (*ticittatā*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
"The mountain-top festival, the picture-gallery training rule, the hip-cloth, female ornaments, perfumes and ointments, and scented sesame paste [are to be avoided] by bhikkhunīs and others..."
Regarding the phrase "rubbing and massaging," it has been stated: "These ten training rules (sikkhāpada) are unintentional and unwholesome states of mind;

however, the intended meaning here is that they are 'unintentional' because they can be committed even without a [specific] intention, whereas when an intention is present, they must be committed with an unwholesome mind, and thus they are both 'worldly offenses' (lokavajja) and 'unwholesome states of mind'. That too is refuted.
Because it establishes the opposite meaning by means of the method already described. Therefore, it should be understood that this statement was spoken precisely to show this distinction:
that even in the case where drinking liquor is unintentional (*acittaka*), the mind is nonetheless unwholesome (*akusala*).
This is the meaning here: the word *ca* in the phrase "and because of not knowing the basis" (*vatthu-ajānanatāya ca*) indicates a specific qualification and is synonymous with *api ca*.

Therefore, that which is defined as "world-transgressing" (*lokavajja*) because it can be committed even without a mind—unlike other offenses except for those involving the world—and which is "unwholesome" (*akusala*) because it can only be committed when the mind is unwholesome;
this definition, characterized by both being world-transgressing and being an unwholesome state of mind, does not apply here to the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor. Here...

However, it is said that there is a distinction. If one asks what that is: it should be understood as "absence of intention" (*acittaka*) precisely because of the non-cognition of the object and because the offense is incurred even without a mind that cognizes the object; there is no further distinction here regarding "absence of intention.

But rather, even on the side of "absence of intention" defined as non-cognition of the object, it is by means of an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*) alone that the fermented liquor (*surāmeraya*) is swallowed.

In this training rule, it should be understood that both in the case of intentional action (*sacittaka-pakkha*) and in the case of unintentional action (*acittaka-pakkha*), there is worldly transgression (*lokavajjatā*) and unwholesome mental state (*akusalacittatā*); this is the distinction here.

For in this context, because it is stated generally as "only by the unwholesome" (*akusalena eva*) without specifying "when the mind is present," it should be understood that both worldly transgression and unwholesome mental state are established in both cases.

In that very *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaṭṭhakathā*), in the explanation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is stated: "The occasion for negligence through fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants has two origins:

from body and from body-and-mind. Here, because of the absence of a conscious mind [in that specific state], the body alone—devoid of the mental factor—is said to have a single origin; and even at that moment when it has a single origin, [it is so described].
The volition by which one drinks is exclusively unwholesome. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on that same passage:
"Herein, the first five [abstinences] are natural offenses (*pakativajja*) because killing and so forth are originated by exclusively unwholesome consciousness;
the remaining ones are conventional offenses (*paṇṇattivajja*). Thus, for all five as well, the state of being unwholesome consciousness is collectively termed "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*).
And natural faultiness has been stated [as a factor]. Yet, among the factors, the factor of knowledge has not been stated. For it is said:
"As for the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, there are these four factors: any one of the intoxicants such as fermented liquor;
the state of mind desiring to drink; the undertaking of the corresponding effort; and the swallowing once drunk. It is not said: [...]
However, there are five factors including the factor of knowing it is *surā*. For if even the knowledge that it is *surā* were a factor, it certainly would have had to be mentioned;
yet it was not mentioned. And just as in this case, so too in other commentaries on the Sutta Piṭaka and elsewhere, the factor of knowing is nowhere mentioned.
Therefore, regarding this [point]: "It is a worldly transgression because it must be committed with an unwholesome state of mind."

Even in the interpretation of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the position that [the offense] is not committed when there is no conscious intent, one must reach the conclusion that the meaning is exactly this: "it is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*) because it must be incurred by unwholesome [action] alone.
Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "If, thinking 'I shall kill this being,' one lies down in that very place [intending to kill] another..."
Just as there is the offense of taking life when one kills because of the existence of the commonality of "living being," so too,
for one who drinks another kind of intoxicant with the thought, "I will drink this intoxicant," there is unwholesomeness because of the existence of the commonality of "intoxicant.
However, just as there is no taking of life when one kills a snake perceiving it to be a stick, so too, for one who drinks an intoxicant perceiving it to be coconut water, [there is no offense].
The statement, “there is no unwholesome [kamma],” was made by comparing [the case] in every respect with taking life;
however, that is highly inappropriate because there is no fixed rule for the mutual equality of all training rules and unwholesome acts such as taking life.
For taking life can be accomplished even by means of a pretext, whereas taking what is not given cannot be so. But that...

It is established even by way of an injunction, yet not in the case of sexual intercourse and so forth. Therefore, it is entirely improper to equate those who are distinct in every respect with those who are associated, even by means of factors such as the preliminary application (*payoga-aṅga*).

If someone were to say, "Just like killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and so forth, are also established through figurative discourse (*pariyāya-kathā*) and the like," why would that not be accepted?
If you argue that it is because there is no such statement, [we reply: here too, "in the same way... [the text continues].
Since there is no statement to the effect that "drinking fermented liquor is similar to the taking of life," this [interpretation] must also not be accepted.

Furthermore, when one who is learned in the Vinaya seeks to refute a point already established by a commentary, he should do so by demonstrating its contradiction with the Suttas, the *Suttānuloma*, and so forth;
he should not, however, do so merely by equating it with another training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that is entirely distinct in terms of its application, constituent factors, and other such details.
For there is no contradiction with the Suttas or other texts in the statement, "Even for one who drinks without knowing it is *surā*, it is indeed unwholesome.
First, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, no Sutta or other passage is found that contradicts this meaning, nor is there any such thing in the Sutta Piṭaka and the rest.
As for what some here say—that because it is stated, "States are preceded by the mind," all unwholesome states [are so] beforehand...
“[The unwholesome states] arise only for one who already knows the basis for transgression. This merely demonstrates that they have not understood the intended meaning of those suttas.
For the statement “mental phenomena are preceded by the mind” does not illustrate the point that unwholesome states arise only for one who has previously known the basis for transgression;
rather, it shows that when wholesome or unwholesome states arise...

This explains the point that [mental factors] arise only by depending on the co-nascent consciousness (sahajātacitta), which acts as their precursor in the sense of being a condition for their arising, and not without consciousness; it does not imply here,

as might be suggested by the statement "it is unwholesome for one who drinks without knowing it is surā," that unwholesome mental factors such as greed can arise even without co-nascent consciousness.
[He] incurs [a fault]. That by which this sutta might be brought forward as a refutation does not exist here;

moreover, there is no contradiction with the Abhidhamma, because it is stated that for one who previously did not know [the object] by way of name, genus, and so forth, wholesome or unwholesome javanas arise in the cognitive process of the fivefold sense-consciousness.
Furthermore, the javanas arising at the six doors for foolish worldlings are, for the most part, exclusively unwholesome.
[Unwholesome states] arise. Wholesome states, however, arise only rarely for them due to the power of strong support (*upanissaya*) such as virtuous friends;

for even when they remain silent, sleep, or dream, unwholesome impulsive moments (*javana*) such as restlessness (*uddhacca*) mostly prevail, and because there is no impulsive moment devoid of both wholesome and unwholesome qualities, [wholesome states] are absent for them.
For unwholesome states follow either the suitability of the object or the suitability of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
They arise according to their respective conditions; in that regard, what is the use of being bound by prior knowledge or lack of knowledge?

However, those [offenses] such as taking life which are accomplished through factors like intention, and those such as drinking intoxicants or holding wrong views which are accomplished even without intention and so forth—having understood each of these exactly as they are, the Perfectly Enlightened One has pointed them out, and one should follow them according to how they were pointed out.

What contradiction with the Abhidhamma is there in accepting this? Thus, because there is no contradiction with the Suttas and other texts, and because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā, the meaning here must be understood exactly in the manner already described.

If this is so, why is it stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "A novice who drinks knowing [it is alcohol] incurs a breach of virtue, not one who does not know"? This is not a fault regarding the breach of virtue.
This is because it depends on the command of the Blessed One, just as there is a breach of virtue for those who follow one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*) and so forth.
For their breach of virtue does not arise merely from the arising of unwholesome states (*akusala*), since it is prescribed immediately following the formal admonition dependent upon the Saṅgha.

Likewise here, the rule is prescribed only for drinking with knowledge, not for drinking without knowledge. For the scope of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is one thing, while the scope of the unwholesome state is another.
For that very reason, among the first five training rules for novices, when even one is broken, all the training rules are considered broken.
However, as for unwholesome action, it is broken by that single instance alone, not by others.

Therefore, it should be understood that even if there is no breach of the moral code (*sīla*) for a novice who drinks without knowing [it was intoxicating], there is nonetheless unwholesome action that has reached the level of a course of kamma (*kammappatha*).

However, regarding the statement made by some in the *Sāratthadīpanī*—“For a novice who drinks without knowing it is *surā*, there is no *pārājika* offense, though there is unwholesome karma”—this has been rejected as being merely their own opinion. [The correct view is:
For a monk who drinks intoxicants starting from the very seed even without knowing it, there is a *pācittiya* offense. A novice, however, [knowing...]

Regarding the statement, "One incurs a breach of virtue while drinking, but not if one does so unknowingly"—for this much alone is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), whereas it is not stated that "it is unwholesome"—the reason given for that is incorrect.

For in the Commentary, at the point of discussing the breach of virtue, it is not said that there is a breach of virtue for novices only when drinking knowingly, and not when drinking unknowingly; nor is it said that it is unwholesome.
However, the phrase "but it is unwholesome" serves as the reason for the absence of unwholesomeness in the case of ignorance, because there is no possibility [of such an offense] in that instance;
furthermore, it is because it has been stated precisely in the relevant section that "it is a worldly transgression (lokavajja) by virtue of being incurred through an unwholesome act alone.
Nor do those teachers who say "but it is unwholesome" [mean to contradict] this very passage from the *Khandhaka-ṭīkā* which clarifies the breach of the novices' virtue.

Having taken [these sources], they spoke; one might say that "only this much was stated in the commentary," yet in fact, having taken the various statements found in the commentary on the *Surāpāna* [offense] and those found in the commentary on the *Suttapiṭaka*, as well as the traditional instruction of the Mahāvihāravāsins, they spoke.
For this is the opinion of those of divergent sects, such as Abhayagirika and others.
This means that for one who drinks while knowing [it is alcohol], it is grasped as unwholesome (*akusala*).

Therefore, what has been stated by some—namely, "For a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*) who drinks alcohol unknowingly, there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*), but it is nevertheless unwholesome"—should be accepted as well-said.
And as for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Even for a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) who drinks unknowingly, alcohol does not enter his mouth..."

Having rejected the statement made by some—“Because it must be incurred by an unwholesome mind that has reached the level of a path of action”—he said, “Indeed, this too should be understood as established by the nature of things (*dhammatā*) for noble disciples, just like the virtue (*sīla*) of the Bodhisatta’s mother when the Bodhisatta was in her womb.
Then, in order to further substantiate its establishment by the nature of things, he said: “Even in another existence...”
For indeed, the noble disciple does not kill a living being nor drink intoxicants even for the sake of his life.
Even if they were to mix intoxicants with milk and put it into his mouth, only the milk would enter, not the intoxicant. How is this so?
Just as when water mixed with milk is drunk by herons, only the milk enters and not the water. This is established by nature.
This statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, “this too should be understood as established by the nature of things (*dhammatāsiddha*),” is likewise not tenable.

For, regarding the phrase “just as the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother is established by the nature of things for the noble disciples,” the “nature of things” pertaining to the Bodhisatta’s mother refers here to the fixed necessity that unwholesome states do not arise, due to the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*) of both the Bodhisatta and herself.
In the same way, for noble disciples as well, it is the very nature of things (dhammatā) that,

by the power of the Path which absolutely abandons the ten courses of unwholesome action— beginning with the taking of life— as well as other unwholesome states that cause rebirth in the woeful states,

there is a fixed rule of non-arising for any unwholesome state caused by the transgression of those respective precepts. For this is not a lack of cause, as would be the case for those who maintain [the view of] inherent nature (sabhāva).

This is what is called "the nature of things" (*dhammatā*). Just as, according to the principle of the nature of things, the existence or non-existence of an effect follows from the existence or non-existence of its cause—and this is not a case of existence or non-existence occurring without cause or condition—so too here, due to the absolute absence of the defilement that serves as the cause for the courses of action such as killing, those [courses of action] are absent;
and for the remaining unwholesome states, because of the absence of their cause...

The existence of one state through another is a natural law (*dhammatā*), not a lack of cause. Therefore, it is well said by some that because of the absence of passion—the cause for the states of misery—the noble ones do not consume fermented liquor even without knowing [its nature].

As for the claim that "even if a stream-enterer drinks without knowing, the liquor does not enter his mouth, because it can only be drunk with an unwholesome mind that has reached the level of a kamma-path," for what reason is that so?
It is not understood that "it was not born beautiful," nor how it is rejected by the statement that it is "established by the nature of things" (*dhammatāsiddha*).

Furthermore, even the statement in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "Having mixed liquor and milk... this is established by the nature of things," establishes that even in the case where drinking liquor is considered unintentional (*acittaka*), it is indeed an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*). For it is said: "Even in another existence..."

When it is said, "Indeed, the noble disciple does not take life even for the sake of his own life, nor does he take what is not given... [and so on] ...nor does he drink fermented liquor," one might consider the possibility of this objection:
"Insofar as the first four courses of action involve a conscious mind, abstaining from them is easy;
however, since the latter—drinking fermented liquor—is devoid of a conscious mind, how could there be abstention from it? Having taken this into account:

Even though he is without consciousness due to his ignorance of the object, since the liquor must be swallowed by means of unwholesome states that have reached the level of a course of action (*kammappatha*), and such an occurrence of unwholesomeness has been destroyed in the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) by the Path itself, therefore there is no entry of the liquor into his throat;
thus, stating the words of the exception (*parihāra-vacana*) which conveys the meaning implied by the sense, [the text says]: "If even for him, the liquor..."

The passage beginning with “and milk” has been stated. Therein, the statement “it enters only the milk, not the liquor” is intended to show that liquor never enters another substance in any way whatsoever;
it is not, however, intended to show the capacity to separate the liquor from milk mixed with liquor.
This is the underlying meaning here: for if anything were to enter milk mixed with liquor, it would enter only the milk.

It is not alcohol. However, in the case of milk, nothing enters that is inseparable from alcohol. This is "established by nature" (*yonisiddha*); the non-entry [of alcohol] into the mouth of water is established by nature.
And here, "nature" (*yoni*) is intended in the sense of "birth" (*jāti*).

Therefore, because of the absence of the cause for swallowing milk-mixed water by those things of the nature of cranes—namely, the physical phenomena known as their mouths and beaks—that non-entry occurs.
The meaning is that it is established. For even in this case of wine mixed with milk, when the milk enters [the stomach], it is still considered the entry of something other than oneself.

"Established by the nature of things" (dhammatāsiddha) means it is established by the nature of things (dhammatā) consisting in the absence of the presence of defilements that serve as the cause for drinking wine in the case of a noble disciple regarding immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma). Thus, here, even in the position that there is no consciousness [at the time of death], because wine must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), [the prohibition applies].
It should be understood that even for noble disciples, drinking is not permitted. Furthermore, it might be argued:

"Even on the side of ignorance, although drinking liquor would be an offense even without an unwholesome mind, the fact that noble ones do not drink is merely a statement intended to show what is proper (dhammata) for them.
That is not so, because it contradicts other passages in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For the meaning must be accepted exactly as it does not contradict those other passages.

Furthermore, the non-performance of the five courses of action, such as killing living beings, even in another life, is indeed the natural virtue (*dhammatāsīla*) of the Noble Ones (*ariya*), provided that their state of mind is the same [as ours].
If it were otherwise, the other four courses of action—just like drinking intoxicants—would not be committed by a noble disciple even unintentionally;
and thus, for Noble Ones who are unaware [of the act], they would not be performed even when accompanied by wholesome or neutral states of consciousness (*kusala-abyākata-citta*).
In cases such as abstaining from taking what belongs to another or seizing the property of others, bodily and verbal activity would not occur;

for if it were not to occur, then just as the act of depriving a living being of life occurred through the walking meditation of the Elder Cakkhupāla, and the touching of the path by what is not the path occurred through the forceful action of the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā, so too, even in the case where drinking liquor is considered unintentional, it must still be avoided because it is unwholesome. Therefore, liquor is [forbidden] for the Noble Ones.
It should be understood that this was stated with the qualification that [the mind] does not enter into another's throat.
Is it not the case that all courses of kamma are said to occur only for one who knows the object? No; because wrong view proceeds precisely through a perverted apprehension.
For how indeed could there be an apprehension of one who is not omniscient as being omniscient, or of the impermanent and so forth as being permanent and so forth?
Wrong view cognizes its object. For if it were to know [the object] correctly, it would not be wrong view at all.
And since it is reckoned among the courses of action (*kamma-patha*), how could there be a rule that the courses of action proceed only for one who knows? If you argue:

"Even while apprehending an omniscient one as 'omniscient,' because it apprehends his specific individuality by thinking 'this is a sentient being,' wrong view also cognizes its object"—we say no. This would also apply to the drinking of liquor.

If it is argued that [the view] does not know because, although there is a reference to the object in the phrase "this," there is an absence of specific recognition as "liquor" due to the similarity in form with the apprehension of "this is not liquor"—then [we reply]:
even though one knows the personhood in the phrase "this," there is likewise an absence of specific recognition as "not omniscient";
thus, the view also does not know the object, and the case is exactly the same. For in this way, they [regard] those [beings] as Buddhas...
"Unbeneficial" means that which is harmful, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others; the same method applies even to the arising of aversion or attachment.
For indeed, all unwholesome states are preceded by perversion (*vipallāsa*).
Moreover, just as when wine is being drunk, its inherent nature is the certain production of unwholesomeness once it has been drunk, so it is with the perception of [something] as milk and so forth.
In a person who drinks liquor, a continuous stream of unwholesome states such as lust and hatred arises even toward their mother, sisters, and so forth, simply by the very nature of the object;
likewise, at the very moment it is being drunk, sharp lust arises.

For this very reason, when the Elder Sāgata drank without realizing [the danger], he suffered the loss of his fivefold higher knowledge (*pañcābhijñā*) and other meditative attainments (*jhāna*), and subsequently experienced a continuous stream of unwholesome states such as disrespect toward the Buddha and others.

It continued until the disappearance of the Surā liquor. For that very reason, the Blessed One also, by way of demonstrating the occurrence of disrespect and lack of skill on his part, explained the fault of *surā* and laid down the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Indeed, there can be no decline of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) without the arising of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
Therefore, even for one who does not know [the consequences], when *surā* is being drunk or has been drunk, it produces unwholesome states (*akusala*) by its very nature.
It should be concluded that this meaning is established both by way of the consequence of the Elder Sāgata’s loss of jhāna,

and by way of the contrast consisting in the fact that noble ones do not allow liquor to enter their mouths due to the absence of defilements; for such an interpretation alone follows the doctrine of the Vibhajjavādins.

As for the assertion that "it is unwholesome only for one who drinks after having [previously] known [the danger]," that is the opinion only of those with divergent views such as Abhayagirika and others.
However, this was written by the authors of the *Gaṇṭhipada* and others according to their own judgment, without realizing it was the doctrine of opponents;
even having entered the circle of those who advocate analysis (*vibhajjavāda*), they continue to corrupt the Dispensation until the present day. It is said that even in former times...
In this very Tamil country as well, there was a certain elder named Nāgasena, who held a distinct sectarian view;
for the purpose of demonstrating the method of crushing the arguments of opponents, he composed the *Kuṇḍalakesīvatthu* in the Tamil language, stating:

"Having understood this unwholesome principle regarding the drinking of liquor, [one understands] all that is to be known—which is infinite due to the distinctions of place, time, and so forth—by means of omniscient knowledge."

"Because it is impossible to know [the object] by way of its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) alone—since that would entail the loss of the infinity of the knowable (*ñeyya*) due to its being delimited by knowledge—and because it is possible to know it only by way of general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) such as impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth";

and "Just as there is a division into name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so on among ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), so too conventional designations (*sammuti*) such as 'person' (*puggala*) and so on must also be a distinct division of entities (*vatthu*). Such is the manyfold method of erroneous meaning.
Having instructed the poet Kabbākāra and having deluded his mindfulness with fallacious arguments regarding that composition, he caused it to be composed;
and based on that poem, this doctrine of schismatic sects persisted for a long time here, mixed with the Vibhajjavāda school.
Later, however, the Great Elder Ācariya Buddhapiya [expounded] the web of views, both external and internal.
Having opened up and established the pure teaching here, even though it had been clarified by the *Vinaya-ṭīkā Sāratthadīpanī*,

some with perverted minds raised their heads once again, relying on the statement in the *Samaṇṇaphala-sutta* that the mind [of drinking liquor] is unwholesome only when associated with a defiled intention (*sacittaka-pakkheva*). This was then refuted by the Great Elders as a censurable doctrine.
Having crushed [the dispute] and separated the monks who had adopted that view, it was settled after a long time in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
For this very reason, we have here rejected this tenet in such detail, lest it should corrupt other proponents of analytical doctrine (vibhajjavādins).
Therefore, the reasons stated and unstated herein should be well understood.
Having observed this, the meaning should be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction with the scriptures.
"The rest" means that even in the case of a conscious being, when perceiving an object, there is no fixed rule that the mind must necessarily be unwholesome;
rather, it refers to all such instances. "They obstruct" refers to [the teaching] beginning with, "There is no fault in a female animal," and so forth.

She prevents the grasping of even a slight indication of non-offense. "Closing the door" means she closes the door that constitutes the cause for the grasping of a slight indication, as stated in the passage beginning with "but [if it is] a human woman.

"Cutting off the stream" means cutting off the uninterrupted stream of transgression by way of those two doors of grasping a slight indication. "Making it more firm" means [by means of] those already mentioned...
The meaning is that, by means of these reasons, they strengthen the offense itself as established by the first formulation, while not allowing any scope for non-offense.

And since that [offense] arises—making it lax in the absence of transgression, in what is not within the scope [of the rule], and even in a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*)—therefore, showing both its arising and the cause of its arising, he said: "excepting... (*aññatra*).
Regarding "excessive pride" (*adhimāna*) and so forth: for this supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), the reason given is "because there is no transgression.
For the phrase "except in a dream," the reason given is "because it pertains to the state beyond [the world]" (*abbokārika*).

In that context, "because there is no transgression" refers to the absence of the intention to deceive—which consists in the act of proclaiming the existence of a superhuman quality (*uttarimanussadhamma*) when such a quality does not exist in one who has evil desires (*pāpicchā*).
Because there is an absence of transgression. For one who is conceited (*adhimānika*), since they perceive what has not been attained as attained, the aforementioned transgression does not exist.

Regarding the term "indeterminate" (*abbhohārika*): although the volition that takes pleasure in liberation and the undertaking [of the effort] are present—as stated in the passage, "Bhikkhus, this volition exists, but it is indeterminate"—nevertheless, because one is overcome by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) and lacks mastery over oneself, [the action is indeterminate].

The meaning is: "because it is a conventional designation" (*abbōhārikattā*), that is, because there is an absence of a designation for the cause of an offense. Here, the word *vā* should be understood as having the sense of conjunction;

alternatively, the reading is "and because it is a conventional designation" (*abbohārikattā ca*). The intention is that both of these supplementary rules (*anupaññatti*) have been stated as making [the act] non-offensive.

Regarding the phrase "when no transgression has been committed," even in times of distress, when monks have not committed a transgression of the training rule—as in the cases of "they did not eat out of scruple" and so forth—[it is non-offensive].
The meaning is: "without having committed a transgression, [the matter] was reported by the bhikkhus due to the arising of their own suffering. "Making it lax" means:
having first loosened the training rule that was bound in a general sense, they make it lax by way of rendering themselves non-offending in their own particular case.
"Providing an opening" means: providing an opening for non-offense. Even in subsequent cases, there is non-offense.
"Making [the rule]" means she demonstrates the state of non-offense by way of that which was given successively.

Even though the training rule had already been laid down, it is said "when the transgression has been committed" because it was formulated on the occasion of Udāyī’s falling into misconduct (*sañcaritta*), having transgressed under the pretext that "there is no fault in [visiting] a momentary courtesan.
"The category of what has been laid down" means, in terms of its actual meaning, the original laying down (*mūlapaññatti*) itself; this is the intended sense.
The method of explaining the narrative concerning the female monkey is finished.
The section of the recitation concerning the narrative of the Vajjiputtakas.
43–44. Regarding the passage in the *Vajjiputtaka-vatthu-kathā* which states, “The Vesālīans...

practiced sexual intercourse,” it should be understood that they went to their relatives’ homes, assumed the appearance of householders, and practiced sexual intercourse under the perception, “We have become householders.
Therefore, he said, “They were struck even by the calamity of their kinsmen,” and so forth. The destruction of their kinsmen was caused by such things as royal punishment.
He says, "There is [destruction] by royal punishment," and so forth. Wealth consisting of grain, gold, female and male slaves, cattle, buffalo, and other riches is called "possessions" (*bhoga*);
since even these are destroyed by royal punishment and the like, he says, "This same principle applies to the second term as well.

By the passage beginning with "Not toward an omniscient Buddha," those who lack faith in the three objects [of refuge] perceive themselves as incapable within the Dispensation (*sāsana*) due to the notion that they are indeed incapable; [the text] shows their own capability.

It should be understood that he said "beginning with desire" (*mayanti-ādi*). Regarding the phrase "among the thirty-eight objects," this is stated in the Pāḷi excluding the light-kasiṇa and space-kasiṇa;

however, together with those two, they become forty. "Wholesome states analyzed" refers to the sublime wholesome states together with access concentration, shown by way of their specific distinctions as "this arises upon this object. "Householder-obstructions" means...

"Engaged among householders" refers to being constantly occupied with [affairs] such as mourning for the deceased. "The impediment of the dwelling" refers to being constantly occupied with new construction and other such matters regarding lodgings.
It should be understood that all impediments whatsoever are indeed included within these two impediments, which are difficult to relinquish.

"By reason of" means by way of a cause. "Not in communion": he said "not in communion" with reference to the meaning that, having been a bhikkhu in that particular existence, one is no longer fit to live in communion with the bhikkhus by any means whatsoever.
"Should abolish what has been laid down": this is stated not by saying "one who has returned should not be admitted into the order," but rather "he should not be ordained."
Since it is stated only to this extent, it is understood that the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) is permitted for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense;

therefore, he says, "But standing on the stage of a novice," and so forth. Because it is said, "Whosoever [is] a monk (*bhikkhu*)," one who has renounced the training is no longer a monk, and since he does not incur a *pārājika* offense regarding sexual intercourse, he is granted ordination with the words, "When he has returned, he should be ordained."
To permit [a transgression] is called "not uprooting a pārājika offense"; therefore it says, "by remaining in the state of a bhikkhu with unimpaired virtue.
The "supreme goal" (uttamattha) is either arhatship or nibbāna itself.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion of the fourfold Vinaya and so forth.

45. "Having extracted" means having drawn out from the canonical text (pāḷi). For it is thus that they extracted the *sutta* and the *suttānuloma* from such canonical passages as: "Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not engage [in debate].
With which five? He does not know the *sutta*, he does not know what is in accordance with the *sutta*," and so forth.
[They say: "There is no offense; such is the learning and the interrogation of our teachers."

They brought forth their own opinions starting from such passages as, "He says," which represents the teacher's doctrine; and they brought forth their own opinion starting from such passages as, "The Venerable Upāli said: 'There is no offense, friends, if it was in a dream.
Since that personal opinion of the Elder was included within the Sutta, it became part of the Sutta.
It should be understood that other [passages] likewise must be accepted only when they are included within the Suttas and so forth, and not otherwise. Then...

"Or having extracted," means having analyzed it; having placed the entire Vinaya Piṭaka together with its commentaries into the four sections beginning with the Suttas, they proclaimed the Vinaya by dividing it into four parts, the intention being that there is nothing existing apart from it.

"It was said" refers to what was stated by the Elder Nāgasena in the *Milindapañha*. [The production of the phonemes] occurs through the places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), the organs of articulation (*karaṇa*), and so forth, such as the throat.

"Having brought forth," refers to the words spoken through one's own vocal intimation; thus, it is the "striking word" (*āhacca-pada*). "Essence" (*rasa*) means the core substance, as in expressions such as "the essence of leaves" (*pattarasa*);

the meaning is that it is the core of the suttas concerning what is prohibited and what is permitted. Alternatively, "essence" refers to the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), because it is stated in accordance with the characteristics without omitting the underlying basis.
The "Teacher-lineage" (*ācariyavaṃsa*) refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) transmitted through the lineage of teachers beginning with the compilers of the Dhamma.
He said: "The 'teacher’s lineage' (ācariyavaṃsa) means the teacher’s doctrine (ācariyavāda).

The phrase "the text in the Vinaya Piṭaka" is stated here by way of specific reference; however, the four methods beginning with the Sutta are indeed found accordingly in the remaining Piṭakas as well.
"Great authorities" (mahāpadesa) means great scope or great range; in terms of meaning, they are [defined] by way of such texts as "That which, monks... and so forth.
Because they are grasped by individuals in various ways through the conformity to what is unallowable and the conformity to what is allowable, they are indeed "methods of meaning" (*atthanaya*).

For even though the Blessed One did not state them explicitly, these are called "great authorities" (*mahāpadesā*) because they serve as the causes for the cessation and engagement in all remaining duties—both those prohibited and their conformities, as well as those permitted and their conformities—and thus constitute a great sphere of activity; it is not, however, [because they are the literal words of the Buddha].
“Monks, that which was stated by me as ‘this is not allowable’ and so forth—this very text, together with its underlying intention, has entered into that Sutta because it is included therein.
For it is said: ‘That which conforms to the Sutta must also be brought down into the Sutta... [etc. ...the Sutta itself is more authoritative.
Now, this text together with its underlying intention is neither to be brought down into the Sutta nor is it to be accepted as such, whereby it would constitute a conformity to the Sutta.”
It may be so. Therefore, based on this intention of the Pāḷi, the meanings as they have been stated and accepted by individuals are in accordance with the Suttas.

However, because it elucidates them, this Pāḷi itself should also be understood as being "in accordance with the Suttas" (suttānuloma). Thus he said: "Those which were spoken by the Blessed One in this way," and so forth.
For, according to the method of the Pāḷi beginning with "O monks," those things such as the *akappiyānuloma* (permissible variations) that are to be accepted by individuals [are established].
The meanings that have been stated are what is meant by the "great authorities" (*mahāpadesa*).
The commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) consist of both the miscellaneous teachings of the Blessed One and those that are in conformity with the discourses (*sutta*).

Because they were compiled and spoken by the Theras who collected the Dhamma according to the sequence of the commentary on the Canon (*pāḷi*), they are called the "Teacher’s Tradition" (*ācariyavāda*); and by this, the commentaries [are indicated].
It should be understood that this [meaning] is included within the Suttas and those teachings conforming to the Suttas by way of its sense.

And just as this is so, one’s own opinion (*attanomati*) is also an authoritative standard; for even the Chief Disciples and others, without relying on the Blessed One’s word and the words conforming to it, would not be able to state any meaning—whether conventional or ultimate—regarding the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya by the power of their own knowledge alone.
Therefore, every word is included within the *Sutta* and that which is in conformity with the *Sutta*.

However, because the *Aṭṭhakathā* and so forth have been collected separately, the remainder—taken from the *Sutta* and that which is in conformity with the *Sutta*—is presented as the Vinaya in four ways. Although [the *Aṭṭhakathā*, etc.
proceed by depending precisely upon the *Sutta* and so forth, they are not included in their own form among them; thus it is said: "In the *Sutta*, the *Suttānuloma*, and the *Ācariyavāda*..."

"Having released," he said, "by means of insight following [the teachings] and by grasping the method. In this context, the meaning is: by means of an insight that follows the discourses (*sutta*) and so forth, and by the grasp of the method obtained through them.
"The doctrine of the Elders" (*theravāda*) refers to the position of the Elder Mahāsumma and others. One's own opinion, even if it is erroneous, is based precisely upon the discourses and so forth.
"He says 'it arises'"; as for "but that," and so forth: "by its own meaning" means by the meaning grasped by oneself through one's own method.
"The text" (pāḷi) refers to the canonical text together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakathā*) which serves as the basis for one's own grasp.

"By the text" (pāḷiyā)—the other person says this to exclude the former—means by the text together with its commentary brought forward by the opponent; the sense is: "having compared both the text and the meaning grasped by oneself."

"According to the teacher's doctrine" (*ācariyavāda*) refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) extracted by oneself and by others. "It both descends and accords" means that it "descends" by way of correlating with what has been extracted by oneself, and it "accords" with what has been extracted by another.

"All very weak" is said because a person who is not omniscient lacks the correct comprehension of the meaning due to the latent tendencies of fault (*dosavāsanā*). [This applies] to the teacher's doctrine by way of a careless reading (*pamādapāṭha*).
Thinking that there might even be a lack of consistency with the Sutta, he said, "The other [meaning] should not be accepted.

By saying "only that which is consistent should be accepted," he shows that only those meanings which accord with the Sutta should be extracted from the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa), because the meanings extracted in such a manner alone conform to the Sutta;
therefore, he said: "For according to conformity with the Sutta, it is the Sutta itself..."

"More powerful" means more forceful. "Irresistible" means unopposable. "Similar to the Saṅgha of the compilers" means similar to the Saṅgha that compiled [the teachings] because of its authoritative nature.

"Similar to the time when the Buddhas were present" means similar to the Buddhas while they were still living; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrases "one who takes up a discourse and speaks," etc.:

one whose habit is to speak after having grasped the meaning as it truly is is a "proponent of his own view" (*sakavādī*). A "discourse" (*sutta*) is that which has been entered into the three councils.

This is the Pāli expression. "An opponent" (paravādī) refers to anyone—whether a resident of the Mahāvihāra or a member of another school—who is habituated to speaking after having grasped the meaning erroneously; such a person alone is called an "opponent" here.

"In conformity with the Suttas" (suttānuloma) means anything whatsoever—whether it has been included in the three councils or not—which, through perversion or deception, is presented as "this has come down from the three councils."

"Conformity with the Suttas" (*suttānuloma*). Some say that "conformity with the Suttas" refers to [texts] in other Nikāyas; however, that is not correct, because both the proponent (*sakavādī*) and the opponent (*paravādī*) must accept only those Suttas and so forth that have been included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*). For he will say:

"That which has been included in the three councils and has come down in the Canon (*pāḷi*) is known and should be accepted," and so forth. Indeed, the proponent does not [accept] the Suttas and so forth of other Nikāyas.
One accepts [the position] by way of authority (*pamāṇato*), such that when those suttas and so forth are shown, one should abide by them; and he will say:
"The opponent shows many reasons and determinations from the suttas establishing its improper nature...
having accepted it, saying 'Well said,' one must indeed abide by what is improper. Therefore, even by the opponent in the three councils (*saṅgītittaye*)...

Even that which has not been included is seen as "not included"; the distinction lies solely in the fact that certain discourses and so forth were not included in the three councils, while those that were included have either undergone corruption in their phrasing or have had their intended meaning interpreted otherwise.
Among these, that which is corrupt is removed; and that which has been interpreted otherwise is addressed for the purpose of demonstrating its erroneous nature.

Then a reconciliation is made with another discourse (sutta) and so forth. However, whatever intention has been grasped by the opponent that is reconciled with a discourse and so forth must also be accepted by the proponent after relinquishing his own position;
thus, it should be understood that for both parties, the discourses and other texts contained within the three councils alone are the authoritative standard.
For this very reason, five hundred discourses are cited in the *Kathāvatthu* regarding the proponent's position.

Regarding the phrase "even five thousand suttas in the doctrines of others," this refers only to what has been included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*) through the diversity of grasping their underlying intent (*adhippāya*);
nothing from other *nikāyas* is included.
"Rejecting" (*khepa*) means a refusal or discarding, thinking, "What is the use of this? "Censuring" (*garaha*) means reviling, thinking, "What does this fool know?"

"Should be brought down into the Sutta" means that it should be brought down by way of reconciling the meaning into whichever Sutta this "conformity with the Sutta" was made because of its conformity to— that is,
into that very Sutta or into another Sutta similar to it— by way of showing how the conformity with the Sutta taken up by oneself accords with it,
demonstrating it after having reconciled it thus: "By this and this reason, it accords with this Sutta."

"Meaning. "This one" refers to the proponent of our own school (*sakavādī*). "The other" refers to the proponent of another school (*paravādī*). "The teacher’s doctrine should be brought down into the Sutta":

whichever Sutta this teacher’s doctrine was promulgated as a commentary upon, it should be brought down into that Sutta—or into some similar Sutta—by way of reconciling the preceding and following meanings.
"A censurable teacher’s doctrine" means it was written down by mistake, or established by those of a different sect; this same method applies everywhere.

In order to show that any "fabricated sutta" (*kūṭasutta*)—that is, statements such as those found in non-Buddhist suttas and the like—should not be accepted, it is said: "A sutta should be brought down into conformity with the suttas," and so forth.
Works such as the *Guḷhavessantara* are treatises belonging to schismatic sects, such as the Mahāsāṅghikas. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), works such as the *Guḷhaummagga* are included.
The proponent (*sakavādī*) speaks by taking recourse to the suttas, and the opponent (*paravādī*) likewise...
By means of the terms "sutta" and so forth, other bases for dispute can also be understood according to the method already stated; therefore, they are not mentioned here.

Having thus shown the general nature of disputes by way of the suttas, the *suttānuloma*, and so on, the passage beginning with "Now, however, this is allowable" (*atha panāyaṃ kappiyaṃ*) is stated in order to show specifically the subject matter of the dispute and its resolution, as well as the suttas and other texts. In the sutta...
Regarding the phrase *ca suttānulome ca*: here the word *ca* (and) has the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*), by which the teachings of the masters (*ācariyavāda*) and so forth are also included.

Therefore, he said: "It shows both the reason (*kāraṇa*) and the determination (*vinicchaya*). In that context, "reason" refers to the cause extracted from one's own judgment based on the method of the Suttas and so forth.
"Determination" refers to the determination found in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "The shadow of the reason" refers to [the term] "allowable" (*kappiya*) within the Suttas and so forth.

Regarding the word *gāha*, it means the shadow of a cause—an obscure reason that is difficult to establish—which serves as the sign for what is "unallowable" (*akappiya*) to one who has grasped [the rule].
The phrase "having reached the Vinaya" is explained as "having come to the investigation of what is allowable and unallowable.
"Should be restrained" means that the transgression committed under the perception of what is allowable must be restrained; the mind intent on preventing that [transgression] should be made firmer.
It must be done. "The stream must be cut off" means that the occurrence of transgression therein must be severed. "In the state of being grave" means in the state of being unallowable (*akappiya*).
"By means of the reasons for the determination of the Sutta" means by the reasons obtained through the Sutta and the determination of the Aṭṭhakathā.
"Thus," etc., is a concluding statement regarding the meaning as previously stated. "An additional reason" refers to the preceding [reasons] among the Sutta and so forth.
"Prior" means either an excessive reason or a manifold reason.
"Uttered by speech" means risen by way of speech; the meaning is that it stands there continuously.
Because it is stated that "the Sutta is the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," the phrase "again, the Sutta" refers to the words of the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas which set forth that meaning.
This is what is intended. "By way of the phrasing" (*anubyañjanato*) refers to both the interrogation (*paripuccha*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In this context, "interrogation" means hearing the meaning of the text from the teacher; "commentary" means the analysis independent of the text.
For both of these follow the text and clarify its meaning through the phrasing, and are thus called "phrasing" (*anubyañjana*). Regarding the Vinaya:
Regarding conduct in the Vinaya, he will himself say later: "one who does not abandon nor depart from the Vinaya," and so forth.
In that context, "establishment" refers to such things as not intentionally committing an offense; therefore, he says, "established by way of a sense of shame.

By this, it is meant that one becomes possessed of shame (*lajjī*). But when the characteristics of a bearer of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) are to be stated, what is the purpose of this quality of being possessed of shame?
He said: "The shameless one," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "even though he is learned," he shows the possession of the first characteristic.

By the phrase "out of desire for gain and honor," and so forth, he shows that in the absence of being established in the Vinaya, the application of the first characteristic does not perform its function;
rather, it performs what is not its function and brings about harm. A quarrel is a prelude to a schism in the Sangha and is called a "fracture" (rāji) of the Sangha.
"Vitthunati" means it distends, or it gasps, or it is unable to remain still; therefore he says "yaṃ yaṃ... and so forth.
"Ācariyaparamparā" refers to the succession of the teachers' interpretations; for this very reason he will say: "Abandoning one's own opinion...
just as the teacher and the teacher’s teacher state the text and its inquiry... and so on.
"It is necessary to know [this]. For there is no purpose in knowing the succession of teachers merely by their names.

"By the connection of what precedes and what follows" means by knowing the relationship between the meaning of a preceding statement and a subsequent statement. "By the meaning" means by the meaning of the individual words, the collective meaning, the intended meaning, and so forth.

"By the reason" means by the logical justification for that meaning. "The sequence of the Elder's teaching" (theravādaṅga) means the order of the Elder's doctrine; the sense is: the order of their analytical exposition.
Regarding the phrase "by these three characteristics": here, by the first characteristic, the fact that the Vinaya has been thoroughly mastered is stated.
By the second, its establishment through both a sense of moral shame (*lajjībhāva*) and immovability is indicated.
By the third, the capacity to judge even what has not yet arrived [in the texts] by means of the appropriate method provided by teachers in accordance with the Suttas and Commentaries is expressed.
"In the matter having been brought forward" means: when the matter of transgression has been brought forward in the midst of the Saṅgha by way of an accusation.

"When what is to be said has been spoken by both the accuser and the accused" means: when that which is to be said—namely, by the accuser such as "I have seen it," "I have heard it," and so forth, and by the accused such as "It exists," "It does not exist," and so forth—has been spoken based on the matter thus brought forward; this is the meaning.

Because the *thullaccaya* and *dubbhāsita* offenses are not included in the *mātikā*, it is stated as “of the five kinds of offenses. “A triad of *dukkaṭas*” refers to the triad of *dukkaṭas* that has come down in such passages as:
“If one perceives one who is not ordained as ordained, and censures or reviles them, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*,” and so forth.
“Or any other offense” refers to: “If one perceives it as the wrong time when it is the right time, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.”
This was said with reference to the "double-dukkata" [offense], beginning with: "If one is doubtful regarding the time, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.

"An intermediate offense" (antarāpatti) refers to an offense stated here and there between the beginning of the narrative and the conclusion of the case being disciplined—excluding the transgression of the specific subject matter mentioned in each respective training rule. However, in this context, it says, "he looks at the subject matter."

Because they were taken separately, the remainder was understood as "intermediate offenses" (*antarāpatti*). "He throws back a firebrand" (*paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati*)—this is found in the training rule concerning fanning (*visibbana-sikkhāpada*).
Therein, he throws back a burning firebrand that has fallen outside from a fire-pit or similar place, having not yet been extinguished;

the meaning is that he places it back again in its original position. However, for one who throws back one that has already been extinguished, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone. "No offense" (*anāpatti*)...

In this context, there are also instances where non-offenses (*anāpatti*) are mentioned here and there— such as, "Monks, there is no offense for one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*) within the domain of psychic power"—
and these too are included in the summary.

As for the statement "it should not yet be called a *pārājika* offense," this refers to the fact that the person who has committed it remains established in the quality of shame (*lajjīdhamma*) and perceives things as they truly are.
Even in the case of an investigation, this was said with reference to such things as taking what is not given, which are difficult to determine.

However, that which is the conscious awareness regarding sexual intercourse and so forth must certainly be stated; therefore he said, "The transgression of the practice of sexual intercourse," and so on.

But in the case of one who, out of shamelessness, does not give a confession and instead engages in evasion, it is impossible to determine even whether his offense is gross, until he [speaks] according to the facts.
If one acts in this way, as long as the Sangha’s doubt regarding the offense does not disappear, one will remain as one who has been expelled.
"Subtle" means subtle due to the subtlety of the mental transformation; therefore he said, "lightness of mind," meaning that his mind is light.
"Those" refers to transgressions. "Based on that" means rooted in taking what is not given, and so forth. That which the teacher...
The statement "speak it," "do that," and so forth, is all said with reference specifically to one who is modest, gentle, and scrupulous.
Even by one who explains [the matter] as it truly is and seeks only purity, it is said that he "should not be called a pārājika," because he is suspected even at the extreme limit of non-offense;
for this very reason, it is called "the shadow of a pārājika. Regarding the phrase "having purified the precepts" (sīlāni sodhetvā): in whatever...

When there is a transgression, a suspicion of a *pārājika* offense arises; in that case, one should purify one's virtues by taking the side that denies the *pārājika* status and by cleansing those offenses through confession (*desanā*) and emergence from them (*vuṭṭhāna*).

The phrase "the thirty-two aspects" is stated as a representative illustration because they are well-known; it is indeed permissible to attend to whatever subject one prefers. The meditation subject is "joined" [to the mind] by means of the root of remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).
By means of non-distraction, it is joined together by the mind through continuity, without showing gaps here and there.
"Formations" (saṅkhārā) is said by way of the meditation subject for insight (vipassanā).

For one who has committed an offense, even a familiar meditation subject does not appear clearly, let alone one involving a pārājika offense; for his mind lacks one-pointedness due to its tendency toward remorse.
However, even for one of pure virtue, if he is prone to excessive applied thought (*vitakka*) and mental distraction (*vikkhepa*), his mind does not become concentrated;
this should not be understood here as being rooted in a defeat offense (*pārājika*).

Rather, it is with reference to the failure of the mind to concentrate due solely to remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) rooted in committed evil that it is said, "the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) does not succeed. Therefore, he said, "by the fire of remorse," and so forth.

By "self" (*attanā*), meaning by means of the mind acting as the instrument, the person (*puggala*) as the agent knows; or, the instrumental case is used in the sense of identity, meaning that the self itself understands.
This concludes the method of explaining the discourse on the fourfold discipline and so forth.
In the *Padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā*:
“*Yādiyo* means ‘as it appears’; since the word *yathā* functions in the sense of the word *yaṃ*, he says ‘connected with this or that.
For by the two words ‘this or that’ (*yena tena*), the meaning of the word *yaṃ* is shown without restriction. [The phrase] “joined to the burden of dwelling” (*vāsadhurayutto*)...
One who is devoted to the task of insight (vipassanā). "Whatever his birth" (*yā jāti assa*) means *yaṃjāti*; the person (*puggalo*) is the same as that which is his birth.

By applying the suffix *-ya* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), it becomes *yaṃjacco*. The connection is: "by whatever lineage (*gotta*), or by whichever lineage—whether he be of such a lineage or of another lineage.
"In regard to virtues" (*sīlesu*) means in regard to natural dispositions. "But then" (*atha kho*) has the meaning of "but rather" (*kiṃ tu*). The sense is: "What is being said? (*kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti*).
"In this matter" means in this context of an offense involving defeat (pārājika). "This [person]" refers to one who is endowed with the aforementioned characteristics.

"Of the noble ones" refers to that which is spoken of thus: "The noble ones stand for the sake of others; this is the solicitation of the noble ones," and not to the wretched person who says, "Give to me.

"By accepting the outward signs" means even in the absence of the thought, "I shall go for alms," there is the acceptance of the outward signs of the renunciant life dependent upon the consumption of alms-food.

By way of acceptance. "Food brought in baskets" means food brought by means of baskets. "Unrighteous" is said because of the absence of the qualities of a bhikkhu, such as the training in higher virtue;
therefore he says, "unreal. The meaning is that those who say "we are bhikkhus" are bhikkhus merely by their declaration, not in reality.
And this is stated because it is possible for one to claim, "We are bhikkhus," even while being otherwise. "We..."

“Bhikkhus”: for even those who do not claim [to be] so are indeed called "professing bhikkhus" (bhikkhu-paṭiññā) by virtue of their assuming the outward signs that are the basis for the conventional designation "bhikkhu," as well as by their accepting a share of the requisites given to bhikkhus. Thus it is said in the *Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā*:

“‘One who is not a practitioner of the holy life, yet professes to be a practitioner of the holy life’—others who are practitioners of the holy life, well-clad, well-dressed, and carrying clean bowls...”

"Having seen those who, after wandering for alms in villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals, maintain their livelihood, he himself acts in such a manner that it is as if he were giving the promise, 'I am a celibate practitioner' (brahmacārī).

Furthermore, when he says, 'I am a bhikkhu,' and enters the Uposatha hall and other such places, he indeed possesses the claim of being a celibate practitioner; likewise when he receives gains belonging to the Saṅgha."
Therefore, it is not permissible for monks who have made such a confession—those whose spiritual lineage (gotrabhū) has reached its conclusion—to enjoy communal meals or shared requisites with them;
it becomes an enjoyment [only] with those who are shameless (*alajjī*).

Furthermore, the definition of a shameless person as one who intentionally commits an offense is stated with reference to the most extreme cases of monks, since the term "shameless" is also seen to be applied to novices (*sāmaṇera*) and others. [As it is said: “With shameless novices...”
For it is said: "One must not even cause manual labor to be performed. Indeed, failing to abide by the practice as prescribed is a characteristic of shamelessness common to all.

Those who are immoral are exclusively devoid of shame from the moment they assume the outward signs [of the monkhood], because they lack the practice as prescribed—just like the Mahāsāṅghika and other sectarian groups, and like those who use the signs for sexual purposes and so forth. As long as...
And as long as their claim to being monks continues, they are indeed monks; however, any enjoyment [of requisites] by them is the enjoyment of those who are shameless.
Furthermore, what is given with the perception that it is for the Saṅgha of monks is said to be "given to the Saṅgha. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Ananda, in a future time there will be those of the lineage (gotrabhuno) who wear the saffron robe around their necks, yet are immoral and of evil character."
"Ānanda, when they give a gift intended for the Saṅgha while those [monks] are immoral,

I say that at that time the offering dedicated to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable. Because it was given by them with the Blessed One’s Saṅgha in mind, the offering became incalculable and immeasurable, even though the recipients were immoral.

If it is argued that [the field of merit] is not [the Saṅgha] because [the gift] was given [to them], no; for among those [persons], they are designated as "dedicating to the Saṅgha" because the lineage-holders (gotrabhū) are referred to as the recipients.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to say, "dedicating to the Saṅgha among any householders or renunciants whatsoever.
And in that case, there would be no purpose for showing the lower limit by saying, "At that time, Ānanda... Therefore, even for the lineage-holders...

There is no gift dedicated to the Saṅgha when the Saṅgha is non-existent; yet, even in that case, a donation given to them at the very least is reckoned as a gift to the Saṅgha and is incalculable, for it does not fail to bear fruit beyond that.
Therefore, based on their own admission, they should be understood as "monks.
"Brahmaghosa" means the supreme sound, or a sound like the voice of Brahmā. "Ehi bhikkhū" is an address meaning "O monks."
In this saṃsāra, which is full of fear, for the sake of completely destroying that fear, enter with your mind the Triple Refuge or the Teaching as a "shelter" and a "refuge.
Having entered, practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*); that is, practice both the holy life of the Teaching and the holy life of the Path.
*Bhaṇḍū* means one whose hair has been shorn. *Vāsī* means an axe for cutting tooth-sticks and so forth.
“Bandhana” means a waist-band (*kāyabandhana*). “Yutto yogo” refers to the application (*yoga*) by way of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*paññā*);
the remainder of the phrase is “these eight are his requisites. The remainder [of the sense] is that he is characterized precisely by those things fastened upon his body.
Although one should have said “three hundred,” it is stated as “three hundred” for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.
Therefore, the Blessed One refers back to what was stated below. For below it was said:
"But I, Kassapa, knowing indeed say 'I know,' and seeing indeed say 'I see. He refers to that; the meaning is: "because I speak knowing, therefore [this is so].
"Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*). "Intense" means great. "Present" means manifest.
"Will it be? means: even before approaching the elders and others, [one thinks], "What if, indeed, a sense of shame and dread of blame (*hirī-ottappa*) were to arise in me?

"Connected with the wholesome" means: based on faultless phenomena (*dhamma*). "Making it a bone" means: making oneself a bone by means of that phenomenon, or making that phenomenon one's own purpose (*attha*) by thinking, "This is my goal. "With the ear applied" means: *(Note: The original text ends abruptly; the provided fragment concludes here.)*

"With ear inclined to the Dhamma. Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself: having directed both the stream of knowledge and the stream of confidence, you should train yourself in this very way, thinking, "I shall listen to the Dhamma with full attention. And:

"Body-contemplation mindfulness accompanied by pleasure"—this refers to body-contemplation mindfulness associated with happiness by way of the first jhāna, both in regard to the foul and in regard to mindfulness of breathing.
Furthermore, the careful reception of this instruction was itself the elder’s going-forth and his full ordination.

The jhāna having the bloated as its counterpart object is the perception of the bloated (*uddhumātaka-saññā*). The fine-material-sphere jhāna having a kasiṇa as its object is the perception of form (*rūpa-saññā*).
These two dhammas of jhāna are indicated here by way of their "perception" aspect. And Sopāka was questioned by the Blessed One.

He said: "They have the same meaning in terms of being of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); only the phrasing is different. "With a mind that has been won over" means with a mind that has been propitiated.
The full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the acceptance of the heavy rules (*garudhamma*) and so forth will be explained further on by itself.
"In the ultimate sense" means by the ultimate limit. The formal act (*kammavācā*) consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) is the procedure for the full ordination.

Because it is the cause, it is the "proper occasion" (*ṭhāna*); and because it is worthy of that occasion, the action free from defects in the object and so forth is called "worthy of the occasion" (*ṭhānāraha*).
This is because an action associated with defects in the object and so forth lacks the inherent nature required to be fit for the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*).
Alternatively, "occasion" refers to the Teaching (*sāsana*) comprised of the three trainings, as it is the cause for attaining Nibbāna; [the action] is "worthy" of that.

Action is worthy of its place. For it is only one who has been fully ordained by means of an action possessing the characteristics as prescribed that is capable of undertaking and fulfilling the entire Dispensation.
Therefore, every function of the Saṅgha, concluding with the perfectly pure formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), is called "worthy of its place.
Thus he said, "by what is worthy of the Teacher’s Dispensation," meaning: by that which is suitable for one who has fulfilled the entirety of the Dispensation, beginning with virtue (*sīla*).

The meaning: although, because this [training] is prescribed for all training rules only for one who has been fully ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), it appears from the literal sense that those pure beings who have been ordained by means such as the "Come, monk!

ordination (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*) lack the incapacity [to commit offenses] or the absence of fault even when they transgress training rules that constitute offenses by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), nevertheless, in terms of the actual meaning, for them too, regarding those offenses by rule—

Even in the case of minor offenses excluded from the world, such as drinking liquor and the like, it is indeed established that one may incur an offense prior to the arising of the Path through lack of intention and so forth.
For it is said: "Two persons are incapable of incurring an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas.
Two persons are capable of incurring an offense: Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs. [This applies] by means of the motion and the third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha*).

"Ordained by means of an act" (kammena upasampanno): this, however, is stated by way of the majority, referring to those monks who are capable of transgressing any training rule and who exist at all times.
"By way of etymology" (niruttivasena) means by way of derivation. "By way of expression" (abhilāpavasena) means by way of conventional usage.
"By way of qualities" (guṇavasena) means by way of the qualities that are the grounds for the conventional designation "monk."

The commentary on the analysis of the terms for the higher training begins with the words "But what is... in order to show that virtue and the other factors, which are the necessary conditions for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), are designated by the terms "higher virtue" (*adhisisa*) and so forth because they are superior to mundane virtues.
In that context, "virtue consisting of five or ten factors" refers to the virtue [practiced] during a period when no Buddha has appeared.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), because [the latter] lacks the necessary condition for the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). However, that fivefold, eightfold, and tenfold virtue which is protected by laymen and laywomen,

as well as by male and female novices and probationers— having understood the qualities of the Triple Gem as they truly are when a Buddha has arisen and being firmly established in faith within the Dispensation—
that too is indeed "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*), because it is a cause for the arising of the Path.

For the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called "higher virtue" (*adhicitta*) among mundane virtues because it is the cause for the arising of the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*), just as [the mundane] higher mind is.
Indeed, no distinction whatsoever is found in the higher mind other than its being the cause for the path of insight, apart from the mundane mind;
and both of these [virtue and mind] are so designated because the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*) is devoid of an essence such as a self (*atta*).
It is struck by the three characteristics; it is rooted in the defects of ignorance and craving that proceed in the mode of "I" and "mine";

and through the excellence of insight—fortified by the powers of virtue and mind—it is capable of utterly destroying those very roots of defect, thereby bringing about the cessation of that cycle of existence (saṃsāra), as well as through the possession of the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as omniscience.

Having understood that the state of being a teacher of the true Dhamma without error is a condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) because it must be undertaken and practiced by one who has practiced accordingly— and not for any other reason—

if that quality of being a condition for turning away is common even to the five precepts and so forth within the Dispensation, why should this [higher morality] not be considered *adhisīla*? For those who abide merely in the five precepts and so forth...
The path arises even for householders such as Anāthapiṇḍika and others. For indeed, there is no arising of the path without higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and higher mind (*adhicitta*).

And although, due to the lack of decisive support (*upanissaya*), that [higher virtue] may not be the cause for the arising of the path in that particular existence, nevertheless, it will certainly exist in another life;
thus, for virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) who pass away while possessing higher virtue alone—
Like the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, he therefore said, "It occurs only when a Buddha has arisen," and so forth.
Even the five precepts and others, when observed while aspiring for *vivaṭṭa* (the turning away from rebirth), occur only when a Buddha has arisen.

However, the statement beginning with "For that is not a formal proclamation" (*na hi taṃ paññatti*) was spoken with reference to the entire Pātimokkha in its most excellent sense; for even the householders' virtue consisting of the abstention from killing, stealing, and so on, is but a portion of that [Pātimokkha].

Only Buddhas, by way of the detailed analysis of the Pārājika Suttas and other sections of the Vinaya, are able to prescribe the higher morality (*adhisīla*) as the proximate cause for the arising of the Path, having completely severed the stream of transgression that obstructs the arising of the Path at the doors of body and speech; others cannot do so.
For it is with reference to the arising of the Path that his higher morality has been described. Therefore he said: "Even from the restraint of the Pātimokkha..."

"And only the virtue associated with the path and its fruits is 'higher virtue' (adhisīla). For that very reason, it is called "higher virtue" because it is based on the Path without any intervening factors.
"Not intended here" means that in this context of the first *pārājika*, it is not intended as "training" (*sikkhā*).
"Worldly minds of the eight attainments" refers to those which are to be entered by worldly people who do not know the true nature of the Dispensation.
This was stated with reference to the eight types of consciousness associated with the fine-material and immaterial jhānas.

For there is no distinction between mundane and supramundane within the sublime (mahaggata) states, such that the qualification "mundane" would serve to exclude the supramundane. Therefore, the qualification "mundane" is employed solely to exclude those sublime jhānas that are to be attained by followers of the Dispensation (Sāsanika).
And as it is here, so too in the case of the phrase "the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere."
In this context as well, the qualification "worldly" (*lokiya*) must indeed be applied. For this alone is the distinction of the mind from "higher mind" (*adhicitta*):

namely, its arising in a person who does not know the Teaching (*sāsana*). And thus, even in the absence of the appearance of a Buddha, the status of higher virtue and higher mind is established for the virtue and mind of those such as the Paccekabuddhas who do know the nature of the Teaching. It is not [established] without the appearance of a Buddha.
This, however, is stated because for others—such as Paccekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas—the teaching lacks the efficacy to serve as a cause for realization (*abhisamaya*).
As for the cause of future latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they indeed teach both virtue and mind;

yet, even though these constitute higher virtue and higher mind (*adhisīla-adhicitta*) by being causes for the Path, they are not designated as such because they are minimal, lack expansiveness, and are not well-known.
It should be understood that the restriction "only when a Buddha has arisen" (*buddhuppādeyeva*) is intended here.

This is because, by means of the commentarial statements such as "one who has attained that [jhāna]," etc., both in this exposition of higher mind (*adhicitta*) and in the subsequent exposition of higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), there is a rejection of only those higher mind and higher wisdom associated with the paths and fruits;
thus, it is mundane (*lokiya*) higher mind and higher wisdom that are intended here. Furthermore, even for one who has attained those two [mundane states],...
