The nature of engaging in sexual intercourse is understood; however, because it is stated in the Canon, "That which is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is the training intended here," it is understood that the mundane training in higher mind (adhicitta) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā) are not intended.
Therefore, the intention in both the Canon and the Commentary should be understood as follows: "Sexual intercourse..."
As soon as the thought "I shall engage in sexual intercourse" arises, mundane higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*) decline;
however, since higher virtue (*adhisīla*) does not decline by the mere arising of such a thought, only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*) is mentioned in the Canon.
In the Commentary, however, it is stated that for a bhikkhu who has attained the supramundane path, even the thought "I shall engage in sexual intercourse" does not arise.

It arises because it is entirely of an unshakable nature; whereas for ordinary persons and even for those who have attained meditative absorption, it may arise due to some cause because it is of a shakable nature.
To show this distinction, it should be understood that when the phrase "one who has entered that [attainment]" is used, only supramundane attainments are excluded.
Regarding the phrase "there is what is given" (*atthi dinnaṃ*): here, "given" refers to the volition of giving (*dāna-cetanā*). The meaning is that there is a fruit for that which has been given.
This same method applies to the phrase "there is what is sacrificed" (*atthi yiṭṭhaṃ*) as well. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), offerings such as *huta* are included.
In this context, "sacrificed" (*yiṭṭhaṃ*) refers to a great sacrifice, a great gift common to all. "Offered" (*hutaṃ*) refers to a substantial honor; whether it belongs to oneself or to others.
Or, the ten courses of unwholesome action, or indeed all unwholesome states, are not called "one's own karma" because they produce what is disadvantageous;

their opposites, the wholesome states, are called "one's own. Alternatively, both the wholesome and the unwholesome are "one's own" in the sense that they are decisive for beings as long as the process of saṃsāra continues, according to such statements as "we are the owners of our karma.
Thus, in this sense of being one's own through the ownership of karma—*kammassakatā*—[the self is established].
The knowledge that arises from the sense of ownership over one's own acquisitions is the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma; this, however, is merely an illustration.
Indeed, all wholesome wisdom leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) that is dependent on the Dispensation is included within the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma.

Furthermore, all wisdom leading to the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*) that is dependent on the Dispensation is called "knowledge in conformity with the Truths" (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*). And that alone is higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*); the remainder is...
All of this should be understood as the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma. For this very reason, the Blessed One included all of it within the fourfold set of knowledges, stating:
"The knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma is knowledge in conformity with the truths; it is the knowledge of one possessing the path; it is the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.
However, as for the insight-knowledge that discerns the modes of the three characteristics, because it serves as an immediate proximate condition for the path—

This has been stated by way of the highest limit. For it should be understood that even the wisdom consisting of the recollection of the Triple Gem and so forth, when belonging to others [than those on the path], possesses the status of "higher wisdom" (adhipaññā) because it serves as a cause for the Path.
The method of commentary on the analysis of the term *sājīva* is concluded.
In the commentary on the analysis of renunciation (*paccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā*):
"When weakness is manifested" means when the state of being weak is made known by such statements as, "What if I were to renounce the Buddha? and so forth.
"Having mounted upon the mouth" refers to the intention that it has been brought to the lips of worldly people in expressions such as "seven or eight [days]" and so on. "Two or three nights."

In this context, just as the expression "two or three nights" (*dirattatiratta*) is stated without interruption for the purpose of including the "three nights" by means of sleeping together with one not fully ordained continuously— rather than taking "three nights" as interrupted by occasional intervals—
it is likewise possible here to understand the purpose of including the "two nights," namely, [the condition of] weakness.

The phrase "without having manifested weakness" (*anāvikatvā*) was stated in order to show that there is indeed a purpose for this inclusion as well; or else, it was stated because [the text] says, "since [there is no offense] in the case of renouncing the training," and so forth.

Now, the phrase "apicā" (moreover) and so forth was stated to show that even without being a mere commentary on the preceding term "without having manifested weakness," there is a distinct meaning of its own.
Regarding the expression "specific and non-specific": here, by whichever sentence the manifestation of weakness itself...
There is a distinction between the renunciation of training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*) and the disclosure of weakness through the renunciation of training (*sikkhāpaccakkhānadubbalyāvikamma*).
However, regarding that statement by which both of these occur, there is neither distinction nor non-distinction; thus, it is "distinction-and-non-distinction" (*visesāvisesa*).
Because the root *kaṭha* is listed among the roots as meaning "to live with difficulty," it is said: "one who has reached a life of hardship" (*kicchajīvikappatta*).
For *ukkaṇṭhana* is *ukkaṇṭhā* (longing); one who has gone away from that is *ukkaṇṭhita*, meaning one who has fallen into a life of hardship.

Alternatively, *ukkaṇṭhā* is that in which the throat is turned upward; a person is *ukkaṇṭha* when, like a herd of cattle whose leader has been led away by a goad, they seek the path of departure due to dissatisfaction (*anabhirati*). One is also called *ukkaṇṭhita* because of having gone away from that dissatisfaction.
Showing the meaning, he said: “dwelling with his throat constricted. And since that state of being constricted is indeed through distraction, it was said:
“one who is distracted,” and so forth.
From the state of a recluse means from the higher ordination (*upasampadā*). By way of a modification of state means having fallen away from the state of a monk (*bhikkhu*), whatever...

One who desires to attain the state of a householder or the like conceives of one's own selfhood as "I shall be this," meaning that one conceives of one's own selfhood in the form of a householder or similar status;
the intention is that it is by way of such a conception of one's own selfhood.
(46) In the Pāḷi, the phrase *yadi panāham* means: "If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would indeed be well."
“Indeed, I shall go away,”—here too the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
He says: “The thought arises in me:

‘I shall renounce the Buddha. (50) “I do not delight” shows the absence of happiness due to the great abundance of suffering in the life of renunciation. “I do not find joy” shows his own lack of delight even though blameless happiness exists within that life of renunciation.
“By that very verbal distinction” means that even after making a verbal distinction, one prevents the communication by another bodily application.

By the phrase “this person desires to abandon the teaching,” etc., although there is a total absence of understanding the meaning of the words due to a lack of skill in speech, [one understands] at least this much of the intended meaning:
“This person, desiring to abandon his status as a renunciant, makes this verbal distinction.”
This shows that even if he knows only that much, it constitutes a formal renunciation (*paccakkhāna*). Therefore, he said: “He knows even this much.
*Padapacchābhaṭṭha* means a reversal of words; all languages remaining after the Māgadhī language should be understood as “foreign languages” (*milakkhabhāsā*).
“Descended into the field itself” means descended into the very field that serves as the locus for the growth of the renunciation of the training.
“Messenger” (dūta) means oral instruction (mukhasāsana). “Instruction” (sāsana) means written instruction (paṇṇasāsana), or it is shown by carving letters on walls, pillars, and so forth.
It is described as “associated with consciousness” (cittasampayutta) with reference to the arising of vocal expression while the intention to refuse is still present in the mind;

the meaning is that it is “originated by consciousness” (cittasamuṭṭhāna). He spoke [the following] to show the distinction in the way of knowing, according to whether it is restricted or unrestricted:

“If this very person should know,” and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the distinction made by the words “speaks” (*vadati*) and “makes known” (*viññāpeti*), it should be understood that this is obtained through the method already stated—that here, the intended meaning is the knowing (*vijānana*) on the part of the one to whom he speaks;

for it is not possible here for the sense to be that he speaks to one person while making another understand. This is because it was stated: “even when only one among them knows. Thus, there are only two.

"Let one know, let one not know"—even if the announcement has been made after thus restricting it to two people, it should be understood that the renunciation is indeed valid if even one among them knows.
"One who suspects" means one who suspects, thinking, "They will stop me. "One who knows the occasion" (samayaññū) means one who knows the conventions of the Dispensation;
however, in this context, one is called "one who knows the occasion" even by merely knowing the underlying intention.

Therefore, he said "discontented," and so forth. Consequently, even if one has fully understood the meaning of the words of the formula such as "I renounce the Buddha," if one does not know the underlying intention—that this person speaks out of a desire to fall away from the state of a bhikkhu—the training remains unrenounced.
On the other hand, even if one does not understand the literal meaning, if one knows that the person speaks because they are "discontented," [the training] is indeed renounced.

There is training. Since the auditory consciousness process involves only the apprehension of the mere sound, whereas the apprehension of the meaning occurs through a succession of mental consciousness processes, he said, "at that very moment," and so forth.
53. *Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna* is a treatise that proclaims the praise of the Teacher’s virtues. *Upāligāthāsu* means in the *Upāli-sutta*.
In the verses spoken by the householder Upāli, beginning with "of the wise one, free from delusion," and so forth.

"According to the literal expression" means exactly as it is stated in the Pāḷi. "Anantabuddhi" and so on are names found in the *Vaṇṇappakaraṇa* (The Book of Praise). However, "the wise one" (*dhīra*) and so on appear in the verses of Upāli.
In that context, "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to omniscient knowledge; because it is the cause for knowing, it is said: "this one has wisdom (*paññāṇa*) [based on] that."
"Bodhipaññāṇo. In such passages as "Svākkhāto dhammo," the word *dhamma* is used to show that it is a synonym for the terms beginning with "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*).
Therefore, renunciation occurs precisely when one says, using these synonyms, "I renounce the well-expounded [Dhamma]," and so forth.
However, when the term is used in conjunction with the word *dhamma*, it is a renunciation according to the literal meaning of the sound.
It should be understood that the same method applies to such phrases as "the Saṅgha is well-practiced" and so forth.

Furthermore, terms such as "wholesome phenomena" (*kusalā dhammā*) are names stated with reference specifically to wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena (*akusalā dhammā*), and so on; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of no fault being incurred in the rejection of unwholesome phenomena.
Therefore, he said: "in the eighty-four thousand aggregates of phenomena" (*dhammakkhandhasahassesu*), and so forth. [This is explained] by the passage beginning with "the first *pārājika*," etc.
It should be understood that this refers specifically to the training rules (sikkhāpada), not to the offenses (āpatti).

"In whose presence" means in whose vicinity. Among the synonyms for teacher (ācariya), the phrase "he who ordained me" is said with reference to one who, without having given the going-forth (upajjha), acted as a teacher and performed the ordination. "In his presence" means in his vicinity.
*Okallako* is a designation for householders whose bodies are emaciated and withered, afflicted by the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth.
*Moḷibaddho* is a householder who has his hair tied up in a topknot. *Kumārako* is a novice (*sāmaṇera*) who is still in the stage of childhood and exceedingly young.
*Cellako* is one slightly older than that. *Ceṭako* is one of middle age. *Moḷigallo* is a senior novice (*mahāsāmaṇera*). *Samaṇuddeso* is...

This is a general term for novice monks (*sāmaṇera*). "One of impure and suspicious conduct" means one who, having become impure, is possessed of a mode of conduct that must be remembered and recalled by oneself with the suspicion, "Has anyone else found out what I have done?
and by others with the suspicion, "Who on earth did this? He is "born of dregs" because of the filth of lust and other defilements that have arisen within him.
"Koṇṭha" is a designation for one who is immoral.

(54) "Those with a triple-root rebirth-linking" is said with reference to those capable of very rapid cognition; it is not [said] regarding those with double roots, because that [rapid cognition] is impossible for them.
"Of a similar kind" refers to a male. "Of a dissimilar kind" refers to a woman. "Resembling a painted figure" means...
"Resembling a form made of clay and so forth. "Of one with heavy wisdom" means, because of the absence of swift engagement with objects, one who is slow-moving; that is to say, one of dull wisdom.
Now, here, for the purpose of summarizing the methods stated in the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā regarding the section on the renunciation of the training:

The analysis should be understood as follows: therein, by means of the phrases "desirous of falling away from the state of a recluse" and so forth, he shows the restriction regarding the mind (*cittaniyama*).

By the phrases "the Buddha" and so forth, he shows the restriction regarding the field (*khetta-niyama*). By the expression "I renounce; let it be held [by you]," he shows the restriction regarding time (*kāla-niyama*). By the word "speaks," he shows the restriction regarding the formal application (*payoga-niyama*).
And by the phrases "Enough for me of the Buddha," "What need have I?", "It is of no use to me," "I am well freed," and so forth...
He shows that there is a renunciation even by way of time when it is not specified; by the word "informs," he indicates the necessity of being understood;
by such phrases as "one who is insane renounces the training" and "in the presence of one who is insane," he indicates the necessity of the person;

and by such phrases as "and he does not understand," he shows the absence of renunciation due to the absence of the necessity of being understood, and by such phrases as "for sport," he shows the absence of the necessity of the intention.

"Desiring to announce it, he does not announce it"—by this, due to the absence of a fixed rule regarding the procedure, [it is shown that] whether one announces it to an ignorant person or does not announce it to a wise person, the success of the act depends solely on the hearing by the very individual for whose sake one announces it, and not on anyone else.
Alternatively, "he does not announce it at all; the training is not renounced"—this, however, refers to the renunciation of the training through the restriction of the mind and so forth.

This is stated for the purpose of showing that it is so and not otherwise. Therefore, having understood the renunciation of the training by way of the mind, the field, the time, the application, and the person, one should know that there is no renunciation in the absence of these factors. How so?
For the renunciation of the training occurs only with a mind desiring to fall away from the state of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and not through mere negligence.
Or by saying "vā" or "ravā. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs through the mind, not by the mere absence [of those qualities].

Likewise, there are fourteen [categories] beginning with the Buddha, ending with "fellow-celibates" (sabrahmacārī)—as stated in "I renounce the Buddha," and so forth—and eight [categories] beginning with "householder" (gihi), ending with "one who is no longer a son of the Sakyan" (asakyaputtiya)—as stated in "Regard me as a householder," and so forth.

Regarding these twenty-two fields of speech, for anyone who wishes to say anything at all among them by means of any synonymous expression, even if they say something [else], there is a renunciation of the training.
Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the field, not by the absence of that [specific word].
In this context, as for what was said: "I renounce it, and you should remember me [as having done so]."

This is a statement regarding the present tense; and as for those four phrases beginning with "Enough for me of the Buddha," which are spoken by connecting them with the preceding fourteen terms according to the method starting with "What need have I of the Buddha? and "I have no need of the Buddha," and "I am well-liberated from the Buddha"—these, without designating a specific time by way of a verb... [the rest of the sentence follows].
And there is a renunciation by way of all verbal expressions, but not for one who utters past, future, or hypothetical expressions such as:
"I have renounced," "I shall renounce," "Do you remember me? "Will you remember me?
or "What if I were to renounce? Thus, it is by way of the present tense and by way of not referring to any [specific] time.
And there is renunciation [of the training], not by the mere absence of that [training]. However, the application (payoga) is twofold: bodily and vocal.
In this regard, by making a vocal utterance in any language whatsoever according to the method beginning with "I renounce the Buddha," there is renunciation through the vocal application alone;
it does not occur for one who performs a bodily application such as writing letters or displaying hand gestures and the like.
Thus, the renunciation occurs through the verbal application itself, and not in its absence.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of persons: he who renounces and he to whom it is renounced.
Regarding these, if he who renounces is not one who is insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain, and as for him to whom it is renounced—
Thus, if he is of human birth and none of those such as the insane are present, there is a renunciation of the training.
For an announcement made by messenger or by letter does not take effect if [the person] is not present.
In this way, the renunciation occurs by way of the persons mentioned above, and not in their absence. Understanding is also twofold: determined and undetermined. Therein—
If, having specified "to whom" or "to which ones," he says, "I announce this to him" or "I announce this to these ones," and if those people—
just as ordinary people in the world would know upon hearing his words at the moment of reflection—
immediately after his speech, by whatever manner, recognize him as a human being, thinking, "This one is dissatisfied," or "He desires the state of a householder."
If one understands the meaning of the words, the training is indeed renounced.
Later on, however, if one reflects, "What was said by this person? and understands it, or if others understand it, the training is not renounced.
But for one who makes the announcement without specifying [the person], if anyone belonging to the human race understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is renounced.
Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of such knowledge, not by the absence of that [knowledge].
Therefore, it should be understood that the renunciation of the training occurs only through these aforementioned factors—mind and so forth—and not otherwise.
The method for the commentary on the renunciation of the training is concluded.
Commentary on the Root Exposition (Mūlapaññatti): 55.

"From here onwards" means starting from the word *duṭṭhulla*. In order to show that sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*) is "grave" (*duṭṭhulla*) not only by its own nature, but also because it is accompanied by grave matters such as looking [at a woman], etc., the words beginning with "because" (*yasmā*) were spoken.
“Of those who are lustful” means those soaked by the passion for sexual intercourse. “Of those who are obsessed” means those whose minds are overcome by the passion for sexual intercourse.
It is said “of those who are similar” because the word *methuna* (sexual intercourse) implies similarity; the meaning is “those who are similar in their passion (*ratta*) and so forth.
And this is stated from a general perspective, because even if one of the two lacks passion, the act of engaging in sexual intercourse is still accomplished by the other.
The word *methuna* (sexual intercourse) is a synonym for the word *ubhaya* (both); for in meaning they are one—the same as *yugala* (pair), *yamaka* (twin), and *ubhaya*.
Therefore he says, "of both who are lustful. Indeed, even in the Canon it is stated: "the union of the two with the two.
In the phrase "by means of the sign" (*nimittena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is that he inserts his own organ into the female organ.
The "sign" (*nimitta*) and the "genital organ" (*aṅgajāta*) are one in meaning. By "sesame seed" (*tilaphala*), a sesame seed the size of a mustard seed is intended;
it does not mean a fruit still enclosed in its husk, hence he says "even the size of a sesame seed.

"In an uncovered place" (*alokāse*) means in a moist spot where the sign—which is naturally concealed—is not touched by the natural wind. Even if such a spot [is affected] by some disturbance of wind or other elements...
Even if it dries up, because there is still a space for fire, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense by virtue of the effort made.
"The middle" (*vemajjha*) refers to the inner surface of the female organ (*itthinimitta*) when a cavity has been made such that one inserts [the member] without touching the four sides.
In the case of the male organ (*purisanimitta*), however, "the middle" is said with reference to the tip of the glans.
"Upward" means with the middle phalanx of the middle finger of the contracted hand as the penis is being inserted;
that is, with the very tip of the finger resembling the back of the middle phalanx of the contracted hand. "Inserting downward" means inserting while touching with the lower part of the male organ;
that is, inserting in such a way that even a space the size of a sesame seed at the bottom surface of the female organ—the non-public area—is touched by one's own organ.
The meaning is as follows: here, "insertion" means merely touching; the same applies to the remaining cases. "Inserting by the middle" means inserting it while being touched by the inner surface;
the meaning is that one inserts it in such a way that it touches the inner surface.
In some instances, for one who inserts it without touching and then withdraws it while it is still in the air, there is no *pārājika* offense, but there is a *dukkaṭa*.
It is like the case of a severed head. "Inserting it while touching with the middle" means inserting it while touching with the tip of the phallus.
"Having contracted it against the back of the middle finger" means having bent the sign against the back of one's own middle finger;
even when inserting it while touching with the upper part [of that finger], the construction is: "like a contracted finger."
Alternatively, it should be connected as "like a finger bent on the back of the middle joint," or it may be construed as "as if inserting a bent finger onto the back of the middle joint.
"By the upper part" means by the upper edge of the contracted sign.

Now, taking four separate positions from among the six previously mentioned below the male sign—specifically the sixth position, which was described as "above"—he says "therein," etc., in order to show the tenfold division of the male sign.
However, the six positions were stated below by way of including those not previously taken up. [The phrase] "even for one inserting it like a measuring rod" means...

For one who inserts [the penis] straight without contracting [the muscles]. "Leather-hinge" (*cammakhīla*) refers to a growth of skin that has arisen at the sign (the base of the organ), like the throat of a sheep or similar animal;

they also call it "woolly swelling" (*uṇṇigaṇḍa*). By using the expression "having lost the sensitivity of the body" (*naṭṭhakāyappasāda*) instead of saying "impaired sensitivity of the body" (*upahatakāyappasāda*), [it is shown that] even when the sensitivity of the body is impaired by some condition while its state as *upādinnarūpa* (clung-to matter) remains, [the act is still an offense] because the physical basis of the faculty (*indriyavatthu*) is present.

This shows that it is indeed a *pārājika* offense. However, it should be understood that even when the female characteristic (*itthinimitta*) has lost its organic integrity (*upādinnabhāva*), its status as a field for a *pārājika* offense is not forfeited, just as in the case of a dead body.
The phrase "by the pleasure of sexual intercourse" indicates that if there is lust for physical contact, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense. "Seeds" refers to eggs.
"Covering the mouth" means that one should not sit without concealing even a laugh arising through negligence by using a fan;
thus it is said that [sitting] without a seat-cloth is disrespectful. Alternatively, "apidhāya" (having covered) means having covered the mouth with a fan;
the meaning is that one should not sit while laughing. "Showing the teeth" means showing the teeth. "With a grinning face" means [thinking], "This is improper speech."

The meaning is: by one who does not shrink back, having developed a sense of urgency regarding the full and complete explanation of the intended purpose. Regarding the commentary on the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*):
"That which constitutes the basis for a *pārājika* offense" refers to those three passages where there is even a space as small as a sesame seed for the insertion of the sign.
All these, including the distinctions of female, male, and so forth, are included here, but not others.

However, in this context, following the wording of the Pāḷi phrase "among those belonging to the animal realm" (*tiracchānagatāya*), it is stated in the feminine gender as "not all," and so on. *Gonasa* refers to a specific kind of snake, which has very large circular spots on its back.
Although turtles and frogs are four-footed, they are grouped with those that are footless due to their commonality of living in water.
“Grasping. “The shape of the mouth” means the shape of the skin of the lips. “A summary of the wound” means an inclusion of the wound.

Regarding the grave offense (*thullaccaya*) in the case of a wound, it should be understood by way of this sutta: “If one inserts [the penis] into what is not the path with what is not the path, there is an offense of grave transgression (*thullaccaya*). “Maṅgusā” means mongooses. “For this very purpose” refers to whoever commits that [offense].
"Defeats" (*parājeti*) refers to the etymological derivation of the very terms *pārājika* and so forth that have been mentioned;
this is because it occurs in this verse of the *Parivāra*. "Fallen away" (*bhaṭṭho*) means fallen away from the Dispensation. "Rejected" (*niraṅkato*) means cast out.
"This" refers to the form of the offense, the *pārājika*. "Severed" (*chinno*) means cut off in the middle.
Regarding the phrase "by regular bhikkhus": here, "regular" (pakatatta) means those who have not committed a *pārājika* offense and have not been suspended.

However, some say: "Since it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that 'it must be performed together with regular bhikkhus,' there is no fault in performing Saṅgha acts such as the Uposatha even together with shameless ones who are actually regular. That is not correct.

Because that meaning is not established by this statement. For if a formal act (saṅghakamma) is performed, it is performed by those who are regular members (pakatatta) alone, and not by those who are not regular members;
thus, this statement is intended to prohibit living together with those who are not regular members.

It does not mean, however, that a formal act must necessarily be performed by all regular members, including those who are shameless (alajjī) and so forth. Thus, it is concerned with the regulation of communal living.

This is because it is prohibited for those who have committed an offense similar to one’s own—even among those who are naturally composed—to perform formal acts (kamma) together with one another or with those who are shameless.

For it is said: "If the entire Saṅgha, when there is an offense similar [to that of others], performs the Uposatha without following the prescribed procedure, then the entire Saṅgha incurs the offense in the manner already described," and so forth. "Where there is the enjoyment of material goods..."
"It is permissible; even the communal enjoyment of the Dhamma is permissible therein.
However, communal enjoyment with those who are shameless is prohibited in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, because performing formal acts (*kamma*) together also constitutes communal enjoyment of the Dhamma.

Therefore, just as in the *Pāḷi*—for the purpose of defining the individual who incurs an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)—"one who has been ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations... this is the monk intended in this context"—so it is here.

In this statement, the restriction that "all those ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) are exclusively persons who incur a *pārājika* offense" is not established,
because there is the possibility of those such as trainees (*sekkha*) who are ordained by a *ñatticatutthakamma* yet do not incur a *pārājika*.
Rather, among those ordained by a *ñatticatutthakamma*, only shameless, foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*) who incur a *pārājika* offense are found, but not others.
In the case of the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) and other such [ordinations], this restriction is established: that they must be those who have already become regular members (*pakatatta*).

Likewise here, it is established as a restriction that only those who are regular members—those worthy of performing the formal act together, free from offenses, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training—are available, and not those who are not regular members.

This is because, due to the absence of the capacity to complete the quorum for non-regular members, there is a restriction regarding their being ineligible for communal living (*asaṃvāsika*). However, as for those who are unconscientious (*alajjī*)...

It should be understood that those who act as mere fillers of the assembly because they facilitate the performance of the formal act (*kamma*), yet do not include those who are not in communion (*asaṃvāsika*)—performing the act by crushing together with them without having performed the required procedure for them—do not lose their state of shamelessness (*alajjitā*).
For it is said: "One shameless person even makes another shameless," and therefore he will say later: "All those who are conscientious (*lajjino*) among these..."
"...dwelling together in regard to [shared] duties and so forth. This meaning will be explained in detail further below.

"In that way" refers to those who are delimited by the boundary (sīmā) and so forth. "Equal training" (*samasikkhatā*) means the training in the rules of discipline (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One through the performance of communal acts, such as performing salutations together, eating together, entering the village together, and carrying out the formal duties (*vatta*), counter-duties (*paṭivatta*), receiving instruction (*uggaha*), cross-examination (*paripucchā*), and recitation (*sajjhāya*).
And that must be trained in equally only by those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*).
In order to show that it is not for those who lack a sense of shame, it is said: “But what has been laid down… [etc. …is called ‘training in common’ (samasikkhatā).

In this context, the training rules (sikkhāpada) are so called because they are to be trained in together—“in common”—by persons possessing a sense of shame, equally and as one, by way of non-transgression and by way of study and inquiry.
Their “training in common” (samasikkhana) is the state of being trained by those with a sense of shame according to the manner already described; this is “training in common.”

The intended meaning is "by name. Regarding the aforementioned cases such as a single act (*ekakamma*), since those who lack a sense of shame (*alajjī*) have not transcended the nature of shamelessness (*lajjidhamma*), they cannot coexist with those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*);
rather, they appear entirely outside of them. Thus he said, "All those who possess a sense of shame," and so forth.
56. The connection is "that which was stated. "The very basis does not exist" refers to female forms made of gold and other materials.

Because the designation "sign" (nimitta) is seen even among the various parts of the body, this was stated in order to prevent the suspicion that there might be an offense involving defeat (pārājika) in those cases.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vinītavatthu* that for one who has developed remorse regarding objects such as plastered walls or paintings, there is no offense of defeat.

57. Regarding the statement "Assā" (it is), which refers to a verb form, he says "hoti" (it is) in order to show its meaning; the sense is "bhaveyya" (it would be). Thus, what was stated as "hoti" [is explained]. In the second interpretation of the meaning, "hoti" is a remainder of the expression (*vacanaseso*).
58. Regarding the phrase "sādiyantasseva" (only for one who consents): here, "consenting" (*sādiyana*) means precisely the arising of a mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse;

therefore, to exclude them, the meaning is shown according to the analogy of the enemies of kings, namely that "the bhikkhus themselves are the enemies.

"Standing" refers to the penis remaining in the interval between the commencement of its extraction after having been thus inserted; or, "standing" means its state of remaining there.

As for "extraction," it refers to the period during which the act of drawing out continues until the tip [of the organ]; thus he says, "one brings forth the intention of enjoyment at the time of extraction."
And here, because there exists the movement of the body— such as the movement of the sexual organ— in one who is being assailed by others,
the movement of the sexual organ and so forth that arises at that very moment through mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*) when the intention to engage (*sevanacitta*) has merely arisen,

Movement is as if it were itself the act; and that [movement] is indeed considered to have been performed by him. Therefore, he incurs the *pārājika* offense arising from both body and mind, just like the case of [the offense for] touching above the knees.

For even in that instance, it is stated that an offense occurs at the mere moment of consent, with the words: "If he should consent to touching... or pressing below the collarbone and above the kneecaps," in the case of a monk.
Regarding bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*), however, because the phrase "one should engage in bodily contact" is stated as the cause for the offense by way of one's own initiative,
it should be understood that even if there is lust for bodily contact on the part of the man being touched by a woman, and even if there is physical movement produced in the woman,
there is still no offense for him due to the absence of his own effort. Some, however, [hold that] this also applies to the scope of the first *saṅghādisesa* offense...
They say: "For one who is being approached by others with force through the hands or other means, there arises a relish for release;
and because of that, if semen is emitted, it is a *saṅghādisesa*, but if it is not emitted, it is only a *thullaccaya*.
"A pit of embers" (*aṅgārakāsu*) means a heap of embers or a trench filled with embers. Not consenting when being approached by a woman is not within the scope of everyone.
He said, "In this [case]," and so forth. "By eleven fires" means by the eleven fires consisting of lust, hatred, delusion, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"Of one who does not partake" means of one who does not consent. "Having extracted the tetrad, he established it":
here, because it refers to a single individual, even a single section on non-offense is presented by way of the four terms—entering, having entered, staying, and exiting.
It is called a "tetrad" (*catukka*). Regarding the phrase "the exposition of the first tetrad":

although one should speak of "five tetrads" according to the method stated for the five sections—including the section on non-offenses—here the status of being a "first tetrad" is stated by attributing unity to them because they share a single path as their object.
For this very reason, he will later say: "There are three pure tetrads by way of the three paths," and so forth.
Commentary on the Seventy-Ninth and Eightieth Tetrad of the Two Hundred and Sixty-Nine (59–60).

“Intoxicated” (*matta*) means intoxicated by liquor and so forth. Because the signs [of intoxication] are not explicitly stated here, they are expressed by the word “unmanifested” (*akkhāyita*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound;
thus he says, “the unmanifested sign. Because they lack qualifying adjectives such as “while waking,” etc., they are called “pure tetrads” (*suddhika-cattukka*).

It has been stated. "Co-students" (*samānācariyakā*) refers to those who are resident pupils under a single teacher. "The lower part of the Ganges" (*aparagaṅgaṃ*) means the downstream portion of the Ganges.

"Vatare" is a particle used in the sense of censure. By the phrase "thus for those who hold the Vinaya in high esteem," the reason for the importance of the decision about to be spoken by the Elder Upatissa is stated.
"Having encompassed everything" (*sabbaṃ pariyādiyitvā*) means having included the entire field of offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) without exception.
Having taken [this up]. For if one were to lay down the rule leaving a remainder, the stream of transgression would flow through even a slight pretext for those who are shameless;

thus he said, "having cut off the stream. It is possible to lay down rules that leave a remainder only in the case of training precepts involving offenses by formal prescription (paṇṇattivajja), such as sleeping together, and not in the case of offenses by nature (lokavajja);
thus he said, "For this," and so forth. Regarding the training precept on sleeping together:
For although, in cases where it is mostly covered or mostly enclosed, a *pācittiya* offense is shown from the perspective of the lower limit,
while a *dukkaṭa* is [shown] for what is half-covered or half-enclosed, nevertheless— because that rule of training (*paññatti*) allows for exceptions—

the *Aṭṭhakathā* shows only a *pācittiya* even in the case of being mostly covered or half-enclosed and so forth. However, here, because the rule of training is without exception, by the Blessed One...
It is shown that, for the most part, there is no *pārājika* offense-field below the point where the sign (*nimitta*) is declared; only a *thullaccaya* or similar offense is found there.
In order to show another supporting reason for the very same legal determination (*vinicchaya*) stated by the Elder Upatissa, [the author] said "Moreover," and so forth.
Even if a tiny sliver of flesh remains at the sign, it is still considered "for the most part declared" (*yebhuyyakkhāyita*).
Furthermore, showing that when the sign has been entirely rubbed away, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), he said: "Beyond that, there is no grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
However, some here divide the anus and so forth into four parts, and state:
"When one has passed through two parts and up to the end of the third part, the rubbing is called 'mostly rubbed away' (*yebhuyyakkhāyita*); beyond that..."
The claim that "there is no *thullaccaya* [offense], and as long as it has been eaten up to the end of the fourth portion, that too is merely a matter of *dukkaṭa*," is incorrect.
It was stated [in the text] that "it should be understood as occurring only in the case of a dead body," because of the statement beginning with "the dead body is mostly not eaten.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "even if it is the sign" (*nimitta*) and so forth refers specifically to a living body, because that alone is the subject under discussion.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even if the skin and so forth of a living body have been completely severed on the aforementioned path," and so on.
"Completely gnawed" means that all the flesh of the sign has been cut away.
"The shape of the sign" refers to the hollow form within the severed flesh, extending as far as the membrane of the testicles.
The form of the female sign consists merely of the inner skin and hide; therefore he said, "entry occurs.
As for the phrase "without leaving out the shape of the sign," this means without leaving out the flesh and so forth within that remains situated in the form of an opening suitable for entry.
By this, he shows that as long as entry is possible, it is indeed the path. Regarding the phrase "a piece of flesh fallen from the sign":
This was said with reference to the internal mass of flesh that is devoid of its characteristic shape.
However, if one cuts around it without disturbing the characteristic shape and extracts the piece of flesh from a dead body where the characteristic shape has for the most part disappeared,
there is indeed a *pārājika* offense for one who proceeds [with the act].
Having thus shown the distinctions found in the body of a living person, he now says "But in the case of a dead body," etc., in order to show them in a dead body.
"In the sheaths of the organs" means in the skin-sheaths of the male generative organs.
Because of such statements as "The nine gates are a great wound," the eyes, nose, and so forth of humans are, by way of being wounds, grounds for a *thullaccaya* offense.
In those cases as well, a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is stated; likewise regarding the dead bodies of humans. Therefore, he said: "on a dead, moist body," and so forth.
Therein, "moist body" is said with reference to one that has not yet begun to decay. "In the field of a *pārājika*" is said with reference to even that which is mostly undecayed.
"In the field of a *thullaccaya*" is said with reference to even that which is half-decayed and so on. Here...
Furthermore, it should be understood that even when the eyes and nose have been mostly destroyed, it is a *thullaccaya* offense;

whereas when they are half-destroyed and so forth, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The phrase "of all [animals]" is stated for the purpose of including other animals besides the aforementioned elephants and so on.
However, regarding the eyes, ears, and wounds of animals, a *dukkaṭa* offense should be understood according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

For it is stated in general terms: “If one causes [the organ] to enter what is not a path by means of what is not a path, there is an offense of thullaccaya,” but it is not specified as being only in the case of humans.

For if the thullaccaya were to apply only to wounds on humans, then [the offense] would also apply—by way of the category of a wound—to the nostrils, the urethra, and the sheath of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as to the mouth-shape of a *paṭaṅga* insect or a frog.

It should not be said [that this is not so], for it has been stated. Therefore, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā are the authority here. The phrase "of animals that have died" is connected with "the dead.
It was stated that there is a thullaccaya for one who inserts [the organ] into the vaginal opening out of lust for sexual intercourse; thus he says, "without inserting it into the vaginal opening.

And what is called "lust for sexual intercourse" is distinct from both the lust for physical contact and the gratification of emission. It refers specifically to the attainment of the two-by-two union.

Passion (*rāga*) arises even toward men and others; therefore, it should be understood that for one who makes an effort toward the body of a woman—even in a case where it is not a field for a *pārājika* offense—there is no *saṅghādisesa* even when semen is emitted.
Rather, there is only a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) or a formal act of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), according to the nature of the field.
By the phrase "not entering," it is meant that even in the absence of the intention to enter through the three [sexual] paths, if there is lust for sexual intercourse (*methunarāga*)...
This shows that contact with the exterior is possible; for that very reason, a *thullaccaya* is stated.

Otherwise, for one who touches the exterior with the intention of insertion, it would have to be declared a *dukkaṭa* alone, since that would constitute a preliminary act (*pubbapayoga*) to sexual intercourse.
Regarding the rule "if he touches organ to organ, it is a *thullaccaya*," this refers to [the passage]: "And you should not, monks, with a lustful mind [touch] the private parts..."
This was stated on the basis of the sutta found in the *Cammakkhandhaka* (the Chapter on Leather), which says: “It should be touched; whoever should touch it, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
In that context, showing the seed for a different interpretation of the meaning for some, he said in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
“With reference to touching by means of the mouth,” that is, by means of parts of the mouth such as the lips, tongue, and so forth.

"Intentionally touching" means with reference to [the act of] contact. "Coarseness" means because of the gravity of the transgression. "Spoken with intentional reference" refers to that aforementioned sutta;
for a sutta is called "spoken with intentional reference" because it was spoken in reliance upon and with reference to a transgression.
"Having carefully observed" means [observing] the touching of the sign by way of the genitals of those who are mounting on the back.

The meaning is: having carefully observed, according to one's own ability, the origin [of the offense], the suitability of merely touching with the genitals those who possess lust for sexual intercourse, the fact that "with the mouth" is not mentioned in the Sutta, and other methods as well.
"Saṅghādisesa" is stated with reference to a human woman. "The path of excrement"—this was stated by way of the introductory narrative (nidāna) in the Cammakkhandhaka.
However, for one who touches the other two paths by way of the sign (*nimitta*), there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) by way of the wound (*vaṇa*).

"In the manner already stated" means precisely by way of lust for sexual intercourse. But for one who, without lust for sexual intercourse and without [focusing on] the sign, touches the urinary passage of a human woman or a female animal by way of the natural opening (*pakatimukha*), there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by way of the natural opening.

As in the case of touching the natural opening, otherwise there would have to be a *thullaccaya* offense even in that instance, which is not appropriate because it is not stated so in the Khandhaka-sutta.

Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) through the lust for bodily contact": whether by way of the [natural] opening or the [other] openings, or by means of another part of the body, for one who touches with the lust for bodily contact, there is indeed only an offense of wrong-doing.

And here, in the case of one who makes an effort toward an external object out of lust for bodily contact, if the sexual organ touches the area that constitutes a *pārājika* offense even though he is unaware [of it], what happens there? Some say:
"Because of the absence of lust for sexual intercourse (*methunarāga*), it is a *saṅghādisesa* in the case of a human woman;
in the other cases, there are *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses according to the nature of the object. Others, however, [say]: "At the moment of penetration, because of the contact..."
They say that because there is consent (*sādiyanasambhava*), it is indeed a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of the forceful approach, as if by compulsion;

this alone is more reasonable. For while a distinction in offenses based on the various types of lust, such as bodily contact, may be found in places other than the three paths, it does not occur within the three paths themselves.
However, in that case, at the moment of consenting to the touch by whatever means, [the offense is incurred].

It is indeed a *pārājika* offense; for that very reason, it is stated to be a *pārājika* by the mere fact of consenting—without having removed the breach of lust—during the entry [of semen] and so forth, even when caused by another’s effort.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Fourfold Breach Regarding the Spread (Santhata): 61–2.
"Of one who has entered upon the path" means of one who has commenced insight (*vipassanā*). "That which is clung-to" (*upādinnaka*) is said with reference to the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*).

"He touches with what is clung-to" (*upādinnakena*) means "he is touched by the body that is clung-to"; thus the meaning should be understood through the instrumental case as the instrument of action (*kamma-sādhana*).
Alternatively, the meaning is: "A bhikkhu acting in this way does not touch anything that is clung-to with that which is clung-to.

"They will cast a slur" (*lesaṃ oḍḍessantī*) means they will establish a slur; the meaning is that they will make a pretext. "Having divided [them] according to the distinctions such as 'spread mats' (*santhatā*)," etc.
Having distinguished [the object] by means of specific qualities such as its shape (*saṇṭhāna*) and so forth.
"By way of shape" (*saṇṭhāyā*) refers to using a term for a part to denote the whole, as in the expressions "the hole of a burnt cloth" (*daḍḍhassa paṭassa chiddaṃ*) and the like.

For just as only one part of a cloth is said to be "burnt" in terms of its substance, that expression for a part is metaphorically applied to the whole cloth; and then, that whole is further characterized by its connection with the "hole," which is to say, the portion that has been burnt.

"Just as people speak of 'a hole in a burnt cloth,' so too here, having applied the designation for a portion of the path to the woman who constitutes the whole [of that path], and then having related that woman to the path already covered, it is said: 'by the anus of the woman who has been covered,' and so forth.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated here: 'The designation for the whole is used for a single part.'"
That is not correct, because by means of the conventional designation for the parts, the whole itself is what is understood.
Otherwise, in the expression "by the anus of one who has spread [a mat]," the feminine gender and the connection with the path would not be possible.
However, when a part is metaphorically designated as the whole, the meaning is simply that part, just as in such cases as "the tree is cut" when a branch is being cut.
"Having wrapped around" is said with reference to wrapping [the head] on the outside itself, without inserting robes and so forth inside the path.
By means of the metaphorical application of the part to the whole (*samudāye avayavūpacārena*), it is said that even a monk is called "one who has covered himself," and so forth.

"To whatever extent it has entered" means when it has entered even as much as a sesame seed. He spoke thus regarding the field of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) because even when the eyes, nose, and so forth are covered, it remains exactly as it was.

"Thullaccaya," and so forth. Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who strikes against a stump": if one inserts a stump inside the female organ and it remains level with the surface or protruding, and one then strikes against it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the striker because there has been no insertion.
However, if the top of the stump—which is itself unclung-to (anupādinnam)—is inserted slightly into the internal space and struck by the male organ...
If he touches it, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense. "Its interior" refers to the inner surface of bamboo, reeds, and so forth.
"Outside the stump" is said with reference to the protruding tip of a bamboo joint or similar object that has been inserted inside.

And just as in the cases of "the female organ," etc., where touching and so forth are mentioned after a stump has been placed in a woman's urinary passage, so it is in all instances regarding the anal passage and the others as well.
The meaning is that the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is to be understood.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse concerning the fourfold classification beginning with the king’s enemies:

"Kerāṭikā" means deceivers. Having first shown the woman-gambler (*itthidhutta*), he now says "or woman-gamblers, liquor-gamblers, and so forth" in order to include and show the other types of gamblers as well.
Commentary on the Section on Offenses and Non-offenses (Āpattānāpattivāra): 66.
There is no "acting according to admission" (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) because two factors are established: the desire to engage in sexual intercourse and the penetration of the path by the path.

However, for one who has already been defiled, the factor of "penetration of the path by the path" is thus established as one factor; [the other], namely the "desire to engage in sexual intercourse," is...
Consent (*sādiyana*) is not established [as a factor]. Therefore, having questioned him, he should be expelled based on his admission that he "consented.
"Right there" means right there in the Great Wood at Vesālī. "Pervading all limbs" means pervading the entire body.
Because it is stated "like blood," it should be understood as being everywhere except in places where hair and so forth are excluded. "He is always insane" refers to one for whom...
This was said with reference to bile that, having moved from the gall-bladder, has always issued outwards. However, it should be understood that for one whose bile,
having moved, remains within the gall-bladder itself, or which issues out only occasionally and then returns,
such a person regains consciousness from time to time and recovers natural health through medicine.
The method of commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*): "Miscellaneous" (*pakiṇṇaka*) refers to the method of mixed treatment. "Origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) means the cause of arising. "Action" (*kiriyā*), and so forth, is merely an illustration.

This is because it includes even non-action (akiriya) and so forth. It should be connected thus: "Wholesome [kamma] together with feeling is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "by way of including all":

this refers to the six origins of offenses (*āpatti-samudāna*) stated as follows: "body, speech, body-and-speech, body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind," by way of including all training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For the origins and so forth pertain to the offense.

Thus it is; [the fault] does not lie with the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself. However, the mention of the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth under the heading of the "training rule" is for the purpose of specifying the particular offense (*niyatāpatti*) of each respective training rule.
For in this way, the distinction between offenses is made known, since the word "offense" (*āpatti*) is common to all types of offenses.
Now, among these six origins, the first three are unintentional (*acittaka*), while the latter...

[The offenses] are with consciousness. The connection [of the sentence] is: "Having understood this miscellaneous matter (pakiṇṇaka) in brief, it is to be known. "That which has six origins" (chasamuṭṭhāna) means that for this [offense], there are six origins;
the same applies to the rest. "There is one originating from the Kathina," etc., refers to those originating from two origins and one origin by way of the head of the origins (samuṭṭhānasīsa).
...the seeing. For there are thirteen headings of origins:

the origin of the first *pārājika*, the origin of taking what is not given, the origin of acting as a go-between, the origin of formal admonition, the origin of the *kaṭhina* robe, the origin of wool, the origin of the *padasodhamma* (reciting the Dhamma together), the origin of traveling on a journey, the origin of traveling with a caravan of thieves, and the origin of teaching the Dhamma.
[The offenses] arising from false boasting, arising from ordaining a female thief, and arising from [acting] without permission.
In this context, by the phrase "there is one arising from six [bases]," the offense arising from acting as a go-between is stated;

because there is no [offense] arising from five bases, it is not said "there is one arising from five," but rather "there is one arising from four," and by this, the offense arising during a journey is [implied].
And that which arises from non-authorization is included. For that which arises by means of the first, third, fourth, and sixth origins is an origin by way of journeying (*addhānasamuṭṭhāna*).
However, that which arises by means of the second, third, fifth, and sixth origins is an origin by way of non-authorization (*ananuññātasamuṭṭhāna*).
By the phrase "there is [an offense] with three origins," the origin of taking what is not given and the origin of reporting what has actually occurred are indicated.
It is included. For that which originates from the three [factors] involving consciousness is the origin of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
However, that which originates from the three [factors] not involving consciousness is the origin of the announcement of [the robe] having been made (*bhūtārocanā*).

By the phrase "there is that which originates from the Kathina," etc., it includes both that which has two origins and that which has one origin, according to the heads of the remaining origins. Therein:
That which originates from the third and sixth [factors] is called the *kathina-samutthāna*. That which originates from the first and fourth is the *eḷakaloma-samutthāna*.
That which originates from the sixth alone is the *dhuranikkhepa-samutthāna*; its other name is also "originating from admonition" (*samanubhāsana-samutthāna*).
Thus, the eight headings of offenses have been shown according to their specific forms.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the remaining five headings of origins—those originating from the first *pārājika*, from *padasodhamma*, from *theyyasattha*, from *dhammadesanā*, and from the ordination of a thief (*corīvuṭṭhāpana*)—are included here. Among these, that which originates from both body and mind is the origin of the first *pārājika*.
That which originates from the second and fifth [rules] is the origin of *padasodhamma*. That which [originates] from the fourth and sixth...
That which originates from all five [factors] is the origin by way of a band of thieves. That which originates from the fifth alone is the origin by way of teaching the Dhamma.

That which originates from the fifth and the sixth is the origin by way of causing a female thief to go forth. And here, among the last three origins involving a conscious state (*sacittaka-samutṭhāna*), each single-origin [offense] is threefold according to its mode of origination; there are also those originating from two factors.

Furthermore, they should be understood as fivefold by way of their origin: either by the first and fourth, or the second and fifth, or the third and sixth, or the fourth and sixth, or the fifth and sixth.
Having thus shown all the training rules (sikkhāpada) in thirteen ways by way of their origin, they will now be shown in five ways by way of action (kiriyā).
To demonstrate this, the words "there too" and so forth were spoken. "Something" refers to a training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

"From action" means from kamma generated by bodily and verbal intimation (*viññatti*), such as digging the earth and so on. "From non-action" means simply by the non-performance of what ought to be done, such as the first *kathina* ceremony and so on.
"From both action and non-action" means, for example, from receiving a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun. It may be [a transgression] from action...
It may be non-intentional, like accepting silver and so forth; it may be intentional; or it may be both intentional and non-intentional, like building a hut and so forth.
The compound *saññāvimokkha* should be understood as a *majjhepadalopī-samāsa* (a compound with the middle term elided), meaning "liberation through the absence of the perception of transgression.
It acquires the factor of consciousness (*cittaṅga*) because it originates only from those origins that involve consciousness. As for the other...

There is no restriction regarding the mental factor (*citta*). This pair on perception (*saññāduka*) is stated by way of non-offenses, whereas the pair on being with mind (*sacittakaduka*) is stated by way of offenses;
this alone is the difference, for they are identical in meaning.

Even that which is to be committed through the doors of body and speech is included within either bodily action (*kāyakamma*) or verbal action (*vacīkamma*). In this regard, it is stated according to what occurs most frequently.

Regarding the phrase "like taking what is not given, false speech, and so forth," it is stated that there are only two pairs—bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*)—by way of such passages as "there is a training rule regarding bodily action.
However, when analyzed in detail, there are three groups when including both bodily and verbal action. For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"And all [the courses of action] are threefold by way of bodily action, verbal action, and both. Therefore, here too...
In the case of taking what is not given and so forth, "bodily and verbal action" is shown by way of both [body and speech].

However, the statement "there is a training rule that is wholesome," and so on, is spoken by applying the name of the cause to the effect—that is, by way of the mind that originates the offense—not by way of the offense itself being a truly ultimate (paramattha) phenomenon such as wholesome or unwholesome, because an offense has a conventional (sammuti) nature. Regarding truly ultimate phenomena such as the wholesome and unwholesome...
For the designation of offenses was indeed established by the Blessed One based on [conventional usage]. For he will say: "That which one commits with a wholesome mind is wholesome," and so forth.

An offense does not possess a paramattha-nature such as wholesomeness and so on, because it would follow that those who are not fully ordained and beginners would be subject to offenses, and because it would follow that there could be no purification of such an offense through confession and other means.

Furthermore, an offense (āpatti) that arises by the power of its cause—possessing the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of unwholesome states and so forth—does not cease to exist even among those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna).

Nor is the destruction of such an offense possible through any means once it has arisen. There is indeed a statement that an offense "disappears" due to its own inherent perishability or through confession (desanā) and other methods;
however, by that [disappearance], the unwholesome state itself does not disappear. This is as in the case of the karma of patricide and so forth.
For indeed, when a monk has committed a *pārājika* offense, the *pārājika* transgression is removed by taking on the marks of a householder and relinquishing his status as a monk;
however, unwholesome acts such as the taking of life do not cease because they possess the nature of *ānantariya* (immediate retribution) and so forth.

Therefore, for the sake of the ten purposes beginning with the restraint of the incorrigible, the Blessed One—depending on the circumstances—having taken as a basis the phenomena of mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*) arising as wholesome, unwholesome, and so on...
It should be understood that an offense is merely a conventional designation (*sammuti*), and it is considered "dispelled" through the performance of the prescribed atonement;
therefore, he said, "There are indeed thirty-two types of consciousness that originate an offense," and so forth.

Here, the distinction between wholesome and other states from the offense is established precisely by their being the originators of the offense. For it is not logical that what originates from that [offense] should be non-different from it.

Because it would entail the consequence of severing the conventional usage of distinctions arising from their origination. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated that from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), the state of being wholesome (*kusalatta*) simply does not apply to an offense (*āpatti*), because of the statement:
"A legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be unwholesome (*akusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*);
there is no legal issue concerning offenses that is wholesome. Furthermore, regarding the state of being unwholesome or indeterminate for an offense...
In order to establish that even at the moment of the arising of a wholesome mind there is the indeterminate nature of form (*rūpābyākatatta*) based on the perception [of its occurrence],
and relying on this statement from the Commentary— that "whatever one commits with a wholesome mind is wholesome, and whatever with the others is otherwise"—

it is said: "Whatever is committed with a wholesome mind" refers to the offense mentioned under the heading of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) which is committed by one possessing a wholesome state of mind.
By this statement, however, it is shown that when it is said that one "commits an offense" (āpajjati), the quality of being wholesome (kusala) regarding that offense is stated figuratively,
not in the ultimate sense (paramattha). For one who commits an offense with a wholesome mind commits an indeterminate (abyākata) offense—

which is comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and consists in the mode of transgressing a training rule (sikkhāpada)— whether it be accompanied by intimation (saviññattika) or without intimation (aviññattika).
Regarding that, with reference to the statement "which one enters upon by means of a wholesome mind," it was said:
"By this statement, however, it is shown that when an offense is being described as 'wholesome,' its wholesomeness is figurative (pariyāyato) and not in the ultimate sense (paramatthato).
Likewise, by the statement "whatever one enters upon by means of an unwholesome mind, that is unwholesome," [it is shown that its unwholesomeness is ultimate].
Since the meaning of the statement, "That which one commits with an indeterminate mind is indeterminate," has already been expressed, one must say regarding the phrase "by the others":
"By this statement as well, the fact that what is called 'the other'—referring to an offense—is unwholesome and indeterminate is shown by way of a figurative expression.
The reason for not saying this [directly] but speaking only on the side of the wholesome is...
We do not see it. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "that which is an offense-dispute (āpattādhikaraṇa) might be unwholesome" is stated by way of a reason;

yet that too is not a [valid] reason, because the state of being unwholesome and so forth has been taught figuratively according to the method explained below—that "whatever one commits with an unwholesome mind is unwholesome"—and because it is inappropriate to apply the designation "wholesome" to an offense. Therefore, there is no such thing as an "offense-dispute."

And because it is described as "wholesome" (*kusala*). For even though an offense may arise from a wholesome state of mind, since it has been prohibited by the Blessed One and is thus a blameworthy phenomenon (*sāvajja-dhamma*), it is not appropriate to apply the designation "blameless-wholesome" (*anavajja-kusala*) to it through metaphorical usage.

This is because the blameworthy and the blameless are mutually contradictory, just as the conventional designations of "arising" and so forth cannot be applied to space and the like, nor can they be applied to birth, aging, and dissolution.

The conventional designations such as "arising" and so forth are untenable from the standpoint of non-abiding and the like; likewise, here too, the designation "wholesome" is untenable because it is contradictory.

However, the designation "unwholesome" and so forth is tenable; yet, by way of metaphorical application to the cause, the claim that they possess the intrinsic nature of the unwholesome and so forth does not avoid the aforementioned faults.
For even in the case of a sutta, the meaning must be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction with other suttas, with what is concordant with those suttas, and so forth.

As for what was stated: "One who incurs an offense with a wholesome consciousness... [omitted] ...incurs an indeterminate offense consisting of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha)," that is indeed incorrect.
Because the aggregate of form is momentary, it would follow that the offense itself would be pacified even without confession or other remedial actions.

If it is argued that the offense is a succession of material phenomena (rūpaparamparā), that is not so; for it would then follow that the offense would not be removed even by means of a remedial action.

For it does not disappear through the teaching on the continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*) and so forth, because it remains dependent upon its own causes; thus, in every respect, the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) of an offense is untenable.

By this very reasoning, that which was stated—namely, "because for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) after lying down, there is the state of an offense due to the occurrence of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) in such a manner by virtue of sharing a bed"—should also be understood as refuted.
However, in this context, regarding those who have entered the attainment of cessation...

Because it arises in dependence solely upon material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), an offense is without mind (*acitta*) and without feeling (*avedanā*); elsewhere, however, it is indeed with mind (*sacitta*) and with feeling (*savedanā*).
In all cases, it should be understood as having the intrinsic nature of a formal designation (*paññatti-sabhāva*).

For this very reason, in the commentary on the training rule regarding malicious speech (*duṭṭhadosa-sikkhāpada*), in order to refute the unwholesome nature and other such qualities imagined by others regarding an offense, it says: "Because there is no offense for the first offender... and so forth.
He himself will state: "It should be understood that the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is merely a designation (*paṇṇattimatta*). Therefore, it is conventionally expressed as:
"The formal authorization of offenses (*āpattisammuti*) has arisen through the Blessed One’s designation for the arising of various wholesome and other states";

and, "It persists until the cause for its subsiding"; and, "It is destroyed by the causes for its subsiding. And even though an offense has the nature of a conventional designation (*sammutisabhāva*),...

For indeed, for one who intentionally commits that offense and fails to perform the act of atonement, there arises both a mass of unwholesome states regarding disregard and an obstacle to the path to heaven;
therefore, those possessed of moral shame do not transgress the rules according to the prescribed method.
And because they do not transgress them, their various virtues such as morality and so forth increase boundlessly—this is how it should be understood. "Only thirty-two" means:
The restriction is made because the intimations of body and speech (*kāyaviññatti* and *vacīviññatti*) arise only together with the causes of offenses;

it is not, however, because all offenses arise only together with them. For indeed, an offense such as "lying down in the same bed" can occur for those who are sleeping after having lain down, as well as for those who have attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) or the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*), through resultant (*vipāka*) or absorption (*appanā*) consciousnesses that do not produce intimations, and through material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).

The eight great functional (kiriyā) consciousnesses, together with the two types of mind-consciousness element that are functionally caused (kiriya-hetuka), constitute the ten functional consciousnesses.

It should be understood that the attainment of supernormal powers (abhiññā), such as the transformation of psychic power (iddhi-vikubbanā), constitutes an offense for one who has not mastered the conventional designations (paññatti).

Furthermore, in this context, some training rules (sikkhāpada) involve only unwholesome consciousness; some involve two types of consciousness by way of the wholesome and the indeterminate; and some involve three types of consciousness.
It should be understood that only this distinction applies, and no other. Regarding "arising from action" (*kiriyāsamuṭṭhāna*):
the movement of the genitals and so forth produced by another's assault is said to be "produced by that very mind" when the mind of indulgence—known as the mind of practice—has arisen;
otherwise, it would have to be stated that "it may be produced by action, or it may be produced without action."

As for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: “‘Arising from action’ is said by way of the majority, because when there is an assault by another, for one who consents to it, it has the nature of arising from non-action,” and so forth—that should not be accepted, because the first *pārājika* offense is not described as arising from non-action in either the Canon or the commentaries.
[Furthermore,] it is said: “In the mind-door, there is no such thing as an offense.”
For it has been said: "How indeed could one who consents to sexual intercourse through the agency of another not consent to the movement of his own body parts, such as the genitals?

It should be understood that in accordance with the mind of consent, the manifestation (viññatti) is indeed produced, albeit subtly, through the arising of mind-born material form throughout the entire body.
Therefore he said: "Because it originates through the door of the body, it is bodily action," and so forth.
In this context, however, the mind is merely an accessory; thus, bodily intimation alone is the cause for the status of being "bodily action" (kāyakamma), not the mind.
Furthermore, in this case, that mind is merely an accessory to the intimation designated as "body," but not to the status of being bodily action itself.
Otherwise, sexual intercourse would have to be called "mental action. Therefore, he said: "The status of being action is not obtained by virtue of that [the mind]."
"Kamma-bhāva" means the state of bodily action (*kāyakamma*). "And all this" refers to this [discussion] beginning with the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
"By way of the training rules" (*sikkhāpada-sīsena*) means by way of the training rules for the purpose of including only those offenses specifically determined by each respective training rule.
The method of explaining the miscellaneous discussion is concluded.
Exposition of the Subjects of Discipline (*Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā*). "What is this? is the question posed out of a desire to speak. "These," and so forth, is the answer.

"Subjects of Discipline" (*vinītavatthūni*) refers to those cases (*vatthūni*) adjudicated by the Blessed One through such statements as, "Monk, you have fallen into an offense. Having extracted each respective case...
An *uddānagāthā* is a verse that serves as a summary by way of giving or by way of showing; it is what is called a "collective verse" (*saṅgahagāthā*) or a "summary verse" (*uddesagāthā*).
A *vatthugāthā* refers precisely to the textual tradition of the cases of discipline (*vinītavatthu*), beginning with the words, "Now at that time, a certain monk...";
it is so called because of its composition as the narrative basis for those respective disciplinary cases, not by virtue of the characteristics of metrical prosody.

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "The narrative of the summary verses (uddānagāthā) is the 'story-verse' (vatthugāthā). "Here" refers to the cases of the Vinaya (vinītavatthūsu).

"Of the second and so forth" means of the second Pārājika and the others. That which painters and other artisans look upon and learn from to produce paintings and the like is "concealed form" (paṭicchannakarūpa); the meaning is "the form of an image" (paṭimārūpa).
67. "The two previous" refers to the two cases concerning the female monkey and Vajjiputta.
These too were included among the subsequent cases of discipline because they had been settled by the Blessed One.
As for the passage beginning "there he felt remorse," although remorse had not previously arisen in them, it was spoken after the monks and the Blessed One had censured them.

This was said with reference to their subsequent arising; that is, it was spoken with reference to what occurred later. As for the passage beginning, "They reported this matter to the Blessed One," and so forth:

after the monks and the Elder Ānanda had first reported the matter to the Blessed One, and after the Blessed One had declared their offense to be a *pārājika*, they became afraid and went there themselves to report their own remorse later on. "Is it true, indeed..."
