When questioned by the Blessed One with the words "Is it true? and so forth, they also confess by way of admitting, "It is true, Blessed One.
The Blessed One likewise determines their state of defeat (pārājika) precisely through their admission of the offense with the words "It is true" and so forth.
However, in the discussion on the subsequent rule (anupaññatti), all of that was not stated; rather, only a small portion relevant to the subsequent rule was spoken. Here too, for them...
It should be understood that this was said for the purpose of showing that these cases had already been settled by the Blessed One.
Some, however, disregarding this underlying intention, claim that these are entirely different cases. *Kusa* means *kusatṛṇa* grass. *Kesehi* means with human hair.
Regarding the phrase *vaṇṇapokkharatāya*: here, *pokkhala* means prosperous and beautiful; its abstract state is "prosperity" (*pokkharatā*).
It is spoken by adding the letter *ra*; the meaning is "perfection" or "beauty. "He surpassed" (*padhaṃsesi*) means he overcame. "He does not smear" (*na limpati*) means he does not adhere. 69.

Nuns who have thus changed their gender, even though they were actually ordained together [with monks], are included among those ordained in both Saṅghas, because the ordination of a nun is superior to the ordination of a monk. In the text, "by them..."
Having used the term "anāpatti" (non-offense) as an accusative case, it should be connected with the phrase "I allow.
Regarding the feminine gender, he says—"the masculine... the feminine form has arisen"—because the feminine form is stated to be the female physical structure beginning with the breasts.
That [gender] does not arise from the immediate proximity; rather, it is precisely what was stated: "the male faculty has disappeared and the female faculty has arisen."

Just as [the faculty of masculinity] exists, so too in the subsequent cases, the inclusion of the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the others should be understood by means of the mention of their respective gender marks (*liṅga*). "Those" refers to the offenses;
this is connected with the phrase "for him to emerge from. The meaning is: "to cause him to emerge from those offenses. To explain how, he says:
"All of them must be performed by the bhikkhunīs," and so forth. By this, [it is shown that] even for a grave offense (*garukāpatti*), whether concealed or unconcealed...
It shows the procedure beginning with the performance of the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight.

"The determination of the descent" (*okkantika-vinicchaya*) refers to the determination regarding the manner of entry, following the relevant context. "By powerful unwholesome [kamma]" means by such acts as adultery.
"By weak wholesome [kamma]" means by wholesome [kamma] that has had its power impaired by the aforementioned powerful unwholesome [kamma], and is therefore rendered weak.

“By weak unwholesome [kamma]” means by unwholesome kamma such as adultery, which has its power impaired by strong wholesome kamma—such as the practice of celibacy—that produces the state of masculinity, and is for that very reason rendered weak.
Because both types of existence in a happy destination (sugati) arise from wholesome kamma, their destruction occurs through unwholesome kamma alone and their arising through wholesome kamma alone;
thus he says “both,” and so forth. However, in a miserable destination (duggati), it is through unwholesome kamma alone.
Both have an arising and a passing away; the distinction between them lies solely in their weak or strong state.

The phrase "having avoided making an appointment" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the offense of a *pācittiya* when traveling along a single road with a nun after having made an appointment by saying, "Come, let us go.
By this, even within the vicinity of a single village, [the offense applies] from outside the village toward the interior of a house...
This shows that even making such an arrangement constitutes an offense. In order to show the method for being released from the offense, he says "thinking 'I...

and so forth. "Outside the village" means within the village boundary (*gāmantara*). It is said, "There is no offense...," because this conforms to the characteristics of non-offense stated in the passage beginning with "The second nun has departed" and so on. "Having discarded" means having renounced. "Modest nuns... and so forth.
"It is possible" (*labbhati*) means that even if there is no inclusion for one afflicted by the suffering of a change of gender, there might still be a falling back to the lower state;

therefore, it is stated "in times of distress" (*āpadāsu*) in accordance with the non-offense [rule]. Taking a companion (*dutiyikā*) along, she must go. Regarding "those who are shameless" (*alajjinīyo*)...
"It is possible": because an offense arises from living together in communal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth with those who are shameless, they belong to the side of the non-existent.
It is said, "they associate. By this it should be understood: "Association with those who are shameless is not permitted.

For if it were permitted, then even in cases such as traveling to another village without a companion, there would certainly be an offense because of their inclusion [in the group], just as in the case of a group of shameless female attendants (*saṅgāhika-lajjinīgaṇa*).
By the statement, "They say that if they are not relatives... it is permitted," [it is shown].
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), this indicates its future status.

Even there, although that statement was not rejected for one who is habitually proud and who finds no delight in the state of a nun—except in the case of trustworthy female relatives—nevertheless, it must be understood that it is certainly not permissible for anyone other than those [trustworthy ones].
"Even in the state of a monk" means even during the time when he is a monk. "Depending on him" means depending on that preceptor (*nissayācariya*).
"Having [done so]. "A preceptor must be taken" means that for the purpose of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), a preceptor must be taken.
"A formal act of the Vinaya" is said with reference to the assignment (*vikappana*). "Must be done again" means it must be assigned again.
"Having received it again, it is permissible for seven days" refers to: "I allow you, monks, the storage [of requisites] by monks for the sake of nuns..."

This was stated for the purpose of showing that it is permissible to consume [the food] after having it received again by monks from the bhikkhunīs, based on the statement: "having had it stored by the monks and received by the bhikkhunīs.
The phrase "on the seventh day" was stated for the purpose of showing that it is permissible to consume it again for another seven days without incurring the offense of *nissaggiya*.
"Of natural sex" means one whose gender has not changed. "He guards it" means he guards it by not relinquishing the formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*);
the intention is that because his state is undifferentiated, he does not relinquish the acceptance.

"Having taken it up himself, he should set it down" means having accepted it with his own hand, he should set it down. "There is an offense for one who consumes it" means there is an offense for one who, after a change of gender has occurred, consumes it again without having formally accepted it anew.

Regarding "returning to the low life" (*hīnāyāvattanena*): here some say that for a regular (*pakatatta*) monk, to take up the marks of a householder with the thought, "I shall become a layman," without first renouncing the training, is "returning to the low life. That is not correct, because by that much alone the state of being a monk is not abandoned.
Others, however, [say it refers to] one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and, having abandoned the claim to be a monk...

They say that even the taking up of the status of a householder's mark constitutes a "returning to the lower state" (hīnāyāvattanā); this is indeed correct. For one who has committed a *pārājika* offense remains a bhikkhu—as long as he conceals it and still maintains the claim to be a bhikkhu—because the *pārājika* rule was prescribed specifically for bhikkhus.
Indeed, it is said, "But whichever bhikkhu... Thus, even while he consents to communal living (*saṃvāsa*), [he is still considered a bhikkhu].

He is not one who lives in communion by theft, nor does he incur an offense such as sharing a sleeping place with another; however, he incurs a *pācittiya* offense for one who reviles him. For it is said:

“If a person is impure, having committed some *pārājika* offense, and another who regards him as pure, having asked for permission, speaks to him with the intent to abuse, there is an offense of abusive speech.
Some, however, say that for those who have committed a *pārājika*, acknowledging the fault and taking on the marks of a layperson constitutes a renunciation of the training.
It is subsumed under that [category] because, by his own admission, he has abandoned his status as a bhikkhu.

For this very reason, in the *Vinayavinicchaya* and other works, "returning to the lower state" (*hīnāyāvattanā*) is not mentioned separately from "renouncing the training" (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), as it is subsumed therein.

Therefore, for bhikkhunīs, the taking up of the layperson’s marks out of a desire to disrobe constitutes "returning to the lower state," which is here [equated with] their renunciation of the training.
They say, "Because of their non-existence, since it must be stated that there is no receiving or relinquishing of them whatsoever"; this too is indeed not to be refuted.

Therefore, for bhikkhunīs who have committed a *pārājika* offense, the taking of the layperson's marks with the thought, "I shall go forth again," should be understood as a falling back to the lower state (*hīnāyāvattanā*).
"Falling away" (*vibbhama*) is also a name for this very thing; for that reason, it is mentioned in the *Khuddasikkhā* as "cutting off, relinquishing, taking, and falling away."
It is stated that one becomes a *vibbhanta* (one who has left the order) by abandoning the formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"By giving away without regard" means by throwing away outside the items already accepted, without having given them to another and even though one has no need for them.

Some [commentators] say: "In the case of items already accepted, [this refers to] the act of relinquishing them before they have been formally accepted, for the purpose of liberation [from the offense]."

Regarding this, some say that even the relinquishing of a mere acceptance is indeed a relinquishing without expectation, just like the formal renunciation (*paccuddhāra*) based on the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of robes and so forth; however, that is not correct, because such a statement does not exist.

For just as in the case of robes and so forth, although the loss of determination through relinquishing without expectation has been stated, a separate formal renunciation (*paccuddhāra*) has also been mentioned, so too should it be stated here. As follows: [text omitted]... as follows.
Furthermore, in the case of robes and other items attached to the body, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) ceases through relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*);
it is not so here. Here, however, even for one who has no regard for the object already accepted, the acceptance is abandoned only when it is released from the body.
For thus it is said: "Let him relinquish it a hundred times; as long as it remains in his own hand, it is indeed still accepted."

Regarding the phrase "by giving without expectation": here, one should only say "without expectation" (*anapekkhāya*), because there is no separate act of giving apart from the state of being without expectation.
For in this case, there is no formal procedure for giving as there is in the case of relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*).
Furthermore, if there were merely a giving away of what has already been accepted, then even food previously accepted could [be given] out of a desire to eat it.
If one were to discard the mere act of receiving what has arisen and receive it again, it could then be eaten at one's pleasure;
in that case, all the various detailed explanations given in the *Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada* (the training rule concerning storing) would be rendered entirely useless. For it is said therein:
“If oil has entered into the knot of a knotted bowl... [etc. ...even when eating from such a bowl on the following day, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” and so forth.
In that context, however, one should have said only this much: “Having released it with a mind free of regard for the receiving-bowl (paṭiggahaṇa), one may eat”;
yet this was not stated. And in some cases, regarding such things as knotted bowls and the like, there is still regard for the receiving-bowl.
Even for one who makes no effort whatsoever to abandon that [desire], the acceptance of food offered there does not cease.

Why? Because the desire to eat again exists within the monk’s bowl, and since that desire persists toward the food already in the bowl, he cannot relinquish the food contained therein without first relinquishing the bowl itself.
It is not possible to relinquish the act of receiving while not relinquishing the food itself.
Therefore, one must conclude that in this context, relinquishment refers only to the relinquishment of the object, and not to the relinquishment of the act of receiving.
For this very reason, in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*) regarding the rule on storing up (*sannidhi-sikkhāpada*), it says:

“Within seven days he resolves upon it, relinquishes it, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burnt, they take it away by force, they take it on trust, having given it away to one who is not fully ordained—having cast it off, vomited it out, released it, and being without regard for it—and having received it back, he uses it.
Thus, in all these cases, only the relinquishing of the object is stated. And here, “within seven days he resolves upon it” [is the first instance].

Because of the declaration of determination for external use, even without relinquishing the physical object itself, the mere restriction for the sake of external use with a pure mind—simply out of a desire not to consume it—is indeed a separate cause for the relinquishment of possession (*paṭiggahaṇa*).
It may be that this was said with reference to the relinquishment of mere possession; and this would be well-said, for it is likewise so.
Furthermore, the relinquishment of what has been received with the intention, "I shall use it later," would not be permissible;
for here, the intended meaning refers to the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for external use.
Indeed, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, regarding the phrase "by relinquishing without regard," it is explained that this means being without need [for the object] without having given it to another.
“By saying, ‘There is no need for this; I will not consume it now,’ regarding the objects [of use];
or by relinquishing without regard [for them], thinking, ‘I will receive it again and consume it later’—regarding the act of receiving:
thus, even the mere relinquishment of what was received is stated to be a cause for the loss of that reception for one who still intends to consume it. This should not be accepted.
However, the preliminary formal act of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding external use must indeed be undertaken.

This [act], however, was not mentioned separately in the commentaries, having been included within the meaning of the canonical phrase: “he relinquishes what is called ‘relinquishing without regard. It should be understood that these words—“is lost,” “perishes,” “is burned,” and “or they take it on trust”—are included within this phrase “they take it.”
"By taking after having snatched away" means by taking [something] from those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna) through force or other such means.
For in the case of fully ordained persons (upasampanna), the act of receiving does not cease even when there is snatching away or taking on trust. "In this place" means in the monastery of the monks.
"Upper growths" refers to trees and shrubs planted by him. "Among the thirteen formal permissions" (sammuti).

In regard to the thirteen formal appointments (sammuti)— namely, the appointees for assigning meals, for arranging seats, for the storekeeper, for receiving robes, for distributing robes, for distributing rice-gruel, for distributing fruits,

for distributing solid foods, for distributing minor items, for accepting gifts on behalf of others, for distributing alms-bowls, for supervising monastery attendants, and for supervising novices— [the rule applies] even though the appointment for the distribution of lodgings during the later period has ceased,

because the absence of the five benefits rooted in the *kathina* ceremony remains the same whether that [later] distribution of lodgings has ceased or not; thus, even if the cessation of the distribution of lodgings exists therein...
Without showing that, in order to show only what must be done by the monks in that case, it was said:
"If [he returns] during the later period," and so forth. "If [he has committed an offense] with unwholesome result... pe...

the *mānatta* penance of six days should be given"—this refers to the *pakkhamānatta* for one who, while living in concealment for a common offense, has either not undertaken the *parivāsa* or has changed his gender (*liṅga*).

This is stated by way of one who is practicing [the penance]. However, if his *liṅga* (characteristic) changes again while he has not yet formally undertaken the *pakkhamānatta*, then after granting him *parivāsa*, the *mānatta* of six days should be granted to him as if he had already completed his *parivāsa*.

There is no granting of *parivāsa* because he did not conceal [his offense] during the time he was a monk. But if he intentionally fails to report it even during the time he was a monk, [then a different procedure applies].
They say that the offense remains concealed, and because of the concealment of the offense, probation (*parivāsa*) must be granted.

It should be understood that even if the gender of men or women who have committed a *pārājika* offense changes, they are not to be granted re-ordination (*upasampadā*), because the state of having committed a *pārājika* is not relinquished within that same personal existence (*attabhāva*).
For this very reason, those such as men whose heads have been cut off are cited as examples for them.
71. “*Tatheva*” means he extends this same meaning [to the following]: whether one is liberated or not. This is said with reference to ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*);
for it is difficult for them to refrain from such an act, whereas for noble ones (*ariya*) such as stream-enterers and the rest, there is no difficulty in that regard.
Indeed, noble ones do not incur an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) or other worldly transgressions.
73. "Tightly closed" (*suphusitā*) means that the lower row of teeth stands touching the upper row of teeth;

the meaning is "not opened. Therefore it is said: "There is no space within the mouth. However, when the flesh of the lips has been torn away, for one who applies [the organ] directly to the teeth, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), because of the contact with the sign outside the sign. This also applies to teeth and the tongue that have protruded outside.
The same method applies here. Those called *nijjhāmataṇhika* (those consumed by thirst) are extremely terrified because their bodies have been scorched by flames arising from the pores of their skin.
By the word "etcetera," hungry ghosts (*petas*) who are afflicted by hunger and thirst, whose bodies consist of nothing but bones and skin, and whose forms are terrifying, are included.
"Having rendered him unconscious" means having acted in such a way that he does not even perceive the treatment being administered.
And by this, it is shown that for one who consents without being unconscious, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

"One whose bodily sensitivity is impaired" means one whose bodily sensitivity has been damaged by disorders such as wind or bile insofar as they prevent the arising of body-consciousness; it does not mean one whose bodily sensitivity is destroyed.
"When the bowl is on the head" refers to when the path has entered the path. "Touching the organ with the organ" occurs solely out of a desire not to insert [the penis].
A *thullaccaya* has been mentioned; however, for one who desires to engage [in sexual intercourse] even there, it is only a *dukkaṭa*. Thus he said, "only a *dukkaṭa* in the vicinity.
(74) By the word *jāti*, in the sense of a *sumana* flower, its supporting thicket (*gumbo*) is intended; thus he said, "of the *jāti*-flower thicket.
And by this, he shows that it is a non-elided compound (*aluttasamāsa*), namely, a forest characterized by *jāti* flowers is a *jātivana*. [The term] *ekarasaṃ*...
Unmixed with the [ordinary] consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (vīthicitta).
77. "When the object has arisen" means when the object of sexual misconduct committed by women has arisen. "A door with tree-needles and thorns" means a door with tree-needles and a door with thorns;
or the reading may be "evameva" (in this very way). Therein, on both sides, there are tree-posts...
Having dug [a pit] there in the middle and pierced it, they insert two or three wooden pegs;

that is called a "wooden-peg door. However, at the time of entering and exiting, having removed those, the door fitted with a covering of thorny branches by means of a closing mechanism is called a "thorn door.
For the purpose of closing a village gate, [one uses] earth, thorny branches, and so forth.

Or, in the case of a door that lacks a mortar and bolt and cannot be closed or opened by one person alone, they attach a single wheel beneath it, by means of which the turning of that wheel makes the closing of the door easy;
it is with reference to this that it is said, "a door equipped with a wheel. For it is the wheel itself, in the sense of being something to be taken hold of, for the purpose of closing and opening.
In the sense of being something to be grasped, it is a "wheel" (*cakkalaka*); a door-panel joined with that is called a "wheeled door," and a door joined with that is a "door equipped with wheels.
However, since two or even three wheels are attached to large doors, he says "on the panels," and so forth.
"In the enclosures" (*kiṭikāsu*) means in the lattices made of bamboo strips, thorny branches, and the like. "The revolving enclosure-door" (*saṃsaraṇakiṭikadvāra*).
"With a wheel-shaped body" refers to the great gate joined with the sliding panels for moving about. "Having blocked it" means having covered it, or having tied it with ropes.
"Only one door with a cloth curtain" includes here also a door with a mat curtain, as it belongs to the same category.
Then, "the monks... were seated"—this was said for the purpose of showing that the monks were present there.

It is permissible to apply attention even while lying down; however, once one has lain down and is falling asleep, it is not permissible to apply attention because one stands on the side of non-exertion.
Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhunī," etc., he says that the closing of the door—just like sitting in private—is permitted for the purpose of preventing women from entering.
"Having climbed up by means of a ladder" refers to the fact that the lower floor is secured with a door-bolt.
It has been stated. Because the wall surrounding it on the four sides is a single continuous unit, it is called "having a single wall.
This was said with reference to what appears in the Pāḷi as "the rear portion.
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by anything whatsoever," here the measurement of the enclosure's height is exactly the same as that stated for what is sufficient for sleeping together.
"Mahāpariveṇa" means a large courtyard; by this, he indicates a place frequented by many people, hence he says "the Great Bodhi," and so forth.
One wakes up when the dawn has risen; there is no offense because one lay down with a pure mind during the night, which constitutes a field where no offense occurs.
"Having woken up, one sleeps again" constitutes an offense if, after waking at the rising of the dawn, one recognizes that the dawn has risen.

Alternatively, having failed to attend to [the duty] or having gone to sleep with a lethargic mind, an offense arises originating from non-action because of the failure to perform what ought to be done—such as closing the door—since the act of lying down performed in a situation where there is no offense is not a constituent factor [of that offense].
For this offense is non-action in such a case, yet at the moment of lying down without restraint during the day, it is action; both are without mental concomitants (*acittaka*).
...and so it should be understood. Even for one who wakes up before dawn but lies down again until sunrise, there is an offense according to the previous method.
Regarding the statement, "Even for one who thinks, 'I shall rise when the sun has risen'... [etc. ...there is still an offense," at what point does he incur that offense? It is said:
not yet during the night, because it is stated, "One incurs it by day, not by night. [This refers to] the *dukkaṭa* offense for disrespect.
However, the *dukkaṭa* mentioned [in the phrase] "he is not released" is not merely a *dukkaṭa* for sleeping during the day, but rather a *dukkaṭa* for disrespect (*anādariya-dukkaṭa*).
Thus, it should be understood that at the rising of the dawn, he incurs an offense that is unintentional (*acittaka*) and originated by non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
If he closes the door and lies down thinking, "I will get up when the dawn has risen," and while the door is [closed] by others...
Even if the door is opened at the time of sunrise, there is indeed no offense for him, because there is no distinction between the portions of night and day regarding the burning of the door.
It should be understood that only a distinction in time is required for the commission of an offense, not for its avoidance;
for it is said: "If one lies down at night without having secured the door. This applies even if someone opens it while he is lying down after having secured it during the day.
There is no offense at the door itself. They say that there is likewise no offense if one does not attend to it oneself, provided there is a reason and the door is open.
"He does not emerge according to the limit" means he emerges only when the dawn has already risen.

The phrase "there is indeed an offense" is said with reference specifically to the root-offense; however, the offense of disrespect still applies to him even if he emerges before dawn—namely, the *dukkaṭa*.

Because it is stated, "he is not released," and because it is said, "he is not released from the *dukkaṭa*," the intended meaning is that even one who has been released from a root-offense (*mūlāpatti*) by rising before dawn is still not released from the *dukkaṭa* for disrespect.
The phrase "he lies down due to sleep" is stated in common parlance; however, since his feet have not been lifted off the ground, this...
One is not said to be "lying down," and for that reason, no offense is stated. Regarding "sleeping while leaning against":
this refers to sleeping while leaning against a pillar or similar object, without allowing even a small portion of the area from the hip bone upward along the spine to touch the ground.
However, for one who allows the hip bone to touch the ground, it is indeed "lying down," for [the posture] is characterized by the stretching out of the back.
It is a bed. Even in cases such as the *Dīgha-vandana*, since the backbones are extended horizontally, lying down itself constitutes the offense;
this must be avoided because in instances such as "he lies at the feet saying 'I pay homage,'" only lying down is mentioned.

There is no offense for that [falling] either, because it occurs at the moment of falling when there is no intentional aim, and because one has risen suddenly once the situation has arisen. However, for one who is unconscious...
Even afterwards it is not within the scope [of the offense]; for him, there is no offense at all, just as at the very moment he fell.
By the phrase "he lies right there and does not get up," he shows that there is no offense even when the object is present; for that very reason, it is said, "there is an offense for him.
"With one side" means having collapsed his body onto one side without lifting both feet off the ground.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, the connection is that this was spoken by the Elder Mahāpaduma;

by this, he shows: "This is the doctrine of the Elder Mahāpaduma as recorded in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. In that regard, because there is a lack of objective domain even for one who is sleeping, the Elder Mahāpaduma stated:
"But because of the lack of an objective domain, no offense is seen. However, the Teachers [state] regarding one who is sleeping...
Because it lacks the state of being unconscious and because it is an object [of perception], they do not say there is no offense. When one is unconscious, there is indeed no offense.
However, the statement beginning with "two people" is a passage from the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself; since that was stated later, it is authoritative.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "possessed by a yakkha," one who has become unconscious is also included here. But as for one lying down on a single side...
It should be understood that one is indeed released from the offense because it was not laid down.

78. “He walks upon the sky”: *pada* means a footprint or a track; therefore he says, “a footprint on the sky. “This is the foremost”: this is the best. “Namely, this”: that which is this. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vimativinodanī*, a commentary on the Vinaya-ṭṭhakathā, known as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The method of commentary on the first *pārājika* is finished.
2. The second *pārājika*:

"By the Peerless One"—that is, by the Jina who has no equal; since the turn for the commentary on that which was proclaimed as the second *pārājika* has now arrived, the construction is: "This is the commentary on this second [offense]."
84. Regarding the commentary on the story of Dhaniya:
It is called "Rājagaha" because it was seized by kings; thus he says, "by Mandhātu. Although it was also possessed by the royal chaplain, it is still considered "possessed by the king";
hence the mention of Mahāgovinda. Furthermore, with reference to the word "city," it is here termed "Rājagaha."

This is the explanation of the neuter gender. Furthermore, it illustrates other modes of expression here, such as "Rājagaha" (the King's House), which is derived from the sense that it is the residence (*geha*) of kings because of its well-ordered protection.
"Vasantavana" (Spring Grove) refers to a pleasure grove; however, it is called "Vasantavana" because it is primarily used for recreation during the spring season.

“Sadvārabandha” (the sixfold door-binding) is a demonstration of the suitability for entering the rains residence. “The Nālaka Path” refers to the path of the great man (*moneyya-paṭipadā*) taught to the Elder Nālaka in the *Sutta Nipāta*.
Regarding “of the five coverings,” this refers to the five consisting of grass, leaves, brick, stone, and plaster.
By the statement, “If he does not obtain [materials]... even he himself should build it,” [it is shown that] except in the case of a boat or a cart, elsewhere—
The statement, “I am one who does not enter the rains residence,” does not permit entering [the rains] by the mere act of making a mental attachment.
It shows that one must indeed enter the rains residence after having sought out a lodging and made a verbal declaration.

For, in the Pāḷi text beginning with “Monks, one should not [enter the rains] without a lodging,” and in the Aṭṭhakathā with the words “even by one who has undertaken the Nālaka practice,” this is established firmly and without distinction.

It has been stated that, even in the absence of a formal dwelling, the undertaking of the rains residence is permitted by way of making it one’s abode—through such passages as, “Monks, I allow you to enter upon the rains residence on a boat”—but it should be understood that this does not apply elsewhere.

"This is in accordance with the Dhamma" means proper conduct (*sāmīcivatta*). "The rules of agreement" refers to those who, at all times, remain heedful, setting aside a fondness for idle talk and the like.

The observances beginning with "one must become" (*bhavitabba*) are the observances of the *tikas*. Regarding the "observances of the Khandhakas," one should resolve upon the observances of the Khandhakas, such as: "The observance of the *khandhaka* for newcomers and others must be fulfilled.
As for the phrase "having spent the rains residence" (*vassaṃvutthā*), the commentary states: "Those who have entered the first [rains] and have performed the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*)."

Since it is stated that "from the first day of the lunar fortnight onwards, they are called 'those who have completed the rains residence'," it should be understood that those who go elsewhere after performing the *pavāraṇā* on the day of the Great *Pavāraṇā*, or even without performing it, may do so only when there is a purpose for a seven-day period;
if there is not, otherwise the rains residence is interrupted and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occurs. "During these three months..."

For it is said: “I enter the rains residence,” and also: “Monks, having entered the rains residence, one should not set out on a journey without having stayed for either the first three months or the last three months. And here it is said: “Having spent the rains residence right here, at the end of the three months...
they departed. The day of the *pavāraṇā* ceremony is also included within those three months. However, some [hold that] “I authorize... [the departure before the end].
When they say, "Monks, since it is stated that 'for monks who have completed the rains residence' [they may perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony] by means of three grounds,
and because the phrase 'having completed the rains residence' refers to the state of having finished the rains,

it is permissible to go as one pleases on the day of the Great *Pavāraṇā* even without the pretext of a seven-day business," that is merely their own opinion; for indeed, regarding those who have completed the rains...

The authorization for the *pavāraṇā* was established for the purpose of excluding those who have not entered the rains residence (*anupagata*), those whose rains residence has been interrupted (*chinnavassa*), and so forth;
it was not, however, intended to show that one should depart without remaining on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, because there is no such occasion here.
Here, the *pavāraṇā* is prescribed for those who are fit to perform the *pavāraṇā*, namely those who have entered the rains residence and have not interrupted it.
As long as they remained until the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, by that much they are called "those who have completed the rains" (*vutthavassa*) with respect to the Pavāraṇā ritual,
because it is understood that a small deficiency or excess does not affect the validity of the count; however, this is not so with respect to the Kathina ritual,
because the three-month period was incomplete, otherwise there would be the contingency of performing the Kathina-athāra even on that day of the Great Pavāraṇā.
“Monks, I allow the monks who have completed the rains residence to spread the *kaṭhina* cloth”— this, as well as the rule, “Monks,

having entered the rains residence, one must not set out on a journey without having spent either the first three months or the last three months,” refers from the literal standpoint to the day following the full moon of the month of *Kattika*, immediately after the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*).
This was stated with reference to the commencement [of the rainy season] and the departure for the journey after the spreading of the *kaṭhina*.
And in the *Parivāra*, having stated, "The month of the spreading of the *kaṭhina* must be known," it further states, "The last month of the rains must be known.

For the time for departing on a journey begins precisely from that time which is the time for the spreading of the *kaṭhina*, and not before that; this applies only to those who have completed the rains residence.

Because of the eligibility for the *kathina* ceremony. For at the very moment when the *kathina* ceremony is not permitted on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, the monks likewise have not completed their rains-residence (*vutthavassa*), since they have not yet performed the *pavāraṇā* on that day.
However, as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Even if it has not been completed in its entirety, by virtue of the portion already completed on that day..."
The statement beginning with “it is indeed completed” and so forth is not correct; for at the end of that day, at the time of sunrise,
one is indeed said to have completed it for that day— just as in the cases of the *parivāsa* and forest-dwelling periods—
and this investigation will become clear in the *Vassūpanāyika-kkhandhaka* below, where we shall explain it in detail.

"Having performed the *mahāpavāraṇā*" means that after entering the first rains-residence (*purimikā vassa*) and demonstrating an uninterrupted rains-residence, this [term] applies even to those who did not perform the *pavāraṇā* due to some obstacle, because they have completed the rains-residence.

"It is not rained upon" (*na ovassiyati*)—this should be understood as a noun derived from the action (*kamma-sādhana*), meaning "not being rained upon"; the sense is: having made it so that it is not soaked. Regarding "unobstructed" (*anavayo*): here...
The prefix *anu* occurs in the sense of distribution (*vicchāya*); thus he says, "one by one" (*anu anu avayo*), and so forth. The work of a teacher is "teacherly work" (*ācariyaka*);
thus he says, "in teacherly work. "Woodwork" refers to pillars and the like. "With oil, copper, and clay" means with copper-clay mixed with oil. 85.
"The state of being made into a hut" means the fact of having been constructed as a hut. When the word *kiṃ* is employed, the suffix for the future tense (*anāgatappaccaya*) is prescribed.

With this in mind, it was said: "Its characteristic," and so forth. Although the Elder had no intention to kill living beings, because many beings died due to his acting without careful consideration, it was said: "Of one who harms living beings," and so forth.
"The state of being drinkable" means the state of being destroyed. "Of those committing the destruction of life"—even though it was not committed by the Elder.
In the case of taking life, it shows the mode of grasping by means of even the slightest subsequent trace (leso) consisting merely in the death of the living beings;
and by that, it is indicated that one should not perform the function of grasping the sign for the subsequent perversion (vipallāsa-lesa), thinking, "I have no such unwholesome deed.
Following the example of what has been seen (diṭṭhānugati) means the following or imitation of the action that was seen.
"Following" means adhering to a particular view or conviction. "To be crushed" means to be trampled or destroyed; this is the meaning.
That even for those who, having obtained [the site] and dwell there, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), is established by the Blessed One’s statement regarding the demolition of a hut.
Furthermore, that [hut] may be made of pure clay unmixed with grass, wood, structural materials such as beams or pillars, or even bricks.

It is permissible for it to be built [of bricks]. For some, having constructed pillars out of bricks alone and then, on top of them, having bound a roof in the shape of a canopy and so forth using bricks alone—devoid of wooden materials such as beams—it makes a dwelling entirely of brick;
such a structure is permissible. Regarding the phrase "built in the form of a brick-house (giñjakāvasatha)": here, *giñjakā* refers to bricks.
A dwelling was built with those very materials; thus it is called a "giñjakāvasatha" (a brick house).
"And also workmanship" means there is also work produced by the labor of those who provide clay, carry earth, lay bricks, and cut timber, for which they are given food, wages, and other requisites.

By this, one should not suspect that the builders of the hut incur guilt or similar liability. It is called "the sectarian banner" because it serves as a distinctive mark of the sectarians themselves; for they [use such things] in these matters...
They dwell in *cāṭi* (clay huts) and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), he shows that the two reasons he has stated are also mentioned in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

Since a hut made entirely of clay is too cold in the winter and too hot in the summer, and is easy for thieves to break into, the alms bowl, robes, and other belongings kept therein are destroyed by cold, heat, thieves, and the like.
It is said: "For the purpose of protecting the bowl and robes. The statement that one may have it cut or broken without fault refers to something that, like this hut, is entirely unfit for use.
However, in the case of things such as umbrellas bound with five-colored threads, only the improper portion may be cut; the remainder is not to be destroyed, because that part is allowable.
One who cuts it becomes subject to censure. For this very reason, he will say: "It should be worn even after breaking a small pot or a beast-shaped [ornament]," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the decision outside the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakavinicchaya*):
concerning the phrase "the cage of slips for holding the umbrella-staff," here, that which is in the middle of the cage-slips and broad at the base—
A *chattadaṇḍa* (umbrella handle) is like an *ahicchattaka* (a type of mushroom), being hollow at the top where they insert the space for the staff to grasp the umbrella;

or it may be a handle that is long by itself. To prevent this from slipping out, they construct a strong lattice-work around the base of the handle where the umbrella ribs meet, and bind it securely with cords.
That spot is called the "umbrella-handle-receiving-lattice"; it ought to be woven there.

By the phrase "not for the sake of color or gloss," he shows that if it becomes glossy through being woven with a single-colored thread solely for the purpose of making it firm, there is no fault therein.
"With the point" means with the tip of the driving tool. "At the base of the handle" means at the end of the handle's root.
*Chattamaṇḍalikaṃ*: a circle of handle-rings bound in a circular shape within the frame of the umbrella. *Ukkiritvā*: having made it uneven, either low or high.
*Nānāsuttakehi*: with threads of various colors. This is stated with reference to those who do it in that manner;
however, even a single-colored thread is not permitted, for it is said: "Only ordinary needlework is allowed. *Paṭṭamukhe*: at the ends of two ribbons.
This was said with reference to the place where [the cloth] is joined together. "At the edge" means at the border of the robe; this was said with reference to the windward side.
"Veṇī" means sewing in the shape of a braid of hair. "Saṅkhalikā" means sewing in the shape of a double-linked chain.
The connection with the standard rule is: "making it a veṇī or a saṅkhalikā. "Agghiya" means having the shape of a *cetiya*.
What they call the "auspicious pillar" (*agghiyatthambha*). "They carve" means they raise it up. "Only a quadrangular shape is suitable" is said with reference to the loops, the rings, and the bands.
Regarding "the protuberances of the corner-threads," some say these are the tips set in the shape of protuberances for the threads that emerge from the corners of the loops, rings, and bands;
they state that those protuberances should be made so as not to be easily discernible after the protuberances have been cut away.
This is their intention. However, some say that there are only two types: the corner-thread (*koṇasutta*) and the pillow (*piḷaka*).
According to their opinion, the threads drawn from corner to corner on the knotted cords (*gaṇṭhika*), the loops (*pāsaka*), and the strips (*paṭṭa*) are called corner-threads.
Those made with a border all around, forming a square pattern, are called pillows. Some [hold] both of these to be for the purpose of making the robe appear distinct [from the rest].
They make it into something altered; to prevent that, it is said, "forms that are difficult to discern are permissible.
This is not, however, because it is entirely outside the range of sight, for it would be impossible to sew it in such a way for the purpose of sewing.
The intention is that it should be sewn in such a manner that no alteration from the original robe-cloth is apparent. Even though it may be apparent prior to the act of dyeing...
Regarding the phrase "when the robe is dyed," he says this because the distinction [of the dye] is not perceived due to its uniform color.

"With gems" means with polished stones such as blue sapphires and the like. However, they say that shoulder-straps, waist-bands, and so forth, because they are not robes, may be rubbed with conch shells and similar materials.
"Ear-threads" refers to those threads that emerge from the four corners and the four ends of a robe sewn lengthwise and crosswise.
This is the name for the strings at the head [of the robe]; having cut that, one should put it on. Therefore he said: "It should be cut when the dyeing is finished.
There is also a single ear-string permitted by the Blessed One; however, to show that although it is similar in name, it is actually something else entirely, he said "but as for that which...
and so forth. "For the purpose of fastening" means for the purpose of binding the robe to the robe-string.
“Gaṇṭhikā” means made of ivory and so forth. “Pīḷakā” refers to those pustules that must be raised by forming them drop by drop.

“In a bowl” means in a personal bowl of three kinds, such as one made of copper and so forth, which is permissible. “It is not allowed” means that the application for coloring it like a gemstone is not allowed;
however, it is allowed for the purpose of coloring it with oil. “On a plate” means made of tin, lead, and so forth. “Not... [The sentence continues: “No, ... [The text ends here.]
Because it was said, "Monks, bowls should be carried with their rims decorated with painted figures," it was stated that "wall-painting is not permitted.
Because it was said, "Monks, I allow you to carve a makara-tooth [design]," it was stated that "a makara-tooth design, however, is permitted"; this, moreover, is even found in the Pāḷi.
This is stated according to the method of what is excluded from the Canon (*pāḷimuttaka-naya*), because it is not included here in the Canon. Other similar cases are to be understood in the same way.
"Writing is not permitted" means that writing made with a stylus is not permitted; however, writing made with colors such as *jāti-hiṅgulika* and the like is permitted.
"On the rim of the umbrella-handle" means on the circular rim of the handle of the water-pot (*dhammakaraṇa*) which has the shape of an umbrella for grasping.
"At the place for binding the water-strainer cloth," some say.
"A water-snake's head" means the head of a water-serpent (*udakasappa*). "Eyes" means [the corners] shaped like an elephant's eye.
"Only one is permitted" means that here, it is not permitted to bind it even by doubling or tripling a single cord; rather, even if there are a hundred [strands], only one [cord] is permitted.

It is permissible to wrap it around the body and bind it; however, when many ropes are joined together and wrapped continuously as one, it should not be called a "bahurajjuka" (multi-rope), because it is stated that such a thing is not permitted.
It should be understood that this does not fall under the category of a *muraja* (drum). For a *muraja* is made by wrapping various colored threads around the frame of a drum in the shape of a drum.
This is said; however, this [type of] *muraja*—which is known as the *maddavīṇā* and is shaped like a *pāmaṅga* (a type of drum)—is suitable for the fringes (*dasā*).
Because it is stated: "The fringes of the waistband wear out; monks, I allow the *muraja* and the *maddavīṇā*," it is permitted.

"Arrangements" (*vidhe*) refers to the arrangements to be made at the end of the fringes for the sake of durability, such as those made with ivory, horn, thread, and so forth. The eight auspicious signs (*aṭṭha maṅgalāni*).
They say [the marks are] a conch, a wheel, a full water-jar, an elephant, a lion, a hook, a banner with a *sovattika* [fringe], and so forth;
they also speak of them by way of a pair of fish, a parasol, a *nandiyāvatta*, and so on.
"Merely a line of demarcation" means merely the boundary-line made at both ends of whatever has been fashioned from ivory and other materials.
Because it is stated as “only straight,” an eye-salve container (*añjanī*) that is shaped like a square or similar form, or one that is crooked, is not permitted.

“In a case” (*sipāṭikāya*) means in a pouch used for storing tools such as axes and the like. They say that an “ārakaṇṭaka” is a long-pointed knife made for the purpose of smoothing out cloth and so forth.
Some say it is “the knife of wood-turners for carving wood and the like. A “round gem” (*vaṭṭamaṇika*) refers to something made round.
A small swelling (*pupphuḷaka*) must be raised. By the word "another," this includes pustules and the like. Regarding "a small knife" (*pipphalika*):
it refers to any small cutting instrument. Regarding "curved" (*valitaka*): at the time of cutting the nails, they make it provided with curves precisely for the sake of a firm grip.
Therefore, by the phrase "that is permissible," whatever other modification exists for the purpose of strengthening the work and so forth—
It is explained that they do this not for the sake of making it glossy, but because that is permissible;
by this, even an iron ring or similar item attached to the tip of a fire-drill staff for the purpose of producing sound through mutual friction is established as allowable.
"The circle" refers to the circular pit for inserting the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇī). It must be perfectly straight.
"Should be bound" is the connection; "on both sides or on one side" is the ellipsis of the words.
The meaning is: "should be bound on both sides of the oil-pressing staff in order to prevent the two ends of the staff from moving.
"In a vessel made of *āmaṇḍa* wood" means in an oil-container made from the paste produced by grinding *āmalaka* fruits. It is said that when [the medicine] is placed therein...
The oil becomes cool. "On a floor-covering" means on a covering to be spread over ground that has been prepared with straw mats and the like.
"A water-jar" includes all varieties of vessels. "Everything...

is permitted" means that even images of men and women are permitted on the aforementioned beds and so forth, because images of men and women are specifically prohibited only in the case of oil containers.
They say that this is because [the oil vessel] was not included [in the list], but rather the beds and so forth were taken separately;
however, even though they say this, since these beds and so forth are articles that must be touched with the hand, one should understand that here only a female form is not permitted.
"Of others" means of those who own the boundary. "By royal favorites" refers to those such as the modest and the gentle who create obstacles to the Uposatha and other observances.

The monks intended here are those who are shameless (*alajjino*) and have broken away from their original affiliation (*bhinnaladdhikā*), because it is improper to perform the Uposatha and other ceremonies together with them;

for that very reason, it is said, "within the boundary" (*sīmāya*). A "shameful assembly" (*lajjīparisā*) capable of providing support to those owners of the boundary refers to an assembly of shameless monks.
"Done by the monks" refers to acts such as the breaking of lodgings (*senāsanabhedanādika*) performed by shameless monks against the shameless monks.
It is said that all of this was spoken precisely for the purpose of restraining those who are shameless, as it ought to be put into practice.
88. "They murmur" means they think low thoughts. The purpose of the murmuring is to censure the monk’s act of theft, thinking, "How indeed can he take what is not given?";
it is not, however, intended to qualify the word *dāru* (wood), because that word is plural.
"Vacanabhede" means in the difference between the singular and plural numbers. "Sabbāvantaṃ" means possessing all members, such as monks, nuns, and so forth.
"Bimbisāro" is his name; here, "bimbī" means gold. Therefore, it should be understood that he is called "Bimbisāra" because of his complexion being like the color of the finest gold.
According to the ancient teachers, he was produced with the measure of twenty māṣas of the most excellent gold.
One endowed with the [proper] characteristics should be understood as a "blue kahāpaṇa. A "Rudradāmaka" is one produced by someone named Rudradāma;
it is said that it is worth three parts of a blue kahāpaṇa.
Furthermore, in a region where blue kahāpaṇas do not exist, even there, the value of goods is determined by five māsakas of refined gold that is free from blackness.

It should be done. "By that" means by one-fourth of a blue kahāpaṇa coin. The phrase "in the case of a *pārājika* offense," and so forth, is stated because *pārājika* offenses were prescribed by all Buddhas;
however, regarding the *saṅghādisesa* and other offenses, as well as their respective bases, there is no difference at all.
The only distinction is that some [Buddhas] prescribe them in every aspect, while others do so only in part. This is all.
This is the distinction. For the Fully Enlightened Ones never, at any time, prescribe a training rule that exceeds or falls short of the offense committed.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya) 92:
Furthermore, because it is stated, "desiring to come," [it refers to] a newly constructed dwelling where humans have never previously resided in any way whatsoever.

It should be understood that when a village has been abandoned by those who have no further attachment, saying, “We shall not enter it again,” there is no need for the formal inquiry regarding entry into the village, because the conventional designation of a “village” no longer applies.

The phrase “for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the forest” means that once the village and its precincts have been shown, the delimitation of the forest as being other than those can be known.

"Within the village" means within a village that is enclosed. However, in the case of an unenclosed site or village, the very place where one stands is considered the location.
"He makes it face the forest" … [omission] … "he guards" means he guards it because, by that means, he has arrived at the place desired by him. From the village...

"Of one who has gone out" means of one who has gone out from an enclosed village. "Kapiñjara" refers to a species of bird raised by foolish people for the purpose of making them fight with one another.
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Sky-Abiding [Sutta]* (Vehāsaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā)

97. In the commentary on *vehāsa* (in the air), the phrase "merely cut" and "merely released" is stated with reference to the act of cutting and releasing, such that what has been cut and released does not remain in its natural place.
98. In the commentary on *udaka* (water), it is said that "what is placed in flowing water does not remain," and thus he says, "in non-flowing water."
“An offense” (anāpatti) is stated with reference to the absence of the *dukkaṭa* offense regarding hand-movements and foot-movements.
“Drags” means he draws it downward from below. “The entire water” means all the water contained within the area touched by the staff.
“The water is not the place” is because the place made by oneself is not the [original] place. “In a lotus thicket” means in a cluster of lotus plants. “A bundle” means a tied cluster.
"Bound in bundles" means bound together by making it small according to the size of a hand.
"Bound as a load" means bound by way of a head-load and so forth. "Root-stock" means a bulbous root (*kanda*).
"A leaf or a flower"—this is said with reference to what stands having entered into the mud. "A drain-pipe" is a channel for the water to exit from a reservoir. "A water-conduit."
"Regarding the *mahāmātikam*: 'He is not to be prosecuted for theft'—this indicates that one is not exempt from the offense in all cases of depriving a living being of life.
'Having charged it to the *mātikā*' means having charged it to the *khuddakamātikā* (the Minor Schedule). As for the phrase 'having died...
they remain': since the dead fish themselves belong to them, there is no theft on the part of one who takes them while they are dead."
Commentary on the Boat Sutta (Nāvaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā) 99.
Regarding the statement, "In the Boat Sutta, there is both a thullaccaya and a pārājika":

here it should be understood that if one discharges [the semen] without first moving it from its place, it is a thullaccaya; however, if one moves it from its place before discharging it, it is a pārājika. In the case of a snare...
He says, “In this regard, the reasoning has already been stated previously,” referring to what was said starting with the phrase “like a tethered pig.
“By way of a ship that has gone astray” means: having fled to another region due to adverse winds, or having broken apart and met with destruction, it sinks into the water;
yet, without reaching the bottom of the earth, its owners have not abandoned it—this is what is meant. By the phrase “and a strong wind having arrived,”...
This shows that this application is performed when there is no wind. "There is no taking away for a person" is stated according to the method of straightening a dried-up root.
This is appropriate when [the object] has not been stepped upon by one's own foot nor lifted up by the hand, but has been bound to another thing such as a staff and set aside;
it does not apply when it has been stepped upon by one's own foot and lifted up by the hand.

However, when one is standing still and the strong wind strikes the umbrella, robes, and so forth, one must abandon the ordinary course and perform a new, more forceful application of effort in grasping, stepping, and so on.

Otherwise, the umbrella, robes, and other items will be lost, or the thief himself will fall [from the boat], and the boat will not proceed at that time. Therefore, in such a case of a new application of effort—

There ought to be an illustration. Since there is no task to be performed at the time when water flows through a dry channel because it is already straight, that does not serve as an illustration here.
However, in the case of a slave who is naturally inclined to run away, one might say, "Go quickly!
and by such means as inducing a hurried pace beyond his natural gait, this should serve as the illustration here; this is our view.

This should be accepted after investigation. Even when a wind arises, if the ship remains in its natural state without making any effort because it is extremely light, this is what is stated in the Commentary; thus it should be accepted.
[End of] the commentary on the *Yāna-aṭṭhakathā*.

100. In the *Yāna-aṭṭhakathā*, "on both sides" means that after a square wooden frame has been placed upon four pillars, a carriage (*sandamānikā*) is constructed on its left and right sides like the two wings of a garuḷa bird, for the purpose of warding off dangers such as wind and heat.
"Yoked with two" means yoked with two oxen. "Unyoked" means...

It is not joined with ox-yokes. A "kappakatā" (a fastening) is so called because it is a support placed at the junction of two crests, with two ends set like the horns of a cow; it stands on the ground with both ends.
Therefore he said, "six places. Or "three or four places" refers to the two [ends] of a non-fastened support.
The connection is as follows: there are three points by way of the wheels, four points by way of the axle-pins (*kappakatā*), and likewise three points for that which is placed upon the ground.
"By the two ends of the axle" means by the two tips of the axle-wood. "By the axle-pins" (*akkhudhīhi*):
the two pieces of wood fashioned at the lower part of the axle-wood to receive it are called axle-pins (*akkhudhī*).
Of those two types of *kappa* that have been fashioned, the four *kappa*-tops are here called "axles" (*akkhuddhiyo*); therefore he said, "and with four axles.
With those [axles] established, there are five locations: the four places where they are fixed and one place where the yoke (*dhura*) is fixed.
The *uddhi* itself is called an "axle-pole" (*uddhikhāṇuka*); in the absence of axle-poles...
Showing the place for the installation of the axle-heads, he said, "having made the arms even," and so forth.

Therein, "evenly" means that without letting the pins hang down, one makes the lower portion of the arms level, cuts a hole between the two arm-boards the size of the axle-heads, and inserts the axle-heads therein; by that—
The lower part of the oars touches the entire ground; therefore it is said, "standing while touching the whole earth.

The remainder is similar to what was stated regarding the boat. By this, if one stops its natural course as it is going thus and leads it to another direction, it is a *pārājika* offense. [This applies] when it has reached any location by itself.
This refers by extension to the principle that if one sells an item and departs without moving it from its place, there is no theft;
however, the price of the goods must still be paid.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning "burdens."

101. In the *Bhāraṭṭhakathā*, regarding the key phrase (*mātikāpada*) "the meaning of the burden" (*bhāraṭṭha*), he says "the meaning of the burden is the burden itself" in order to show its significance.
"In the front part of the throat" means in the anterior portion of the throat. "The upper cavity of the throat" refers to the upper opening of the neck.
"In the middle of the chest-limit" means in the center of the boundary of the chest. "Not commanded by the owners" means...
If this [goods] had been commanded by the owners, saying, "Take this burden and give it at such-and-such a place," then the goods taken by him would constitute a deposit (*upanikkhitta*);

and even for one who removes them from the head or elsewhere with a thieving mind, there would be no theft (*avahāra*), but only [theft] upon the relinquishment of responsibility by the owners. Therefore, in order to distinguish this from the status of goods deposited (*upanikkhittabhaṇḍa*):
It has been stated; for that very reason he will say: "But because there was no formal command by them, it is a *pārājika*. "Shaking" means tossing [the head] from the top of the head;
if one were to toss it, the *pārājika* offense would occur at the mere act of tossing. Therefore he says: "even as much as a hair's breadth from the head," and so forth.
"And this which" refers to this analysis (*vinicchaya*).

Commentary on the Discourse on the Monastery (Ārāmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā) 102. Regarding the phrase "he seizes the monastery" in the Discourse on the Monastery: this act of seizure is indeed permissible even in the case of land, standing goods, and so forth belonging to others.
However, since in the case of monasteries and other such immovable properties, seizure generally occurs only through the means of legal seizure (abhiyoga), [the term is used here].
In this very passage, the application (*abhiyoga*) is stated; thus, it should be understood that by this method, it can be known in all instances.

"By the application of taking what is not given" refers to the application together with the act. Because the application was made upon the object itself, this *dukkaṭa* offense occurs by way of that concurrent application.
"Himself also" refers to the instigator as well. "What shall I do? What shall I do?"—thus, it is simply a matter of "what-is-to-be-done."
"One who acts as if promising to do so" is a *kiṅkārapaṭissāvī*; the state of being such is *kiṅkārapaṭissāvibhāva*.

In that [state], it is said to be "the state of being under one's own control. *Ukkoca* means a bribe. "An offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) for all" refers to those who administer false judgments and the like.
At the very moment of performing the action—the cause for both parties to relinquish their responsibility—such as [thinking] "this is the owner of the object," etc.

It should be understood that this constitutes a *pārājika* offense. However, if the owner’s doubt and relinquishment of responsibility arise sequentially, then at the moment of consciousness that initiates the effort, it is indeed a *pārājika*, not a *thullaccaya*.
If only doubt arises, then it should be understood that it is only a *thullaccaya*; this principle applies everywhere as appropriate.

It should be accepted. By way of laying down the burden alone, there is defeat; thus, it shows that one who does not lay down the burden, thinking "I am not released," is not called defeated even if he is distressed.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Monastery.
103. In the commentary on the term *vihāra*, "vihāra" refers to the entire monastery, defined as the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*).
"Pariveṇa" refers to a separate area within that monastery, demarcated by walls or other such boundaries. "Āvāsa" refers to a single dwelling place.
Because the property belonging to a group has designated owners, it is possible to have the responsibility for its maintenance relinquished; thus he said:
“However, in the case of a group consisting of Dīghabhāṇakas and others,” it is said. Here too, if even one person does not relinquish his responsibility, he indeed protects [the property].
This same principle applies everywhere regarding the property belonging to many.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning fields.

104. In the commentary on the field (*khetta*), regarding the phrases "having crushed" (*nirumbhitvā*) and so forth, the term "of one who takes" (*gaṇhantassa*) should be construed with each [verb] individually.
Therein, "taking after crushing" means that without cutting off the tip of the rice stalk, one grasps it with the hand exactly as it stands, pulls it, and takes only the amount of seed.
"Each one" (*ekamekaṃ*) refers to a single rice stalk. Regarding the phrase "in whichever seed," etc.
Having restrained [the meaning], it should be applied respectively to the cases of hiding and so forth.

From the statement, "As soon as he has released it from its binding," it follows that when that seed or other object has been freed from its binding—even if it has not yet been removed from that place—there is no absence of the location [of the original offense], and thus it is indeed a *pārājika*.
However, in the case of something such as the head [of a corpse] which has either been sewn together with the inner lining and so forth, or is joined as a single unit, for that...
It should be understood that if one releases [the animal] from its bonds, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; if one releases it from any other place, there is a *pārājika* offense.
Therefore, he said "by means of a rice-stalk," and so forth. "With husks" means together with the straw. "By a stake" means by a wooden post.

In this context, both simultaneous application (*sahapayoga*) and the laying down of the burden (*dhuranikkhepa*) are possible regarding the moving of the stake and so forth. Here, "moving the stake" and so forth refers to simultaneous application.
And when that has been done, if the owners do not relinquish their burden and still desire to take it back up, there is no forfeiture yet; for,

having learned that "such-and-such a royal favorite, a monk, desires to take the field and so forth after shifting the boundary-stake," and based on his strength and his nature of being harsh and so on,
[the matter must be resolved] before the actions such as shifting the boundary-stake have even reached completion.
The owners relinquish their responsibility; there is no theft because the responsibility was relinquished even before the completion of the effort.
However, when the relinquishing of responsibility occurs through the very act of moving the stakes and so forth, only then is there theft.
For this reason, it is said here: "And that is by the relinquishing of responsibility by the owners. [This refers to] the state of having moved the stakes and so forth.
In this case, even the acceptance [of the gift] without knowing [the donor's intention] should be understood as a relinquishment of responsibility.
"Thus in all cases" refers by extension to the aforementioned matter, such as the shifting of a rope and so forth. "The measuring-stick" means a measuring rod.
"If one has buried the wood and intends to take it up with that very same [amount]," then there is a *thullaccaya* when one [end] has not yet come out, and a *pārājika* when it has come out.

If it is at the end of the wood, it is a *pārājika* offense. If he intends to take it by covering the space between his feet with thorny branches and the like there, making it impossible for anyone else to enter, then it is a *pārājika* offense at the final branch; therefore it is said:
"he is able to make it his own by means of the surrounding branches alone," meaning that only after having buried the logs and constructed the surrounding branches does it become his property.
The meaning is "he is able to do. To clarify the very same point already stated as "the boundary of a field," it is said "the embankment of a rice-paddy.

And this inclusion by means of a stake, a path, and so forth, is indeed applicable even to monasteries and the like. Commentary on the Discussion of the Eight Kinds of Sites (Vatthu-aṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā).
105. In the *Vatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, "of three walls" refers to three types of walls made of brick, stone, and wood. 106.
In the *Gāma-aṭṭhakathā*, the phrase "what is called a village" is not stated in the *Pāḷi* because the definition of a village has already been fully explained previously.
Explanation of the *Arañña-aṭṭhakathā*.
107. In the *Araññaṭṭhakathā*, "having pierced straight through" means having pierced directly.

"Of one whose characteristics have been severed" refers to [a tree] for which signs such as marks have been made by those who, having purchased it from the owners of the forest, took possession of it.
By the phrase "covered with bark," he indicates that because the owners have no regard for it, it has been abandoned for a long time; therefore, he says, "it is permissible to take."
If the owners still have a sense of ownership, it is not permissible.

"Those [buildings] are built and inhabited" means that those houses and so forth have been constructed, completed, and are being lived in by people. "Timber" refers to the timber remaining after the construction of the houses and so forth.
"It is permissible to take them" is said because the owners no longer have a claim to them.
If they see him at the time of taking [the goods] and, being attached, stop him, it is certainly not permissible to take them.

When told, "Give [it]," one must indeed give it; thus, for one who has gone after forming the intention, "I will give it," when told, "Give it," there is no offense in departing without giving it if it was not previously asked. Even later, when urged by them, it must indeed be given.
"Having seen it, he goes away, [thinking] 'it is to be given as a gift for the goods'"—for one who has gone with a pure mind, there is no forfeiture of the goods.
Even if one passes through a place of watchfulness with a pure mind, though a thought of theft subsequently arises, there is no theft because the place of watchfulness has already been passed.
However, some say: "Even in the case of timber that has been carried anywhere, since it remains the property of the owners of the forest, [there is no offense]. Again...
Some say that if one goes having generated a thieving mind, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense; however, that is not correct.

This is because the offense is stated to occur precisely upon the transgression of the guarded place—as in the passages, "Having reached the guarded place... [and] he passes beyond through lack of mindfulness," and "He passes beyond that place suddenly," etc.—and because the text specifically refers to the transgression of the guarded place when it says, "But this, with a thieving mind..."
It is stated: "For one who carries it away while moving through the air, there is likewise a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, as for the reason given—that "even when logs have been carried to any location whatsoever, they remain the property of the owners of the forest"—that is not a reason for the commission of a *pārājika* offense outside the place of protection;
rather, it is a reason for the obligation to restore the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*), precisely because they are their property. It is by virtue of being their property...
For even if something is prepared outside [the customs post], it becomes subject to the payment of goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*);
otherwise, there would be no such payment, as in the case of crossing over a customs barrier. Only what is given by travelers becomes the property of the customs officers, not what is not given;
therefore, for one who crosses that place from any source with a pure mind, there is no payment of goods. But here, [it belongs] to the owners of the forest.
Because it belongs to another, it must be restored in every case; for that very reason, this [act] becomes more serious than even a customs checkpoint in the forest.

For if there were theft whenever the thought of stealing arises even outside the place of watch, then the restriction of location expressed by the phrase "having reached the place of watch" and so forth would be rendered meaningless, since the thought of stealing could occur anywhere.
Because it must be said that a *pārājika* offense occurs when [the object] has arisen [in the sense of being moved].
Therefore, one must reach the conclusion here that for one who goes outside the place of protection with a thieving mind, there is no taking away (*avahāra*).

However, regarding the phrase "for one carrying [it] with a thieving mind," this refers to the specific location which, once crossed, means that both the forest and the place of protection have been passed. That location...
The meaning is: "even for one who goes by way of traversing through the air.
108. Regarding the commentary on the Discourse on Water: a large-mouthed water-jar is a *udakamaṇika*; it is also said that "a jar with a rim is a *udakamaṇika*."
They say: "Therein" means in those vessels. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even with living beings," one includes even unallowable earth.
"For the purpose of protecting the pond" means for the sake of guarding the pond so that, when great water comes, it does not break the embankment of the pond.
"Overflowing water" refers here to the excess water [escaping] from one high side of the pond.
“Nibbahana” (a conduit) is so called because one flows out or goes forth by means of it; it refers to a channel for the exit of excess water.
The water flowing therein is called “nibbahana-udaka. A “niddhamana-tumba” is a water-outlet pipe made of bricks and the like for the purpose of growing crops and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “having made the boundary weak,” even if one does not make it weak, in the aforementioned application—
Having set a limit and stepped out [of the field], one must indeed perform the distribution in accordance with the value of the water used.

This is said with reference to whatever extra profit arises from that cause—excluding the labor of sowing seeds, cultivation, and so forth—for they have no duty to perform, nor should they be given a share of this. And this refers to young crops.

It is appropriate for one who destroys standing water; however, when a crop has not yet been produced at all, one who destroys the water must pay only the value of the water, and not the entire value of the crop, because the compensation is due only for the specific article destroyed.
Otherwise, for one who steals goods placed by others for the purpose of trade and so forth, both [the value of the goods and the profit] would be required.
Having taken it, one might have to pay the value of the goods as compensation, yet we hold that this is not appropriate. Regarding the phrase "by the relinquishing of responsibility by the owners":
in this context, if the pond or field belongs to a single person, there is a *pārājika* offense through the relinquishing of responsibility by that very person;
however, if that pond is common to all, or the fields belong individually to each person, then [the offense applies] only to that specific individual.

The offense occurs upon the relinquishing of the burden; furthermore, even if the fields are common to all, it should be understood that the *pārājika* offense applies only when all have relinquished their burden, not when they are absent.
"Not having gone out" means not having departed; the meaning is that [the person] remains right there in the pond. "The opening of the main drain for others" refers to the opening of a small drain.
“Even before it has arrived” means while [the water] has already emerged from the pond and is still standing in the great channel.

“If it has not emerged, what is bound is well-bound” means that as long as it has not emerged from the pond, there is no obligation to pay for goods (bhaṇḍadeyya), because the water is common property to all; this is the intended meaning.
However, once it has emerged, it becomes the private property of the individual; thus he said, “If it has emerged, what is bound is subject to payment for goods. Here...
However, because it was not included in the Minor Schedule (Khuddakamātikā), it was not recognized as theft;
rather, this pair—“if it has not yet left the pond and has not reached the mouth of the channel belonging to others,” and “if it has not emerged, it is well-bound;
if it has emerged, it is bound and must be made good”—was stated for the purpose of applying them respectively to the two alternatives mentioned above. There is none [of this].
Regarding the term *avahāra* (theft): here some say, "There is no theft, but there is an obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*)," but that is not correct.

Regarding the phrase "the object... does not amount [to theft]": the intended meaning here is that because the water in a reservoir is common to all, it does not constitute property belonging to another.
Commentary on the Story of Dantapona (109):
Regarding the story of the tooth-sticks, because they were set aside for the purpose of being taken as much as desired— without being divided,
