with the thought, "Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus enjoy them as they please," since there was no theft from that point onward and they were left unprotected.
And because it is common to all, it is not like other property belonging to the Saṅgha; therefore, even for one who takes it with a thieving mind, there is no act of theft (*avahāra*).
One should connect this with the thought that some elders might say, "Let them eat [it], the novices will bring more later.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding forest trees.
110. In the discourse on the forest-guardian (*vanappati*), the phrase "because it was supported" refers merely to the supporting of a tree that has been cut down and is about to fall;
it does not refer to its having previously stood encircled by creepers such as *marica*.
For even when such a tree is cut, there is no offense of theft, just as in the case of a creeper encircling [a tree] mentioned in the *Araññaka-kathā*. By the words "it stands upright,"...
The unique sense of "dislodging from its place" (*ṭhānācāvana*) shown here is the complete severing [of a tree] such that it is no longer connected by creepers and the like;
it is the releasing [of the tree] from every part touched by space and so forth, unlike the previous case. However, some say:
"Because it remains slightly shaken by the weight of the tree, there is indeed dislodging from its place. That is not correct, because [the shaking occurs] due to the tree's touch.
Because it cannot be exceeded by five or six modes in any part of space.

"He clears the opening for the wind" means that just as the wind, having arrived, fells a tree, so he clears it by cutting away and removing the branches, thickets, and so forth that stand obstructing the path of the wind's arrival.
"Or a frog-thorn" refers to the tip of the tail of a frog.
They call it "standing thorn," and some also call it "uneven fish-thorn.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse on stealing:
in the discourse on stealing, "stealing" refers to that which is being taken away by the owner of the object; and that [object] is worth one *pāda*.

"Pārājika indeed" means that because he did not specifically observe, "I will not take the end," but rather observed it generally, thinking, "I will take this," and thus desired to take even that portion which was merely a part of the cloth, it is stated as a pārājika offense.

"Together with the carrier of the goods" (saha-bhaṇḍahārakaṃ) means accompanied by the carrier of the goods; because the substitution of the letter *sa-* is optional, the word remains as *saha* itself, meaning "together with the carrier of the goods."
"Quarreling with him" means [engaging in a dispute]. "Full of apprehension" means having become fearful due to the thought: "If I approach and take his goods, he might strike me with a weapon.
"Stepping aside to one side" means, out of fear itself, not approaching him but stepping back from the path oneself.
"Threatening" means by means of harsh speech as well as bodily gestures such as brandishing a weapon.
And having intimidated them. "Uninhabited" (*anajjhāvuttha*) means unappropriated. Even goods that one is not intent upon through attachment are called "uninhabited";
thus he said, "It should be given to those who have it brought.

By this, even for those who have previously relinquished their attachment, if a sense of ownership (*sakasaññā*) subsequently arises, that property belongs to them alone, even if they take it by force because of that sense of ownership.
This shows that there is no fault in taking it, as it is the theft of one who does not give it. However, if the owner has doubts—thinking, "It was first relinquished by me;

is this now my property or not?"—it is not permissible to take it by force, because it has reached a state where it must be taken again only through the power of the [owner's] own perception of ownership. "For one who does not give it, there is a *pārājika* offense."

By this statement, it is shown that even if the thief has the perception that the goods belong to him, it is not permissible to fail to give them back as long as the owners still have affection for them.

The phrase "in others" refers to the *Mahāpaccarī* and other such works. By saying "there is no deliberation," he shows that this is the very meaning because there is no rejection [of this view] even in those texts.
Commentary on the Discourse on Deposits (Upanidhikathāvaṇṇanā) 112.

Regarding the discourse on deposits: when an item has been placed in one's own hand for the purpose of safeguarding it, and during times such as a royal upheaval or civil unrest, [one takes it] without having performed another formal act—such as the act of returning it to its secure place—thinking, "I will not take it," and so forth.

“Now I will not give it to him; he will not give it to me now”—even though both have sat down in their respective places and thus relinquished their responsibility, there is no offense of theft (*avahāra*).
However, some here say that because the effort to recover [the goods] has been made, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense;
this is merely their own opinion and should not be accepted as authoritative. For at the time of recovery, his...

There is no intention to steal; however, at the moment the intention to steal arises—thinking, "I will not give this to him now"—there is no bodily or vocal effort that serves as the cause for the owner’s abandonment of responsibility, by which he would incur an offense.
For this offense does not originate from non-action (*akiriyasamutthāna*). The phrase "he is still guarding it while intent on giving" refers to the act of misappropriation (*avahāra*).

It should be understood that in making a false statement such as "I do not take it because it was not said [to me]," there is only a *pācittiya* offense, not a *dukkaṭa*, because in the absence of a thieving mind, there is also an absence of the preliminary effort (*sahapayoga*). Even if one says with the mouth, "I will give it," ... [and so on] ...

up to "it is a *pārājika*," in this case, by which effort is the offense committed? It is certainly not by the first effort, which is the act of returning the goods, because at that time there is no thieving mind.
Nor can it be said that, by means of the preliminary effort of saying "I will give," the effort is permissible even when a thieving intention exists at that time.

It is replied: When one, though repeatedly requested by the owner with the words "Give," does not give, but by some preliminary effort makes known to the owner his own unwillingness to give—and by which [effort] the owner, knowing "This man is procrastinating because he is unwilling to give," relinquishes the burden—[that effort constitutes theft].
There is an offense for him by that very same means of action. For in this case, there is no release through a pretext regarding the goods deposited.
Indeed, even if one shifts the burden onto the owner by using such pretexts as "When was it given to you? or "Where was it given to you?"—because of the desire not to give—it is still an offense.
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: "What are you saying?... Thus, by shifting the burden upon both parties..."
“...is a *pārājika* offense for a bhikkhu. It should be understood that there is an exemption from this rule only in the case of having another person take what belongs to another on one's behalf;
it does not apply in all instances. Regarding the phrase “because it was placed in his own hand”:

here, because the item was given into his own hand by the owner and he stands in the position of a storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), there is no theft even if the item is moved from its place; however, if he takes it with a thieving mind, [it constitutes an offense].
It should be understood that he is not released from the *dukkaṭa* offense.
"The same method applies" means that the *pārājika* offense belongs to the thief at the very moment of lifting [the goods]. Why? Because it is stated that the identifying mark is common to others.
It is appropriate when one takes another thing that is exactly like it; therefore, by way of the identifying mark and the location, it must be something similar to that.

It is appropriate for someone else to take it; the intention is that it is only appropriate for one who takes it after the thief has removed it from the spot he observed and some other similar bowl has been placed there in its stead.
Thus, even if the thief has moved the bowl he observed during the day elsewhere and placed other similar bowls in its place, [the offense applies] to the thief later at night.
It is shown that the arising thought of theft arises by taking as its object another similar bowl placed in a location observed during the day.
"By the track of the footprints" means by the track of the footprints of the thief who goes away after taking the bowl brought out and given by the Elder.
It is logical [to say] that he takes one that is not similar; for [the Elder] had taken one that was not similar.

The intention is as follows: since there is no act of theft at the moment of grasping, the theft is only logically established by the very step taken during the movement with the thought, "Having taken this, I shall go," based on the perception that what has subsequently come into hand-reach is either "that" or "another.
There is no *pārājika* offense; it should be understood that even at the step-by-step stage, there is no *pārājika*, just as in the case of a deposit.
"Village gate" (*gāmadvāra*) is stated by way of showing the initial point for entering the village, since the monastery is established outside the village;
the meaning is "inside the village. "In both cases, there is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) upon taking it out" is stated because the Elder was not the storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*).
For if he had been the storekeeper, everything would have been merely deposited; regarding goods that have been deposited...
Furthermore, even when one takes with a thieving mind, there is no theft for the elder; rather, it is the thief alone who commits the theft.
"For both there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that because the item was the elder's own possession, no theft has occurred on the part of the thief since he received it from its owner;
yet because both took it with an impure mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing for both.
"Because it was taken by command" means because it was taken at the command given by the Elder, such as "Take the bowl and robe.

"He enters the forest; he must be made to proceed step by step" refers to [the case where] the Elder, having set out from the monastery with the instruction, "Take the bowl and robe, let us go to such-and-such a village and wander for alms," [dictates the pace] even on the path to the village and throughout the entire village.
Because it has been delimited by the path, the offense is stated to occur for one who goes by stepping along the footprints even after having stepped off the path.
For indeed, from the boundary of the monastery's outer precinct onwards, as far as the boundary beyond that village, all of this constitutes the precinct for movement under the elder’s authorization;
however, it does not extend further than that. For this very reason, it is said: "If he crosses the boundary, there is a *pārājika* offense."

And it is said: "In the case of exceeding the vicinity of the village, it is a *pārājika* offense. This same principle applies even when sending someone back for the purpose of washing robes and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "without standing or sitting": having entered the monastery, if one stands or sits without setting down the burden on the ground from one's head or other parts of the body, and while resting, a thought of theft arises again once that previous thought of theft has subsided—[this constitutes the offense].
If he goes after having lifted it up, he should be made to pay for its removal. If he sets it down on the ground and then picks it up again and goes, he should be made to pay for its removal.

Why? Because whatever was to be done by the command of the one who gave the order has been completed by that much. [This applies when he says,] "We will go to the interior of the village," without specifying "to such-and-such a village."

When it is stated without qualification, they say that all the village resort areas where one has previously entered for alms even before reaching the vicinity of the monastery are indeed "field" (*khetta*).
"The rest" refers to everything such as setting out on the path, approaching the monastery, and so forth.

"It is exactly like the previous case" means that although it was taken without formal authorization, because it was taken after informing the owner, everything—including the monastery precincts and so forth mentioned below—is indeed "field."
This has been stated. "The same method applies" refers by extension to the method stated in the passage beginning with "having conceived a thought of theft on the way," and so forth.
"Or having made a sign" means when a sign has been made such as, "My robe is soiled; who indeed will dye it and give it back to me?
"In the very same manner as stated" refers to the section concerning going with an elder who has not been instructed, taking his bowl and robe.
In the same manner as previously stated. "On one side" means on one side of the monastery because of its great size, without showing oneself.
"Consuming while having a thieving mind" means that when a thieving mind has arisen, he consumes it by wearing it in the very manner of his lower and upper robes without moving from his place;
however, for one who moves from his place while possessing a thieving mind, there is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) at the head [of the act].
"Placing the burden on the shoulder," as in the case of carrying loads and so forth. "It may be lost in any way whatsoever" means it is lost by fire and so forth, or by someone else;
by this phrase, it should be understood that even the person by whom it was deposited is included.

"Of the other" refers to the thief. Regarding the phrase "for one who takes the other, there is a *pārājika* offense in the case of its removal": here, [the text continues] "having entered, your garment..."

Because he was released from the state of being a deposit by the words "Take it," and because the owner—who was taking the other item—still possessed an attachment to his own cloak, it is stated that "there is an offense of defeat (pārājika) in the case of a withdrawal.
However, if the owner is truly free of attachment, thinking, "Let this belong to me or let something else; what does it matter? I have enough with this," then for the thief...
It should be understood that there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*). "They do not know" means they do not know because they did not hear the words spoken by him.
"The same method applies here" should be understood to mean that even if they know [the truth], if they do not mentally accept it, the same method applies.
"They reject" should be understood to include mental rejection as well. "While the vicinity exists" means...
When there is a place for excrement and urine near the storehouse. Regarding the phrase "when I am dead and the Saṅgha’s lodgings are ruined":
even if only this much is said—"We shall kill him"—it is permissible to open [the door], because it is stated that [the offense] does not apply since he stands on the side of the sick;
for there is no illness greater than death, nor anything more out of bounds. "The door..."
Even when it is said, "Having cut [the cloth], we shall take the requisites," it is indeed permissible to open [the storehouse].
"One must have companions" means that they too, having sought [items] through alms-round and other means, should give whatever little they possess from their own belongings.
"This is the proper conduct" (sāmīcī) refers to this duty for those residing in the storehouse.
Lolamahāthera was dull-witted, deluded, and lived in a state of constant distraction. "By the others" means by the other bhikkhus dwelling in that very same monastery cell.
"Vihāravārika" refers to one appointed for the duty of guarding the monastery; it is the guardian of the cell who takes his turn according to seniority.
"Nivāpa" means food and wages. "When they had gone out to meet the thieves" refers to the thieves.
Having learned of their arrival, [the monks] went ahead even earlier [than the thieves], thinking, "We shall make a noise," and when they went toward the thieves;
likewise, when they followed along the path, thinking, "We shall bring back the goods plundered by the thieves"—the same principle applies.

"Having made a fixed arrangement" means having established a restriction such as, "The rice-gruel and meal from such-and-such a family is for the monastery attendants alone. Two or three ladlefuls of gruel.
"Receiving four or five *salākabhatta* meals"—this is merely an illustration;
whether it be less or more than that, one should understand that the measure is simply receiving enough for oneself and one's attendant.
"Looking after those who are dependent" means having them look after the monastery. "Of one without a companion" means of one who is without a helper.
"Having oneself as one's second" (*attadutiyassa*) means: he has only himself—that is, the body—as his companion and no other; thus he is "one who has himself as his second.
Regarding the phrase "the elucidation of the meaning of both of these," and so forth, it should be understood that by all of this it is shown that the turn of each [individual] need not be reached.

"For the sake of the constant practice" (*pākavattatthāya*) means: for the sake of the practice consisting of the rice gruel and cooked food that must be prepared daily. "They set aside" (*ṭhapenti*).
The donors set it aside. "Having taken that" means having taken that portion being given by the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others.

"It should not be caused to be taken" means that even if there is an extra personal requisite set aside for one who dwells in the open air (*abbhokāsika*), or if there is an attachment toward a portion belonging to the Saṅgha such as robes and so forth, that too must indeed be caused to be taken.
"Twofold" means double what is received by others. "By turn of the fortnight" means by turn of the half-month.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Toll-house (Suṅkaghātakathāvaṇṇanā) 113.

Regarding the discourse on the toll-house: "Toll" (*suṅka*) refers to that place where royal officials strike [those who do not pay] and seize the property of those who fail to give it, even by way of confiscation;
thus the meaning should also be understood in this way. This very meaning has been made clear.

"To do that" and so forth was stated. Regarding the phrase "he steps beyond the second foot": here, having set aside the first foot as the boundary, the offense of *pārājika* occurs the very moment the second foot is lifted.
Even if, after lifting it, one does not place it outside, it is considered as if it were already standing outside;
this should be understood to apply in all instances of stepping across a footprint. Having turned around...

Regarding the statement, "If one places the inner [part] outside, it is a *pārājika* offense," this was said with reference to turning [the cloth] by first lifting the inner part while standing outside, or by lifting them simultaneously.
For as soon as it has been lifted while standing outside, everything has indeed gone outside. However, if he, even while standing outside, first [lifts] the outer fold...

If one places it inside first, and afterwards lifts up the inner part and places it outside, even then, because it has not been separated due to its remaining as a single connected whole, no theft is seen to have occurred.

However, some say: "Since it is stated that 'if it falls to the ground and returns inside again, it is indeed a Pārājika offense,' then even when the outer casing has entered inside, because it was previously situated outside, [there is no offense]."
Some say: "One is released [from the offense], but if the packet is still inside, it is first [an offense]; or later, as soon as it is merely placed outside, it is indeed a *pārājika*.

That is not correct. Since there is no connection with anything else when it has been dropped on the ground outside, it is correct to say that even when it has entered inside, it is indeed a *pārājika*; however, this [other case] is because of its being connected with that.

It does not coincide. Therefore, just as there is no state of being joined together for that which has gone inside the boundary, so too it is understood that the conventional usage [of "joined"] applies only when the external status of both is established; this should be accepted after investigation.
As for those who say that the meaning of *parivattitvā* is *nivattitvā* (having turned back), they have taken the sense of "he places the inner [boundary] outside."
"There is no doubt at all in this regard that it 'becomes' [an offense]. "Tied together" (*ekābaddha*) is said with reference to the binding by means of a rope at the end of a carrying-pole (*kāja*).
It is merely placed at the end of the pole without being tied; as for "an offense of defeat" (*pārājika*):

if the value of the object is one *pāda*, it is indeed an offense of defeat when it is placed outside the end of the pole held externally, because there is an absence of being "tied together" with what is placed inside—this is the intended meaning.
"Leaving it while the vehicle is moving... and so on... "He leaves it" means he leaves it either after having entered the toll-house or without having entered it.
"Standing outside the toll-station" means it stands outside because it has been brought out by means of vehicles and the like.
Some, however, alter the reading to "placed outside" (*bahi ṭhapita*) and explain the meaning as "placed outside even before [reaching] the toll-station"; that is not good.
Even when the vehicle has been stopped after entering the toll station, there is no offense because it is as if it had already departed. However,
if someone who has entered within the toll station realizes it is a "toll station" and, with a thieving mind, turns back by the way he came and goes away,
there is an offense for him as well— provided that they collect the toll from those traveling in that direction.

It is indeed a *pārājika*. "In this instance" refers to the removal [of the child] by means of vehicles and so forth. "Therein" refers to that training rule concerning wool (*eḷakaloma*). 114. Regarding the commentary on the discourse on living beings:
"Entrusted" in the discourse on living beings means that when parents are taking out a loan, [they say], "Until the debt is repaid, this [child] is yours..."

"Let it be near [us]," he said, and it was handed over to the creditors. "There is no theft" means that because the parents have not relinquished their son, and because the son does not belong to the parents, there is no theft.

However, they say that by the statement, "The wealth increases at the place where it has gone," it is shown that the debt of the one who took the son as a hostage includes both the interest and the wealth taken as a hostage.
The phrase "born as a slave" is stated to indicate the superior characteristic; however, one born to a non-slave woman in the womb of a slave woman is also included herein.
"Having been plundered from another country" means having been plundered by royal thieves and others who seize the wealth of other lands.
"He says, 'Live happily'" means he speaks with a thieving mind, desiring to cause [the child] to flee from the presence of his own masters.
However, if one does not intend it thus, but says out of compassion, "Go in peace and live happily," there is no theft;
yet there is a debt (a liability). Regarding the second phrase:
if he will certainly take back the second phrase, the monk incurs a *pārājika* offense at the very moment he says, "Live happily after having fled. For him, there is no offense of *pārājika*.

This shows that even if one does not increase the momentum through speech, one is not released from the *dukkaṭa* offense. Since it is stated, "one should take what is not given, which is reckoned as theft," the act of taking itself is what is expressed;
therefore, according to the manner in which it was stated, one is released [from the offense].
This concludes the commentary on the four-line discussion.

117. Regarding the phrase "the rest not included in the text" in the *Catuppada-kathā*: because the term *pasu* (beast) applies universally, it refers to animals other than those such as elephants mentioned in the text.
*Bhiṅkacchāpa* refers to a young elephant so named because it makes the sound "bhiṅkā bhiṅkā.
*Antovatthumhi* means within an enclosed area. *Bahinagare ṭhitassa* refers to one standing outside an enclosed city.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). However, in the case of an unenclosed city, even for one standing inside the city, the very place where he stands constitutes the "spot" (*ṭhāna*).
"A broken gate" means a gate that has been damaged by himself. Regarding the phrase "one who is lying down," here too the word "binding" (*bandho*) must be supplied and connected;

therefore he said, "two for one who is lying down. Regarding the phrase "he causes to be killed": here, because there is a simultaneous application (*sahapayoga*) for one who removes [the victim] with a mind of theft (*theyyacitta*), [the offense is established].
They say it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the spy (*ocarakakathā*):

in the statement, "By means of a stratagem, one is released from taking what is not given," this was said with reference to the employment of an agent; however, in cases such as making a direct accusation oneself, there is no release even by means of a stratagem.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Custodian (Oṇirakkhakathāvaṇṇanā): In the discourse on the custodian, "oṇī" means brought near (*oṇīta*); the sense is "brought.

A commodity placed in the presence of a custodian is like a deposit (*upanidhi*); it is for the purpose of guarding it by placing it in a secure location, not by leaving it unattended in the place where it was originally set down.
Because that article was placed there for the purpose of being looked at for only a moment, the one who has removed the guard incurs a *pārājika* offense by the mere act of moving it from its place.
Commentary on the Discussion of Conspiracy (*Saṃvidāvahārakathā*):
In the discussion on conspiracy, "having conspired" (*saṃvidhāya*) means having made an agreement. By way of such an order, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

It is stated, "provided that a *pārājika* offense is not possible. For if those commanded by him carry away [the goods] according to the command, they incur a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of the command.

Even in the case of the canonical text which says, "When many have made a plan together and one person steals the goods, there is an offense of *pārājika* for all," the offense for the commanders occurs at the very moment of the command.

It should be understood that it must be taken from the one who is carrying it away. When several monks command one person, saying, “Go and bring it,” the same principle applies to the statement, “In the case of its removal, there is a *pārājika* offense for all of them,” and so forth.

Whether the physical act (*sāhatthika*) belongs to the one who gave the command (*āṇattika*), or the command belongs to the one who performed the physical act, they do not constitute a factor for one another because they occur at different times; thus, they are not factors for each other.

It is so because for one who steals with his own hand, the offense occurs at the moment of moving the object from its place, whereas for one by command, the offense occurs at the very moment of the command; thus, because the times of the offenses differ, they are distinct.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the act of appointment (*saṅketakamma*).

119. Regarding the phrase "in the same manner as stated for the secret agent (*ocāraka*) in the discussion on the act of appointment (*saṅketakamma*)," this refers to the method stated in the passage beginning with "if the goods are inevitably carried away," and so forth.
In the Canon, the expression "before or after that appointment" (*taṃ saṅketaṃ pure vā pacchā vā*) means "before or after that appointment.
The same principle applies to the expression "before or after that sign" (*taṃ nimittaṃ pure vā pacchā vā*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Sign-Making (Nimittakammakathāvaṇṇanā) 120.
In the discussion on sign-making, acts such as scratching the eyes and so forth are minor and temporary;
therefore, it is not possible to steal that property at that very moment. One must take it immediately after the sign-making.
Because it has been undertaken, one is said to "steal" by means of that very sign (*nimitta*).

If this is so, does it not follow that the claim that this is merely a preliminary effort before the meal attains the status of a valid authority? It does not. For the act of making a sign (*nimittakamma*) is not subject to a limitation of time in the same way as the act of making a convention (*saṅketakamma*).
Indeed, the act of making a convention is stated in terms of time, whereas the act of making a sign is stated in terms of action; this alone is the distinction between them.
“Whether he steals that property before or after making that sign, there is no offense for the one who was the original owner”—

this, however, is stated with reference to one who takes it before the making of the sign, as well as to one who, even though the sign has been made, takes it later on his own initiative without having begun the act of stealing.
Commentary on the Discussion of Commands (Āṇattikathāvaṇṇanā) 121. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of non-confusion in the discussion of commands":

because one performing the acts of a convention or the acts of a sign does not merely perform the act of a convention regarding times such as "before the meal," nor only the act of a sign such as "winking an eye," but rather—
In this way, one takes up goods of such color and shape, or even engages in a dispute;
one also issues commands according to a sequence of persons, such as "Tell so-and-so," or "Let him tell another," and so forth.

Therefore, regarding these acts of signaling (*saṅketakamma*) and acts of signs (*nimittakamma*) when commanded according to the time—such as forenoon and so on—according to actions such as scratching the eyes, and according to the sequence of goods and persons:
Confusion arises regarding the absence of convention; for the purpose of removing that [confusion] and attaining non-delusion:

having formed a perception of the sign (nimitta-saññā) by means of what was spoken by the instructor, and having made a sign-perception (*saññā-ñāṇa*) as the basis for such a grasp—namely, grasping it at dawn and so forth, or during the acts of rubbing the eyes and so on—as being endowed with such color, shape, and other qualities, he who instructs [does so]. Thus [he speaks].

"Bhaṇḍaṃ" has been explained. "This principle applies everywhere" means that in all instances where an order is involved—both those mentioned below and those yet to be mentioned—the Vinaya-principle consists in the state of the offenses such as pārājika being established at the very moment of the ordering;

and because, at the moment of the ordering, there is an absence of the instigator’s effort or a mind of theft at the moment the ordered act is brought to completion, [the offense is determined] at the moment of the ordering.
"It is a single offense" is called a "logical argument" (yutti) because it is established through reasoning.
Since it is stated that "there is a thullaccaya for the one who is the root," even though [the gift] was accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, there is only a dukkaṭa for Buddharakkhita and Dhammarakkhita.

But why, in this case, is it said that the teacher incurs a thullaccaya? He says: "Because the great multitude," and so forth. And the "great multitude" refers to Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita.
This was said with intentional reference [to a specific case]. "The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) belongs only to the one who is at the root" means that the wrong-doing belongs to Buddharakkhita.
And this was stated first with reference to the wrong-doing at the moment of the command, for the purpose of showing the absence of a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the one at the root;

it was not, however, stated with reference to the possibility of another wrong-doing arising for Saṅgharakkhita on account of his receiving [the gift], for he did not [act] by a single course of action.

He incurs two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Some, however, say: "Because it is not stated in the Canon as 'of one who is at the root' due to the difference in phrasing, but is stated in general terms as 'if he receives it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' this was said with reference to Saṅgharakkhita’s offense of wrong-doing.
Although that does not accord with the Commentary, it appears to be consistent with the Canon.
For there is no offense in the act of receiving it. By this very principle, it should be understood that in the preceding sections as well, those who receive [the gift] commit a *dukkaṭa*.
Some say: "If one writes on a leaf or on stone and so forth, 'Theft must be committed,' and leaves it there, it is indeed a *pārājika*";
however, that refers to when it is written with such specific restriction as, "The goods are in such-and-such a person's house."
One should investigate whether this is logical, rather than assuming it was written without restriction.

By the phrase "similar to the fruit immediately following the path," it means that just as for noble persons (ariyapuggala), when the fruit immediately following the path arises, the task of cultivation (bhāvanākicca) culminating in the subsiding of defilements is said to be accomplished;
so too, when this volition (cetanā) that accomplishes the purpose arises, the task of commanding (āṇattikicca) is indeed accomplished.

He shows this, and therefore he says: "Therefore, one is defeated at the very moment of the command. The meaning is that one becomes defeated at the very moment of the volition that originates the vocal effort of the command.
The method of commentary on the discussion of the command is finished.
Commentary on the Classification of Offenses (Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā) 122. "In this and that" refers to things such as those situated on the ground or on dry land.

In the Canon, the term "appropriated by another" is used with reference to what is claimed by a person. By these three phrases—"touches," "makes tremble," and "moves from its place"—[the offense is defined].

The fifth factor of theft (*avahāraṅga*) has been stated as being accompanied by prior effort (*pubbapayoga*). Furthermore, the phrase "removes from its place" (*ṭhānā cāveti*) is merely an illustration;
it should be understood that all efforts, such as commanding and so forth, as well as the abandonment of the task (*dhuranikkhepa*), are to be included here.
(125) The term "removal from its place" (*ṭhānācāvana*) is stated here in accordance with the Pāḷi text, since the abandonment of the task is also to be included.
This same method applies everywhere in what follows. For there, by the phrase "not perceiving it as one's own," the fact that it is possessed by another is stated;
by the phrases "not taking it with confidence" and "not for a limited time," the perception that it is possessed by another is stated;

or rather, it should be understood that by these three [phrases], both the fact that it is possessed by another and the perception that it is possessed by another are stated. "Not inhabited" (anajjhāvutthakaṃ).
“Not inhabited by anyone” (*anajjhāvutthaka*) refers to wood, grass, leaves, and so forth in the forest that have not been claimed as “mine” through the act of appropriation.
“Discarded” (*chaḍḍita*) refers to anything whatsoever that was first appropriated and later discarded due to a lack of need. “Severed at the root” (*chinnamūlaka*) means it is lost;
it is severed at the root because the root known as attachment (*ālaya*) has been cut. “Ownerless” (*assāmika*) refers to those things such as the uninhabited and so forth.
Property without an owner is shown by way of three aspects. "Both" means that which is without an owner and that which belongs to oneself.
131. Commentary on the classification of non-offenses:
"Arising in that very same personal existence" means arising as a peta-existence within that very same dead body.
Regarding the statement that "there is nothing at all to be said about a garment caught on trees and the like," this was said with reference to what has not been guarded by people;
however, if it is guarded and protected by men appointed for shrines, sacred trees, and so forth, it is not permissible to take it.
The statement "if only a small amount has been consumed... it is permissible to take" was said with reference to the absence of the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
To eat meat by snatching it away from one who is eating it with a hungry hand is indeed improper, both because it diminishes compassion and because it stems from greed.
For this very reason, those of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsika) do not even stop a dog that is eating food from their own bowl after first scaring it away;
for they regard the non-snatching of food from such creatures as being just as skillful as giving them a gift of food.
It should be understood as exclusively unwholesome; for that very reason, he will say: "And it should not be undertaken out of compassion for others.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion:
When one person is lifting a single heavy load consisting of timber and so forth, [others] say, "Take hold! Lift it up!"
The term "taking by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*) and "by command" (*āṇattika*) is stated with reference to a situation where bodily effort coexists with vocal effort.

However, in a case of theft occurring in the manner, "You take this object; I will take another," what is taken by oneself is indeed "by one's own hand," while what is caused to be taken by another is indeed "by command";
therefore, even if the value of both together reaches five months [of wages], it is so designated.
It does not constitute a *pārājika*; rather, depending on the value of each individual article, there is only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) and so forth. For it has been said:
"The act of commanding (*āṇattika*) is not a factor for the act of doing with one's own hand (*sāhatthika*)," and so on.

Even if one, out of a desire not to give back an article that has been deposited or an article to be paid, evades by saying "I will give, I am giving," or harasses by remaining silent, or by various bodily gestures and such actions—
"He caused another to lay down the burden" means "it arises from action"; thus it is stated.
The method of commentary on the word-analysis is finished.
Commentary on the narrative of the training rule (*vinītavatthu*).
135. Among the *vinītavatthu* passages, "niruttipatha" (the path of language) refers to language itself as the means for grasping various meanings;
thus he says, "in mere conventional expression. "Gone according to his karma" indicates that he has passed from that state of existence as a peta into the state of being dead.
"In heat" (*abbhuṇhe*) indicates that the body possesses warmth due to the proximity of death; thus he says, "in a warm body."
Even when it has reached the state of a corpse, it is indeed "broken" because of its being broken from its fresh state. "A dissimilar body" refers to a woman's body.
The phrase beginning with "on the head," etc., is stated with reference to the arising of a mental transformation in a place below the neck and above the knees;
for one who does not touch it anywhere, it is well done. For even a dead body, in whatever manner...
They say that for one who intentionally makes physical contact, there is only the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for touching what is not a forbidden part; this is indeed correct.

For the *dukkaṭa* incurred even when the object belongs to the category of an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)—namely, in the case of a woman’s form such as her mind and so forth—does not cease to apply when the object is the body of a woman who constitutes the basis for an offense of defeat.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding the basis of crossing a thicket of *kuśa* grass.
138. "By force" means by strength. The phrase "it will be a cloth; I shall take it" is stated by way of showing a prior mental projection that arose before the actual grasping of the bundle.
However, at the moment of grasping, the intended meaning here should be understood as:
"If it is a cloth, I shall take it," and thus he takes the bundle; it does not mean that he first draws it out from outside.
Thinking, "I shall take it once I have recognized its state as a garment," he therefore said, "It is an offense of defeat (pārājika) at the very moment of lifting.

Otherwise, even for one who takes it while thinking, "I will not take it now; I will take it later when darkness has fallen or when it is time to discern it," or "While looking at it now, I am making it come into my hand"—for such a person too, there would be an act of theft at the moment of taking; and that is not logical.

Because at that time there is an absence of the final determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*) regarding the seizing. For it is only through the volition of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*)—just as in the case of unwholesome acts like the taking of life—that [the offense is established].

Indeed, for one who seizes a living being with the thought, "I will kill him later," there is no taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*) even when that being has died, because the volition to kill has not yet been put into practice.
Likewise here, in the case of one who thinks, "I will steal when the sun has set," and so forth...
Even if one is moved from the place by means of a determination regarding time, there is still no theft at that moment, just as in the case of a determination regarding space.

However, when the time arrives at that determined place, if one goes away with a thieving mind without having set down the goods on the ground, it appears that there is theft by way of the steps taken.
Therefore, there is the determination of goods, the determination of space, and the determination of time.

All three types of hypothetical cases (parikappa) should be understood. However, it is our view that the *Aṭṭhakathā* does not mention the hypothetical case of time separately after having combined it with the hypothetical case of place;
this should be investigated and accepted accordingly.
"He should be made to act word by word" is said because he was tested without being allowed to set [the foot] down on the ground. "Possessed" (pariyuṭṭhita) means "obsessed" (anubaddha).

"The hypothetical assumption (parikappa) is seen" means that at the moment of seizing, the hypothetical assumption is seen; it shows that, according to their opinion, there is no act of theft (*avahāra*) at that time.

"Because it was taken after having been seen, the hypothetical assumption is not seen as an act of theft" means that later, having examined it outside and recognized it as being a garment, it was subsequently taken with a thieving mind;
therefore, because the hypothetical assumption made previously is not a constituent part of the theft, [it is not considered an act of theft].
If one were to know, "This is a *sutta*," then taking it would indeed constitute theft (*theyyāvahāra*). Therefore, the designation "tentative taking" (*parikappāvahāra*) is not seen [in this case].

Because a hypothetical assumption such as "If it will be a cloth (*sāṭaka*)" is not present at that time, it is merely "taking" (*avahāra*) alone, and not "tentative taking"—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, regarding the "tentative taking of goods" (*bhaṇḍaparikappāvahāra*), [the text says]: "If it will be a cloth..."
By saying, "I shall take it," he shows that the action occurs at the very moment there is no formal determination regarding the goods. Therefore, he said:
"Whatever is merely imagined—that which is unseen—is theft for one who takes it while remaining fixed in that state of imagination.
If this is so, why is it that the "theft by opportunity" belongs to one who steals after seeing the goods, whereas the "theft by imagination" would belong to one [who acts] otherwise?
This is not a fault, because that mental construction (*parikappa*) has as its object an item that has not yet been seen;
for it is said that the "mental construction of space" refers only to an item already known from having been seen previously.

Although the Sutta statement, "Thinking it was that, he took it away," is expressed with reference to one who takes it while determining "this is that very same thing," nevertheless, in this case where [the thought] occurs thus, "I shall take that"— (End of excerpt)
Even in the case of a preliminary plan (*parikappa*), because there is a certainty regarding the act of taking with the thought "I shall take," it establishes the meaning of theft;
thus it was extracted [from the text], and for that very reason it is said, "it coincides.

"Some" refers to certain teachers within the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself. By the passage beginning with "In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however," he shows that the view of "some" is to be disparaged, and that the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* alone is more appropriate.
“Ornaments and trinkets” refers to finger-rings and the like. “Having dropped the *kusa* grass” means having dropped a marker made of reed or made of palm leaves and so forth.
Even when the *kusa* grass has been removed from the other side of the enclosure, the exchange of the *kusa* grass has not yet occurred;
thus it is said, “he protects it during the removal. By the statement “it is a *pārājika* offense as soon as it is released from the hand,” this indicates the displacement from its original place.
This shows that "stepping on the straw" (*kusasaṅkāmana*) is a distinct offense (*avahāra*) apart from "abandoning the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa*).

For it should be understood that all offenses of theft, when being accomplished through the methods of acting by one's own hand, commanding another, or intending [the act], converge in meaning within these three:
causing displacement from the place, abandoning the burden, and stepping on the straw. The other [offender] takes away his portion; in the taking away, there is a *pārājika* offense.
It was stated [in the previous case] because of the non-disappearance of attachment (*ālaya*) toward one's own portion; however, when there is no attachment whatsoever, there is no theft.
Therefore, he said: "Even for one who takes what remains after having searched, there is no theft at all.

Regarding the phrase "even though knowing, 'This is not mine,'" the word "even" (*pi*) includes one who, while being in doubt about it, nevertheless takes it with a thieving mind. "Siveyyaka" means produced in the kingdom of Sivi.

"Having had it made allowable" means having had it cooked. Regarding "in that case there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)," it should be understood that because there is an absence of the act of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), even though there is a concurrent effort, a wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is not mentioned. "By those who have been authorized" means by those authorized by one who has been formally appointed.

"By one who has been authorized" means by one authorized by the owners. "Property to be given" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) does not constitute an offense of defeat (*parājika*) because it was given by those who were formally appointed and so forth; it is not [actually] existing.
However, because it was taken after specifying a person, it is called "bhaṇḍadeyya" (a fine to be paid for the object).
"Given by another" means given by someone other than the four [officials] beginning with the one formally appointed. "Taking" means taking after saying, "Give another's share.
"Of another" means either without pointing out a specific person, saying "Give another's share," or by counting false years.

When one takes [an item] from the property of a householder, there is no obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) even if it is given by the owner or by someone authorized by him with the command, "Give this to him";
however, when it is from the property of the Saṅgha, there is such an obligation. To show this distinction, the phrase "by one who is not authorized or not commanded," and so forth, is stated again.
"Being given by the others" means being given by one who is authorized or by one who is commanded. Thus...
"Taking" means taking by saying, "Give me another portion as well," or by counting false years. Regarding the phrase "but by the owner":

here the word *pana* indicates a distinction; thus, it is meant that there is a distinction when the owner himself gives or causes [the gift] to be given to one who takes either by saying, "Give me another portion as well," or by counting false years.
The intention is that what is given by Sudinna does not constitute "bhaṇḍadeyya" (the price for stolen goods).

However, in the previous case, when one takes the property of a householder being given by the owner or by one authorized by him, saying, "Give another person's share," it becomes "bhaṇḍadeyya" because there is no other [share] for the second person; thus it remains the property of the owner. But here, when it is being given by those very people themselves, [saying] "another... [the distinction applies].

It is said that for one who takes [an object] after saying "Give me a share" or after counting false years, since it was said "Give," there is no forfeiture of goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*)—setting aside the mere act of requesting from a stranger—but rather it is considered "well-given.
However, they say that for one who takes goods given by someone acting under the command of one who is not the owner, there is indeed forfeiture of goods;
yet in this case, as in the case of the fourfold bowl, only the status of theft (*avahāratā*) is appropriate.

However, in the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha, even if one says, "Give it," since there is no individual owner, it should be understood that the obligation to pay the value of the goods (bhaṇḍadeyya) applies even when it has been given by one authorized [to do so].

Regarding those who cause the goods to be brought back, the phrase "the obligation to pay the value of the goods" is used because of the statement, "he is satisfied when it is taken"; this refers to one who is not satisfied [with the initial decision].
It is stated that even if something belonging to others has been taken, it must be returned. Because of the statement, "It should be distributed among those who are present," one says:
"It is permissible for one standing within the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā) alone to take the goods to be shared," since the goods to be distributed reach only as far as the precinct boundary.
Regarding the term *bhaṇḍadeyya* (goods to be given): even if both [the thief and the owner] have a claim to them, they are not given to the thief, but only to the owner.

It must be given even by a thief, because it is to be given back to the owner. "In this same manner" means that when an object is taken with the perception that it is a refuse-rag (*paṃsukūla*), it is a debt to be repaid;

however, if it is taken with a thieving mind, it is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*). "While they were departing" means while they were fleeing after abandoning the village. "Without distinction" means without referring to specific qualifications such as whether there was an intention [to steal] or not.
In general. The mere fact that it is accompanied by breath is the criterion for its being an offense, because the owners have relinquished their ownership.

"From that" means from what belongs to the community (*gaṇa*) and so forth. "He gives for the sake of supporting a family" means he takes it under the impression that it is a discarded rag (*paṃsukūla*) or a trust deposit (*vissāsika*) and then gives it;

in that case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and the obligation to pay the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) on account of supporting a family. However, if there is a mind of theft (*theyyacitta*), even when giving for the sake of supporting a family...

Even for one who accepts it, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense. In cases involving less than five *māsaka* coins and so forth, there are *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses together with the *dukkaṭa* for corrupting families.
The phrase "designated for the purpose of lodging" is stated for the purpose of showing that there is a *thullaccaya* for one who gives [the property] out of a sense of ownership (*issaravatā*).
Even if it was given for other requisites, if one—without a mind of theft—out of a sense of ownership or for the sake of supporting the family, [gives it] to relatives and so forth...
If one gives [it away], there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and it remains an object that must be restored.
"By way of lordship" means: thinking, "Who can stop me from giving? I alone am the authority here," thus acting out of one's own sense of power.

An offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) occurs for one who gives—whether for the sake of supporting a family or for some other reason—a heavy object designated for the purpose of a dwelling, because such an object is of great value.

And "to be given as a bribe" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Regarding "the penalty" (*gīvā*): here it should be understood that in the case of a [piece of land] designated for the purpose of a dwelling, the penalty is together with a *thullaccaya*; in the other case, it is together with a *dukkaṭa*.

"Eaten right up" (*sukhāditameva*) is said because, having stood within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*), they divided it, made it their own property, and ate it. For that which belongs to the Saṅgha is connected to the monastery and is subject to distribution (*vebhaggiya*).
150. Goods situated outside the secondary boundary (*upacārasīma*) must be divided only by monks situated inside the secondary boundary;
it is not to be divided by those standing outside the secondary boundary.

Regarding the phrase "I exclude what has been spoken": this refers to the charging of a monk who has already spoken with a fault such as a *pārājika* offense that arises after he has been told, "Exclude [what has been spoken]."
Or [it is so called] because of attributing a fault to householders by saying, "The venerable ones speak without making a distinction.
153–5. *Chātajjhattaṃ*: by that hunger, by the fire of the stomach, it is heated; the meaning is that it is scorched or oppressed.
*Dhanukaṃ*: a small bow-shaped stick for hanging things on. *Maddanto gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ*: he goes along crushing [the crops]; "bhaṇḍadeyya" means... [text fragment].
In this case, a single valuable object, such as a pig’s snout, should be given; for when there is a single bond, others do not become attached to it.
“Adūhala” means a mechanical stone, by which deer, being overwhelmed, are unable to escape.
“It goes afterwards” means that instead of going by means of the effort made [by others], it goes of its own accord afterwards. Even in the cases mentioned below, it is the same in such instances.
The same method applies here. "Having requested protection" means having gone to the presence of the king's men and requested protection for no specific purpose.
"The mouth of the fish-trap" means the opening through which the fish enter into the trap.
"Of the elders" refers to the visiting elders (*āgantuka-thera*). "Of them too" refers to the resident monks (*āvāsika-bhikkhu*) as well. "For the sake of use" means...
Having performed the procedure to be done for the Saṅgha, it is for the purpose of using [the property]. The word "in the taking" (*gahaṇe*) should be understood as a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*).
"Where" (*yattha*) means in whichever monastery. "Of others" (*aññesaṃ*) means of other guests.

Even among those guests, they are not independent because it has been given by donors or by monks specifically designated for the sake of robes to those who dwell continuously in the lodgings; therefore, it must be distributed.
They have no authority to eat [the fruit]. Even those who are guests, wishing to enter that monastery during the rainy season retreat or other times, must take [fruit] for the sake of robes.

They should abide by an agreement, such as: "We shall divide and consume the fruits from so many trees, while we shall maintain the dwellings with the fruits from the others. Thus, without dividing all the various fruits, they should agree:
"We will divide and enjoy the fruits from these many trees, and we will attend to the lodgings with the fruits from the others."

Or, [the agreement] should be observed by incoming monks regarding the established agreement of resident monks who are properly providing [resources], thinking, "We shall procure requisites such as almsfood," or "We shall set aside even a small portion and offer it solely for the sake of the four requisites.
This very meaning is indicated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* by the word "not independent" (*anissarā*), and in the *Mahāpaccarī* by the passage beginning with "of the four requisites," and so forth.
It has been shown by way of detailed exposition. Regarding the phrase "by way of use alone" (*paribhogavaseneva*), the particle *eva* here is used out of its proper place;
it should be construed as: "having divided that very [offering] by way of use. "In this" (*ettha*) means in this monastery or in this kingdom.
"Requisites for lodgings" (*senāsanapaccaya*) refers both to the lodging itself and to what has been set aside and designated for its purpose. This includes one or two excellent lodgings.
"Setting aside" means that, in order to show the same point again by way of contrast, it is said:
"But having cut off the root of the basis, one should not bring them forward.
The meaning is: having cut off the root of the basis consisting of the lodgings, all the lodgings should not be relinquished. However, some here [interpret] "one or two excellent lodgings..."
They say that this point was stated [in the commentary]: "Even by those distributing [the goods] starting from the lowest quality, the dwelling sites themselves must not be distributed.
This is indeed appropriate, because this meaning must necessarily be stated;
otherwise, some might think that even the actual physical sites should be distributed.
"Having posted a notice" means having posted a notice stating: "Having protected so many trees, so much [wood] must be taken from them.
"Having made a sign" means having established a convention. "Children" refers to anyone who guards them, such as their sons, grandsons, and so forth;
all of these are here called "children. "From there" means from the aforementioned collection of timber. "Having asked permission" means [having asked] the community of workers.
"Having asked for permission. "Having brought all of that" means having brought it back temporarily even without asking permission.

"This very bhikkhu is the owner," etc.: because he had it built from the beginning using timber and other materials belonging to himself, and because he looked after it and shared in the use of the Saṅgha’s dwelling, this very person is the owner; and it is stated that he should not be evicted from there.
"Water-worship" refers to worship such as sprinkling water on the courtyard of a cetiya. "By way of duty" means solely out of faith, not for the sake of wages or other benefits.
"With its foundation" means together with the ground. "Wall" refers to the wall of a house. "Rampart" refers to a surrounding enclosure wall. "From there" means from the abandoned monastery.
"Having brought [materials] from there, a dwelling was made" refers to the monks residing in the neighboring villages.
Having brought timber and other materials from an abandoned monastery, a dwelling place was constructed.
Regarding the statement, “He uses it for his own personal enjoyment,” it is said, “He does not give it to those who arrive as seniors,” in order to clarify that very meaning.
“Mixed with a fourth part of water” means mixed with one-fourth [of its volume] of water.

In the Pāḷi, it is stated: “There is no offense, monks, for one who has committed a pārājika,” because [the goods] were given into Thullanandā’s hand specifically for her by the owners, and because she used them with a mind free from theft.

Even if she had used them with a mind of theft, there would still have been only the obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*), because they stood in the place of goods deposited as a pledge. Regarding the case of the shared rice-pot: “another’s...”
Regarding the story of his arrival with the words, "Give me my share":
by the phrase "out of compassion for that family" and "for the sake of preserving their faith," etc., it shows that he did not do so for the purpose of gathering the family to himself.
[He set] a prior time limit, saying, "As long as the children ascend the palace, let the palace remain within their reach. 159.
Because it was established by means of a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it remains there only for the duration of the time-limit set;
thereafter, the palace goes back to its original place of its own accord. And that departure occurs as if produced by the withdrawal of the supernormal power (*iddhi*);

thus it is said, "The Elder withdrew his supernormal power. For when one acts in this way through the knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), there is no physical or vocal exertion.
There was no intention to steal because the palace itself had already been searched; therefore, it should be understood that the Elder acted thus thinking, "In this case, there is no taking away.

Alternatively, just as one might lure away hogs and other animals bound in a snare by showing them bait after bringing them into a palace out of compassion for the children, so too [was it with] the children brought in for execution.

Even when climbing onto a palace and subsequently withdrawing [the intent], there is no offense here because the intention was one of compassion; furthermore, it does not constitute "goods to be returned" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) due to the absence of physical or verbal application. For only when physical or verbal application exists is there an offense or "goods to be returned.
Therefore, the Blessed One did not say, "There is no offense, monks, for one whose mind is not thieving," but rather: "There is no offense..."

“Monks, for one possessing psychic power, there is no offense within the domain of psychic power. This much he said. Regarding the phrase “within the domain of psychic power,” the intended meaning should be understood as follows:

there is no such thing as an offense in the domain of a psychic consciousness that is purely mental-door-based, which does not originate from bodily or vocal exertion (such as taking another’s property), and which consists solely of a mind free from theft.
However, what is prohibited? It is improper to perform a miracle of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*). Such is the objection.
Having intended this, he said: "There is no offense for such a resolution-iddhi.
For by this very sutta, "There is no offense, monks, for one possessing iddhi within the domain of iddhi," it is established that resolution-iddhi (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is not prohibited.
[This refers to] the manifestation of elephants and so forth externally without abandoning one's own natural form, as in: "Being one, he becomes many."
That which is described as having arrived "because it is accomplished by way of resolution" is called *adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*.
That power (*iddhi*) described thus—"having abandoned his natural form, he displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga... [and so on]...
he displays even various military arrays"—is called *vikubbaṇā-iddhi*, because it proceeds by way of transformation through the abandoning of one's natural form. But of oneself...
Having established one's natural form according to its own nature, the external manifestation of elephants and so forth is not called "transformation power" (*vikubbaniddhi*);
rather, it should be understood that transformation power is the creation of one's own form itself in the shape of an elephant or other such forms.
"By one who has conquered the defilements" means by one who has won over the defilements; the meaning is "one who is free from defilements. "Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*). By that...

The construction is as follows: there exists no other training rule (*sikkhāpada*) equal to the second *pārājika* training rule that is interwoven with many methods and provides a determination of its profound meaning. In this context, "meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), while "determination" (*vinicchaya*) refers to the determination independent of the canonical text;

that which possesses these two profound aspects is "that which provides a determination of profound meaning. "When immersed in the subject matter" (*vatthumhi otiṇṇe*) means by way of an accusation (*codanā*).
Or, it refers to when one has fallen into the matter of taking what is not given in the midst of the Saṅgha, either by oneself confessing one's own transgression or by another doing so.
"In this" means in the matter of having fallen [into an offense]. "Determination" means the defining of what constitutes an offense and what does not.
"Even in the case of a permissible matter" means even in the property belonging to one's mother, father, or others, which is suitable for one to take for oneself.
Thus ends the method of commentary on the second *pārājika* in the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the Vinaya, known as the *Samantapāsādikā*. 3.
The third *pārājika*.
"By three" means by way of the doors of body, speech, and mind.
162. Regarding this first explanation of the source [of the narrative]:
"Now, that which was previously described as 'at the time of a Buddha and at the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch, it was a city,' and so forth..."
It has been stated that Rājagaha attained its full development only upon the arising of a Buddha;
to show that this is the same in the present case as well, it is said, "And this city too. By this, he shows that it is not only Rājagaha and other such cities [that have developed].

The passage beginning with "Named Mahāvana" and so forth is stated according to the opinion of the Majjhima-bhāṇakas and Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas; however, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas [state] "together with the Himalayas..."
They say it is "a great forest standing as a single, solid mass. "Covered by a circle of swans" means concealed by a circle of swans;

the meaning is that it has the shape of a flock of swans. "A discourse for the purpose of turning away from the body" is a discourse for the arising of dispassion toward the body born of karma (*karaja-kāya*).
"Desire" (*chanda*) is weak lust; "lust" (*rāga*) is strong lust. "Hair of the head, hair of the body, and so forth"—this refers to the matter stated in brief.
In order to show this by way of analysis, the passage beginning with "Those who... and so forth was stated.

Regarding the phrase "by way of fivefold divisions": since there are five divisions for each of these synonyms, it is called "fivefold division" (*pañcapañcappabheda*); thus, by means of this "fivefold division," the specific nature of the synonyms should be understood according to the external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*).

"Regarding 'the foul' (asubhāya)": this refers to the matrix of the foul (asubha-mātikā). Since the feminine gender is used in the genitive case in view of the matrix that is to be described, he says, "having set forth the matrix," and so on.
"Analyzing that" means analyzing the matrix. "The performance of the task" (phātikamma) means the bringing about of the result.
"Abandoning five factors": this is the state of having abandoned five factors by way of the departure from the five hindrances, such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), and so forth.
The possession of five factors should be understood by way of the arising of the jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth when absorption (*appanā*) is reached.
Regarding the phrase "excellent in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics," here the excellence in three ways refers to the beginning, middle, and end of the jhāna;
and the possession of ten characteristics refers to the characteristics of those same beginning, middle, and end.

And these [qualities] should be understood. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "By the very exposition of the ten characteristics, the threefold excellence—which is the support for that [jhāna]—also becomes manifest; therefore, 'In this regard, these... and so forth is stated.
Regarding that, "this is the *pāḷi*" means that this is the *pāḷi* concerning the subject matter of the exposition of the ten characteristics. "Purification of the way" (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*)...
The purification of jhāna from hindrances such as the nivaranas occurs through the preliminary practice leading up to the stage of the lineage-determining state (gotrabhū).
Since this purification is primarily established by previous causes and also serves as a condition for the intensification of equanimity (upekkhā) and so forth, it is therefore said:
"Purification of the way is first. The phrase "intensification of equanimity" is used because there is no longer any need for things such as further purification.
Therein, "intensification of equanimity" refers to the intensification [of the mind] through the accomplishment of the function of neutral equanimity (*majjhattupekkhā*).

However, although that [equanimity] is manifested simultaneously with the purification of the impediments, it is stated as "intensification of equanimity in the middle" for the purpose of showing that it is accomplished precisely by means of that purification.

"Gladdening" (*sampahaṃsanā*) is the cleansing [of the mind] by way of the accomplishment of the function of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) which effects the non-transgression of the basis, the phenomena, and so forth.
Since that [encouragement] is indeed established only through the accomplishment of every duty that ought to be done, it is therefore said:

"Encouragement is the conclusion. And although these three excellences are obtained at a single moment, they are described in terms of beginning, middle, and end in order to show that they proceed by way of the relationship between cause and effect;
however, this does not refer to the three moments of the arising, presence, and dissolution of the jhāna.

It should be understood that [the practitioner] obtains it in due order. Regarding the phrases "he enters upon the middle sign of concentration" and so forth, the "middle sign of concentration" refers precisely to the absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) proceeding in even balance.

For that is "middle" because it does not fall into either of the two extremes known as laxity (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*); and it is so called because it places the mind with particular distinction upon a single object.
Concentration itself is called the "sign of concentration" (samādhinimitta) because it is the cause of further distinctions;

the meaning is that one enters upon it or acquires it. Because one has entered thus by means of the middle sign of concentration, one leaps forward and becomes established there in the single-pointed object that is the domain of absorption (appanā).
Furthermore, since that mind, being thus purified, has nothing further to be purified, [it remains stable].
A person who does not exert effort in purification is said to "look on with equanimity" at the purified mind.

Likewise, one who has entered into serenity (*samatha*) through the attainment of its state, and no longer exerts effort toward further concentration, looks on with equanimity at that which has entered into serenity;
for, having thus abandoned association with the defilements due to the state of having entered into serenity, it remains established in unity. Furthermore...
One who does not exert effort toward the manifestation of unity is said to "look on with equanimity" at the manifestation of unity.

Regarding the phrases "born therein," and so forth: those pairs-of-coupled states (yuganaddha-dhammā) consisting of concentration and wisdom that are born in that jhāna-consciousness when it has been thus nourished by equanimity—their encouragement, purification, and cleansing by way of their nature of not overstepping one another—[is what is meant].
And there is encouragement by way of the single flavor of liberation, because the faculties such as faith are liberated from the defilements;

and there is encouragement by way of the carrying and the proceeding of that energy which is "conducive" (tadupaga)—meaning it is suitable for those states that possess the single flavor of non-transgression—and of that "conducive energy" itself. At that moment, [there is encouragement] of the aforementioned states...
It should be understood that both encouragement in the sense of cultivation and purification are accomplished precisely through the fulfillment of the function of purifying knowledge.
Thus, the phrases "the mind has reached a state of threefoldness" and so forth are words of praise for that very mind.
"Endowed with applied thought" means having attained excellence by way of the factor of applied thought (*vitakka*). "The mind is endowed with resolution" means...
That which is endowed with concentration—defined as the uninterrupted flow of the mind upon that very same object—is stated here by way of the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga).
However, it should be understood that the phrase "endowed with concentration" (samādhisampanna) is stated by way of the faculties (indriya).
"Contracts" (paṭikuṭati) means it shrinks back. "Recoils" (paṭivaṭṭati) means it turns back. "A piece of sinew" (nhārudaddula) means a fragment of sinew.
“Payuttavācan” means one whose speech is intent upon the search for requisites. “Daṇḍavāgurāhī” means by means of snares (vāgurā) consisting of long nets attached to sticks.

“Samaṇakuttako” means one who performs the duties of a recluse, such as wearing the saffron robes and so forth. Regarding “Vaggumudā,” although it should be called “Vaggumatā” here— [the rest of the passage follows].
Showing that worldly people spoke [of it] as "joy," he said, "regarded as delightful" (*vaggumatā*).
"Regarded as delightful" means it is considered pure; therefore he said, "regarded as merit" (*puññasammatā*). It is regarded as merit because it purifies and leads beings to the goal.
163. *Māradheyya* is Māra’s domain, his place, or his dwelling; in its essential meaning, it refers to the phenomena of the three planes of existence.
In this context, however, the five strands of sensual pleasure are intended; that is the realm of Māra.
Thinking, "Will this mere sham ascetic be able to transcend it by means of adopting the state of an ascetic based on whatever root of spiritual urgency has arisen? he spoke thus.

But he did not say, "He will be able to transcend it through the attainment of Arahantship, by way of non-relinking in the three realms of existence," for [he thought] only of beings [passing away] through death.
Because the deity was the one who had obtained the attainment of liberation from *saṃsāra*. For there is no rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) anywhere for those who are dead.
In this sense, it must be exactly so; by this meaning of depriving others of life, it must be exactly so in its nature as liberation from *saṃsāra*.
"They deprive themselves of life, and they also deprive one another of life."
Because it was so stated, it should be understood that the statement "he deprived all those five hundred bhikkhus of life" was made by way of the majority.
Therefore, setting aside those ordinary (puthujjana) bhikkhus who themselves deprived themselves and one another of life,
as well as the remaining ordinary bhikkhus, this [refers to] depriving all the noble ones (ariya) of life.
"It was lost" is how it should be understood.
164. "From solitude" means from seclusion. "They received the recitation and the interrogation" means they received them in the presence of their respective teachers;
and having received them, they waited upon the Blessed One together with their teachers. But at that time...
The givers of the recitation and so forth approached the Blessed One with the bhikkhus who had become emaciated; it was with reference to them that the Blessed One asked.

[This concludes] the commentary on the discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatisamādhi). 165. Although mindfulness of breathing is included among the ten recollections (dasānussati), it is mentioned here to show that it is suitable for many bhikkhus at that time.

They are included once again because the Blessed One taught them to those [beings]. The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is similar to the meditation subject on foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*);
however, the four formless attainments (*āruppa*) are unsuitable for beginners, and thus their omission here should be understood accordingly.
"Another method" means another means for the attainment of Arahatship. "The sequence of meaning and application" refers to both the meaning (*attha*) and the sequence of application (*yojanākkama*).
"By way of inhalation" means taking the inhalation as the object; this is what is meant.

"Establishment is mindfulness" means the act of standing by, having approached that very inhalation and exhalation through non-forgetfulness; the meaning is that the quality of standing in such a manner is called mindfulness.
Now, wishing to describe the person by way of mindfulness itself, it is said: "He who inhales," and so forth. Therein, "he who inhales":
The meaning should be understood as: "his mindfulness, having approached the breath, stands [there]," and so forth.
"Born of unskillfulness" means born of ignorance (*avijjā*). "In an instant" means in the very moment of its own occurrence.

This concentration, which serves as the foundation for the Noble Path, is said to have "reached the growth of the Noble Path" because it gradually increases until it effectively becomes the Noble Path itself.
“An illustration by way of a simile” (*opammanidassana*): here, the simile itself is the *opamma*, and this is its demonstration.
Non-Buddhists who know mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) know only the first four modes, not all sixteen;

therefore, [the author] says “all modes,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “thus his lodging”: here, “thus” (*evaṃ*) refers to the manner already described for the mindfulness of development (*bhāvanāsati*).
