The meaning is that mindfulness alone binds the mind to the object, not its absence; by this, he shows that for one who is muddled in mindfulness, dwelling in the forest is useless and unsuitable.

"The remaining seven kinds of lodgings" refers to what is stated thus: "a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, and a heap of straw. [These are] conducive to the three seasons and conducive to one's temperament and conduct.

He points out that [this posture] is conducive to the three seasonal periods beginning with summer, the three elements beginning with phlegm, and the three types of temperament beginning with delusion;
that firmness is achieved through sitting cross-legged; that the movement of the inhalations and exhalations is made comfortable by keeping the upper body erect;
and that the means for grasping the object is indicated by fixing mindfulness directly in front.

"Na paṇamantī" means they do not bow down. "Pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ" means having established mindfulness—which is grasped in every way and characterized as an escape because it is the opposite of forgetfulness—as the highest mindfulness and circumspection; this is the meaning.
"Satova" means being indeed endowed with mindfulness. "By thirty-two modes" refers to the long, short, and so forth, as presented in the four tetrads.
By means of the thirty-two aspects spoken of by dividing the sixteen bases into two—namely, inhalation and exhalation. "By way of long inhalation" means by way of a long inhalation;
this is a designation made by eliding the case-ending (*vibhatti-lopa*). Alternatively, it refers to the inhalation spoken of by the Blessed One as "long.
"One-pointedness of mind" is called "non-distraction" because it is the opposite of distraction.

"Of one who understands the one-pointedness of the mind. "By way of inhalation while contemplating relinquishment" means being one who contemplates relinquishment by way of inhalation; or there is the reading "by way of inhalation while contemplating relinquishment," the meaning of which is "by way of the inhalation of one who contemplates relinquishment.
Inhalation (*assāsa*) is the initial outward movement of the breath, whereas exhalation (*passāsa*) is the subsequent inward movement.
"He says 'out-breath' (passāsa) [meaning] out-breathing," and "in-breath" (assāsa) [meaning] the air going outwards, and so forth.

However, in the commentaries on the Suttas, it is stated in reverse order by way of drawing [the breath] in: "In-breath (assāsa) is the breathing inwards; out-breath (passāsa) is the breathing outwards.
Therein—referring to the air going outwards and entering inwards—the internal air goes out first.

This is the connection. Some say: "By the passage beginning 'for all those lying in the womb,' it is shown that one should understand the breath-in (assāsa) as the wind exiting outward according to the sequence of the child's movements. And here, the method of the Sutta itself [shows this]:
"For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the breath-in, both body and mind become agitated by a mind that has fallen into internal distraction."

It should be understood that this accords with the following passage: "For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the inhalations and exhalations, both the body and the mind become agitated, excited, and trembling due to the mind being distracted externally.
"By way of duration" means by way of the duration of time. For this word *addhāna* refers to both time and place.
And it is also the designator [of time]. Therein, by means of the phrase "Just as," etc., the periods of time are shown by way of similes.

Now, in order to clarify the long and short duration of the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of the specific periods of time corresponding to those [similes], the passage beginning with "Thus" is stated. "Crumbled and scattered" means by way of many distinct portions.
And herein, regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths in the bodies of elephants and so forth, and in the bodies of dogs and so forth—
It should be understood that "long" and "short" are spoken of by way of time-periods (*addhāna*) distinguished as long and short durations;

this is because of such statements as, "having slowly filled the long duration known as the personal existence (*attabhāva*)," and so forth. "Of them" means of beings. "They" refers to the inhalations and exhalations.
"A short duration" means a brief period of time. "In nine ways" refers to [the changes] of one who is devoted to the practice of meditation (*bhāvanā*), from before to after.
For one who has not yet attained distinction, the three modes mentioned at the beginning occur solely by way of duration;
and these manifest as inhalation for some, exhalation for others, and both for still others—thus they are stated with reference to three types of persons.
Likewise, there are three by way of desire, and likewise three by way of gladness; thus, by these nine modes. "By one mode" means:
In the case of long inhalations and so forth, [it occurs] by way of a single mode.
"In what is reckoned as a duration" means in a selfhood (attabhāva) reckoned as a long spatial duration, or even in a temporal duration;
likewise for "in what is reckoned as short" below. "Zeal arises" refers to the cultivation that brings about successive excellence.
Because of having gained a sense of satisfaction, a wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) characterized by an especially strong wish to act arises therein.

"By way of desire" means by way of the desire that has thus proceeded. "Joy arises" means that, due to the subtler state of the inhalations and exhalations, the greater tranquility of the object, and the fact that the meditation subject (kammatthāna) has entered its proper course, joy accompanied by the developing consciousness (bhāvanācitta) arises.
"Delight" means that fresh joy (*pīti*) arises, distinguished by its minor grades and so forth.
"The mind turns away" means that when the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) has arisen, the mind withdraws from the natural in-and-out breaths.

"Equanimity becomes established" means that when concentration—distinguished as access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*)—has arisen upon that counterpart sign, there is a state of looking on with indifference because of the absence of further effort for the sake of producing the jhāna.
It exists; furthermore, this equanimity should be understood as "equanimity regarding the middle" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

"Knowledge of contemplation" (*anupassanāñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge that contemplates the sign by way of serenity (*samatha*), and contemplates the name-and-form dependent upon that [sign] by way of insight (*vipassanā*) through the medium of inhalation and exhalation.
"The body is the foundation" (*kāyo upaṭṭhāna*): the body, consisting of inhalation and exhalation, stands having approached [the mind].

In this context, "establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is not simply mindfulness (*sati*); rather, mindfulness is both establishment and mindfulness in the sense of being established through its own essence and in the sense of remembering. Regarding the phrase "therefore it is so called," etc.:

that which is the contemplation of the body itself—both the aforementioned body of inhalations and exhalations and the physical body (*karajakāya*) that serves as its support—in terms of its impermanence and so forth, or in terms of its nature as permanent and so on, or its nature as female, male, a sentient being, a soul, and so forth.
Or, without contemplating [the breath] as such, there is the contemplation of the mere body of inhalation and exhalation and its state of impermanence and so forth.

Through that contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), there is the cultivation and increase of the foundation (*paṭṭhāna*) known as mindfulness. "Cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body" (*kāye kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā*):

this is the summary meaning. "By way of the limited" (*ittaravasena*) means by way of a short duration. "Such" (*tādiso*) refers to both long and short. "Color" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to the forms such as long and so forth.
"At the tip of the nose" (*nāsikagge*) means either at the tip of the nose; by the word "or" (*vā*), the meaning is "or on the upper lip. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means:

because [the meditator] previously applied attention with the thought, "I shall make the entire body of in-breaths and out-breaths known and manifest according to its beginning, middle, and end," he subsequently, by means of a consciousness associated with knowledge that has arisen accordingly, [perceives] that body of in-breaths and out-breaths.

Thus, making it known and manifest, he both inhales and exhales; therefore, being such, he is said to "train himself, thinking: 'I shall inhale and exhale experiencing the whole body,'" but the intention is not that he is called this merely by the thought, "In the future I shall do so.
"Of one who has become thus" means of one who makes known the beginning, middle, and end.

"Restraint" (*saṃvara*) means either mindfulness or energy. "Nothing else at all" refers to the preliminary mental application (*pubbābhoga*), such as the thought, "I shall make the entire body known," and so forth.
In the phrase "in the arising of knowledge, etc.," the word "etc. includes the calming of the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), the experiencing of rapture, and so on.
"Bodily formation" refers to inhalation and exhalation; for although it is mind-originated, its occurrence is dependent upon the physical body composed of the four elements.

Because it is conditioned by that, it is called "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*). "At a time when [the body] is not yet mastered" means at a time when the meditation subject has not yet been undertaken;

the meaning is that at that time, both body and mind are not yet mastered for the purpose of undertaking it. For, by the words "he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect," there is the mastery of the body;
and by the words "having established mindfulness directed to the front," [there is the mastery of the mind].

The "comprehension of mind" has been explained. "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means strong or gross; it is stated with a change of gender, for what is intended here is the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).
Alternatively, this is an adverbial qualification of the action, meaning "it proceeds having become excessive. "Of all alike" refers to both types [of persons].
It is said that "it is subtle in the comprehension of the great primary elements" with reference to the application of insight by way of the four elements.

"Insight having the characteristics as its object" refers to the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*). From the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) onwards is strong insight;

prior to that is weak insight. "By the method stated previously" means by the method stated in the section on calm (*samatha*), beginning with "at a time when [the mind] is not yet grasped," and so forth.
"By means of interrogation and clarification" means by means of questions and their resolutions. The passage beginning with "How... is from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*; therein, "how" [is explained].
"Trains" (*sikkhati*) is the syntactical connection. "It is said, indeed," and so forth, is the statement of the objector (*codaka*). "It is said, indeed" means "it is thus.
The objector's intention is that [the practitioner] brings the inhalation and exhalation to total non-existence.

"By the perception of wind" (*vātūpaladdhiyā*) means that due to the absence of the wind of inhalation and exhalation, there is neither the arising nor the increase of the developing consciousness (*bhāvanācitta*) which has that [wind] as its object. This is the meaning.
"And they do not strike here"—*nanti* is merely a particle. "Again, 'it is said' (*iti kira*)" and so forth is the response to the aforementioned objection.
In that context, "if he trains in the manner stated by me, namely, 'he trains' (*sikkhati*)," such is the meaning. "There is development" (*pabhāvanā hoti*):
even though the gross bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) subside, subtle ones still remain; thus, there is indeed development.

The intention is that it indeed increases. "In a bronze vessel" means in a bronze bowl. "The sign" (nimitta) means of the sign—that is, the mode of occurrence of those sounds. "Subtle sounds" refers to the after-sounds (anurava).
"Even by having the subtle sound as the sign-object" means even by having the subtle sound itself as the sign, which serves as the object of focus.
"Ābhisamācārika-sīla": here, *abhisamācāra* means "excellent conduct"; that itself is *ābhisamācārika-sīla*.
This is a designation for the virtue included within the Khandhaka observances (*vatta*).

The statement "I guard the virtue" refers to the virtue included within the two Vibhaṅgas. "Āvāsa" (residence) refers to the impediment of residence. The same applies to "family" (*kula*) and so forth.

The same method applies here. "Work" (*kamma*) refers to new construction (*navakamma*). "Success" (*iddhi*) refers to the mundane success (*pothujjanikā iddhi*); it is an impediment to insight (*vipassanā*).
"It should be severed" means it should be severed by means of the methods for severing each respective impediment as described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Devotion to yoga" (*yogānuyoga*) is the application to the cultivation of yoga. "Regarding the thirty-eight objects" (*aṭṭhatimsārammaṇesu*)...
This is stated by way of the eight kasinas mentioned in the text, excluding the two—namely, the light-kasina and the space-kasina;

however, there are actually forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). "In the manner already described" refers to the fact that these serve as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the practice of yoga.
"By this very meditation subject" means by this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati). [The text mentions] the Great Elephant Path.
He goes forth as if leading [the disciple] out, as if making a great highway for the path of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and showing it to him.

Regarding the teacher of the aforementioned type: this refers to the teacher described below in such passages as, "Having produced the fourth jhāna by means of this very meditation subject, and having developed insight, he attained Arahantship," and so forth.
This is indicated by the description beginning with, "Dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem."
They also say that the type of teacher described in the *Visuddhimagga* is intended here. "Five-jointed" means having five sections;
the meaning is "five parts. "Learning the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) means learning the text on the meditation subject.
"Inquiring about its meaning" refers to inquiry concerning the meditation subject, or inquiry regarding doubts therein. "The appearance of the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānaṃ*)—
"Apprehension" (*upadhāraṇa*) means that for one who is thus devoted to development, the sign (*nimitta*) establishes itself in this way.

Likewise, "the absorption of the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānappanā*) means that jhāna enters in this way. "The characteristic of the meditation subject" refers to its essential nature (*sabhāva*), which is the reaching of the summit by means of establishing through the stages of counting, following, and touching, having brought the development to excellence. This is what is meant here by "development."
It is the discernment [of the object]; therefore it is said: "the grasping of the specific nature of the meditation subject.

"Free from the eighteen faults of a lodging" refers to: being large, being new, being dilapidated, being situated on a main road, being possessed of stumps, leaves, flowers, and fruit, being desirable, being situated near a city, wood, or fields, the presence of incompatible persons, and being situated near a port.

It is free from these eighteen faults of a lodging: being near a border region, being near the boundary of a kingdom, being unsuitable, and not finding virtuous friends. It is "endowed with five factors of a lodging":
"In this case, monks, the lodging is not too far away, nor too close; it is well-served for coming and going; by day..."
It is not crowded at night, with little noise and little clamor, free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles;
furthermore, while dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick arise without difficulty;
moreover, elder bhikkhus dwell in that lodging... In this way, bhikkhus, is a lodging [proper].
“It is endowed with five factors.
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, [the dwelling] was endowed with these five factors of a lodging: herein, being not too far [from the village], etc., constitutes one;

being not crowded during the day, etc., constitutes one; being free from gadflies and the like, constitutes one; the obtaining of robes and so forth, constitutes one; and [the presence of] elder monks.
"Abiding alone"—in this way, the five factors are to be understood.

"By one for whom minor impediments have been severed" means by one through whom the minor impediments have been severed by the removal of long hair and so forth, and by the performing of such tasks as cooking, dyeing, and sewing of bowls, robes, and other requisites.
"The fatigue caused by food" refers to the exhaustion resulting from eating.
"Learning from a teacher" (*ācariyuggaha*) means learning from a teacher; it refers to the entire procedure for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), not merely the "learning" mentioned previously.
"Even a single word" means even a single portion.
"Carrying along" (*anuvahana*) means the continuous proceeding of mindfulness by way of following after the in-breaths and out-breaths. Since...
However, there is no separate attention by way of touching as there is by way of counting and so forth;

rather, it is shown that counting and so forth should be performed only at the place touched. Demonstrating this by taking up "touching," he said: "Touching is the place touched. "Fixing" means stabilization (*samādhāna*);
but since absorption (*appanā*) has concentration (*samādhi*) as its primary factor, he said: "Fixing is absorption."
Insight (*vipassanā*) is the observation of the characteristics such as impermanence (*aniccatā*). The path (*magga*) is the turning away from occurrence and from signs.
Fruition (*phala*) is purification (*pārisuddhi*) by way of the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of those" refers to turning away and purification.
"Fragment" (*khaṇḍa*) means breaking up by way of counting, such as "one, three, five," in the manner of skipping one and so forth. Alternatively, "fragment" means...
One should not show an interruption in the middle by omitting a certain period of time and then resuming the counting;
for if one shows such a break, distraction arises from the inquiry, "Is my mind inclining toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) or not?
Therefore he said, "Has it reached its peak for me? and so forth. And this [interruption] is as follows:
This was said with reference to one who, having shown [the breaths], attends to them for a longer period by way of counting.

For he might think thus, relying merely on the non-distraction thus obtained. As for the phrase "taking that which appears," this is said concerning one for whom only one of the inhalation or exhalation first appears;
however, for one for whom both appear, both [should be taken].
Having grasped them, they should be counted. By the phrase "whichever presents itself," it is also indicated that one should grasp whichever of the two nostril-winds is manifest;
thus it should be understood. Although only one appears at a time in each nostril, for one who observes and counts them, both gradually become manifest;
therefore he says, "the in-breaths and out-breaths become manifest. Thus...
The connection is: "It must be counted very quickly, very quickly. Thus, in order to show the occasion for beginning the rapid counting, it was said:
"Counting this also by the previous method," and so forth. Therein, "by the previous method" means by the slow counting.
By the phrase "having become manifest," [it is shown that] at the time the slow counting was commenced, because of the lack of clarity in the mind, the subtle inhalations and so forth—
This shows that when they are not yet clear, and later when they have become clear, one should abandon slow counting and perform rapid counting once they have become clear.
Rapid counting occurs, in the literal sense, only in the cognitive process of absorption (*appanāvīthi*) which proceeds uninterruptedly;

it does not occur in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), because there is an interval between the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Therefore, he says, "as if proceeding uninterruptedly. "In the same manner as before" means:
By means of rapid counting. One is said to "cause the mind to enter within" by attending to the air entering within.
"This" refers to this set of inhalation and exhalation. "Following" is simply the act of attending to the point where [the breath] touches;
it is not following the inhalation and exhalation themselves. Therefore he said: "And that is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end. By way of establishing the touching.

By the phrase "there is no separate attention," it is shown that there is no attention consisting merely of fixing and touching without following, as there is in the cases of counting and touching; rather, having withdrawn counting,
one attends by means of both following and touching until absorption arises, at which point [the attention] is of absorption.
This indicates that one indeed attends to the arisen [consciousness] for the purpose of following it and for the purpose of fixing it;

however, in the Aṭṭhakathā, only this much was stated—"one attends to it for the purpose of following, for the purpose of contacting, and for the purpose of fixing"—in order to show that there is no attending to it for the purpose of fixing without [first] following it. This is how it should be understood.

That which does not measure or decide absolutely is "near to conceit" (*mānassa samīpa*); this is an illustration by means of a similar established example, such as the proof of what is to be proven by means of what is already proven, for instance:
"like a *gavaya* is like a cow. "Lame" (*paṅguḷo*) refers to one who is a cripple. "Swing" (*dola*) refers to a hammock. "Of those playing" (*kīḷatan-ti*) means of those who are sporting.
"At the base of the pillar of attachment" (*upanibandhanatthambhamūle*) is said with reference to the tip of the nose and the mark on the face.
"From the beginning" means starting from the point where the meaning of the object of comparison is shown.
"The sign" refers to the sign for anchoring the mind, namely the tip of the nose or the sign at the mouth.

"Not an object for a single consciousness" means that because inhalation and exhalation do not occur simultaneously, all three are not objects for a single consciousness; rather, it is the sign together with either the inhalation or the exhalation [that serves as the object].
The meaning is that only two [factors] become the object simultaneously.

"And for one who does not know the three things" means for one who does not find these three things—namely, the sign, the in-breath, and the out-breath—by way of making them the object. The word *ca* (and) indicates contrast;
by it, he shows the contrast, implying: "And this being so, there follows this undesirable consequence. "Cultivation" refers to the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).

“How do these... [etc. ...attain distinction?”—this is the formulation of a question intended to explain, by means of the simile of the saw, the very same matter already stated in the verse of the response.
In this context, the word *kathaṃ* (how) should be applied to each [term]: “How are these [states] unknown... [etc. ...how does one attain distinction?
*Padhāna* (exertion) is the energy that brings about the development [of the path]. *Payoga* (application) is that which suppresses the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Application to development" (*bhāvanānuyoga*) means the excellence culminating in Arahantship. "Exertion" (*padhāna*) is the effort of cutting down a tree. "Application" (*payoga*) is the act of cutting that very tree.

Although the phrase "he attains excellence" is not explicitly stated in the simile here, it must nevertheless be applied according to the sense. The passage beginning with "Just as a tree... is the correlation of the simile. [The term] "at the tip of the nose" (*nāsikagge*).
Or, "on the sign of the mouth" refers to the upper lip, which has received the name *mukhanimitta* because the nose is fixed (*nimiyati*) or covered (*chādiyati*) by it,

as in the case of one with a long nose. "This is the striving" means that the exertion of energy by which both body and mind become fit for the work of cultivation is here called "striving" (*padhāna*).
He shows the cause by means of the fruit. "Impurities" refers to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "Thoughts" refers to wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth;

or, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna through the abandoning of the hindrances, he speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and the others by means of the phrase "the subsiding of thought.
"This application" means this application consisting of the practice of the meditation subject (*kammatthāna*), which serves as the cause for the attainment of jhāna. "Fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
"They are abandoned" means that even the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned by way of total eradication through the penetration of the path.
"They come to an end" means that likewise, even the seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) become entirely gone, without remainder, to the extent of their very destruction.
"This is the distinction" refers to this sequence of abandoning the fetters and so forth, which is obtained gradually by depending upon this concentration. This is its [distinction].
The meaning is "a distinction of concentration. Thus, the words "these three things" and so forth constitute the concluding statement.
"Complete" means entirely full due to the fulfillment of the sixteen bases. "Successive" means by way of gradual sequence. "Cultivated" means thoroughly developed.
"This world" refers to the world of aggregates and so forth; he illuminates it with the radiance of wisdom.
*Idha* means in this place. *Assa* refers to the saw, which serves as the simile. It should be construed as "the purpose for bringing it [into use].

*Nimitta* refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). They say that "adorned with the remaining jhāna factors" means adorned with the remaining jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
However, one should rather say "with sustained thought (*vicāra*) and so forth," because, in the primary sense, applied thought does not exist in the state of absorption (*appanā*). For it...
“Absorption (appanā) and access (byappanā)” is what has been indicated. For when this is so, the word “the rest” (avasesa) becomes appropriate;

or else, having taken concentration—which is the most prominent among the jhāna factors due to its association with applied thought—to be absorption, it is said: “And the establishing called absorption, adorned by the remaining jhāna factors, is accomplished.
However, for some, [it begins] from the time of attention by way of counting itself.
Here, the passage beginning with "In due order... it becomes like a bowl," which will be explained later on, is found in ancient manuscripts;
therefore, this reading should also be written here, though it must be understood as having been omitted through the error of scribes.
As for the passage beginning with "When the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased," etc., one should also investigate the bodily formation according to the method stated below.
It was brought forward in order to show the method of investigation. "From the place" means from the location previously grasped by way of contact.
"The sign should be established" means that the perception which grasps the sign in its previously grasped mode should be established upon the place of contact.
For this very purpose is meant the method of establishing the non-manifested object, which is designated as the "establishment of the sign."
"Dependent on a cause. "It" refers to the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*). It is called "weighty cultivation" because it is difficult to develop;
thus he says, "weighty cultivation. "Having wandered" means having taken up its range. "The sign" refers either to the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) or the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*);
for both are mentioned here together. For the three similes beginning with the tuft of cotton apply to the learning sign, while the rest apply to both.
“Like the form of a star” means like the actual form of a star. “Due to the diversity of perceptions” means due to the diversity of the perceptions that occurred prior to the appearance of the sign.
“Perceived” refers to what is conceptually constructed by the perception of meditation; it is not actually produced because it does not exist [as a real object].
Therefore he said, “it appears as diverse. “It becomes thus” means it appears thus to one devoted to meditation. “Thus” [refers to the manner described].
This being so, the meaning is that mindfulness (*sati*) consists in the fixing of the mind precisely upon the sign (*nimitta*) in the manner already described.
"From this point onwards" means starting from the arising of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). "Upon the sign" means upon the counterpart sign.
"They fix" means fixing the mind by way of fixing. "Various aspects" refers to the various aspects mentioned as "the four colors. They discern them.
"Vibhāvento" means making them disappear. For from the moment the sign arises, those modes [of breathing] seem to vanish for one who does not attend to them.

The construction is as follows: "By discerning the various aspects of both the in-breath and the out-breath, or by fixing the mind on the sign produced by the in-breath and out-breath, he indeed binds his own mind. However, some explain it as "vibhāvayanti."
They explain the meaning of "distinguishing" (*vibhāvento*) as making known or making manifest; this would be appropriate in the sense of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
This is the meaning here: by distinguishing the various aspects of the in-breath and out-breath, one understands them;
then, fixing the mind upon whatever sign (*nimitta*) is obtained therein, one gradually binds and settles one's own mind [upon it].

"Defilements" refers to the remaining defilements. "Seated right there" means they are withdrawn, having not obtained the assistance of the hindrances. "In the access stage" means in the state of access concentration.

"By way of characteristic" means either by way of their intrinsic nature, such as suppression, or by way of their intrinsic nature, such as impermanence. "The resort" refers to the village for wandering for alms.
That place where suitable alms-food is difficult to obtain is unsuitable; the other is suitable. "Speech" refers to...
Discourse based on the ten topics of talk is suitable; the other is unsuitable.

Regarding the remaining factors, such as the dwelling place and so forth, one should understand that whatever causes an unconcentrated mind to become concentrated is suitable, while the opposite is unsuitable.
However, for one who thus avoids the seven kinds of the unsuitable and cultivates only what is suitable, yet...
Since absorption does not occur [without preparation], he spoke the words "making the basis pure" and so forth, showing the tenfold skill in absorption that must be accomplished therein.

Therein, "making the basis pure" means making the internal physical basis—the body—pure by means of cutting hair and nails, etc., and making the external basis pure by means of washing and preparing robes, lodgings, and so forth. For in this way...
Knowledge also brings about the accomplishment of its pure function. "Balancing the faculties" means making the faculties, such as faith and the rest, equal.
"Skill in the sign" means proficiency in guarding the sign acquired through meditation.
Regarding the passage beginning with "At whatever time the mind should be restrained," it refers to the times when the mind [is to be restrained] due to causes such as excessive exertion.
When the mind is to be restrained due to restlessness, then by not cultivating the three beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga*),

there comes to be restraint of the mind through the cultivation of the three beginning with tranquility (*passaddhi*). When his mind is to be exerted due to sluggishness caused by excessive laxity of energy and so forth,
then by not cultivating the three beginning with tranquility, [he should cultivate] those beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena.

By the cultivation of these three, there is an uplifting of the mind. When his mind becomes dispirited due to dullness in the application of wisdom and other such factors, then there is for that mind an arousing of urgency, termed "encouragement," by means of reflecting on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency and so forth.
However, when, through practicing in this way, it is neither sluggish nor agitated but is dispirited toward the object—

When the mind is proceeding evenly and has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*), then there is equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanā*) by way of not engaging in the functions of exertion, restraint, or encouragement.

"Inclination toward that" (*tadadhimuttatā*) means inclination toward concentration (*samādhi*); the meaning is being bent, sloping, and leaning toward concentration. "In this" (*ettha*) refers to this very contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

"One who desires to attain purity" means one who desires to realize the fruit (*phala*) and one who desires to enter the attainment (*samāpatti*). In this context, first, by way of discerning and turning away [from formations], one desires to realize the fruit immediately following the path (*maggānantara-phala*).
Thereafter, by way of discerning [the fruit itself], one also desires to enter the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*);
thus the meaning should be understood. Regarding the passage "from adverting and entering... up to attaining mastery": here...
Having emerged from the attained jhāna and reviewing each of the jhāna factors, such as initial application (*vitakka*) and so forth, when the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is interrupted and,
immediately following the arisen adverting consciousness, sense-sphere impulsion moments— having as their object whichever jhāna factor was reviewed—
proceed uninterruptedly, alternating with the life-continuum, then his mastery over adverting is accomplished. That...
Furthermore, the capacity to enter jhāna immediately after the desire to do so is called mastery of entering (samāpajjana-vasī).
The capacity to maintain the jhāna for a moment as short as a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps is called mastery of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī).
Likewise, having quickly become possessed of the jhāna for a moment, the ability to emerge from it by way of the arising of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is [mastery of emergence].

Capability is what is called mastery in emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*). Here, the mastery in resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*) and the mastery in emergence are distinguished by way of the difference in prior preparation—namely, [the resolve] "I shall attain [this attainment] for only this long a moment," and "Having been possessed of jhāna for only this long a moment, I shall emerge from jhāna"—but not by way of a difference in their essential nature.
These are what are called "skill in attainment" and "skill in emergence. Mastery in review (*paccavekkhaṇa-vasī*).

However, it is spoken of specifically in terms of mastery over adverting (āvajjanavasi). For in the cognitive process of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇavīthi), mastery over adverting arises because of the swift occurrence of adverting;
and mastery over reviewing arises from the simultaneous emergence of the subsequent impulsion-moments (javana).

Thus, it should be understood that mastery over reviewing is established precisely through the establishment of mastery over adverting. "Having discerned the factors of absorption" (jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvā) means [having discerned] those associated with the absorption-consciousness.

Having discerned the jhāna factors by way of their characteristics and so forth, [one discerns] "their support," which is the support for those primary elements that serve as the physical bases (vatthu-nissaya).

And this is stated according to the method of the Suttas, because the material body—the decad of the physical basis—is supported by the primary elements; it is not according to the method of the Paṭṭhāna.
For primary elements contained within one group (kalāpa) do not [serve as the support] for primary elements contained within another group.
They function as dependence conditions (*nissaya-paccaya*); however, according to the method of the Suttas, they should be understood as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
For it should be understood that all conditions not included in the *Paṭṭhāna* are subsumed under the decisive support condition according to the method of the Suttas.

"The material phenomena dependent on that" refers to the derived material phenomena (*upādā-rūpa*). Regarding the phrase "or the object, door, or basis of material phenomena as they have been delimited": here—

It should be connected as follows: the object consisting of the form of hair and so forth as it has been grasped, the object of the physical basis (vatthu) according to the method explained previously, and the doors of the eye and so forth—which have appeared by way of the grasping of the physical body that is their support—along with the consciousness together with its associated mental states, flow [toward them].
"The smith's bellows" means the bellows used by smiths for blowing the fire. "Corresponding" means suitable to that. "Of that" refers to name-and-form (nāmarūpa). "Having seen that" means...
"Having seen the conditions such as ignorance and craving": he "crosses over doubt" means he transcends the sixteen-based perplexity that proceeds in the manner of "Was I indeed in the past?

and so forth. "By way of comprehension by groups" (kalāpasammasana) means the comprehension of the five aggregates—past, future, and present—as impermanent and so on, by taking each portion of the past and so forth from among them as a single group.
"Comprehension by groups" refers to that [comprehension] by way of its influence.
"In the prior stage" means in the stage prior to the contemplation of rise and fall, which is included within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way.

"Radiance and so forth" refers to radiance, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolution, exertion, equanimity, establishment, and attachment. Among these, "resolution" is faith. "Establishment" is...

"Being present. "Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) here means neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*). And herein, the nine factors beginning with the "appearance" (*obhāsa*) are called "defilements" (*upakkilesa*) because they serve as the basis for the defilement known as craving (*taṇhā*), which is characterized by attachment;
whereas attachment itself is a defilement both by its own nature and by being the basis for those [other] factors.

"Becoming disenchanted" means becoming disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*), which is preceded by the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*). [This refers to] the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*), equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*), and the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*).

Immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) has reached its conclusion, one becomes dispassionate toward and liberated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by means of the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) that arises [thereafter].
For it is said that one is "liberated" at the moment of the fruit (*phala-khaṇa*), while one is "being liberated" at the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "of nineteen kinds": this refers to the path, fruit, and Nibbāna that arise individually immediately following each of the four path-moments (*magga-vīthi*), as well as the remaining defilements (*kilesa*) that have been abandoned.
By way of the five things to be reviewed, it consists of nineteen types. For the Arahant, there are nineteen because of the absence of any remaining defilements.
"Of him" refers to one who practices the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.
"Two jhānas accompanied by rapture" means the first and second jhānas in the fourfold system, which are associated with rapture. "Of that" refers to...
By that yogi. "At the moment of attainment" means at the moment of having entered [the meditative state].
"By way of the object" means that rapture is experienced through the apprehension of the counterpart-object (*paṭibhāgārammaṇa*); it is because the object is experienced.

For when the object is known, the mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika*) that have that as their domain are themselves said to be experienced by one's own nature, both in terms of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and their general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).

And because there is no doubt regarding its subsequent grasping. "At the moment of insight" (*vipassanā-khaṇe*) means at the moment of seeing by way of the object of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
Thus, the very grasping of rapture (*pīti*) by way of its impermanence and so forth is called the "experience of rapture" (*pīti-paṭisaṃvedana*) due to non-delusion.
"By way of long inhalation" means by way of the long inhalation which has become the object; for one who understands thus, that is rapture.
The connection is with the phrase "is clearly experienced. "Of one who understands the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind" means:
of one who understands through wisdom associated with that [state] the one-pointedness of the mind called "non-distraction" which is included within jhāna.
For just as rapture is clearly experienced by way of its object, so too are the states associated with it clearly experienced.
"Thus they are. "Mindfulness is established" means that mindfulness associated with jhāna, by way of long inhalation, is established upon its object;
it is said to be "established" even in the jhāna that has that as its object. The meaning in the passages beginning with "by way of long exhalation," etc., should be understood in this same manner.
Thus, the experience of rapture shown in this way is [to be understood] from the perspective of the object and from the perspective of non-delusion.
And in order to show [this] by way of analysis, it is said: "by adverting," and so forth. Therein, "by adverting" means for one who is adverting to the jhāna.
"That rapture" refers to that rapture included within the jhāna. "By knowing" means by knowing through the medium of the object at the moment of attainment;
the connection is that "for him, that rapture becomes clearly experienced. "By seeing" means by means of knowledge consisting in vision, from the perspective of the jhāna.
“For one who sees after emerging”: for one who reviews the jhāna. “For one who resolves the mind”:
for one who resolves the jhāna-consciousness, thinking, “I shall remain possessed of jhāna for this much time.
Thus, by way of mastery over the five kinds of mastery, through the door of understanding jhāna, the experiencing of rapture from the object is shown.

“Adhimuccati” means for one who has faith; the intention is that this occurs by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). The same method applies to “exerts energy” (*vīriyaṃ paggaṇhati*) and so forth.
Regarding “to be directly known” (*abhiññeyya*), it refers to the Four Truths to be known by distinguished wisdom;

the construction is “directly knowing [them] by means of path-wisdom preceded by insight-wisdom,” and so on. Likewise, regarding “to be fully understood” (*pariññeyya*) and so forth, [the construction is] “fully understanding [them],” and so on.
The construction should be understood. Therein, "to be fully known" refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
"The remaining phrases" refers to the phrases "experiencing pleasure" and "experiencing mental formations.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "feeling, etc.," perception (*saññā*) is included; therefore he says, "two aggregates. This is for the purpose of showing the plane of insight (*vipassanā*).

It is stated [that there is no bodily pleasure] because, under the heading of bodily pleasure and so forth, one perceives the miscellaneous formations (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra*), whereas in calm abiding (*samatha*) there is an absence of bodily pleasure.
"That" refers to cessation (*nirodha*) expressed by way of the method of "tranquilizing.

"By the method already stated" means by the method stated regarding the bodily formation, beginning with the words: "For this bhikkhu, at a time when it was not previously discerned," and so on. Feeling is stated under the heading of joy; thus, by the designation of "joy" (*pīti-apadesena*), feeling is indicated.
Feeling has been mentioned; the intention is that it is included under the contemplation of feeling because of the inclusion of the term "pleasure.
Regarding the two sections on mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*): this refers to these two portions, namely, "experiencing the mental formation" and "tranquilizing the mental formation.
It is stated that "feeling associated with perception" is mentioned because of its presence in the contemplation of feeling. That "the experiencing of the mind" is to be understood [in the same way].

This is stated with reference to the method described by the passage beginning "from the object" and "from non-delusion. "Citta" refers to the consciousness associated with jhāna and the consciousness associated with insight (vipassanā).
"Āmodeti" means he rejoices through the joy (pīti) associated [with that consciousness] which has the jhāna as its object.
"At the moment of insight," etc., refers to the moment of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) as previously described.
The method of commentary on the discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is finished.

167. Although the Noble Ones neither take their own lives nor those of one another, nor do they incite others to do so, nevertheless, among the dead ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) according to the three aforementioned modes, [there was] Migalaṇḍika...
It is stated that they are "mixed with noble persons" because there exist even those noble persons who have been killed. Alternatively,

it should be understood that this is said because there are also those who, having killed themselves while still ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), developed insight at the time of death, attained the noble path, and then passed away.
172. "Without regard for the phrasing" is said because [the offense] was not stated in accordance with the phrasing, such as "having known" or "having recognized.

"One who knows it is a living being" is stated in order to show that even if one does not know it is a human being, the offense of a *pārājika* occurs solely through the perception of it as a sentient being.
It has been said. "Having intended by way of murderous volition" means having thought with a murderous volition, [thinking] "I shall kill this person.
"Having planned" means having delimited it with the mind thus, "I will kill. "Having fully resolved" means having made a firm determination;
therefore he said, "having sent forth a mind free from apprehension. "The matter has reached its culmination" refers to the term *sañcicca* (intentionally) as denoting the preceding action.
The meaning reaches its ultimate limit through the demonstration that even what has been stated—namely, the transgression—is associated with death at a later time.
"Wool of birth" (*jātiuṇṇā*) refers to the hair of a lamb born on that very day. "Of such appearance and likeness" (*evaṃ vaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ*) means of such color and shape.

"Or beyond that" (*tato vā uddhaṃ*) is said with reference to having reached the state of an *abbuda* (embryo) and so forth during the second week and subsequent periods. For one whose momentum has subsided...

"It is a condition for the continuity" means it is a cooperative condition (*sahakārī-paccaya*), not a productive condition (*janaka*). For karma alone is the productive condition for the kamma-born material phenomena that arise moment by moment;

and that [karma] is only able to produce them when it has previously arisen during the course of existence and, remaining unimpaired, obtains the fourfold continuity of matter as its cooperative condition, and not otherwise.

It is already established that for individuals whose eye-faculties and so forth have ceased due to any obstructing condition, even though karma exists, it is unable to produce the eye and other faculties.
"Overstepping" means causing to overstep, that is, destroying. "In the manner already stated" refers to the method of overstepping the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

It is of the very kind already described. *Atipāta* (excessive killing) is the excessive or swift killing that does not allow what is by nature subject to falling to fall slowly, through the very force of its own momentum;
the killing of a living being (*pāṇa*) is *pāṇātipāta*. *Āthabbaṇikā* means those who know the *athabbaṇa* (Atharvan) Veda.

*Athabbaṇa* refers to what is prescribed by the *athabbaṇa* Veda. "They employ spells" means [by means of] such things as abstaining from salty food, using grass mats for bedding, and visiting cemeteries.
They recite mantras through various applications, and by means of that, a result such as the killing of living beings according to their desire arises;
therefore, that is included within bodily and verbal action. *Īti* means affliction. *Upaddava* means an even greater affliction than that.
*Pajjaraka* means a feverish state. *Sūcikā* means a piercing pain as if being pierced by needles. *Visūcikā* means colic accompanied by such pain.
*Āmātisāraṃ*: diarrhea caused by undigested food. *Pakkhandiyanti*: bloody diarrhea. *Vijjaṃ parivattetvā*:

having recited one’s own lore—such as the Gandhāra-lores and so forth—which has been made a means of livelihood, by way of the sequence of chanting mantras. *Tehi*: by those means. *Payojanaṃ*: the instigation or setting in motion.
*Aho vatāyaṃ*: "Oh, may this [person]... *Taṃ kucchigataṃ*: that which has entered the womb. *Gabbhaṃ*: this refers to that which has entered the womb.
“Womb”: *kulumba* means womb; or it means family (*kula*), or household (*kuṭumba*)—this is what is meant.

“By means of supernormal power consisting in development” is said with reference to the supernormal power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*). The intention is that [the claim] “that is merely by their wish” does not accord with the meaning of the Sutta.

For it should be understood that in the Sutta, the phrase “one possessed of supernormal power, attained to mastery over mind” is stated specifically by way of the supernormal power of the *atharvaṇa* (magical) arts, and not by way of supernormal power consisting in development.
Regarding the phrase "otherwise one would seek," the meaning might, according to the literal sense, be merely the act of seeking;
in that case, the meaning would be "merely having sought," that is, by the mere acquisition of weapons and so forth after having sought them.

For it is said that "weapon" (*sattha*) is the name for everything used as an instrument of killing, such as stones, ropes, and so on—hence he says "clubs" and so forth. Because one kills (*sasati*) or injures (*hiṃsati*) by means of this, it is called a weapon; thus he states "clubs" and so forth to include all such instruments of slaughter.
"Laguḷanti" is a designation for a club (*muggara*). "Satthasaṅgaho" refers to the inclusion of weapons mentioned in the *mātikā* as "one who carries weapons.
It is "because of the method stated later" because it follows the method explained in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for the second term, which was stated later by way of conclusion.
It is "stated for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of the word *citta*" because the word *citta* has a manifold range of meanings, such as "variegated" (*vicitta*), and so forth.
It is stated [in this context] in order to exclude others and to restrict [the term] to consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
174. "One is bound by karma" means one is bound by the karma of taking life; the meaning is that this karma has been accomplished by him.

"In both ways" refers to the distinction between being specifically designated (*uddissaka*) and not being designated (*anuddissaka*). Or, "by that disease later" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) even in the future.
This shows the occurrence of killing with reference [to that object].
And thus, even if the success of the command—“When you are able, then deprive him of life”—is achieved only after a long time, the killing occurs at the very moment of the command.

Furthermore, in cases of permanent application such as digging a pit, even when a being who has already taken rebirth dies after the application was performed, the killing is still an object of the future.

He is reborn. As for what was stated in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*—that "five training rules have only the present as their object"—that was said with reference to the abstention from killing and so forth, and should not be understood as referring to the acts of killing and so forth themselves.
"With another mind" means with a mind that does not intend to kill. "He dies by the second blow" means without the first blow.
The meaning is: "He dies by the second [blow] itself. "By the first blow itself" means: at the very moment of the volition that originates the first blow.
Although the first blow is not able to kill by itself, it becomes the cause for the destruction of life when it obtains the second;
therefore, since death is not accomplished without the first blow, it is [classified as] "the preliminary effort" (*payoga*).
And because it connects with the phrase "and by that [act] death [occurs]," one is bound by karma through the first stroke alone, not by the second, since that was administered by another's mind.
And as it is here, so it is in the case of another person administering a second stroke and so forth.
However, if the person who administers the second stroke also possesses the intention to kill, then for him too—
It should be understood that because [the being] has already died through one's own action, the act of taking life occurs at the moment of that action.

"For the purpose of clarifying the nature of kamma and offenses" means for the purpose of making manifest the classification of kamma such as the *ānantariya* (immediate) offenses, and the classification of offenses such as the *pārājika* (defeats).
Even in the case of a mistaken perception, such as thinking, "I am killing a sheep," [the object is still identified] as "this one," referring specifically to the one lying there.
Because it is grasped in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), one remains bound by karma according to the actual state of things; thus he said, "this object," and so forth.

"And he becomes a slayer" means that he is bound by the kamma of taking life. Because the volition (*cetanā*) of killing directed toward those who possess great qualities, such as a mother, is extremely reprehensible (*mahāsāvajja*), it is stated:
"In this case, however, the volition is cruel."
"Red-stained" means stained with blood. "While performing an action" means while performing the action of battle. "Gone according to the intention":

even if the warrior is not pierced but only the father is pierced after having pierced the warrior, there is no lack of offense (*visaṅketa*) because the intent to kill exists in regard to the father as well; it is exactly the same even when only the warrior is pierced.
The meaning is that there is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*); that is, there is no kamma of taking life committed against one’s own father.
"Teach him thus" means he instructs him by way of teaching the manner of piercing, such as "stand on the ground with your feet thus," "take up the bow and draw it thus," and so forth.
"Strike him thus" means "taking a firm sword, strike thus. "Kill him thus" means thus...

"Kill them by inflicting torture. This is stated because both [the commander and the executioner] have made an effort for the purpose of killing anyone at all, without specifying that "so many lives are to be taken.

For if the commander gives the order, "Pierce him thus; when pierced in this way, so-and-so will die," with the perception that it is a specific person, then the commander is bound by the kamma only upon the death of that specifically designated individual.

They say this. If one who has been commanded shoots an arrow aiming specifically at "so-and-so," while the commander gave the order without specifying [the victim], it should be understood that the commander is bound by the kamma for the death of anyone [who dies], whereas the one who was commanded is bound only for the death of the specified person.
"In the middle" means in the middle of the elephant's back. "By this" refers to the scriptural statement beginning with "having resolved, he commands," and so forth.
"Regarding that" refers to the case of commanding.

Although the specific details of the action have not been recorded in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), because the specific details of the action— such as "pierce thus," "strike thus," or "kill thus"—
are mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*), these specific details of the action, which have come down through the succession of teachers, [should also be understood].
Presenting [the meaning] by taking it from the comparison with the Pāli text, he said: "Another method," and so forth.

"Piercing" (*vijjana*) means piercing with spears, arrows, and the like. "Cutting" (*chedana*) means cutting off hands, feet, and so forth with swords and the like. "Breaking" (*bhedana*) means splitting or making into two parts the head and other limbs with clubs and the like.
"The shell-headed" (*saṅkhamuṇḍaka*) refers to having the skin of the skull, together with the hair, torn away and [covered] with coarse gravel...
The practice of "conch-shell shaving" consists of heating a leaden cauldron and using it to produce the color of a conch shell [on the head].
By the word "etcetera," one includes such things as the *biḷaṅgathālika* (the "bile-pot" punishment) and so forth.

Furthermore, the specific rules regarding striking, piercing, and so on, in particular parts of the body—such as "striking the chest," "striking the back," or "striking the neck"—are also merely specific types of actions.
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), this [term] is included even for cases where death is caused by entering into specific parts of the body, such as the head or the neck;
however, regarding the commentary passage in the *Sāratthadīpanī* which says, "Strike him in front and kill him," etc., the explanation of its intended meaning is as follows:
"Because the front part and so forth are similar in nature to the [original] object, they are included by the mention of the 'object' itself; thus he said, 'striking in front,' and so on."

Since that [definition] was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding the specific nature of the action in the context of whether or not one inflicts a wound on a part of the body such as the head or the skull, it is not appropriate here.
For a "discrepancy regarding the object" (*vatthuvisaṃvāda*) consists solely in killing one person when another was commanded to be killed;
it does not consist in a discrepancy regarding the bodily location where one was commanded to strike. Therefore, he said: "Having deceived the object... [etc.]"
Then he kills another. Or [he says], "Kill by striking from the front... and so on... up to "...there is no bondage of kamma.

This, however, is understood to have been stated in order to show the absence of bondage of kamma even in the case of the "instruction" (āṇatti) offense, by means of a specific distinction in the action (*kriyā*) despite the lack of a formal agreement (*visaṅketa*).
Therefore, rather than merely saying "killing without deceiving the victim," it says "according to the instruction."
The specification of the particular action is also shown; otherwise, the statement "according to the command" would result in being rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, in the description of the object (*vatthu*), it is stated only as "the object is the living being to be killed," and not as "also the part of the body to be struck according to the command.
Therefore, even striking [the victim] from the front is indeed a specific action.
"It is included" is our position; it should be accepted after investigation. "By way of a specific object" means by way of a specific deceased being, such as a mother and so forth.
"A specific action" refers to a specific action such as an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed. "A specific offense" refers to a specific offense such as a *pārājika*.
"Whenever at the forenoon" means at the forenoon of any day whatsoever, other than the day on which the command was given.
Regarding the phrase "standing in a village," the mention of a "village" is intended to specify the person, not to specify the location;
therefore, it is said that "wherever one kills, there is no discrepancy.

By this, when there is no desire to restrict the time, place, weapon, posture, or specific action, for the commander who desires death by whatever means possible, [the offense is established] by virtue of what has issued from his mouth.
It is made known that even when there is a discrepancy in the stipulated conditions of place, time, and so forth, one is nonetheless bound by the kamma.
However, for one who— though desiring death itself at any place, at any time, and in any manner whatsoever—

desires to be released from the impulsion of unwholesome states due to a lapse in time and other factors, and thus makes a stipulation regarding time and so forth under some pretext, [he incurs] the *pārājika* offense of "human form" (*manussaviggaha-pārājika*).
It should be understood by reflecting on how, because there is no release even through a change of circumstances, one remains bound by karma despite the lapse of time or other conditions;
however, some do not accept this, so it must be investigated. "With the snout" means with the very tip. "With the sword-hilt" means with the handle of the sword.
By saying "this person goes," it is the individual who is specified by the act of going, not the posture itself; therefore he said, "there is no lapse of conditions."

Even when it is said, “Kill the long one,” because there are many things that have a long shape, and because it has not been specified by a characteristic unique to others—such as “Kill such-and-one who is long and of such-and-such a kind”—it is said that “he commands without specifying.
For this very reason, he says, “I kill whatever is like that. And here, having mentally specified one among the many things with a long shape, [the command is given].
They say that even when [the order] has been spoken, because it is not restricted by speech, there is no breach of convention if someone else similar [to the intended victim] is killed.
Since, apart from oneself, the characteristic factor of perceiving a living being as a living being is absent in another person's life, there is no act of taking life;
thus he said, "The one who gives the command is released. When there is a restriction of location, such as "seated in such-and-such a place," directed toward oneself—

It is said that "for whomever, wherever they may be sitting, a murderous intent arises directed toward their life-faculty (jīvitindriya), neither the killer nor the one who gives the command is released. For when one points out a specific location, it is because one intends to kill whoever is sitting in that place;
yet at that time, one is not oneself present there. Therefore, it refers specifically to the person sitting there together with that location.
It should be understood that the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is the object, not the self. However, if one sits down there oneself and,
having specified only one’s own sitting place, says, "Kill [him]," and another person sitting there is killed,
then the murderous volition (vadhakacetanā) occurs with respect to the life of both that person and oneself, provided that the other person is killed there.

It should be understood that the one who gives the command is bound by the offense. In such a matter, the determination of the movement of the mind is within the domain of the Buddha and not within the domain of others;
therefore, he said, "Thus, no disregard should be shown here.
In this way, first of all, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the teacher who commands, provided that the one being commanded does not act according to his intention.
At the moment of the teacher’s command, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, if he proceeds according to his intention, then at the moment of the command, there is precisely that which is later described as a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
But if he necessarily causes him to be killed, then at the very moment of the command, there is a defeat (*pārājika*) for him, as it is later stated: "There is an offense of defeat for all."

It should not be understood that there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or grave offenses (*thullaccaya*). Regarding "there is also wrong-doing for them": this refers to the wrong-doing incurred by Buddharakkhita and the others due to their reporting [the deed]. And this [consequence] is consistent with the case where Saṅgharakkhita’s life was not taken, according to the rule of the formal instruction (*yathāṇatti*);
if his life had been taken, they too would incur a defeat offense (*pārājika*) at the very moment of their reporting. "As soon as it is accepted" means necessarily...
This was stated for the purpose of illustrating the nature of the act of receiving, not to show that a grave offense (thullaccaya) occurs at the very moment it is received.
For if he is certain to receive it but will not bring the formal act (kamma) to completion,
it should be understood that the teacher incurs a grave offense at the very moment of his command.
“The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) applies only to the root [act]”—this is merely an illustration of the method found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*;
it is not, however, what he himself intends. Therefore, he says, “Such being the case,” and so forth; the meaning is: “such being the sense according to the method stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
“There would be no offense in the acceptance” refers to the acceptance of death from an executioner, saying, “Very well, excellent!”

There would be no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭāpatti) even in such a case; thus, first of all, there is a dukkaṭa even for an object that is not gross—how much more so, then, for accepting [a gift] for the purpose of death?
It is for the sake of showing this that the acceptance of a go-between and so forth are cited.

Furthermore, when there is a dukkaṭa for rejoicing in the acceptance of a go-between and so forth, it is for the sake of showing the rejoicing in death, thinking: "Oh, may such-and-such a person be killed!"
The intention is indeed: "I shall kill him," regarding the acceptance of the death [of another].

By the restriction that "this is an *dukkaṭa* for the one who accepts it," it is shown that there is no offense at all for the original instigator (*mūlaṭṭha*) on account of the acceptance by Saṅgharakkhita;
because there was no prior agreement, he incurs only the *dukkaṭa* for the first command. However, some say: "Even for the original instigator..."
They say, "It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," but that is not correct, because it is impossible for two offenses of wrong-doing to arise from a single act.
"In the previous manner" refers to the immediately preceding description of the messenger who did not refuse. "This" refers to the offense of wrong-doing.

"Because of the absence of opportunity" means that since the grave offense (thullaccaya) pertaining to the primary agent is being discussed, the offense of wrong-doing for the one receiving [the message] is not mentioned due to the absence of opportunity.
However, the intention is not that there is an absence of an offense.
175. Because he himself was the senior elder of the Saṅgha, it is said, "at the time of attendance. Regarding the statement "for every word, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)":
this refers to speaking not with the intention, "Let anyone who hears my words kill this person," but merely by way of expressing a longing for death.
Because it has been stated thus, even the speech such as "thieves will not kill him" is said to be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding "with reference to two": this means with reference to two individuals, or with reference to the death of two.

Even though the volition that initiates the action is one when praising death for both, it attains a state of intensity characterized by being described as "two acts of taking life," which then enters into rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
Because it has a great result (*mahāvipāka*), it is called "a heap of unwholesome deeds" (*akusalarāsi*). The same principle applies even when one praises death for the sake of many people.

As for the phrase "so many acts of killing" (*tattakā pāṇātipātā*): since the volition (*cetanā*) proceeds by taking as its object all the present and future life-faculties (*jīvitindriya*) of as many beings as will die upon hearing the praise, there are "so many acts of killing."
The meaning is that while the result of the process (*pavattivipāka*) must be given by as many volitions (*cetanā*) as there are, that single volition alone is capable of giving it;

however, it should be understood that regarding the rebirth-result (*paṭisandhivipāka*), both the volition itself and the preceding and succeeding volitions are each individually capable of giving it.
"From whose hands" means from the hands of those relatives, those who have invited him, and so forth; and this refers to the monk’s [handling of] the root-value of money (*rūpiyamūla*).

This was said with reference to non-existence; that is, if one releases [the book] after taking the price oneself, it should be understood that even if the price is not taken, the fact that the book has been made the property of its owner is the authoritative criterion here.
"Those curious to see the writing" means those who, having seen beautiful characters, or wishing to look at it thinking, "What kind of book is this? desire to examine it.
"Because it is an application for the taking of life" means because it is an application that brings to completion the separation of life from the body.

However, for one who disturbs a living plant for the purpose of digging a pit, or for the purpose of obtaining a spade and so forth, or for the purpose of producing iron seedlings, or for the purpose of a spade-handle and so forth, there is only a *pācittiya* offense.
This is because there is an absence of an application for the taking of life, as in the prior application for the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*).

Just as in the case of the second search and so forth, it should be understood here that where there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), there is a dukkaṭa, and where there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) such as false speech, there is indeed a pācittiya.
"In measure" means in the measure determined by oneself. "Having trimmed" means having trimmed away the raised portions.
"The last dust-tray" means the very final dust-tray. [This is said] because of the desire to finish with the thought, "This much is enough."
The volition that accomplishes the very last application is the "concluding volition" (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*).
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, this is stated with reference to one who completes [the act] by digging while the application remains unceased even on a single day;
however, in other commentaries, it refers to one who acts with the intention, "Let him fall into this and die," on a single [day].
This was said with reference to one who, having dug a little on one day, completes it by digging a little more on the following day;
in this way, the mutual contradictions between the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathās) should be understood. "By their own nature" means either unknowingly or through negligence.
"Even Arahants are included in the collection" refers to those who, though not wishing to die, are carried away by others.
It is stated that the death of Arahants is possible. "In the manner previously described" means according to the method stated as: "Those who desire to die will die here.

"A discrepancy" (visaṅketa) means that because [the act] was directed toward those who desired to die and those who desired to kill, there is no karmic bond regarding the death of those who did not desire to die; this is the meaning.
"Having removed what has fallen there outside": this is said because death occurs as a consequence of falling there.

It should be understood that even if one who has fallen into a pit dies after staying for a short while before departing—whether he is killed after being seized, or dies while walking afflicted by a disease contracted from falling there, or dies by tripping and falling upon rocks and the like—the pit-digger is not released from his liability.

Because the intention "desiring not to die" is possible [in that case], it is stated that even for one who has died after being unable to emerge from a spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), there is a *pārājika* offense.
If it is argued that no falling is seen because it is stated "[having been] reborn," there is no contradiction, for in that instance, his very rebirth itself constitutes the falling.
Since he is a matricide when his mother—who had fallen and undergone a change of gender—has died...

It is not only one who kills a human male; therefore, with the intention that the offense occurs by virtue of the victim having fallen [into such a state], it is said that "the form of falling is the measure.
However, this is not a valid reason, because even when the gender is transformed, the continuity of the single stream of existence (*ekasantāna*) has not ceased.
This is so even for one who deprives of life a mother or a father who has become human, even if their gender has been transformed.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The action is an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). However, by whatever nature beings are born, by that very same nature they die;
that indeed is their nature even when grasping another form. Thus, it is said: "The form of death itself is the criterion;
therefore, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The latter position is the authoritative one. This being the case, [the text says] in the *Pāḷi*: "Whether a *yakkha* or a *peta*..."
If a yakkha or a peta, or a form belonging to the animal realm or the human realm, falls upon it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When it has fallen and painful sensation arises, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If it dies, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya). Why was this said?
There is no fault here; for after first showing its own form as "a yakkha or a peta," even if it assumes another form...
In order to show that [the offense applies] even when [the being] is already present as a *yakkha* or a *peta*, it is stated: "or one appearing in the form of an animal or a human.
Therefore, the construction here should be made thus: "a *yakkha* or a *peta* appearing in the form of an animal or in the form of a human.
However, some say: "It appears as if a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is mentioned by singling out animals who exist in human form."
That is not appropriate, because it must be stated that [the victim] was either an animal or a human being, and because this distinction is not mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

By the phrase "even when [the victim] has died in the form of a *yakkha* or a *peta*, the same principle applies," he extends the application of the grave offense (*thullaccaya*) by taking the appearance at the time of death as the criterion. "For nothing" means without a root-offense.
"He is blameless" is because there was no preparatory effort (*payoga*) made toward him in that instance; however, if even he...
In this context, he said "fallen thus," and so forth, demonstrating that whatever one does there, one is not released.
Therein, "thus" means "done by me in this way. "They will not perish" means they will not go out of sight;
the intention is that they will not escape. Or, "they will be easy to extract"—this shows the purpose for filling up a deep pit.
The intention is that once the pit has been made wide, it will be easy for us to seize and kill [the victim] quickly.
The phrase "when remorse has arisen" is said with reference to the primary agent (*mūlaṭṭha*).
However, if even the subsequent person, having obtained [the victim], performs some act of the kind described therein and then acts likewise when remorse arises, the same rule applies to him as well.
The phrase "the earth that has been produced is produced" is stated for the purpose of showing that even when another pit is dug later on, one is still released;
it should be understood that one is indeed released even if, having made it like the earth already produced, one pounds it well again and fills it more firmly.
"Harder" means having bound it together with successive layers of bamboo strips for the sake of making it stable, or [binding] that very [earth] itself.
Or, having tied a slack snare tighter, he leaves it there. "A post" (*khāṇuka*) refers to a post for binding the snare-staff.

"Having cut a reed growing there, he is released"—this means that because a staff standing as it was in the forest had not been cut at its base and had been left there made fit for binding a snare, someone else might bind a snare there; [but] one standing at the base...
It is not released; however, it is said that it is released only after being cut at the root and broken into pieces, for the purpose of demonstrating this.
"With ropes" means with ropes made by twisting fibers once. "Twisted by oneself" means twisted by one's own hand, having been made thin and doubled or tripled.
