"Having unwound" means having restored it to its original state. "Even while guarding" means...
"Even one who guards [the tree] by treating it as diamond, diamond.
(177) "The 'support-tree' (*ālambana-rukkha*)" is said with reference to one grown there.

"Having made it for that very purpose" means having had a tool such as an axe made by means of raising iron spikes and so forth, specifically for the purpose of killing. "Ordinary" refers to a natural tool made by others.
The meaning is that, having obtained [it], it is established in the sense of being a root (*mūla*). "It is released" means the sense of being a root is released.
"An uneven circle" refers to an unevenly smeared area on beds, chairs, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having spoken, he places a sword nearby": here, even when placing it nearby after thinking it in the mind rather than speaking it with the mouth...
The same method applies. "By the previous method" means by the passage beginning, "from whose hands the price was taken," and so forth.

A "disease of a discordant type" (visabhāgaroga) is so called because it causes deformity such as leprosy (*kuṭṭha*), or because it is an obstacle to the continuation of life, such as through boils or pustules. 178.
"The same method applies even to what is pleasing": by this, [the commentator explains] that which is a pleasing form in the phrase "he brings about a pleasing form."
It shows that one should apply [the text] such as: "he places it near him," or "he stands possessed of a form pleasing to himself," and so forth.
"Having adorned [him], he brings him near" means he brings him near with the intention: "Let him die having withered away from lack of food. For this very reason it is said:
"If he dies out of fear, there is a failure of the agreement (*visaṅketa*). Having withered away from lack of food...
In the phrase "dies," the remainder of the text should be understood as "an offense entailing expulsion" (*pārājika*).
"Mahākacchu" is a specific kind of vine-fruit; its shape is like a cat's paw, and it has fine hairs that are painful to the touch.
"Haṃsapuppha" refers to the wing-feathers of swans and other such birds. If it dies by its own nature, there is no offense—meaning there is no *pārājika*.
It was said with intentional reference [to the offense], because one is not released from the *dukkaṭa*.
(179) Regarding the phrase "unintentionally" (*asañcicca*), he said "by means of this effort," and so forth, because this refers to the lack of observation regarding an effort that leads to death.
Furthermore, the phrase "of one who does not know" (*ajānantassa*) refers to the performance of an effort involving poison and the like that leads to death.
He said, "It was spoken with reference to ignorance," regarding the passage beginning with "by this one will die.

He said, "Not for one who intends death," meaning that this was spoken with reference to the absence of the intention to die even in one who knows they are undertaking a means that produces suffering;

thus he said, "for one not desiring death," and so forth. "Due to the absence of continuity" means due to the absence of the uninterrupted occurrence of the mental pathways of dejection (*domanassa*).
The method of commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.
Commentary on the cases of training (vinītavatthu) 180.
"By way of conventional usage" means by way of the preliminary conventional usage, at the moment of the decisive volition of one who intends death.
The intention is that, due to the absence of compassion (*karuṇā*), it is not like the releasing of a pig caught in a snare out of pity.
The phrase "according to its lifespan" (*yathāyu*) is stated by way of a synonym as "according to its continuity" (*yathānusandhi*).
He said, "in which no fold is discerned," because below [that point], if anything exists, it takes on a fold. And this reflection (*paṭivekkhaṇa*) is for householders.

"It should be understood as 'belonging to oneself' (*santake eva*). In the Pāḷi, 'having raised the pestles' (*musale ussite*) means that two pestles have been placed leaning against a wall, having propped each other up.
'A wooden implement for the mortar' (*udukkhalabhaṇḍikaṃ*) refers to a wooden object brought in for the purpose of a mortar.
'An obstruction' (*paribandhaṃ*) means an obstruction to eating; it is said to be an obstacle to food."

181. Regarding the term *aggakārikā*: although one might explain the meaning as "the foremost act" (*aggakiriya*) because the word *kārika* here denotes an abstract state, since it is impossible to give away an "act," one must understand that what is intended here—by way of figurative usage—is the alms-food itself associated with that foremost act known as giving.
Thus he said, "The alms obtained first," and so forth.
182–3. "By means of sticks, clubs, picks, shuttles, and so forth": here, a *daṇḍa* is a long stick; a *muggara* is a short one;
a *vema* is the weaving implement of weavers, by which they beat the stretched-out thread. "By the alteration of case-endings" means by the transformation of grammatical cases.
"The attainment of distinction" refers to both concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Special attainment" (*visesādhigama*) means the acquisition of supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*).
"Having declared" (*byākaritvā*) means having announced; this is stated for the purpose of showing that a special attainment has been reached.

For monks who possess a sense of shame (*lajjībhikkhu*) will inevitably declare their attainment so that others may follow their example; yet, even without declaring their attainment, one might still cease taking food.
It is not permitted; for since the cutting off of food was authorized solely for the purpose of removing obstacles to attainment, it must certainly not be done once that attainment has been reached.
But is it then permissible to announce one's attainment? To this he says, "to those who are like-minded," and so forth.
"Or washing their belongings" means washing their robes. "A washing-stick" means a stick for washing robes.

185. Regarding the phrase "having caused it to be crushed, he causes it to fall," it is stated that this constitutes a *visaṅketa* (non-agreement) because the original instruction was not carried out.

However, if the one giving the order speaks figuratively—referring to both the act of crushing and the act of causing it to be crushed—by saying, "Having crushed it, cause it to fall," it should be understood that there is no *visaṅketa*.
Because it was stated, "or he should praise the appearance of death," he says: "A 'synonym' (*pariyāya*)..."
"There is none"—the intention is that there is no release from the offense by way of a formal method.

For one who gives medicine even before conception for the purpose of preventing birth, thinking "the embryo will perish after having arisen in the womb," in the case of those who die accordingly, there is a bond of karma;
[but] for one who gives it with the intention that "it shall not arise in the womb" [there is no such bond].
Once given, whether they die or not, there is no binding by karma.

"Those who share the same Dhamma" means those who, within the teaching of a single Teacher, have undertaken the training together; or those who are engaged in the state of training according to the precepts of the Dhamma.
By the phrase "those of equal virtue and faith," etc., it is meant that this does not apply to those of bad character or those with differing views.
This shows that it may be obtained even when not made. "From a place where kinsmen have invited" means from a place where one's own kinsmen or theirs have invited.
An invitation (*viññatti*) that has not been made by noble ones (*ariya*), in the sense of being improper or never having been done before, is called an "unmade invitation.

"He prepares" means he procures. Regarding the statement "it is not permissible to fail to make [the invitation]," they say there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here, precisely because of its impropriety.
In this context, it should be understood that the prohibition concerns non-performance [of the duty], not on account of an offense.
"As long as the relatives see" means as long as his relatives see.

"Paternal aunt" (pitubhaginī) means the father’s sister. "Maternal uncle" (mātubhātā) means the mother’s brother. "They are unable" means they are not capable of performing [the service]. "They do not request" means...
Out of shame, they do not ask. Because it is stated, "having made an intention (*ābhoga*)," there is indeed an offense for one who gives otherwise.

However, some say, "it is permissible to give even without making an intention"; that is not correct, because in the Canon, regarding the preparation of medicine, an intermediate offense is shown by stating:
"There is no offense for the monk regarding a *pārājika*, but there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."

Because it is prohibited by way of its general nature (*sāmaññato*), it should be understood that an offense is established by the Sutta itself for one who acts in a manner not specifically mentioned in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For this very reason, the Commentary also states: "belonging to those very [people]," and so forth.

"Others" refers to those who are not blood relations; thus he says: "through the succession of their children," and so on. "Family circle" (*kulaparivaṭṭo*) means the lineage of kinsmen within a family.
"Of one who prepares medicine" means of one who prepares it according to the aforementioned method;

however, even for one who gives it without forming the intention, "I shall give this as a temporary loan," there is an intermediate offense of *dukkaṭa*, yet—provided it is done without wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) or corrupting a family—it does not constitute such a fault.
Therefore he said: "There is neither the act of a physician nor the offense of corrupting a family. For [this applies] when it is the property of relatives.

It is permissible to take [medicine] even after asking for it; therefore, there shall be no corruption of families or similar faults in that regard. "In all instances" refers to all phrases such as "of the younger mother," and so forth.

The statement "We are bringing [it] for the preceptor" is said for the purpose of showing the procedure to be performed by those who have been commanded by the preceptor, saying, "Bring medicine for my relatives.
And by this, [it is shown that] even for novices and others, [there is no fault] regarding another person’s [belongings], provided there is no expectation of reward.

This shows that making medicine [for oneself] is not permitted. By the phrase "having sought it in the manner already described," he extends the meaning stated by the phrases "by means of the conduct of alms-gathering" and "by means of one's own kinsmen or novices.
By the phrase "without expectation," even when providing for guests, thieves, and so forth, one should not think, "People are indeed helpful," and thus expect gain from them for oneself.

"By one who does not expect anything in return. The intention is that for one who acts with expectation, there are faults such as performing medical treatment and bringing disgrace upon one's family. However, there is no fault in doing so when it is done with the thought:
"When such assistance has been rendered, they will gain confidence upon learning the virtues of the Teaching, or they will become benefactors of the Saṅgha.
Some, however, [hold that] even for guests and other persons whose presence is prohibited, [one may act] without expecting anything in return...
If they say, "It is permissible to give," that is not correct; for it would follow that the distinction between what ought and ought not to be done would be rendered meaningless.

One should simply state this much: "For one who does not expect anything in return, it is permissible to give and to perform [services] for all. Furthermore, this lack of expectation is stated solely for the purpose of preventing faults such as wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) and the defiling of families (*kuladūsana*), in the context of this practice known as the preparation of medicine.

It should be understood that one is released from that offense simply by giving to those who have been permitted—such as newcomers, thieves, and others—for the purpose of being freed from an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*).
For that very reason, in order to show a place where this should not be done even by one who does not expect anything in return, it is said: "to a faithful family," and so forth.
By the phrase "they ask," it is indicated that wandering about by alternating between those who have seen and those who have not seen the sick is improper.
He shows this. However, they say that even for one who asks and expects a reply, a figurative discourse (*pariyāyakathā*) is not permissible.
"He conversed" means that, without expecting anything in return, he thus initiated a mutual discussion.

"The portion of a teacher" means the status of a medical teacher by way of prescribing medicine without violating the conduct of the Vinaya. That which was being accepted for the purpose of honoring with flowers—
Since silver is inherently subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) by virtue of being one's own property, he said, "having had it accepted as something allowable" (*kappiya*);

the meaning is: having rejected it by saying, "Silver is not permitted for us, but flowers are permitted for the purpose of flower-worship," and so forth, and having had it accepted through an allowable transaction.
If, when told "Recite a protective charm (*paritta*)," they do so, it is said that "it should not be done," because it would be like performing medical treatment or a layperson's work.

However, when told "Recite the Dhamma," since this is a request for the Dhamma, the Dhamma may be recited even by one who has not been requested, let alone by one who has been requested; thus it is said "it should be done. "Having moved the thread and rubbed it all over" means:
It is said that when one has performed this protection with the thought, "I shall enter here under this protection," the protection is then considered to have been entered therein.
Regarding the passage from "From the monastery... down to "...an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," they say this was spoken with reference to an unrelated householder.
As for "having sprinkled water on the feet," this was stated according to the custom in that region; for it is said: "In that place..."
They sprinkle water on the feet of the monks sitting according to the *pāḷi* for the purpose of allaying disease and so forth,
perform a protective recitation (*paritta*), and having placed a thread [around the feet], they say, “Recite the *paritta*,” and then depart.
For if they were to remove the thread while this is being done, people would think it is an ill omen, or the disease might not be allayed.”

Therefore he said, "The feet should not be removed. Just as when seeing a dead body, so too when merely seeing a cemetery, the perception of death arises, thinking, "This is the place where born beings go to their destruction"; thus he said, "When visiting a charnel ground...

it is permissible to go under the heading of a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), thinking, 'We shall acquire mindfulness of death. This was said without resorting to figurative interpretation (lesa-kappa).
If one says, "Let them come for the sake of an entourage," it is permissible to go even with a mind that has arisen in purity.
"Almsfood not touched" means that its first portion has not been taken; the meaning is that it has not been consumed.
"It is worth a kahāpaṇa" indicates that the donors have prepared many kinds of food and given it with due respect. "In a bowl" refers to a bowl belonging to the Saṅgha.
"In a bowl made of bronze and so forth" includes a plate here as well. By the phrase "it is not allowable," he indicates that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Of a murderous thief" refers to a notorious thief who seeks to seize a kingdom. The connection is: "even when [the food] is not being given, they become angry, thinking, 'They are not giving.
This refers to the resentment arising between oneself and another due to the failure to obtain material goods or the Dhamma.
“Patisanthāra” (hospitality) is the covering up or closing of a gap or opening; it is, moreover, twofold: by way of material goods (*āmisa*) and by way of the Dhamma.
With reference to hospitality consisting of material goods, it was asked: “To whom should it be performed? To whom should it not be performed?
To make clear the meaning stated in brief as “It should indeed be performed for a guest...,” [the text] speaks of the guest:
He spoke beginning with the words “tāvātītaṃ. By the phrase “whose provisions are exhausted,” he shows their state of being without means of subsistence and their worthiness as objects of compassion;
by this, it is established that it is not permissible to give even to prosperous donors and others who are strangers, provided they are the opposite of those [in need].
When rice and such are to be given, it is said: “It should not be said at an improper time... etc. “By one who does not expect anything in return.”
Having said this, the words "human beings," and so forth, were spoken in order to demonstrate the manner of the expectation [of a reward].
However, it is not permissible to give even without expecting a reward to those who have not been authorized, because that would be a misappropriation of what was given in faith;

furthermore, when there is an expectation [of a reward], there is also the defilement of the family. "Having cleared away" means having caused the people plundering for three leagues all around to flee. "A variegated rug of choice cloth" refers to a carpet variegated with many kinds of excellent forms, such as men and women.

187. Among the group of seventeen, because one had previously been killed by the poking of a finger, it is said that "the remaining fifteen persons" refers to all except for one who was sitting with his belly resting upon [another].

"Like millstones" means like stones placed upon a millstone. "With the intention of performing formal acts" means with the intention of carrying out formal acts such as the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*).

"Having summoned" means having caused [a spirit] to enter. "Having made a form and cutting off its hands, feet, and so forth" means that after summoning a non-human being into that form made of flour and other materials, they cut off its hands, feet, and so forth.
"One might kill Sakka, the king of the gods"—this was said by way of exaggeration; for such powerful *yakkhas* do not deserve to be struck with a weapon.
Even in the battle between the devas and asuras, there was no death for them due to the striking of weapons. 188.
"A blow must not be given"—this is the connection [of the rule]. For one who strikes a non-human being with a mind of anger, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense.
For one who strikes with the intention of medical treatment, it should be understood as an *anācāra* (improper conduct). A palm leaf... [etc. ...should be tied.
It is said that non-human beings flee by means of binding them with palm leaves; furthermore, it is not permitted for laypeople to perform this as a medical treatment.

Regarding the passage beginning, "Even one who has been crushed by a tree does not die," whatever needs to be said about those cases will be explained by the author himself in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the Bhūtagāma training rule; that should be consulted there.
"Requisites made of wood" refers to those things set aside after being cut by certain people, which are thus possessed.
For in that case, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated for one who intends destruction by means of not displacing [the fire] from its place.
It is also stated that there is a *dukkaṭa* even with the intention of sport, referring to making a fire on dry grass and the like;
however, if one acts with the intention of play upon things that are moist, there is indeed a *pācittiya*. *Paṭaggi* is a fire that is opposed to, or moving against, [another fire].
Giving even grass and other such things while they are wet is permitted;

when one sees a forest fire approaching from afar, instead of giving [the wet materials] all around the monastery at once, one should begin from one side and slowly burn them all around the monastery so that even a large fire is unable to reach the monastery. Thus, all around the monastery—
Having cleared an open space, a counter-fire should be set; it goes toward the forest fire, meets it, and merges with it, thereby being extinguished along with it.
"Performing a protective rite" means providing protection by cutting down trees and grass on all sides, digging a trench, and so forth;
thus he says, "covering the ground all around the grass huts," and so on.

191. Regarding the phrase "an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) because of entering the field": since even one of the two is included within it, it is an offense entailing expulsion because of entering even one of the fields mentioned as "by two.
However, when it is restricted by the rule, "only by two murderers, not by one," they say that if he is killed by only one, there is no offense entailing expulsion;
this applies likewise to cases such as "only two men" and so forth. This is because of the prior application of the act of cutting off the head.
No other application (payoga) that cuts off the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is found;
rather, it is by the first application that his life-faculty is cut off. Therefore, it is said, "of one who has his head cut off.

As for the reason stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, "because the life-faculty does not exist," that is not a valid reason, because [the mind] is a continuity of consciousness dependent upon the life-faculty.
Because movement occurring over the course of a day—such as that involved in lifting up, setting down, and so forth—is impossible without [the momentum of] speed.
For the body does not move like leaves, cloth, and the like by the force of the wind;

nor can it be said that the mind-born intimation (*cittaja-viññatti*) and so forth, which operate during the act of lifting, are themselves the cause for setting down and other such actions, because they occur in discrete, interrupted moments. Even those who have not previously acquired momentum...
For instance, when a certain species of reptile is cut in two, it continues to move in both directions for a few moments as soon as it is severed;

and in that case, the five-door adverting consciousness, remaining in the portion where the heart-base is located, arises having taken as its object the tangible impression impinging upon the body-sensibility in both portions;
thereafter, it is precisely that [consciousness] which becomes the registration-consciousness (tadārammaṇa).
In this manner, body-consciousness arises by way of succession— once in one part and at another time in another part—

and from that, within the heart-base itself, there arise the receiving and other process-cittas (interrupted by the life-continuum) as well as mind-door process-consciousnesses that produce intimation; for it is these that move, vibrate, or quiver throughout both parts.
Or rather, due to the mind’s rapid revolution, both sides appear as if they were moving simultaneously at a single moment.
This should be understood as being just like the experience of a being whose entire body is submerged in hells such as Kukkuḷa;
just as bodily-consciousness and pain arise throughout his whole body at one and the same instant, so too should this case be regarded. Thereafter...
However, in that part where the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—along with the material form born of residual karma—ceases, bodily consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*) does not arise there;
it arises only in the part associated with the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), continuing until the cessation of the life-faculty.
Is it not the case that in hells and other realms, since the body is a single connected whole, the arising of bodily consciousness is logically appropriate throughout by way of succession?
Let it be so; but how is it when [the body] has split into two and is divided into two parts? This is not a fault.

For in the case of a body, there is no such thing as "being bound together" (ekābaddhatā) apart from ultimate phenomena (paramatthadhamma), unlike the "whole" (avayavin) and other such concepts of rival theorists.

Rather, "being bound together" is simply the simultaneous arising of many [factors] dependent upon a single causal complex, such as karma. And in that state, through the encounter with adverse conditions such as a blow from a weapon—
Even for distinct [factors] such as karma and so forth, their dependence on the aggregate does not cease;

as long as that [dependence] does not cease, the occurrence of consciousness therein remains uninterrupted. However, distinct material phenomena born of karma, as well as other remaining material phenomena in the continuity of the mental stream, are unable to persist for long by way of providing support, and until—
As long as they persist, they remain conditions for consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and by means of consciousness, there occurs the arising of other states such as movement and locomotion in them.
Therefore, even in the case of a headless trunk (*kabandha*) at the moment it is running, the life-faculty accompanied by consciousness (*saviññāṇajīvitindriya*) certainly exists;

and that [life-faculty] falls quickly only through the application of the decapitation itself, because any other application produces a specific change in the body only after that initial [application].

Because the deed has been accomplished, he should be understood as being bound by the kamma of one who has actually severed the head. "Of such a kind" means similar to the case of the headless trunk (kabandha).
"Of this case" refers to the case of the execution ground. "In the exposition of the meaning" means in the elucidation of the matter consisting of being killed by a single person or by a single act.

192. The connection is: "It is permissible through the consumption of food. However, because it has been stated thus, [it is said]: "Salted sour gruel (*soyīraka*) is for the duration of a watch (*yāmakālika*)."

Some say [it is seven-day medicine]; others, however, because it is stated that "for the sick it is as usual, but for those who are not sick it is mixed with water," say that "like sugar, it is seven-day medicine.
Thus, in the *Vimativinodanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā...
The method of commentary on the third *pārājika* is finished.
4. The fourth *pārājika*:
Commentary on the account of the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River.
193. "Adhiṭṭhema" means we agree. "Having composed his posture" means having made it conform to his exertion (*padhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "if there were no connection with the future," he supplies the ellipsis "it will be spoken" to mean "if there were no connection with the future.
To the question, "How does a past statement [bhāsito] come to be connected with a future statement?", he says: "But the characteristic... and so forth.

For in such a case, those learned in the science of grammar state that when there is a connection between the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*), by the rule "conditioning factors [are applied] when there is a connection between roots," the conditioning factors are valid even if they are prescribed at an incorrect time. 194.

By the word *vaṇṇavā* ("possessing color"), the state of having newly arisen color is expressed. By the phrase *pasannamukhavaṇṇā* ("with a clear facial complexion"), [the clarity] of the facial complexion...
Excessive thinness has been mentioned. By the phrase "the complexion of the skin is serene," the serenity of the natural body-complexion itself is stated according to the method already described.
Since nourishment occurs through the very support [of the body] because the sense-faculties are derived matter (*upādārūpa*), he said: "because the space occupied is full.
He said this because the fullness of the heart-matter (*hadayarūpa*) is indeed stated just as the fullness of the fivefold clarity (*pañcappasāda*).
"Of the faculties with the mind as the sixth": the connection is that those who applied themselves to the summary and the inquiry did not attain this beauty of the body.
Regarding "yathā tanti," here *tanti* is merely a particle.
Regarding "catucakkam," here the postures (*iriyāpatha*) alone are called "wheels" (*cakkam*) in the sense of proceeding.
195. *Upalabbhanti* means they are seen; the sense is that they are known. *Pacanto* means one who oppresses, or one who himself burns houses and so forth, or one who causes others to burn them.
*Uddhato* refers to one whose nature is characterized by restlessness (*uddhacca*).

*Unnaḷo* means accompanied by an elevated and empty pride, like a stalk that has grown tall. *Capalo* means endowed with fickleness through such things as the decoration of one’s bowl and robes. *Mukharo*...
"Harsh speech. "With natural faculties" means that because they are unrestrained, their faculties remain in their natural state, just as they were during the time they were householders.
"The establishment of postures, etc."—by the word "etc.," it should be understood that the inclusion of the use of requisites and ordinary conversation is intended.
"Dwellings inhabited by monks who live according to the most austere way of life through the Great Noble Lineages" are called "dwellings esteemed by the world. "To bring to maturity."

To transform [the mind] by means of amazement. Regarding the phrase "when one is not successful in the alms-round," this should be connected with the words "wandering on a tour of the countryside," and not with "teaching the scriptures" and so forth;

for those terms were spoken to show the duties to be performed both in one's own place of continuous residence and in the countryside, and they perform them under the heading of proper conduct (*vatta*).
Not for the sake of gain; therefore he said, "a string," and so forth. "With difficulty" is a synonym for this very term, "with exertion.
Both of these are stated with reference to the effort required to fulfill the perfections (*pāramī*). "By way of being common property" means by way of being the property of the Saṅgha.
"Having stolen it because of its being such" means having stolen it because it is not to be distributed or divided, and not by way of moving it from its place.
This is the intended meaning; therefore, he said, "one incurs the dukkaṭa offense for corrupting a family.

Regarding the word *asantam* (non-existent), *abhūtam* (unreal) is a statement of the reason; the meaning is that it is non-existent because it has not arisen. *Kitavasseva* means like a gambler catching a bird. *Kerāṭikassa* means of one who is crafty.
*Gotrabhuno* are those who merely follow and bear [the lineage]; thus they are "shramanas in name only."

Meaning: "Difficult to delimit" means that because suffering is infinite, it is difficult even for the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) to know it by way of numerical delimitation as "suffering is this much";
however, it is not impossible to know it in its specific nature (*sarūpa*), for that is not outside the scope of a Buddha’s knowledge.
Commentary on the Basis for Overweening Pride (*adhimāna*).
196. "Arahatta" means the fruit of the highest attainment (agga-phala).

"With the eye of knowledge" means with the eye known as the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), or else with the eye of knowledge associated with the fruition-consciousness itself. For even by means of the knowledge associated with oneself, something is said to be "seen by oneself" because of non-delusion;
thus, the meaning is that [the Buddha] sees even that which was not seen by him [in that specific moment]. This is by way of being the abandoner of all defilements (kilesa).
Because one understands (*ājānāti*), or understands completely in every respect, it is called "full knowledge" (*aññā*); this refers to the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
By way of metaphorical designation (*tadupacārena*), however, its fruit is also so called; thus he said, "They declared full knowledge," meaning they declared *arahatship*.

"He sets aside [the attainment] in between" means he sets aside overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding the stage of the trainee (*sekhabhūmi*). "Not seeing the manifestation of defilements" refers specifically to those [defilements] to be abandoned by the three preceding paths.
This is stated with reference to the defilements (*kilesa*), not to the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) and so forth.
Commentary on the Training Rule with its Analysis (Savibhaṅgasikkhāpada): 197.
"Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to the qualities attained by supreme persons such as the Buddhas, who are superior to ordinary human beings.
He said: "Superhuman states," and so forth. In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase "And these states exist in me," the word *me* (in me) is merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
An inquiry concerning that which is to be attained—that is, the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and so on, which is designated as "attainment"—is an "inquiry into attainment.
And since that inquiry occurs generally with respect to the absorptions and so on, [the text now specifies] therein either the first absorption or one among the second and so forth.
Or even there, among the objects such as the kasiṇas, which object is it? Or among the supramundane states, is it the stream-entry path, or one of the paths beginning with the once-returning path?
Or even there, is it the emptiness liberation, or one of the liberations beginning with the wishless liberation?
Thus, in order to show the manner of questioning by way of distinguishing each individual category, it is stated in the Pāḷi:
It should be understood that the question, “Furthermore, of which states are you a possessor? has been shown; therefore he said, “In the first path, etc.
That sequence of practice by which the supramundane attainment is reached is the preliminary practice, the way of arrival (*āgamanapaṭipadā*).
When asked, “It is not purified,” he speaks by overstepping the sequence of practice. “He should be removed” means by you.
One should be led away from the conceit of having attained [the goal] by the thought that this cannot be attained according to the stated sequence.

Because of being unattached even to the four requisite conditions when they are available and permissible, it is said: "with a mind like a hand in space. The construction is: "the explanation is similar to what was stated.
The practice is similar to the practice of one whose taints are exhausted because the defilements have been well suppressed. And this—
This was said with reference to one who claims to have attained *arahatta*; hence he said, "of one whose taints are destroyed," and so forth.

Thus, the claim of a person whose defilements are well-suppressed that they are still practicing the duties of a trainee (*sekha*) cannot be investigated by means of this arousal of fear, nor by the production of saliva upon seeing sour things and the like;
therefore, it must be accepted on the basis of his word alone: "This bhikkhu has delivered a perfect declaration."
This was not stated solely with reference to one who is fearless; it should be understood as being stated with reference to even certain ordinary persons (puthujjana) of a courageous nature,
who are free from fear, and who— even when presented with objects that provoke lust, such as sour fruits like jujube and tamarind or pungent condiments—
remain entirely purified and devoid of the arising of saliva or the activity of craving.

"Those of evil desires" (*pāpiccha*) is defined as the characteristic of imagining qualities that do not exist; thus he said, "whosoever here," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes the textual passage beginning with "one who is faithless.

"The ascetic life (*sāmañña*) is wrongly grasped" means that the ascetic life, known as the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), is wrongly grasped—that is, poorly taken up—due to broken virtue and so on.
For that person, it leads to hell, meaning to the suffering of hell, in that very hell.
"Draws near" means it causes [the defilements] to arise. "Loose" means made by acting sluggishly or with a lax grasp;
or it is "loose" because it is taken up with guile (*satha*) or deceit (*sāṭheyya*). "The wandering life" (*paribbaja*) refers to the state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*).

"Furthermore" (*bhiyyo*) means that it scatters yet more dust upon the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth that was already present previously. "The state of a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhubhāva*) is established merely by an unrighteous profession.
The state of being a bhikkhu. Regarding the phrase *ajānameva* (“only not knowing”): here the word *eva* functions as a restriction, meaning “only not knowing. There is also the reading *ajānam-eva*;
in that case, however, it should be construed as “I know thus, I see thus.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (*Padabhājanīya*).
199. And thus, the grasping at the first jhāna and so forth is expressed as "I know the first jhāna, the second jhāna, and so on.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the jhānas of foulness (*asubha*), etc.," it includes the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), the kasiṇa jhānas, and the formless (*āruppa*) jhānas rooted in the kasiṇas.
Regarding "liberation" (*vimokkha*), it is the fourfold path; showing its names such as "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and so on by way of its qualities:
He said: "But as for 'they say,' etc. For the path receives its name by way of five reasons:
either by its own essence (*sarasena*), or by its opposite (*paccanīkena*), or by its qualities (*saguṇena*), or by its object (*ārammaṇena*), or by its arrival (*āgamanena*).

For if equanimity regarding formations emerges after having comprehended formations as impermanent, the path is liberated by the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*). If [it emerges] after having comprehended them as suffering..."
He emerges; he is liberated by the desireless liberation. If he emerges after having comprehended [the aggregates] as non-self, he is liberated by the void liberation;
this is what is called "by its own essence. But because he has arrived here abandoning the sign of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence in formations, it is therefore "signless.
Through the contemplation of suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure, the desire, and the aspiration.
It is "wishless" (appaṇihita) because it has come about by abandoning [craving]. Through the contemplation of non-self, the perception of self is abandoned;

by way of seeing the emptiness of self, it is "empty" (suññatā). This is its name from the perspective of its opposite. Furthermore, it is "empty" (suññato) because it is empty of lust and the other [defilements];

it is "signless" (animitta) due to the absence of the signs of form and so forth, or specifically the signs of lust and so forth; and it is "wishless" (appaṇihita) due to the absence of the wish for lust and the like.

This is called its name according to its qualities. Because it takes as its object Nibbāna—which is empty of lust and so forth, signless, and desireless—it is called "empty," "signless," and "desireless"; this is its name according to its object.
As for its arrival, it is twofold: arrival by way of insight and arrival by way of the path. Among these, on the path, there is only arrival by way of insight.
Furthermore, regarding the fruit: there is the arrival at the path immediately following the path, and also the arrival at insight during the attainment of fruition.
Because of the aspect of contemplation of non-self, the path is "empty"; because of the aspects of contemplation of impermanence and suffering, it is "signless" and "desireless.
Thus, insight gives its own name to the path, and the path [gives its name] to the fruit; this is the name derived from the manner of arrival.

“Emptiness” (*suññatta*) means seclusion (*vivittatā*). Since lust and the other [defilements] are themselves the "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) in the sense of being a basis for settling, he said, "of the aspirations of lust, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding the phrase "of this true knowledge" (*imissā vijjāya*), they speak with reference to each individual true knowledge, such as the true knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-vijjā*).
Thus, even if one does not mention the name of a single [specific] true knowledge, if one says, "I am a possessor of the true knowledges," one becomes subject to a defeat offense (*pārājika*).
This is the intended meaning in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*. However, he is not speaking with reference to the science of architecture (*vatthuvijjā*) and so forth.

"By way of each single category" means, according to the method stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, that without making a distinction for the supramundane, it refers simply to "one who is an obtainer of the foundations of mindfulness" by way of each single category.
"Therein" means among those categories. The "abandoning of the defilements" is as follows:
In order to establish that even a mere absence is "supramundane" because it pertains to supramundane functions, the passage beginning with "But that... was stated.

"The mind is unobstructed from lust" means the state of the mind being unobstructed from lust; thus, the meaning is that it is "free from the hindrance of lust" precisely because it is liberated from that lust.
This should be construed with the phrase "the five true knowledges. Regarding the expression "not come," here in the word-commentary [it says] "knowledge is the three..."
Because it is stated as “true knowledge” (vijjā), the meaning is that the remaining five knowledges have not been included.

“Because it is supramundane (lokuttara) by nature” means that, due to the absence even of the conditioned (saṅkhata) which is common to mundane phenomena, it is entirely unmixed with mundane things, being supramundane. “Another” refers to the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and so forth;
the connection is that this too has been rejected right there [in that same work].
200. Regarding the phrase "having brought it back again, it was not joined with the first jhāna and so forth," some say that "the reading is *paṭhamajjhānenā*" (by means of the first jhāna);
that is indeed appropriate, because there is no other jhāna to be included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). For there is only one "broken wheel" (*khaṇḍacakka*) based on the first jhāna.
Since the word "spoken" (*bhaṇita*) can also function as a nominative agent, he says "or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth. By which...
One speaks falsely with a particular state of mind; it is not possible with that very same mind to know, "I am speaking falsely.

However, from time to time, through other mental-door processes (*manodvāra-vīthi*), one knows, "I am speaking falsely"; thus it is said, "For one who is speaking, [the thought] 'I am speaking falsely' occurs.
This is the meaning demonstrated here: that false speech is endowed with three factors. This is the sense.
*Davā* means suddenly. *Ravā* is the speaking of something else by one who intended to say another, due to a lapse.

"Knowledge of that" (*taṃñāṇa*) is knowledge of that; its state is "the state of knowledge of that" (*taṃñāṇatā*). The meaning is that it is self-cognized through the relationship of object and subject between the knowledge and [the state].
"Convergence of knowledges" (*ñāṇasamodhāna*) is the convergence of many knowledges at a single moment; the meaning is their simultaneous arising. By which...
“By means of the mind one knows ‘I shall speak falsely’”—this is stated by combining the preliminary volition (*pubbabhāgacetanā*) and the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhānacetanā*) together.

The meaning is: by whichever mind—both as the preliminary volition and as the decisive volition—one knows the sentient beings and formations (*saṅkhāra*) with whom one is to deceive; by whichever mind one intends, “I shall speak falsely. For that very reason... [etc.]
"Should be relinquished" means that by that very same consciousness, having made that very mind of false speech the object— either thinking "I am speaking falsely" or "it has been spoken"—
the bhikkhu knows it; thus, in the three moments of the volition that reaches its conclusion in the preceding and succeeding stages,
a person knows both the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself within a single moment by means of that one consciousness.
The intention here is that this state of knowing must be relinquished because, at that time, it is the object itself that is manifested; thus he said, "For it is not," and so forth.
If the intrinsic nature of knowledge is not known, how does the subsequent consciousness know?
To this he said, "The preceding, the preceding," and so forth. In that context, by the words "I shall explain," etc., [he refers to] the preceding preceding consciousnesses arisen in the three times.
The meaning is that it serves as a condition for the successive arising of each subsequent consciousness that arises by taking itself as its object.

"By that" means: by that reason that, in the three moments, consciousnesses must be known by other consciousnesses, and those [subsequent ones] necessarily arise from each preceding consciousness; it is by that reason—this is the meaning.
"In that being present" means "when it exists in the prior stage. "I shall speak"—the remaining two [stages]—this pair, namely "having been spoken," will not exist;

thus the construction is simply "that is not there. It "appears as one" refers to the fact that even though the moments are distinct, they should be grasped as "that very same thing" due to their uninterrupted arising.

“By way of the misplacement of strong grasping” means by way of the misplacement of a firm grip. “Of the very weak” means of the very weak grips. “By way of relinquishing one’s own state” means by way of relinquishing the state of what belongs to oneself.
(207) “Because of being terrified” means because of being made to flee as if fear had been produced. Since one who has been thus made to flee does not return to that place again, he said:
“By way of showing the state of not returning. Those who know the meaning of words [explain] the word *kheṭa*.

"He recites it in the *Uttāsaṭṭha*," he says; "this is its meaning," and so forth. "Aṇusahagata" means minute itself, or associated with minuteness, or joined with the state of being minute—such is the meaning.

This was stated with reference to cognizing immediately after the speech by its very nature. However, even if no verbal expression is made, but rather a convention is established such as,
"Whosoever shall depart first from this residence, we shall know him to be an Arahant," then for those in a monastery who have made such an agreement,
the offense of *pārājika* occurs at the moment of departing first— even if that moment has not yet passed, or even at the mere act of setting out.
It is as in the account of the arrival [of the Blessed One], where a certain bhikkhu first departed from that residence thinking, "Let them know me as an arahant.

Therefore, someone standing beyond the range of intimation might, by means of the divine eye, perceive a bodily movement, or by means of the divine ear-element, perceive a vocal utterance.
Having heard it, one knows; thus it is shown that it is not a *pārājika*.

In the canonical text, regarding the section on "knowing" (*paṭivijānantassa āpatti pārājikassa*), at the very moment a syllable is uttered or a bodily action is performed such that another person understands the meaning—such as "this one has attained the first *jhāna*," and so forth—from that point onward, during the preceding utterances of syllables and other such activities...
It should be understood that after having committed a *thullaccaya*, one incurs a *pārājika* at the very moment of the application [of the act] when one subsequently recognizes it;
for in this context, the *thullaccaya* itself serves as the preliminary stage (*sāmanta*). For this very reason, the teacher Buddhadatta stated:
"The *dukkaṭa* is described as being the preliminary stage of the first [offense]."
"But for the remaining three, a grave offense (thullaccaya) has been declared"—this is what was stated.
And this meaning should be understood as being included in the sutta: "For one who does not understand, there is an offense of a grave nature.
Regarding the phrase "by way of learning, interrogation, and so forth," it is because no prior cultivation has been made regarding the meanings of terms such as *jhāna*, *samādhi*, and the rest.
Having heard [this], and not knowing that "the matter is such," one thinks merely, "Some distinguished quality of a recluse has been acquired by him";
this shows that even when it is known by another, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the non-offenses (*anāpatti*).

"Of one whose intention is not to misrepresent" means: when one speaks such words as "Friend, I do not fear death," without reflecting that "by saying this, I have proclaimed a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)," and while speaking thus, one is said to be answering with something else from the standpoint of conventional usage;
hence it is said, "of one answering with something else. "Fearing" means...

"By means of a vehicle," and so forth, has been stated. The term "by means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) is used with reference to the psychic power consisting of higher knowledge (*vijjāmayiddhi*), because such power is impossible for one whose intention is mere deception.

*Dhammadhātu* means omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), or the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. *Upapatti* means the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

In the reading *vitudentī*, [the phrase] "from the spaces between the ribs... [is understood].

"It is indeed a marvel" (*acchariyaṃ vata*) means it is worthy of being struck by the fingers (*acchara*) because it is censurable. "Become as eyes" (*cakkhubhūtā*) means they have become like, or arisen as, eyes for the world;
the meaning is also that they are similar to eyes. "Of that very same karma" (*tasseva kammassā*) refers to that very act of slaughtering cows.
If the meaning "he is reborn in hell" were taken as referring to that very same [volition], it would follow that many rebirths arise from a single volition;
and this is not logical, just as it is impossible for multiple sprouts to arise from a single seed of a mango tree or the like.

Avoiding that [objection], he said: "accumulated by various volitions of his," and so forth. By this, the prior volition and the subsequent volition at the moment of the cow-killer's deed [are distinguished].
"Decisive volition" (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*): Even in a single act of killing, there are many volitions; it is unnecessary to speak of various acts of killing.
In this context, he shows that after being cooked in hell by one volition, one is reborn in this state of existence as a peta by another volition belonging to the *aparāpariya* (subsequent) class.
Therefore, he says: "either the remaining karma or the sign of the karma."

And here, with reference to the arising of a result similar to the action (*kamma*), only the action and the sign of the action (*kamma-nimitta*) are included, not the sign of the destination (*gati-nimitta*); therefore he said, "The sign was simply a heap of bones.
In the text, *vitacchantī* means they pluck [the flesh] as if scraping it away with their beaks; *virājenti* means they scratch it off.

It crawls (*ulati*) by way of its limbs (*maṅga*), thus it is a “crawler” (*maṅguli*); the meaning is that it moves about in a deformed and loathsome manner. “Mental play” means a playful, improper conduct according to one’s own whims. 231.

"Petaloka" (the world of the departed) refers to the world—the assembly or dwelling place—of those who have gone (*itānaṃ*) from a happy destination to a miserable destination due to preeminent unwholesome karma.
*Vā*. "With hand trained" (*katahatthā*) means those whose hands are well-trained in the art of archery; the meaning is that they are capable of hitting a target without missing.

"Those who have performed the shooting" (*katupāsanā*) refers to those for whom the casting of arrows (*asana-sarakkhepa*) was performed upon approaching a royal assembly and the like by way of displaying their skill;
the meaning is that they have demonstrated their craft on every occasion. "Broken down" (*pabhaggo*) means shattered; the meaning is defeated.

Regarding "the immovable concentration" (*āneñjasamādhi*): although the immovable concentration exists even when the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) have ceased, it is specifically the fine-material-sphere concentration (*rūpāvacara-samādhi*) that is subject to arising due to the "thorn of sound" (*saddakaṇṭaka*).
Therefore, he says "immovable, unshakable," and so forth. By the phrase "obstacle to concentration," he refers to applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest;
however, this [fault] was mentioned merely as a matter of improper conduct (*anācāra*), even though it had arisen during the First Enlightenment (*paṭhamabodhi*).

therefore, this training rule, though formulated later, was included by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma as a case already settled under its heading. [This applies] to disciples.
In order to show the absence of recollection in reverse order, it is said: "not in reverse order.

"A difficult task was performed" means that even though the continuity of consciousness was not seen during the immediately preceding period of five hundred kappas, and without being confused, one grasped the relationship between cause and effect—even by inference—regarding the rebirth-linking of the subsequent third existence along with the death-consciousness of the previous life.
This was said because it is difficult for disciples to achieve. "Penetrated" means similar to having penetrated.

Just as if one were to pierce the tip of a single hair from the tail of a yak that has been split into seven strands with the tip of another hair, standing at a distance and shooting as if drawing a bow—so too, it is said that this [task] was accomplished by him as something difficult to do.
"Etadaggaṃ" means "this is the foremost. "Yadidaṃ" means "this which.
[Commentary on the Conclusion, 233]:
"Idha" refers to the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga. "Uddiṭṭhapārājikaparidīpanaṃ" means by way of the recitation of the Pātimokkha among the training rules (sikkhāpada).

This is an exposition of the offenses specified under the *Pārājika* rules, but it is not an exposition of every offense that appears in the entire *Pārājika-vibhaṅga*, because heavy offenses (*thullaccaya*) and others also occur therein; rather, it is an explanation of the *vibhaṅga* as stated by that very word "specified.
Regarding the four [offenses] not shared with the bhikkhus: these are *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*, *vajjappaṭicchādikā*, and *ukkhitānuvattikā*.
"Eight bases" means that these offenses of defeat (pārājika) are prescribed exclusively for bhikkhunīs and are not shared with the bhikkhus.

"Deficient in the basis" (vatthuvipannā): "basis" (vatthu) refers to the state of being a candidate for going-forth and full ordination; she is deficient by virtue of that mere basis, meaning her basis is defective.
"Possessing a rebirth-linking without roots" (ahetukapaṭisandhikā) states the reason why the Path has not been attained.

Although the path does not arise even for those with two roots, they are nevertheless able—by remaining in the stages of going-forth and full ordination—to accomplish the cause for the path in the future.
Those without roots, however, are unable to accomplish it even by remaining in the perfectly pure fourfold purification of virtue;
therefore, it should be understood that they too are "deficient in the basis" (vatthuvipanna) on account of that. [They are] "those who have committed an offense involving defeat" (pārājika).
Due to the failure of their karma, they incur defeat at the very moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Even for those such as *theyyasaṃvāsakas* who, while remaining in the state of a householder, strive in insight meditation (*vipassanā*), the arising of the Path (*magga*) is impossible within that particular existence;
therefore it is said, "the Path is barred. That which hangs down due to its length is called a "pendant" (*lamba*); one who possesses such a thing is...

It is long. To that extent, he is not yet defeated; however, it is only when one inserts that long sexual organ into one's own mouth or anus with the intention of sexual intercourse that one is defeated.

Here, however, it is specifically the insertion into the anus that is intended, because insertion into the mouth is stated only for one whose back is supple due to having performed the preparatory exercises. For even that [anus] has become supple through such preparation.
One becomes subject to a *pārājika* offense only when, having bent over the back, one takes hold of one’s own *aṅgajāta* with the mouth; it is not [an offense] for merely [bending].

Furthermore, for one who takes hold of one’s own anus with the mouth, or the anus or the urinary passage of others, or for one who touches a male organ with a male organ—even in the case of inserting one organ into another—[the same applies].
It does not constitute a *pārājika* offense because, by the very act of inserting the other [organ] into the male organ, it is designated as sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*).

"She sits upon another's genitals" means that while the other person is lying on their back and their genitals are functional, she inserts her own anus into them and sits upon them; this is merely an illustration, as it applies to the genitals of others as well.

If one causes [the organ] to enter the anus and even consents, it is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*). However, if one is forcibly made to enter [the organ] into the anus or the mouth by another and does not consent, there is no offense at all.
In this context, non-consent is difficult to maintain because [one must] avoid [the act].
Furthermore, in this regard, if one remains in the status of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) while killing either one's mother, father, or an Arhat, [there is no offense].

Because it is mentioned separately to show that one who violates a bhikkhunī does not even receive the going-forth as a sāmaṇera, it should be understood that the four [offenses], beginning with matricide, are included within the third and first pārājikas respectively.

2. The Section on the *Saṅghādisesa* Offenses. 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Emission of Semen.
234. *Terasaka* means that which has thirteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) as its measure; thus it is the "Thirteenfold" chapter.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "By the distinction of the receptacles" means by way of the four receptacles of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood.

thus, because the *sambhava* emerges from the ear-lobes... [and so on] ...and the *sambhava*.
Therefore, the construction should be understood as follows: "The third [statement] was well-spoken.
*Dakasota* refers to the path by which the emitted [semen] exits from the organ; it is said to be the region of the genitals.

And this semen, among the seven bodily elements such as lymph, blood, and so forth, belongs to the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), like the marrow in the bones and other such things, being comprised of the four intermediate elements.

It exists throughout the entire body even of very young infants who subsist on food; however, it begins to shift from its location starting from the age of fifteen or sixteen due to the sensual lust arising in beings.
Once shifted, it becomes mind-born through the state of the water element and enters the urinary stream.
From the point of entering the urinary stream onwards, it is produced by the physical nutriment conditioned by the mind.
It is like the discharge of mucus from the brain when it is disturbed.
However, for those who lack the obsession of lust through its total eradication (*samuccheda*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and so forth, there would be no emission of semen.
Thus, the emission of semen from its respective location is produced solely by a mind of lust, not by its natural state; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā*:
“‘Emission of semen’ means it is originated by lust”: here, only the emission of semen is said to be originated by lust, not its natural state.
However, although the semen-element exists even in the six classes of sense-sphere deities, it does not flow from its place due to the power of the couple’s union, even when lust is fully manifest;
rather, remaining in its very place, it undergoes some kind of transformation.
It should be understood that this brings about the immediate subsiding of feverish passion and results in the completion of the sexual act.
However, some say that for them, the pleasure of physical contact itself constitutes the fulfillment of the sexual act.

Furthermore, it should be understood that because both those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and non-returners (anāgāmī) are entirely devoid of sensual lust, they do not even undergo the transformation of the semen-element. This applies to the Brahmās of the fine-material realm (rūpī-brahmā) as well.
However, because it is produced by lust for sensual pleasures that has been suppressed and because its life-force is not sustained by nutriment, the semen-element (*sukkadhātu*) is entirely absent.
The phrase "in the same way" refers by extension to such passages as "one makes an effort toward the sign through the relish of emission," and so forth.
Since it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that "emission" (*vissaṭṭhi*) means "falling from one's place," why is it said [in the text] "merely upon entering the stream of water"?
He said: “The descent into the stream of water here,” and so forth. “Here” refers to all three versions. “Having consented” means:
having made an effort toward the sign, and then, when remorse arose, having dispelled the relish for emission. “To restrain in the interim” means:
not allowing the stream of water—which had fallen from its place due to his own effort toward the sign—to descend, but restraining it in the interim. By means of the relish for emission...

Even when one performs hand-massages and the like, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even if emission occurs; however, because there is no intentional effort directed toward the sign (*nimitta*), there is no offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).

Thus it was said: "If [one performs] hand... [etc. ...there is no offense. Regarding the statement beginning with "and here, descending into a river," this refers to the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) already stated; hence it was said: "This is the legal decision common to all teachers."
The condition known as the "disturbing condition" (*khobhakaraṇapaccaya*) refers to conditions such as unwholesome medicines, lodgings, food, and so forth.

"Various kinds of dreams" refers to those corresponding to the disturbed elements, such as wind and the rest. "Previously experienced" includes both what was previously undergone and what was previously imagined by the mind;
for this expression encompasses even heavens, hells, other lands, and so on. It may also occur through a desire for benefit or a desire for harm.
This was said in order to show the intention of deities regarding what is beneficial or harmful.
The phrase "for the sake of benefit or for the sake of harm" was spoken with reference to benefit and harm as they must exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
But surely, objects being presented by deities do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*); how then does a person see them, or how can deities [present] those things which are non-existent?
Regarding the phrase "they provide," he says "so tāsanti" and so forth, having in mind the exhortation.

By that—merely by the thought of the deities, "Let him imagine thus"—the mind of one who is sleeping falls away from the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-santati) and proceeds as it is being imagined according to the very order intended by the deities.
Thus, the objects being imagined by him are provided by the deities.
This shows that those names exist and that he sees them through the power of the deities (*devatā*). In such passages as "like the mother of the Bodhisatta,
[she saw] the sign of obtaining a son," the appearance on the day of the Bodhisatta’s descent into the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā,
showing how a certain great white elephant had entered her right side, is the "sign of obtaining a son."

This is called a dream. Now, for our Bodhisatta, on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, at the time when night was turning to dawn, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha," he made the Himalayas his pillow, placed his left and right hands in the eastern and western oceans respectively, and set his feet in the southern ocean;
thus, alone, he lay upon the great earth with a bed of *tiriyā* grass known as *dabbatiṇa*.
One [tree] was of a species of grass with a stalk as thick as a ploughshare, rising from its navel and instantly reaching and remaining fixed in the sky at many thousands of yojanas;
another remained fixed, having been climbed up to the level of the knees by white worms with black heads on their feet;
and various four-colored birds came from the four directions and settled at the base of its roots.
The appearance of a white color, and the Bodhisatta’s walking back and forth atop a great mountain of filth without being soiled—these are called the five great dreams.
And these, in their respective order, signify: his attainment of perfect enlightenment; the proclamation of the Noble Path among gods and humans;
the taking of refuge by householders; and the going forth from the four castes, beginning with the Khattiyas.
It should be understood that these are the premonitory signs for the attainment of *arahantship* and for remaining unstained by the four conditions.
The sixteen dreams are indeed manifest. "Exclusively true" is said because of the certainty of the arising of the fruit.
However, in all cases, the vision is indeed distorted. Among the four root causes, such as the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*), [the dream occurs] through two...

He said, "One sometimes sees a dream for three reasons," namely, "due to association and disturbance. "Disturbance of dreams" refers to the distinction between the true and the false nature [of the dream].
Regarding the phrase "an object such as a visible form-sign (*rūpanimitta*)":
here, it is a visible form other than the sign of karma (*kamma-nimitta*) or the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*) that serves as the object for consciousness.

"Sign" (*nimitta*) means the sign of form (*rūpanimitta*). Those [signs] such as the sign of a being (*sattanimitta*) which have that [sign of form] as their first are the "signs of form and so forth.

That life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) which has those signs of form and so forth as its object is "that which has the signs of form and so forth as its object. "Such as these" refers to those having the signs of form and so forth as their objects, as well as those associated with greed and so forth.
"By the all-encompassing mind" means by the ordinary process-consciousness (*pakativīthicitta*) of one who has awakened. What?
The intention is that one cannot be said to "see a dream" because there is no occurrence of consciousness dissociated from the state of being awakened from sleep;
therefore, he says, "the non-existence of the dream itself would follow.

By the phrase "overcome by monkey-sleep," [he refers to] the wholesome or unwholesome cognitive process of the mind-door (manodvāra-vīthi) which is separated by the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-santati) occurring through the influence of sleep.
And he shows that one sees; therefore he says, "That which is sleep," and so forth. "Released from two extremes" means released from the two extremes known as the wholesome and the unwholesome.
"At the moment of adverting and its object" is stated with reference to what is capable of arising in the mind-door, because in dreams there is an absence of the cognitive process of the five doors.
And here, because they are described as having those [objects] as their object even in dreams, the resultant states of the sense-sphere—
even though they occur through perversion by way of imagining forms and so forth that have been experienced or previously heard as having occurred in the past—
are said to have limited objects because they occur by depending upon and imagining limited phenomena; however, this is not because they grasp limited phenomena in their actual form.

It should be understood that [this] occurs precisely because they have come into being. And thus, for those states of lust and so forth, which are accompanied by kamma-result and which arise having superposed the forms of "woman," "man," and so on, as well as for the rebirth-linking and other resultant consciousnesses that arise having apprehended those objects, the status of having a limited object (*parittārammaṇatā*) and the status of having the sign of the kamma as their object (*kammanimittārammaṇatā*) are indeed established.

However, the object consisting of the counterpart-sign of the *kasiṇa* and so forth—which is conventional (*sammutibhūta*) and distinct from the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the actual phenomena—is...

One should understand that the mental states and mental factors (citta-cetasika-dhammā) which have arisen and proceed for a period of time through access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā), etc., are precisely what are meant by "objects not to be classified within the triad of limited objects" (parittattike na vattabbārammaṇā).

"Svāyaṃ" means a dream. Because its limited object is merely imagined through perversion (vipallāsa), it is said to be "of weak basis" (dubbalavatthukattā); the intention is that it lacks mastery over an object that does not actually exist. Therefore, he says: "because it has arisen regarding what is not its proper domain," and so forth.
"Of the class of offenses" (*āpattinikāyassa*) is stated in accordance with the masculine noun *saṅghādisesa*.
"Of this" (*assa*) means of this class of offenses that one wishes to emerge from; therefore he said, "What is meant? and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by conventional usage" (*ruḷhisaddena*):
here, even for a word that has been derived in reference to a whole, its established application to a single part of it is called "conventional usage" (*ruḷhī*); by means of that...
A word connected with conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) is a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*); [the text refers] to that.
He states the reason for the conventional usage with the words "in a part," and so forth. And "at the time" means the time shown by the phrase "in the stiffening of lust," and so forth;

when it is said "in the stiffening of lust," the time is understood by implication as meaning "at the time when the stiffening of lust has arisen, he releases [himself]. "Of the ninth intention" means of the intention of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhippāya*). "The basis" means the object (*visaya*).
238. "Lomasā" means those who possess body hair; thus, they are hair-bearing creatures. 239.
"By means of release" means by means of the application of releasing. Regarding the phrase "associated with the relish of release": here, the desire for release is the "relish of release";

265. Regarding the case where one says, "Come, friend, you be my novice," and commands another; [the offense applies] to that which is performed by him.
Because one relishes the movement of the sexual organ through the pleasure of emission, that movement arises even from a monk’s mind of relishing;

however, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by the very act of commanding. Furthermore, regarding one who performs an action even by force when not commanded by another—
If one consents through the pleasure of emission, then even when there is emission, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense—just as in the first *pārājika*;

if there is no emission, it is a *thullaccaya*. However, the teachers say that if there is no volition for the pleasure of emission, then even for one who consents out of lust for physical contact, there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* even when there is emission; and this is indeed correct.

Regarding the case of gazing intently (*upanijjhāyana*): "the genitals" refers specifically to the urinary passage of living women, and not any other part. 267. "Flower-garland" (*pupphāvalī*) is a particular kind of game.

Having done so, they sit with both feet extended there and fall [upon them]; there is also a reading, "a row of flowers" (*pupphāvaliya*). Regarding the phrase "of one who inserts":
because it has two objects due to the agent's role as an instigator, the accusative case is used for both "sand" and "the organ.
Here, three factors should be understood: volition, the preparatory effort, and the emission.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.

Because light coming from outside is obstructed, there is indeed a dense darkness on the inner side of the door-panel;
it is with reference to such cases that it was said, "when these are opened, there is darkness," and so forth.
At the moment the brahmin woman touched her own limbs, she remained compliant with her improper conduct and said nothing.
Because it was spoken at the moment of praising the bhikkhu, he said, "having observed,
'He seems desirous of going forth,'" meaning "having observed him as if he were desirous of going forth.
He said, "his own misfortune," because such being overwhelmed by others on the part of women is indeed an extreme disgrace.

In order to show the meaning that "they call this a body" by way of its specific bodily nature, the passage beginning with "Or else" (*atha vā*) was stated. The statement "insulting...

However, for one who is wearing a lower garment (*sanivatthāya*), if he lowers his hand from the top [of the head] and places it upon the upper garment (*sāṭaka*) while it is over the lower garment, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). From the upper garment...
If, having caused [the hand] to enter, he touches [her] starting from the shank, it is again a *saṅghādisesa*.

"In the exposition as described" means in the exposition of bodily contact as previously stated. "By that" means by whatever reason there are the factors such as the perception of the object; by that reason.
The construction is: "He should make heavy for the monk" means he should manifest [the offense] as stated in the exposition of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

"Having become dispassionate toward perception" means having failed in perception. "This object" refers to what is mentioned in this training rule; it is stated with reference to the absence of an offense for anyone who touches anything—whether animate or inanimate—that has not been mentioned [specifically].

"Lusting" means lusting specifically through the desire for physical contact. "Dispassionate" refers to one who is free from the lust for physical contact, speaking with reference to a mother or similar person.
"An offense of wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa) is stated with reference to one who takes hold [of her] out of maternal affection and so forth; even one who is dispassionate...
However, for one who takes hold of a woman out of lust for physical contact, there is indeed a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

This is the connection [to the rule] as it accords with this textual passage (*pāḷi*). If you ask, "How does it accord?"—for if, when the thought "I shall take hold of what is attached to the body of a woman" has arisen, the perception of her as a woman were to be lost, then even in the taking of what is attached to her body, there would be no *thullaccaya* (grave offense) either.

Because the *pāḷi* states that there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) precisely when there is the perception of a woman, therefore, for one who takes hold of a body with the thought, "I will take hold of what is connected to the body of a woman," the perception of a woman is not said to have been lost.

Thus, for one who takes hold of a body with the thought, "I will take hold of what is connected to the body of a woman," there is both the perception of a woman and the lust for bodily contact; [and] regarding the taking of the body...

And this very statement by the Elder Mahāsiva—“and whatever possibilities [arise], one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense according to the actual state of affairs”—is consistent with this canonical text (*pāḷi*).

For in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), regarding one who encircles [women] with his arms with the perception, “I am taking hold of them,” a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is stated on account of those who are in the middle; for it is not [the case that] for him... Because a dark woman is difficult to distinguish from a blue one, she is referred to as “black. 279.
“With the intention of indulgence” means the intention of indulging in the pleasure of touch. In the section on touching what is attached to the body, it is by way of what is attached to the body.

The discernment of contact is to be understood. The statement that there is no offense because there is no offense in a mere arising of thought is said with reference to the absence of an actual effort, even when one consents to the bodily movement being performed by a woman, since no bodily movement occurs through a mere lust for physical contact.
