By that intention, the agitation of the sexual organ necessarily arises of its own accord, and since it is considered "done by him," it is stated as a *pārājika* offense.

By that same method, it should be understood that even in the first *saṅghādisesa*, an offense occurs through the possibility of the agitation of the sexual organ arising, even when one consents to the effort being performed by another.
Regarding the fourth [offense]: "And he does not exert himself with the body..."
And in this section, “he does not discern contact,” the word *api* (also) indicates that, as in the third section, there is no effort (*vāyāma*) either.

Furthermore, the phrase “as in the case of sitting on a seat [given] by one who has relinquished [the robe]” should be understood as an illustration of the mere absence of the discernment of contact, and not of the absence of the preliminary application (*payoga*).
Regarding the term “with liberation as the aim,” here it is because of the mind’s rapid transformation (*lahuparivatti*).
Even if lust for physical contact arises from time to time, there is no offense so long as the intention for liberation remains uninterrupted;
however, when that intention has been interrupted, there is indeed an offense.
This is the method of commentary on the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*).
281. "In this case, one should not say 'Take it'" refers to the offense of *dukkaṭa* committed by touching [the robe] with a bodily contact based on worldly affection (*gehasita-pema*).

However, if one says "Take it" to someone who is unable to grasp the cloth or other items out of compassion—and who is sinking in the water due to being overcome by necessity—one may, out of compassion, take hold of her hair or similar parts without hesitation, provided one does not consider them untouchable (*anāmāsa*).
Even if one takes hold of her with the intention of releasing her and pulls her along, there is no offense. For it is not improper to lift up a mother who is dying.
This same principle applies to a woman who is not a relative as well.

The word "mother" is used to show that even taking hold of one's own eminent mother is not permitted. However, regarding what is to be done for her, the same applies even when doing so for other women.

There is indeed no offense when there is no intention [to use it], as there is no distinction [in the nature of the act]. *Tiṇaṇḍupaka* refers to a head-ornament made from the roots of *hirivera* and other plants.

"Having turned it over" means having removed it from its state of being one's own lower garment (*nivāsana*) and so forth. However, it is permissible to touch it for a short time for the purpose of worship and the like.

Regarding "the hair-comb, tooth-pick, needle, and so forth": this is explained by dividing it into two parts—the hair-comb made from cloth rags and the like for the purpose of adorning the head, and the tooth-pick and so forth—and thus shows the meaning in sequence as that which is to be taken for the purpose of the comb-case and the purpose of the tooth-pick equipment.
Having tied up a mass of hair, there [one should place] crosswise...
A tooth-pick made for cleaning the teeth is the same as a tooth-pick used as an ornament for the head;

having treated them as one and the same, they should be placed in a case and carried about. Thus, the construction should be understood as "the equipment consisting of the case and the needle," where the needle is the instrument for its respective function.
A "cloth-image" refers to one made of plaster and the like, depicting female animals that constitute an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
Even that which is made by way of shape is likewise not to be touched.
That which is made by displaying female forms and so forth, or by means of cloth, walls, and the like—provided one does not actually touch the female form—it is permissible to make use of it.

In such cases where there is no lust for bodily contact, there is no fault in touching what is attached to the body. Regarding the phrase "having broken [it]," this refers even to things not to be touched, such as sticks, stones, and so forth.

Because this is stated in the commentary on the *Bhedaṇa* [Sutta], and because it is also stated in the Canon (*Pāḷi*) that there is no offense even for touching [a child] with the intention of rescuing it in times of distress;

this is the meaning that must be understood. As for the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, "But she must not be touched," our view is that this was said with reference to an object that is not being measured (or weighed).
“Having resolved upon the path” means having generated the perception of the path, thinking, “This is the path. “Having prepared [a seat] and giving it” is said by way of formal courtesy;
however, even if they say, “Sit down without having prepared a seat,” it is also permissible to sit down after having prepared one oneself.
“Grown there” means those that remain as living organisms (bhūtagāma) without being cut down.
Because it is stated, “while playing,” there is no offense for one who touches [it] when a requisite condition exists.

However, it is not permitted in any way to touch what belongs to a bhikkhu that is fit for use, because it is a transgression. The phrase “I will give it to those who are not fully ordained” refers to taking [it] without having received it.
There is no fault in taking it after having received it for one’s own benefit, because it lacks the quality of being untouchable (*anāmāsa*).
"Maṇi" refers to every kind of gem other than beryl (*veḷuriya*), such as the *jotirasa* and so forth. "Beryl" (*veḷuriya*) is a gem the color of fresh *veluva* wood;
some also say it is the color of a cat's eye (*majjārakkhi*) or a mandala. "Stone" (*sila*) refers to a very smooth black stone the color of green gram or black beans.
They say that stones which have come to be designated as gems—even those of red, white, and other colors, provided they are well-polished—are likewise untouchable (*anāmāsa*). "Silver" (*rajata*)...

It is not permissible; even if it was given by householders after being mixed [with other substances], if it remains in the form of gold or the like within the medicine and can be separated, such medicine is also not permissible. However, if it has become indistinguishable, it is permissible.

It should be seen. It should be connected as: "the conch-shell trumpet, the polished and perforated one, and the one inlaid with jewels. "Perforated" means having holes made for the purpose of being used as a jewel or similar object.
"Inlaid with jewels" means variegated with gold vines and the like, and studded with gems such as pearls; by this, the conch-shell trumpet [is described].
This shows that anything else mixed with gems is likewise "untouchable. The same principle applies to stone as well.

"The rest" refers to everything remaining after excluding those things associated with gems.

Since it is stated, "in a place where money is discarded," it is established that it is permissible for a person who discards money to touch gold and silver and then discard it.
"To play with" means to touch and move [the object] here and there. "It is said" means it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

Because it resembles *keḷāyana* (a type of brass). *Ārakūṭaloha* is a specific kind of artificial metal with the color of gold.

that which is made by mixing lead and tin is *vaṭṭaloha*; and that which is made by mixing mercury and tin is *hārakūṭaloha*.

[This is] the name. However, because it is stated that "it belongs to the category of gold" (*jātarūpagatika*), some say that for one who takes hold of it, there is also an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

"All allowable" (*sabbakappiya*) refers to the touching, guarding, and so forth of the requisites for lodgings made of the aforementioned gold and other materials.

"It is allowable to accept even the whole [object], thinking, 'I shall make it a permissible article. Here too, after breaking something or separating it, it may be touched.
Regarding the phrase "shields, lattices, and so forth": here, a "shield" (*phalaka*) refers to a wooden board held in the hand for protection against arrows;

a "lattice" (*jālika*) refers to a net-like structure made of iron, metal, or other materials to be fastened on the head and so on for the purpose of protecting the eyes. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), armor and similar items are included.
The term "untouchables" (*anāmāsāni*) is stated with reference to fish-nets and other such things that obstruct others, but not with reference to protection against arrows.
This is because he lacks the equipment for weapons. For that very reason, he will say later: "It is for the purpose of warding off the obstruction of others," and so forth.
"Of the seat" means of the cetiya surrounded by a paved terrace (*paribhaṇḍa*). "I shall bind it" means I shall bind it so that crows and other birds do not defile it.
"A *bheri-saṅghāṭa* is a drum with its skin joined together; a *vīṇā-saṅghāṭa* is a lute with its skin joined together"—thus it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

It has been stated [in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*]: “Because there is no distinction [from the previous definition] based on the statement ‘lutes, drums, and so forth, bound with leather,’ and because the commencement of a specific explanation beginning with ‘But in the *Kurundi*’ and so on, it should be understood that the collection of binding accessories for drums and the like is called a ‘drum-lute ensemble’ (*bherivīṇā-saṅghāṭa*), taking the word *saṅghāṭa* to mean ‘that which is joined together. A hollow bowl (*tuccha-pokkhara*)...”
The *pokkhara* (head) of an unbaked leather drum (*avinaddhacamma-bheri*) and a lute (*vīṇā*).

"With the leather applied" (*āropitacamma*) means that which was previously applied and later removed from it, being merely the head-leather set aside separately, and not including the remaining accessories.

However, when including those accessories, it is called a *saṅghāṭa*; this is the distinction. "Covered" (*onahita*) refers to having applied the leather to the drum-heads and so forth, [securing them] with leather straps and the like.
[The text] is to be adorned with all the requisite articles.
In the Pāḷi, "of a paṇḍaka" means by a paṇḍaka. "At the time when it is capable of causing a pārājika offense" means at the time when it has not become putrid.

It should be understood that even in every situation where there exists passion for bodily contact and so forth, as long as the female form is discernible, the dukkaṭa offense of inappropriate touching does not cease.
Because it cannot be moved by means of displacing the walkway and so forth, it is not designated as "connected to the body"; thus, a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) is stated.

282. A "single-path walkway" (*ekapadika-saṅkama*) is a narrow bridge. Because of the statement "pulling," a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) applies only to a rope that is capable of being moved, and not to another [type of rope] which would end up against a wall, a pillar, or the like; hence he says, "that which is a large rope," and so forth.

It should be understood that it is explained here that even for one who touches thin cords or sticks that are capable of being moved by him, but does not move them, there is indeed a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). "To be concealed" means to be hidden by means of covering and so forth.

The five factors here are: a human female, the perception of her as a human female, lust for bodily contact, the exertion [of the effort], and the touching of the hands or other parts with that [lust].
The commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech. 285.
In the third [rule], "connected with what is not the true Dhamma" means connected with sexual intercourse. "Fools" refers to those who do not understand well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
One who does not know—whether through intoxication from liquor or by being insane and so forth—is included in this very category even if unaware.
"It does not yet reach the head" means that the culmination known as the status of being a *saṅghādisesa* offense has not been reached;
however, because it is not combined with intercourse on the road, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Disparages" means she utters words that cause disparagement. "Gives offense" means she establishes an offense.

Regarding the phrase "by three," it is stated that because the words beginning with "one who observes the signless" are capable of being construed even as non-gross offenses, there is no restriction to the anus and so forth;
however, by those eight words, it should be understood that there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), as in the case of the Paribbājikā-vatthu.
"Only the size of a keyhole" means the size of a keyhole. "Dry channels" is said because, due to the dryness of the urinary channels, the red color disappears.
"Pure" means even those not joined with terms such as sexual intercourse (*methuna*). "Joined only with the act of sexual intercourse" is merely an illustration;
for even with respect to the anus or the urinary passage, one might say in reference to the signless (*animitta*): "Your anus or urinary passage is like this," and so forth.
Even when [the act] is completed, these are indeed grounds for an offense. 286. "A grave offense" refers to a *pārājika* offense committed by a nun who has raised her knees above the waist. 287.
"Laughing, laughing" is merely an illustration; even if not laughing, if one speaks in any manner whatsoever manifesting to a woman one's own perverted state of mind, there is indeed an offense.
"From body and mind" means that it originates from both body and mind for one who illuminates [the area] by means of a hand-gesture.
288. "Therefore, it is a *dukkaṭa*" means it is a *dukkaṭa* because of not recognizing [the offense];

however, if there is recognition, it is indeed a *thullaccaya*, as in the case of the nun (*paribbājikā*) in the relevant rule, because it is not a "field-word. For if she recognizes it in the case of a "field-word," it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

It might be [an offense] like the two bases for requesting sexual intercourse; however, although those two bases should have been mentioned under the fourth Saṅghādisesa (regarding lewd speech), they are mentioned here because they occur merely through the pleasure of lewd speech.
Thus, what happens when one speaks using the term "field" to a woman who does not understand? Although this is indeed a specific offense, [it is not so classified] in the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.

It is not stated [that there is a *saṅghādisesa*]; rather, in this case, there must simply be a *thullaccaya*. For indeed, regarding the phrase "not a field," it is stated that there is a *dukkaṭa* for one who does not recognize [it as such], and a *thullaccaya* for one who does recognize it. However, regarding the phrase "a field," when there is recognition, only a *saṅghādisesa* is stated;
therefore, when there is no recognition, it is appropriate that there be only a *thullaccaya*, and not a *dukkaṭa*, as compared to the case of "not a field."
It should be understood that this leads to the undesirable consequence (pasaṅga) of there being no distinction [between the cases].

And just as it is here, so too in the fourth training rule (sikkhāpada), it should be known that for one who understands the phrase "not a field," there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); for one who does not understand it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
but for one who understands the phrase "a field," there is a grave offense. In the Pāḷi, *navāvuta* means "ninefold-woven" (*navavīta*).
288. "With reference to unrighteousness" means with reference to sexual intercourse; for that receives the designation of "sowing" because it deposits the seed for the production of offspring.

"Sinks down" means it flows away, or the meaning is that it transmigrates. The five factors here are: a human female, the perception of her as such, lustful desire for the sound of her indecent speech, the making of it manifest by that [speech], and the awareness of it at that moment.
The commentary on the training rule regarding indecent speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Service According to One’s Own Desire (Attakāmapāricariyā-sikkhāpada) 290.
Regarding the fourth [training rule]: "Alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to the gathering together of alms-balls of food being offered by others into one's bowl;
thus, it is called the "food of alms. By virtue of its similarity to that, anything else whatsoever obtained without the practice of begging for alms from monks is also so designated.

It is called *piṇḍapāta* (almsfood). It is called a *paccaya* (condition) because it goes toward (*eti*) what is approached (*pati*); thus he said, "in the sense of being a support (*patikaraṇa*), it is a condition.
Alternatively, it is a condition because it goes toward (*ayati*) or proceeds as an antidote (*paṭipakkha*) to disease and suffering.
"Suitable" means beneficial. "By the city's defenses" means by those who protect the city by surrounding it. A moat is a defensive perimeter for kings' houses.

They say that these seven—the moat, the rampart, the pillar, the crossbar, and the watchtower—are the requisites of a city. "White requisites" refers to the ornament of purified virtue (*visuddhisīla*).
For here, the Noble Path is intended by the term "chariot," and right speech and the other factors are called its "requisites" in the sense of being ornaments.
"Wheel-vigor" means the wheel of vigor. "Life-requisites" [refers to...]
The causes for the maintenance of life. "To be procured" means they must be properly brought forth or sought after. 291.
"In the vicinity" means in such a place where, standing there, one is able to make a request. Regarding the phrase "desire, cause, service, and purpose," in the Pāḷi it is stated as:
"one's own desire, one's own cause, one's own intention, one's own service."

Among these four points thus stated—namely, sensual pleasure (*kāma*), cause (*hetu*), and service (*pāricariyā*)—the meaning (*attha*) is indicated through the intention of the analytical statement (*viggahavākya*) according to the first alternative (*atthavikappa*) mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "The rest" refers to the single term "intention" (*adhippāya*).
"The phrasing" (*byañjana*) means mere phrasing; the sense is that it is mere speech because it is not applicable to the first alternative. This same method applies to the second alternative as well.
In order to demonstrate the meaning already stated by correlating it with the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), the following was begun:
“When it is said, ‘for one’s own desire, for one’s own sake, for one’s own service,’ the wise will understand. This is what is meant:
when “for one’s own sake” is said, the meaning “for one’s own benefit” is understood; [and] when “for one’s own desire” and “for one’s own...

When "service" (*pāricariyā*) is stated, the meaning understood is "service through desire. Therefore, by means of these three words, the wise will understand this alternative interpretation of the meaning:
"service for one’s own desire" (*attakāmapāricariyā*).

However, when "one's own intention" (*attano adhippāyaṃ*) is stated, because the word *adhippāya* has the same meaning as the word *kāmita*, [the meaning is understood as "service according to one's own wish"].
The wise will understand this meaning through the distinction that "service to one's own desires" (*attakāmapāricariyā*) refers to the sense of desiring what is intended for oneself.

"This is the foremost" (*etadaggaṃ*): this is the best. Although in the training rule concerning indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā-sikkhāpada*), the solicitation for sexual intercourse is indeed mentioned as "she asks and she entreats," that was stated by way of the lust for indecent speech; here, however, it is [by way of] oneself...
“By way of lustful passion for sexual intercourse”—this is the distinction.
In the *Vinītavatthu* [cases], the statement “give the first portion” is said for one’s own benefit;

however, it should be understood that in the training rule regarding indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*), even if spoken for the sake of another, the offense applies to the speaker. “Subhagā” means beautiful through such qualities as sovereignty and the like.
[The factors are: being a human female; the perception of her as such; lust for the fulfillment of one's own desires; the solicitation for that fulfillment of desires;
and the awareness at that moment. These are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the fulfillment of one's own desires is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Matchmaking (Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada) 296.
In the fifth [rule], "by cleverness" means by knowledge of their own nature (*sabhāva-ñāṇa*). "Possessing discernment" means endowed with the movement of that knowledge of their own nature.

"By proficiency" means by the trained knowledge regarding what is to be done by women. "By intelligence" means by the presence of understanding even regarding those things to be done by women for which one has not been trained.
By means of wisdom. *Chekā* refers to those skilled in cooking and so forth with the body. *Āvahana* (bringing home) is the taking of a bride;
it is the bringing [of her] to another family according to the prescribed rite, which is the giving away of the girl. *Vivāha* (marriage) is the sending [her] to another family;

it is the bestowing of the girl. 297. *Randhāpana* is having food cooked. *Pacāpana* is having curries and other dishes prepared. *Na upāharanti* means not given. *Kaya* is called "taking"; *vikaya* is called "giving. Having grouped both of these together, it is termed "commerce" (*vohāra*).
300. By the phrase “it is not permissible to perform a miracle,” it is indicated that there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

Because it is stated, “It must be given by one who has been defeated,” one who does not give it is to be dealt with as having abandoned his responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*). “*Acirakālādhikārika*” means that which has a connection (*adhikāra*) to a recent time;

it refers to a go-between (*sañcaritta*). Alternatively, the reading is “*acirakālācārika*. The construction is: “that for which there is conduct (*ācāra*) or transgression (*ajjhācāra*) in a recent time.”

301. Although those such as the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) and others also incur offenses that are formal transgressions (paṇattivajja), such as acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), because these [other types of ordination] do not occur at all times and are few in number, the author here provides the word-commentary beginning with "yvāyaṃ" specifically with reference to one who is fully ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma).
"Sañcaraṇaṃ" means going about; he who possesses this is a "sañcarī."

The state of that is *sañcaritta* (mediating). Therefore he said, "the state of mediating" (*sañcaraṇabhāva*). One who mediates is a mediator (*sañcaraṇo*), namely a person; the state of that is the state of mediating (*sañcaraṇabhāvo*).
The meaning is: "that state of mediating between a woman and a man. Regarding "in the state of a wife" (*jāyābhāve*), it means for the sake of being a wife (*bhariyabhāvāya*).

Regarding "in the state of a lover" (*jārabhāve*), it means for the sake of being a husband (*sāmibhāvāya*); the sense is "for the purpose of that. [This occurs] in the sense of a cause (*nimittatthe*).

For this is a word in the locative case. Although the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for the phrase "in the state of a paramour" (*jārattane*) is stated in the feminine gender as "you will become a paramour" (*jārī bhavissasi*), in the explanation (*niddesa*) of the phrase "should enter into mediation" (*sañcarittaṃ samāpajjeyya*), it says:
"Either sent by a woman, he goes into the presence of a man; or sent by a man, he goes into the presence of a woman."

Because it is stated, "he goes," in order to show the manner of speech that should be used even in the presence of a man, the commentary uses the term "in the state of being a paramour" (*jārattaṇe*);
since this designation applies equally to both women and men, it says: "One who reports a woman's intention to a man reports it in the state of being a paramour.
However, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the construction of both phrases is made specifically by way of reporting a man's intention to a woman; following that [method],...
It is possible to understand even the manner in which a woman’s intention is communicated to a man.
Now, demonstrating the meaning according to the method stated in the Pāḷi, he said, “Moreover,” and so forth.
The phrase “you shall become a husband” is expressed by way of a masculine synonym because the word *jāyā* (wife) is restricted to the feminine gender; it means “you shall have a fixed husband.”
The meaning is as follows: "You will become a lover" means the intention is that you will approach [her] by way of sexual misconduct.
(303) "Serivihāraṃ" means wandering according to one's own will. "Attano vasaṃ" means under one's own command.

Since the word *gotta* applies to those of the same clan, and the word *dhamma* applies to those who practice the Dhamma, he said "by those of the same clan," and so forth. In that context, "sagottehi" means by those of the same lineage.
“By those who share the same Dhamma” means by those who should practice together within the teaching of a single Teacher, or by those belonging to the same family or religious tradition.
For this very reason, he said, “a single Teacher,” and so forth. “Included in the same group” means included in such groups as florists and the like.
“With an owner” means protected. “With legal penalty” refers to one for whose departure a punishment has been established by the king. Of the latter...

"Of two" refers to those who are protected by a master and those who are under punishment. "There is misconduct" means that for those women, there is misconduct on their part as well—just as there is for the men who have gone to them—because they possess a husband.
"Not the others" means that among the eight types beginning with those protected by a mother, there is no misconduct [on their part] because they lack a husband;
rather, misconduct belongs only to the men who have gone to them, since they are protected by their mothers and the rest.
For men are not permitted to go to a woman protected by anyone whatsoever;
however, women who have been taken as wives by any man are not permitted to go to another man, but not for any other reason than that she herself is the owner of her own touch.
Indeed, mothers and others do not protect them for the sake of their own enjoyment of those touches.
They merely forbid intercourse with men. Therefore, because women have not been forbidden by anyone from contact and because the contact is their own, there is no sexual misconduct for them;
however, for men, because they enter places belonging to others that have been forbidden by others, it should be understood that this constitutes sexual misconduct.

"By means of wealth" (*bhogena*) means for the sake of wealth. "One who has taken hold of a water-pot" (*odapattakinī*) refers to one who has grasped a water-pot after touching it. Since the army itself is indicated by the word "banner," he says "of one with raised banners," and so forth.
(305) "Corrupted externally" (*bahiddhā vimaṭṭhaṃ*) means it was announced elsewhere. "She will accomplish that action":
this is said with reference to her capacity to accomplish that action, whether or not she actually accomplishes the task after having been informed of it.

It should be understood that even when a boy or a girl has not been informed, and they are sent by their parents or others into the very presence of those same parents or others within the Dispensation, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to the fulfillment of the three factors consisting of receiving, examining, and reporting back.
This applies specifically to the person for whose sake the message was sent; even if one reports it to the mother or others of that person, it remains a field of offense.
The passage beginning with “I renounce the Buddha” was cited in order to demonstrate the state of being immersed [in saṃsāra].
This should be understood as having been cited on account of the commonality of proficiency, even though there is a distinction between proficiency in speech and proficiency in reasoning.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with “But that” was stated to avoid the fault of that example and to show conformity with the Sutta. Regarding the phrase “it accords with this,” the intended meaning is as follows:
Just as there is no breach of the agreement for one who, having not informed her himself, tells others such as his pupils and tests them before reporting back,
so too there is no breach for one who, for the sake of informing her, tells her mother and others—
even though they may or may not carry out that action. For even if those people, such as the mother, remain silent...
"He brings back" means there is no discrepancy in the designation.

"She manages the household duties" thus she is a *gharaṇī*. The intention is that for one who speaks of another [person], the designation of the object is like a command regarding taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth, even though there is a discrepancy in the designation.
And "by way of the primary status" (*mūlaṭṭhāna*); here, for a man, it refers to his mother and so on.
Because she is the fundamental basis for the sending of the message, she is called "the one who stands as the root" (*mūlaṭṭhā*).

322. Regarding the passage in the Canon stating that "for a woman protected by her mother, the mother sends a monk," this refers to either sending a monk to her own daughter saying, "Let him be the wife of such-and-such a man," or [sending him] to a man or to his kinsmen.
It should be understood that she sends [the girl] to his presence with the message, “Let my daughter become the wife of such-and-such a person.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. “Because of the method stated previously” means because of the method stated under the first *saṅghādisesa* offense.
“At the end by one” means by a single word. “He departs from right there” means he leaves that very spot without calling her back.
“Without rejoicing”: this is said with reference to one who acts in such a manner.

Even if there is rejoicing, one who does not report it to the Teacher is indeed said not to investigate. “In the manner stated in the third phrase” means in the manner stated by the passage beginning, “He, without rejoicing at her words,” and so forth.
In the Pāḷi, “having had the pupil investigated” means: “This one [is] theirs...”
"Is he capable of speaking?"— having thus tested him by means of his pupil. However, if that pupil remains silent after accepting the instruction,

it should be understood that for the teacher who reports that occurrence back [to the Saṅgha], there is likewise a *saṅghādisesa* offense, just as in the case of reporting the silence of one's mother or others when they have remained silent.

In the fourth section of the Pāḷi, although it is not explicitly stated that there is no offense when one who is going fulfills the purpose but one who is returning fails to fulfill it, the phrase "there is no offense in the fourth case" is spoken having already implied this by way of the underlying meaning.

340. "Of craftsmen": carpenters and others—namely, the five types of craftsmen consisting of woodworkers, metalworkers, weavers, dyers, and barbers—are called "craftsmen. Regarding the phrase "by such a person... there is no offense":

this is stated with the understanding that even such service for a householder does not constitute [a formal] duty. "Originates from the body": this refers to one who is unaware of the formal rule (paṇṇatti), or unaware of the state of being fit to speak, or unaware of both.
It originates from the body. This same method applies to the other two [doors] as well.

They are "fit to be spoken to" (*alaṃvacanīyā*) because, whether they be women, men, or both, since their desire for the state of wife and husband has been completely relinquished, they are no longer subject to being addressed or spoken to with such things as "Do not do this!
for the sake of a future reunion; thus they are "fit to be spoken to."
"Alaṃ vā kātuṃ arahanti sandhānavacanametesu itthipurisesūti alaṃvacanīyā" means that they are "to be spoken to with the word 'alaṃ'";
the intention is that, without the word of one who effects a union, they do not join together and are indeed abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "having known the designation (paṇṇattiṃ)," it should be stated here as "or [having known] the state of being one to whom the word 'alaṃ' applies. For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*...

“Having understood both of those,” and so forth, was said. If one writes down one’s own intention on a letter and gives it to someone without having informed the bhikkhu, saying, “Give this letter to so-and-so,” there is no *sañcaritta* (mediating) offense for the one who takes it away.

For this training rule is *acittaka* (without conscious intent) solely by way of not knowing the state of being a medium of communication (*paṇṇatti-alaṃvacanīya-bhāva*), and not by way of not knowing the entire state of acting as a go-between (*sañcaraṇa-bhāva*).

In both the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā, only the act of announcing (*ārocana*) is shown. Therefore, for the purpose of clarification, it should be understood that an offense occurs only for one who announces—either by body or by speech—even by means of sending a letter, provided they have knowledge [of the matter].

341. "In whatever manner, in whichever regions" refers to the giving of a letter, the informing of kinsmen, masters, and so forth, which must be performed in order to make known the state of having relinquished [the object], as determined by each respective locality.
This shows the reason; and this is stated with reference to what is taken as a wife by formal marriage.

However, in the case of women who have come together by their own desire, as well as for a momentary mistress, it should be understood that the mere absence of lust in the man's mind is sufficient to constitute the state of being "fit to speak to.
In the phrase "in the case of indecent acts, etc.," the word "etc. includes adultery and acting as a go-between.
In this context, although human women and men are not explicitly mentioned in the text— despite such statements as "a woman means a human woman,

not a female yakkha"— nevertheless, since only human women are specified in passages such as "ten kinds of women protected by their mother," and because men must likewise be understood according to that same principle, it is human women and men who are intended here.

Therefore, the five factors here are: that those with whom one enters into matchmaking must be of human birth; they must not be persons who should not be spoken to; there must be acceptance [of the proposal]; there must be investigation; and there must be the bringing back of the message.
The commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Building of a Hut (Kuṭikārasikkhāpada) 342.
Regarding the sixth [rule]: "By this much" means by this much timber and so forth. "Of indefinite measure" means of indefinite measure in terms of timber and so forth.
"Cutting off the root" means by way of making it one's own property after releasing it from the state of being another's possession; such is the meaning.
When one asks in this manner, there is both an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for requesting from an unrelated person and an offense of wrong-doing for accepting male or female slaves;

this is because [the practice] is prohibited in the Commentaries based on the statement: "He abstains from accepting female and male slaves. "One's own work" refers to the work of killing living beings.
And this wrong-doing is stated for the purpose of avoiding the fault of taking life, not for the purpose of avoiding the request itself. Even without specifying...
“‘It should not be requested’ is stated for the purpose of showing respect; however, there is no offense for one who requests manual labor with a pure mind.
‘It is permissible to have it done as one wishes’ means that it is permissible even without requesting in such terms as ‘I request manual labor, please give it.
Even for one engaged in their own duties, there is no formal act of intimation (*viññatti*) when having them do this, as it is merely for the purpose of showing respect.”
However, it was stated after making a distinction.
"For the purpose of indicating that everything is allowable" means for the purpose of indicating that all things are entirely allowable.

Regarding the statement, "It is permissible to say, 'Give the root,'" because one first says, "We shall give the root," there is no *viññatti* (formal request) even though the words "the root" are a general term applicable to both allowable and unallowable objects.

It is stated [in the text] because, for those who have completed their work of service (*bhatikicca*), there is no acceptance of unallowable things (*akappiyavatthu*) since they cause them to be given.
"Not inhabited" (*anajjhāvuttha*) means unappropriated (*apariggahita*).

Regarding the phrases "one desiring to have a bed... made," "cloths (*cīvara*) and so forth," and so on: for one desiring to have a cloth made by weavers who are neither relatives nor invited (*aññātaka-appavārita*), [the following applies].
It should be understood that although there is no offense of *dukkaṭa* regarding the act of causing [a weaver] to weave by means of manual labor or solicitation,
there are nevertheless *pācittiya* or *dukkaṭa* offenses as appropriate under the training rule concerning the causing of robes to be woven.
"Unsuitable coins and so forth must not be given" refers to giving— even if received through a *kappiya-kāraka*— by saying, "Give this coin for the purpose of performing manual labor."
"It is not allowable" has been stated. Although no fault is seen in causing someone to give for work previously performed, nevertheless they say it is simply improper.

However, there is no fault for one who causes wages to be given through a figurative expression using allowable terminology, whether for the purpose of work already done or for the purpose of work to be done.
"Allowable" means proper conduct; the intention is that no offense occurs.

"Having had it made allowable, they should be accepted"—this was stated for the purpose of avoiding the disturbance of the seed-field when fanning away flies from a branch while cutting leaves and so forth, and to avoid accepting dust and the like that might adhere there.

When there is no suspicion of either of these two, there is no fault in not acting in that manner. Regarding rivers and the like, because the water is not enclosed (apariggahita), one may say, "Bring [it]."

"It is allowable," it is said. Because of the statement, "It is not to be used if brought [in this manner]," even after one has confessed the *dukkaṭa* incurred through the act of requesting (*viññatti*), for one who uses that object again, there is still a *dukkaṭa* for that subsequent use;
it is not allowable for any of the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*). Furthermore, "one must not have manual labor performed by shameless monks or novices."
Because it is stated in general terms, it is not permitted to have anyone perform any manual labor for one’s own benefit.
However, there is no fault in the case of those who are shameless (*alajjī*) and continue to perform tasks such as fanning even when being restrained.

Furthermore, it is permissible to have them perform work for the *cetiyas* and so forth. And here, because it is said "by shameless novices (*sāmaṇera*)," [it implies that] "intentionally committing an offense..."

The passage beginning with “he incurs [an offense]” and so forth describes the characteristic of the shameless (*alajjī*) from a superior perspective; it is stated by way of illustration based on those who have received full ordination (*upasampanna*).

Therefore, it should be understood that even for those who claim to be monks—such as novices (*sāmaṇera*) and others down to those of the lineage (*gotrabhū*) in the sense of their outward signs—who are devoid of that specific characteristic yet are immoral (*dussīla*), the characteristic of being shameless consists simply in their deliberate failure to abide by the practice as it has been prescribed. This is to be taken as a common feature shared by all such persons.

"For one who causes [an ox] to be brought," the offense of *dukkaṭa* occurs: at the moment of requesting it, by reason of the request; and at the moment of its acquisition, by reason of consenting to the ox.
For even if an ox is obtained for one's own sake without being requested, it is not permitted to consent to it, because it has been stated:
"He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. Therefore he said:
“Even from a place where one has been invited by relatives, it is not permitted to ask for [food] so as to cut off the root.

And here, although there is no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the act of requesting, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing both in the requesting of an improper object and in the acceptance of it. “Having guarded” means having protected it from dangers such as thieves and the like.
“Having tended” means having nourished it by providing grass, water, and so forth.

However, it is permissible in a place where one has been invited by kinsmen; because the cart must be accepted, it is permissible to ask for it on the grounds that its [original] source has been cut off.
"It is permissible for a limited time" means it is permissible in both cases. Regarding axes and so forth, even those belonging to an individual are permissible;
thus he said, "This same method applies to the axe," and so on. And this same method applies to creepers and the like, as well as to things owned by others.
It should be applied. The phrase "only when it is worth a heavy object" is said with reference to formal request (*viññatti*).
However, regarding taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), if one takes something owned by another—even a blade of grass—with a thieving mind, it is indeed theft (*avahāra*);
one must be dealt with according to the value of the object. In the phrase "creepers and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes bamboo and other items mentioned in the Canon. Therein:

In whatever place substances such as yellow orpiment (haritāla) or vermilion (hiṅgulaka), even in small quantities, are of great value, there even that which is less than the size of a palm fruit is indeed a "heavy object" (garubhaṇḍa), and it is not permitted to request it. This is "requesting" (viññatti).
Among the methods such as indirect speech (parikathā), speaking by way of circumlocution, such as saying "the lodging is crowded," is "indirect speech."

It is called *obhāsa*. When one does not speak directly, but rather speaks in such a way that the intention—such as "Is a pavilion not suitable for the monks?"—is made manifest, this is called *obhāsa*.

*Nimittakamma* is the making of a sign for the purpose of producing requisites, by means of preparing the ground and so forth for the sake of lodgings and the like. They "depart" (*ukkamanti*) means they go away.
344. “Maṇikaṇṭho” means one who has a jewel on his neck. “Devavaṇṇaṃ” means the state of being a deity. 345.
In the text, when the Blessed One said, “I have need of a bowl,” he caused the bhikkhu to speak thus even though he had no need for a bowl, by means of the words of the Sotthiya mantra.
That bhikkhu also spoke the words commanded by the Blessed One, thinking, “I am speaking.”
He said this, and thus there is no falsehood for him. Alternatively, it should be understood that the statement "I have need of a bowl" has the same meaning as "May they give me a bowl.
This same principle applies here as well to the phrase "I have need of a gem.
Therefore, it should be understood that there is no fault in speech for one who speaks or causes others to speak in such a manner.
349. *Uddhamukhaṃ littā* means smeared on the upper side; *ullittā* means smeared all over. For those who smear the interior of the roof generally smear it facing upwards;
therefore he said, "smeared on the inside" (*antolittā*). *Adhomukhaṃ littā* means smeared on the lower side; *avalittā* means smeared all over.
For those who smear the exterior generally smear it facing downwards; therefore he said, "smeared on the outside" (*bahilittā*).

The phrasing would be reversed because the term "by the one causing to do" (*kārayamānena*), which is a causal agentive expression, does not have "by the one doing" (*karontena*) as its synonymous alternative—

that is, it is not a simple agentive expression. Therefore, in the *Niddesa*, the meaning of the word is established by using the instrumental form of the action itself— namely, "by the one doing or by the one causing to do"—
which is consistent with the various headings (*uddesapada*) such as "by the one causing to do."

If it were [taken] as a verbal derivative (*kate*), the grammatical form would be contradictory; however, the intention is that the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states "doing or causing to do" in the nominative case (*paccattavasena*) in order to show the meaning established through semantic force (*sāmatthiya*) rather than by explicitly showing it through the literal sense of the words (*padatthavasena*).
Therefore he said, "only the mere meaning," and so forth. [This refers to] that which is obtainable both from the literal sense of the words and from semantic force.
"Only the meaning" is the sense. For whatever must be practiced by one who is having [a building] constructed, that very same thing must also be practiced by one who is doing it oneself;
this is the implied force (*sāmatthiya*) to be seen here.
"Specification" (*uddesa*) means that which is to be specified as the subject matter. "White work" (*setakamma*) refers to the application of white-colored plaster for the purpose of making it white.
Or, even if a thin coating of plaster has been applied, if it is measured together with that [coating], it would exceed the prescribed measure;

therefore, to dispel such doubt, he said, "it is *abbhokārika*. The intention is that by this, it does not fall under the designation of "exceeding the measure," because the plaster is not a constituent part of the hut.
To demonstrate the method of explaining the aforementioned meaning, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth. Therein, "in length..."

The intention is that by not saying "and in width," but rather using the word *vā* (or) in the sense of an alternative—saying "either in length or in width"—it is made clear that an offense occurs even if it is increased on only one side.
"Three cubits" means three cubits by the standard cubit (*pakati-hattha*);
some also say it refers to the "carpenter’s cubit" (*vaḍḍhakī-hattha*), but that [is not accepted] because [the definition] says: "Wherein... this is reckoned as a hut."
This contradicts [the rule] "it moves," because even in a hut measuring three cubits, a bed of standard measurement can easily be turned over by the hand of a carpenter.

Furthermore, the phrase "or less than four cubits" is stated with reference to a bed that meets the minimum measurement and is not fit to be turned over. For if it were four cubits by the standard cubit (*pakati-hattha*), even then...
If a bed that fits the measurement of a *kuṭī* (hut) does not fit [within it], then it is simply not a *kuṭī*;
therefore, the measurement must be understood as being determined solely by the dimensions of the bed. "A bed of proper measurement" means a bed of the smallest permissible measurement.
For that is nine spans or eight spans of a natural cubit; any bed smaller than that, including the headrest, is not permitted.
One is unable to lie down with one’s feet extended after setting them aside. “Even if it is smaller than the [prescribed] measure” means even if it is smaller than the maximum measure;
this is stated so that there may be no doubt that the selection of a site should be made even for that which possesses the minimum measure.

“A paste of mud” (kalalalepa) refers to a coating made with some kind of clay, such as a paste of red ochre and other materials applied for the purpose of coloring the surface white, red, or otherwise.

Therefore he says, "it is indeed non-sticky. By this, he shows that when a thick paste is applied to ponds and the like, it enters into the category of what is called "plastering" only when it is applied with clay.
A "wooden door-frame" (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa) refers to a square wooden frame consisting of two door-posts, upon which they lean a door-panel with its upper bolt and close the door.
"Even after looking" means even after having looked; the meaning is "even by way of a formal act of looking. It should be understood that the letter *o* has been substituted for the prefix *apa*.
"Even a place where the range [of elephants] is fixed": here, the path of regular travel for elephants departing for their range is also included.
"Of these" refers to lions and the rest. "Range-ground" (*gocarabhūmi*) means a place for taking food. "Not taken" means because it is to be rejected.
The meaning is: "not taken" and "not forbidden. For the place where lions and other such animals take their food is not fixed, as it is for elephants;
rather, wherever there are living beings such as cattle or buffalo, they go quickly even to distant places to take their food.
Therefore, that [taking of food] is not forbidden for them; rather, it is the fixed path of travel from their lair that is forbidden.
Because they are fixed [in place]. "Of other wild animals" means of forest buffaloes and the like. "For the sake of health" means for the sake of being free from affliction.

"The rest" refers to the sixteen types beginning with those dependent on grain stores; these should be understood as being subject to affliction through disturbances such as crowds of people, great crushes, house robberies, and physical injury.
"Abbhāghāta" means that which is struck (*abhi-ghnantī*) here. This is the same meaning as what was called a "house of enmity" (*verighara*).
It is said that it was "made for the purpose of killing thieves" in order to clarify this point.
"Dhammagandhikā" means those who, by means of the Dhamma—that is, by the method of punishment—perform the amputation of hands, feet, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the term "gandhikā," that piece of wood or plank upon which they place the hand or other limb and then cut it off is called by that name. By this...
And the place that has been marked out. In the text, "situated on a street" means situated on a carriage road.
"Situated at a crossroads" means situated at the junction of four carriage roads. "By cart" means by a cart for carrying goods such as bricks, plaster, and so forth.
"Pācīna" (the site to be built upon) refers to the designated area to be constructed, starting from the ground level of the dwelling up to the top of the roof.
Upon which they establish walls, pillars, and so forth. Therefore he said, "From that point on," and so forth.

Although there is no distinction here between prior effort and simultaneous effort as there is in the case of taking what is not given, nevertheless, the demonstration of their classification must be made by breaking it down;
thus, this is for the purpose of showing the delimitation by way of the hut's division.
"Made": for the purpose of that, meaning for the purpose of roofing it. "Thus made": made either without a formally designated site or exceeding the prescribed dimensions.
"Leaf-hut" (paṇṇasālā): they plaster both inside and out so that the leaves, grass, and chaff do not fall away;
it is with reference to this that it is said. For this very reason, he will say later: "he plasters a leaf-hut."
The phrase "or within the plaster" (*antolepe vā*) and so forth was stated with reference to one who wishes to finish [the work] by means of internal plastering.
The same principle applies here as well regarding "or external plastering" (*bahilepe vā*). The word "in that" (*tasmiṃ*) should be construed as "placed either in the door-panel or in the window.

"Its opening" (*tassokāsaṃ*) refers to the gap that constitutes the space for that door-panel or the like. "Having enlarged it again" (*puna vaḍḍhetvā*) means having made the space previously established small...
Having further enlarged that [opening] by breaking through the door, the window, or the gaps;
"placed" means having brought it to the door-bolt or the lattice-window, and having established it within that gap, whether it has been enlarged or not;
"the plaster does not adhere" means that the plaster applied all around does not [adhere] together with the door-bolt or the window as it was thus placed.
"Ghaṭīyati" means it is not joined as one; this is what is meant. "Taṃ" refers to either the door-enclosure or the window.

"The Saṅghādisesa occurs at the very first" means that because the plastering was completed by joining [the parts] all around them beforehand, the Saṅghādisesa offense occurs even before the door-enclosure or window is set in place.

"By means of plastering alone" means that even for windows and such, which are made of bricks, there is an offense by means of plastering alone on all sides because there is no space for plaster in those windows, or because they are made of bricks;

alternatively, some explain the meaning as "even in the case of windows and such, by means of the plaster joining together with the plaster of the wall. "Therein" means in the leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*). "To the extent of eight finger-breadths for the sake of light..."

"Leaving it aside and plastering" means that when one leaves an opening of about eight finger-breadths between the wooden planks of a wall and applies plaster only as far as that, doing so for the sake of light while leaving the rest of the wall surface unplastered with the intention, "I will plaster this opening later"—in such a case of leaving it aside, there is no offense;
this is the intended meaning. However, if one does not do it in this way, but [leaves it] for the sake of light at all times...
He establishes [the offense] by way of the window-opening; when the window-frame and the door-panels have been joined together, the plastering is also joined.
Showing that it is a *saṅghādisesa* from the very first moment, he says "If," and so forth. Since only a mud-wall comes under the category of "plastered with mud," he says:
"If one makes a wall of mud, there is an offense when it is joined together with the roofing-plaster. Of both...
“Non-offense” means that because the first coating has not been applied, it is impossible for the second to be designated for oneself.

(354) “For the purpose of showing the classification of offenses” means that therein, “in the case of a site with living beings and without space, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); and because of the ground having been prepared without confessing the offense, and because of exceeding the measurement, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)”—thus it is for the purpose of showing the distinction between the offenses themselves.
(361) “When the work on the hut is not finished” means when the work on the hut—right up to the completion of the plastering—is not finished even by a single lump [of material].
The phrase "or for another person" is stated for the purpose of showing that there is no offense for one who is the original owner (the *mūlaṭṭha*).

However, even for the one by whom it was obtained, if they bring it to completion, there is indeed an offense; for according to such statements as, "If one brings to its conclusion what has been left unfinished by others, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)," and so forth.
Furthermore, even an action previously performed [by another] is considered from the time it is received [by the offender].
It is indeed considered to have been done for one’s own sake; therefore, even that [building] must be completed by giving it to the Saṅgha or to novices (sāmaṇera) and so forth.
As for the phrase “or for another,” this should be understood as being said with reference specifically to one who has not yet received full ordination (anupasampanna).
However, some maintain that there is no offense in completing a hut obtained from another, provided it was originally intended for one’s own sake.

“They say ‘because it has not been done. “To be cleared away” means that they must be destroyed by means of clearing away. “Having made level with the ground” means having made it even up to the surface of the clearing.
“A cave” refers to a mountain cave. “For no plastering is applied here” is said because of the absence of a plastered covering.

Or, because it has been specifically permitted as distinct [from a hut]. If they apply plaster inside the upper part of a cave for the purpose of painting and so forth, it does not count as an *ullittakuṭi* (a plastered hut), and it is indeed permissible.
They call a particular type of dwelling—a square gabled house constructed of bricks and the like, with a single central peak, not too high—a "cave" (*guhā*); even one as large as that is permissible.
There is no offense for one who is whitewashing or plastering [the interior].
"Earth-cave" (*bhūmiguhā*) means a cave in the ground (*umaṅgaguha*). Regarding the phrase "in the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathāsu*):

in the commentaries on the *Kukkuṭacchikageha* and other such passages, after it has been stated that "a grass hut is a *kukkuṭacchikageha*," the commentators further explain it by saying, "the roof [is made] with poles... and so forth; this is how the construction should be understood.
It should be seen as follows: "Having made a lattice with poles" means having set up poles lengthwise and crosswise, and having constructed it like a net by binding them with creepers and the like.
"And that" refers to the state of being plastered on both sides (*ullitta*). It is stated with reference specifically to the roofing;
that is, it is said with reference to the plastering of both the interior and the exterior of the roof. Even in the case of a mud wall, even without a coating of plaster on the walls...
Since an offense can arise even from the mere joining of the plastering of the roof with the wall, it should be understood that the plastering of the roof itself is the primary factor.

Nevertheless, because of such statements as: "If one builds a stone foundation below for the purpose of warding off termites, but having left it unplastered, applies plaster only on top, and the plaster does not adhere, there is indeed no offense," and so forth.
For the purpose of joining the plastering of the roof, the plastering of the entire wall must necessarily be desired;
for even if one part of it is not plastered, the plastering of the roof cannot be joined. Therefore he said, "the plastering is not joined. "In this" means in the grass hut.
And it is not only in a grass hut that there is no offense due to the conditions of construction and lack of space, but also in rock shelters, caves, and so forth.

In this way, by means of this method, it has been shown by implication that even for one building a hut for the sake of another, there is no offense due to the conditions of "commencement" (*sārambha*) and so forth.
In that context, the words beginning with "yaṃ pana" (but as for what... were spoken in order to avoid contradiction with the Canon (*pāḷi*). This is the intended meaning here: [regarding] another...
For one who builds for the sake of a preceptor or others, there is no offense even on account of such causes as hostility;

however, that statement in the Pāḷi, "for the three builders of offenses, there are three *dukkaṭas*," was spoken for the purpose of showing the offense incurred by one building for another's sake, and not because of causes such as hostility.
Rather, it is due to the non-completion of the hut exactly as it was authorized.

"Regarding the phrase *āpattidassanatthaṃ* (for the purpose of showing the offense): therein, *yathāsamādiṭṭhāya* means that when a monk has given an instruction while departing, saying, "Build a hut for me;

let it have its site designated, be free from harm, and have a surrounding space," the intention is that this refers to the causal condition of the act of building, rather than the sequence of the command given by the one who causes it to be built. However, in some places..."

In the manuscript, immediately after the reading, "There is no offense for one who has another [monk] build a hut even though it has reached the characteristics of a *kuṭi*," etc., the reading "But whatever offense belongs to the craftsmen" and so forth is seen; that alone is more appropriate.
For when this is the case, the intended meaning therein becomes clear.

"Having stated 'there is no offense'": this means that because it was intended solely for the purpose of a dwelling place and was not restricted [to a specific recipient], it is stated that there is no offense.

"One who builds without having it designated": this refers even to one who builds [a hut] of the proper measure. "Without intention": this means without the intention of knowing the formal rule (paṇṇatti).

The state of being any one of the "overturned" [types of roofing], the occurrence of the lower limit of measurement, the fact that the site has not been designated, the exceeding of the proper measure, and the fact that it is for one's own use.
A dwelling-house consists of seven parts, including the plastering and the construction, or six parts, excluding the measurement of the structural members and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the building of a small hut (*kuṭikāra*) is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding the building of a monastery (*vihārakāra*).
365. Since even the genitive case is desired for the agent in the seventh application of the word *pūjā* (worship), it is stated: “or worshipped by the village.

With reference to the fact that [the sense-faculties] exist within the material elements (*rūpa*), their state of being a single faculty is spoken of; thus he says, “with reference to the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*).
For they maintain that even the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) belongs to the primary elements (*bhūtagāma*).

366. Regarding the phrase "there is no origination from action": it means that there is no origination from mere action alone, apart from non-action (akiriyā) which is defined as the non-indication of the object. For this [non-indication] originates from both action and non-action.
In this training rule, in the expression "or monks," the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction; by that, [it implies]: "He may have a large vihāra built..."
"And not having caused monks to be brought [to him]"—this combines both the act of doing and the act of not doing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a dwelling is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Malice.

380. In the eighth [verse], the connection is with the phrase "surrounded by a rampart. Regarding the expression "furnished with gate-towers and watchtowers": here, a *aṭṭālaka* (watchtower) is a specific type of structure built upon the ramparts for the purpose of warfare, which is curved in shape and provided with openings for discharging arrows.

"Of sixteen kinds" refers to the sixteenfold practice consisting of full understanding (*pariññā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) to be performed respectively regarding each of the four Truths along the four paths.
"Out of respect for them": those monks, appearing weary, gathered at the place where the meal-assigner was stationed.
"Out of respect for the monks" means out of reverence (*gāravena*) and shame (*lajjāya*) when showing one's own exhausted body before the monks while requesting them to recite the *uddesa*.

"Thirteenfold" refers to the thirteen formal appointments (*sammuti*): the designator of meals, the assigner of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the distributor of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, the distributor of hard foods, the dispenser of trifles, the assigner of outer cloths, the assigner of bowls, the supervisor of monastery attendants, and the supervisor of novices.

In the Pāḷi, the word “apisū” is a particle synonymous with “apicā. “Thus in all instances” means that regarding common bedding such as seats and so forth, one should understand that one may have it prepared after having made a separate determination for each case—such as the time of entering, exiting, and the arrangement of the agreement.
For this is the nature of things created without prior specification; it occurs by way of those things created [on the spot].
It has been said; however, having made a determination such as, "Let so many speak this and that, let so many remain silent,
let them assume various modes of posture and activities, and let them have various colors, shapes, ages, and genders," and having performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*),
entered the attainment, emerged, and then made a resolution (*adhiṭṭhita*), they appear in whatever manner is desired, each distinct from one another.
[They] exist. "A baseless statement" means a meaningless statement. 383.
"Food for those wandering alone" refers to food that, because it is very pleasant, should be given separately so that everyone may obtain it.
"By way of a derivative expression" (*taddhitavohārena*) means: "This has four as its measure; thus it is a 'tetrad' (*catukka*)," by way of such a derivative expression. "Existence" (*bhava*).
"It must have happened. The phrase "the past part of the day" is said with reference to the very moment of distributing the voting sticks on that same day.
"Yesterday" (hiyyo) has the same meaning as "today" (ajja). For this reason they said, "Tomorrow we... and so forth.
"Smuttering" (padhūpāyanta) means smuttering by way of repeatedly arising anger. In the text, "kissa maṃ" means "for what reason for us? (kena kāraṇena mayaṃ).
384. Having formed “sarasi tvam” into one sentence, having formed “kattā” as ending in the *ritu* suffix denoting the agent (*kattar*),
and having formed “asī” into a single sentence together with the supplied word (*ajjhāhāra-pada*),
he says “atha vā” and so forth in order to show that “evarūpam” and “yathāyaṃ bhikkhunī āha” should each be joined with two separate sentences.
"Ujukam eva" (straightway) means that the first apprehension of the meaning, by way of the suffix -tva, is "straight"; this is the intended sense.
The second word "dabba" is a synonym for "wise" and so forth; thus he said, "Indeed, O Dabba, the wise are not [merely] 'dabbas'.
"Nibbeṭhenti" means they release one from fault. "Vinayalakkhaṇe tantaṃ" means establishing the tradition (āgama) regarding the subject matter of the characteristics of the Vinaya adjudication.

In the Pāli, regarding the passage beginning with *yato ahan* (“since I was born”), the meaning should be understood as follows: from the time I was born until now, I do not recall engaging in sexual intercourse even in a dream, nor have I been a practitioner of that sexual act.
Therefore, he said, “even in a dream,” and so forth. Now, to show the construction by way of a single sentence, he says, “Alternatively (*atha vā*),” and so on.

It was said: "It does not fit" means that because her statement does not accord with the statement of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), and because that lack of accord arose precisely from her being notoriously immoral among the bhikkhus from long ago, the intention is:
"Therefore, expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā."
"Go away, go away! Go far away, you who do not belong to me. Perish! means: "Go out of sight. "She is not one who acts" means:
she is not one who acts by means of a groundless accusation. "He becomes the perpetrator" means:

if she has not been expelled on the basis of her confession—"I have defiled the venerable one"—then the Elder becomes the perpetrator of that offense because he has established her as a defiler of bhikkhunīs. He is not a perpetrator [otherwise].

He is "one who has not committed [the offense]" because the Blessed One said, "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā," based on her general reputation and without regard for the specific admission she had made.

For if the Elder had been the actual perpetrator, he would certainly have had to state, "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā for this very reason," by pointing to that specific fault; since he did not say so, [he is one who has not committed it].
The intention is that because it was stated, "And investigate these monks," rather than saying,
"Investigate the matter [of the robe]," it is established by implication that the nun Mettiyā deserved expulsion for another offense,
that the charge against her was groundless, and that the Elder was not the perpetrator.
“His own sutta” refers to a forged sutta accompanied by the phrase “by his own admission. Regarding the statement “the Elder was the perpetrator,” this is the intended meaning:

in your own doctrine, without stating “by his own admission,” the expulsion of that nun was ordained specifically within the context of the case presented as “Expel the nun Mettiyā,” which deals with the common ground [of the offense]. Thus, in your position, the Elder...

He is not the author [of the rule]. However, when it is stated, "by his own admission," since the offense of *pārājika* was already established previously, the Elder [Dhammarakkhita] is not the author of our position because it is accomplished by the destruction of that [offense] through her own admission.

Furthermore, for the Mahāvihāravāsins as well, when it is stated, "by his own admission," the destruction of that [offense] is prescribed only in the case of the specific matter (*vatthu*) that has been entered into, and not otherwise.
The intended meaning is "by way of commonality. "In this" means in these two positions or in the two suttas.

"That which was stated later" means that what was stated by the Mahāvihāravāsins is the logical one; the reason it is investigated is that the correctness of the latter position has been examined, [stating]:
"In that case, the *saṅghādisesa* offense leading to rehabilitation... [and so on] ...it did not destroy the impurity itself."

The meaning is that it has been analyzed according to the method that will be explained. By the statement, "One incurs a *dukkaṭa* for defaming a bhikkhunī," the doctrine of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is shown.

"Therein" means among those [offenses] consisting of *dukkaṭa* and *pācittiya*. Regarding the term *dukkaṭa*, one should understand the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) of the doctrine of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* as it was stated.
Having shown this, in order to demonstrate the intended meaning of the *Kuruṇḍi-vāda*—which states that it is a *pācittiya* offense—it is said:

“In the latter method as well,” and so forth. The meaning is: by the force of the prescriptive words for a *saṅghādisesa* and other offenses, even though the intention to deceive is the same, there is a distinction such as the act of slandering (*anuddhaṃsana*) and so on.
However, for a nun [committing this] toward a monk, it is a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the nun...
For a monk who reviles [another], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having thus clarified the intended meaning in both of these commentarial statements, he now says "In that regard...

and so forth, in order to point out the fault in the latter position regarding the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) and to establish the former position regarding the offense of wrong-doing. Therein:
In the case of intentional lying (*sampajāna-musāvāda*), a separate *pācittiya* is stated apart from the [general] *pācittiya*;

the intention there is that it is not included within that [general category]. Therefore—because a separate *pācittiya* has been prescribed for groundless accusation (*amūlaka-unnaddhaṃsana*)—the previous method refers to the doctrine of a *dukkaṭa*.
Having thus shown the doctrine of *dukkaṭa* and *pācittiya* as intervening [between them], now...
In order to clarify the meaning that is already evident, the passage beginning with “likewise, a bhikkhunī” is commenced. Therein, “likewise” means:
just as for a bhikkhu who slanders a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, the offenses of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa* were stated, so too [is it here].
It was stated in general terms that there is no forfeiture (*nāsanā*) on account of these; however, for this [offense], there is forfeiture by means of the *dukkaṭa*.
The intended meaning is that it does not exist. "Immoral" means those who have committed a *pārājika* offense.
(386) "By way of diversity of mode" means by way of the diversity between the mode of being corrupted and the mode of corrupting.
"Discontented" means unsatisfied; thus he said, "not happy. "Not inspired with confidence" means one in whom confidence has not been produced. The word *khīla* denotes a state of rigidity.

And because there is a sequence regarding refuse, he said: “The mind... [up to] ...a stake. “Not arrived at” means not approached or reached by means of rapture, pleasure, and so forth. Therefore he said: “not entered into.

Regarding the phrase “by which it is called corrupted” and “by which it is called agitated,” here “by which it is called corrupted” refers to that by which it is called corrupted, and “by which it is called agitated” refers to that by which it is called agitated.
It should be understood that both what was stated [in the summary] and what was stated in the word-commentary apply here.

Regarding the phrase "by two": it refers to the two terms "anger" and "hatred" mentioned as "by that anger and by that hatred. However, since in terms of actual meaning it is only hatred that is shown by both, he says, "it shows only the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). "By which" means by which dissatisfaction.

"By way of one who has been accused": the intention is that if "by way of one who has been accused" were also intended [to include cases] where there is no basis (*amūlaka*), then the word-commentary would have stated, "that which is called 'without basis' is that which has not been committed.
"That which is a *pārājika*" refers to any one among the nineteen *pārājikas* appropriate for a monk. However, in the word-commentary, only those found in the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga* are taken.
It is said, “by one of four [ways]. Here, “this is immeasurable” means that whether the person has committed an offense or not, this lack of uprooting is not a factor for the offense;

rather, the intention here is that only the desire to cause a downfall—whether through a perception of purity, thinking “this person has not committed an offense and is pure,” or through doubt regarding a person who has either committed or not committed an offense—is the factor here.
“‘In the same way’ (tatheva) refers by extension to this meaning: ‘by the ear of faith’ or ‘by the divine ear.
‘Suspicion arising precisely from following what has been seen’ is called *diṭṭhaparisaṅkita*. The same applies to the remaining cases. ‘Or without having seen’ is stated in its most extreme sense;
even if they have departed after having seen [the fault], there is no offense. ‘Of these’ (*imesaṃ*) means ‘by these. ‘Will do’ (*karissanti*) refers to that very moment.”
This is a demonstration of the manner in which [the offense] arises; however, it later rebukes him with the suspicion that "it was done by this much time.
There is no rebuke based on the thought that they will not do it. The phrase "Ariṭṭha was drunk" is a demonstration of the sign of the smell of liquor wafting from the mouth.
For Ariṭṭha was a permissible medicine possessing a color and scent similar to liquor.
In the passages beginning with "The seen has a root," there is shown the state of having or not having a root for the occurrence or non-occurrence of misconduct.

In the passage beginning with "There is perception based on what was seen," however, there is shown the state of having or not having a root for the occurrence or non-occurrence of the perception of what was seen.
Regarding the phrase "Having seen, and being one who perceives it as seen, he reproves": here, the person whom he reproves is someone other than himself who is transgressing.
If one sees someone emerging from a concealed place and accuses them with the recognition, "This is he," it is included [in the offense].
This same method applies to cases based on what has been heard and so forth. Regarding the phrase "with the root" or "with the root of recognition":

here, if one accuses someone who has committed a *pārājika* offense by means of the root of having seen it, etc., and with the impure recognition that "this person has committed it," one is said to accuse "with the root. As for "having the root of recognition": [it refers to when one accuses based on a perception rooted in such factors].

Thus, because there is the possibility of non-offense: when one perceives a person as having committed an offense—whether they have actually committed it or not—with respect to what has been seen and so forth, or with respect to the roots such as what has not been seen;

and when, perceiving [the offense] through what was seen, heard, and so on, one reproves that person by means of those roots such as what was seen, this is called "reproving based on perception. There is no offense in these cases.
The meaning in the section on offenses should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated here.
“Standing nearby” means standing within the range of sight and hearing for the purpose of communicating through hand gestures or vocal sounds;
this is the meaning. Some, however, say “standing within twelve cubits,” but that is not correct.
This is because later on, when demonstrating the non-offense by way of contrast, it says: “by sending a messenger, a letter, or a message.”
Only this much has been stated; it is not, however, said that "if one reproves [the monk] after releasing him from a distance of twelve *hatthas*, the offense does not reach his head.
"Word by word" (*vācāya vācāya*) means that for the one who reproves, there is an offense for every single word even if he speaks for the entire day after having been instructed once.
"He too" (*sopi*) refers to the one who was instructed. And for him, even without saying "I have seen it too," etc., if he perceives it as "groundless" (*amūlaka*), [there is an offense].
