If one speaks with the intention of causing another to fall away, saying "You have committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)," even if one speaks of it generally without making that statement exactly like the words of the other person, there is still an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
However, even if the intention is to expose [the fault], if one merely repeats what was said by another, saying "So-and-so spoke thus," there is no offense entailing suspension. But if...
If one says that something was said even when it was not said by another, there is indeed an offense.

Regarding the phrase "many [accusers] toward many [accused] on many grounds," here the term "many" indicates—by way of specifying the plurality of those accused—that there is a distinction between the sections in the first three cases due to the plurality of those accused.
For, in the case of a single [accused], there is a distinction based on the plurality of the grounds for accusation and the accusers.
This tetrad has been stated; since another tetrad is also obtained by way of the plurality of the one being accused, there is indeed an octad.

In connection with the charge of groundless accusation, the passage beginning with “Who, however, is entitled to accuse? was commenced in order to show the characteristics of a charge based on grounds and so forth.
As for the Sutta beginning with “Having heard it from a bhikkhu, he accuses,” this refers to those who [report] the failure of others to the accuser.
They proclaim [the faults]; at that very moment, they do so while standing in the position of accusers.

And because the other person—having accepted their words—is able both to accuse and to cause one who does not accept the accusation to accept it through those starting from the first accuser down to the end of the sectarians' disciples, they should be understood here as being designated by way of the status of disciples.

Regarding the phrases "having sent a messenger," and so forth: it means having sent a messenger with the instruction, "Go and accuse him thus," or having sent a letter or the original message to one who is capable of accusing him. "At the proper time" means at the moment of ordinary knowledge.
"Of the two heavy offenses" refers to the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses. "Wrong view" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) is the ten-based view proceeding in the manner of "there is no gift," and so on;
"extremist view" (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*) is the view that grasps at the extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism.

"Of the six [offenses] prescribed on account of livelihood": this refers to the *pārājika* offense involving superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) which must be committed even for the sake of livelihood;
the *saṅghādisesa* offense regarding matchmaking (*sañcaritta*); the grave offense (*thullaccaya*) incurred by saying indirectly, "He who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant";
the *pācittiya* offense for a monk’s requesting exquisite food; and the *pācittiya* offense for a nun’s requesting exquisite food.

Regarding the six [offenses] mentioned in the *Parivāra*—namely, the *pāṭidesanīya* and the *dukkaṭa* for requesting soup and rice—it is not the case that these offenses were prescribed solely on account of one’s livelihood (*ājīva*), because they may also be committed in other ways, such as through acting as a matchmaker (*sañcaritta*).

Nevertheless, this was stated with reference to the commission of these offenses specifically on account of one’s livelihood; the meaning is that they are indeed prescribed on account of one’s livelihood. And it is not only...

These very [offenses], as well as others that must be committed for the sake of livelihood—such as through taking what is not given, corrupting families, killing living beings, and performing surgery—exist;

however, it should be understood that they are not mentioned separately because they are included within the six categories of offenses beginning with the *pārājika*, which are grouped under the heading of "offenses" (*āpatti*).
Furthermore, the statement "it does not reach the head" was said with reference to the *saṅghādisesa*; the formal accusation, however, has indeed been made.

"Thirty" (*tiṃsāni*) means those which possess thirty; thus it is said they are "in excess of thirty. The same method applies here to the term "ninety" (*navutāni*). Regarding the phrase "by one wishing to take up the *attādāna*":

because it is to be taken up by oneself, because it is to be grasped through the roots of views and so forth, and because it seizes another without allowing them to struggle, it is called a "charge" (*codanā*, lit. taking up of self); [the phrase means] by one wishing to take up that charge.
"Desiring to act"—this is the meaning.
"By a committee" (*ubbāhikā*): it is called a committee because by means of it they extract (*ubbahanti*) or separate those who are shameless, whether through censure or by settling a quarrel;

it refers to the formal authorization of the Saṅgha, and by that [authorization]. "Adjudication" (*vinicchana*) means precisely the adjudication by those monks authorized by that [committee]. "In an assembly crowded with the shameless" (*alajjussannāya*).

Indeed, when the ten factors for settling have been brought forward in the assembly, two or three monks endowed with those factors should be appointed right there by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*), as prescribed;
and those so appointed, either sitting separately or within that very assembly, should adjudicate that legal dispute after announcing: "Nothing should be said to others."
"Kimhi" means "in what matter" (*vatthusmiṃ*), that is to say, "in which failure" (*kataravipattiyaṃ*).

Regarding the phrase "Kimhi naṃ nāmā," even if it is spoken in any language by which it is understood—namely, "In which failure do you charge him?"—it refers to the accuser's lack of knowledge regarding the Vinaya;
for one who is unable to discern, [thinking]: "He asks me 'in which' among the failures of virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood."
It is a question, but not for one who does not understand even the mere meaning of the words such as "in what" (*kimhi*).
For an investigator does not ask a foolish accuser in a language with which he is unfamiliar, "In what [is it] not? Nor is this statement "Do you not know even 'in what'?
intended merely as a verbal quibble; rather, when it is asked, "By which failure? it is possible to reply, "By such-and-such a failure."
It should be understood that this was said with reference specifically to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) of the statement "you do not know.
For this very reason, after stating, "The method (*naya*) should be given to the modest fool," he spoke the passage beginning with "In what will you charge him?

For failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*)," which is merely an exposition of the underlying intention regarding the granting of the method; it is not, however, a demonstration of the mere synonymous alternatives for the words "in what" (*kimhi*) and "him" (*naṃ*).

For a fool, even when he understands the meaning of the statement, "In which failure do you accuse me?", is unable to discern the various types of failure or the specific nature of the failure with which he himself is being charged;
therefore, because of that very ignorance, he should be reproved as shameless.
Furthermore, the phrase "in what? is merely illustrative; it may also be understood in any other way whatsoever.
Having made it known that [the offense] was unintentional, he must indeed be released.
Because of the statement, "For the restraint of refractory persons," and so forth, it is said: "Laid down for the purpose of restraining the shameless...
etc. For the word *ehiti*—the syllable *hi* here should be understood as an augment (*āgama*), meaning "he will come. By way of the continuity of what has been seen...

"By the method of what has been seen. The meaning is that even when the fault has become manifest through the sequence of question and answer, it must be dealt with as an offense solely by means of the shameless person's admission that "it is impure," which is the acknowledgment of the fault.
However, some say: "Since this [acknowledgment] does not exist for a shameless person, it must be dealt with as a non-offense solely by means of the admission of purity."

Some say that "this meaning is included here," but that is not correct, because it would result in the investigator being rendered purposeless, as the accuser alone would have to stand by having admitted his own shamelessness.
For in this context, what is intended by "admission" (paṭiññā) is specifically the admission of the removal of fault.
Therefore, he will later say: "He does not give an admission [saying], 'This too does not exist,'" and so forth.

"‘For the purpose of illustrating that meaning’ means for the purpose of illustrating that even when the fault of one who is shameless has become manifest, the matter must still be dealt with according to his promise to abandon that fault.
‘Those who oppose the meaning,’ which is to say the subject of dispute, are ‘opponents of the meaning.

‘Having given notice’ means having made a sound for the purpose of interrupting their speech and for the purpose of making them face [the assembly]. ‘Unfit to decide’ means by way of the perception that [the case] is ‘impure.’"

This was said with reference to the impossibility of investigating [the matter], because [the accuser] has entered the side of the accuser (*codaka-pakkha*) and thus stands outside the state of being an investigator (*anuvijjaka*). For it is only when there is doubt that it is possible to investigate;
however, when there is a view of impurity, everything stated by the one who has been accused appears untrue—how, then, could there be an investigation in such a case?

By the phrase “he will simply be expelled in that manner,” it is shown that without making a formal decision, this act of separation from the Saṅgha—just like the *liṅga-nāsanā* (expulsion by change of gender)—is also one type of expulsion (*nāsanā*). “It has been transgressed” means he has intentionally fallen into an offense through negligence.
“From the very beginning, there is no such thing as one who is shameless (*alajjī*)”—this is said for the sake of protecting his faction.
"He does not give his consent" is the statement of the cause for the arising of this characteristic of shamelessness.
From the time it is concealed, he is indeed called "shameless"; the meaning is that his previous state of conscientiousness no longer protects him.
"He does not give his consent" means that he does not give his consent thinking, "If I speak of the fault I have committed, those who follow me will break away."
"He does not stand in his place" means he does not stand in the position of one who possesses a sense of shame; the intention is that there is transgression in both body and speech.

Therefore it was said: "No formal decision should be given. The intention is that even though the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) had been settled previously by the admission of those on the opposing side, because it has not been properly settled, this [person] will likewise be one who has caused its ruin.

"Having understood the procedure regarding those who accuse and those who are accused" means: having understood the action that must be performed by the investigator (*anuvijjaka*) toward both the accuser and the accused, as stated in such passages as, "You will be satisfied with our judgment.

"The judgment is in the middle" means: the meaning is that the conclusion of the investigation—whether it be an offense (*āpatti*) or no offense (*anāpatti*)—is what is called the "middle" of the investigation.
He says, "There are two roots," because they speak by making what is rootless have a root. Regarding the phrases "I shall speak at the proper time" and so forth:

one who speaks after having obtained an opportunity is said to speak at the proper time. One who reproaches [others] at places such as the voting hall (*salākagga*), the rice-gruel line (*yāguagga*), or while on the alms-round (*bhikkhācāra*) is said to speak at the improper time.
One who speaks with the desire to remove [another] from a state of fault is said to speak for the sake of benefit (*atthasaṃhita*).
"One whose mind is defiled" means one whose mind is characterized by the defilements (*doṣa*). "Regarding the fifteen qualities" refers to the five qualities stated as:

"purity of bodily conduct, likewise purity of verbal conduct, a mind of loving-kindness toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, great learning, and being well-versed in both *Pātimokkhas*," as well as: "I shall speak at the proper time," and so forth;
and [the remaining ten are] compassion, the desire for welfare, sympathy, and the restoration from offenses.
"Having the discipline as the primary concern" refers to these fifteen qualities. Therein, by "compassion," compassion (*karuṇā*) is shown.
By "desire for welfare," the seeking of what is beneficial is meant. By "sympathy," the joining [of others] with that benefit is meant; by these two, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is shown.
By "the emergence from offenses," the establishing [of others] in the state of purity is meant. Having accused [them] regarding the matter and reminded them, [one obtains] their admission...
"Carrying out the formal act according to what was admitted after having brought the matter forward is called 'having the Vinaya as the primary concern.

In the sense of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) means in the sense of that which is to be brought forward; the meaning is 'in the sense of that which is to be settled by the methods of reconciliation' (*samatha*).
To show that variety: although it is not intended here [in this specific context], that variety is shown by way of enumerating the meanings."
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). For this very reason, he will say: "The remaining [terms] are stated by way of the extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*).
By the phrase "that which one has in view" (*yaṃ adhikicca*), etc., the fact that the word *adhikaraṇa* functions as an accusative (*kamma-sādhana*) is stated.
"Grasping" (*gāha*) is the grasping of the mode of accusation in the mind, thinking, "I shall accuse such-and-such. "Volition" (*cetanā*) is [the thought], "I shall accuse."

"Mental action" (cittakamma) refers to the mental activity characterized by arisen states of mind. "Intolerance" (akkhanti) is the inability to endure anger that has arisen upon seeing the failure of one who has been reproved;
it may also refer to any collection of mind and mental factors occurring in such a manner. "Discourse" (vohāra) is speech proceeding from the occasion of reproving.
"Designation" (paṇṇatti) is the conceptual designation of a name conceived by the mind proceeding from the occasion of reproving.
"Having taken up the charge" means having taken up the accusation mentally. "That legal issue" refers to that legal issue characterized by the taking up [of the charge].
It ceases because volition is momentary, and that [volition] has reached a state of settlement; thus, in this context, an undesirable consequence should be understood.
Likewise, in the subsequent passage, by the phrase "he remains silent," he shows the cessation of conventional expression. Therefore he said:
“‘That legal issue will have reached a state of settlement’— having thus shown the conclusion established in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that ‘therefore,
the designation (*paññatti*) is the legal issue,’ and having now shown that even this has been rejected by some, and having further refuted that [position] as well,
in order to support the status of the legal issue for the very designation stated in the commentaries, [the text says]: ‘That...’”
He said, "But this," and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows: "The apprehension that 'this, namely, designation (paṇṇatti) is the legal issue (adhikaraṇa),' is contradictory.
This is because one might hold the notion that an offense such as a *pārājika* is either exclusively of an unwholesome nature or of an indeterminate (*abyākata*) nature;
thus, the Sutta passage beginning with "the *pārājika* offense of sexual misconduct" would be contradictory when interpreted according to the doctrine that the legal issue is designation.

It was extracted in order to demonstrate this. Therefore he said: “For they... because of their absolute unwholesomeness,” and so forth. “They” refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*).

Regarding the phrase “that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed rootless,” it is stated “and that which is this” and so forth, in order to show that here the term *adhikaraṇa* intends specifically the rootless offense of defeat (*amūlakapārājika*).
As for the passage beginning with “But since...,” however, it refers to the rootless offense of defeat intended here.
This has been undertaken to show that the state of being a designation (*paṇṇattibhāva*) is thus appropriate.

In this context, the phrase "by which designation" refers to the name-designation (*nāma-paṇṇatti*) set forth by the accuser as "one who has committed a *pārājika* offense," and so forth, even though the person is pure by nature.
"Designated" means spoken of. "Because it occurs in relation to the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)" means [it applies] even when [the offense] does not exist, but is merely mentally imputed.
Because it functions as a verbal designation (*vācaka-bhāva*) regarding the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).

Thus, having shown the manner in which the legal issue of an offense is established (*paññatti-bhāva*) in this training rule by way of a designation of name (*nāma-paññatti*), he now says "or because...
and so forth, in order to show it also by way of a designation of meaning (*attha-paññatti*). "Merely a designation" means...
The meaning is that it is merely a designation of an object mentally attributed by way of a mode of existence to that which does not exist.
"And that indeed here" means that, according to the method just stated, the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for this designation exists only here, in this very training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"Some" refers to certain [commentators]. "That is not appropriate" refers to what was stated by some in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the locus.

Having negated the status of being a mere designation (*paṇṇatti*), in order to establish the status of wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth as ultimate reality (*paramattha*), [the opponent] has presented it with elaboration (*papañca*) by saying, "But this is an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) for sexual intercourse," and so on;
the meaning is that this is not logical. He states the reason for this with the words, "For one who is a beginner" (*ādikammikassa*), and so forth;
and by that, if in that doctrine what is called an "offense" were either unwholesome (*akusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*), how could there be an offense for a beginner?

Could there be non-offense? For her too, because unwholesome states and so forth have arisen, it cannot be said that [offense] exists only from the time the Blessed One laid down the training rule until the point of the actual transgression;
for in the case of sexual intercourse and other such acts, unwholesome states and so forth arise even prior to the laying down of the training rule.

For that very reason, there would be the undesirable consequence of offense even for those not fully ordained, since unwholesome states and so forth arise in them as well, such as in the case of those who are ill.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no offense even for a subsequent rule (anupaññatti). Now, if it is thought:

"It is not only unwholesome states and the like, but rather, offenses such as the unwholesome arise only for one who knows that [an act] has been prohibited by the Blessed One," that too is without substance;
for in the case of sexual intercourse and so forth, for one who transgresses without knowing the promulgation of the training rule (sikkhāpada-pannatti)...

Because it would follow that there is no offense, and because an offense has the intrinsic nature of being unwholesome and so forth, even the unity [of the act] in a single effort and so on would not exist.
For indeed, for one who touches a woman throughout the entire day without ever releasing her from his body, only a single unwholesome state arises;
whereas for one who touches many women and then departs, many [unwholesome states] arise—by which [the distinction between] the unity or plurality of the offense would be established.
It should be understood that this is shown by including such improper [statements] as "it might be" and so forth.
In that context, "the basis" (vatthu) refers to the transgression; for that is called the "basis" in the sense of being the occasion for the formal designation of an offense.
"The clan" (gotta) refers to a conceptualized mode of generality, in the sense of excluding the application of the term "Buddha" from acts such as taking what is not given.
"Lineage" (*gotta*). "Name" (*nāma*) refers to a designation for that which does not exist [as a substantial entity].
Furthermore, it should be understood that the offense (*āpatti*), which is the referent of the name "Pārājika," is a designation of meaning (*atthapaññatti*).

As for the suttas cited by them, such as "A legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) may be wholesome" and so forth, and "A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be unwholesome" and so forth—that too [does not apply] to the disputes and so on [themselves].

As for what should be said here regarding the fact that the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth was taught by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*), that has already been stated in detail in the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary on the first *Pārājika* origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), for the purpose of clearing up points of error; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
The author of the *Sāratthadīpanī* holds the view that the offenses are indeed unwholesome (*akusala*) in nature; for this very reason, he states here as well: "Therefore..."
“Having shown that the *paṇṇatti-adhikaraṇa* (the legal category of designation) is the conclusion established in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), [the author] now says ‘But this...

and so forth, in order to show that even that is not tenable. Thus, taking his own position to be the position of the commentator (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), he pointed it out without even considering the contradiction with the text; for here, the master Buddhaghosa does not [accept] the commentary’s doctrine.
In order to show that [the previous position] was incorrect, he began with the words “But this, however,” and so forth;
for he himself states further on, “It should be understood as being merely a designation (paññatti-matta) of a legal issue arising from an offense.

Alternatively, having shown the error of certain people who have misapprehended it, he began again wishing to refute that [misconception]; for it is for this very reason that he says at the end, “some (eke).”

It should be understood as follows: if quarrels and so forth were themselves wholesome (*kusala*) and so on, it would follow that their respective means of settlement (*samatha*) would also possess those same qualities.
However, since designations (*paññatti*) are not applicable to ultimate realities (*paramattha*), he said, "by means of the wholesome and other types of settlement.

It is only the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) which, by their very nature as designations, are subject to settlement; it is not the case that the various ultimate realities, such as the wholesome and so forth, are themselves subject to settlement.
By showing the conclusion of the matter already established above—that it reaches pacification by itself through its momentariness—it is said:

"Thus, in this sense of 'legal issue' (*adhikaraṇa*). The meaning is that, according to the method already stated, it is to be legally settled (*adhikaraṇīya*) by means of the methods of pacification (*samatha*).
By the phrase "here, a certain person," the specific type of dispute intended here is excluded.
*Anuvāda* means both censuring on account of failures and formal accusation. In this context, *upavadanā* refers to reproach and abuse.

This is stated with reference to the five classes of offenses included in the Schedule (*mātikā*). *Kiccayata* means that which ought to be done. Regarding the phrase "of the exposition according to the sequence of words": here, "exposition according to the sequence of words" refers to the word-analysis (*padabhājana*);
thus, the meaning is "of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) together with that."
387. Regarding the word *assa*, it is the genitive case used in the sense of the agent; thus he says, "by this accuser," and so forth.

However, the phrase "but in the case of that which is rooted in what has been seen" refers to the section of the Pāḷi beginning with, "it occurs to one who is committing an offense involving defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*) having seen [it].
In that context, "committing an offense involving defeat" refers merely to the act of seeing [the monk] sitting in private with a woman and so forth.
The person was seen by him, but not by way of seeing the path, the entering upon the path, and so forth.
For if he had seen him in that manner, he would have been one who perceives that person as impure;
and for one who accuses another—whether pure or impure—with a perception of impurity, there would be no *saṅghādisesa* offense. "There is no offense for one who sees an impure person as pure."
This is because of such statements as, "In one who is impure, there is the view of impurity," and so forth. Therefore, even upon merely seeing [a monk] sitting in private with a woman,
if one perceives him as pure— or is in doubt— thinking, "This faithful son of good family does not incur a *pārājika* offense," yet then accuses him by specifying,
"I have heard that he has committed a *pārājika* offense," etc., it is indeed a *saṅghādisesa*.
It should be understood that for one who does not perceive it as impure, there is only a light offense due to lying and so forth, even though he has seen it or heard it. However,
if he intends to cause another to fall from their pure view, yet speaks only of what was seen, such as sitting in private and so on, while omitting what was not seen— namely,
the grounds for a *pārājika* offense such as leading someone along a path that is not a path, or saying "you are no longer a *samaṇa*" and so forth— [then the offense is different].
If he does not speak, there is no offense for him. However, for one who speaks more than what is true—because of saying "seen" when it was "not seen"—there is indeed an offense.

Furthermore, if one who, being conscious of impurity due to the first *pārājika* offense such as sitting in private with a woman, intends to cause another to fall away and commits the taking of what is not given, yet says "I saw her" or "I heard [of her]" and so forth, for him too there is no *saṅghādisesa*.

Some say: "It is because of the perception of impurity regarding what is impure. Others, however, say: "Since there is an absence of the perception of purity regarding the offense for which one accuses another of a *pārājika*, it is indeed an offense [of the *saṅghādisesa* class]. This is correct. For it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Regarding the *pārājika* with which one accuses another, knowing 'this person has not committed this,' and with the intention of causing him to leave [the Saṅgha]... [it is] a *saṅghādisesa*."
By this method, the analysis should also be understood for those cases rooted in what has been heard and so forth.

"In other [instances] mentioned" refers to those mentioned in the context of verbal abuse and the like. "Lustful" means one who is soaked by the persistence of misconduct that constitutes an offense involving defeat (pārājika) through all three doors.
"Become like dregs" means having become like refuse; the meaning is that one is devoid of essence.
*Koṇṭha* means a thief; the meaning is "one who is immoral. *Jeṭṭhabbataki* refers to a sectarian (tīrthika) appointed to the service of the goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī;
it is said that she was called the "elder sister" (*jeṭṭhā*) of the goddess Kāḷakaṇṇīsiri. *Yadaggena* means "by which reason" or "to whatever extent";
the same principle applies here for *tadaggena*. The passage beginning with "it is not allowable" (*no kappati*) is intended solely to illustrate the state of being doubtful.
"Thus it is said"—this is the intention of the Elder Mahāpaduma.

(389) "In this regard" refers to the formal accusation. The intention of one who accuses another of an offense with the thought, "I shall perform a formal act such as censure," is called the "intention regarding the formal act.
This applies to one who accuses another of an offense with the aim of having them emerge from that offense through the sequence of granting probation and so forth.

The intention is the intention to leave [the offense]. For one who accuses another of an offense for the purpose of preventing the Sangha from performing the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, the intention is the intention to suspend the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā.
"In the absence of the person... down to... an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that there is an offense of wrong-doing even for one who reviles or abuses while accusing.

"In all cases" means in all commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Because the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are formal acts consisting of a motion (*ñatti*), the suspension of the Uposatha or Pavāraṇa occurs only while the motion is still being carried out, not when it has been concluded.
And since that motion is said to be "concluded" only when the syllable *yya* is reached, he says: "It is not permitted when the syllable *yya* is reached."
They say that one who is not a lay follower (*anupāsaka*) is no longer even a lay follower (*upāsaka*) because his going for refuge has ceased.
By the phrase "one who speaks the Dhamma indiscriminately," it is shown that one who speaks selectively must first be granted leave.

"Having confessed the offense" means having confessed the offense incurred by causing [the other] to grant leave. "One who accuses another is one who has attained the status of being fully ordained (*upasampanna*)."

In this context, there are five factors: (1) the perception of purity or doubt regarding that [offense]; (2) the groundlessness of the charge of a *pārājika* offense brought forward by way of what has been seen and so forth;

(3) the formal accusation and instigation of the charge by specifying, with the intention of causing a fall from the community, "You are one who has committed a *pārājika*," and so on, in the presence of the accused;
and (4) the accused's understanding of it at that very moment. These are the five factors here.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning corrupting faults is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning corrupting faults: 391.
Regarding the ninth [rule], "a nun named Mettiyā," even though she had been expelled for renouncing her gender, she is referred to here by her former designation.

This is stated having been taken up [from the source]. "Of another portion" (*aññabhāgassa*) means of that other part (*koṭṭhāsa*) reckoned as the state of being a goat belonging to the animal kingdom, which is distinct from the elder’s state of being human and being a bhikkhu.
"This" (*idaṃ*) is expressed in the neuter gender in a general sense; the meaning is "this goat.
"Another portion" (*aññabhāgo*) refers to the other part reckoned as the state of being a goat belonging to the aforementioned animal kingdom; "of this other portion" (*aññabhāgassa idaṃ*).
"Aññabhāgiya" means belonging to another part according to the first analysis; "it has another part" according to the second analysis.
By both analyses, it is called a "goat. Now, explaining in detail the very same meaning expressed by both analyses, he says, "For that which...
and so forth. Therein, "that goat which was mentioned belongs to another part" is what is designated as *aññabhāgiya*.
The construction is: "he obtains. To show the meaning of the second grammatical connection (*viggaha*), the words beginning with "or he" (*so vā*) were stated.

Regarding the phrase "it should be understood as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*"), here too the word "he" (*so*), which was previously mentioned as the goat named "Dabba Mallaputta," must be brought forward and connected.
For it is with reference to that goat—the basis for the designation of the name "Dabba"—[that this is said].

With reference to this. "Those monks" refers to those monks who are conducting the inquiry. Because the offense is defined by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), it is said that "the inclinations belong to the persons themselves.

393. And as for that accusation stated at the end... [etc. ...it refers to the various types of accusations such as: "A monk is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense; he has the view that it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
If one accuses him of a *pārājika* offense," and so forth.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Although there is a commonality among the seven offenses in that each is a *pārājika* and so forth, he says, "But because...
it does not exist," because there is also a dissimilarity based on the objects such as sexual intercourse and taking what is not given, and based on their intrinsic natures such as lust and hatred.

"In the manner already stated" refers to the manner stated by the phrase "based on similar and dissimilar objects," and so forth. This is the characteristic of the action (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*); attention to that is [the practice].
And because it is a sign of unimpaired karma, it is called "karma" by way of metaphorical designation for the fruit; thus he said, "because it arises depending on that.
Because probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth arise depending on the *mānatta* and so forth, the phrase "the former, the former," etc., was stated.

395. "Having made it have a basis" means having made it refer to a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). "Of long and so forth" refers to the characteristics (*liṅga*) such as long and short. "Of seen and so forth" refers to those previously seen, and so on.

408. "Perceiving it thus" means that having seen another person engaged in sexual intercourse or similar acts, one perceives it as such, thinking, "This is he. The constituent factors are similar to those stated under the first offense of corruption; however, here the act of taking even a slight portion [of the matter] is additional.
The commentary on the second offense of corruption is finished.
10. Commentary on the First Offense of Schism in the Saṅgha.
410. Regarding the tenth [type of person]: for those who, due to their weakness, are unable to concentrate the mind through dwelling in the forest and so forth;

for the sake of making an end to suffering, in that very existence, the mere words and phrases—consisting of the grasping and retaining of the Buddha’s word—are supreme for them, but not the attainment of the Path;
thus he is "one for whom words are supreme" (*padaparamo*). *Abhisambhuṇitvā* means having accomplished or brought to completion. From the perspective of the Dhamma...
It is departed from the Dhamma; it is indeed rejected. This was stated because of the words: “Monks, one who does not have a dwelling place should not enter the rains residence.
It is with reference to this very statement that the text also says, “for eight months,” and so forth.
“By three points” means by the three points concerning the root of impurity. And herein, because monks depend upon eating morsels of almsfood obtained from the four families, [it is said:]
Because families free from the consumption of fish and meat are rare, and because there is a suspicion that even the food and curries obtained there might have come into contact with fish or meat,
the sustenance of the monks' bodies would be difficult to maintain;
therefore, the Blessed One, without prohibiting fish and meat altogether, prohibited only that which was impure according to the three criteria (*tīhi koṭīhi*).
For if the Blessed One were to prohibit it in every respect, the monks—even when dying—would not eat food suspected of contact with fish and the like;
consequently, they would have to receive rice, grain, and so forth, store them away, cook them themselves, and eat them.
For this purpose, [the Buddha permitted] male and female slaves as well as mortars, pestles, and the like as requisites for the monks, along with their bowls and other items.

It should be understood that, as in the case of the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas), it must necessarily be permitted to take [the robes], such that there would be only a residence for householders and not a residence for monks (bhikkhu-āvāsa). "Net" refers to a fish-trap; "snare" refers to a deer-trap.
"Is allowable" means: if no suspicion arises from their words, it is permissible; however, it is not permissible to apply the "trace-allowance" (lesakappa) to those words.
For this very reason, he will say: "Whatever one is free from doubt regarding, all that is allowable.
"Meat that has come into circulation" means dead meat that has been brought into the marketplace and so forth for sale.

Regarding the phrase "not prepared specifically for the sake of monks," the word *eva* (only/just) is used here in the sense of exclusion; it should be connected as "not prepared exclusively for the sake of monks."
Therefore, it should be understood that even if [the recitation] is performed by mixing [the *bhikkhu*-formula] with the *maṅgala* and other formulas, it is not permissible.
However, some, taking the restriction to mean "according to how it stands," say "it is permissible"; that is not good.
By the word "permissible" (*vattam*), he shows that there is no offense.
They endure for an *asaṅkheyyakappa*; some say this refers to an "age of life" (*āyukappa*).
For an *asaṅkheyyakappa* is one-fourth of a great *kappa*, and they say that one-twentieth of that is the "age of life" for one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha.

However, that does not accord with the commentary on the *kappa* in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, because of such statements as, "He is released only at the destruction of the *kappa*. "Brahma merit" means supreme merit.
Regarding the phrase "a kappa in heaven," it should be understood here that a duration of a kappa refers to a succession of rebirths (*paṭisandhi-paramparā*).

"By one who holds different views and belongs to a different communion" (*laddhi-nānā-saṃvāsaka*) is said because the description emphasizes the state of being; this refers to one who follows a suspended person (*ukkhitto-anuvattaka*).

"By one who [differs] through action and belongs to a different communion" (*kamma-nānā-saṃvāsaka*) refers to one who is suspended (*ukkhitto*). Because the phrase "should strive for schism" is stated separately, it refers to that which leads to a schism (*bhedana-saṃvattanika*).

It should be understood that it is appropriate to perform an act of formal admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) against one who, having taken up and maintained a legal dispute, was previously striving for a schism in the Saṅgha by means of seeking partisans and so forth. Furthermore, this is to be connected with the phrase "this is a schism in the Saṅgha.

"By means of an act" refers to an act such as a motion (*apalokana*). "By means of recitation" refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. "By means of discourse" refers to various kinds of arguments.
"By means of the expression 'non-Dhamma is Dhamma,' etc."—the meaning is: by making it known to others.
"For the sake of proclamation" (anusāvanāya)—the meaning is: by repeatedly whispering into their ears for the purpose of making them adopt one's own tenets;

that is, by speaking. "By the taking of voting tickets" (salākaggāhena)—this refers to [the process] after having thus encouraged their minds through such proclamation so that they enter one's own faction.
By means of taking voting tickets (salāka), saying, "Take this ticket for the sake of identification.

And here, it should be understood that the formal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the primary cause for a schism in the Saṅgha, whereas worldly discourse and so forth are merely preliminary stages to the schism.
"Exalted" (abbhussita) means risen up. "Should dwell" (accheyya) means should live.

Because of the statement, “One who is conscientious will guard [the secret],” the burden of reporting out of fear of an offense falls upon those who are conscientious; thus it says, “by monks who are conscientious.

For one who is unconscientious, there is indeed an offense even if he does not report it. Regarding the phrase “for one who does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” this refers to an offense of wrong-doing according to the number of individuals to whom they speak separately. “By one who is able” means by one capable of going; the meaning is “by one who desires to go.”
However, the offense should be understood as applying only within a distance of half a *yojana* for one who is not ill.
(416) With reference to the existence of *dukkaṭa* and other offenses arising from the motion (*ñatti*) and so forth, it is said: "There is no offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
"His" refers to Devadatta. Since there was no formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) at all when the training rule had not yet been laid down, [it is said]: "For..."

It is said: "for one who transgresses a training rule that has been laid down. Indeed, the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) was authorized by the very one who laid down the training rule.
By the phrase "authorized specifically," he refers to what was authorized with specific reference [to a case], such as: "I allow you, monks, the chewing of cud for one who chews cud," and so forth.
"In the case of non-offense" means in the section concerning non-offenses. "The offense should be laid upon him" means...

He should be charged with an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) for the purpose of formal admonition. "The offense itself has not arisen" means that the offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) has indeed not arisen.
It is "liberation through perception" because one is released by the absence of the perception [that one is committing an offense], as in the thought, "I do not relinquish it.

It is "with mind" (*sacittaka*) because it is accompanied by the conscious mind that knows, "I do not relinquish it. One who is unconscious, or afraid, or distracted—even if [the act] ought to be relinquished—[is not at fault].
Or, if he does not know that “he will perform an act,” there is no offense for him.

Herein, there are four factors: the endeavoring toward schism; the formal admonition by means of a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*); the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*); and the non-renunciation in one’s mind, thinking “I will not relinquish it.”
The commentary on the first Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada is finished.
11. Commentary on the second Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada: 418.
In the eleventh [offense], since it is permissible for an appointment (sammuti-kamma) such as that of a committee (ubbāhikā) to be made even for many people, therefore: "Not indeed..."
It should be understood that the statement, “The Saṅgha performs an act against the Saṅgha,” was spoken with reference to an act that must be carried out by way of censure.

Furthermore, regarding the factors here, one should understand them to be exactly as stated below, with the addition of “striving for schism” and “not following [the Saṅgha’s] instruction” in place of [the previous factors].
The commentary on the second training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha is finished.

12. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Being Difficult to Correct (Dubbacasikkhāpada). 424. "Insulting speech" (*vambhanavacana*) means speech of reproach. The word *saṭa* has the same meaning as the word *patita*.
And because that qualifying term is placed last, he says: "grass, sticks, and leaves fallen here and there.
"By anyone" means by someone such as a preceptor (upajjhāya) who is like the wind and so forth. 426.
Enmity (*upanāha*) is simply persistent anger; resentment (*khila*), however, is a stronger attachment to anger than even that, difficult to release.
"Counter-accusing" means standing in opposition to the accuser. "Disparaging the accuser" means assailing him with speech.
"Reversing the charge" means attributing the offense to the accuser by saying, "You too are guilty of an offense. "Concealing" means hiding [the fault].
"By way of one's own conduct" means through one's own behavior. "Not making amends" refers to what the accuser says.
When asked about his conduct in such a manner as, “At the time you said, ‘I saw this person commit an offense,’ what were you doing,
what was he doing, where were you, and where was he?”— to fail to provide an account after being questioned; and by the introductory statement,
“For whomsoever there may be an offense,” all offenses whatsoever are included— therefore it says, “for whomsoever...”
“May it be,” and so forth. Herein, the constituent factors are similar to those in the first case of schism in the Saṅgha; however, this is the distinction:
whereas in that case there was an effort toward schism, here it should be understood as making [the monk] one who is not to be spoken to.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the abusive monk is concluded.
13. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Corrupters of Families (Kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada) 431.
Regarding the thirteenth [rule], *Kīṭāgiri* is the name of that market town (*nigama*). With reference to it, it will be stated later:
"The monks Assaji and Punabbasuka must not dwell at Kīṭāgiri. Furthermore, their banishment was from the village or market town, not from the entire district (*janapada*).
Furthermore, because of its association with that [mountain], the district itself came to be designated as "Kīṭāgiri"; thus he says, "in the district of such a name.
Therein means in Sāvatthī. At the place of the front means in the position facing [the city], that is to say, near the gate of Jetavana.
By two clouds means by the two clouds of the rainy season and the winter. Because it was augmented by six teachers of groups...
It is said, “excessive.

Regarding “of water”: since it will be stated separately that this refers to “the sprinkling with allowable water” (*kappiya-udaka-siñcana*) of unallowable water, and since it will also be stated here that “even when using unallowable expressions for the purpose of planting trees for the sake of a monastery and so forth, the sprinkling with allowable water and the like is permitted,” [it follows that] here too...
Having made a distinction, the sprinkling of allowable water (kappiya-udaka) and so forth is shown separately.

Just as physical actions such as pounding and digging are included under the category of unallowable transactions (akappiya-vohāra), so too are actions such as straightening a dried-up furrow included under allowable transactions; thus it says, "straightening a dried-up furrow.
Herein, even the removal of old leaves and the like is included. This is because the opinion of the *Mahāpaccarī* alone is the authoritative standard.
This was stated later. He said, "And not only the remainder," etc., in order to show that even in the case of unallowable speech (*akappiya-vohāra*), certain things are permissible.
"Any kind of summary table" (*mātikā*) means whether dry or not dry. "Therein" refers to the planting of trees for the sake of a monastery (*ārāma*) and so forth.

"In that way" is said with reference to having them written down by means of allowable speech (*kappiya-vohāra*), synonyms, and so on. And by this, [it is meant] for the purpose of supporting families (*kulasaṅgaha*).
This shows that even tying [the thread] oneself is not permitted.
Anticipating the objection, "Why is it not permitted to tie it oneself for the purpose of worshipping the sacred object (vatthu)? he says, "Is it not the case that...," and so forth.
Just as it is permissible to plant [trees] oneself on allowable ground for the sake of a monastery or similar purposes, so too [is it permissible] for the purpose of worshipping the sacred object.
The opponent’s intention is: "Why is it not permissible to plant [the seed] oneself? The response begins with "It is said," and so forth.
Now, why does he say, "But not in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*"? For even what is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries is indeed authoritative;
thus, there is no contradiction here. However, regarding the planting by oneself—which was not mentioned in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*—there is the sprinkling of water mentioned in that very same [text].

Because it is stated [there] that this is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of demonstrating the method of combining [the texts], the word "you might think" (*maññeyyāsī*) should be connected with the phrase "how could that be? The intention here is as follows:

although the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) does not explicitly mention planting [trees] oneself, it certainly mentions pouring allowable water (*kappiya-udaka*) on them oneself; therefore, just as for the sake of a monastery (*ārāma*) and so forth...
It is permissible to sprinkle *kappiya-udaka* (water for ritual use) oneself; likewise, why should it not be permissible to tie up [trees] for the purpose of honoring the site?

That too is not contradictory. For that which was stated—namely, the prohibition of tying up and so forth even for the purpose of honoring the site, while permitting one to plant and water oneself for the sake of the monastery and such—is not inconsistent with the preceding or following context when compared with the Pāḷi.
To show how this is not contradictory, he says, “For there,” and so forth. “There” refers to the context of planting and watering.

Since it is specified as “flowering shrubs” (*mālāvaccha*) when the general practice of supporting families with flowers and such is being discussed, it is understood that what is intended is planting specifically for the purpose of supporting families;
thus he says, “When speaking of ‘flowering shrubs,’ etc. This has been stated: “They plant flowering shrubs...”
It has been said: “They plant themselves, they water themselves, or they cause others to water. But “except for” means:
except for planting flower seedlings and so forth for the sake of a monastery and the like. “Method” (*pariyāya*) means a way, a mode of expression, or a specific purpose;
the intended meaning is that there is no lack of purpose because it serves to maintain one’s family. Thus, in this context...
When the word *pariyāya* is understood in the sense of both performing an action oneself and causing another to perform it, then—
setting aside the prohibition against tying a knot or having one tied found in the Pāḷi phrase “they tie themselves up or have [others] tie them up”—
the absence of fault is established regarding the act of having [something] tied by means of subsequent permissible words such as, “Know this; thus made, it will look beautiful.”
“By means of books” (*ganthehi*): this is intended as the causing of others to write because it refers specifically to the commissioning of writing through an order.
In that context, one should understand the presence of an indirect method (*pariyāya*) there and its absence here;

for in passages such as “they plant flowering shrubs,” there is the presence of an indirect method consisting of both doing and commissioning, due to the existence of the qualifying term “flowering shrub” (*mālāvaccha*), which indicates the purpose of gathering a family.

Having understood that this particular term is absent because there is no mention of such specific distinctions in passages such as "they tie" (*ganthenti*), one should know that it is indeed well-stated; this is the construction of the sentence.

"Everything should be understood according to the method already explained" means that everything—such as planting and so forth, as well as causing to be tied and so forth—should be understood exactly according to the method handed down in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). He concludes by stating: "No doubt should be entertained here."
"In taking, etc. means in the acts of taking and so forth for the purpose of worshipping the shrine.
"Taking for the sake of young women, etc."—the intention is that this specifically prohibits the act of taking young women and the like. Therefore he said, "In the section on taking," and so forth.
*Mañjarī* is a cluster of flowers. *Vaṭaṃsaka* is a floral ornament made for the purpose of wearing upon the ear.
And that is called a "tuft" (*vaṭaṃsa*). A "central cluster" (*kaṇṇikā*) is the name for many flowers or garlands tied together as one;
they also call it an "ear-ornament. "Like a necklace" means like a pearl necklace. "With what is allowable" means with allowable water.
"Of those two alone" refers to the two: defiling a family and improper use. "An offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*).

In the case of sprinkling for the purpose of maintaining the family, whether one sprinkles oneself or causes another to sprinkle by means of either a permissible or an impermissible expression, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

However, in the case of sprinkling for the purpose of consumption, whether one sprinkles oneself or causes another to sprinkle by means of an impermissible expression, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

"Due to the multiplicity of applications" means that in the case of performing it oneself, there is a multiplicity of both bodily application and verbal application, as well as in the case of causing it to be done.
A garland produced by knotting is "knotted" (*ganthima*). The same principle applies to the remaining types as well.

"It is not allowable" means it is not allowable even for the purpose of honoring the physical relic; the meaning is that it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "It is allowable" means it is allowable for the purpose of honoring the physical relic;
however, even for one who has it made using allowable terminology for the sake of supporting families, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
“Nīpa flower” means the *kadamba* flower. “In the same manner as before” refers to the method stated in the passage beginning with “for a bhikkhu,” and so forth.
With reference to everything stated in the passage beginning with “in a plantain trunk,” it is said: “that is indeed too coarse.

The meaning is that in all cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both for the act itself and for causing it to be done by means of an improper word. [The phrase] “for the purpose of piercing the flower... [is used].
Because the phrase "even to tie a thorn [to it] is not permitted" is intended as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*),
some say that even tying it with a rope for the purpose of making a flower garland or hanging it is not permitted; others, however,

maintain that since the word "thorn" is specified for the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not permitted to tie only a thorn for that purpose, and this is according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
They say this; it should be accepted after investigation. A "flower-receptacle" (*pupphapaṭicchaka*) is a flower-holder made of sticks and so forth;

this too, whether it be a peg (*nāgadantaka*) or otherwise, must be taken only if it has a hole. "A cluster of *aśoka* branches" (*asokapiṇḍiya*) refers to a collection of *aśoka* branches or flowers.
A "Dhamma-rope" (*dhammarajju*) is [a rope] used for the purpose of inserting flowers between the railing and the rope that encircles the *cetiya* and other such structures.
“Binding-string. Some say: “It should be bound like this, either loosely coiled or within the coils of a string, for the purpose of inserting flowers.
“A crest-garland” means a garland hanging from the top of the Dhamma-seat and so forth. “Of those very [flowers]” means of the blue lotuses and so forth.
“With a fiber or with a stalk” means having split the flower-stalk, [the garland is made] with a fiber that remains attached to the flower, or with a stalk.
And because it is bound by only a single bond, this flower does not fall under the category of "seed-planting" (*bījagāma*), as it has not entered into the five types of seeds, just like a leaf;
therefore, there is no fault in plucking it even without having it made allowable (*kappiya*).
Furthermore, the blooming of a bud that has already been severed is not a characteristic of growth, because that which is too young lacks such a state; rather, it pertains to a matured bud.
When the moisture of leaves has been exhausted, their state of separation itself is the "opening" (*vikāsa*);

thus, it is called "the opening of a severed bud" (*chinnamakuḷavikāsa*), as it is inferior to the "opening of an unsevered bud" (*acchinnamakuḷavikāsa*), or it is seen as being associated with wilting.

Furthermore, that which occurs when a withered leaf does not become withered upon contact with water is common even to betel leaves and the like; therefore, it is not a characteristic of growth, according to the Pāli commentaries and other texts.
Furthermore, nowhere has the preparation (kappiyakaraṇa) of flowers been mentioned; therefore, it is understood that a flower is entirely seedless.

This should be accepted after due investigation. Because it is stated, “as in a bag,” it is established that it is permissible to place them in a flower-bag, or in a binding similar to a bag, or in any kind of robe.
"It is not permissible to bind" refers to binding with ropes and the like; however, it is indeed permissible to bind the flower itself with uncut stalks and fibers.
"And it should be seen as a flower-cloth" means that for one making a flower-cloth, it is done by way of taking and bringing back long rows of flowers.
This was said with reference to filling [the space]. However, carrying [the flowers] across [the boundary] is called "weaving" (*vāyima*), not "filling" (*pūrima*).

Because it is stated in general terms as "he lets it pass beyond the front limit," there is indeed an offense for one who passes beyond by way of encircling [the area], whether or not he causes the front edge of the flowers to touch [the boundary].
"It is permissible to bind" refers to [binding] that which is devoid of flowers.
It is permissible to bind [the cloth] with ten million threads of thread.
The phrase "having carried it once or having enclosed it" refers to the previously mentioned enclosures around cetiyas and so forth, as well as the making of flower-canopies.
"Filled by others" means stretched out lengthwise. "Woven" means to carry it crosswise; however, even that [crosswise carrying] may be done only once.
It is not permitted. "By one who places flowers" means by one who places even unstrung flowers after having caused them to touch one another.
"A hanging wooden ball" refers to a hanging ornament shaped like a small jar (*ghaṭikā*) at its lower part, or shaped like a wooden toggle.
"A ball made of thread" is what is called a *geṇḍuka*. "In all cases" means in all instances, including those involving strung flowers and so forth.
*Recakanti abhinayaṃ*: the meaning is that they display the manner of acting, saying, "Dance thus"; some also say it means "whirling oneself around like a wheel. *Ākāseyeva kīḷanti*:
they play in the air itself, playing while both speak with their mouths, saying, "This sāri has been led by me to such-and-such a square.
*Jūtaphalake*: on the gambling board. *Pāsakakīḷāya*: of the game of dice. Of the two...

The game of *jūta* consists of throwing pieces made of wood, ivory, or other materials, measuring three finger-breadths in size, onto a board after marking dots on its four sides by counting one and so forth; then, removing the pieces according to the dots seen on the upper side.
*Mañjaṭṭhi* refers to the resinous sap from the heartwood of the *mañjaṭṭha* tree. *Salākahattha* is a term for a bundle of palm nuts, dice, and the like.
[This is] the name. In the Pāḷi, "on the sword" (tharusmiṃ) means on a blade. "Hissing" (usseḷenti) means they emit a hissing sound from their mouths;

the meaning is that they produce a great, indistinct noise. "Clapping" (apphoṭenti) means they make a sound by striking the doubled left hand with the right hand. "Face-drum" (mukhaḍiṇḍima) means a drum-like face.

432. In the compound *tesam*, he refers even to the subordinate members (*pabbāni*). *Bondu* means fickle; the meaning is that his bodily elements (*dhātu*) were sluggish. *Bhakuṭim katvā* means having made a contraction of the eyebrows. *Nela* means faultless. 433.

In the text, the address “Sāriputtā” is an address to both Sāriputta and Moggallāna according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*); for that very reason, the plural number is employed. 435.
“The eighteen rules of conduct (*vatta*)” refers to [the precepts] beginning with “one should not ordain [without permission]” and ending with “one should not associate with [unauthorized] monks.”
The concluding sections consist of the eighteen rules of conduct found in the Kammakkhandhaka. "Na pannaloma" means those whose hair does not stand on end;
the sense is that they do not act in a favorable manner.

(437) "If she gives what belongs to another, it is a dukkaṭa offense"—this is said with reference to giving by way of a trusted deposit. "A thullaccaya offense"—here, there is likewise the liability for compensation for the goods as well.
"And that too is for the purpose of venerating the physical remains" means that even when giving flowers to one's mother and father,

they should be given solely for the purpose of venerating the physical remains; this shows that it is permissible to give them to one's parents with the thought, "They will live by selling this," whereas for other relatives,
it is only for a temporary period, since only the phrase "for the purpose of adornment or for the purpose of venerating the *śivaliṅga* and so forth" has been stated.
It is permissible to give it. "By the novice monks who are relatives" is said for the purpose of releasing them from their household duties.
"The others" refers to those who are not relatives; even by those novice monks, it should be brought [to the teacher] under the heading of service (*vatta*) toward the preceptor and teacher.
"A small portion" means even half of a half.
"Novices... they set aside" is said with reference to that which is neither guarded nor protected. "In this or that place" means either on the path or in the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*).

"They are not permitted to have it given by novices" is said because it would be as if the novices were being made to perform work for householders; however, it is not because giving flowers is not permitted even for novices.
And it is said: “‘By oneself alone,’ and so forth. By the phrase “stated without distinction,” he shows that this does not apply to everyone.

The expression “of those whose provisions are exhausted” is said with reference to newcomers. Even in the case of trees that have limited fruit, one who says, “The fruits here are beautiful,” and so on, is indeed performing an act of social bonding (*kulasaṅgaha*); therefore, he says, “but one should not speak in such a way.”

“Tree-bark” means the bark of a tree. It is called “heavy property” because it is not to be distributed. “In the manner stated” shows that even the giving of leaves constitutes family support in the same way as flowers, fruits, and so forth, were stated previously.
“Of the kind mentioned before” refers to the training rule first mentioned in the passage beginning, “Venerate the Blessed One’s feet in my name.
“Depart, venerable sir,” was said by way of a formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*). Again, “Depart, venerable sir,”...
This too is stated by way of the duties for one who has undergone the formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*).

Furthermore, in this context, since the offenses to be prescribed regarding the various kinds of misconduct committed by Assaji and Punabbasuka toward their teachers were already laid down in other training rules (*sikkhāpada*), those are not prescribed here;
rather, in order to effect the restraint of those who corrupt families through the formal act of banishment, [the rule] was established right there.

It should be understood that this training rule was formulated for the purpose of formal admonition regarding those who, without having been suspended, cause the Saṅgha of the makers [of the schism] to fall into states such as being swayed by favoritism (*chandagāmitā*).

"Similar indeed to the first schism of the Saṅgha" means that here, just as there was striving (*parakkamana*) in that case, so here one should see the causing of falling into states such as favoritism; the rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who corrupt families is finished. Regarding the concluding commentary:
the connection is that "the others, however, should be understood as [offenses] up to the third time. For even one who is aged, having come [to visit] on a single day—
Having failed to arise in the two immediately preceding days, it arises on the third day;
thus it is called "the third-day [fever]. However, that which fails to arise even on the third day and arises only on the fourth day is called "the fourth-day [fever].
It is with reference to this that he says, "Just as on the third," and so forth. By the phrase "against one's will and helplessly," the failure to perform a remedy is indicated.

Because shamelessness (*alajjilakkhaṇa*) is an obstacle to heaven and liberation, it is shown that a person who has committed an offense is not permitted to delay, thinking, "I will undergo the probation later," and that the Saṅgha must grant the probation even against his will. Regarding the passage in the Canon:
"A monk who has completed the *mānatta*... [is] to be rehabilitated" (*abbhetabbo*), this means that whichever monk has completed the *mānatta*, that monk is to be rehabilitated.
In this way, the application of the two terms *bhikkhu* should be understood. And those monks are "to be censured" (*gārayha*) because they conceal their deficiency;
they are to be reproached by incurring an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Proper conduct" (*sāmīcī*) means the customary duty (*vatta*).
Thus [ends] the *Vimativinodanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The method of commentary on the Thirteen [Saṅghādisesas] is finished.
3. The Section on the Undetermined (Aniyata-khaṇḍa). 1. Commentary on the First Undetermined Training Rule (Paṭhamāniyata-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā).

443. Because of the general designation by the word "sons" (*putta*), or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), daughters (*puttī*) are also included; thus he says, "and many daughters. "Immediately after that" means immediately after the monks' meal. 444–5.
"That action" refers to that action of sexual misconduct and so forth. In the text, the phrase "secrecy of the ear" is stated by way of an extraction of the meaning;
however, in the subsequent training rule, it is stated as "nor indeed in a concealed place," and so on, regarding this very training rule.
Having excluded the [visual] object (*visaya*), because the ear— which constitutes a different category of object—
is mentioned separately in the statement, "It is sufficient to address a woman with indecent words," it is here intended that only the eye is meant,
as indicated by the words "in a concealed seat" and so forth, and because it is stated, "it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse."
And for that reason he said, “Even though,” and so forth. “Delimitation” means the defining of the offense of sitting in private.
Now, demonstrating the delimitation of the offense by means of the eye alone, he said, “Even if,” and so forth.
By the phrase “of one whose door is closed,” he shows that because of the state of being concealed, it is the privacy of the eye that is intended, not the privacy of the ear. Therefore he said:
“There is no offense for one whose door-panel is closed... [etc]...”. For by closing the door-panel, the privacy of the ear does not disappear;
rather, it is the privacy of the eye that disappears.

The phrase “even within twelve cubits” is intended to show that there is absolutely no offense regarding the grave verbal transgression (duṭṭhullavācā) that would otherwise be incurred due to the privacy of the ear as mentioned in the second training rule.
It has been stated. For one sitting more than twelve cubits away does not incur an offense of indecent speech there, because of the absence of secrecy for the ear;

likewise, it would not be appropriate to state the general rule as "he does not incur an offense," but rather it should be stated specifically that "he incurs no offense regarding the offenses of sexual intercourse or bodily contact. Therefore...
Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "within twelve cubits" was stated precisely to show that there is no offense whatsoever if one does not speak to him.

For if he were speaking with reference only to the privacy of the eye, he would not have said "within twelve cubits," because even if one is sitting at a distance beyond that, privacy of the eye is still possible when it is unobstructed. This is because while sitting and dozing...
Overcome by drowsiness, he opens his eyes for a short time and closes them for a short time; therefore it is said, "Even while sleeping, one commits an offense.
"Having attained the fruit of stream-entry" is stated from the perspective of the final limit. "Claiming to be sitting" refers to [the act] through sexual intercourse, bodily contact, and so forth.
The meaning is: "one who admits to sitting in private. Therefore he said, "by an offense entailing expulsion," and so forth.
"Not one who does not admit" means that even an unashamed person, if they do not admit [the offense], is simply not to be dealt with for that offense.
For as long as he does not admit the fault, he should be described as "neither pure nor impure"; however, he is to be dealt with according to the sequence of the rule. For this has been stated:
“A confession is made among those who are conscientious; it does not exist among those who are unconscientious.
Even if the unconscientious one should speak much, one should have him act according to the connection of the rule.

Regarding the phrase “while confessing” in the context of sitting and so forth... “that bhikkhu should be made to act by that [confession]”—here, although the word “while confessing” is not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi, it is stated as such because it is understood from the context.
"Make them speak"—though he himself was free from suspicion due to his supernormal power (*iddhi*), he said this while instructing them:
"Without investigating, you have made even those like me speak ill of yourselves, saying, 'The Elder sat in private on a single seat with a woman.
Do not do so again. This is the intended meaning. "You did it thus": [end of quote].
The meaning is that, while this special attainment was indeed to be concealed, he acted in this way solely in order to inspire confidence in him. "You should protect this" means:
do not reveal this superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) to others. 451.

"In sitting together, there is an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*): when the pleasure of sitting in private is occurring, it is an offense of expiation. However, if he [the other person] is one who takes pleasure in sitting in private...
If, having dispelled [the desire], one is occupied with something else—such as attention to a meditation subject—or has fallen asleep, there is no offense at all.
Therefore he said, "when enjoyment has arisen. By the phrase "of a woman who is sitting," he shows that there is an absence of enjoyment at the moment of sitting.
For if enjoyment were to arise at the moment of sitting, one would have to rise because of it; otherwise, there is an offense.
Just as in the case of a woman who rises up again and again and sits down repeatedly, even there, for a bhikkhu who rises up, there is no offense;
therefore, they say that the offense of sitting in private (*raho-nisajjā*) is also originated by non-action (*akiriya-samutthāna*).

However, this is an indeterminate training rule (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*), and both this one and the following one were not laid down separately as distinct designations of offenses regarding sitting in private and so forth.

Because they were laid down among the various training rules for offenses. However, these [offenses] such as the *pārājika* and so forth were laid down by way of dividing them into two categories according to the facts, specifically for the purpose of showing the method of adjudication by the investigators when someone has been accused of such offenses.
And since these alone are sufficient for the nuns to grasp the method of adjudication, therefore, for them...
It should be understood that these have not been stated separately. However, the classification of factors (*aṅga*) here should be understood according to whichever offense one confesses.
For that very reason it is said: "This rule is undetermined" (*aniyata*).

Here, because the Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, and Pācittiya offenses mentioned by way of the undetermined [rule] all share the same origin and other characteristics as one another, it is said: "The origins and so forth are exactly the same as those of the first Pārājika."
The commentary on the first undetermined training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second undetermined training rule: 452.
Without stating, "One must not sit down alone with a woman...," it says, "It is forbidden."

Because it is stated [in the Vinaya] with the words “by a woman,” etc., the word “alone” (*eko*) as a nominative singular does not agree with the negated term; rather, it should be stated as “of one” (*ekassa*).
Proving this, he says: “For otherwise,” and so forth. 453.

“The courtyard of the *pariveṇa* and so forth” means the platform of the *pariveṇa*. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), [he includes] the *cetiya-māḷaka* and other such structures enclosed by walls and the like.
He includes [it]. "Included within" means included precisely in the unhidden place. Here, the connection is that even a woman commits no offense.
But why does a woman commit no offense here only, and not under the preceding training rule?
Because this training rule is formulated with reference to wicked speech (*duṭṭhulla-vācā*) rather than sexual intercourse (*methuna*). For it is only sexual intercourse...
Women conceal one another in the great forest, just as they did when the door was opened while the bhikkhu had fallen asleep;
however, they do not conceal grave offenses. For this very reason, it is said in the training rule on grave speech (*duṭṭhullavācā-sikkhāpada*):
"Those women who were modest went out and complained to the bhikkhus. Therefore, it is said: "Even a woman incurs no offense."
It is said; they also state the reason as "because it is an unconcealed matter.
Since improper conduct and lustful glances can also arise through the body, "privacy of the eye" and "privacy of the ear" are intended in this training rule (sikkhāpada);
thus he said, "one who is not blind, one who is not deaf," and so forth. However, some [interpret] the passage in the Vibhaṅga, "not fit for the formal act," as follows:

Because it was stated only that "one is not able to engage in sexual intercourse," and it was not said that "one is not able to enter into physical contact," even in a situation where there is no concealment,
if one sees the absence of others in private, one might think that physical contact with a single woman can still be committed; thus, even one who is deaf,
standing within a twelve-fathom radius where speech can be heard, [is subject to the offense].

They say: "Because a blind person does not even know whether physical contact exists or not, the phrase 'one who is not blind' and so forth was stated in order to avoid the offense of bodily contact, even if one has not mentally considered the possibility of making a lewd gesture with the body.
However, as for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, namely, "He is called 'not blind' by way of bodily contact," that—

This was stated without taking into account the possibility of a coarse or lustful manifestation through the body; it should be understood that this also applies by way of physical contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*).
For this very reason it was said: "In this training rule, only the seclusion of the ear is intended... [etc.]...

However, some have said, 'Both kinds of seclusion are intended here,' but that should not be accepted. As for that which was [stated] for the purpose of proving the absence of seclusion regarding the eye:
The statement, “For in an uncovered place, privacy for the eye does not exist,” and so forth, is not correct;
because even if one stands at a very great distance, it is impossible to perceive either the radiance from the body or the grasping of the hand, and so on.
For this very reason, the phrase “privacy for the eye” is mentioned in the Pāḷi, while it is not rejected in the Aṭṭhakathā. And this is not the only case...
It is not prohibited; rather, it is stated that "one who is neither blind nor deaf does not [commit an offense] even if he is blind or not deaf.
Therefore, both types of privacy (raha) must be understood here. By the phrase "within twelve cubits," this shows that the privacy of the ear is delimited by a distance of twelve cubits.
However, as for the privacy of the eye, it is where one standing [at such a distance] cannot perceive bodily gestures and so forth.
It should be understood that he must be distinguished by the fact that [the offense] is not recognized [by others].

However, the phrase "even one who is deaf but has sight" is stated with reference to the *saṅghādisesa* offense of improper speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*). Regarding the statement "an improper offense is mentioned," the meaning should be taken as follows: an improper offense is mentioned in addition to those mentioned in the preceding training rule;
it does not mean, however, that only an improper offense is intended here, for bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) is also included.

Because it must be included. For that very reason, only this much was stated: "having avoided an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)," for otherwise it would have had to be said, "and bodily contact.
As for the phrase "originating from three" and so forth, however, it refers to the offense of Saṅghādisesa involving indecent speech, which was not mentioned in the preceding training rule.
It is stated [as such] by way of that [preceding rule], because bodily contact and so forth are already mentioned in the previous training rule; however, some say that they are not mentioned here.
This should be understood after careful investigation.
The commentary on the second *aniyata* training rule is finished.
