The method of explanation for the Indeterminate [offenses] is finished.
4. The Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa), 1.
The Subchapter on Robes (Cīvaravagga).
1. Commentary on the First Kathina Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 459.
*Samitāvī* means one who has stilled evil. *Gotamakacetiya* refers to a monastery built at the site of the shrine of the Yakkha Gotama. 461.
*Navamaṃ vā dasamaṃ vā* is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. *Sace bhaveyya* means "if it should happen to anyone."
There might be doubt. "Similar to what was stated" means similar to the tenth [chapter], that is, similar in its sectioning; some also write it as "exactly as stated.
Regarding the word "to preserve," one should understand that the words "he says" (*āha*) are to be supplied to the text.
463. "The putting away of the needle" refers to its storage in a needle-case; this is for the purpose of showing that all needle-work has been completed.
It has been stated. "This" refers to the lost robe. "Of these too" refers to the lost robe and so forth;
by this, he demonstrates the absence of the obstacle of robes. "Of the second obstacle" refers to the obstacle of the dwelling-place.

And here, by the demonstration of the absence of two obstacles through the two phrases "when the robe is finished" and "when the kaṭhina has been spread," [it shows] for one who has had the kaṭhina spread...

This indicates that it is permissible to keep an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) for as long as five months, provided that neither the obstacle of robes (*cīvarapalibodha*) nor the obstacle of residence (*āvāsapalibodha*) has been removed.
"Ending with departure" (*pakkamanantikā*) means that departure occurs within [the five-month period];
the remaining terms should be understood in the same way. The detailed explanation for these will be made clear in the places where they appear in the text.
“*Dasāhaparamaṃ kālaṃ*” (for a period not exceeding ten days) is an expression denoting absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). For this is what is meant:
… [omission] … “the state of having ten days as the limit” is a mere indication of the meaning of the term *dasāhaparamatā*;

for it is precisely “the state of having ten days as the limit” that is expressed here—thus should the construction be understood. The passage beginning with “this is the meaning” is intended to show the specific intended meaning of the very term *dasāhaparama*.
It has been stated. In that context, "this much time" means the period described as "at most ten days"; this is the meaning of "this much time.
*Khoma* refers to a robe made of *khoma* cloth woven from *khoma* fibers; they say it is made of flax. *Kappāsika* is that woven from cotton fibers;
the remaining types are to be understood in the same way. *Kambala* is a cloth woven from threads made of the wool of sheep and other animals.
"Bhaṅga" refers to all types of linen thread and so forth, or a robe woven from some of these mixed together.

Some say that "bhaṅga" also includes those made of wool. However, the six types of robes—dukūla, pattuṇṇa, somāra-paṭa, cīna-paṭa, iddhija, and devadatta—are not mentioned separately because they are merely variations of these [primary materials]. For instance, dukūla is a variation of sāṇa (hemp).
*Anuloma* means made from wool. It is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* that "patuṇṇa" is a specific type of silk (*koseyya*).

Fabrics produced in the country of Sōmāra and the country of Cīna are called *sōmārapaṭa* and *cīnapaṭa*. These three—patuṇṇa and the others—are similar to silk because they consist of threads spun by insects.
*Iddhija* refers to robes produced through the merit-power (*puññiddhi*) of those who have come as monks (*ehibhikkhus*).

The *kapparukkha* (wish-fulfilling tree) garment and that given by the gods consist of one or another of the fine fabrics such as *khoma*; these are the "conformable" (*anuloma*) types for all of them.
With reference to the ordinary human *vidatthi*, it is said, "two *vidatthi*s," and so forth.

By this, it is shown that what is acceptable as a substitute (*vikappanupaga*) is a length measured by a carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakīhattha*) and a width half of that. For it is said: "The *sugatavidatthi*..."
"Now, for a man of medium height, three *vidatthis* are equal to one and a half cubits (*hattha*) by the carpenter’s measure," as stated in the commentary on the *Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*.
Therefore, it is established that twelve *aṅgulas* of the Sugata’s measure constitute one *sugata-vidatthi*, which is one and a half cubits by the carpenter’s measure.
And having established this, [it follows that] eight *aṅgulas* of the Sugata’s measure...
It also accords with the passages where it is stated as being "the measure of a carpenter’s hand.
Regarding the phrase *taṃ atikkāmayato*: here, *taṃ* (that) refers either to the robe (*cīvara*) or to the time (*kāla*).

*Tassa yo aruṇo* means the dawn that has passed from the day on which the robe was acquired. *Saddhiṃ cīvaruppādadivasena* means together with the very first moment of the day on which the robe was acquired.

The meaning is "together with the sunrise that has passed. And although this is understood from the word itself—since the Blessed One, after stating "at most ten days," further stated "on the eleventh day at sunrise"—it is expressed as "together with the day the robe was acquired" for the purpose of correlating the preceding and following statements.
For if it were simply said "on the tenth sunrise," it would coincide with the "at most ten days" rule.
For it is by way of the future dawn that constitutes the limit of the day’s end that a day is said to have been "passed";
it is not, however, by way of the dawn that constitutes the beginning of the day, because such [a definition] is not adopted in the case of the *parivāsa* (probation) and other observances.
Here, however, the Blessed One spoke of "the rising of the dawn on the eleventh day" in order to show the delimitation of the beginning and end of the day; therefore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*...

Taking the dawn that marks the beginning of the day and which is dependent upon that very day, it is stated: "At the rising of the dawn on the eleventh [day], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
Here, "dawn" (*aruṇa*) should be understood as a specific radiance, thick with redness and increasing, that precedes the rising of the sun. "To be addressed" (*vacanīya*) refers to the Saṅgha.
"The distinction of the statement" (*vacanabheda*) means that it should be spoken in such ways as: "He remembers two offenses during the motion (*ñatti*)," and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
“‘Perception does not protect here’—this was said with reference to both one who is in doubt and one whose perception has not transcended [the object].
‘Even for one who has such a perception’ means even for one whose perception has not transcended it or who is in doubt.
He states the distinction regarding what is ‘not lost’ (anaṭṭha) as ‘by way of taking by force’; for even that which is taken by way of theft is considered ‘lost’ in this context.”
"There is no offense in receiving one made by another," and so forth, is said with reference to a sitting rug (*nisīdana-santhata*).
For if someone has made a new sitting rug without leaving a Sugata-span (*sugata-vidatthi*) around the edge of an old rug,
then even though that [new rug] is an article to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*), there is no offense for one who receives it from someone other than that person and uses it.
This meaning applies to all [rules] involving forfeiture (*sabba-nissaggiya*) as well, because they are established through relinquishment. 469.
"To determine the three robes" means to determine them by their specific names, such as the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*), and so forth.

"Not to assign [them]" means not to assign them under that name; one who has assigned his three robes in this manner does not remain a wearer of the three robes (*tecīvarika*). Regarding those three robes determined by him:
This shows that the procedure to be performed through non-separation and so forth must not be carried out; however, it does not mean there is a fault in making a formal assignment (*vikappana*).
Regarding the phrase "after that," some say it is permitted to use [the robe] after having assigned it for more than four months;
others, however, say that after assigning it, it is permissible to keep it until the following year; and still others...
However, they say: "There is no fault in assigning [the robe]; having thus assigned it, one may use it after determining it by the name of 'requisites' (parikkhāra) and so forth.
"Five fist-measures" (muṭṭhipañcaka) means a measure of five characterized by the fist;
the intention is that one should measure it by making a fist for the fifth hand after measuring four hands. Some, however, say: "Five fist-hands is 'five fist-measures' (muṭṭhipañcaka)."
"Therefore, even the five [fingers] must be measured with the hand made into a fist," they say.

The same principle applies here to the term "fist-measure" (*muṭṭhittika*). He said "by means of the upper robe" (*pārupanena*), etc., because it is possible to cover the three circles with an inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) that is two cubits long.
"Excessive" (*atireka*) means more than the measure of the Sugata’s robe. "Deficient" (*ūnaka*) means less than the five-fist measure, etc.; by that—
And this shows that the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes does not take effect upon them.
"I relinquish this outer robe" (*imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmi*) means: "I set aside this determination of the outer robe; I renounce it.
"By making a movement of the body" means by touching the robe with the hand or by moving it. It should be determined by means of speech.
In this context, it should be understood that the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by means of both body and speech is included, because of the statement "without having touched with the body.
"Two kinds" means it is twofold by way of being within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*) or beyond arm's reach (*a-hatthapāsa*).
Therein, "arm's reach" (*hatthapāsa*) is said to be two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*); some say it is twelve cubits, but that [is not] here.

It does not coincide. The phrase "in a neighboring monastery" (*sāmantavihāre*) is said with reference to a location that is situated within the range for observing where the robe has been placed. Even if it is situated far from there, one must still determine it by observing the place where it was placed.
In that case as well, the only criterion is the observation of the fact that the robe was placed there; for it is impossible to observe the location in every respect. In one [instance]...
It is not permissible to resolve that [a robe] placed elsewhere than in the monastery has been set aside there.
Some, however, say, "Even if it is resolved in that way, there is no fault"; this does not accord with the Aṭṭhakathā and should be investigated.
"With robes set aside by means of resolution" means with robes set aside under the name of "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*); for that very reason, "this..."
By saying “I relinquish,” he demonstrates the relinquishing of the requisite cloth.

Furthermore, one who observes the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the three robes, if unable to make up, dye, and wear within ten days a garment obtained through rag-robes (paṃsukūla) and so forth, must pass those ten days having formally determined it as a requisite cloth; otherwise, [he would incur an offense].

This shows that it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "From the time it has been dyed, however, it is not permitted to set it aside;

one is then called a 'thief of ascetic practices' (*dhutaṅgacora*). The statement "they must be resolved upon again" is said with reference to one who wishes to use them after resolving upon them by the names of the three robes, such as the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth; for another, however, there is only the previous resolution.
It should be understood that [the word] *alaṃ* is used. By the phrase "it must be resolved again," it is shown that even a mere drop of water (*kappabindu*) must be given.

Because the formal act of granting the boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā-sammuti*) is possible within a fixed boundary (*baddha-sīmā*), there is no difficulty in maintaining it there; thus he said, "it is difficult to maintain in an unfixed boundary (*abaddha-sīmā*).

Regarding the offense of expiation involving cutting (*chedanaka-pācittiya*) for [a robe] exceeding the proper measure, he said, "not exceeding the proper measure. Beyond that, having relinquished [the robe],...
"Should be assigned" means that after the determination has been relinquished beyond the four months of the rainy season, it should be assigned;
by this, it is understood that the determination remains in force for the period above those four months of the rainy season, because there is no need for its relinquishment thereafter.
And as for what is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The rains-bathing cloth [is kept] even beyond the months of the rains; the itch-covering cloth [is kept] until the subsiding of the illness..."
As for what was stated [in the Vinaya-mukha], “He abandons the formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna),” that is not found in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
And in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*, regarding the passage, “There is an offense committed in the winter, but not in the summer,” this is said:

“If one wears a rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) that has been formally resolved and set aside on the first day of the month following the full moon of Kattika, one commits an offense in the winter; according to the *Kurundi*...”
However, it has been stated that "one incurs [the offense] in the winter by not relinquishing [the robe] on the full-moon day of Kattika"; this too is well-stated, for it has been said:
"One may determine [the robe] for four months, and beyond that, one may assign it.

In this regard, the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the condition of wearing [the robe], whereas the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* states it is due to the condition of not relinquishing it; therefore...

According to the method stated in the *Kurundi*, it is understood that even when the month of the rains has passed, the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloak) does not lose its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the loss of determination, the fact that it is lost through the passing of the month of the rains or the disappearance of an illness is not mentioned even in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, according to the method found in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the determination remains in force until the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*).
It should be accepted. Because it was permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is said: "Even this, though dyed merely by a change in color, is allowable.

By the statement "but two [other types] are not allowable," it is shown that—as with the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth—a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) does not take effect on a second one, and thus it becomes an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that there is no offense, referring to the absence of the function of use (*paribhogakicca*) by way of the robe.
This is as in the case of a rug given for the purpose of bedding requisites.
As for the statement, "The rug must also be determined," that is not restricted to being for the purpose of the lodging alone, because it is included among the nine types of robes;
therefore, having determined it by its own name and set it aside like a requisite cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa), as follows...

It should be understood that it must be used in exactly that manner. Regarding the *pāvāra* (woolen blanket) and the *kojava* (felt rug), although these are included among the "spreading cloths" (*paccattharaṇa*) and so forth because they are so designated in common worldly usage, they are mentioned separately here because they were specifically given for the purpose of bedding and furniture.
The phrase "by returning to the lower state" refers to one who, having committed the ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*), still remains under the designation of a monk.

It is said with reference to the assumption of the layman’s marks or the marks of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) by one who has gone over to the faction of the non-Buddhists (*titthiya-pakkanta*) and by a nun (*bhikkhunī*), due to their lack of regard for their status as a monk or a nun.
Some say it is said with reference to the adoption of the state of a layperson without having formally renounced the training (*sikkhā*);
however, that is not correct, because even in that case he remains fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and because he has not relinquished his ownership of the robe.
“Of a robe of standard measurement” is said with reference to the lower limit of measurement.
“While putting on two robes” is said with reference to the practice of doubling the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) when entering a village.

By the phrase “this method [applies] as well,” it includes such points as that in any of the robes endowed with the standard measurement, a tear or a breach causes the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) to be lost.
The intention [of the phrase] "there is no other final measure" (*aññaṃ pacchimappamāṇaṃ*) as it appears in the Sutta is that there is none.

Now, in order to clarify that very point, the words beginning with "yañhi" were spoken; however, that does not accord [with the Sutta], because the lower measures such as the five-fist-widths and so forth for the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and other garments have not been mentioned in the Sutta—this is the intention.

Regarding the phrase "one makes it large or small": here, even when one makes a robe that was excessively large into one possessing the minimum measurement of five fist-breadths and so forth by cutting it all around, the place being cut during the process of dissection does not count as a "hole" (*chidda*), and it is established that it does not lose its status as a formally determined (*adhiṭṭhāna*) robe;
thus it is said, "having joined [the pieces], he cuts it, yet it is not destroyed."

And it is settled by means of speech. However, if the requisites cloth (*parikkhāra-coḷa*) is cut down to a size smaller than the maximum limit for what is subject to formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*), one loses the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), because the formal determination has no basis [in such a small piece].

It should be understood that once those pieces are sewn together again, they must indeed be formally determined anew. Some, however, say: "Even if the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā-cīvara*) is cut in two..."

Each individual section must be of the maximum permitted size; the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) remains valid for only one section and not for the others, because it has been stated that "two [sections] are not permissible.
They say that this same method applies to the sitting-cloth and the itch-covering cloth as well.
*Sammukhe* is the nominative singular form meaning "in the presence"; and that is a qualification of the act of assigning (vikappana). Therefore, "in the presence" (*sammukhe*)—
They explain the meaning by treating the ablative case as having the sense of the locative; thus, "in the presence of" (*abhimukhe*) is the meaning.

Alternatively, "assignment in the presence" (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) means an assignment by one's own speech while face-to-face. "Assignment away from the presence" (*parammukhā-vikappanā*) should also be understood in the sense of the instrumental;
this alone accords with the canonical text (*pāḷi*). [The phrase] "the state of being present or absent" (*sannihitāsannihitabhāvaṃ*)...
Regarding "the state of being near or far": by this much it is sufficient to establish [the robe], because the function of the formal assignment (*vikappanā*) is completed by just that much;

thus, it does not become an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), meaning that upon the lapse of ten days, it does not give rise to an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Regarding "it is not permitted to use...":

if one uses it oneself without having formally relinquished it (*apaccuddharaṇa*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); however, if one formally assigns it (*adhiṭṭhāna*) or gives it away to others, [there is no offense].
This was said with reference to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
By the phrase "even using and so forth are permitted," it is meant that using, giving away, and designating [the robe] are also allowed;

by the word "also" (*api*), the meaning is that even storing it is permitted. And by this, when the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) has been performed, the robe becomes indeed a robe that has been formally assigned (*vikappita*).

It is not an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). However, this indicates that one who wishes to formally determine (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) it by means of the name "three robes" (*ticīvara*) and so forth must do so;
otherwise, it should be used only after having been designated as a robe to be assigned to another (*vikappitacīvara*). Some, however, say:
"That robe which has been assigned should be kept stored until the time of use, without having it formally relinquished (*apaccuddharāpetvā*); but when the time for use arrives..."
Having had it relinquished and having made a formal determination, it may be used.

For if one were to have it relinquished even before that time, then because the relinquishment itself would preclude the need for a formal determination, it would become what is called "extra robe-cloth";

and upon the lapse of ten days, there would be an offense entailing forfeiture and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Therefore, only that which is to be set aside without being used should be formally determined.
They say, "Once the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) has been performed, it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) within ten days;

and as for what is stated in the Commentary—that 'from that time forward, even using [the robe] and so forth are permitted'—that contradicts the Canon (*pāḷi*)," but this is merely their own opinion. For in the Canon, it says:
"He determines it within ten days," and "he designates it himself (*sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ*)."

Because it is stated in general terms that “if one uses [an object] after having assigned it but without relinquishing it, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” and also that “there is no offense if he gives it back,

or if one uses it with his trust,” and because the Commentary does not show a relinquishment by saying, “I relinquish this robe or this assignment,” but rather says, “Use what belongs to me,” [it follows that there is no offense].

Because it is stated that the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) occurs through the very act of using [the object] and so forth— without first releasing one's own ownership by saying, "I give it back" or "Relinquish it"—
and because it is stated that from that point onward even using [the object] and so forth are permissible, it follows that even without a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*),
there is a separate allowance for use and for depositing; thus, immediately after the assignment (*vikappanā*), one should have it relinquished and, without making a formal determination, [use it].
It appears that this is a separate formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma): namely, to use and to store a robe that is not one of the three robes (ticīvara) but is fit for assignment (vikappanāraha).
Furthermore, since it is stated that many bowls may be assigned and relinquished, it is established that by means of such relinquishment their status as "extra" bowls (atirekapatta) is shown;
thus, it follows that only one among them need be formally determined (adhiṭṭhātabba).
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method handed down in the Aṭṭhakathā.

"He is not skilled in designations" means that when a designation has been made in this way—"Immediately after [the designation], it must be relinquished in this manner"—he does not know the formal act (vinayakamma) [of relinquishment].
For this reason he said, "he does not know how to relinquish. By this also, it should be understood that immediately after the designation...
“The relinquishment must be performed.
This statement is one spoken without distinction; that is, it is a statement made using a term common to the three robes and so forth.
However, regarding what was said here—that it “appears as if contradictory”—in order to dispel that suspicion of contradiction, [it says]: “By way of the summary of the three robes... [etc.]”
It is said, "the opportunity for formal assignment (*vikappanā*) has been granted.

Although this is stated in general terms as "he determines (*adhiṭṭheti*) or assigns (*vikappeti*)," the specific meaning that "one may also assign the three robes" is not established here, because it is stated with the qualification: "one may determine the three robes, but one may not assign them. However, whatever is to be determined, that he determines; and whatever is devoid of the three robes...

The meaning is established as follows: "that should be assigned" and "he assigns that. Therefore, no contradiction between what precedes and what follows is seen here, because the general statement remains restricted precisely to what has been stated as its remainder.

As for what was said here to show the procedure for assigning even the three robes—"the three robes by way of the designation 'three robes'" and so forth—therein, "by way of the designation 'three robes'"...
While these robes are being carried about, it is not permissible to set aside even one of them and formally assign it to another; however,
for one who wishes to carry about another set of three robes by way of the "three-robes" designation after removing either one or all of them from the existing set of three robes,
or for one who wishes to use all his robes as requisites-cloths after relinquishing the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes.
Or, if it were intended that one may relinquish a previously determined robe and then re-assign it,
then the statement beginning with "he wishes to live apart from one of his three robes" would be consistent with the Canon.
However, if he again wishes to determine that very same robe by means of the determination of the triple robe for the sake of the ease of living apart...

It might have been stated with the intention that "having relinquished [the robe], one designates it," but that does not accord with the statement, "one may designate the three robes, but one must not relinquish them.

For if the three robes were to be relinquished and designated just like the remaining robes, then this very statement— “one may designate the three robes, but one must not relinquish them”— would be contradicted.
It would be purposeless with respect to the remaining robes, as there is no distinction from the three robes (ticīvara).

Therefore, the statement "he designates" (*vikappeti*) is said specifically with reference to one who is devoid of the three robes; thus it is understood that it is not permitted to designate the three robes themselves.

For this very reason, the word "designates" is not mentioned in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*) for the second *kaṭhina* rule; having investigated this, [one should act] so that it does not contradict the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
In this context, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) should be understood as follows:
In cases such as "I give to you," because the object has been relinquished, it becomes the property of the recipient even if they do not mentally accept it;
thus, the recipient is entitled to take it at the desired moment. The phrase "of such-and-such a person" refers to one who is present in person (*parammukhe ṭhitaṃ*).
"He says. However, the passage beginning with "to whom it pleases" and so forth is stated with reference to the state of being ownerless due to the relinquishment by both parties.

The statement "that is not appropriate" is said because the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) arrived at refers specifically to taking on trust within ten days, whereas here [the robe] was taken by means of a pretext for the purpose of making the forfeitable robe (*nissaggiyacīvara*) permissible; so say some.
However, they say: "No fault is seen when [the robe] has been taken away by others who are like oneself, or when it is recovered after having been accepted in trust.
By "not formally determining" (anadhiṭṭhāna) is meant the intention of not performing what ought to be done by body or speech. [The factors for the offense are:
the robe being one's own property, its being of the proper kind and size, the state of having severed the impediment [of travel], its being an extra robe, and the passing of ten days.
These are the five factors here.
The commentary on the first Kathina training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udosita training rule.

473. Regarding the second [term], *avippavāsa* (non-separation): the meaning is that it refers to the formal agreement (*sammuti*) to be made when non-separation is to be accomplished, or when the absence of the fault of separation is to be established.

475. Regarding the phrase *paṭisiddhapariyāpannena*: this refers to being included among the three robes for which separation is prohibited; by mentioning one part, it indicates the metaphorical application of the whole to its component.

478–9. Regarding the phrase *ettāvata*: this refers to the term "enclosed" (*parikkhitto*). Regarding the word *sabhāya*: it is stated that through a change of gender (*liṅgabyattayena*), the word *sabhā* (assembly) is expressed.
Having spoken thus, he further demonstrates by using the term "sabhāye" himself that there exists a synonym for the word *sabhā*—the word *sabhāya*—which is connected with the neuter gender.
Alternatively, there is the reading: "In 'sabhāyaṃ,' by means of a change of gender (*liṅgabyattayena*), 'sabhā' is expressed.
The meaning of "by means of a change of gender, 'sabhā'" is that the word *sabhāya* is a synonym for the word *sabhā* that is connected with another gender.
"He goes to the assembly" means he goes to the *sabhā*. "There is no need to stay" means there is no need to stay even within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*) of the robes;
this is the meaning. "Of that" refers to the street. Regarding the phrase "the arm's reach of both the assembly and the door must not be abandoned":
here, because the beginning and the end are included, the street and the houses situated between the assembly and the door are indeed included as well.
And here, one living in dwellings with doors and verandas must avoid the faults of entering villages, sharing beds, and so forth, and should instead remain properly concealed and so on.

However, it should be understood that if an assembly hall (*sabhā*) has been built like a common hall for the purpose of being a residence for everyone, it is permissible to stay there at one's ease, just as in a monastery within a forest retreat (*antarārāma*).
Furthermore, because it is enclosed, it constitutes a single access point (*ekūpacāra*); whereas because it is unenclosed—
Extending this by way of analogy even to dwellings and so forth, he says, "By this very method," and so on.
Dwellings and the like situated outside the village are included here, because those located within the village are already covered by the mention of the "village" itself.

"In all cases" refers to the fifteen locations, such as villages, market towns, and dwellings. Regarding the phrase "enclosures and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the absence of enclosures.

There is no single common boundary (*ekūpacāra*) or distinct separate boundaries (*nānūpacāra*) even for those belonging to a single family and so forth, because the defining characteristics of such boundaries do not exist.
Furthermore, in this context, the enclosure (*parikkhepa*) applies only to a caravan that has settled somewhere for a few days, not to one that is still traveling.

482–7. Outside a village, a storehouse (*bhaṇḍasālā*) or warehouse (*udosita*) built by owners on the seashore or similar locations is what is meant by the phrase "of vehicles, etc. A "pavilion with a flat roof" (*muṇḍacchadanapāsāda*) refers to a palace that is not excessively high, provided with a courtyard (*candikaṅgaṇa*), and devoid of spires, turrets, garlands, and the like.

489. *Pariyādiyitvā* means having encompassed. Regarding the "exclusion of rivers" (*nadīparihāra*), some say that because the exclusion of rivers is not mentioned separately—as it is for separate villages and so forth—it refers simply to the reach of one’s hand from the robe. Others, however, say:

"By this statement in the Commentary, the exclusion of rivers is established as a separate rule; one must not let go of the reach of one’s hand over a river. *Vihārasīmaṃ* means the boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīma*).

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). And here, although the monastery belongs to various families, because the non-separation from the robe is possible everywhere within the boundary of the non-separation zone, and because that [boundary] is primary, the exemption from the caravan rule does not apply there;
thus it is said, "one must go to the monastery and dwell. The phrase "in the vicinity of the caravan" refers to the aforementioned internal boundary.

It has been stated. In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase "there is a caravan belonging to various families; having deposited one's robe in the caravan, one must not go beyond hand’s-reach," it is the "hand’s-reach of the caravan" that is intended here.
(490) Regarding "a field belonging to a single family," he speaks with reference to what is unenclosed.
491–4. "Vihāra" means the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*). In this context, it is said with reference to the inner courtyard and so forth of the specific vihāra where one resides;

and here, the fact that it belongs to a single family or the like is determined by way of those who caused it to be built. "Of the place touched by the shadow" refers to the area within the distance of a stone thrown straight down.

Regarding the phrase "on the path of arrival": the construction is that it refers to those islands situated in the middle of the ocean which one would be unable to reach and return from on the very same day.
Regarding the word "the other": it refers to the robe in the eastern direction. By the passage beginning with "At the time of the Uposatha...

[it] increases," the extreme distinctness of the seven-intermediate-space boundary for common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsa*) from the seven-intermediate-space limit for being separated from one's robe is shown.
This is shown as follows: when many bhikkhus sit together and, having each placed their own robe within a boundary of seven *abbhantara*s all around,
carry it about, the boundary of each individual *sattabbhantara* starting from the sitting place of each bhikkhu is distinct and manifold, not one and the same up to the edge of the assembly.
Because it begins from the boundary of the assembly (*parisa*). For that reason, in that case, there is neither increase nor decrease according to the size of the assembly;

this is not so with the seven-intermediate-space boundary (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*). For that [seven-intermediate-space boundary] remains one and the same, even if it extends for a league (*yojana*), being cut off by seven intermediate spaces all around from the very limit of the assembly.
Therefore, it increases or decreases according to the assembly; thus, it is indeed another [kind of] seven-intermediate-space boundary.
It should be understood that "open space" (*abbhokāsa*) refers to an exemption from the offense of being separated from one’s robes, which is delimited by the interior of a dwelling.
Whatever needs to be said regarding this matter, we shall explain it precisely in the discussion on boundaries (*sīmākathā*) within the *Khandhaka*. 495.
"He descends into a river" means he descends after releasing the reach of his hand (*hatthapāsa*). "Having placed [the robe] outside the village" means because it must not be uncovered.

It has been stated: "The disciplinary act (vinayakamma) should be performed. Having first performed the disciplinary act with respect to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) placed outside the village, one should afterwards put on the upper robe and perform it with respect to the inner robe (antaravāsaka).

And here, because the expression "disciplinary act" applies even to that which was placed outside the village, one may release [the robe] even while it stands out of sight; it is relinquished (nissaṭṭha).

It should be understood that it is permissible to give [the formal support]. Because there was an intention to go with those who were young, it is said: "But the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended.
Regarding the phrase "for a moment... it is suspended": this is said because the intention to go, though present, has been interrupted.
However, for those who rise even before dawn and go with the intention [to travel], even if dawn breaks while they are on the way, [the support is not suspended].
It subsides because it is stated that "it ceases by dawn. For this very reason, it is said: "Having entered the village...

it does not subside. Because there is an underlying intention (*saussāhattā*) in the passage beginning with "without taking each other's words," the subsiding at the moment of departure is not mentioned. "By the danger of cows" means by the charging of young calves and cows.

“By fear of being struck with a horn”: regarding the statement “the dependence (nissaya) is suspended,” this is said because those who have stayed [overnight] due to fears such as those of cattle cannot determine for themselves, “I will depart before dawn,” since they must remain until the danger has subsided;
therefore, it is impossible to make such a restriction. However, where it is possible to make such a restriction, there the dependence is not suspended even if dawn breaks in the interval.
It is like [the case of] young monks who have entered a village for the sake of medicine.

Regarding the phrase "within the boundary of a village," he speaks with reference to a village established after the formal authorization (*sammuti*) of the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).

Since it must be authorized excluding both the village and its precincts (*gāmūpacāra*), [the robes] of those who have entered—namely, teachers and pupils who have gone separately—are not [separated from them], because of the existence of the non-separation boundary. As for the robes...
They become subject to forfeiture; the dependence (nissaya) does not cease because of the presence of encouragement.
"On the way" means on the road for those who are returning after hearing the Dhamma.

By the phrase "here there is no relinquishing," it is shown that, unlike formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappana), relinquishing (paccuddharaṇa) must also be performed by means of the body.
This shows that it is to be performed by means of either body or speech. "The non-performance of what is to be performed by body and speech" refers to its origination from body and speech.

Herein, there are four factors: the state of having determined the three robes, the state of not having spread the kaṭhina, the state of not having obtained formal authorization, and staying apart during the night.
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Kathina Training Rule: 497.
Regarding the third [rule], the phrase "to store with expectation of a robe" in the Pāḷi means to store it while there is still an expectation for a robe.

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "when a bhikkhunī’s robe is finished," the meaning of the instrumental case should be understood here in the sense of the agent (*sāmivasena*), just as in the second *kathina* rule. 499–500.
As for "given as 'I give it to you,'" this refers to what is given by saying, "Venerable sir, I give this out-of-season robe to you.
The intention is that even this is called "given specifically for a time" (*kāle ādissa dinnaṃ*). However, this is a statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*; in the *Pāḷi*,...

The phrase “given specifically even at the proper time” is stated by way of a summary (atthuddhāra) in order to show all that which is applicable through the commonality of the expression “out-of-season robe” (*akālacīvara*),
just as the first indeterminate offense (*aniyata*) was shown by way of a summary for the ear. For indeed, what is given specifically to the Saṅgha even at the proper time—

like an out-of-season robe arising at an improper time— is [to be understood] by those who have spent the rains residence in the presence [of the robe], and by those who have not spent the rains residence.
Furthermore, in order to show that it is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*) because it is common to all [robes] in being subject to distribution, the text states by way of a summary:
"even if given specifically at the proper time.

However, this does not mean that a robe obtained by distributing [the gains] from that [fund], whether obtained out of season or during the proper time, does not receive the one-month or five-month grace period for those who have completed the rains residence.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that when there is no expectation regarding the robe-cloth, one obtains the ten-day exemption; and in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well,
in order to show by way of a general summary all that is included under the common expression "given specifically," it says, "it is given to a single person, saying,
'I give this to you,'" but not [referring to] what is obtained in that manner or what is obtained out of season.
It should be understood that this is intended to show that for those whose *kaṭhina* has not been spread, the robe must be determined within ten days;

otherwise, it would contradict the Canon and the Commentary. For instance, in the training rule on the *accekacīvara* (urgent robe), it is stated that even an urgent robe that arises out of season "may be kept until the time for robes. And in its commentary, regarding the month of the *pavāraṇā*:
For a robe that has arisen on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, when the *kathina* has not been spread, the period of grace is said to be one month plus eleven days;
when the *kathina* has been spread, it is five months plus eleven days. Referring to that very period of grace, [the text says]:
"But from the sixth day onwards, even a robe that has arisen which is not an urgent (*acceka*) robe, as well as a robe that has been set aside..."

"It is said that he indeed receives this privilege. Therefore, it should be understood that whether at the proper time or not, an extra robe (atirekacīvara) obtained in any manner whatsoever receives the appropriate privilege for one month or five months after the rains-retreat has been completed.

However, the connection is that the word-commentary (padabhājana) was stated without saying "in this way" (evaṃ). In that context, "in this way" (evaṃ) refers to what is stated in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā).
Regarding the phrase “tato ce uttarī,” the meaning stated is “beyond one month”; this [objection] refers to that.
The intention is that the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*) does not state the meaning in this way, but states it otherwise.
“Tāva uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ” is in the nominative case. “Mūlacīvaraṃ” is in the accusative case. “Attano gatikaṃ karoti” means immediately after.

On the second day and subsequent days, if one sets aside a *paccāsā-cīvara* (an expected robe) that has arisen, not for more than a month, but rather establishes it as one's own for no more than ten days, this is called "making it one's own. Beyond that, regarding the term "*mūla-cīvara*" (the basic robe):
here, "*mūla-cīvara*" is a singular noun. For that [period] begins from the twenty-first day onwards, on the twenty-second day and so forth.
If one sews together and joins an expected robe (*paccāsā-cīvara*) with one’s own [robe] and, instead of returning it within ten days,

makes it one’s own possession by keeping it for nine days or less, then it is permissible; however, an expected robe that has not been sewn together and kept separately must be returned within ten days at the very latest.
In the Pāḷi, *dasāha* means "within ten days. In such passages as *ekādase uppanne*, the meaning is "arisen on the eleventh day," or else this very reading (*ekādasāhe*) should be accepted.
The phrases "arisen on the twenty-first day" … pe … "it should be made [into a robe] within nine days," etc., are stated with reference to the day the expected robe material arose.
For that very reason, it is said: "On the thirtieth day … pe … it should be determined on that very day."
“‘Another expected robe... [and so on]... ‘should be made’—this was said specifically regarding an expectation that still exists.

However, if the expectation from the intended source has been cut off—thinking, ‘From now on I shall not receive a robe there’—and one generates an expectation elsewhere by any means whatsoever, then the original robe must not be determined; in every respect, [the determination is lost] due to the expectation.”
If the ten-day period has elapsed for a basic robe that was interrupted [in its acquisition], it must be determined on that very day.
Regarding the statement that even a "hope-robe" (paccāsā-cīvara) may be determined as a requisite cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa), this is said with reference to a dissimilar robe that arose earlier.
"Mutually" (aññamaññaṃ) means one and another; this is indeed the reading. As for the factor (aṅga) here, it is exactly the same as what was stated regarding the first *kathina* ceremony.
For in that case there is only the transgression of ten days, whereas here there is the transgression of a month; this is the distinction.
The commentary on the third training rule concerning the Kathina is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes (Purāṇacīvara).
503–5. Regarding the fourth [section], "the dismissal of food" (*bhattavissagga*) means the releasing of food into the stomach;
its meaning is the entry or swallowing, which constitutes the act of eating. Some also say it is the "dismissal of food" by way of the conclusion of the meal.
In that context, *nāma tvam* means "you indeed," or alternatively, *tāya nāma tvam* is the meaning. *Pitā ca mātā*...
And the ancestors, as well as the father and mother of the father—the grandfathers—these very ones, by virtue of being a pair, constitute a "yoke" (*yuga*).
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "as far back as the seventh ancestral yoke," that is, the grandfathers.
For, by the inclusion of the term "grandfather," both the maternal grandfather and the paternal grandmother are indeed included. Beyond the seventh yoke, they are "unrelated" (*aññātaka*).

It should be understood as follows: "She" refers to the bhikkhunī. "Father," "mother," "paternal grandmother," "maternal grandfather"—in each and every instance of the action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the bhikkhu.
This is stated because by the single verbal act of commanding, "Wash it," all the actions conducive to that [washing] are commanded.
(506) Because washing is inseparable from that [command], it is said: "having made a bodily gesture" and "within twelve *hattha*s."
Because it has been so stated, there is no offense at all for one who, without manifesting a desire to have [the robe] washed by means of the body, performs the acts of throwing or sending [it];
nor is there an offense for one who, having left the twelve-cubit vicinity, stands outside and performs the acts of throwing or sending by commanding through body or speech.

"By a single instance" means by the first case. "Five hundred" means those whose measure is five hundred. Even a nun who has changed her gender from the state of being a monk is indeed one who received full ordination on one side (ekato-upasampannā) in the presence of monks.
"Having taken it as temporary" means: having requested it for a limited time for one's own use, such as for wearing it for a few days.
Here, there are three factors: [the robe being] an old cloth, standing in the vicinity and commanding a nun who is not a relative, and having her wash it and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes. 508.

Regarding the fifth [training rule], "when the training rule has not yet been laid down": this refers to when the training rule concerning departing from the community had not yet been laid down. "Perfection of parts" means:
The excellence of the five parts beginning with the hair. "Showing it on the palm of the hand itself" indicates that the rest of the body is not visible from the palm of the hand.

510. *Vihatthatāya* means "by being struck down," that is, by being disintegrated; the meaning is "by being unmixed" or "by being without refuge. Therefore he said, "because of being thoroughly pierced," which means "because of being wounded.
*Parivattabbaṃ* is "to be turned over"; *pārivattakaṃ* is just that; the meaning is "being given after having been turned over."
As in the previous training rule, there is no restriction of a twelve-fathom radius here; thus he said, "having left the vicinity.

"Except for an exchange" means, setting aside that which one takes as an exchange after giving even a piece of a myrobalan fruit, or having made the intention, "I will give [this]," [and receive that]. By the phrase, "That does not coincide because of its lack of conscious intent,"...
It indicates that there is no offense even by way of not recognizing her status as a bhikkhunī, just as in cases such as not recognizing her kinship.
513–4. It is a *pācittiya* belonging to the triad [of offenses], thus it is a "triad-pācittiya" (*tikapācittiya*); the meaning is "a *pācittiya* of the triad.

Regarding the phrase "alms-bowl bag, etc.," he speaks with reference to those items that do not require formal dedication (*anadhiṭṭhānupaga*). As for the expression "what need to mention the alms-bowl bag, etc.?"—this refers even to a large one.
There is no offense regarding a robe made of bark-fiber because it has not reached the status of being formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhāna*);

this shows that what need be said about those things which cannot be resolved upon—because they lack the minimum size required for formal assignment—is even more obvious. Furthermore, it is indeed not permitted to accept alms-bowls, bags, and so forth that have reached the minimum size for formal assignment.
Acceptance is an action (*kiriya*); non-exchange is a non-action (*akiriya*). [This refers to] the state of a robe that has reached the status of being fit for formal assignment.
The absence of an exchange and receiving from the hand of one who is not a relative—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the acceptance of robes is concluded.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding requesting from one who is not a relative.

515. In the sixth [offense], "paṭṭo" means simply "cloth. In the Pāḷi, the term *dhammanimantanā* refers to an invitation based merely on the duty of proper conduct (*vattabbācāra-dhamma*) toward ascetics;
it does not mean an invitation made out of a desire to give. For that very reason, it is said, "she will request.
Indeed, what is called "requesting" (*viññatti*) occurs only from one who is neither a relative nor one who has invited [the monk].
517. Regarding the statement, “One should come having covered [the ground] with grass or leaves,” this implies that the destruction of living plants is permitted;

thus he says, “nor by the ravaging of living plants,” and so forth. Furthermore, even one who first assumes the outward marks (liṅga) with a pure mind but later adopts a different doctrine is still one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka); thus he says, “even after putting on [the robes], the doctrine must not be adopted.”

Regarding the phrase "the dwelling which one first enters": here too, even when entering for the sake of a monastery, robes, or other necessities, one must go having covered oneself with grass or the like;
one must certainly not come naked, because a general offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) has been stated for such an act.
"With rags" means with pieces of cloth made from discarded cotton. "By use alone" means by using [the robe] after failing to obtain another robe.
"Decayed through use" means that the robe has become worn out and unsightly through being used, having become tattered and torn; thus it is "decayed.
Regarding "for the sake of another," here too the phrase "for relatives who have invited him" carries over; therefore he says, "for his own relatives who have invited him," and so forth.
However, in this case, it refers to the purpose of another person for whom one's own robes have not been stolen or lost, and who has not invited him.
The meaning to be understood is that there is no offense for one who makes [the food] known while using what is subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*);
otherwise, there would be no distinction from the phrase "for those who are relatives or have invited [him]. For this very reason, he will say in the immediately following training rule:

"In the commentaries, however, it is stated that 'in the place of relatives or those who have invited... only the proper measure is permitted,' but that does not agree with the Canon (*pāḷi*)," and: "But since this training rule..."
It was prescribed precisely within the context of requesting for the sake of another; therefore, the phrase “for the sake of another” is not stated here.

Furthermore, the four factors in this case are: the robe being of a permissible kind, the absence of a [valid] occasion, the request made by one who is not a relative, and the acquisition through that [request].
The commentary on the training rule regarding requesting from an unrelated person is finished.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule (Tatuttari-sikkhāpada), §§ 522–524.
Regarding the seventh [rule], "a cloth-shop" (*paggāhikasāla*) refers to a cloth merchant’s stall; for there, merchants display their cloths for sale.
Because it is a place for viewing, it is called the "Hall of Reception.

"Of that robe" means of the robe that is to be accepted. By the phrase "one who possesses the three robes," he shows the absence of any other robe—such as one deposited in a monastery—that might be exempt from being cut up.
If such a robe existed, it would not be permissible to ask for one. Having worn it only temporarily, for oneself...

One should obtain a robe; even for one who does not receive it even on a temporary basis, requesting it—even as if one were clearing away vegetation from a site and covering it with grass and leaves—is indeed permissible.
"By another" means by means of a robe that has not been stolen or is not entirely [new]. Regarding the phrase "two lost," it is stated "two should be accepted" because of the context.

526. "It does not accord with the Canon" means that it does not accord with the Canon passage stating, "There is no offense in the case of relatives or those who have invited one," because that [passage] was spoken specifically regarding the contingency of an offense for requesting more than that.
The statement, "It is not said 'for the sake of another,'" illustrates this meaning: that there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense for requesting more than that for the sake of another.
And that *pācittiya* offense would belong either to those for whose sake one requests [the robe], or to the requester alone;
it could not belong to the former because they did not request them, nor to the requester because he did not request them for his own sake.
Therefore, even for one requesting [a robe] for the sake of another, a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* is not seen [in the texts]. However, in the *Pāḷi*...

They say that because the training rule (sikkhāpada) operates by way of being dependent on one’s own approval, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned in the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra);
and this appears reasonable, yet it should be accepted after careful investigation.
Herein, there are four factors: the state of having an extra robe, the cause such as it being lost, requesting from one who is not related, and the acquisition thereof.
The commentary on the subsequent training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Set Aside (Paṭhamupakkhaṭasikkhāpada). 528–531.
In the eighth [rule], the phrase "whoever should" refers to the donor. *Paṭaka* means simply a cloth (*paṭa*). "Of little value..."

The statement “he causes it to be made” is said with reference to the non-offense regarding the *nissaggiya-pācittiya*; however, on account of the solicitation (*viññatti*), there is indeed a *dukkaṭa*.
For in the Sutta, “without having been previously invited,” the act of soliciting is stated as the cause. Furthermore, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:
“Excessive desire for robes, soliciting from one who is not related, and the acquisition through that—these are the three factors here.”
The state of requesting from one who is unrelated has been explained. However, some say:

"Even if the donor has not personally stated in one’s presence, 'I wish to give,' it is permissible to have [the goods] brought at whatever value he intends to give. This does not accord with the commentary on the Rāja-sikkhāpada (the training rule concerning kings), which states:
"Whether by messenger or by the donor himself, [one says]: 'A cloth-fund has been brought for the sake of the Venerable One.'"

Even when [the gift] has been announced, it is prohibited to have it brought from the presence of those such as a "mouth-ornament" (mukhavevaṭiya) or a "maker of what is allowable" (kappiyakāraka), because that is forbidden there.
For it is said therein: "These two are called 'unspecified makers of what is allowable' (aniddiṭṭha-kappiyakāraka); one should behave toward them just as toward strangers who have not been invited...
nothing at all should be said to them. And this is merely for the sake of instruction: 'By means of a messenger, [one may send] the purchase-price for a robe..."
"‘One may send it’ means that even when one brings it oneself and gives it for the sake of alms-food and so forth, the same principle applies.

For it is said that "nothing need be said" regarding the mouth-cleanser, the kappiya-kāraka (the one who makes things allowable), and others, because—even though the object has been relinquished by the donor—they have not been specifically designated [by the donor] with the words, "Take the robe, alms-food, etc., from such-and-such a person"; it is not, however, because of the mouth-cleanser and others [being inherently improper].

Because it is his own property, therefore here too, for one who speaks without having been invited by saying, "Tell me whatever you wish," whether by the donor himself or by a messenger, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the term "in relation to the increase of value": this training rule (sikkhāpada) concerns what occurs in dependence on an increase in the value of a robe;
it does not concern alms-food and so forth, because in the case of those, an increase in value constitutes only an offense of wrong-doing, whereas in the case of high-quality alms-food—

And it should be understood that this is because it is a *pācittiya* offense of the pure (*suddhika*) class. For that very reason, the factor of "excessive desire for robes" (*cīvare bhiyyokamyatā*) is stated [in the rule].
The commentary on the first *upakkhaṭa* training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the second *upakkhaṭa* training rule.
533. In the ninth [offense], *paccekacīvaracetāpannā* means "cīvara-purchase funds designated individually";
the meaning is "cīvara-purchase funds designated separately by each person. *Ubho va santā ekena* means "being both together as one";
the meaning is "having both become one."
The commentary on the second *upakkhaṭa* training rule is finished.
10. Commentary on the King Training Rule (Rājasikkhāpada) 537.

Regarding the tenth [rule], "ajjaṇho": this is said by adding the letter *ha* where "ajja no" should have been said, and by changing the letter *na* to *ṇa*. Therefore, it says, "on one day today, for us."

538–9. As for what was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe”—this was said to demonstrate purity of transmission (*āgamanasuddhi*);
for if one were to send [the gift] saying, “Give this to the monk named so-and-so,” because the transmission would be impure, it would concern an improper object (*akappiyavatthu*).

If it were not possible for the monk to designate even a "maker of what is allowable" (kappiyakāraka), then— since that [gift] would consist of an object subject to forfeiture or an object of wrongdoing,
namely an unallowable cloth-fund intended for robes, and since there would be no purity of the source regarding the statement, "Give this to such-and-such a monk"—
and since the messenger's speech would also be impure according to the method set forth in the training rule (sikkhāpada), it is entirely proper to issue a prohibition.
However, it is not possible to say, "We shall accept the robe," nor can one designate a steward on that basis,

because both the messenger's words regarding the arrival and the [messenger's] own statement are impure. But in order to show that— according to the method found in the Pāḷi— if there is purity regarding the arrival according to the method stated in the text,
then even if the messenger's words are impure, it is permissible to do everything according to the method stated in the training rule (sikkhāpada).

It has been stated. And by that, the following meaning is established by implication: just as it is permissible to designate a messenger even when his speech is impure provided his arrival is pure, so too it is permissible [to designate him] even when his arrival is impure provided his speech is pure;
thus, since there is no need to speak of the case where both are pure, this refers specifically to the case where both are impure.
It should be understood that it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The one who makes [food] allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) would also not need to be pointed out.

However, as for what was stated here in the *Sāratthadīpanī*—"No specific purpose is seen for either the arrival [of the *kappiyakāraka*] or his purity or impurity," and so forth—that was stated without having observed the intended meaning of the statement in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Because it serves a purpose through the methods already described, such as the purity of its arrival and so forth.

As for the undesirable consequence (aniṭṭhappasaṅga) stated here—that "even one who speaks by way of improper terminology on the part of a messenger sent by a master using proper terminology should be pointed out as a maker of what is improper"—that undesirable consequence does not actually occur, because it is precisely what is intended. For thus it is said in the training rule (sikkhāpada):

Thus, when a messenger speaks using improper terminology, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept this robe-fund," the attendant must be designated by means of a proper transaction (*kappiya-kamma*), because of the purity of the messenger's arrival;
however, if the messenger's arrival itself is impure, then even by means of a proper transaction, the attendant is not to be designated.
Therefore, there is indeed a distinction between the purity and impurity of the messenger's arrival.
The purpose [of this]. But how is the purity of the arrival known through the messenger’s words? This is not a heavy burden.
For the purity of the arrival must be sought only when the messenger speaks using improper terminology (*akappiya-vohāra*), and not otherwise;

and in that case, it can be understood by questioning him according to the sequence of his statements and by means of logical reasoning (*yutti*) and so forth. For here too, in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*):
By the messenger’s statement, “The purchase-money for the robe has been brought,” it is understood that the robe was bought and sent specifically to be given.
For if the purity of the delivery were not established in every respect, a refusal would indeed have to be made.
And in the Pāḷi, the passage beginning with “But we accept the robe” [is given] even though the messenger’s words are unallowable, because of the purity of the delivery.

This was stated for the purpose of showing the method of proceeding when [the robe] exists. The passage beginning with “This indeed… one should not say, ‘Give it to him’” was stated for the purpose of avoiding the acceptance of unallowable things.
The passage beginning with “He has been summoned” was stated for the purpose of showing that “only when the messenger has spoken thus again is it permissible to admonish him, and not otherwise.
The passage beginning with “One should not say, ‘Give me a robe…’” [was stated for the purpose of showing the proper conduct].

When one says, "Exchange this for a robe for me," because one has designated oneself as the "proper agent" (kappiyakāraka) for accepting the money brought by a messenger, one is effectively engaging in the commercial transaction of money—saying "Give me a robe...
exchange it for a robe for me"—since one is dealing with the money itself; thus, one incurs that fault.
It was stated [in that context] for the purpose of avoiding [the offense] from afar, as in the case of accepting silver in the midst of the Saṅgha after it has been relinquished.
For it is said there: "One should not say, 'Bring this' or 'bring that.

Therefore, it should be understood that this was not stated for the purpose of avoiding the fault of requesting; otherwise, it would follow that one could not even say, "Friend, I have need of a robe."

For that very reason, since there is no suspicion of trading in silver among those designated by a messenger, it is stated that one may have [the robe] brought even after appointing another person as the *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable).

Even in that case, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: rather than saying, "Having exchanged [the value] for silver appointed by the messenger, have the robe brought," one should simply say, "Have the robe brought. This is the proper occasion (*ṭhāna*).

Regarding the phrase "he breaks the occasion" (*bhañjatīti ettha ṭhānaṃ*): here, "occasion" (*ṭhāna*) is a term for both a standing place and a reason. Therefore, by sitting on a seat, one breaks the standing place as well as the reason for their coming;

they do not understand the purpose for which they arrived. However, when one does not disturb the standing place but rather breaks only the reason for their coming during the acceptance of alms and so forth, one does not break the standing place. Thus it is said: "He breaks the reason for their coming. Some, however—
Some say that "by accepting material gifts and so forth, one also breaks the *ṭhāna* (the standing rule)," but this does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

The passage beginning with "Whatever robe-fund for him... is an instruction on the procedure to be followed by the person who was designated as the attendant (*veyyāvaccakara*) when the robe has not yet been produced.
Thus, when the monk has spoken to the owners of the goods, they give after having been exhorted.
It is permissible [to say], "The owners, having been urged, are giving it," because this is stated in the context of there being no offense.

By that, it is established that there is no offense for one who, without urging them himself, has lay followers (upāsaka) and others urge them in turn; even if they urge them seven times and cause the robe to be given, there is no offense for him, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) is not a direct command (anāṇattika).
One who has not been designated by anyone else, but has attained the status of a personal attendant (*mukhaveyyāvaccakara*) through his own mouth—that is, by his own word—is a *mukhaveyyāvaccika*.

By the phrase "because of a desire not to investigate," it is shown that even Noble Ones (*ariya*), though possessing [the goods], may say "there is none" in common parlance without the intention to deceive, because they do not wish to give what is available.
This is from the *Meṇḍaka-seṭṭhi-vatthu* in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*.
The statement beginning with “There are, monks,” and so forth, is indeed what is called the Meṇḍaka training rule (sikkhāpada).
The phrase “in the hands of those who make things allowable” refers to a messenger-designated kappiyakāraka, and not to one designated by a bhikkhu or one who is undesignated.
Therefore he said: “And here there is no authority for a formal charge,” and so on.
The connection is with the phrase, “when they themselves have brought it and give it. By the words “for the sake of alms-food and so forth,” he shows that it is not for the sake of robes alone.

By the words “the same method applies,” he shows that even when gifts are given for the sake of alms-food and so forth by various types of kappiyakārakas (authorized agents) designated by the owner of the property, all matters such as the formal motion regarding the place and so forth must be performed according to the method explained below.

Because it is stated, “without referring to the Saṅgha...,” when people speak by touching [the object] and saying, “We give this for the sake of a dwelling for the Saṅgha,” and so forth, it must indeed be refused.
The phrase “the Saṅgha accepts” is spoken in the highest sense;
however, even when accepting for the sake of the Saṅgha in the case of a group (gaṇa) and so on, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) both in the act of acceptance and in the subsequent use.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for accepting [it].

This is not correct, because an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for the sake of the Saṅgha, a shrine, and so forth. "He accuses" means that even though he knows there is no fault in him, he accuses him out of anger or greed, saying, "This is a gift to be given.
For it is he alone who, by reason of lying and so forth, incurs offenses such as expiation or wrong-doing.
One becomes guilty of an offense; however, for one who speaks with the perception that it is a debt but then desists upon realizing there is no fault, there is no offense.

It is said that "it should not be accepted" because a pond has entered the domain of a field. When someone gives [something] saying, "Let the Saṅgha enjoy these four requisites," it is permissible; here, [the phrase] "for the purpose of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus enjoying the four requisites... [is used].
It is also permissible to say, "I give a pond," or "I give a pond for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to enjoy the four requisites," or "I give the four requisites arising from this pond.
This is stated with reference specifically to what is given for the purpose of the Saṅgha’s enjoyment; however, even if such a pond, field, or the like is given to an individual person—
It is not permitted. However, for one with a pure mind, wells, lotus ponds, and so forth, are permitted for the purpose of using water.
For it is stated in all such cases by way of the Saṅgha alone, beginning with: "There is a reservoir belonging to the Saṅgha; what [is to be done] with that?
Regarding the word "hand," it means "under one's control. The phrase "when told 'set it down'" is said by way of formal courtesy; even if not told, there is no fault in one who sets it down.

Therefore it is said: “It is permissible to ward off water. Even during a time of drought, it is allowable to release [the water] after having threatened [the owner]; however, if one does not release it, there is the obligation to pay the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
“He gives again” means he gives again after having taken it back; the connection is that even in this way it is allowable. By this [it is meant]:
by whatever authority [one acts], with the perception that “this has been relinquished by the monks; it is ownerless,” [he acts] himself...

This shows that what is given after having been taken is permissible. The phrase "I shall explain the determination regarding allowable speech" (*kappiyavohāre*) is an elliptical expression [to be supplied].

"By means of water" (*udakavasena*) means for the purpose of using water. The phrase "of those with pure minds" (*suddhacittānaṃ*) is said with reference to those who act by their own hand and by means of allowable speech.
"For the purpose of producing crops"—even for those with such impure minds, however, acting themselves...
It is indeed permissible to have [the work] ordered by means of allowable speech (*kappiya-vohāra*) without having performed it oneself.

As for the statement, “It is not permissible to appoint a steward (*kappiyakāraka*),” this was said because it is “inappropriate” (*asāruppa*) that a pond be made by one’s own hand or other such means;

however, no offense (*āpatti*) is understood for the Saṅgha either for the one who appoints [the steward] or for those who consume that requisite (*paccaya*), according to the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā. Or rather, in this matter...
An offense is to be incurred. "By a conscientious bhikkhunī" means by one who possesses a sense of shame;

the intention is that it applies even more so when a lack of conscience is involved in having clay-digging and such tasks performed. "In a new crop" refers to a field where harvesting has not been done before.

By the word "kahāpaṇa," he shows that the act of causing grain to be harvested is itself unallowable for her; furthermore, regarding the procedure of causing grain to be harvested, there is merely a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), and not as [a grave offense] as in the case of causing [money] to be harvested.
Regarding the statement, "If one says, 'Sow it! Plant it! it would be improper for everyone," he said, "without saying [this].
In the phrase "such a portion," he speaks with reference to this as well: "such a number of kahāpaṇas.
For even if that were said, since kahāpaṇas were not available at that time, what arises in the future is indeed permissible for others. Therefore he said, "That is improper for him alone."
Furthermore, for all such preparatory acts as well as for the actual consumption, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Some, however, say: "The offense occurs only in the consumption of the grain, not in the prior preparatory acts. That is not correct;

for it would be improper to claim there is no offense when one performs those very preparatory acts—such as measuring and guarding—the subsequent consumption of which constitutes an offense. This is according to the method of exegesis (*pariyāyakathā*).

However, there is no offense in all such cases. For this very reason, it is stated that [the act] is unallowable when there is a specific instruction such as, "Bring this and that with so many grains of rice.

The same principle applies to the exchange of kahāpaṇa coins. Furthermore, statements such as "The object exists in such a manner, yet there is no one to make it allowable" serve as proof in this context.

Regarding the statement, "I give a forest... it is permissible": because it is a place of residence, it is permissible for an individual to accept it with a pure mind. Regarding the statement, "We give a boundary": because it is expressed by a general term such as "monastery boundary" (*vihārasīmā*) and so forth, it is said, "it is permissible.

Even when stated as "a service-provider" (*veyyāvaccakara*) and so on, it is permissible to accept a slave for an individual, because it was specifically authorized [by the Buddha] with the words, "Monks, I allow you an attendant (*ārāmika*)," and that too according to the sequence of acceptance and use established by Pilindavaccha.

It is not by way of the householders’ method of enjoyment as slaves. However, it should be understood that all things such as fields and so forth are permissible for the Saṅgha alone, because taking them for an individual is not permitted in the Pāḷi.
The statement "we give to the monastery" refers to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha;
this is because there is a prohibition found in the Suttantas, beginning with: "He abstains from accepting fields and lands."

Since the Great Elders of the Council, knowing the Blessed One’s intention that [the offense] was established by the Blessed One even as a causal basis for an offense, stated that this entire exposition outside the Canon (pāḷimutta-vinicchaya) concerning the acceptance of fields and so forth is based on that, it should be understood thus.

Herein, there are four factors: the designation of a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable), the act of entrusting by means of a messenger, exertion beyond that [entrustment], and the acquisition [of the object] through that [exertion].
The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Robes, is completed. 2.
The Chapter on Silk.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Silk (Kosiyasikkhāpada) 542.

Regarding the first [offense] of the second [training rule], the term *kosiyakāraka* in the Pāḷi refers to those who produce cloth and such items from silk thread—that is, from the cocoons produced by silk-spinning creatures (*kosakāraka-pāṇa*). *Saṅghāta* means destruction. 544.
Because it is stated as "not woven" (*avāyima*), there is no offense in making [the item] after having woven it. *Missetvā* means having mixed it with sheep’s wool.

"By acquisition" means by completion; since it is stated that "it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) when one brings it to its conclusion," there are three factors here: the mixing with silk, the making or having made a rug for one's own use, and the acquisition.
The commentary on the training rule regarding silk is finished.
547–552. The second and third [offenses] are likewise clear. However, in this context, the absence of intentional intent (*acittakatā*) should be understood in two ways:
first, by way of making a rug out of purely black hair while perceiving it as a mixture of white and other colors;
and second, by way of making a rug out of black hair that exceeds the two-part limit, while perceiving it as not exceeding that limit.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Six Years (Chabbassa-sikkhāpada) 557.

Regarding the fourth [training rule], in the phrase "having evacuated excrement," he says, "they discharge both feces and urine," with reference to the meaning of the verbal root *miha*, which means "to sprinkle.
