Here, the absence of intentional consciousness (*acittakata*) should be understood by way of those who have less than six years of seniority yet suspect themselves to have more than six years, and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule on six years is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana-saṇṭhata-sikkhāpada) 565.
Regarding the fifth [rule], "it will be seen therein" means that it will be seen by the wise due to one's improper conduct according to one's own private agreement.
The three factors beginning with the forest-dweller’s practice (araññakaṅga) are stated in the Canon as the primary factors among the triad of requisites, such as lodgings.
It should be understood that they undertook the remaining [precepts] as well.

566. "Desiring" means longing for. Because it is merely a spread (santhatassa) and because it is an accessory of lodgings, it lacks the status of a robe (*cīvara*) and there is no need for its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhātabbatā*);
thus he said, "by way of the perception of a fourth robe," meaning by way of a mistaken perception.
However, some say: "This so-called 'seated rug' (*nisīdanasanthata*) is only the sitting cloth (*nisīdanacīvara*) among the nine types of robes, and nothing else.
Just as in the rule regarding the sitting cloth (*nisīdana-sikkhāpada*), it is said here in this rule, 'A seated rug is called that which has a fringe,' and in its commentary:
'Having spread it out like a rug, at one corner, [measuring] a Sugata-span..."*
Some say: "Because it is stated that 'having split the cloth in two places across its width, three borders are made; with those borders, it is called a *sadasa* (with-border),' [this applies here].

This is not correct, because no specific measurement is prescribed here, because a sitting mat (*santhata*) is not a robe that has been sewn together (*avāyima-cīvara*), because it lacks the status of being subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānūpaga*), and because it is not mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). [This concludes the section on] the sitting mat robe (*nisīdana-cīvara*).
However, they arrange pieces of rag-patches from the six kinds of robes so that, though they are merely strips, they appear as if they were a properly proportioned spread.

For this very reason, the word "like" (*sadisa*) is used in the expression "like a spread" (*santhatasadisa*); therefore, it should be understood that it is that very robe which becomes subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*), and not this [the rag-patches themselves].

567. Herein, the state of being unintentional (*acittakatā*) should be understood by way of two factors: taking up [a measure] with the perception that it is less than a *sugata-vidatthi*, and perceiving it as not deficient when it is actually deficient by a *sugata-vidatthi*.

Since it is stated that there is no offense when making [a bed] solely for the purpose of a canopy or similar uses, there is indeed an offense even for one who makes it for the purpose of lying down. It is not permitted to use [beds made of] silk; and among the black varieties, those that are purely black...

This was stated because the materials were unallowable. For that very reason, it is stated in various places in the Pāḷi: "If one obtains and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)";
however, regarding the other two cases, it is stated: "there is no offense.
In this regard, it should be understood that in the fourth case there is no offense even when making it for the sake of another, whereas in the fifth case there is an offense of wrong-doing.

However, because it is spoken of as a gift that has been relinquished, there is no fault in taking it; nor is there any fault in using it, provided it has been disentangled and prepared in accordance with what is allowable (*kappiya*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting mat (*nisīdana-santhata*) is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sheep’s Wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*).
572. In the sixth [case], the phrase “of one who has set out on a journey” is stated by way of illustration (*vatthu*).

It is likewise not permitted to carry [medicine] beyond three *yojanas*, even if it was obtained at one’s place of residence. The statement “if there is no one to carry it” is made by way of suitability;

for if there is someone to carry it, there is no fault in carrying it oneself. “It is indeed an offense” because it was carried without being instructed [to do so]. This applies to both sides [of the rule].
He states the reason as “because of her desire to go,” meaning because she has not ceased her intention to go.

He states the reason for the side of pure mind alone as “because of being without consciousness. It does not apply because it was stated that there is no offense only in the case of avoiding [the act] by having someone else carry it.
“While not coming” means while standing. “Below” means on the ground.
575. *Taṃ harantassa* means: for one who carries it from more than three *yojanas* starting from the place of the first acquisition;
this is the meaning. For when carrying it in that manner, it is permissible to carry it up to three *yojanas* from the place where it was returned by thieves after having been stolen.

However, some [hold that] because it is stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* regarding the *Aṅga* country that "the first acquisition" refers to the second acquisition, [the limit is from the second acquisition].
Some say that there is no offense even when traveling more than three *yojanas*, but that is not correct;
for even the second acquisition [of the robe] occurs at the place of acquisition, just as when one travels again from the place where one went for the purpose of staying.

Regarding "the waist-band and so forth," it is said that what is placed inside a double-layered waist-band and so on is like what is placed in a bag, and is not considered a finished article; the same applies to the opening of a storehouse.
The five factors here are: being unmade, being newly acquired, exceeding three leagues [in distance], having it brought back, and the intention not to dwell [there].
The commentary on the training rule concerning wool is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Washing of Sheep’s Wool (Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpada) 581.
Regarding the seventh [training rule], in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), it says: “If one has someone wash a finished article that has not been used.

Here, having someone wash a finished article such as a woolen blanket (*kambala*) that has already been used constitutes an offense under the training rule concerning the washing of old robes (*purāṇacīvaradhovāpanasikkhāpada*).
To prevent that [misunderstanding], it is stated: "an un-used manufactured article. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the washing of wool is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Money (Rūpiya-sikkhāpada).
583–4. In the eighth [case], since even a single kahāpaṇa made of gold is included within silver, he says, "or made of gold.
"Or made of rūpiya" means a kahāpaṇa fashioned by using silver as the material (rūpa). "Ordinary" refers to the common kahāpaṇa used nowadays.
"All this" indicates everything stated in both the training rule (sikkhāpada) and its analysis (vibhaṅga). It is fourfold.
The connection is with the term *nissaggiyavatthu* (an object involving forfeiture) itself, and not with the immediately preceding word *rajataṃ* (silver).
Now, showing those four kinds of objects involving forfeiture according to their specific nature, he says "silver," and so forth.
In that context, although only the silver *māsaka* was mentioned below—and not silver alone—nevertheless, in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is stated as "gold and silver" (*jātarūparajataṃ*).

To show that this was also stated by way of the word itself, "silver" (rajataṃ) is mentioned separately. However, since it is already established by the matrix-word (mātikāpada) in the word-commentary (padabhājana), it is not mentioned there;

rather, it should be understood that the passage beginning with "silver means a kahāpaṇa coin" is stated to show how it is included together with that [matrix-word]. A "gold māsaka" (jātarūpamāsako) is a gold coin. "Of the aforementioned classification" (vuttappabheda).
The classification stated by the phrase “made of silver or ordinary [copper]” and so forth. *Paṭa* means a cloth or garment.
“An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) alone” means that for the recipient alone, there is an offense of wrong-doing on account of the acceptance;

however, regarding the use [of the gift], for all those who use the requisite arising from the cause of pearls and so forth—which are devoid of grain—after they have been accepted by the five types of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.

It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, some say: "Even grain received from the five types of persons associated with the Dhamma is not permitted for anyone to consume, just as pearls, fields, and so forth [are not].

The statement, 'This is unallowable for him alone,' was spoken solely with reference to the distribution of grain that has arisen on land belonging to the Saṅgha through a transaction involving allowable goods (kappiyavohāra)."
The passage beginning with "One hundred or one thousand" is stated to show the manner in which [the use of] money occurs at its lowest limit;
it is not, however, intended to show that "one must act in this way alone.

He said, "It should not be said, 'Place it here,' because taking it up occurs when [someone] says, 'Place it here,'" since [money] is not allowable (kappiya) because it has not been touched. ...pe... It is allowable because it has not been touched.

Therefore, things arising from that [allowable source] are allowable; thus, it stands supported by what is allowable (*kappiya*). However, since even what arises from that is not allowable when there is improper conduct (*dubbicāraṇā*), it should be understood as standing supported by what is unallowable (*akappiya*).
By the phrase, "nothing whatsoever was bartered for with that allowable article," it is shown that if something has been bartered for, there is no way to consume it.

Because it was purchased with unrenounced money after having been received. This indicates that, having made such a renunciation in the midst of the Saṅgha and having discarded [the object], one must confess the *pācittiya* offense. However, some say:

"Even though the article subject to renunciation (*nissaggiya-vatthu*) was received, the purchased allowable goods were renounced to the Saṅgha; then, having exchanged the unrenounced money through the *kappiyakārakas* (monks who manage allowable goods)..."
They say, “It becomes like an allowable article that has been brought [for the Sangha]; therefore, it is permissible to divide and consume it even without [the usual] means.
This does not accord with the discussion regarding the set of four bowls and so forth.

In that context, it is shown that a bowl exchanged for money is simply not to be used at all, and not that there is a procedure for relinquishing it. “Having placed as a deposit” means by the kappiyakārakas (those who make things allowable).
This was said with reference to the purpose of increasing [the number of robes]. It is called "unallowable" because it has been taken by means of that object.
585. Regarding the phrase, "by one who does not attend to the fallen spot," this should be understood as demonstrating a state of indifference.
"By way of false attribution" is said with reference to the reporting of what is untrue through indirect speech and so forth. "Enjoyment by theft" [is explained as follows].

This was said because it has not been permitted by the Blessed One, the Master of requisites. "Debt-like enjoyment" is said because one enjoys things without having performed what ought to be done even though it was permitted by the Blessed One;

and by this, he shows that virtue dependent on requisites fails. "In each act of enjoyment" means in each act of enjoyment after having repeatedly released [the object] from the body. "It should be reviewed during the last watch of the night."

The application (*yojanā*): Regarding the phrase "it stands in the place of the utilization of what has been received" (*iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne*), they say that here even retrospective reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*) on the past—such as "the robe which was utilized by me yesterday," and so forth—is appropriate.
Regarding "in each act of utilization" (*paribhoge paribhoge*), this refers to the instances of entering within from the point where water falls, as well as in sitting and lying down.
"It is appropriate for it to be a condition through mindfulness" (*satipaccayatā vaṭṭati*) means that it obtains the state of being a condition for reflective mindfulness (*paccavekkhaṇasati*).
It is permissible. This shows that mindfulness of reflection must necessarily be maintained both in the receiving and in the consumption [of the medicine].

Therefore he said, “having established mindfulness,” and so forth. Some, however, explain the meaning as follows: “The conditionality of mindfulness means that when the requisite exists—that is, when the cause for the consumption of the medicine is present.
For them as well, the phrase “when the requisite exists” refers to the discernment of the presence of the requisite.
The meaning should be understood as "it exists," because virtue is not purified by the mere presence of the requisite conditions.

By the statement, "An offense occurs even for one who does not actually consume [the requisites]," the breach of the *pātimokkha-saṃvara* (vow of restraint) is shown, but not that of the virtue dependent on requisites (*paccaya-nissita-sīla*), since the latter is purified through retrospective reflection on the past.
However, regarding this and the other requisites, by the expression "consumption like a debt" and so forth...
The breach occurs only in the virtue dependent on requisites; thus should the distinction between these two be understood.
Having thus shown the purification of virtue dependent on requisites, he said, "For purity is fourfold," etc., in order to show all forms of purification in that same context.
Therein, it is called *suddhi* because one is purified (*sujjhati*) by means of teaching and so forth, or because one is cleansed (*sodhīyati*).
Or purity: the fourfold virtue (*sīla*). Therefore, it was said: "Because of purification through confession," and so forth.

Here, by the mention of "confession" (*desanā*), both formal rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhāna*) and the admission of being a non-Bhikkhu for those whose roots [of the offense] have been severed are included.

For even in the case of those whose roots are severed, the Bhikkhu-virtue that was previously protected remains called "purified" by means of rehabilitation from the offense of a defeat (*pārājika*); consequently, their attainment of the Path (*magga*) also comes to pass.
It is a "legacy" (*dāya*) in the sense of that which is to be given; those who take it up are "heirs" (*dāyādā*).

Regarding the phrase "of the seven trainees" (*sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ*), it should be understood that even the noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) are included here, because their enjoyment of freedom from debt is subsumed under the enjoyment of the legacy.
The *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* is the discourse that proceeds with the words: "Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things," and so forth. In that [discourse]:
The meaning should be understood by bringing in the word *me* (of me) as follows: "May they not be my heirs to material things. For it is in this way that the meaning stated is established.
"Sharing with one who is conscientious" refers to the state of being mixed by means of the Dhamma and material gifts. The same principle applies here regarding "with one who is unconscientious.
By the statement, "Indeed, from the very beginning there is no such thing as an unconscientious person," there is a suspicion regarding those seen and unseen [to be unconscientious].
This shows that a name should not be given [to a pupil] except when there is a reason such as having seen or heard [of his qualities].

"Those who have become one's own burden" refers to the co-residents (saddhivihārikas) and others. "If he does not desist" means he does not desist from following wrong courses or from the enjoyment of requisites provided by the Dhamma.
The statement "there is no offense" refers to those who are shameless, in regard to requisites obtained according to the Dhamma and to formal acts (dhammakamma) performed according to the Dhamma.
It has been stated. For even those who consume requisites arising from such acts as defiling a family, or who perform illegal formal acts (*vaggakamma*), incur an offense.

Because it was said, "The use of requisites—whether according to the Dhamma or not the Dhamma—is to be understood by way of the requisites themselves," the aforementioned use by the conscientious [monks]...
It should be understood that this has been stated both by way of conditions and by way of single acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Dutthadosa-sikkhāpada*, it is said of two shameless persons who stand in the position of accuser and accused, even with reference to the enjoyment of the Dhamma:

"Live together, sharing a common enjoyment. This is because there is no contradiction in their mutual enjoyment of the Dhamma and material gifts (*dhammāmiṣa*). [This applies] only to those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjinam*).
For it is not permitted for one who lacks a sense of shame (alajjī) to share either of these two types of enjoyment with another.

"Enjoyment of the Dhamma" (dhammaparibhoga) should be understood as both the communal living described by such terms as "a single formal act and a single recitation," as well as the entire non-material enjoyment consisting of the granting and receiving of formal dependence (nissaya), and so forth.
This is because of the statement: "He who possesses a sense of shame (lajjī) is not to be dealt with according to an offense."
It should be understood that there is an offense for one who supports a shameless person. "The other as well" means even the conscientious one.

By this, it is shown that when a conscientious person supports a shameless person—whether out of a desire for gain such as praise and so forth, or out of a preoccupation with material things, or out of worldly affection—he indeed causes the Dispensation to disappear. Thus, [this applies] among householders and others.
“Supported by this, the shameless one, having gained strength and overcome those who are gentle, will before long cause the teaching to become contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.
By the statement, “The enjoyment of the Dhamma is also permissible there,” he shows that the enjoyment of the Dhamma is weightier than the enjoyment of material things;
therefore, it must be practiced with extreme avoidance of the shameless. [And] by the statement, “It is permissible to learn through support in the Dhamma,”...
Because the teaching is declining due to the prevalence of shamelessness, and because those who possess a sense of shame are insufficient,
it is indeed necessary to uphold the teaching by ordaining even shameless individuals as regular members to complete the quorum for the higher ordination and other rites,
by winning over some of the shameless through the enjoyment of the Dhamma and material gifts, and by restraining the rest of the shameless group.

However, some say: "Because it is stated that 'the text is what stands at the limit,' the enjoyment of the Dhamma consists only in the mastery of the texts, and not in [performing] a single legal act (*ekakamma*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is permissible to perform legal acts such as the Uposatha even together with those who are shameless; there is no offense.
This is not correct, for among the many enjoyments of the Dhamma, such as the single legal acts and so forth, even when performed with one who is shameless...

This is because, in this context, only the texts have been extracted by way of illustration in order to show the enjoyment of the Dhamma (dhammaparibhoga) appropriate for the state that must be practiced together [with them].
For it cannot be said that a procedure such as a single act (*ekakamma*) and so forth is not an enjoyment of the Dhamma;

since there is nothing whatsoever that is not included among the "non-material gifts of the Dhamma" (*dhammāmisa*) due to its lack of physical substance (*anāmisatta*). It is for this very reason that, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, within the discussion on the preservation of the Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisandhārakathā*), [it is stated]:...

“The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be explained; the Dhamma should be taught... [etc.]... the acts of rehabilitation, emergence from probation, penance, and temporary exclusion should be granted;
one who deserves admission should be admitted; one who deserves full ordination should be ordained... [etc.]...
this is called ‘the preservation of the Dhamma’”—thus, even the formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) and so forth are shown as categories of the Dhamma. Among those categories of the Dhamma:

When the Uposatha and other ceremonies are performed out of consideration for shameless monks—such as for the sake of completing the quorum—or when the study of the Dhamma or the formal acceptance of dependence (*nissaya*) is undertaken in their presence, this is called "the enjoyment of the Dhamma" (*dhammaparibhoga*), because it is both the Dhamma and an act of enjoyment.

It is not permissible to perform such acts without such conditions; for one who does so, it becomes the "enjoyment of the shameless" (*alajjiparibhoga*) and constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, that which [is done] toward a hundred shameless monks...

If one performs acts such as the formal act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and so forth, or supportive acts such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, or the granting of instruction and inquiry (*uggaha-paripucchā*), without regard for [the recipient's] suitability, that is merely the Dhamma itself, not its "use" (*paribhoga*). It is permissible to perform these for those who are suitable;

like the giving of material gifts (*āmisa*), there is no offense. However, even the granting of formal dependence (*nissaya*) or the granting of the thirteen permissions (*sammuti*) and so forth is not permissible, because they are causes for the enjoyment of the observance of duties and counter-duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*).

Furthermore, it is not permissible for one who is greatly shameless (*mahā-alajjī*)—one who acts contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya—to perform services such as the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for his co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and others, nor is it permissible to provide them with instruction or answers to their questions;
rather, this constitutes an offense (*āpatti*), and only an act of censure (*niggaha-kamma*) should be performed against him.
For this very reason, the support of the shameless is also prohibited. This is also evident from the avoidance of partaking in the gift of the Dhamma and material goods (*dhammāmisa*).
For indeed, the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct (*dummaṅku*) is intended;

and that [restraint] is for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of those who are well-behaved (*pesala*), for the establishment of the True Dharma, and for the support of the Vinaya, since the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) has this very purpose.

Therefore, whatever serves as a prop for those who are difficult to correct, or leads to the uncomfortable dwelling of those who are well-behaved, or to the decline of the True Dharma and so forth—all that, whether it be an object of use (*paribhoga*) or not an object of use, [is to be avoided].
It is not permissible to do so; those who act in this way cause the Dispensation to disappear and incur an offense.

Regarding the enjoyment of the Dhamma and material requisites, here the enjoyment of the Dhamma—such as the performance of formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—by those who are shameless leads to the uncomfortable dwelling and the decline of the true Dhamma for those who are virtuous, whereas the enjoyment of material requisites does not do so to that same extent.
For it is not merely through the enjoyment of the basic requisites by the shameless that the virtuous [are affected].

There is an uncomfortable dwelling and so forth through the enjoyment of the things already mentioned, whereas by avoiding those very things, there is a comfortable dwelling and so forth. For instance,
shameless individuals who have transgressed the training rules, having entered into the Uposatha and other ceremonies,
must be addressed by the bhikkhus with words such as, "You commit transgressions at the door of the body and the door of speech," and in accordance with the Vinaya.
Those who do not desist must be thoroughly restrained by means of such measures as banishment from the Saṅgha;
for if one does not act in this way but continues to live together with them, they remain indeed shameless, according to the saying: "Even a single shameless person makes a hundred shameless ones.
For if they were not thus restrained, they would increase strife and the like within the Saṅgha, thereby obstructing communal acts such as the Uposatha ceremony.
Having caused discomfort for those who are well-behaved, and gradually increasing their following like Devadatta, Vajjiputtaka, and others, they would—
by illustrating their own misconduct according to the Dhamma and Vinaya, and even by causing a schism in the Saṅgha—
cause the Dispensation to disappear before long; however, when they have been restrained through all possible means by being excluded from the Saṅgha and so forth...
There is no calamity. For it is said:
"Relying upon a person of immoral conduct, the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, the formal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed, and there is no concord...
[etc. ...But when those of immoral conduct have been restrained, all this calamity [ceases]."
"There is no [conflict], and thus the well-behaved bhikkhus dwell in comfort.

Therefore, it should be understood that the enjoyment of the Dhamma—beginning with formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—must be carried out with even greater seclusion from shamelessness than the enjoyment of material things; for it causes offenses and is the cause for the decline of the True Dhamma.
Furthermore, the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, and the formal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed. Thus...
This is also established by the fact that the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains the non-performance of Saṅgha formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) together with those who are shameless (*alajjī*);
likewise, in the discourse on the conduct of a monk whose gender has changed as he goes to a nunnery (*bhikkhunupassaya*), it says:
"They are pleasing, supportive, and modest; having offended them, one must not go elsewhere. If he goes..."
"She is not released from the offenses of crossing between villages, crossing a river, staying apart at night, or being in a group, nor from the offense of withdrawing...
[etc. ...because they are shameless and yet provide support; even so, it is permitted for her to abandon them and go elsewhere.
Thus, regarding the taking of a second companion and so forth among those who are shameless, heavy offenses such as crossing a river are permitted in order to avoid the offense of communal living.
It is understood that even more serious than that is the offense of living with one who is shameless, because it is the cause for the decline of the true Dhamma.
Indeed, teachers do not permit the transgression of a grave offense in order to avoid a minor offense or a situation where there is no offense;
likewise, in the commentary on the term "living together," it says: "By all persons who possess a sense of shame..."

"Because they must train together, it is called 'training together' (*samasikkhātā*). Here, since all those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjino*) dwell together in these matters such as formal acts (*kamma*), and not even one of them is seen outside of that [community], therefore, taking all of them together, this is what is called 'communal living' (*saṃvāso*).
In this way, it is shown that communal living—consisting of formal acts and so forth—is permissible only for those who possess a sense of shame.
If this is so, why is the shameless one (*alajjī*) not included among those who are not in communion (*asaṃvāsika*)?

This is not a contradiction, because those who are taken as completing the quorum for a formal act (*kamma*) that becomes invalid are specifically understood to be those who are "not in communion" due to having committed a defeat (*pārājika*) or other such offenses that render them unqualified (*apakatatta*).
However, there are also shameless ones who remain qualified (*pakatatta*); if they serve to complete the quorum and thus bring about the formal act, [the act is valid] solely on that account.
By acting through a course that leads to ruin, they become like those who have committed an offense, mutually incurring a similar transgression.
This is because for worldlings (*puthujjana*), both shamelessness and modesty are bound to specific moments of consciousness (*cittakkhaṇa*) and are not constant at all times.
For when a mind of intentional transgression arises, one who is shameless resolves with the thought, "I shall not do such a thing again."

They are indeed possessed of a sense of shame; however, among them, those who do not desist even when exhorted by the virtuous, but repeatedly transgress, are precisely those with whom one should not live together—not the others, because they have entered into the nature of shame.

For this reason as well, it was permitted that one should perform the Uposatha and other rites only after purifying oneself by excluding the shameless from the community of those with whom one must not live, so as to avoid them. Thus, [the Buddha said]: "Pārisuddhiṃ..."
By the words, “Venerable sirs, announce [any faults]; I shall recite the Pātimokkha,” and so forth, it is shown that it is improper to perform the Uposatha when the assembly is not pure.
Furthermore, by saying, “Whoever has an offense, let him reveal it...

[until] there is well-being,” the manner of performing the Uposatha is described as establishing even those who are shameless in the quality of shame. Then, [the question is asked]: “Are you pure in this matter...? and so forth.
In the passage, "Are you pure here, venerable sirs? and in the context of the purity-observance (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*), "I am pure, venerable sir;
may you remember me as pure," the purity of those performing the observance in this manner is thus revealed.

Furthermore, the procedure for the postponement of the observance ceremony for those who do not remain silent after being addressed is stated; [this applies] to those who in every way do not abandon the quality of moral shame (*lajjidhamma*).
The prohibition against granting or receiving formal dependence (*nissaya*) due to the unsuitability of co-residence,

as well as the performance of disciplinary acts such as censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) and the procedure for rendering one who is shameless and belongs to a faction— along with his retinue— unfit for co-residence by means of the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*),

have been explained. Therefore, according to the methods of the Suttas and the words of the Commentaries, whether they concern those who are regular members of the Saṅgha (*pakatatta*) or those who are not (*apakatatta*).
It must be concluded here that communal residence—such as performing formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—with all those who are shameless is not permitted;
for when they do so, there is indeed an offense, since all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were established solely for the purpose of restraining individuals who are difficult to manage.
For this very reason, at the Second Council, even though they were regular monks (*pakatatta*), the Vajjiputtakas, being shameless, were dealt with with great severity by the Elder Yasa and others.
They were separated from the Saṅgha through formal effort (*vāyāma*). For among them there were none who were *asamvāsika* (excluded from communion) due to a *pārājika* offense or the like;
this is because the ten grounds mentioned by them pertain to minor offenses (*lahukāpatti*).
"In his presence" means in the presence of the Elder Mahārakkhita. "A harsh leaf" refers to that which is known as a *khara* leaf.
The object is something resembling gold. When silver has been given by donors under a misunderstanding, it is not permissible for them to take it back again with the thought that it is their own;
nor is it permissible to give it [back] saying, "Take this forfeitable object. Thus he said, "Look at your cloth.
Even though he spoke thus, since there is no need for forfeiture—as in the case of a lost object—the offense must still be confessed.

For even when one is without mindfulness, if one takes that object with one's own hand—such as cloth or other items—and gives it saying, "I give this," then because the act of relinquishment is present, it is indeed a gift, just like giving something of great value while intending to give something of little value.

Furthermore, even if the recipient knows that the item is being given while they themselves are without mindfulness, there is no taking what is not given, because it has been given by the donors; therefore, [this does not constitute] money.

It is indeed an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). However, some say: "Such a thing does not exist; for that very reason it was said here, 'I see your rag'. That we do not accept; it should be investigated. 586.

"Of a single limit" (*ekaparicchedāni*) is said with reference to what may be an act (*kiriya*) and what may be a non-act (*akiriya*). Here, there are three factors: the nature of gold and silver, the state of being intended for oneself, and one of the acts such as taking up [the object].
The commentary on the training rule concerning money is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning trading with money: 587.
In the ninth [training rule], the fourfold objects subject to relinquishment, beginning with gold and silver (*jātarūpa*), are included here by the very term "money" (*rūpiya*).

He said: "The exchange of gold and silver. Regarding "the exchange of what has been accepted": this refers to the exchange of money (rūpiya) that has been accepted, whether by means of allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra) or unallowable terminology (akappiya-vohāra).
In the text, "ghanakaṭa" refers to bricks and so forth. As for the term "money" (rūpiya) in such passages as "gold-colored [coins] and so forth," although it refers exclusively to—
Although silver was not explicitly mentioned [in the preceding rule], it should nevertheless be understood as being included by the very term "money" (*rūpiya*).

It should be supplied [to the sense] that only pure monetary exchange is what is being discussed. Regarding the phrase "perceiving money as money," etc., there is a remainder of the text: "I shall explain the legal determination.
In the canonical text, the expression "perceiving money as money" is stated with reference to one's own property being given away by oneself.

"Exchanges for money" means [exchanging] what belongs to another. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. In that context, the term "non-monetary" (arūpiya) includes even the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

However, in the final triad, the application should be understood everywhere according to this principle: "If one perceives what is non-monetary as monetary and exchanges it for money, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
And in this triad, by the term "non-monetary," only a permissible object (kappiya-vatthu) is meant.
The object of the *dukkaṭa* offense was not included [in the list], because at the end it is stated: "there is no offense for the five together.

Nevertheless, even though the object of the *dukkaṭa* offense was not included, it is established by logical principle that a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs for one who exchanges an object of *dukkaṭa* for another object of *dukkaṭa*, or an object of *dukkaṭa* for a permissible (*kappiya*) object. And that [offense] pertains to the object of *dukkaṭa*.

Whether through a perception of it as such, a perception of it as not such, or through doubt, [the offense] still occurs even for one who exchanges [it], because this training rule (sikkhāpada) does not involve the mind (acittaka).
"Together with five" means together with five fellow-followers of the Dhamma (sahadhammika).

Now, regarding the meaning stated by the phrase "by means of an article involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu), or an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu)," etc., [the following is] the literal form in the Canon (pāḷi):
In order to show that even in the future [this rule] is obtainable by way of the same principle, the passage beginning with "For whoever this... was stated.
And here, because non-material goods exchanged for material goods—even if relinquished—are still unallowable (*akappiya*) for everyone, they do not constitute a forfeiture (*nissaggiya*);
rather, they must simply be relinquished so as to be used after having been relinquished. However, this [present case] is merely to be discarded.
The offense is indeed a *pācittiya* that must be confessed by means of an exchange;

therefore, the Blessed One did not state the triad beginning with, “If one perceives money as money and causes something not consisting of money to be purchased, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*,” because in all three cases, since what is being exchanged is not money, the designation *nissaggiya* would be inappropriate, as only money is to be forfeited (*nissajjitabba*). For it is only when money itself has been forfeited...
The procedure for dealing with monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others is shown in the Canon (*pāḷi*), but not for that which is non-material (*arūpiya*).

Therefore, it was stated here in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)—"This triad should be understood even though it was not mentioned"—solely for the purpose of showing the occurrence of a mere *pācittiya* offense, and not for the purpose of showing that the object (*vatthu*) is subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
For this very reason, regarding the fourfold set of bowls (*patta-catukka*), [it is said]: "It is not possible by any means to make it allowable..."

"‘To make’ and so forth was stated. This is our interpretation (*khanti*). Or, ‘of one’s own’ and so forth was stated in order to demonstrate how the third triad is established by means of the second triad’s method of conformity.

Herein, this is the intended meaning: because, just as when one exchanges one’s own non-monetary goods for another’s monetary goods, since the presence of monetary goods occurs at one end [of the transaction], it is called ‘trading in money.’"
Thus the second triad was stated [with the words] “it is likewise. In this way, there would also be a third triad to be stated regarding one who exchanges his own silver for another’s non-silver;
however, because that is established by the second triad alone through the commonality of the side of silver in both cases, it was not stated in the Pāḷi.
In that context, "on one side exclusively in the side of silver" means on one extreme limit within the side of silver.
Alternatively, there is the reading “on one side, with what is of a monetary nature.

Now, regarding the second triad, in order to show the classification of offenses when exchanging items that are the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) with items that are allowable (kappiya)—which constitute the meaning of the term “non-monetary” (arūpiya) in the phrase “with what is not of a monetary nature”—the passage beginning with “by means of an item that is the basis for an offense of wrong-doing” is commenced. By means of an item that is the basis for an offense of wrong-doing...

The phrase "the basis for an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭavatthu*) and so forth is stated in order to show that, even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the text (*pāḷi*), the meaning can be obtained through the method of reasoning (*naya*) when there is the possibility of exchange with something that is a basis for an offense of wrong-doing. In this context, "by this" refers to the training rule concerning trading in money;

and by that, he shows that there is also the absence of intention (*acittaka*) regarding the offense of wrong-doing. Regarding the phrase "except among those who share the same Dhamma" (*aññatra sahadhammikehi*): "among the five... [and so on].

It is stated because of the words, “there is no offense”; by that [statement], it establishes that the training rule concerning buying and selling is based solely on allowable things (*kappiyavatthu*).
The connection with the preceding context is: “this... was said with reference to [the exchange of] goods and the bartering of money.
*Iha* means in this training rule; *tattha* means in the training rule concerning buying and selling.

Having thus shown the classification of offenses regarding the exchange of money and so forth by means of an improper object (*dukkaṭavatthu*), the passage beginning with “But by means of a permissible object (*kappiyavatthu*)” is now commenced to show it by means of a permissible object as well.
In this context, “by that very [means]” refers to by means of a permissible object itself.
The phrase “having acquired money” is stated by way of the most extreme case; for one may also acquire even an improper object such as pearls and the like.
Even that which has been caused to be done by the five [types of persons] is likewise not permitted.

"Causes to be produced" means either producing it oneself by going there and saying, "Give this coin and so forth to the laborers and cause the seed to be produced," or causing it to be produced by commanding another.

It is called "greatly unallowable" (*mahā-akappiya*) because it is defiled from the very moment of the seed itself and because there is no other original owner; for he [the one who took it] was [seized] by thieves...
Even if it was recovered after being stolen, it is not permissible for anyone who knows [the circumstances].

For if it were permissible, the teachers would have said that what was stolen is permissible, just as in the case of reservoirs and the like. It cannot be made allowable by any means whatsoever—not by relinquishing it to the Saṅgha, nor by acts such as having thieves steal it back;
and this [object] remains in its original state, and because it is rooted in that [original act], [it remains impermissible].
This was said with reference to things existing in the form of *vatthumutta* (gold-dust) and so forth.
For it is impossible by any means to make even an article of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭavatthu*) or an article rooted therein into something allowable (*kappiya*) in that same form.

However, if that monk were to exchange that article of wrongdoing or that article of allowable property for money again, it would be possible to make other allowable items after having that money forfeited.
It should be understood as "it would be.

Regarding the phrase "he buys a bowl," it should be known that this includes having a monastery attendant or others buy it on one's behalf, such as by saying, "Go and buy a bowl from a smith's workshop for this amount of kahāpaṇas or the like.
For this very reason, in the commentary on the Rāja-sikkhāpada, [it says] "by so many..."

It is said: "If one says, 'Bring saffron robes for these kahāpaṇas,' or 'Prepare rice-gruel and so forth with this much,' whatever they bring for him is unallowable for all [monks]. Why? Because the kahāpaṇas have been handled.

By this statement, that which was called "without an instruction" (*anāṇattika*) regarding the training rule on trading in money (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra-sikkhāpada*) in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* is [refuted].
It does not agree. Not only does it not agree with this [commentary], but it also does not agree with the Canon (pāḷi).

For in the Canon, regarding the exchange of ghee, etc., for money that has been relinquished by means of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), etc., it says: "He should be told, 'Friend, please take note of this.
If he asks, 'What should be brought in exchange for this? he must not be told, 'Bring this or that. Rather, what is allowable (*kappiya*) should be pointed out: 'Ghee...'"
The phrase beginning with “or” was stated precisely to exclude the exchange of money. Even when one asks, “What should be brought for this money?
and is told, “Bring this,” it is understood—by virtue of the context—that the monk has been instructed by the command, “Bring this for this money.
Therefore, in order to avoid that exchange of money, one should not say, “This or that.”

A refusal was made with the words "Bring it," yet even in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), it is not stated that "one points out [the goods] to a preparer of what is allowable" (*kappiyakāraka*).

However, in the training rule concerning buying and selling (*kayavikkaya-sikkhāpada*), it is stated accordingly; therefore, this case involving a blanket (*sāṇattika*) should be understood as being buying and selling without an instruction (*anāṇattika*).
"Because the price has not been relinquished" means that the price by which the bowl was purchased must be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Because it has not been relinquished, this shows that only the money itself must be relinquished, and not the non-monetary items derived from it.

For if he were to exchange that money for other money, then after having him relinquish that according to the method set forth in the training rule on trading in money, he would be permitted to use the remainder. By the phrase, "because the original capital was not accepted,"...
This demonstrates that the root [offense] pertains to what belongs to a householder, and by that very fact, shows that the offense of trading in money does not arise for what belongs to a bowl.

For the fault of trading in money occurs only with respect to what belongs to the five classes of fellow-practitioners (*sahadhammika*). In that regard, there is a *pācittiya* offense for one's own property, whereas in the other case, there is a *dukkaṭa*.
"Having relinquished" (*nissajjitvā*) is said in the sense of giving, not in the sense of a formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*). Therefore, it is said: "having filled it with ghee."
The two factors here are: either the state of being silver in the wealth with which one exchanges it, or its state as either the object exchanged or that by which it is exchanged.
The commentary on the training rule concerning trading in silver is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Buying and Selling (Kayavikkaya-sikkhāpada) 593–5.
Regarding the tenth rule, in the Pāḷi: "Know it" (*jānāhi*) means "examine it right now"; the intention is that this cannot be discarded later.
"By this one" refers to the monk who is giving; "this" refers to what is being returned by the other party. As for the remaining kinsmen...
In order to show that even the state of being such [a field] can arise from the misappropriation of what was given in faith (*saddhādeyya*), it is said: "But [if one takes] one's mother or father.

Regarding the phrase "it is not possible to reject that," here, just as when one gives money to laborers and they dig on ownerless land to produce iron seed, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) even though the goods were taken from those who were paid for their labor.
Some say that it is the same here [in this case] as well, but that is not correct. For an iron seedling produced by digging up ownerless ground belongs to the laborers;

and for one who gives silver to them for that purpose, there is indeed a transaction involving silver, just like the buying and selling of dye-bark and so forth through an improper transaction—even though such an item is the property of another.
In this case, regarding such matters as washing clothes and so forth, there is no [offense]; therefore, the *pācittiya* here must be understood solely by the authority of the Commentary.
597. Regarding the phrase "gives thinking, 'There will be merit'":
if a monk, even though he knows his own goods are of little value, says without mentioning it, "Examine them right now and take them; do not have regrets later," and the other person—

And if one, unaware of the high value of what is being given to oneself, gives it away saying, "Whether less or more, let it be yours alone," and then departs—as in the case of Upananda’s taking of the wanderer’s robe—there is no offense for the bhikkhu.

However, if the donor later returns with the perception that it was his own and feels regret, he should be given back whatever was taken in excess. Whichever item one exchanges for another, [that is the basis for the offense].
The three factors here are: that both of them are allowable things, that it is contrary to the Dhamma, and that it results in buying and selling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Silk, is completed.
3. The Chapter on Alms Bowls (Patta-vagga) 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Alms Bowls (Patta-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 602.
In the first [training rule] of the third chapter, "thirteen and a half palas" means measured at thirteen and a half palas by the Magadhan standard of weight.
Some say this was said with reference to one who takes water, and likewise with reference to one who takes a limited amount of barley, beans, and so forth.
However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla states: "A natural four-handfuls make a *kuḍuva*; four *kuḍuva*s make a *nāḷi*;
sixteen *nāḷi*s of that [measure] make a *doṇa*; and they say that this [Magadhan *doṇa*] is twelve *nāḷi*s by the Magadhan *nāḷi* measure."
It has been stated. "The Tamil *nāḷi*" is said with reference to the ancient *nāḷi*. That consists of eight *kuḍuva*s by means of four-fistful *kuḍuva*s;
two such *nāḷi*s take the measure of one Magadha *nāḷi*. However, the ancients say, "The Sinhalese *nāḷi* takes three *nāḷi*s";
according to their opinion, the Magadha *nāḷi* is equal to the four-*kuḍuva* *nāḷi* currently in use.
Four *nāḷikas* of the Damila measure constitute one; from that, half of a Magadha *nāḷika* plus what is reckoned as a Damila *nāḷika* is called a *pattha*.
And by this, it accords with the canonical statement: "A small bowl is one that takes a *pattha* of cooked rice.
This is also [confirmed] by worldly people:
“‘Worldly’ and ‘Māgadha’—these two measures have been declared;
the worldly is sixteen *palas*, while the Māgadha is considered double that.
Thus it is shown that in the world, the Magadha *nāḷi* is double the size of the ordinary *nāḷi*; and when understood in this way, [the measure] of the small bowl...

And she became one who took only as much alms-food as was necessary for her sustenance. For it is not possible to sustain oneself by seeking almsfood with a bowl that has less than eight *kuḍuva* measures of rice;
even if one were to seek out a large quantity of food, it would not suffice. For this very reason, it is said in the commentary on the Verañjā Chapter:
"A *pattha* measure is the amount of a single *nāḷi*, which is sufficient for the sustenance of one man. And it is also said: 'This *pattha* of rice is not enough...'"
It is stated, "for two," and there is the tradition that "it suffices for two or three for each person"; therefore, it should be understood here according to the method explained [in those sources].

Regarding the phrase "proportionate to the mouthful of rice" (*ālopa*): since it is stated in the *Brahmāyu Sutta-aṭṭhakathā* that "the measure of a condiment (*byañjana*) is indeed a fourth part of the rice," it should be understood that a condiment proportionate to the mouthful is precisely a fourth part of the rice. [The phrase] "only following the course of the rice" means...
The meaning is that they would have the habit of entering into the very midst of the rice, not seeking out their own space.
"In mere names" means in mere names such as "the middle bowl," "the middle-small bowl," and so forth. 607–8.
"In each instance of the mouthful" means in each instance of the practice of swallowing after the final [portion] has been taken; "in each morsel" means in each morsel.
The meaning: "Having made" means having completed the process of cooking. "I will set it aside after cooking" is said with reference to the dark-colored (black) variety of cooked rice.
"Hollow" refers to the hollow space two finger-breadths below the rim of the mouth. The rest is exactly according to the method explained in the first *kathina* [rule].
The commentary on the bowl training rule (*patta-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Fewer than Five Repairs (Ūnapañcabandhana-sikkhāpada) 609–613.
Regarding the second [training rule], the remainder of the Pāḷi is: "I shall satisfy those bhikkhus with my bowl.

By the term "without a bowl" (apatto), it also indicates the relinquishing of the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Even in the case of a bowl with fewer than five repairs, the determination is as it is for a bowl that is not fully baked.

It does not grow. Because it is stated, “or with a triple patch,” it is permissible to cover a hole in an iron bowl with allowable metals such as copper, bronze, and so forth. For this very reason, it is said, “with a metal disk.

In this training rule, it should be understood that there is an offense even for one who requests an allowable bowl that is not black in color. Regarding an established bowl, it must have fewer than five repairs.
The four factors here are: being intended for oneself, not having made a formal request, and obtaining it by means of that [request].
The commentary on the training rule concerning less than five-fold binding is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Medicines.

618–621. In the third [case], after the Elder Pilindavaccha had first refused, saying, "Great King, a monastery attendant (ārāmika) has not been permitted by the Blessed One," he later consented to the taking of slaves even under the name of "monastery attendants" for individuals, with the words, "I allow you, monks, a monastery attendant.
Consequently, fields, land, and so forth were accepted even through formal transactions (kappiyavohāra).
It is understood that it is not permissible to accept [land] for individuals, as this has not been authorized in that manner.

For when it is stated, “He abstains from accepting fields and lands,” and so forth, since the acceptance of one [type of property] for an individual has been prohibited, the fact that the others likewise must not be accepted for individuals is established by implication. And as for what was done by the Elder Pilindavaccha for the family of donors...

The creation of a grass hut by means of a golden garland for the sake of a girl should be understood as having been done because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, there is no offense for one possessing psychic power within the domain of psychic power," and thus it does not constitute the gathering of families and so forth.

However, some say that since those whose taints are destroyed lack the desire for gain, there is no corruption of livelihood even when gathering families; that is not correct, for even those whose taints are destroyed...
Because one must avoid alms-food and other requisites that are causes for the ruin of one’s livelihood. For it was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“I would not break my livelihood, even at the cost of giving up my life. And the Blessed One said: “Food sung to with verses is not to be eaten by me,” and so forth. 622.
*Uggahitaka* means what has been taken up by oneself for the purpose of consumption. *Sayaṃ karoti* means he makes it himself by cooking it.
“Before the meal” means that it is permissible only on that same day before the meal, because it was received with its physical basis intact.
“Self-made” refers to what is made by boiling milk and butter. “Only non-material” is said with reference to that which is before the meal on that same day.

As for the question, “Why does cooking for oneself not constitute a *sāmaṇerapāka* (offense of cooking for oneself) for one who eats today what was self-made and non-material? he says: “While heating the butter,” and so forth.
"By those already received" is said with reference to milk and curd. The construction is: "What is made from what has been received should be applied as an ointment and so forth.
"In the same manner" is said with reference to an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiyāpatti*). "In the case of unallowable meat-ghee" refers to the ghee of elephants and other such animals.

"But here," however, means that there is a distinction regarding butter. "Washed is allowable" means that even receiving washed [butter] is not allowed; otherwise, it would be considered "received with its source" (*savatthuka*), according to the intention of the Elders.
However, because the substance [of the curd] has been separated from the Mahāsivatthera, it is not considered "received with a physical basis" merely by being joined with lumps of curd and so forth;

therefore, the intention is that they received only what had been extracted from the buttermilk, and having washed it or cooked it, they consumed it as something entirely free of meat (nirāmisam), but they did not consume it at an improper time together with the lumps of curd and such. Thus he said:
“Therefore, for one consuming butter... [etc] ...it is not called ‘received with its base still attached.
In this context, the meaning is that even if one has received it while it was unwashed, when consuming that butter, one should remove the curds and so forth before eating it.
“It will go to destruction” means it becomes non-material; therefore, the meaning is that it is permissible even at an improper time. “To this extent” means:

"By even a mere trace clinging to fresh butter"—that is, by that which has not yet received the designation "curd" and so forth, being still unseparated; the meaning is "by [butter] that is not yet curd.
By this, he shows that what is cooked together with curd and other substances already accepted separately falls under the category of "what is accepted with its own base" (*savatthuka-paṭiggahita*).
"In that too" means even when it has become free from meat. However, for those who are scrupulous, the intention regarding the acceptance is as follows: [The text continues: ...in the acceptance...
As long as the curd and other ingredients have not mixed their flavors with the rice, it is not considered "cooked by oneself" (*sāmaṃpakka*), just like a lump of sugar taken together with the meal.
However, that [curd] must be washed before being cooked; otherwise, at the moment of cooking, because its flavor has mixed with the curd-lumps and such being cooked, it becomes "cooked by oneself.
Once those [ingredients] are exhausted, it remains "cooked by oneself" only. Therefore, it must be entirely free from meat.
"It must be cooked. For that very reason, the cause is stated as "because it was cooked together with the food-stuff (*āmisa*).

Herein, this is the analysis: in the absence of being accepted with a physical basis (*savatthuka*), when a monk has cooked [the food] together with the food-stuff, either the fault of self-cooking (*sayaṃpāka*) or the state of being for the time being (*yāvakālika*) might be suspected. Among these, first, the fault of self-cooking does not apply here.
It is possible because of the seven-day time limit. For whatever food, such as curd and so forth, is contained therein, that has indeed perished.

Now, if one suspects that [the medicine] might become "cooked with its own base" (savatthukapakka) because it was cooked together with the lumps of curd and other items received [as alms], then the reason should be stated as "because it was received together with the food," and not "because it was cooked."
And thus, the opinion of the "Half-Elders" (Upaḍḍhattherā) alone would have to be accepted.

In that case, even food prepared by novices and others would be considered "only for the time being" (*yāvakālika*), just like ghee and so forth made by those not fully ordained using milk and other ingredients they have received;
however, this is not tenable, because butter and other items obtained through alms-round may come into contact with curdled milk (*takkā*) and other types of raw meat (*āmisa*).
Because it would entail the consequence that [the food] must not be consumed. For there is no rule stating that householders only pour [food] into bowls after they have washed or cleaned them;
moreover, this contradicts the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Just as rice grains and so forth that have fallen there do not cook, in the same way...
having cooked it again, he gives it; by the same method as before, it is permissible for seven days."
Therefore, here, not even the sign for the arising of remorse is seen for those who are scrupulous. And just as in this case, so too the sign is not seen for the statement:
"A conscientious novice may release the cooking of meat by having it melted over the fire in such a way that the fallen grains of rice and so forth do not cook... [and so on] ...it is allowable. If—
For if this were stated for the purpose of avoiding contact with what is only for a limited time (*yāvakālika*), one would have to act accordingly oneself;
furthermore, the suspicion of contact with foodstuffs (*āmisa*) such as ghee given by householders would not be dispelled.
Indeed, householders do not melt [the butter] in this way, remove the rice and so forth, and then cook it again; rather, they cook the milk and so forth together with the medicinal ingredients.
Having added it, just as milk and such things go to exhaustion, so too cooked medicine, oil, and the like given by others would be only *yāvakālika* (permissible for the duration of the day);
yet even that is not appropriate for the purpose of making curd and so forth, because it is stated that "having cooked it again, one gives it.
Therefore, without harboring scruples regarding the opinion of the Elder Mahāsiva, even butter that has not been washed may be used on that very day or on subsequent days.
It is permissible to cook ghee and so forth mixed with rice and other ingredients by oneself, having first melted them in the fire and strained them,
and then to cook them again for the purpose of making buttermilk and the like.

In that case, even though it exists at the moment of cooking, because the *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed within the same day) has already had its flavors blended (*sambhinnarasa*), it is not subject to the formal designation [of being *yāvakālika*].
One must reach the conclusion that even food accepted with a physical basis (*savatthuka*) or accepted beforehand (*purepaṭiggahita*) is not subject to formal designation (*abbohārika*).
For this very reason it was said: "Up to this point, it is not called 'accepted with a physical basis'.

However, when a monk or others mix clarified butter (*navanīta*) and so forth with milk or other edible foods (*āmisa*) that were accepted separately, and [prepare] medicine such as cooked oil (*pakkatelādi*), [it is permissible].
It is counted as having been received with a physical basis (*savatthuka*), because there is no absence of the designation [of "time-bound"] for that which has entered into it.

However, when milk and so forth—which were not previously received among the medicines—have been added to oil that was cooked [by non-ordained persons], even though it was cooked by those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) and even though it was received with a physical basis, it does not constitute storage (*sannidhi*); therein, the milk and so forth that were added [are likewise not considered stored].
At that moment, because it has been received previously, it falls under the offense of *sambhinnarasa* (mixed flavors).

However, if it has not yet been received, or if even in other substances such as cooked oil and so forth, the flavor of raw meat (*āmisa-rasa*) is still discernible, it should be understood that it remains strictly *yāvakālika* (permissible only until the same day).
"Having taken" means having taken it oneself.
"Having strained and taken" means having strained it for the purpose of removing the rice grains and so forth, and having cooked it again for the purpose of removing the whey and so forth;
this is the meaning. "With medicines kept after having been received" refers to those received for more than seven days;
by this, he shows that even ghee and other substances mixed with them do not become [forbidden] if they were received for more than seven days. "At the time of the *vaddali* festival."
"At the time of the rains" means at a time when there is no sunlight.
"Because it has been produced" means because it has been separated from the category of *yāvakālika* (food for the duration of a day);

by this, he shows both the absence of the status of *yāvakālika* in oil by its very nature, and the monk's admission of the status of *yāvakālika* through his acceptance of it as having a physical basis (*savatthuka*). "Both" refers to that which was made by himself and that which was made by others.
623. [The commentator] says, "excepting human beings," because this is an illustration specifically of the grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Mixed" means strained. "Three offenses of wrong-doing" is said with reference to the three *dukkaṭas* incurred with every swallow.
Although [the act of] receiving, cooking, straining, and so forth at an improper time is for the purpose of consumption, [it is still an offense].

Although no offense is mentioned in the Canon (Pāḷi) or the Commentary regarding previous applications, nevertheless, an offense must certainly exist here because one is doing what has been prohibited,
just as in the case of accepting food at an improper time or food allowed for the watch of the night for the sake of nourishment.
This is because the dregs of a cooked medicinal oil into which milk and such have been added fall into the category of "solid food" (āmisagatika), and therefore, together with that—
It is not permissible for a bhikkhu to accept oil, nor to cook it. Therefore it was said: “He is scrupulous as if regarding cooked oil and gruel.
If [they ask], “If it is not permissible because it has been cooked together with fat, why is this not permissible?
they say: “Venerable sir... it is permissible. Because of excessive scrupulousness, the Elder said: “This too, friend...”
"It is not permissible," he said. Having observed that fat was permitted solely for the purpose of curing disease, he later accepted it, saying, "Very well.
Regarding the phrase "by honey-bees called *madhukarīs*," this is a qualification of only two types of small bees.
Some say that "madhukārikā" refers to the *madhukarī* bee;
others, however, say that there are three species of honey-bees including those. "Bumblebees" (*bhamara-makkhikā*) are large *paṭalaka* bees.
"Resembling slime" means it has become thickened due to being dried or cooked. "The other" refers to thin honey.

“Taking sugar-cane juice as an example” indicates that even the sap extracted from sugar-cane is to be used for seven days, because it is stated in the Pāḷi in general terms as “produced from sugar-cane.
However, what is stated in the Suttanta-aṭṭhakathā—“If it is sugar-cane, it is to be used as long as the day; if it is sugar-cane juice, it is to be used for a watch of the night;
if it is molasses, it is to be used for seven days; if it is the skin, it is to be used for life”—[is explained as follows].

It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the fact that mango juice and other such substances become "time-bound for a watch" (*yāmakālika*) due to being mixed [with other substances];

however, because it is not a statement of the Vinaya, that [specific rule] is not authoritative. For this very reason, it is said: "by means of unstrained mango juice received before the meal," and so forth.

Only that which is free from meat is permitted there, because anything "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*) that has entered into it is not subject to formal censure; this applies to sugar as well.
It is said that even though dregs (*kasaṭa*) are present there, because they have been cooked and dried, they partake of the status of being "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*).
For if they were "only for the time being" (*yāvakālika*), then due to having been cooked by oneself, they would be unfit for consumption even before midday.

The phrase "because it was received with its substrate" (*savatthuka-paṭiggahitattā*) is said with reference to the dregs remaining in the sugarcane juice after it has become crushed and broken up; and by that [phrase], it refers to what has not yet been strained.
This shows that what has not been formally accepted is permissible for seven days when prepared by those who are not fully ordained.
"Burnt sugarcane treacle" refers to that made by heating sugarcane over a fire. "Pounded sugarcane treacle" refers to that which has been cut into small pieces, pounded, pressed, and cooked.
"Even though that dregs exist there, they lose their status as 'yāvakālika' (food for the day) at the time of ripening"; thus he said, "that is appropriate.
"Made with cold water" means it was made by crushing madhuka flowers with cold water, straining them, and cooking them;
some say it was made without crushing them, but no reason for this is seen there. "Cream of milk" means the froth of milk. *Madhukapuppha* (madhuka flower).
The passage beginning with "pana" (but) is commenced in order to show the basis for the fermentation of craving even in that which exists as a substance for the time-being (*yāvakālika*).

"All of them" refers to the five [medicines], such as ghee and so forth. To resolve the objection—namely, "Why must these, while performing the function of nutriment, be consumed in this specific way?"—the author presents the specific instruction regarding medicine;
and in connection with that, all those specific items are treated together.
To show this, it is said: "It is sevenfold," and so forth. Because they are medicines in their natural state (*apakati-bhesajja*), they are "loathsome" (*vikaṭa*);

because they are repulsive, and because they are great poisons due to their capacity to carry [the venom], they are "great loathsome things" (*mahāvikaṭa*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "ordination, etc.," items such as the *gaṇa-aṅgaṇa* (the communal bowl) and sandals are included.
"He resolves" (*adhiṭṭheti*) means he generates the thought: "This is for external use"; thus, by way of having no expectation regarding its use, [he resolves].

The intention is that one relinquishes the acceptance [of the food]. Thus, even in the case of other "timely" (kālika) foods, when there is a restriction made with a pure mind—due to a lack of desire to consume them—for the purpose of external use, the acceptance is relinquished; this too should be understood as a distinct reason for relinquishing acceptance.
625. Regarding the passage, "If two... it is not allowable," the text here has been omitted; however, the text should be understood in this way:
“If what belongs to two people has been accepted by one and not yet divided, there is no offense for either of them after seven days have passed;
however, it is not permitted to consume it. For otherwise, even the application of the words would not be included [in the formal definition].
It is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that “this very reading is also shown in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. For both...

“Non-offense” is stated because [the rule] has not been analyzed. “But it is not permissible to consume it,” this is stated on account of the statement: “It may be consumed as stored for a maximum of seven days.

By the phrase “because it was relinquished by the one who received it,” he shows that the word “relinquishes” is used here with reference to giving to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*). [Regarding] the fully ordained...
In the case of an object given without expectation, although the act of receiving has not ceased, the state of being one's own property has indeed ceased;

therefore, there is no offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). An offense of relinquishment occurs due to these two causes—namely, the fact that it was received by oneself and the fact that it became one's own property—not by either one alone.
However, in the case of giving to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) without expectation, both of these [conditions] are absent.
One relinquishes; here, "use" (paribhoga) is permissible, because in a gift given with expectation, the characteristic of giving (*dānalakkhaṇa*) is absent.
Furthermore, it should be understood that under this scriptural term "he gives away" (*vissajjeti*), even discarding without expectation—without having given it to anyone—is included.
And the phrase "having given without expectation" is stated solely for the purpose of showing the procedure for relinquishing after receiving. Regarding the receiving:
For once it has been relinquished, its subsequent use after being received again will be permissible;

and that relinquishment occurs through the abandonment of one's own proprietary claim over the object. By this it is established that when there is an expectation of consuming the object, what is called "the giving away of what was received" does not exist as a separate act.
Otherwise, [it would follow that] even while one is indifferent to receiving, one would be receiving...

It might be said: "Having relinquished it, he receives it again and eats it. By the phrase "because it was not [previously] received," it is shown that even if something belonging to one person has been received by another, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
The word "thus" refers to the state of having been relinquished with a pure mind, without forming the expectation, "I shall take it again."

The phrase "for the purpose of showing there is no offense for one who uses [it]" means the intention is to show that there is no offense regarding the *pācittiya* and other offenses rooted in the *nissaggiya*.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of showing there is no offense in the act of using," the intention here is to show that there is no offense concerning the *dukkaṭa* mentioned in relation to physical use and so forth of what was obtained after having been relinquished (*nissaṭṭha*). [This applies to] the state of ghee and other substances having been accepted.
"Belonging to oneself" and "exceeding seven days"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning medicine is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*).
628. On the fourth [fortnight], on the full moon day of Jeṭṭha and Mūla... [etc. ...it is stated that the "preparatory period" (*karaṇakkhetta*) applies even to the first half-month.

This was stated with the understanding that the phrase "having made it, it should be worn" means that having made it either in the first or the second half-month, it must be worn only in the latter month;
for it is stated as an offense specifically regarding the wearing [of the robe].
As for what is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “The last month of the hot season is the field for seeking [robes];
the last half-month is also the field for making and wearing them,” that was said with the understanding that they must be made and worn within that very same half-month.
When the meaning is taken according to the method explained here, there is no contradiction.

“The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for breaking the rule” was said with reference to those who have not previously given a rain-cloth (vassikasāṭikā). Therefore he said, “Those people,” and so forth.
Those called “givers of rain-cloths by nature” are those who give them every year without having invited either the Saṅgha or themselves [to accept the invitation].
630. By the phrase “he receives a six-month exemption,” it is indicated that even during the rainy season, he receives an exemption until the final day of the rains retreat.
The expression “one month” is stated by counting together with the final *uposatha* of the winter season; for on that very *uposatha* day, that original robe must be made, otherwise—
Regarding "from forfeiture": by way of one day, two days, and so forth... "both obtained and finished"—herein, the meaning should be understood as follows:

[the robe-cloth] is both obtained and finished when the commencement of the rains retreat is one day away; or when it is two days away... or ten days away; or when it is obtained and finished within the rains retreat itself.

In this regard, if a *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-season robe) is obtained on the full moon of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī and is finished on that very same day by means of the permissible methods of dyeing,
it is said to be "both obtained and finished one day before the commencement of the rains retreat.
By this same method, if it is obtained on the sixth day of the bright fortnight and finished [on that same day], it is [obtained] ten days before...
It is said: "Obtained and finished during the entry into the rains. From the full moon of the first month of Kattika until that same full moon, it is said: "Obtained and finished within the rains.
After the full moon of the first month of Kattika, as long as the robe season has not yet elapsed, even if one has not formally determined [the robe], it is still considered obtained and finished.
The intention is that it is permissible to set it aside.

And here, although it is stated without qualification that "it must be formally determined within that very ten-day period," if one obtains [the robe] before the rains retreat when the commencement of the rains (vassūpanāyikā) has not yet arrived by one or two days, etc., one may keep it without exceeding the ten-day limit by means of those [extra] days.
Starting from the day of entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*), one should determine [the robe] only when it has arrived within the designated field (*adhiṭṭhāna-khetta*);
however, even if it were finished before that time, it should not be determined if it exceeds ten days, because that is not a field for determination.
Such a robe, however, should be determined on the very day of entering the rains residence; for if one does not determine it, at the rising of the dawn...
It is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). If one asks, "What is the purpose of the phrase 'when ten days have not yet elapsed'?
