It is stated for the sake of showing that if the robe is finished even before the ten days [of the *kathina* period] have passed, it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) on the very day of the entry into the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*).
For this very reason, it says: "If the ten days have elapsed, it must be determined on that very day."

"The meaning is: 'If ten days remain, one must not let the robe season pass' means that if ten days remain within the three-month period—that is, from the seventh day until the full moon of Kattika, when nine days remain before the end of the robe season—whatever [robes] are obtained then, and whatever is finished [made], one must not let the robe season pass.
For it is said: 'When one month of the hot season remains, a monk should seek out a rainy-season robe.'"

Having stated that the field for seeking [robes] is thus, because it is said, "One should determine the rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) for the four months of the rains," it is established that even if one has made [the robe],
it must not remain undetermined for even a month; and since what is not made does not count as a rain-cloak,
and the failure to make it is due to some deficiency rather than negligence, therefore, on account of its not being made during the four months...

One obtains this exemption; however, when it has been determined within the designated field (*adhiṭṭhānakkhetta*), and not yet made [into a robe], one obtains exemption by means of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) regarding the ten-day limit during the robe-making season.
This is the meaning obtained here. "Why? is a question for the reason according to one's own judgment.
"Therefore" is because of the statement that the rain-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) must be determined only during the rains. The Sutta says: "One should determine the three robes."
In this context, this has been cited specifically to establish the absence of a fixed time limit for the remaining robes; for there is no other purpose for it here.

By the statement from the Kurundi commentary beginning with "When should it be determined?", it refutes the idea that "it may be determined at any time whatsoever," and instead demonstrates that the determination must be made within ten days. Regarding the phrase "one whose robe has been cut" (*acchinnacīvarassa*) and so forth in the Canon:
this refers to one whose remaining robes have been cut or whose remaining robes have been lost. For these...
It is stated that there is no offense regarding the seeking and wearing [of robes] at an improper time. For that very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:

"There is no offense for one who wears [a robe] due to an emergency—thinking 'thieves are carrying off my unworn robe,' whether the robe has been stolen or lost—or for those who are insane, and so forth.
However, here in the *Samantapāsādikā*, this non-offense regarding the forfeiture is [derived] from the *Pāḷi*.

It should be understood that this was stated—"of one whose robes have been stolen," and so forth—in order to show the non-offense for a naked person bathing who incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense [for not bathing], rather than to show that "one succeeds by oneself" without demonstrating this [latter point]. For this non-offense does not apply if it is not stated that one succeeds [by oneself].
[The factors are: the robe being designated for oneself, seeking it at an improper time, and the acquisition of it through that [seeking].
These, then, are the three factors for the offense of seeking [robes]. For the offense of wearing [a robe], however, there are four factors:
possessing a robe, the absence of an emergency, the [robe] being one's own rainy-season garment, and wearing it at an improper time.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the rainy-season garment is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Taking Away of Robes (Cīvaraacchindana-sikkhāpada) 631.

Regarding the fifth [offense], in the phrase "whatever... he takes away" (*acchindīti*), one should connect it by supplying the following: "Whatever robe I gave you, I gave it with the perception that 'it will go away with me,' and not otherwise; yet, being angry, he took it away. Thus it should be applied. 633. "One *dukkaṭa*":
If he is commanded and necessarily takes it away, there is only a *pācittiya* at the moment of the command.
If he does not take it away, it should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at that very moment. Regarding "many offenses by a single utterance":

if one who has been commanded takes [the robe] away without obstruction, then at the very moment of the command, there are offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the number of items, because the offense is incurred at the very moment the action is performed;
however, the robe itself becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) only when it has actually been taken away.
...it occurs. If he does not take it away, it should be understood that there is only one *dukkaṭa* at the moment of the command.
In this way, the method should be known for other similar cases as well. 635.
"He will take up the preceptorship" indicates the giving [of the candidate] while he is a novice; and by that, having given him while he was a novice, at the time of his full ordination—
It indicates that even for one who seizes [the robe], it is a *pācittiya*. The phrase "having given a robe to a bhikkhu himself" is stated by way of the highest limit (*ukkaṭṭha-vasena*).
However, it is permissible to have it brought back; this is stated because, as long as the formal act (*kamma*) has not been performed, it is similar to a wage (*bhata*).

[The factors are: the robe being of the lowest allowable size and fit for assignment (*vikappanupaga*), having been given by oneself, the perception that it is one's own, the person being fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the seizing or causing to seize out of anger.
These are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the taking away of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting by means of a thread.
636. Regarding the sixth [offense], the *vītaṭṭhāna* is the name for that square wooden frame upon which they wrap [the cloth].
That by means of which they beat it after inserting the thread crosswise, thereby bringing the cloth to a state of density, is called the *vema*.

By the phrase "in the other case, likewise there is a *dukkaṭa*," it is shown that from the time one begins to weave until the aforementioned limit is reached, there is indeed a *dukkaṭa*, but not before that during the preliminary efforts of weaving.

Regarding the instruction "one should resolve upon it while it is still stationary": once it has been resolved upon a single time, the cloth thereafter remains within the state of having been resolved upon;

there is no further need for the act of resolving. However, if in the meantime the cloth is separated into distinct, delimited portions by setting aside the fringes, it should be understood that each portion must be resolved upon individually. And in this context, [the rule concerns] allowable thread.

Having taken [the cloth], there is no offense for one who causes an unwholesome weaver (*akappiya-tantavāya*) to weave—even if he is not invited by a stranger—by means of such indirect phrases as, "There is thread, but there is no weaver," and so forth.
For this very reason, the commentary on the *Mātikā* explains the word "should cause to be woven" (*vāyāpeyya*) with the meaning:
"He should cause it to be woven by means of an unwholesome request, saying, 'Friend, please weave a robe for me. Thus speaking to an unwholesome weaver...
"Causes to be woven" means nothing other than that. 640.
Regarding "there is no offense for [the purpose of] sewing a robe," and so forth, they say that there is no offense by virtue of this very training rule;

however, because it was requested for something not yet made, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). [The factors are: the cloth being unallowable, it being designated for oneself, and the request for an unallowable weaving by an unallowable weaver.
"Causing to weave": these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning verbal intimation is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Great Weaver.
642. In the seventh [offense], the phrase "should give even a little" is a demonstration of a variation in the application; however, giving (*dāna*) is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) here.
For this very reason, it is stated in its analysis (*vibhaṅga*): "even so much as reciting the Dhamma. The rest here is self-evident.
It consists in approaching weavers who are unrelated and have not been invited and making a formal request (*vikappa*), regarding a robe.
The four factors here are: addressing oneself, the increase of the Sutta by his word, and the acquisition of the robe-cloth.
The commentary on the Mahāpesakāra-sikkhāpada is finished.
8. Commentary on the Acceka-cīvara-sikkhāpada.
646. Regarding the eighth [offense], it is said, "starting from the sixth," etc., because the robe-time arises on the eleventh dawn after the robe has been obtained.

And because it is stated as "not yet ten days having elapsed," even if ten dawns have arisen starting from the fifth day before the full moon, the robe does not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Together with the full moon day, there are eleven days.
"Are obtained": by this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), only this much is permitted;

it shows that from the sixth [day] onwards, all robes that arise do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) until the end of the robe-season, solely by virtue of the first *kathina* training rule.
650. Now, the specific exemptions regarding the various robes as they are obtained through the first *kathina* and other training rules—
Showing this by combining [the cases] together right here, he said, "Of extra robes," and so forth.
The reading, "When the Kathina has not been spread, it is one month plus eleven days;
when the Kathina has been spread, it is five months plus eleven days," is the one that accords with the Pāḷi. However, some say, "One month plus ten days; five months plus ten days."
They say that it must be recited [in the Suttavibhaṅga], but that is not correct, because otherwise it would have to be stated as "nine days remaining.
Furthermore, regarding the statement here in both the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Granted, this is already established by the rule 'an extra robe may be kept for ten days at most';
nevertheless, the training rule was established by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), demonstrating a meaning as if it were something new."

They write this down, but that is a scribal error, because it has been stated: "The time for storing robes that have arisen from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā is shown.

And it should be understood that it was precisely based on this scribal error that the teacher, the venerable Buddhadatta, said: "It is considered to be at most ten days; [any period] beyond that is a month's neglect," and so forth.

The meaning is: when one has previously resolved upon another robe similar to an "urgent" (*acceka*) robe, and then, with the perception that it is an "urgent" robe, one lets the robe-season pass by means of another robe that is similar—being similar in its time of arising, its appearance, and so forth—for that reason, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated here, as well as the absence of an offense;
otherwise, a *pācittiya* would have to be declared for all three cases alike. This also applies to a robe that is not an "urgent" robe.
It should be understood that for one who lets the robe season pass, it is indeed a *pācittiya*, just as in the case of the "urgent robe" triad (*accekacīvarattika*). Here, there are four factors:

(1) the urgent robe being of the maximum allowable size and having come into one's own possession; (2) its arising when less than ten days remain until the full moon of the Kattika month of the cold season;
(3) its not having been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned by means of a formal assignment (*vikappita*); and (4) the passing of the robe season.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hurried robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning danger:
Regarding the ninth [rule], because it is said that "a house here and there" refers to a village, he says "within the village."
In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase “having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna,” the word “attaining” (*upasampajja*) is cited together with its nasalization (*sānusāra*).

It is with reference to this that he says, “as in the case of ‘attaining’ and so forth. The phrase “of that too” refers to the analytical term “of those who have completed the rains-residence” (*vutthavassāna*).
Furthermore, the genitive case in *vutthavassāna* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*); and by this, [the meaning is applied] to the preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
It is established that for those whose *kaṭhina* has not been spread, even during the month of *kaṭhina*, the practice of "not undertaking" [the robe] is not permitted;
otherwise, the training rule itself would be rendered meaningless—so it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "from the place eligible for the enclosure":
here, starting from the vicinity of the houses situated at the village boundary, one *leḍḍu-pāta* (the distance of a stone-throw) [is the limit].
This refers to a place that qualifies for enclosure. In the *Visuddhimagga* it is stated: "In the case of an unenclosed area, starting from the first stone-throw.
The word "that" (*taṃ*) refers to that first dwelling-place and so forth.
However, in the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that one should measure the distance between the two stone-throws after excluding the precincts of both the monastery and the village itself.
Because it was stated, “In Kosambī, a certain bhikkhu was ill,” it is said that “the authorization for those at Kosambī (kosambaka-sammuti) was permitted.

By the phrase, “And he had gone toward the western direction,” it is meant that for one who has deposited his robe within an inhabited area and is staying in that monastery, it is permissible to be separated from the entire robe-month; beyond that, elsewhere—
This demonstrates that when there is a necessity for travel, a separation of up to six nights from one’s dwelling is permitted. Therefore, he said:
“Having returned to the lodging, one may cause the seventh dawn to rise,” and so forth. “Having stayed” means having caused the dawn to rise.
“Right there” means in that very place where one had gone. The factors [of the offense] in this case, however, are stated in the Commentary itself.
The commentary on the training rule concerning suspicion is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Planted:
"A young tree planted by someone" is said with reference to that which has been planted by a specific person. It is not [a tree] grown of its own accord.
Having gathered what is being mixed together, it is permissible to offer it anywhere. "Seeing it standing" means seeing that which remains after the portion has been taken.
Regarding the phrase "give it wherever you wish," there is no fault even if one specifies, "Give this to so-and-so," because it was said, "according to your own preference.
As for the fact that [the gift] was dedicated to the Sangha, having understood that, for oneself—
Dedication and acquisition: these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dedication is finished.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Bowls, is concluded.
Thus ends the method of commentary on the Thirty [Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules] within the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the Vinaya, known as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The first part is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary Dispelling Doubts on the Vinaya Piṭaka (Second Part)
5. Pācittiyakaṇḍa 1.
Musāvādavagga 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvāda-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

1. Regarding the phrase "of the minor rules" (*khuddakānaṃ*) in the first training rule of the Chapter on False Speech (*Musāvādavagga*), they say that "the word *khuddaka* is a synonym for the word *bahu* (many). "In those" (*tattha*) means in those chapters, or among the minor rules.

When others state that the reason given—"because it must be known"—is inconclusive (*anaikantika*) because it applies even to Nibbāna, which is its opposite, [the author] says: "This reason was not stated by me"; thus he sets forth that argument.

To conceal [the fact], he further says, "I said 'subject to birth,' and so forth. Since one should say "sampajānan" (knowing), the form used here is a grammatical designation with the elision of the nasal vowel; thus he says "jānanto" (knowing).
Regarding "sampajānamusāvāde" (in the case of deliberate lying): having previously known the falsity of the matter being spoken by oneself, [one speaks it].
And [it applies] to one who speaks a falsehood while knowing [the truth] at the moment of speaking. Therefore he said, "having known," and so forth.
In the phrase "in a falsehood" (*musāvāde*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; thus, in this context, it means that the *pācittiya* offense is for the purpose of speaking falsely.
This same meaning should be understood in other similar instances hereafter.

3. He says "speech" because one speaks by means of it; thus he says "wrongly," and so forth. Just as in the expressions "he pierces with a bow" and the like, the phrase "seen with the eye" is stated in its conventional sense;
therefore, he says "by means of the coarse [form]. 11. Regarding the phrase "it will have been committed": here too, because it is stated with a definitive conclusion, a false speech has occurred.

"An offense" refers to an offense of expiation (pācittiya), not a wrong speech (dubbhāsita). For that [offense] occurs for one who, out of malice, addresses another with the ten grounds of abuse, beginning with birth and so forth.
They brought them along. There are three factors here: the falsity of the object, the intention to deceive, and the effort to make that person understand the matter which one desires as the object.
For if there is no falsity of the object, even if it is understood through the intention to deceive, it is not a lie; it is merely an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Therefore, that too must be understood as a constituent factor. For one who speaks falsely for the purpose of proclaiming a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), there is a *pārājika* offense;
by way of figurative expression, there is a *thullaccaya*. For the purpose of slandering with a groundless *pārājika*, there is a *saṅghādisesa*;

for false speech and the like involving slander with a *saṅghādisesa*, there is a *pācittiya*; for those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies] to high or low birth and so forth...
For one who reviles with anger, there is an *dukkaṭa*; for one who speaks merely falsehoods, a *pācittiya* is stated here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning false speech (*musāvāda*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech (*omasavāda*).

13. "In the second [case], it causes the rim that was previously established on the ground to reach the ground again" means that after the portion of the rim already established on the ground has been rotated, it is caused to be established on the ground once more.
15. "In the past" refers to the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*). Those called "flower-scavengers" are those who carry away the impurities of the womb and so forth.

"Stone-worker's craft" refers to the work of a carpenter, such as the carving of stone and the like. "Counting by hand gestures" is counting by the mere contraction of the fingers. "Finger-joint counting" (*acchiddaka-gaṇanā*)—[is]...

“Name” refers to counting by ones, tens, and so forth, after having placed a marker (sāri). By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the collective counting that occurs through addition, multiplication, subtraction, division, and so on, is included.
One who is proficient in this knows, even upon seeing a tree, “there are this many leaves here.
Because of the expression “in *ya* and *bha* for sexual intercourse,” he says “the letter *ya*, the letter *bha*,” and so forth.

16. "Not by the first" refers to the training rule on false speech (*musāvāda-sikkhāpada*). Even that [offense] is an offense: even when one speaks using terms distinguished by prefixes and the like, one is to be dealt with for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone.

26. "Badly spoken" (*dubbhāsita*): because this is stated as a general term, the teachers say that even for one who speaks in the absence [of the person addressed], it is indeed "badly spoken," even though it is not included in the Canon (the *Pāḷi*), since there is no more minor offense than that; furthermore, it cannot be considered a non-offense here.
Because it is improper. Regarding the term "all beings" (*sabbasatta*), those learned in the meaning of words include even animals and the like here.

35. For those who speak with a primary intent toward instruction or with a desire to censure evil, there is no offense even when anger arises from time to time, because of the mind’s state of rapid transformation.
Since verbal abuse can occur even through a mere bodily gesture, [this offense] has three origins (*tisamutthāna*).
And it is said, "bodily action. However, in the *Parivāra*, after rejecting the other origins by stating, "Regarding the fourth origin of offenses...

one might incur a *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech). This should not be said," and so forth, because only the fifth [origin] is mentioned, he says: "But here, the offense of *dubbhāsita* originates from speech and mind. For, out of a desire for sport...

Even when one insults by means of body, speech, and mind, only speech and mind constitute the factors for the offense, and not the body, even though it exists—as in the case of the offense of teaching the Dhamma, which occurs through bodily gesture alone.

However, although there is no offense of *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech) here for one who insults, it should nevertheless be understood that there is indeed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) due to the training rule prohibiting bodily play. [This applies to] one who is fully ordained.

The three factors here are: reviling by means of terms such as "birth" and so forth without using a designation for another [person], knowing that [reviling], and the absence of having the welfare [of the other] as one's primary concern, and so on.
The commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Slander (Pesuññasikkhāpada) 36.
Regarding the third [offense]: "Those among whom strife has arisen" are called *bhaṇḍanajātā*. "Slanderous" (*pisuṇā*) means that which grinds;

the meaning is that it causes division among those who are united. One who possesses such speech is "slanderous" (*pisuṇo*); the action of such a person is "slander" (*pesuñña*). This is how the meaning should be understood here.
Here too, for one who utters slander by means of the ten bases beginning with birth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);

for the other bases of abuse, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, they say that for one who utters [slander] by means of bases other than those of abuse, there is only an offense of wrong-doing.

Regarding the case where, having heard a monk abusing another monk under the pretext of birth and so forth, one utters slander to that monk—this applies when the intention is either to win favor or to cause a schism.
"Another person," "that [person]," and "the act of learning"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning malicious talebearing is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning the memorization of verses.

45. In the fourth [case], it is similar to the preceding phrasing: regarding the word *anicca* in the phrase “form (*rūpa*) is impermanent,” he speaks of the word *anicca* in the phrase “feeling (*vedanā*) is impermanent” as being identical to that. A collection of syllables is stated to be without inflection (*avibhattika*).
A phrase (*pada*) is stated to be ending in an inflection (*vibhattianta*).
"One line" refers specifically to a single verse-line (*gāthāpada*). "By counting the lines" means by counting the verse-lines of the gāthā.

"Without reaching" means without having spoken together [with the other]. By this, it is shown that if the novice speaks the first line while the last line of the gāthā is being recited, there is indeed an offense; it must be stated by the other [monk] only when he has become silent.
"Based on the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathānissita*) refers to the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) recorded in the three councils (*saṅgītittaya*).
Even now, such commentary statements as "Just as the leopard, having hidden itself, seizes the deer," still exist;
and they say that even what was spoken by the teacher Buddhaghosa and others according to the method of the ancient commentaries should be included here.
"Dependent on the Pāḷi" refers to works such as the *Udānavagga-saṅgaha*. "Dependent on turning away from the round" (*vivaṭṭūpanissita*) means dependent on Nibbāna.
"Of the Elder" refers to the Elder Nāgasena. The treatises such as the *Maggakathā* and others [are meant]. 46.
The phrase "in the letters of the Pāḷi," etc., is stated with a change of gender; the meaning should be understood as "by means of the letters," and so forth.

48. "Having left the vicinity" means: having left the twelve-cubit space around the assembly, there is no offense for one who speaks with reference to others, provided they do not speak to a person who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) standing or sitting nearby.

However, if one speaks with reference to someone even though they are sitting at a distance, there is indeed an offense. "Directs" means: he converses together [with them]. The factor of the offense is the state of being one who is not fully ordained.
Reciting the dhamma with its stated characteristics word by word, and reciting it together—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the memorization of words is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sleeping in the Same Bed.
50–51. "In the fifth [offense], this is the illustration," is the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the expression *dirattatirattaṃ* ("two or three nights"): here, the inclusion of the term *dirattaṃ* (two nights) is for the purpose of poetic ornamentation; it should also be understood as being for the purpose of showing that an offense occurs only for one who stays continuously for three nights and then sleeps on the fourth day and so forth, and not for one who sleeps by skipping days (*ekantarika*) or by other intervals. For [the duration] is distinguished by the two nights.
When "three nights" is mentioned, it indicates that the three nights must be consecutive. "With five coverings" means with bricks, stone, plaster, grass, and leaves.
"By way of being mastered" means by way of being well-practiced. It should be one and a half cubits high, as measured by the carpenter’s cubit.
"A single precinct" (ekūpacāra) is that which, having been entered by a single path and having reached the open space, is suitable for circumambulation on all sides.

Although this [dwelling] has many doors, it is indeed a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*). However, if they block it off with walls and the like and construct separate doors, it becomes multiple precincts (*nānūpacāra*).
But if they do indeed block it off and do not construct separate doors, it should be understood as "this too is a single precinct, like a chamber whose door is closed with clay and so forth.
Otherwise, having entered the chamber, [if one goes] to the porch and so forth...

"Even for one who has the door of the womb closed with clay and other materials while those who are not fully ordained are lying down—thereby being exempt from the offense of sharing a sleeping place—and then opens it at dawn, there would be no offense.

Regarding the statement, "For each of their actions, the monk incurs an offense," some say: "Because it is not performed through physical exertion, it originates from non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*)."
The offense is stated [to occur] at that very moment because there is an absence of action for one who is sleeping.
For this training rule may originate from action, and it may originate from non-action. He says that its origination from action is stated by way of its predominance.
And as this is so, so too is sleeping during the day. For this [offense occurs] through failure to perform duties and through lack of restraint over the sense-doors.
They say, “There is also that which arises from non-action. And this appears to be reasonable; it should be accepted after investigation.
The phrase “of one whose wall is not connected with the upper floor” is stated for the purpose of showing that there is nothing at all to be said regarding one whose wall is connected.
Since there is no suspicion whatsoever for one lying on the upper floor, [the text says] “in the lower palace,” and so forth.
It has been stated. "In various approaches" means outside the ladder used for climbing up.
"By way of a hall-enclosure" means by way of the form of a hall. By the term "half-wall," he shows the shape:
where walls are built on three or two sides, but the roof does not reach [the fourth], that is a half-wall (*aḍḍhakuṭṭaka*).
"Named. A "hair-fringe" (*vāḷasaṅghāṭa*) is a fringe made from hair-figures placed upon pillars and so forth within the enclosure. Regarding the phrase "outside the enclosure":
if there is no enclosure on a particular side, and the ground there is high, then even if it is within a *nibbaka* (a span) below the high ground on both sides, there is no offense.

This is because, in that case, there is no conventional designation for "lodging" (*senāsana*). Now, if the base is low and stands at the same level as the ground on the lower surface of the lodging, then an offense occurs everywhere within the *nibbakosa* (the space below the eaves) in the direction free from enclosures, due to the absence of a defined boundary.
It should be understood that outside the enclosure itself there is no offense, as there is no demarcation. "Or a full circle," and so forth.
This was said with reference to a lodging that has an open courtyard in its center for the purpose of water-bathing.

In that context, "with an unconfined interior space" means that they do not construct a wall no less than one and a half cubits high, having delimited the passage on both sides of each individual cell by means of a vestibule, so as to enter through an open courtyard; such is the meaning. "Enclosure of the cells" (gabbhaparikkhepo) refers to this.
This is said with reference to the walls of the chambers situated on all sides in the case of the Caturassapāsāda and other such structures.

"Arranged separately" means that the rows of chambers in each individual direction are called "arranged separately" because there is an absence of chambers in the other directions, or even if they were present, because they are not connected to one another by means of wall-roofs. That... [etc.]
Regarding the phrase "spoken with intentional meaning," it is stated therein that there is no offense by way of a *pācittiya*, but not by way of a *dukkaṭa*.

For a room of such a kind—where the front is open due to the absence of walls in three directions and possesses only a wall on one side—is called "partially covered" (*cūḷaparicchanna*) even though it is completely enclosed. Therefore, there is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. However, if the front of that [room]...

In other directions as well, whether they build a wall on one side or on all sides, it should be understood that when it is entirely covered, half-covered, or otherwise, there is only a *pācittiya* offense.

Regarding the phrase "referring to the front of a house built on the ground without a raised platform," this refers to the front of a house constructed on the ground without having erected a high structure; in such a case, if it is unenclosed, there is a *pācittiya*.
"Non-offense" is what has been stated here. If the front porch (*pamukha*) is on a high foundation, the intention is that the porch is counted as being enclosed by that very foundation.

"Therein" refers to the Andhaka commentary. Having stated the measurement of the floor (*jagati*), it means that the height of the foundation is such that one lying on the natural ground does not see what is situated above the floor. Thus, it is "high" or "very high."
Having stated the measurement of height, a palace constructed by extending straight upward in a single direction is to be understood as having the arrangement of a single hall (*ekasāla*).
Those constructed in two, three, or four directions in the shape of a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*) and so forth are to be understood as having the arrangements of two halls (*dvisāla*) and so on.
Furthermore, the distinction from the preceding [description] here consists solely in the illustration of the various types of halls. "Encircled" means surrounded.
This refers to the perimeter of the front part.

53. Since the *pāḷi* presents "half-covered and half-surrounded" as the starting point for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), everything exceeding that—such as "fully covered and half-surrounded," and so forth—even if not explicitly mentioned in the *pāḷi*, constitutes an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

It should be understood that this is shown by way of the basis [of the offense], because the training rule is a fault by definition (*paṇṇattivajja*), and because one must remain firm regarding what is grave.
"Seven *pācittiya*s" is stated by taking the two *pācittiya*s mentioned in the Canon as a single unit in a general sense. 54.
In the Canon, the phrase "having departed before dawn on the third night, he dwells again" is stated according to the strictest limit (*ukkaṭṭha-vasena*).

It has been stated that, however, if one does not go out but rises before dawn and remains seated inside the roof-covering, there is no offense even if one shares the same sleeping place on the following day.

"It has the appearance of a *senāmaṇḍapa*": it is said that in the island of Sri Lanka (Sīhaḷadīpa) there is a gathering hall (*sannipātamaṇḍapa*) of this name, which has a high foundation, is entirely covered, and yet lacks any surrounding enclosure; it is with reference to this that [the text] says this.

It has been stated. Here, one-fourth [of the roof] is the *cūḷaka* (small pinnacle); two parts are a half; and two out of three parts constitute a majority—by this method, the terms "covered with a small pinnacle" (*cūḷakacchanna*), "completely covered" (*paricchanna*), and so forth, are to be understood.

The three factors here are: a lodging that constitutes the basis for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); lying down there together with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*); and the setting of the sun on the fourth day.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sleeping together is finished.
6. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Regarding Sleeping Together: 55.
In the sixth [case], even for one who sleeps with a woman on the fourth day, there is only this single training rule.

An offense. Some, however, say there are two offenses because of the preceding rule as well; that is not correct, because it is stated with the gender-neutral term "by one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannena*).
It is appropriate to state that for a neuter person (*napuṃsaka*) who lies down on the fourth day, there is a *dukkaṭa* along with a *pācittiya*.
Although in this case the *Pāḷi* mentions the *dukkaṭa* specifically in reference to a paṇḍaka, it is [applicable] in accordance with that.

However, for one who lies down with a person possessing both sexual organs (purisaubhatobyañjanaka), there is a *dukkaṭa* offense by this [present rule], and on the fourth day, a *saddukkaṭapācittiya* by the previous [rule].
As for a female possessing both sexual organs (*itthiubhatobyañjanaka*), our opinion is that she belongs to the category of women.
They say there is no offense regarding a dead woman. A lodging whose substance is subject to a *pācittiya* offense: lying down there together with a woman.
"Sunset": these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning sleeping in the same room is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Teaching the Dhamma.
60. In the seventh [case], the connection for the phrases beginning with "not with a *yakkha*" is with the words "except with one who is wise.
The intended meaning should be understood as follows: "Except with a man in human form who is wise, not even with a *yakkha* or the like.

For it is not permitted to teach while standing together even with such a person. However, it is certainly permissible to explain the meaning in the respective local dialect according to one's preference.
The non-performance here consists of either changing one’s posture or causing a man to shout within a twelve-fathom radius. The five factors here are:
teaching a dhamma possessing the stated characteristics beyond the six types of speech; the woman possessing the stated characteristics;
the absence of a change in posture; the absence of a wise man; and the absence of a question-and-answer session.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the preaching of the Dhamma is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Reporting of What Has Occurred (Bhūtārocanasikkhāpada) 77.
Regarding the eighth [rule], the term *antara* means even before the time of final Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase *atikaḍḍhiyamānena*: "Venerable sir, please speak."
"Have you attained [anything]?"—being thus pressed and being excessively constrained. When such conditions exist, one must certainly speak.

Regarding "the quality of learning, mastery, and virtue": here, proficiency in the meaning is the quality of learning (*suta-guṇa*), while proficiency in reciting the text is the quality of mastery (*pariyatti-guṇa*);
this is how it should be understood. By the phrase "or because of the absence of distraction of mind," even the state of being afflicted by painful feelings that distract the mind is [excluded].
This shows that for the Noble Ones (ariya), [this offense] does not exist.

"By what was not previously stated" means by what was not stated in the fourth Pārājika. Furthermore, this training rule (sikkhāpada) arises exclusively from a state of non-intentionality (acittaka-samuṭṭhāna) due to the lack of knowledge regarding the formal rule (paṇṇatti-ajjhānana), because the Noble Ones do not transgress the formal rules. And for those who have attained meditative absorption (jhānalābhin),...
Because one whose mind is hostile toward transgressing the Teacher’s command has fallen away from meditative absorption (jhāna), it is impossible for the report to be true.

Herein, there are four factors: the truth of the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), the reporting to one who is not fully ordained, the understanding [of the offense] at that very moment, and the absence of another excuse.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the reporting of what is true is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Proclamation of a Grave Offense (Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada) 78.

Regarding the ninth [training rule], "it might occur there": someone might have such a thought regarding that matter. Establishing it as firm by means of the very words of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) through logical justification, he says, "And by this also," and so forth.
82. "The first five training rules" refers to the five beginning with the taking of life. "The remaining ones" refers to those beginning with eating at improper times.
The emission of semen and so forth is indeed transgression. For a monk who has not committed the final offense, there are three factors here:
the presence of a specific location, the reporting to one not fully ordained, and the absence of authorization from the Saṅgha.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the reporting of grave matters is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Digging the Earth (Pathavīkhaṇana-sikkhāpada) 86.

Regarding the tenth [rule], since it is stated that there is no offense when the earth consists of very little dust or clay, it should be understood that even with half-dust or half-clay, it is indeed a *pācittiya*.
For it cannot be said that this is merely a matter of *dukkaṭa*, as it is distinct from both what has been produced and what has not been produced.
Because there is no third earth.
"It is allowable" means that in this case, one may dig a lotus pond because the location is not restricted;
since this refers to digging the earth, it constitutes an offense under this very training rule, and not under the training rule concerning plant life (*bhūtagāma*).
When both [cases] are intended by the statement, however, there are two *pācittiya* offenses.
"Water-film" (*udakapappaṭaka*) refers to that which, when water has entered into the ground, remains as a thin layer of fine dust or clay covering its upper surface;
even when that water has dried, that film remains moving in the wind—that is called a water-film.
"Akata-pabbhāra" is stated for the purpose of showing a place that has not been artificially leveled;
for it is only in such a place that an anthill can occur. "Mūsikukkara" refers to a heap of dust made outside by mice having dug [into the ground].

Because of the mention of "covering" and so forth, the earth becomes covered only by rainwater falling directly from the sky, and not by water that falls upon a roof or similar structures and then [flows down] from there.
It should be understood that [the bedding] becomes damp from flowing water. "Pavilion pillar" means a pillar of a branch-pavilion (*sākhāmaṇḍapa*).
"Having lifted up" means having raised it. "From there" means from the old lodging-place.
88. "Great clay" refers to wall-plaster. "A path already formed," "known as such," and "either digging or causing to be dug"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on False Speech, is finished.
2. The Chapter on Living Beings and Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Plants (Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada) 89.
Regarding the first [offense] in the second section, "being unable to restrain oneself":

this refers to the incident in the *Sākhaṭṭhaka-vimāna* where, while a branch was being cut, he saw the deity’s son brought forward by the goddess to prevent its cutting; yet, despite seeing this, he did not desist from the impulse to set down his axe.

The meaning is: "being unable to turn back. Regarding "the nature of a tree" (*rukkhadhamme*): it refers to the behavior of a tree. For indeed, that which is unshakable regarding cutting and so forth, like trees, is called "the nature of a tree.
"Uppatitaṃ" means arisen. "Bhantaṃ" means running about. "Vāraye" means one should restrain. "Itaro" refers to that which has arisen.
The meaning is that one who does not restrain anger is not a supreme charioteer, like a person who merely holds the reins for kings, vassals, and others.
"Like the poison of a black snake" means like the poison of a black serpent that has spread and pervaded the body following the track of its fang-wound.
"He abandons this shore and the further shore" means he abandons the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiyasaññojanāni*) by means of the third path. "This shore and the further shore" refers to...
For "this shore" (*ora*) is said to be this side. Alternatively, "he" refers to the bhikkhu who, having dispelled anger by means of the third path, stands firm;

the meaning is that he abandons "this shore" by means of the path to *arahantship*. In this context, "this shore" (*ora*) means one's own personal existence (*sakattabhāva*), or the internal sense-bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*).
"The further shore" (*pāra*) means the existence of others (*paraattabhāva*), or the external sense-bases (*bāhirāni āyatanāni*). Abandoning desire and lust for both of these, [he crosses over].
"It is said: 'He abandons this shore and the further shore.
(90) "Bhavanti" means they increase. "Ahuvaṃti" means they have come into being. Therefore he says, "born and grown.

"The village of the bhūtas" refers to the collection of the great elements (mahābhūta) when they are gathered together in the form of green grass and so forth; it does not refer to a village distinct from those.
To show that [the term "village"] signifies non-existence, it is said: “Or, the village is simply the primary elements (bhūtā).

With reference to the root-meaning of the word *pātabya* as “to drink” (*pā pāneti*), he says: “The state of being something to be consumed. And since that state of being consumable consists precisely in cutting and so forth, he says: “Of that...
[arising] from the conditions of cutting and so forth, which have arisen in the village of primary elements.”

91. Here, the word *jāta* is used in the sense of "born" (*vijāta*), as in the expression "a woman who has given birth to a son" (*puttaṃ vijātā itthī*). Thus he says "they have been brought forth" (*pasūtāni*), meaning that the leaves and roots have been produced.
"Showing them" means showing those seeds. Since the cause is understood through the very presentation of the effect, he says: "By means of what is produced from the seed, the seed is shown. 92.
By the phrase "the group of beings arisen from a seed is the seed," with the elision of the final member of the compound, [it refers to] "that which is produced from a lotus plant..."
He shows that this is a conventional expression (vohāra), as in the case of [the phrase] "a lotus flower" (*pupphaṃ padumaṃ*) and so forth.
When it says, "that seed which is called a 'class of beings' (*bhūtagāmo*)," he speaks with reference to the leaves and roots that have already been produced.

"According to the literal meaning" (*yathārutaṃ*) means according to the text. Because it is said "intentionally" (*sañcicca*), one rises even after knowing that [an insect] is clinging to the body, by the perception: "I shall remove it."
It is permissible because of its absence. By the mention of "endless" (anantaka), the *sāsapamattikā* is included; for that is the name of that species of moss.
Because it lacks roots and leaves, it is called "an incomplete habitat of beings" (*asampuṇṇabhūtagāmo*). It is included within the category of "seed-habitats.
Even though it does not grow, because it is rooted in a habitat of beings, it is said: "it is included among the rootless habitats of beings. [Regarding] the coconut...
He speaks by way of an exclusive category (*āveṇika*).
*Seleyyaka* is a certain type of fragrance produced from stone. "From the time it has blossomed" means from the moment it has opened.
"Taking the umbrella" means taking it while it is in full bloom. However, as for the bud, even without disturbing the bark of the tree...
It is not permissible to take [the fruit] while it is unripe; it is permissible when it is fully blossomed (ripened).
"With hand-fickleness" means with dexterity of hand. The statement "water should not be kept" refers to water for one's own drinking;
however, it is permissible for others because it is not being stored for their benefit. Therefore he said, "by one who wishes to eat it oneself. Regarding the trees whose branches grow...
Even if the roots are not pulled out, it increases by the mere removal of leaves.
In that regard, even if one does not perform what is allowable (*kappiya*), it is permissible to disturb cut coconut husks, bamboo stalks, and so forth.

Because it was said, "I will show the place for walking meditation (*caṅkama*)," there is no fault for one who steps on them solely with the intention of walking meditation or the intention of traveling along a path, nor for one who sits upon the grass with the intention of sitting.

“By means of allowable conventions for recluses” means by means of the allowable designations used by recluses. Even seeds that have not yet been extracted are called “allowable for recluses” because they possess the status of being allowable.

“Seeds that are not [yet] seeds” refers to young mango fruits and the like. That from which the seed must be extracted or separated is called “that from which the seed has been extracted,” such as jackfruit and so forth.
Although it was stated using the past tense (“having said it is allowable”), it is expressed in this way by way of the prior action.

However, because of the statement that "the seed-planting area must be cleared of forest [growth] by means of fire, weapons, and so forth at the very moment of speaking," it is not permitted to do so beforehand;
furthermore, this should be demonstrated as consisting only of cutting and breaking, without performing the two [other methods].
And when the monk performs it, it must be done only after someone has said in whatever language, "Make it allowable" (*kappiyaṃ karohi*). This is for the purpose of protecting the seed-planting area.
"Furthermore, it must be made allowable (kappiya)" means that because the act of making it allowable is the very first requirement.
Since it is stated, "It is permissible to do so even in a basin," it is indeed permissible to pierce the kernel or the seed wherever it may be, even after it has been removed from the basin.
In this context, there are three factors: a living plant (bhūtagāma), the perception that it is a living plant, and either the destruction or the causing of destruction.
The commentary on the training rule concerning plants is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule concerning speaking otherwise:
"Speaking otherwise" means that one evades with a different, inappropriate statement what has been said by others for the purpose of exposing one's fault.

98. That speech which proceeds by way of evading one thing with another is called "one who speaks otherwise" (*aññavādaka*) because he speaks of or reveals something other than the matter asked about; thus it is said: "This is the name for evading one thing with another.

"This is the name for one who has become silent" means this is the name for the state of silence; or rather, this is the reading itself. "To charge one who speaks otherwise" [is explained as follows].
To bring a charge of speaking otherwise. *Vihesakaṃ* means the state of being a harasser. 99.
In the text, "not wishing to disclose" means wishing to conceal. 100.

Regarding the offense of wrong-doing mentioned in the text as occurring when one has not been charged with speaking otherwise, it refers to the practice of evading by saying one thing while meaning another.

This is logical; however, according to the method found in the Aṭṭhakathā, for one who evades the truth with a falsehood, there is a dukkaṭa offense together with the pācittiya. When the charge has been brought, by this very [rule], there is a pācittiya.

Some, however, say that "there are two pācittiyas along with the pācittiya for false speech," which should be investigated. Even for a first-time offender, there is no offense for false speech by this very [rule].

It must be seen. The three factors here are: being subjected to a formal legal act (*dhammakamma*), being interrogated regarding either an offense or its basis, evading one matter with another out of a desire to conceal it, and remaining silent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who speak otherwise is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reviling (Ujjhāpanaka-sikkhāpada) 103.

Regarding the third [rule], because the root *jhi*—which has the sense of "thinking"—possesses multiple meanings, it can also carry the sense of "looking"; therefore, it is said, "causing to look. As for the phrase "through desire" (*chandāya*), this is a grammatical inversion of gender;

thus he says, "by means of desire" (*chandenā*). 105. To cause another monk to think of oneself as inferior by speaking of one's own faults in the presence of others is called "reviling" (*ujjhāpana*).
But "reviling" (khiyyanā) is the manifestation of a fault by a bhikkhu through mutual conversation, rather than speaking to others;
this is the distinction between these two. 106.
"He causes another who is not fully ordained to revile" means he causes another person who is not fully ordained to revile him, or [he causes] that person...
"In his presence" means that one reviles that person who has been ordained and approved by the Saṅgha in the presence of that person who has not yet been ordained.
Here too, it should be understood that the grounds for *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) arising from censuring through falsehood, as well as the non-offense for a first-time offender,
are stated by this very training rule, because the *pācittiya* offense for lying is not excluded in all such cases.
The six factors here are: being authorized by a formal legal act (*dhammakamma*); having received full ordination; not having gone on a wrong course;
desiring to disparage that person; and the person in whose presence one speaks. [Also included are] that person’s state of having received full ordination, and either complaining or criticizing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning complaining is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Lodgings (Senāsana-sikkhāpada). 110.
Regarding the fourth [rule], *apaññāte* means "when it was not well-known.

However, the intention is that the Blessed One laid down this training rule first, taking into account the specific purpose consisting of storing [the robes] for eight months in pavilions and the like; thus he said: "I allow..."
By stating, "O monks, for eight months," and so forth—in a manner similar to a subsequent rule (anupaññatti)—it was not stated as a separate subsequent rule.
However, in the *Parivāra*, this statement of permission is considered the locus of a subsequent rule; thus it is said, "there is one subsequent rule.
"Newly woven" means a bed recently covered with a cloth that has had its fringes removed. "Covered" means [covered] with an allowable hide.
"Covered": for these [things] do not quickly perish due to the rain. "An open-air dweller who lives in the highest [spot]" is merely an indication of his pleasant mode of practice;
however, even for one living in the highest [spot], a robe-shed (cīvarakuṭi) is indeed permissible. "Because it follows the body" explains that the monk remains seated right there;
by this, it shows that if he himself goes elsewhere out of fear of the rain, an offense occurs. For those who are open-air dwellers...
Even that which has been given by donors for the sake of companions must certainly be protected by one who protects himself.
By the phrase "having observed whether clouds have arisen," it is indicated that even in the summer, when clouds have risen, it is not permissible to leave [the robes] in the open air.
"In this or that place" refers to those various open spaces such as the courtyard of a cetiya and so forth.

They were deposited after being restrained. "Starting from the middle and directed toward the foot-base" means that where, having swept all around, the sand is always heaped up in the middle of the courtyard by gathering the refuse there;
this was said for the purpose of showing the procedure to be performed there. Alternatively, the sand should be carried away toward the base of a high structure.
Alternatively, some explain the meaning as follows: "Wherever sand has accumulated in the corners, one should begin from there and carry it toward another direction.

Others, however, say: "It is stated that, in order to avoid disturbing the already swept area by the tread of one's feet, one should stand oneself in an unswept spot and carry the sand toward one's own feet."
In this context, no purpose for the expression “starting from the middle” is apparent.

To show that the distinction of a crab’s feet from others lies merely in their being curved, and not in the specific manner of inserting the feet into the legs, the passage beginning with “or whoever else” was stated. “Of him” refers specifically to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
Regarding the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for sitting... [etc. ...here, having recognized the absence of rain, one thinks, “I will come later and lift it out.”
There is no offense for one who departs with the intention [to return]; he must indeed return by that means.
"Having obtained permission" means having received the words, "Go;
do not stay here. "An obstacle for the residents alone" means sitting down without saying anything to the newcomers, thinking, "The residents themselves will remove it."

Even at the gates, it is an obstacle only for those residing there. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī-vāda*, the intention is that it applies even to those who are merely sitting there, without having said, "This is ours.

Because it is stated, "having spread [it] oneself or having had it spread," and because it was established without formal instruction (*anāṇatti*), the reason for the *dukkaṭa* offense is stated. An *ussāraka* is a reciter; for he [recites] higher and higher.
One who causes the recitation of the Pāli text to proceed and circulate is called an *ussāraka*.
(112) "Made for the purpose of protecting the color" means made by sewing together pieces of cloth and so forth.

"It should be spread on the ground" means that if a rug (*cimilika*) is available, it should be spread upon it; if not, it should be spread directly on the bare ground. "Only for the purpose of carrying lion skins and the like..."
By this [term] "prohibition," it is shown that for one's own use, it is not permitted to carry around items such as beds and chairs by spreading them out and then folding them up again;
however, using them as floor coverings and the like does not constitute "carrying around" for oneself.
For in the Khandhaka, it says: "There were things spread out both inside the bed and outside the bed..."
Having thus prepared them for their own use on beds and so forth, a prohibition was made regarding the practice of keeping them:
“Monks, large skins such as lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins must not be worn. Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated. A wooden stool is simply a stool made of planks. A foot-scraper is a piece of wood or plank upon which one rubs and cleans one’s unwashed feet.

113. Because it is stated, “He goes with the thought, ‘I will come back and take it up,’” there is no offense even when one goes for another reason, provided that one has not asked permission and still has an expectation of returning.
For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: “The fact that the beds and so forth belong to the Saṅgha;
the spreading out or having them spread out in a place characterized as described; the absence of obstruction; the absence of an emergency; and the lack of expectation.”
"Transgressing the range of a clod-throw": thus, six factors are stated here together with indifference.
The commentary on the first training rule regarding lodgings is finished.
5. Commentary on the second training rule regarding lodgings.

116. In the fifth [case], *pāvāra* and *kojava* refer to specific types of rugs with raised wool placed specifically for use as floor coverings. It is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that only this much was said. "From the lodging" means from the very last of all the lodgings. 117.

To show the same matter as stated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* with further detail, the passage beginning with "Even though it has been stated" is commenced. "There is nothing further to be said" is stated because the root of the tree is already well known. "It perishes" means it is destroyed.
118. That by which one weaves a bed or a bench is the "weaving of beds and benches. A "rock-cave" is a mountain cave.
By the phrase "asking for permission is a duty," he shows that there is no offense. [The factors are:
a bed with the stated characteristics, its belonging to the Saṅgha, spreading it out or having it spread out in a dwelling with the stated characteristics, and the absence of obstruction.
The absence of an emergency, departing for another region without regard [for the dwelling], and crossing the boundary of the precinct—these are the seven factors here.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Encroaching.
119. "Having entered close by" means having entered into the vicinity.
122. "Having set aside the precinct" means having set aside the precinct of one and a half cubits.
The four factors here are: [the dwelling] belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing that it is not to be vacated, the desire to cause inconvenience, and sitting or lying down within the precinct.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting down intruding [upon others] is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Expelling: 126.
Regarding the seventh [rule], "gate-houses" refers to gate-towers.
128. “It is not permissible to eject [a monk] from the entire Saṅghārāma”—this was stated because it is inappropriate.
For there is no offense under this training rule for one who causes ejection with an unperturbed mind for the sake of censuring evil, since it is stated [in the rule]: “being angry and displeased.
No other offense is seen [in such a case]. In the Pāḷi, in passages such as “he ejects one who is shameless,” [the condition refers to] the state of the mind.
Because of its quick turnover, there is no offense even if anger arises from time to time, since the act of ejecting is undertaken solely on account of such factors as shamelessness.

In this case, there are three constituent factors: a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, the person being ejected being free from states such as being a quarrelsome maker of strife while ordained, and the actual ejection or causing another to eject out of anger.
The commentary on the training rule concerning expulsion is finished. 8.

Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Upper Story of a Cell (Vehāsakuṭi-sikkhāpada) The eighth [training rule] is self-evident. Herein, there are four factors: a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha; an upper story cell whose ceiling does not strike the head; its being used as a lower level; and sitting or lying down on a seat with detachable legs placed without a support.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hut for one living in the air is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning a large dwelling (Mahallaka-vihāra-sikkhāpada). 135.
Regarding the ninth [rule], since it is stated that "a 'large' dwelling means one that has an owner," there is no offense in the case of a hut built by personal solicitation.

They say: "Of which" means of the dwelling (*vihāra*). "That [area] is also devoid of the precinct (*upacāra*)" means that when a door is opened, the wall it strikes becomes devoid of the precinct for a distance equal to the width of the door on all sides; this is the meaning.
It is called a "light-opening" (*ālokasandhi*) because it connects or joins with light and a window; thus, the door is being referred to. From the precinct of the door and the window...
For one who repeatedly performs plastering and so forth elsewhere, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the counting of the lumps.
However, some say: "Because it is not mentioned as an offense of expiation in the Canon, it is an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "It should be resolved upon" means it should be prepared.
"Standing on green [grass], he resolves upon it": for one who covers [the ground] while standing in a field possessed of green [grass], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The meaning is "an offense of wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa). Some, however, say that for one building a monastery on such a site, it is a dukkaṭa;
that does not accord with the Pāḷi.
136. "Covering straight up" refers to the covering starting from the edge of the opening and extending as far as the ridge-pole, the roof-peak, the pinnacle, and so forth.

First, there is the straight covering with bricks and so forth. However, because this [type of] covering—by which the entire monastery is covered at once—is considered a single course (ekamagga), the text says "two courses" and so on.
They say that even covering by way of successive layers (pariyāyena) should be applied according to this same method; and this is also supported by the text: "He had it covered again and again."
This accords with the commentary’s statement: “And all this roofing should be understood as being above the roof.

In the Canon, the phrases “for one who roofs with a path” and “for one who roofs by way of a method” are stated for the purpose of showing the different modes of roofing, such as with bricks and so forth, or with grass and leaves.
However, some [commentators] maintain that [the phrase refers to] “a roof already covered by a row [of tiles].”
They say that starting from the edge of the roof covering, taking the single layer of roofing directly upwards as "one course," the phrase "two courses" and so forth is stated;

however, this does not refer to the entire roof covering of the monastery. They claim this same method applies even to a roof covering by way of layers, but that does not accord with the Pāḷi and its commentaries.
Regarding the phrase "for the third path": here, *tatiyāya* is a dative case used in the sense of the accusative; thus, the meaning is "to the third path. Or rather, this very reading [is correct].
It is said that "it is obtained by means of grass and leaves," which refers to covering it with grass and leaves and then plastering the exterior and interior on top.
For it is stated that there is no offense for a simple grass hut. "Of the three paths" refers to the paths themselves.
"Of the three coverings" means of the three types of roofing. "Of the three methods" follows the same principle here as well.
The three factors in this case are: the state of being a large dwelling, the state of being one's own residence, and the further formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding large dwellings is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇakasikkhāpada) 140.
Regarding the tenth [rule] in the matrix: "Water with living beings" means one should sprinkle it with grass or clay, or discard it;
or alternatively, having taken water, one should sprinkle it outside, and in that water [one should place] grass or clay.
“Having brought, one should throw in” means that it should be understood as having been brought in. Therefore he said, “Even if it be the measure of a cartload,” and so forth.
“This” refers to the rule for throwing grass or clay. “Stated” means stated thus in the matrix (mātikā) as “grass or clay,” or stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
And this training rule (sikkhāpada) is stated with reference to external use by way of its subject matter, because internal use will be explained separately.

Both of these, being formulated as "containing living beings" (sappāṇaka), are called "offenses of formal rule" (paṇṇattivajja) because they are prescribed for pouring [water] even in the absence of a murderous intent (vadhakacitta).
However, when a murderous intent is present, it is [an offense] by another training rule alone.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); it should not be understood as being [an offense] by this alone.

The four factors here are: the water containing living beings; the knowledge that "the living beings will die from being sprinkled"; and the sprinkling of grass or the like with such water for some purpose other than the intention to kill.
The commentary on the training rule concerning living beings is finished.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanavagga), is completed.
This same chapter is also known by the name "The Chapter on Living Beings" (Bhūtagāmavagga).
3. Ovādavagga 1. Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā 144. Regarding the first [rule] of the third chapter:

*tiracchānabhūtaṃ* means "that which has become a screen," that is to say, "that which has become external. *Samiddho* means "complete. *Sahitattho* means "conducive to welfare. It is "profound" (*gambhīro*) by virtue of its profundity of meaning and so forth.
145–147. *Parato* means "furthermore" or "beyond. *Karonto vā* means performing [the action] externally. *Vibhaṅge* refers to the *Jhānavibhaṅga*. *Caraṇaṃ* is the foot for proceeding toward Nibbāna.

*Yadassa* means "whatever belongs to him. *Dhāreti* means he maintains it without letting it perish. *Parikathanatthaṃ* means for the purpose of delivering discourses on specific teachings by way of miscellaneous talk.
*Tisso anumodanā* refers to the three types of thanksgiving associated with the benefits of giving, such as meals offered to the Saṅgha.

There are these three kinds of thanksgiving: thanksgiving with the *Nidhikuṇḍa Sutta* and others on occasions such as entering a house for a blessing; thanksgiving with the *Maṅgala Sutta* and others on auspicious occasions such as the entry into a home;

and thanksgiving with the *Tirokuṭṭa Sutta* and others on inauspicious occasions such as funeral meals. "The determination of what is action and what is not action" refers to the determination stated in the section on actions at the end of the *Parivāra*.
"By way of concentration" means by way of serenity (*samatha*) preceded by that [concentration]. "By way of insight" (*vipassanā*)...
It blows by way of dry-insight (sukkha-vipassanā) beginning with the purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi).

He is "one who goes in the four directions" (cātuddisa) because, for the sake of guarding his own virtue, he is capable of going wherever he wishes due to his independence from others; or because these [four directions] belong to him, or because he is excellent in them.
"In the higher discipline" (abhivinaye) means in the discipline of restraint known as the Pātimokkha-restraint, or in the Vinaya Piṭaka which elucidates it.
"Vinetuṃ" means to train and to explain. "Paguṇā vācuggatā" means they should be made proficient and committed to memory both by way of the text and by way of the meaning;
that is, they should be mastered through the method of internalizing them orally. Here, some provide an interpretation based on the meaning alone.
"Abhidhamme" refers to the phenomena of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-dhamma) as defined by their characteristics, functions, and so forth. It is said that formerly, the Great Elders...

In order that the scriptures (*pariyatti*) would not disappear, they handed down each section of the Dhamma—such as the *Dīghanikāya* and so forth—to individual groups, saying, "You must preserve this both according to the text (*pāḷi*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); if you are able, learn even more.
In this way, they handed down the entire Dhamma by means of the textual tradition (*gantha*); therein, those monks were known by the name of "reciters of the Long [Discourses]" (*dīghabhāṇaka*).
They are designated as "reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya," and they are not permitted to learn another portion once they have abandoned the section that has become their own responsibility.
With reference to this, it says: "If he is a reciter of the Majjhima," and so forth.
In that context, "the three lower sections" refers to those below the Mahāvagga: the Sagāthaka-vagga and the Nidāna-vagga.
The Khanda-vagga consists of these three sections. The phrase "starting from below the Tika-nipāta" is said with reference to the Eka-nipāta and Duka-nipāta.
The *Dhammapada*, together with its *vatthu* stories, should be mastered along with one's own *Jātaka*;
it is not permissible to go beyond that—this is the intention of the Mahāpaccarī school. The phrase "from there" refers to the *Dīgha Nikāya* and so forth.

It was prohibited with the words "that is not permissible" because there would be no one—even among the bhikkhunīs—to compile and preserve the True Dhamma, nor anyone skilled in the connections between preceding and succeeding sections and so forth.
As for the statement that it is not said that anything should be learned in the Abhidhamma:
herein, since the analysis of the triads of skillful states and so forth is found in the Vinaya, and the path of serenity and insight is found in the Suttantas, [the Abhidhamma is not required].
Furthermore, without the study of the Abhidhamma, it is not understood; it is as if one has entered into darkness.
Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of the Abhidhamma by way of the grasping of the Sutta and Vinaya has already been stated, and thus it was not mentioned separately.
Just as when it is said, "Food should be eaten," it follows—even though not explicitly stated—that "condiments should be consumed," because they are inseparable from it.
It should be understood as being thus constituted.
"With words and syllables that are well-rounded" means: by that [speech] in which the syllables—whether soft, hard, and so forth—are well-rounded, that is, complete, in their respective places.
"Of the city" (*porī*) means: belonging to the city; the meaning is: the speech of the city-dwellers. "Without flaw" (*anelagaḷā*): here...
[He] emits saliva, [which is] free from its dripping. Regarding the term *kalyāṇavākkaraṇo*: here, speech itself is the "utterance" (*vākkaraṇa*), meaning the sound of articulation.

One who possesses a beautiful, sweet utterance is "one of beautiful utterance" (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇo*). It is said, "or bodily contact with a fully ordained nun," and so forth, because one is incapable [of the offense] through sexual intercourse with a fully ordained nun alone, and not with a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*).
148. "With valuable articles" means with articles of great value. "To one ordained on one side" is a locative expression used in the sense of the accusative.

Those ordained in the presence of monks are called those who have changed their gender or the five hundred Sakyan women. However, for one who exhorts these women who are ordained on one side, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
149. "Not having been invited, they wish to go" means that having been invited, they do not wish to go at the conclusion of the meal;
rather, they wish to stay right there. "From" (yataḥ) means from the nunnery. "Having requested" means having requested, [thinking]:
"We too shall stay by means of the exhortation brought by you. "There" (tatra) means in that nunnery. In a residence devoid of monks (abhikkhukāvāse).
If she remains for the rains residence, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if she departs, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Anticipating the objection, "Which of these offenses should be avoided?", he says, "That [offense] must be guarded against.
The meaning is that the offense rooted in departing during the rains residence must be guarded against, as there is a reason for not being guilty of the other one.
Therefore he said, “In times of distress,” and so forth.
“For the sake of exhortation” means for the purpose of requesting exhortation. “Two or three” means by two or by three; here the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
“With what is pleasing” means with bodily action and so forth that produces confidence. “Let him accomplish” means let him accomplish the threefold training.
The state of not being authorized, the state of a bhikkhunī’s full ordination being complete, and the giving of the eight garudhammas by way of exhortation—
these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding exhortation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sunset (Atthaṅgata-sikkhāpada) 153.
Regarding the second [rule], *kokanada* is a specific kind of lotus; it is said to have many petals and to be endowed with excellent color.
This is the meaning here: just as the lotus known as *kokanada*, so too is the lotus with its blossoming face, which has not lost its qualities or its fragrance.
Behold the Perfectly Enlightened One, Aṅgīrasa, who—like the sun in a cloudless sky—blazes with his own splendor and shines forth from that very state, with rays of light streaming from his limbs.
"Dust-remover" (*rajoharaṇa*) is the name for a wiping cloth, so called because it wipes away dust from the body. These verses were spoken preceded by the emission of radiance.

It is called an *obhāsagāthā*. However, in the *Visuddhimagga* and other texts, verses such as “Lust is dust, but it is not called ‘dust’ (*reṇu*)” are referred to as *obhāsagāthās*, yet this is not the verse beginning with “Of one whose mind is exalted” (*adhi-cetaso*).

Furthermore, because this is an *udāna* verse of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, it does not appear in the *Udāna-pāḷi*; it is stated there that this is not an *udāna* verse of the Elder Ekudāniya. But here...
Since it is stated in the Pāḷi itself, it should be understood that this is also a *udāna-gāthā* of the Elder.

And here, for one who exhorts even by means of a non-weighty rule (*agarudhamma*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The three factors here are: the setting of the sun, full ordination (*upasampadā*), and exhorting.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the setting of the sun is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters (Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada) 162.

The third [training rule] is likewise straightforward. Herein, there are four factors: entering the nuns’ quarters, being fully ordained, the absence of a [valid] occasion, and admonishing [the nuns] regarding the heavy rules (garudhamma).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the nuns’ quarters is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Material Gain (Āmisa-sikkhāpada) 164.

In the fourth [offense], even if one speaks with the perception that one is exhorting for the sake of material gain, though one is actually indifferent to material gain, there is no offense because this training rule is dependent upon a specific mental state (sacittaka).
The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are: being fully ordained (upasampanna), and having received formal authorization (sammuti) in accordance with the Dhamma.
The state of being free from worldly gain and speaking thus out of a desire for disrepute—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning worldly gain is concluded.
169. The fifth training rule, concerning the giving of robes, is self-evident.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sewing Robes (Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpada) 176. Regarding the sixth [rule], "the duty concerning the Kathina" (kathinavatta):
