this is said with reference to entering into a state of assistance for one's fellow celibates who are making robes during the Kathina month. "Having deceived" means not saying, "from your relatives," but merely saying, "from a certain bhikkhunī."
Having said this, and having heard the words "of a single bhikkhunī," they perceived her as not being a relative; thus he said, "because of being directed toward what is improper.

Herein, there are three factors: that it belongs to a bhikkhunī who is not a relative, that it has reached the state of being used for wearing as an inner or outer robe, and that it has been sewn or caused to be sewn in the manner already described.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sewing robes is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Arrangements: 183.
Regarding the seventh [offense], "Let us go, sister; let us go, noble lady," an arrangement made with a monk as the primary party is what is meant by "arrangement."
The other [case] concerns one who was previously a bhikkhunī. "A single journey-path" means a path reckoned as a single journey taken together.
"Yesterday" means tomorrow. "Tomorrow" means on the third day.
"Of the two kinds mentioned" means of the two kinds mentioned: traveling on foot and traveling by vehicle. "No access [zone] is obtained" means...
The "vicinity" (upacāra) described for a walled village and so forth—such as the distance of a single clod-throw—is not applicable here because of its proximity.
By this, it is shown that in this context, "village" (gāma) is intended only as the interior of the house, not the entire village territory.
Furthermore, even there, it indicates that an offense occurs only upon stepping across the vicinity where such a boundary exists. Therefore, he said: "at least a ratana apart," and so on.
And here, "entering the precinct" means precisely entering within the precinct.

In this regard, even one who does not actually enter [the village] but travels by a path that lies within two *yojanas* outside the precinct, is said to have traveled after having entered the entire village precinct situated within two *yojanas* on both sides of the road. This applies even when traveling by a path that goes beyond two *yojanas*.
One traveling [by boat] should not be made to account for the distance by the reckoning of a village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*), but rather by the reckoning of half a *yojana* (*addhayojana*).

This being so, in the immediately preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*), an offense by way of the reckoning of a village precinct is established only for one traveling along the bank of a river by means of a boat.
For it is impossible to enter within the precinct of a village by means of a boat. Of the three...
A crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*) is a place where roads meet.

Regarding the phrase "arranged within this interval," the intention is that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) does not apply only when arranging [the journey] among the aforementioned chariot-riders and so forth, but also on the intermediate path.
"For one exceeding half a *yojana*" means for one exceeding half a *yojana* when no village is present; for even in that which constitutes the domain of a village...
Within a distance of half a *yojana* in the forest there is no village; this too is intended here as "forest" (*arañña*) that is without a village, not places such as the Viñjhā forest.
185. Regarding "in the destruction of a kingdom": it refers to the ruin of a kingdom. "Mounted on a wheel" means mounted on either the wheel of postures (*iriyāpatha*) or the wheel of a cart.
For both [of these], the undertaking of the journey after making an agreement, the absence of a signal, the absence of a specific time, and the absence of an emergency [constitute the offense].
Entering another village or traveling beyond half a *yojana*: these are the five factors here.
However, for one who travels in concert with those such as those ordained on only one side, there is an offense under the training rule concerning women (*mātugāma-sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning traveling in concert is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Boarding a Boat (Nāvābhirūhana-sikkhāpada) 189.
Regarding the eighth [rule]: “One bank... pe ... continuously” means that the state of being continuous is described by way of villages situated within a distance of half a *yojana* from the river.
“A forest without a village” is stated because of the absence of any such situated villages. “On a bank-side without a village,” and so forth.
However, this was stated with reference to a river that is more than one and a half *yojanas* wide.

For in the case of a river narrower than that, even when traveling through its middle, since both banks are reached within the space of half a *yojana*, the offenses must be delimited by counting the intervals between villages and by counting half-*yojanas*.
Therefore it is said: "A [river] one *yojana* wide... [and so on] ...by counting half-*yojanas*."

It is stated, "they are *pācittiya* offenses. For by that very same reasoning, it is already established that the counting of offenses occurs based on the bank situated within half a *yojana* of a river that is less than a *yojana* in length.
This supports the meaning already expressed in the passage beginning with, "In all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In that regard, although a *pācittiya* offense is not mentioned for oceans, ponds, and so forth, nevertheless, for one who has the intention for sport—
In this context, it should be understood that there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense;

for even one who initially intends to play, if he subsequently falls asleep on the boat, or if he applies proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), an offense may still arise when crossing between villages and so forth, because it is a fault of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
Furthermore, it should be known that three levels of intention (*ticitta*) are stated for this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the training rule regarding boarding a boat is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule regarding cooked food:
Regarding the ninth [rule], the text states: “For a trainee nun... there is no offense in all cases except for the five kinds of cooked food.”

This was stated with reference to the non-offense (anāpatti) under this training rule (sikkhāpada). For one who consumes what has been obtained through requests or conversations initiated by five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (sahadhammika), there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The five factors here are: that it was prepared by a bhikkhunī; knowing it to be so; the absence of instigation by a layperson; the state of being food; and the swallowing of it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning maturing [beings] is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting in Secret. 198.
Regarding the tenth, "by means of Upananda’s fourth training rule," this refers to the training rule concerning sitting in secret with a woman.

This was said with intentional reference; however, it should be understood that it was stated thus because it is the fourth among the rules laid down concerning Upananda in the fifth section of the Acelaka-vagga.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sitting in private is concluded.
The third chapter on Exhortation is finished.
4. The Chapter on Food.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms from a Lodging House.
206. In the first [sutta] of the fourth section, *imesaṃ yeva* means "of these very [heretics]" (*pāsaṇḍānaṃ*). *Ettakānaṃ* means "of so many" within this heretical sect. 208.
Regarding the phrase "whether going or coming," this should be understood in terms of half a *yojana*.

Furthermore, that which is prepared for others, or even that which is prepared by non-Buddhist ascetics (*titthiya*) who have no faith in the monks—even if it is prepared out of a sense of commonality—it is not [permissible] for the monks.
It is indeed permissible. In this context, there are three factors: [eating] a meal at a public rest-house, not being ill, and having stayed overnight.
The commentary on the training rule regarding meals at public rest-houses is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Group Meals.
209. Regarding the second case, "having overpowered" refers to the archers employed for the purpose of killing the Blessed One after he had been overcome.
Is it not established that this training rule was promulgated during the time of Ajātasattu, given the statement, "He even caused the king to be killed"?
This being so, [it is said in] the Pāḷi: "Now at that time, the kinsman and blood-relative of the King of Māgadha... and so forth.
"Does this not contradict [the passage] beginning: 'He went forth among the Ājīvakas... and said this to Bimbisāra'? It does not contradict it.
For it is said that from the time of Bimbisāra onwards, that Ājīvaka would occasionally invite monks and give alms;
even during the time of Ajātasattu, when the training rules had been laid down, he sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, and the monks..."
Being apprehensive, they restrained him. Therefore, it should be understood that this matter is shown from the very beginning.

215. *Aññamaññaṃ visadisaṃ rajjaṃ* means a kingdom that is dissimilar to one another; those who have come from such [kingdoms] are *verajjakā*. And because they are of various kinds according to birth, clan, and so forth, the meaning is also "those from various kingdoms" (*nānāverajjakā*).
217–8. Since this training rule is understood by way of the matter itself, its purpose as a group meal is established.

It should be understood that, by not stating it explicitly, the *padabhājana* (word-by-word commentary) shows that eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*) is established precisely through the act of being invited.
Therefore, he said: "In two ways," and so forth. Because it is stated, "by whatever synonym," eating in a group occurs even under the general name "Take food," and so on.
However, regarding the instances in the Canon such as traveling on a journey, where it says, "Eat right here," [the rule does not apply].
The feeling of remorse regarding what has been said should be understood as having been committed precisely because it was spoken while referring to items such as boiled rice.
"Taking together" means they stand together and take [the food] without letting go of each other’s twelve-fathom space.
Because it was said, "Give us all four our meal," the text (commentary) states: "You, for one bhikkhu..."
Because it is stated in such passages as “Give food,” it should be understood that a formal request made under the name of “food” constitutes a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*);
furthermore, this applies even if the request was made by someone else, provided that all those eating together accept it from one source.
However, for one who eats a request made separately, there is indeed an offense according to the training rules concerning fine foods and the like.
"Having cut off the incoming strip (*āgantukapaṭṭa*) and made it a subsequent pledge," this is said with reference to the robe-material being prepared.
"He sets it aside" means he fixes one end by tying it to the robe.
"He sews the returned [end]" means he turns the second end of that same [strip] over and sews it down. "He fastens the incoming strip" means, while making it adhere to the robe, he repeatedly—
In various places, he binds it with thread. "He strikes" means that having taken [the material] according to its measure, he strikes it with a stick or other tools.
"He makes thread" means that he winds it into the form of strands and so forth. "He twists" means that he rolls the multi-stranded thread into a single unity by hand or by means of a spindle-stick.
"He performs the turning" means that he prepares the turning-stick and its frame.
Having inserted a thread-ball into it, having placed it in bamboo tubes or similar objects, and having caused it to rotate, they pull it starting from the end of the thread.
220. "With an uninvited fourth" means: that group of four monks in which the fourth is uninvited;
thus it is for the others as well. Therefore he said, "of five groups of four. "Having brought them together" means: having joined them with those [others]. A group (gaṇa).
"It is broken" means that it is not a Saṅgha invited [as a group].
Regarding the phrase "when they have accepted and departed": here, at the moment of accepting an improper invitation, there is no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for the preliminary action;
however, regarding the act of requesting, at the moment of the request itself, an offense of wrong-doing arises according to the other training rules.
It should be accepted. "Accept the invitation" means: receive the meal offered as an invitation. And "those [foods]" refers to the groats and so forth;
because they were taken later by one of those monks, they were not taken together.
By the statement, "The distributor of meals must be wise... [and] must release [the food]," it is meant that the distributor of meals, regarding an improper invitation—
When one has consented, it is considered consented for everyone. This shows that for those taking [the meal] together, there is the offense of *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group).
Because of the fear that the messenger, having arrived at the door, might say again, "Take the food," it is stated, "without standing at the village gate.
Here, the three factors are: the state of eating in a group, the absence of a [valid] occasion (*samaya*), and the act of swallowing.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating in a group is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating in Succession: 221.
In the third [rule], the phrase "the sequence of meals is not fixed" means that the sequence of meals should be assigned according to the sequence of families.
"Not fixed" means not stationary; "uninterrupted" means occurring without interval.
Having added jujube fruits, rice gruel and so forth are called "jujube-sauce" (*badara-sāḷava*).
In the Canon, regarding "successive eating" (*parampara-bhojana*): it refers to the meal of another that follows the meal of the one by whom one was first invited.

While eating. Although *vikappanā* (the assignment of property) is not included in the *mātikā* here by way of being a subsequent ordinance (*anupaññatti*), it is nevertheless counted as one of the "four subsequent ordinances" in the *Parivāra*.

In this regard, although the *Aṭṭhakathā* establishes *parammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the absence of the person) by mentioning it after the *Mahāpaccarivāda*, nevertheless, *sammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the presence of the person) must also be accepted.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The monk who, in the presence of one of the five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, says, 'I give my expected meal to you,' or 'I assign it to you,'" and so forth.

(229) Regarding the phrase "milk or juice," this is said with reference to the five kinds of edible food that remain after the main meal; because these are not considered "food" [in the strict sense], there is no offense even if one drinks them out of order. Therefore, he says, "by one who is eating," and so forth.

Because it arises through the non-performance of the act of *vikappanā* (assignment) by way of non-action, it is said to be "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*) as it originates even from speech. In this case, there are three factors: eating in succession, the absence of a proper occasion, and the swallowing of food.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating in succession is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kāṇamātā.
231. In the fourth [offense], "paṭiyālokaṃ" means the western direction; the meaning is "the back direction.

Even for one who takes it under the perception that it was prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey and so forth, there is indeed an offense because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is unintentional (*acittaka*).

It is called "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*) because an offense is incurred even by saying, "Give this to his hand," for one's own sake. It possesses the characteristics of the aforementioned cakes and porridge.
The five factors here are: being without remainder, not going with a mind of non-relaxation, [the food] belonging to one who is unknown, and receiving more than [allowed].
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the first training rule concerning invitations (pavāraṇā).

237. By the phrase “without saying ‘ti’ three times,” it is shown that the word *iti*—which is obtained through the inherent force (*sāmatthiya*) of the verb *kata*—should not be uttered once the act has been performed.
However, in this context, it should be understood that even when used by those who are unaware of it, the food becomes *atiritta* (leftover) precisely upon being made so.
238–9. To show that the term “*pavārito*” (invited to stop eating) is derived in the sense of the agent, the phrase “one who has performed the invitation” (*katapavāraṇo*), etc., was stated.

The phrase beginning with "And it has also been said" (*vuttampi cetaṃ*) was stated specifically to establish that the word *bhuttāvī* (one who has finished eating) is indeed meaningless [in this context].
*Tāhi* means by those [flour-masses]. *Sattumodaka* is an uncooked preparation made by moistening flour.

However, they grind the flour, make a dough, moisten it, form it into cakes (*pūva*), and cook them; he does not invite [the guest] to partake of that. [He must remain] standing precisely in a place where [food] is to be refused.

Because it is stated, “he refuses,” it should be understood that there is no invitation (*pavāraṇā*) for whatever belongs to one who is shameless, or for what belongs to the Saṅgha and so forth which has not reached oneself, due to such refusal. Regarding the limb that is closer:
for one who stands outside the reach of the hand and gives by leaning forward, the head is the closest limb; it must be defined by its lower limit.
“Having brought toward oneself” means having brought it forward. “He says, ‘Take this food’” means he says this without having brought anything at all.

Because the mere verbal offer was not intended, even if one has begun to take it with a ladle but has not yet lifted it, since it was previously brought in this manner, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*);
therefore it is said, “it is indeed brought. “As soon as it is removed” means...
"Immediately upon being separated from the vessel. "In the case of two equal portions" means even when the portion carried by the server and that carried by another are equal.
Regarding the phrase "take the broth," since only the meat broth was mentioned by name as the object of the invitation, there is no offense for one who refuses it.
In the cases of "fish broth" and so forth, because the meaning of "fish and broth" is possible, [the refusal] applies to the substance as well.
Such a case constitutes an invitation (*pavāraṇā*); it is indeed an invitation even for one who refuses what has been brought by silence, without saying, “Take this.
*Karambaka* is a designation for a mixture. For that which they prepare by mixing many things together is called “*karambaka*.
Regarding the phrase “thinking it was prepared specifically for him,” it is stated that because the substance itself is allowable, he is indeed already invited.
If it was specifically prepared for that person, there is no prohibition. This is the intended meaning here;

he speaks with reference to the very point stated in the passage beginning with "by whom [one] has been asked. However, the reason in this case is difficult to see: the reason why an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is possible due to the greater quantity of food is difficult to perceive;
otherwise, even in the case of *karambaka* (rice-porridge), if there were a large amount of fish and so forth, an invitation would [still] occur.

The intention is: "it should be so. And just as the reason here is difficult to see, it should be understood that the reason for the subsequent statement, "Take the mixed [food]," is likewise difficult to see.

Furthermore, the reason stated as, "But this is indeed mixed with rice," and so forth, does not accord with the statement, "One does not invite [others] when there is less [food]. To give separately means...

The meaning should be understood as follows: by saying “Take the broth,” and so forth, he gives it separately by means of speech; however, he does not separate the broth, etc., from the food by means of the body.

Even when they have not been separated in that way, since an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is impossible for one who refuses [the food], it is stated by name as something excluded from the invitation, just as in cases such as when rice-gruel mixed with solid food is brought and one says, “Take the rice-gruel.”
Alternatively, the intended meaning here should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict what precedes and follows.

Regarding the passage beginning with "a ship or a bridge," even though one stands for a moment at the time of boarding a ship and so forth, and although boarding and the like must be performed, there is no such thing as "standing" because one is intent on going;
however, due to being crowded by people, it is impossible to perform [the action] because there is no space.
It is not permitted. "Without moving" means without shifting it to another place or upwards from the stated location;
however, one is allowed to turn it over right there in that same spot. Therefore he said, "In whichever direction," and so forth.
"Or unallowable food" refers to that which has arisen through such things as corrupting families; that is what is meant by the term "unallowable. Mixed with that [is also unallowable].

This shows that the rice and so forth have become *atiritta* (leftover). Therefore, having removed whatever there is that is not properly made—such as roots, fruits, and the like—the remainder must indeed be eaten.
He is not permitted to make it again; thus, if it is placed back into that same vessel, it is considered "made" together with the first making.
Regarding the phrase "it happens": that same person is not permitted to do it again; another person is permitted. For once it has been done by one, another is permitted to do it again.
However, in another vessel, it is permissible for either that same person or another to do it.
Therefore he said: "That by which it was not done must be done, and that which was not done must be done. Thus, "done in this way" means done in another vessel.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if it is mixed with food," it should be understood that even food stuck to the mouth and so forth must be cleared away before one may eat the remainder.

(241) It should be regarded as originating from non-action because the state of being "remainder" is not established by merely commanding with words. In this context, there are three factors: the fact of having been invited to eat, the food not being "remainder," and the swallowing at the proper time.
The commentary on the first rule regarding invitations is finished.
6. Commentary on the second rule regarding invitations: 243.

Regarding the sixth [rule], because it is stated in the matrix (mātikā) as "when one has eaten," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the conclusion of the meal. [This applies when] one has been invited...
The five factors here are: perceiving it as such, the expectation of being invited, an invitation brought by one who has not yet finished his meal, and the completion of the meal.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning invitations is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Eating at Improper Times 247.
Regarding the seventh [training rule], "dancers' dances" (*naṭānaṃ nāṭakā*) refers to the performances of dancers, such as *Sītāharaṇa* and others. 248–249.

Regarding "in the case of fresh food, for the purpose of fresh food": this means that when fresh food such as cakes (*pūva*) is available, one should perform the function of fresh food by means of those very fresh foods.
They neither fulfill nor accomplish the purpose or function, which is defined as the removal of hunger.

One might object that it is possible for something to perform the function of nutriment in one location, while failing to perform that function in another location due to differences such as the local soil or mineral content;
therefore, he says, "in those various countries," and so forth. However, some [commentators] say: "In one..."
They also say that this was stated in order to show that even for one who is performing the function of eating in one country, it is not permissible at an improper time in other countries as well.
"By way of natural food" means by way of performing the function of eating according to its own nature, uncombined with other foods that are only for the time being.
"There is only confusion" refers to names that have multiple meanings and those that are not well-known.

In this case, there would only be confusion. For that very reason, we too have omitted [the mention of] the "root-root" and so forth by showing alternative synonyms, since they must be understood from the *upadesa* (instructional manual) itself.
"Yaṃ" refers to the *vaṭṭakanda* (circular tuber). "Muḷāla" is simply the thick, young root; it is the "top" of trees, creepers, and so forth, meaning the lower part.
This has been stated by summarizing what was already said. The term "unripe" is used to show that the fruits of the *acchi* tree and others are permitted for life (*yāvajīvika*) even when unripe.

Regarding the phrase "the seeds of the *harītakī* and so forth," some say that the kernel (*miñja*) is "to be taken at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*), but that is incorrect because it is not mentioned in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
*Hiṅgu* is the exudation that flows from the *hiṅgu* tree. *Hiṅgujatu* and the like are merely preparations (*vikati*) of *hiṅgu*.
In this context, *hiṅgujatu* is the exudation made by boiling the stalks and leaves of the *hiṅgu* tree. *Hiṅgusipāṭikā* is the exudation made by boiling the leaves of the *hiṅgu* tree;
some also say it is made by mixing [the leaves] with something else. *Taka* is [the exudation] from the tip of the [stalk].
"Exuding from the bowl" (*nikkhantasileso*): this refers to that which has exuded from the bowl. "Exuding from the leaf" (*takapaṇṇi*):

this refers to what has been made into a paste by frying it on a leaf; they also say it is that which has exuded from a stalk. In this context, there are three factors: being at the wrong time, being within the proper time, and being swallowed.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating at improper times is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding storing food. 252–3. Regarding the eighth [rule]:
“Such” means without curry or condiment. Whether it be *yāvakālika* (food for the day) or *yāmakālika* (food for the watch of the night)… [omission] …it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Although here in the Pāḷi the terms *khādanīya* (hard food) and *bhojanīya* (soft food) include only what is to be consumed during the day (*yāvakālika*) and not what is to be consumed during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*), nevertheless, there is the statement:
“There is no offense if one eats after having stored it for the watch of the night,” and also here:

“Monks, by means of what is to be consumed during the watch of the night, seven-day [medicine]... [and so on]... lifetime [medicine], if received on that very day, is allowable during the watch; once the watch has passed, it is not allowable.”

Because it is stated elsewhere and because of the force of the expression "yāmakālika" (lasting for a watch of the night), it should be understood that the commentators, who knew the Blessed One’s intention, have explained "yāmakālika" as referring specifically to the object of the offense of storing food (sannidhikāraka-pācittiya).
The word "yaṃ" refers to the bowl; this is used in the accusative case in relation to the action of rubbing. "The finger-mark is visible" means...

Even in the absence of moisture, it is perceived due to the smoothness of the bowl. "That which" refers to what is for the time being (*yāvakālika*) and what is for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
"Only not relinquished" means that, because of a lack of concern, it has not been given to one who is not fully ordained;

and this is said with reference specifically to the objects such as those for the time being, and not to the act of receiving them while they are still there. For it is impossible to receive [an object] while remaining in that place without having relinquished the object itself.
It is possible to renounce [the bowl], yet there is no such statement [in the Vinaya].
If there were, it would contradict the statement: "If the bowl is not well-washed... [and] while eating, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

For one who is striving to remove the food by washing, there can be no expectation regarding the act of receiving [the bowl], which would otherwise give rise to an offense of expiation for eating on the following day.

However, since the expectation that exists regarding the alms-bowl also extends to the material goods contained therein, the state of being free from expectation regarding material goods cannot be found here;
therefore, it is said that accepting [food] without having abandoned one's attachment to material goods incurs a *pācittiya* offense on the following day.

Now, if it is thought: "Insofar as the state of being free from expectation regarding material goods is not found here, in that same measure there is also no freedom from expectation regarding the act of acceptance."
"It is not obtained. If that were the case, it would follow that wherever there is expectation for material goods (*āmisa*), there also expectation for acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) does not cease;
and thus, giving without expectation regarding acceptance could not be spoken of as a separate category.
Furthermore, if this [expectation] were intended in the Commentary as a cause for the relinquishing of acceptance, then this [interpretation] is even more appropriate.

This must be stated separately, just as there is the relinquishing of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-vijahana*) through renunciation (*paccuddhāra*), even when one is still in possession of the robe out of expectation for it.
And since this method exists, it has been said that there would be no such thing as "fixing" [the bowl] upon bowls that have been struck by the *gaṇṭhika* (the bowl-fastener).
Therefore, as for what was stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "If, having renounced it to another, even though it is not given, should [it be] received... [and so forth].

"The acceptance is relinquished by giving it away without expectation; that too is permissible on the second day," and so forth—this should not be accepted as authoritative. Regarding "natural food" (*pakati-āmisa*), this refers to cooked rice and other allowable foods that are to be consumed within the proper time (*yāvakālika*).
"Two" refers to [food] received before midday that is to be consumed during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
For one who eats before the meal with a mouth containing food, there is one offense on account of the condition of storing up (*sannidhi-paccayā*);

and for one who partakes of what is mixed with what is to be consumed during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) by means of a vessel for what is to be consumed during the day (*yāvakālika*), there is one offense on account of the condition of not being left over (*anatiritta-paccayā*). Thus, there are two *pācittiya* offenses. Regarding the "two alternatives" (*vikappa-dvaye*), this refers to the two sides of the classification:

with food (*sāmisapakkha*) and without food (*nirāmisapakkha*). There is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*): there is a grave offense in the case of human flesh, and an offense of wrong-doing in the remaining cases. [This concerns] the state of being for the day (*yāvakālika*) and for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
The state of being stored and its consumption—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning storing food is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Luxurious Foods.
259. In the ninth [section], regarding foods mixed with delicacies (*paṇītasammissa*), the phrase "delicate foods" (*paṇītabhojana*) is used.

However, since foods were already mentioned previously in the text, they are not explicitly shown here as being well-known; rather, because they are mixed with such delicate items, they are called "delicate foods.
To demonstrate their classification, it is said: "That is to say: ghee, fresh butter," and so forth.

Regarding the term *sappibhatta*: although here the meaning can be understood as "rice mixed with ghee" or even "ghee and rice," since it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "there is no such thing as *sappibhatta* in the way there is *sālibhatta* [rice with salt]," one cannot take it to mean anything else.
For in such instances, the teachers of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathācariyā*) alone are the authority.

“Roots” refers to allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). Therefore, regarding the statement “there is no offense,” they say that although there is no *pācittiya* due to the absence of a prior agreement (*visaṅketa*), one is not exempt from the *dukkaṭa* for [offering] soup and boiled rice.
Furthermore, the phrases “with allowable ghee” and “with unallowable ghee” are stated with reference to the status of the meat as either allowable or unallowable.
261. The Mahānāma training rule refers to the subsequent training rule concerning the invitation for requisites for four months.
For one who is not ill, even when requesting at a place where no invitation has been made, it is permissible provided one establishes a limit of time or a limit of medicine;
however, it is not permissible to request beyond that which was invited by the Saṅgha, nor, even within the limits, to request for anything other than what is required for medicine.
Regarding the statement, "He is equal to one who requests medicine because of illness," it is said that he must be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Here, there are four factors: the food being of a superior kind, the person not being ill, the obtaining [of the food] through a request not made by oneself, and the swallowing [of the food].
The commentary on the training rule concerning superior food is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Teeth-Cleaning Wood (Dantapoṇa-sikkhāpada) 263.
In the tenth [rule], "tightly bound" (*ghanabaddha*) means bound by thick flesh; the meaning is that the body is firm and compact. 264.
"The mouth-door" (*mukhadvāra*) refers to the opening below the mouth; the meaning is the throat-pipe (*galanāḷika*). And thus...
Even that which has entered through the nose is considered as having entered through the mouth-door; however, that which is merely placed in the mouth is not considered "entered.
By "food" (āhāra), what is intended is that which is to be swallowed at the proper time (kālīka), and not water.

For even though water may be included among medicines, it is strictly non-time-bound (akālika) because it is only the [other] food that is subject to the time-restriction once accepted. Indeed, the formal act of acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) does not apply to water. Therefore, by that very monk...

Even for one who eats solid food together with water that has been boiled, water that has been received long ago, or water that has stood in an unallowable hut, there is no fault such as cooking for oneself (*sāmapāka*).
For it will be said: “If a bhikkhu boils water for the sake of rice-gruel... it is permissible,” and so forth.
However, the bhikkhus did not understand this intention at that time; therefore, he said, “without correctly discerning the meaning,” and so on.

265. *Rathareṇumpīti*: dust resembling the dust that rises when a chariot is moving. By this, it is shown that even if something finer than that is seen whirling in the air, it is not to be reckoned [as a hand-span]. *Akallako* means one who is ill.

Regarding the phrase “or to take it... by its near side,” even for one standing upright in the air and taking what has been lifted by another, the range of the hand must be delimited starting from the sole of the foot—which is the nearest part of the body—and not from the edge of the head.
"Starting from" is what is being shown. In this context, for the phrase "by the near side," the meaning should be understood as "by the lower side.

Furthermore, here, because in the commentary on the *Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada* it is stated, "If a monk is sitting, starting from the rear edge of the seat," and so forth, the delimitation is shown by starting from the far side of the limb closest to the recipients.

Here too, it should be understood that the range of the hand (hatthapāsa) must be delimited starting from the lower surface of the recipient’s foot, which is situated in the air and constitutes the near limit, down to the toes which constitute the far limit;
and for the donor, starting from the lower surface of his own toes, which constitute the near limit. It is by this same method [that the measurement is determined].

Even when one is lying on the ground and receives [an offering] from the hand of someone sitting on their head, the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*) must be measured starting from the neck—the far limit being the area near the head—and not from the soles of the feet.
This should be understood accordingly even in the case of giving while lying down; for it is said: "That limb which is nearest."
“With the perception of receiving” means with the perception produced [in the mind] thinking, “I shall receive it with a bed or the like.
By this, he shows that there is no need to utter the words “I receive. In certain commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) or in some sections.
“On a plank that cannot be carried” means on one that cannot be carried by a man of medium strength. “Having wiped and having received” means even when it has been wiped...

This was stated for the purpose of receiving [food] when there is the appearance of dust particles, but not when there is none. "That, however" refers to the alms-food already held in the hand above, without having received the dust that has fallen.

"There is no offense" means there is no fault such as that of improper conduct (*durupaciṇṇa*). Even if one has taken it without first saying, "I will give this to one who is not fully ordained," and so forth, it was stated [in that way] to avoid the Vinaya-offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even if it was taken without doing so, once it has been received...
There is no offense at all for one who consumes it. The phrase "having given to one not fully ordained" is also stated because it conforms to the previous mental application (*ābhoga*).
"With a caruka" means with a small vessel. "Because it was brought" refers to the moment it is being given.
However, at the time of taking it away after having given it, if ashes or drops fall [onto the ground], it must be received again, as it constitutes a fresh offering (*abhihāra*).
They say it is "gone away. It is appropriate to set it aside while saying, "I shall remove it so that it does not fall.
If one removes it with the conventional perception [of its being gone], the act of offering is not interrupted, and it is indeed considered accepted.
It is permissible to take it even from the rim of the bowl; thus, it is permissible to reach out one's hand and touch the upper part of the rim of the bowl while it is being offered.
“Having stepped on with the foot” means having stepped upon it with the thought, “I shall receive it with my foot. “Some” refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri.
“Merely a matter of words” means that there is only a difference in the mere sound of the terms *paṭibaddha* and *appaṭibaddha*;
it remains merely connected to the body. Therefore, the intention is that their statement should not be accepted.

"Having him bring it by means of that person" means: having commanded the one who went to the presence of the monk [to whom the food belonged], saying "bring him here," it is permissible for the other [monk] to have it brought by that person;
this is the meaning. "Not beyond that" is said with reference to what was not personally accepted on that very day.
However, they say that what was accepted on that very day may be consumed even if it is not re-accepted on subsequent days and so forth.
“They perish” means they go to destruction; the intention is that there are no offenses of a grave nature (thullaccaya) or of non-receiving for those [particles] because they are mere dust.
By the phrase “arisen anew,” it is shown that in the case of sugarcane and so forth, because they are freshly attached, it is not subject to the formal designation [of an offense].
“The same method applies” refers to the fault of storage and so forth. Therefore he says, “For it is not,” and so on.

This shows that when all five factors of receiving are fulfilled, that which has been taken with the desire to swallow it is indeed called "received," because receiving is permitted only in regard to things intended for swallowing. Likewise,
oil and other substances that have been taken and set aside for external use may be received and consumed provided there is the desire to swallow them.

In the passage beginning with "Of some," even for the sake of those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), although the food may be placed somewhere, the act of receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is not lost the moment it is released from the hand;
rather, the act of receiving is lost only when it has fallen into a vessel.
And since the vessel is still being looked after by the monk for the sake of the following day, the food contained therein is like that which remains in a bowl that has not yet been washed.

It should be understood that because there is a suspicion that [the bowl] does not relinquish its status as a formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa), it is stated that "it must be placed in the hand of a novice.
For in such cases, one should not seek logical consistency; one should simply proceed according to the manner in which it has been stated.
By the phrase "rice gruel contained in the bowl," even if the rice gruel touches the rim of the bowl, it has not been formally accepted or taken up.
This shows that [the offense occurs] when the monk is touched against his will. "He makes [her] take hold" means he causes her hand to touch [the object].
"A load suitable for receiving" means a weight that can be lifted by a man of medium build. "It must not be covered up" is said with reference to what has been released from the hand;
however, if one covers with the other hand what is still held in the hand, or even if it has been released from the hand...
There is no fault for one who, having touched [the vessel], lets down the upper lid.

"He receives" means: if a large branch held above for the sake of shade should break off by any means and dust clinging to it should fall into the mouth, he receives it after having had it made allowable (*kappiya*). "In a *kuṇḍaka*" means in a large jar.

"In that too" means even in the case of exchanging alms-bowls. "Having had [it] taken" means having had something not formally received (appaṭiggahita) that is suitable for the proper time (kālika) taken.
"Of the second elder" means that after he has had the first elder relinquish it by saying, "Give the elder’s bowl to me," he gives it to the second elder. "But here" refers to the exchange of bowls.
The reason is as follows: "Just as novices [might think], 'From this [person], let us also..."
The thought arises, "She is giving [it]," but they say that this is not the reason; and that is correct.
However, for one who does not have such a thought, it is permissible to eat even without turning [the food over].
"To remove what is constantly moving" means to remove stones, gravel, and so forth after having moved them. "It should be placed on the hearth" refers to when there is no fire.

This was said with reference to a cooking pot (*uddhana*). Regarding the churning of what is being cooked in the pot, he says, "it is both self-cooked," because the uncooked rice grains that were on top fall down and cook.
When the bowl is placed on a stand, it means the bowl containing food not yet formally accepted is set aside for the purpose of being accepted again.
"By the very mention of 'one'": this refers to the inclusion [of the food] by way of not discarding it again after it has already been included among the requisites of the novices (*sāmaṇera*).

"It is permissible to eat": this is stated because the column of smoke was received on that very day. "A serving of rice," etc., is an exposition regarding eating at the improper time (*vikālabhojana*) as a secondary discussion connected to what is not formally declared (*abbhohārika*).
"With sea water": with that which has not been formally received (*appaṭiggahita*). "Hailstones" (*himakarakā*): [so called].
Sometimes they are specific types of water that have become solidified, like stone markings formed by falling rainwater; there is no need for formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) regarding them.

Therefore he said, "they are merely of the nature of water. By stating "it is permissible only before the meal," he shows that although it is not subject to the offense of eating what has not been formally accepted (*appaṭiggahita*), it is nevertheless subject to the offense of eating at the wrong time (*vikālabhojana*).
"It clings" means it shows the color of clay on both the mouth and the hands. "Thick" means that even if it does not cling to the hands or mouth, it should still be accepted.
"Merely a coating" indicates the absence of dust or milk. "It sprinkles; it should be accepted" is said because the scent of the flower-essence becomes apparent.
"In the great elements" means in the great elements such as earth and so forth, which are dependent upon the bodies of living beings.
"Everything is permissible" means that everything dependent upon one's own body or the bodies of others is permissible;

the intention is that because it conforms to what is not forbidden meat, it does not give rise to a grave offense (thullaccaya) or the like. "It falls" means it falls after being severed from one's own body. "Having cut it from a tree," etc.

Because it has been so stated, it should be understood that it is permissible to dig the earth for the sake of clay, and likewise to cut any other medicinal root, leaf, or the like, and to consume it even without making it into ash and even if it has not been formally accepted.
In this case, there are four factors: the state of being unaccepted, the state of being unauthorized, the absence of the condition of being cleared by smoke and so forth, and the act of swallowing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks is finished.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Food, is completed.
5. The Chapter on Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-vagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) 273.
In the first [rule] of the fifth section, the phrase "in my name" refers even to that which has been given by a monk after having placed it on the ground.
[The factors are: being of another sect, not being permitted, being edible, and [giving] with one's own hand for the purpose of eating.
"Giving with an unfixed vessel": these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning naked ascetics (acelaka) is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning inciting [to give] (uyyojana).

274. In the second [offense], there are three factors: the desire to engage in improper conduct; the incitement of one who is fully ordained for that very purpose; and the transgression of the vicinity of that person.
The commentary on the training rule regarding incitement is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Being with Food.
281. Regarding the third [offense] in the Pāḷi, "in a small house": here, a "small house" is intended as one less than five cubits in width.
And in that case, even if one does not leave the hand's reach from the door-frame (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa), there is still a crossing over the ridge-pole (piṭṭhivaṃsa);
thus it says, "having crossed over the ridge-pole. "Whether made in such a way or that way" means having raised it onto the ridge-pole.
Or [the offense occurs] by not having made [the formal act], or by making it without having formally proposed it.
283. In the text, "those free from lust" (*vītarāga*) includes those whose lust is not currently manifest (*apariyuṭṭhita-rāga*) as well as non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
"With mind" (*sacittaka*) means with a mind that has entered [into the act] and is seated [therein]. It refers to the presence of husbands and wives whose lust is manifest (*pariyuṭṭhita-rāga*).
Being in a sleeping quarters, the absence of a second monk, and sitting down intruding [upon another]—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating with [another] is finished.
284–289. The fourth and fifth [rules] have their meanings already explained.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Conduct (Cārittasikkhāpada) 298.

Regarding the sixth [offense], because it is stated that "there is no requirement to announce [the offense] after having searched," if one who should not be searched for is seen in a place suitable for approaching, even if he has gone beyond the range of hearing for ordinary speech—
Having approached while standing still, one must ask for permission. Therefore he said: “Moreover... [etc. ...whomever he sees, he should ask that person for permission,” and so forth.

In the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), because it is stated specifically regarding the interior of a monastery (*antarārāma*) and so on, there is an offense even for one who crosses from the monastery into the village street without a permitted reason; however, this does not apply only to one who crosses the precinct of a house (*gharūpacāra*).
As for what is stated in the Canon: “For one entering the precinct of another’s house... [etc. ...when he steps over the threshold with his first foot,” and so forth.
This was said. It was said with reference to one who has entered a village;

nevertheless, even for one who does not step onto the vicinity of another’s house but goes along the middle of the street, stands facing the door of whichever house he desires, looks at the people, and then departs, there is likewise a *pācittiya* offense.
Regarding this, some say: "For one passing through the street, there are offenses corresponding to the number of times he crosses the vicinity of a house."
Others, however, say: "It is by way of the number of families [visited] for whose sake one has gone. The five factors here are:
accepting an invitation to any one of the five kinds of cooked food; failing to inform a monk who is present; going from the house of a supporter to another house;
not passing beyond the midday hour; and the absence of a valid occasion (*samaya*).
The commentary on the training rule on conduct is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule: 303.

Regarding the seventh [rule], "Mahānāma": he was the son of Sukkodana, the elder brother of the Elder Anuruddha, and the elder brother of the Teacher. The Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana, while the Elder Nanda was the son of Suddhodana himself.
305. In the Pāḷi, “you shall bring [the medicine] at the proper time” means you shall spend the present day, or it means you shall bring the medicine tomorrow.

Regarding the statement, “There is an invitation (pavāraṇā) that has both a limit for medicine and a limit for the night,” the medicine specified in the third section must be taken only within the specified time limit, not beyond it. Otherwise, it would be separate.

It should be understood that there is no purpose [in making such a request]. The three factors here are: the Saṅgha’s invitation being limited, the requesting of medicine beyond that limit, and not being ill.
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Marching Out with an Army (Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpada) 315.
Regarding the eighth [offense], the phrase "one by one" includes here an army consisting of two divisions as well as one consisting of three divisions.
The two factors in this case are: going without such requisite conditions and so forth for the purpose of seeing an army of four divisions set out for battle, and seeing it in an unauthorized place.
The commentary on the training rule regarding being stationed with an army is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Staying with an Army: 319.
In the ninth [rule], there are two factors here: "the fourth sunset while with an army" and "not being ill."
The commentary on the training rule concerning military camps is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Military Parades (Uyyodhika-sikkhāpada) 322.

Regarding the tenth [rule], the meaning of “how many lakhs have you won? in the Pāḷi is “how much have you obtained? Herein, there are two factors: going without a legitimate reason to see a military parade and so forth, and seeing it in an unauthorized place.
The commentary on the training rule concerning wrestling is finished.
The fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics, is completed.
6. The Chapter on Drinking Liquor.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Drinking Liquor (Surāpāna-sikkhāpada) 328.
Regarding the first [offense] in the sixth chapter, the Pāli text states:

*kiṇṇapakkhittā* means that which is made by adding what is called *kiṇṇa*—the seeds of liquor such as grain sprouts—and so forth, instead of adding leavened bread (*piṭṭhapūva*) and the like. *Sambhārasaṃyuttā* means that which is compounded with many ingredients such as mustard seeds and so forth.
The juice of flowers such as *madhuka*, *tāla*, and coconut, having been fermented for a long time, is called "flower-liquor" (*pupphāsava*).
Likewise, there is fruit-liquor (*phalāsava*) from fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*). Grape juice is honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*). Sugarcane juice is molasses-liquor (*guḷāsava*).

The juice of various ingredients such as the three myrobalans (*tiphalā*), tamarind (*tikkaṭuka*), and so forth, having been fermented for a long time, is called "mixture-liquor" (*sambhārāsava*). "Starting from the seed" refers to the aforementioned flour and other substances.
From the moment it is placed in the vessel for the purpose of immersion.
329. *Loṇasovīraka* and *sutta* are specific medicinal preparations compounded from many material ingredients.

Regarding the training rules concerning those who are mobilized (*uyyutta-sikkhāpada*), the fact that they are "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*) while being "unintentional" (*acittaka*) is according to the method previously stated; thus, in that regard, there is nothing [further to be said].
It should be understood that this was stated by the phrase "and here, due to ignorance of the basis," etc., precisely to demonstrate that specific distinction—
such as being a worldly offense— even on the side of a mindless state, because of the presence of unwholesome mental states established by the specific nature of the uncommon basis.
As for what remains to be said here, it has been explained in detail in the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary on the first *Pārājika*.
It should be understood that this was stated by way of purifying the point of transgression. Herein, there are two factors: the state of being fermented liquor and the drinking thereof.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of *surā* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Prodding with the Fingers 330.
In the second [offense], the two factors here are: having the intention for amusement, and touching the body of one who is fully ordained with one’s own body.
The commentary on the training rule on prodding with the fingers is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Joking (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada) 338.
Regarding the third rule, in the phrases "perceiving it as joking when it is joking" (*hasadhamme hasadhammasaññī*) and so forth:

when there is something to be done, such as the mere act of laughing, one attends to it by perceiving that which is joking as "joking. Thus, it is by way of perceiving the joking as "joking" [that the offense occurs].
The meaning should be understood as follows. "Hauling up" means bringing a boat standing in the water onto the bank.

"In the sections on falling and rising" refers to the movement by way of jumping up and down like a frog on the surface of the water, performed by means of throwing a single pebble for that purpose. The water reaching above the ankles is due to the intention to laugh.
"Playing" consists of two factors.
The commentary on the training rule concerning laughing is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect.

344. In the fourth [case], "in accordance with the Sutta" refers to the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*); they also call them the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For one who is fully ordained, the two factors are: speaking what has been prescribed and showing disrespect.
The commentary on the training rule regarding disrespect is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Terrifying.
345. In the fifth [offense], there are two factors: being fully ordained, and making an effort with the desire to frighten someone within the range of their sight or hearing.
The commentary on the training rule regarding frightening is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Fire.
354. In the sixth [offense], "the firebrand has fallen" means it has fallen outside of the fire-pot. "Extinguished":

for one who extinguishes a firebrand and then rekindles it by throwing it into the fire in the pot, there is a *pācittiya* offense; likewise for one who merely throws fuel [into it], or for one who rekindles an extinguished fire in the pot by blowing on it with the mouth or other means.
The absence of such causes as illness, etc., and the desire to warm oneself, [constitute the factors of the offense].
"Setting on fire" refers to three factors.
The commentary on the rule concerning fire is finished.
7. Commentary on the Rule Concerning Bathing.

357. Regarding the phrase "the city was closed" in the seventh [case] of the text: it should be understood that the king, desiring to bathe for a long time, gave permission, saying, "I shall dwell in the outer park having provided protection; close the city and guard it," and they did so.
"Asambhinna" means "unadorned"; that is, on that day, he had merely woken up without having again taken up his ornaments.
The intention [is as follows]: in the Middle Country, the two factors are the shaving of less than half the head and the absence of the [proper] occasion and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning bathing is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning disfiguring [the hair].

368. Regarding the phrase "with a new robe obtained on the eighth [day]": here they say that even a robe obtained for a short time as a temporary loan for the purpose of wearing it—which was not previously made allowable (*akatakappa*)—is included.

369. Since it is stated in general terms that "new means not made allowable," a robe used by another monk after he had applied the *kappabindu* (the mark of allowance) is indeed considered "made allowable" (*kata-kappa*), whether one obtains it from him, or receives it from someone else.

It should be understood that there is no such thing as "new. Because it is stated, "to wear as an undergarment or to wrap around," they say that even a shoulder-tied saffron robe must be made permissible (*kappa*) since it is to be wrapped around.
"Leather-blue" (*cammakāranīla*) means blue leather being dyed blue; some say it refers to what is naturally blue.
Regarding the aforementioned robe, its state of not having been made permissible and its state of not being one of the eight robes, etc., [are established].
The three factors beginning with "wearing" [the inner robe] are complete.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making [robes] discolored is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reassignment.

374. "With whom" (*yena*) in the ninth [offense] means with whomsoever, or in whose presence; such is the meaning. The three factors are: the failure to relinquish what has been personally assigned, the state of the robe being subject to assignment, and the use [of the robe] without trust.
The commentary on the training rule concerning assignment (*vikappana*) is finished. 10.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Non-Resignation of Robes (*cīvara-apanidhāna*).

378. In the tenth [offense] of the Pāḷi, by the word *api* (even) in the phrase "even one who merely intends to laugh," there is included one whose mind is not intent on theft but who, out of anger, desires to cause suffering, as well as one who desires to proclaim disrepute.
For this very reason, it is stated as "threefold feeling. For a fully ordained monk (*upasampanna*), there are two factors: the setting aside of bowls and so forth, and the desire to harass, etc.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the storage of robes is finished.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Alcohol, is completed.
7. The Chapter on Living Beings.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Intentional Killing of Living Beings (Sañcicca-pāṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 382.
Regarding the first [offense] of the seventh [training rule]: "One who shoots an arrow at a living being is an archer (*issāsa*).

The connection here is that there is no such thing as "life" (*jīvita*) existing separately [from the body]. In this context, "living beings" (*pāṇa*) refers to sentient beings (*satta*). "A careful person should perform their duty" means...
Having observed that there is no harm even to small creatures, one should perform the duties such as warming [the water] and sweeping in this manner.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the intentional killing of living beings is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada) 387.

Regarding the second [rule], "in a place where water is settled": this refers to ground consisting of mud, stones, and so forth. "Therein" means in water that has been made permissible (kappiya-udaka). The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the training rule concerning water with living beings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada) 392.

Regarding the third [rule], because it is stated, "having gone into the presence of that bhikkhu," the offense is a *pācittiya* for one who reopens [the case] in the very presence of the person whose legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*) was settled by a formal act of the Saṅgha. However, if one reopens it in their absence, it is merely a *dukkaṭa*.

395. Because it is stated, "If one reopens [a case] that is a legitimate act (*dhammakamma*), perceiving it as an illegitimate act (*adhammakamma*), there is no offense," [this refers to cases involving] disrespect and so forth.
The reopening itself is not unwholesome; rather, it becomes unwholesome through the perception that it is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*) or through doubt.
There are three factors: the state of having been settled according to the Dhamma, the knowledge [of this], and the reopening.
The commentary on the training rule concerning reopening is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada) 399.

Regarding the fourth [rule], it is stated under the heading of "abandoning the burden" that one indeed incurs an offense. "The person who is the subject" (vatthupuggala) refers to the person who has committed the offense.
For it is only when there is a desire to conceal it that the necessity of reporting it to another is stated; [this applies] to the person who is the subject of the matter.

The intention is that since there is no such thing as "reporting," it is indeed concealment. "The limit is severed" means that even if the offense continues through a succession of individuals, once one relinquishes the burden by thinking, "I will conceal it," the limit of the offense is severed. 400.
"Emission of semen and physical contact with one who is not fully ordained—this constitutes gross misconduct."

Regarding the phrase "by name," one should investigate whether this contradicts the commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of a grave offense (*duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada*), which states:
"For one who is not fully ordained... [omission] ...the first five training rules refer to what is called a 'grave offense' (*duṭṭhulla*) as transgression; the remaining ones are not grave offenses.
However, for him, the emission of semen, physical contact, a grave offense, and lustful intent are indeed called transgressions. This is stated with reference to affection for a person.

Furthermore, it should be understood that when one conceals [an offense] out of fear, thinking, "Others will criticize me," it is precisely at the moment of concealment that aversion (paṭigha) arises;

therefore, it is described as "painful feeling" (dukkhavedanā). For one who has been fully ordained, there are two factors: the recognition of a grave offense (duṭṭhulla-āpatti) and the relinquishing of the burden due to the desire to conceal it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning grave offenses is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Under Twenty Years of Age: 402.

Regarding the fifth [training rule], "the craft of form" (*rūpasippa*) refers to the craft of coin-exchanging. One who has completed the twentieth year, counting from the time spent lying in the womb, is called "twenty by conception" (*gabbhavīso*).
404. "The full moon day of the departure" refers to the full moon of the month of Āsāḷha, which is the full moon immediately following that of Sāvaṇa.
"On the first day of the fortnight" refers to the later date for entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*).

The meaning is that they confer the higher ordination (*upasampadā*) on one born during the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*), after having dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months. "Thirty nights and days make a month; twelve months... [make a year].
Because of the statement, "the year [is thus]," it is said that "four months are lost.
"They postpone the rains" means they draw the rains upward; the meaning is that they enter the rains after discarding one month as an intercalary month.
Therefore, every third year consists of thirteen months. "Taking those two months" refers to [the period] from the full moon of the departure [from the rains retreat].
The Great Pavāraṇā lasts until the day of birth. Therefore, for the sake of those two months yet to come, one takes the two months obtained from the extra month (adhikamāsa).

Thus he said: "One who, having performed Pavāraṇā, will become twenty years [of standing]," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having become free from doubt," this refers to taking one extra month from the eighteen years, and then [counting] even within those twenty years.
This was said with reference to being always twenty years old in full, by way of subtracting four months for the sake of the fourteenth day [of the lunar month].
"Having performed the *pavāraṇā*, he will become twenty years old" means that when the day of the Great *Pavāraṇā* has passed, he will become twenty years old including the month of the womb.
Therefore, because even the months of the womb are included in the calculation...
Therefore, "twenty-one years old" is said with reference to being twenty years of age by birth. 406.

"He ordains another" means he ordains while acting as either a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or a teacher (*ācariya*). "He too" refers to the one who ordains being himself unordained. The two factors are: being less than twenty years of age, and knowing that [the candidate] is so while acting as a preceptor and ordaining him.
The commentary on the training rule regarding those under twenty years of age is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Traveling with a Robbery Caravan (Theyyasattha-sikkhāpada). 409.
In the sixth [rule], there are three factors: the state of being a robbery caravan, making an arrangement after knowing [the plan], and traveling without a pre-arranged signal.
The commentary on the training rule on traveling with a robbery caravan is finished.
412. The seventh [training rule] is exactly as previously stated.
8. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Training Rule: 417.

Regarding the eighth [rule], "obstacle" (*antarāya*): it is called an "obstacle" because it comes (*eti*) or arrives in between (*antara*), that is, in the middle; it refers to misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth.
“Ānantariyadhammā” means volition and other such states that are fixed toward the production of a fruit in the immediately following existence.
The phrase “not of heaven” is stated because the act of defiling a nun does not constitute an immediate offense (ānantariya).

However, for one who forcibly defiles noble female disciples (ariyasāvikā) or even virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇaputhujjana), it is indeed an immediate offense. This constitutes an obstacle to liberation (mokkhantarāyikatā).
However, even for a lustful bhikkhunī who is of natural character, it is stated that there is no arising of the Path in that very existence for one who violates her.
In that existence, only the views of non-restraint, rootlessness, non-action, and nihilism are the factors of fixed wrong view.
The mention of eunuchs and so forth is merely illustrative. All rebirth-linkings with two roots or without roots are indeed obstacles to kamma-resultant states.
Because even those with two roots have not yet attained the Path. *Ayaṃ* means Ariṭṭha.

*Rasena rasaṃ* means having equated the flavor of the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure with the blameless flavor of consuming requisites. *Upanento viya* means as if joining them together; or rather, that very reading (*upanento*) is the text.

Regarding the simile of the skeleton (*aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā*): here, because it is devoid of flesh, the bone itself is called a "skeleton" (*kaṅkala*). In the sense of being a hindrance (*palibhañjanaṭṭhena*).
In the sense of being inevitably subject to falling. "In the sense of excessive striking" means in the sense of striking excessively.
In the Canon, the passage beginning, "Thus by the Blessed One... [it was said] ...it is not capable of being an obstacle," is stated in accordance with the specific instance (*vatthu*).
However, failing to grasp it in this way, one might instead grasp whatever was spoken by the Blessed One in a distorted manner and, even when others speak to the contrary, refuse to let go.
Even for one who is conversing, it is permissible—by following the stated method and applying the formal statement of *samanubhāsana* (admonition) accordingly—to charge him with an offense;
and having selected any one of the three grounds, such as the non-acknowledgment of an offense, the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) may be carried out.
Even without performing the *samanubhāsana*, as soon as the monks have said, "Venerable sir, do not speak thus," [the procedure may proceed].
It should be understood that a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) may indeed be carried out even for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of not relinquishing one's adherence.
There are two factors: the legitimacy of the legal act and the failure to relinquish [the view] after being admonished.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Associating with One Who Has Been Suspended (Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpada) 424.

Regarding the ninth [rule], because it is stated that "one who has been suspended and not reinstated," it should be understood that a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) had been carried out against Ariṭṭha.
425. Since the word "under one roof" (*ekacchanne*) is used in the Canon in a general sense, it refers even to lying down under one roof when they are in separate precincts.

For one who does not know the designation—even for an Arahant—and for those who follow one who has been suspended, there is likewise an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The two factors are: the state of not having performed the *anuddhamma* (restoration), and engaging in social intercourse and so forth after knowing [the suspension].
The commentary on the training rule regarding social intercourse with one who is suspended is finished.
10. Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule (Sikkhāpada). 428.
In the tenth [rule], *pireti* is a particle used in the sense of addressing. The remainder is exactly according to the method explained in the two preceding training rules.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule is finished.
The seventh chapter on Living Beings is finished.
8. The Chapter on Those of the Same Dhamma.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Those of the Same Dhamma.

434. In the first [offense] of the eighth chapter, there are two constituent factors: the statement made by one who has been fully ordained (*upasampanna*) regarding what has been prescribed, and the statement made under some pretext by one who does not wish to train.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those in accordance with the Dhamma (*sahadhammika-sikkhāpada*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning remorse (*vilekhana-sikkhāpada*).
438. In the second [case], "shamelessness" (*alajjitā*) means by way of being shameless. The same applies to the remaining cases.
The definition of shamelessness beginning with "one who intentionally commits an offense" and so forth is stated specifically for monks and nuns;

however, for novices and others, as well as for householders, it should be understood according to their respective training rules (*sikkhāpada*), such as the concealment of transgressions. Regarding the definition of conscientiousness (*lajjilakkhaṇa*) as well...

The same method applies here as well. Although one might act in this way even when remorse has arisen—doing so by suppressing it—or even when acting while perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, it is done precisely because of a lack of shame at that very moment.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that remorse and the other categories are mentioned separately. The Vajjiputtakas are those who illustrate the ten points;
they are proponents of such views as "bringing from another," "ignorance," "doubt," and "being instructed by another. Herein, [the term] *arahattaṃ*...

Those who, having seen the emission of semen from deceivers who claim [to be arahants], hold the view that "deities belonging to Māra’s host have introduced impurity," are called proponents of the doctrine of external instigation (parūpahāravāda).
Regarding the Arhat, there is ignorance in not knowing the names and so forth of all persons, such as men and women;

there is doubt due to the state of uncertainty regarding those things; and there is the doctrine that there exists the communication of knowledge from another, because one comes to know the names and so forth after hearing them from others.

The doctrines of ignorance, the doctrines of doubt, and the doctrines of seeking clarification from others—the distinctions between these and those such as the Mahāsaṅghikas—are explained in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise.

Regarding the phrase "the four paths and the fruits," it should be understood that by the word "and" (*ca*), the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) are also included.
"Some" refers to those who uphold the scriptures and preach the Dhamma; "others" refers to the Paṃsukūlika elders who uphold the practice.
But as for the passage beginning with "The others, however," this is the intended meaning: when the elder Dhamma-preachers heard the discourses brought by the elder Paṃsukūlikas, they said:
"As long as the Suttantas endure, and as long as the Vinaya shines, so long will they see the light, just as when the sun has risen."
“When the Suttantas have disappeared and the Vinaya has been forgotten,
there will be darkness in the world, like when the sun has set.
When the Suttanta is preserved and remains intact, the practice is preserved.”
“Firmly established in practice, the wise one does not fall away from security from bondage.
Having cited this sutta, they establish their own position, saying that the very study (pariyatti) comprised by practice—which stands by way of not incurring a *pārājika* offense—is the root.
Therefore he said: “If five monks who are guardians of the four *pārājikas*... [etc.]”
“They shall cause the Dispensation to reach growth and expansion. By this it is established that when the time has come to an end and one cannot find a group of modest monks (lajjigaṇa),
the holder of the Vinaya (vinayadhara) must, by gathering even those who are shameless (alajji) who are of natural character,
associate with them through the sharing of the Dhamma and material goods, and by ordaining many sons of noble family (kulaputta), it is proper for him to uphold the Dispensation.
It is to be seen. The two factors are: the desire to reproach, and the disparaging of the training rules in the presence of one who is fully ordained.
The commentary on the rule concerning causing remorse is finished.
3. Commentary on the Rule Concerning Confounding.

444. Regarding the third [case], the phrase "what need be said, then, of more" means that if there has been a previous occasion of sitting [to hear] the Pātimokkha being recited in detail by those other monks beyond the section on the two types of views (diṭṭhadvatti), what indeed needs to be said there?
The intention is that there is no release from the offense. And "it must be dealt with according to the Dhamma" is the tradition (tanti).

The instrumental case is used in the sense of the cause; the meaning is "by means of that. What is meant is: "In whatever manner the Dhamma and the Vinaya are established, in that same manner one must deal with that offense.
There are three factors: the imposition of delusion, the fact of having heard it three times, and the delusion of one who intends to delude.
The commentary on the training rule concerning seduction is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning striking. 451.
Regarding the fourth rule, in the Pāḷi text the phrase "with something connected to the body" includes even the throwing of stones and other objects that are released from the hand.
