452. "With a lustful mind" refers to the passion for physical contact. However, regarding striking with the intent of sexual intercourse against men and others, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even for one who, with the intention of releasing [an animal], strikes a snake or similar creature with the tip of a staff to free a frog or the like, there is no offense at all.
Being angry and striking a fully ordained person (*upasampanna*) without the intention of releasing him—these are the two factors [of the offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning striking is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning clods of earth. 457.
Regarding the statement, "In the fifth [rule], it is an *dukkaṭa* offense because it was given without the intention to strike," what here is this *dukkaṭa*? Is it on account of the striking?
Or is it on account of spitting? It is indeed on account of spitting, not on account of striking. For if there is no desire to strike, it is not logical that any offense should arise on that account.
However, because spitting does not possess its own inherent nature [as an intentional act], an offense of expiation (pācittiya) does not arise on that account;
yet, because the action was performed with an impure mind, there is no exemption from the offense here.
"Engaged" means it should be understood that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) has been stated.
458. "In the previous" refers to the immediately preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The remainder is exactly the same as the previous one.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hand-strike (*talasattika*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Rule Regarding Groundless Accusations (Amūlaka-sikkhāpada) 459.
In the sixth [rule], the phrase "while seeking protection for oneself" is stated for the purpose of showing that this is not an accusation rooted in enmity (*veramūlikā anuddhaṃsanā*).
At the moment of the accusation, however, only a mind of anger arises. For this very reason, it is called "painful feeling" (*dukkhavedana*).
It has been stated. The remainder is exactly according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the training rule concerning groundless charges is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning causing remorse.
464. For one who has received full ordination, there are two factors: the desire for discomfort and the causing of remorse.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the causing of remorse is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eavesdropping.
471. That which is heard is "suti," meaning speech. Being near that is "upassuti.
If the meaning were taken as "that wherein one hears is 'sutī'," it would follow that one stands in another place where there is no hearing, merely near the place of hearing.
Furthermore, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), in order to show the meaning of the word *upassuti* itself, it says "standing where... and so forth.
Not merely the sound of what is being heard.

473. "In a single unit" is said because of the commonality of origination, whether from non-action or from action. The two factors are: the intention to accuse by one who is fully ordained, and the hearing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reviling (Khiyyana-sikkhāpada) 474.
In the ninth [offense], there are three factors: it being a formal act of the Dhamma (dhammakamma), knowing [it to be so], and reviling after having given one's consent.
The commentary on the training rule on reviling is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Departing (Pakkamana-sikkhāpada) 481.

Regarding the tenth [training rule], there is the legitimacy of the formal decision (*vinicchaya-kathā*). Having understood that, there are two factors: starting from the formal act (*kamma*), and for one who is within the same boundary and belongs to the same community (*samāna-saṃvāsika*), the relinquishing of the reach of the hand (*hattha-pāsa-vijahana*).
The commentary on the training rule on departing is finished.
11. Commentary on the Weak Training Rule (Dubbalasikkhāpada) 484.

In the eleventh [rule], there are two factors: being fully ordained and having received formal authorization in accordance with the Dhamma; and, after giving a robe to the Saṅgha, speaking out of a desire to disparage them.
The commentary on the weak training rule is finished.
489. The twelfth [sutta] is exactly as previously described.
The eighth chapter, the Sahadhammika-vagga, is finished.
9. The Rāja-vagga.
1. Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 499.

Regarding the first rule of the ninth chapter, the phrase “one whose womb is pure” (*saṃsuddhagahaṇika*) occurs in the Pāḷi. Here, “womb” (*gahaṇī*) refers to the region of the mother’s belly known as the seat of the fetus;
she is called “one whose womb is pure” because it has not been touched by the semen of another man. [She is like] a consecrated noblewoman (*abhisittakhattiyā*).
The three factors are: both [monks] not having departed from their own sleeping quarters, and the crossing of the threshold without having been made aware [of it].
The commentary on the Antepura training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Ratana training rule.
506. Regarding the second [offense], "of a dwelling" (*āvasatha*): here, whether it be within the monastery grounds or elsewhere, wherever one's own place of residence is, that is called a "dwelling.
"Out of desire or out of fear": out of desire for carpenters and the like, or out of fear of those favored by the king.
"Even when it has become crowded with people... they suspect": in that place which was previously devoid of people, they later suspect it when it becomes crowded with people.
Even though it was given, because they had forgotten it at the time of departure and did not see anyone else, they suspected that very monk. "Appropriate" means:

having personally taken a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) among allowable goods, showing it to lay followers and others who are appropriate for unallowable goods, and then either directing them toward merit such as at a cetiya or having them give it away, and then departing without concern. "Having incited" means: having requested it.
The three factors are: being caused by another; the absence of the perception that it is a rag-robe obtained through trust; and taking it up or the like for reasons not permitted.
The commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (Ratana-sikkhāpada) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time (Vikāla-gāmappavesana-sikkhāpada).
508. In the third [section], "talk on fear" refers to talk concerning the fear of kings, thieves, and so forth, or the fear of disease, non-human beings, famine, wildernesses, and so forth.
"Talk on streets" refers to talk about well-laid-out roads and the like. "Talk on water-stations" refers to talk about watering places for cattle, or talk about female water-carriers.
"Talk on departed relatives" refers to talk about deceased kinsmen. "Talk on diversity" refers to...
That which is freed from what has been said and what will be said—namely, talk of various natures that is purposeless—is called "talk about the world" (*lokakkhāyika*).
This refers to discourse proceeding by way of explaining the nature of the world, such as: "By whom was this world created?

and so forth. Talk about the ocean (*samuddakkhāyika*) should be understood in the same way. "Thus is existence, thus is non-existence"—discourse proceeding after stating some such or other purposeless reason is [called] "talk about origins" (*sammutikkhāyika*).

Such is the talk of existence and non-existence (*itibhavābhavakathā*). Herein, "existence" (*bhava*) is threefold: eternalism (*sassata*), growth (*vuḍḍhi*), and sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*); "non-existence" (*abhava*) is its opposite.
Thus, together with these six kinds of talk of existence and non-existence, there are what are called the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
Alternatively, even though talk of forests, mountains, rivers, and islands is not explicitly mentioned in the text, it is included by the word "such" (*iti*).
These are collectively called the "thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk. Regarding the phrase *iti vā*: here the word *iti* signifies a manner or mode, and the word *vā* signifies an alternative.
Therefore, the meaning to be understood is: "he speaks such a kind of useless talk as this, or something else of a similar nature.

It is stated because [the person] must be asked for permission. "In the same manner as described under the taking of what is not given" refers to the second throw of a clod of earth.

Regarding the phrase "within the monastery," etc.: here, on festival days and the like, when people are circumambulating the village wishing to worship a statue of the Conqueror (Jina) or similar objects, or when they have requested the monks for the sake of pacifying illness and so forth—by those monks...
Some say that it is permissible to circumambulate the village by way of the middle of the street even without performing the procedure of being well-covered and so forth;
however, this should not be accepted, because it is not mentioned in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) and because it is prohibited by the rule: "If one does not descend from the path...

[etc. ...it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Even when the Elder Ānanda was reciting the protective chant (*paritta*) while circumambulating Vesālī, he [ensured] being well-covered and so forth.
It should be understood that this was done either without causing offense or before a training rule had been laid down. However, some say:
"It is permissible for those staying within the monastery grounds or other such areas to enter the village street by way of going out to meet or coming to welcome those of venerable standing.

Even that is not permissible to do with respect to one who is entering between the houses; it is only permissible to do so at a suitable place such as the interior of the monastery or another appropriate location.
However, it appears that it is permissible to do so for one who is traveling specifically for that purpose; this should be investigated.
There are two factors: entering a village at an improper time without having asked permission from a monk present, and acting without authorization.
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada) 520.

Regarding the fourth [offense], "vāsijaṭe" in the Pāḷi means "on a needle-case. The two factors [for an offense] are: its being made of bone and so forth as a needle case, and its acquisition by oneself through making it or having it made.
The commentary on the Training Rule on the Needle Case is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Beds and Stools (Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpada) 521.
Regarding the fifth [rule], the phrase "by his disposition, O monks, that foolish man is to be known" means that he is to be understood as a hollow person due to his base disposition;
thus, the hollowness of a person who is greedy for inferior requisites is to be understood.
This is the intended meaning. In this training rule and in the five that follow, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) occurs only upon the acquisition of what one has had made for oneself.
However, regarding its use, as well as that of others, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The two factors [for an offense] are: the state of being a bed or chair exceeding the proper measure, and the acquisition through making it oneself or having it made.
The commentary on the training rule concerning beds and chairs is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Stuffing with Cotton: 526.
Regarding the sixth [rule], "poṭakitūla" refers to the cotton derived from grasses and shrubs. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stuffing with cotton is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting Mats (531–536).
In the seventh [rule], there are two factors: the exceeding of the prescribed measure for the sitting mat, and its acquisition through one’s own making or other means.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats is finished. 537–547.
In this same manner, the factors [of the offense] should be understood for the eighth, ninth, and tenth rules as well. The rest is easy to understand throughout.
The ninth chapter, the Rājavagga, is completed.
The method of commentary on the Minor Section (Khuddakavaṇṇanā) is finished.
6. The Section on Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa).
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Confession (Paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

553. Regarding the first of the *pāṭidesanīya* rules, "the demonstration of the manner in which one should confess" means the demonstration of the manner in which an offense should be confessed in the presence of a junior.
By this characteristic, it can also be understood that the manner in which many offenses should be confessed in the presence of a senior is to be known.
In this regard, the method is as follows: "Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy state."

Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* rules that are unsuitable, the application [of the formula] should be understood in the same way for multiple [offenses]. However, in the presence of a senior [monk], the construction should be understood as: "Venerable sir, this is a censurable matter... regarding censurable matters, venerable sir. In this context, "unsuitable" (*asappāya*) means that which creates an obstacle to heaven and liberation.
It refers to taking food that is to be consumed during the day directly from the hand of an unrelated nun who is standing within a village.
"Swallowing" consists of two factors.
The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished. 558.
In the second [rule], the two factors are: the act of dismissal by one who is fully ordained and has not been authorized, and the swallowing of food without having been restrained.

563. In the third [offense], there are three factors: being designated as one in training (sekkha), not being invited while within the vicinity of a house, and eating after taking non-staple food (aniccabhatta) and so forth for the sake of one who is ill.

570. In the fourth, there are two factors: the lodging being a suspicious place belonging to others, and the swallowing by one who is not ill of what has been accepted within a monastery—namely, a non-staple food (yāvakālika) that was not permitted and not announced. The rest is self-evident.
The method of commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya rules is concluded.
7. The Section on Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa). 1. Explanation of the Chapter on Being Well-Rounded (Parimaṇḍalavagga). 576.
Regarding the training rules (sekhiya), since even those duties prescribed in the Khandhaka on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka) must be practiced, they are likewise training rules (sekhiya). Therefore...
In the case of the *pārājika* rules and others, no such delimitation was made in the *pāḷi*.

Furthermore, for the purpose of demonstrating the method of conduct (*cārittanaya*), instead of saying "if a bhikkhu wears [his robe] hanging down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," the *pāḷi* is recorded everywhere as "the training is to be observed.
However, because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that "there is an offense of wrong-doing," [this applies] in all cases to the act of showing disrespect.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) should be understood [to occur].

By the word "measure" (*matta*) in the phrase "only eight finger-breadths," both slightly more than that and slightly less are included. For this very reason, it is stated that for one who is sitting, even a measure of four finger-breadths [is sufficient].
Indeed, it is not the case that for one who is sitting the measure is only four finger-breadths, while for one who is standing it is exactly eight.

It is not possible to fix [the measurement] definitively because of the possibility of deficiency or excess. Therefore, it should be understood that, in accordance with what is appropriate, it is the lower robe (*nivāsana*) itself that is intended by following the eight-finger-width rule.
For this very reason, he will say: "But whichever bhikkhu has dry shanks," and so forth.
In the *Kurundi*, emphasis is placed on the phrase "there is no offense for one who does not know," meaning that there is no offense even for one who is learning [the rule] while remaining ignorant.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Therefore, one must train in the constant practice of wearing the lower robe and the upper robe; for one who does not train, it is indeed a lack of respect.

By the inclusion of the term "all around" (*parimaṇḍala*), lifting up even the lower robe is prohibited; thus he said, "either lifting it up or letting it down. "With a conscious mind" (*sacittaka*) means with a mind that discerns the object.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, according to the method of the Elder Upatissa...

Taking into account its status as a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), it is stated: "It is 'with consciousness' by means of the consciousness that cognizes the object (*vatthu*) and the consciousness that cognizes the rule (*paṇṇatti*).
In this context, the cognition of the object need not be mentioned separately;
for by the cognition of the rule, that too is included within it, since one who cognizes the rule understands: "For one who transgresses this object in such a manner, there is an offense."

"It is said that 'one cognizes'. In this regard, according to the doctrine of the Elder Upatissa, it is held that for one who knows only the physical object—such as a lower robe that is not properly rounded—but does not know the designation (*paṇṇatti*), there is no offense at all among all those in training, due to the absence of disregard for the transgression of the designation.
However, that is not tenable, because in the *Kosambakakkhandhaka*, even for one who leaves water remaining in a latrine, there is an offense despite the absence of knowledge of the designation.
Because it is stated [in the Vinaya] regarding an offense (*āpatti*). For it is said there: "Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had fallen into an offense...
later on, he came to hold the view that there was no offense in that offense," and so forth. And in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) regarding this, it says:
"You do not know here that this is an offense, do you?—'Yes, I do not know.'—'Very well, friend; here there is an offense.'"
"If it has occurred, I shall confess it. "But if, friend, it was done unintentionally and through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense.

Thus it is said that he held the view that there was no offense for that transgression; likewise, it is said that "one who speaks what is not Dhamma" refers to one among those who follow the suspended monk.
For since the Khandhaka observances are included within the Sekhiya rules, the method stated therein applies to these as well. Here...

And what has been stated for them is indeed common to both. For that very reason, the method regarding offenses (āpatti-naya) stated here—namely, "there is no offense when it is done unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness"—is also shown there.

Therefore, standing by the opinion of the Elder Phussadeva, all training rules involving a conscious state (sacittaka) pertain solely to the mind that recognizes the objective basis (vatthu), not to the mind that recognizes the formal rule (paṇṇatti). [The cases of] "desiring more," "concealing broth and condiments," and "perceiving blame" [are thus explained].

It appears more appropriate to understand that two training rules involve offenses against the world (*lokavajja*) with unwholesome minds (*akusalacitta*), while the remaining ones involve offenses by way of formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*) with three types of mind and three types of feeling (*tivedana*).

For this very reason, here the commentary on non-offense is given solely by way of not knowing the basis [of the offense], stating: "‘Unintentionally’ means: ‘I shall put it on so as to hang in front or behind,’ thus unintentionally," and so forth.
It is not by way of a consciousness that understands the formal rule (paṇṇatti).
Moreover, this is also established by the defining statement: "That for which, on the side of those with consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, is a worldly offense (lokavajja).
For here, the phrase "on the side of those with consciousness" is stated precisely by way of a consciousness that understands the objective basis (vatthu); otherwise, [it would not be so].

By way of the consciousness that discerns the formal rule (paṇṇatti), since all training rules (sikkhāpada) would, in the category of those involving a conscious mind, necessarily entail unwholesomeness of the mind, it would follow that they could not be offenses by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja) alone;
furthermore, this statement would be purposeless, as there would be no training rule to be excluded by such a statement.
Nor [is it the case] regarding the Sekhiya rules, by way of the consciousness that discerns the object (vatthu).
In the case of those with a conscious mind, there is a restriction that the mind is exclusively unwholesome, as in the case of killing living beings and so forth,

by which worldly transgression (*lokavajjatā*) would follow here. However, this scriptural statement, “dependent on disrespect,” was spoken regarding the act of transgression committed through the three types of consciousness after having recognized the underlying matter (*vatthu*),
not regarding the transgression committed with an unwholesome mind after having recognized the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).
It should be accepted. Otherwise, it would contradict both the sequence of the Khandhaka-pāḷi and the commentary;
this is our view. Or rather, one should seek the intended meaning here in such a way that no contradiction arises.
Disrespect, the absence of a cause for non-offense, and wearing the lower robe unevenly—these are the three factors here. And as it is in this case, [so it is elsewhere].
The same applies everywhere. The only distinction is the application of the third factor (*aṅga*) by way of performing the opposite of what was stated in each respective instance.

577. Regarding the second [rule] and those following: "clothed in white" refers to those wearing white garments and so forth. "Even in the monastery" is said with reference to times such as the assembly of the Saṅgha or attending upon the Buddha.
578. "Having fastened the neck-tie," etc., is an illustration of the method of concealment. By the phrase "having covered the neck," etc.,...
Because it has been so stated, there is an offense for one who intentionally does not cover the neck and the wrist.

Here too, because of the commonality with the *parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada*, one should put on the robe in a circular manner (*parimaṇḍala*), having lowered it by at least four finger-breadths below the circle of the knees and without letting it hang down. 579.

"Sitting after opening [the robe]" refers to the practice of wearing the robe over one shoulder (*ekaṃsa-pārupana*), as is done in a monastery; it is said [here] for the purpose of residing [in a lay dwelling].
Because it is stated, "of one who has entered [for residence]," even when sitting for a very long time for purposes such as teaching the Dhamma or reciting parittas— without the intention of staying—
one must sit only while fulfilling all the duties toward the household. Furthermore,

since among the training rules concerning sitting it is stated that there is no offense for "one who has entered for residence," [this applies specifically to] entering a house for the purpose of staying.

Even when approaching [the dwelling], one must go only by keeping everything well-covered and so forth, without disturbing anything. For it is said, "having entered for residence," but not "while entering.

However, some say: "Having first gone to each individual [dwelling] and taken possession of it for residence, it is permissible for others to go there as they please after that. Others, however, [say]: "By the owners of the house..."

Some say: "As long as you reside [here], we give this house to you; therefore, it is permissible for others who do not intend to dwell there to go and sit there at their pleasure, just as in an intermediate monastery (antarārāma).

All of that should not be accepted, because such a statement was never made, because it lacks the characteristic of a gift (dāna-lakkhaṇa), and because by that much alone it does not attain the status of a monastery (vihāra).

And: "Even one who gives while saying, 'I give this house to you for as long as you remain seated,' gives it only for a limited time, because the characteristic of giving consists in the relinquishment of the object.
(582) They say that the phrase "measuring four cubits" is stated with reference to the cubit of a carpenter.
584. "Having lifted up his robe" refers to the lifting [of the robe] by way of showing the body-binding cloth (*kāyabandhana*) and so forth above the waist;
for it is permitted merely to take up the bowl while wandering for alms. For that very reason, it is said:
"But at the time of sitting, the water-strainer (*dhammakaraka*)," and so on. For at the time of sitting, the water-strainer is [taken from] the bowl-bag or similar items hanging from the shoulder.
As he is taking it out, it should be seen even above the waist; the intention is that it must be taken out without showing [the body] in that manner.
Furthermore, when sitting on a seat, one should sit having lifted up the robe already worn, but without lifting the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) from the calves.
However, because the phrase "one who has entered for the night" is stated in this very training rule, regarding those things connected with sitting—
Since it is not mentioned in the sixth and eighth [rules], even one who has entered his residence must sit with well-restrained senses and downcast eyes.
For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, without stating any distinction between them, it is said here alone: "But for one who has entered his residence, there is no offense.
The commentary on the section on "Complete Circumference" (*Parimaṇḍala-vagga*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Excessive Laughter (Ujjagghikavagga).

586. Although the offenses concerning laughing excessively and making little sound while seated are connected with the rules for sitting, it is not stated that there is no offense for one who has entered a dwelling;
rather, it is stated only in relation to shaking the body and so forth. However, in some manuscript copies of the Pāḷi, this is treated by way of abbreviation (peyyāla).

Because it is confused, it is not clearly understood. Furthermore, it should be seen that there is no offense even when one teaches the Dhamma or recites the Pātimokkha within an inhabited area (*antaraghara*) amidst a great noise, provided the sound does not reach beyond the assembly; this is because such was the practice of the Elder Ānanda, the Elder Mahinda, and others.
The commentary on the *Ujjagghikavagga* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Chapter on Standing (Khambhakata-vagga) 603.
Regarding the phrase "having made a perception regarding the bowl": this is said to show the meaning of *pattasaññī*, which means one who possesses the perception of grasping [the food] in the bowl.

604. *Oloṇī* is a certain preparation of sauce (*byañjana-vikati*). Some say it is the flavor of sour gruel, curd, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "meat broth, etc.," all remaining preparations of sauce are included.
605. *Samabharitam* means arranged. It "descends below" because, being leveled by hand due to the availability of space all around, it falls down.
The cakes placed on the edge of the bowl are called "cake-earrings" (*pūvavaṭaṃsaka*) because they were placed there in the shape of an earring.
However, some say: "Having taken the bowl and arranged the alms-food so that it was shaped like a stupa..."

They say that for one who takes [food] while it is being given, there is an offense; however, when the bowl has reached the hand and is being given, it is permissible to take even what is heaped up (*thūpīkata*).
This must not be accepted, because the term "level to the brim" (*samatittika*) is stated in a general sense using the neuter gender.
The commentary on the section concerning those leaning on a support is finished.
4. Commentary on the Chapter on Thoroughness (Sakkaccavagga) 608.
Regarding the term *sapadāna* in the fourth chapter and those that follow: here, *dāna* means "breaking" (*avakhaṇḍana*).
That which is devoid of breaking is *apadāna*; together with *apadāna* is *sapadāna*. This is said to mean "without interruption" or "in regular succession."
Therefore he said, “Without making a limit here and there,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “in an intimation,” he speaks with reference to the training rule concerning the intimation for soup and rice.

By the words “there is nothing to be said,” he shows that everything is understood from the text itself. In that context, within the text, in the phrases beginning with “unintentionally,” only the basic matter is stated.

For one who incurs an offense while eating after having understood [the rule], if they subsequently understand the formal proclamation (*paṇṇatti*) and, wishing to discard what has entered the mouth, swallow it because it had entered against their will, that is called "swallowed unintentionally" (*asañcicca*); in that case, there is no offense.

Furthermore, when eating that same thing either because one’s attention was directed elsewhere or with the perception that "this is not [forbidden] food," it is called "through lack of mindfulness" (*asatiyā*).

613. Regarding the phrase “for the sake of another”: this was stated with reference to the absence of an offense under this training rule (sikkhāpada), because it was prescribed specifically for one who, having requested [food] for their own sake, eats it themselves.

However, when requesting on behalf of five types of fellow practitioners (pañcasahadhammika) in a place where one has not been invited by an unrelated person, at the very moment of the request, according to the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) and in accordance with the Suttas—

One is not exempt from the dukkaṭa offense of making a request for what has already been stated. It should be understood that at the moment of eating intentionally, both oneself and others are not exempt from wrong livelihood. 615.
“A hen’s egg is too small”—this was said by way of what is improper; the offense occurs only when [the food] is excessively large.

It should be understood thus. However, for one who eats, there is an emergency here in the sense of eating quickly—even if the food is large in quantity or not perfectly rounded—due to fear of robbers and the like.
In this way, it should be understood accordingly for the other cases as well.
The commentary on the Chapter on Careful Eating is finished.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on Lumps (Kabaḷavagga) 617.
However, when a lump has not yet been brought to the mouth and the mouth is opened, because there is no purpose [in opening it], the phrase "in times of distress" is not mentioned.

The same applies to other similar cases. 618. "The whole hand" refers to the fingers as parts of the hand, as in expressions such as "hand-gesture" (*hatthamuddā*). Therefore, it is not permitted to place even a single finger into the mouth.
The commentary on the Kabaḷavagga is finished.
6. Commentary on the Surusuruvagga 627.
In the text, *sītīkata* means "afflicted by cold. *Silakabuddha* is a term of derision; for when people see something resembling a stone, they say, "This is a Buddha."

628. By the statement, "It is permissible to eat after inserting the fingers into the mouth," he shows that there is no offense for this training rule (sikkhāpada) even when one licks the fingers that have entered the mouth, as well as for the training rule concerning the insertion of the entire hand into the mouth.
This same method applies to licking the bowl with the hand or the lip with the tongue when eating thick gruel and the like.
"It is allowable" refers by extension. "Therefore" means that it is not allowable to lick [a bowl] that is devoid of thick gruel and the like.
634. "A *vilīva* umbrella" is one made from bamboo tubes.
"Fastened in a circle" means that after placing sticks in a circular form across long sticks, they are bound with cords; the long and crosswise sticks are perfectly straight.
Setting aside those that are firmly bound crosswise, and having made them contractible by means of long sticks, they are bound crosswise with cords.
"Made with a stick grown there" means made together with palm leaves and so forth cut from a stick [growing] there.
"Of a sunshade and sandals" means [those made] after inserting the tip of a sunshade handle and setting the sunshade upright.
They sit or stand in the shade below, under such a canopy.
*Cāpa* is a type of bow resembling a curved bamboo staff. *Kodaṇḍa* is a type of bow made from a reed-staff.
The commentary on the section on *surusuru* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Chapter on Sandals (Pādukavagga) 647.
In the seventh chapter, "fallen from a tree" means he fell while grasping a hanging branch. "In the Pāḷi" refers to the text that elucidates his own conduct.
"Dhīratthu" means "let there be shame"; the sense is, "let there be censure. "By way of a cause for falling into the lower realms" (vinipātanahetu).
By way of being the cause for falling into the lower realms. *Tvaṃ* is the nominative singular used in the sense of the accusative; or rather, the reading is simply *taṃ*. *Asmi* means "stone.

(649) "It should not be told" was said because the Elder had asked about the point of his own doubt. Since he had asked in order to know the junior monk's proficiency regarding the meaning, it was appropriate for him to speak by way of posing a question to the teacher who was seated on a high seat.

652. Regarding the phrase "and here, by 'spittle' (kheḷa), nasal mucus (siṅghāṇikā) is also included": it should be understood that it is permissible to take a mouthful of water, as well as sugarcane refuse and so forth, out of the mouth itself and discard them in the water. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Pādukavagga is finished.
The method of commentary on the Sekhiya rules is concluded.
655. There is nothing further to be said here regarding the methods for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).
Thus ends the method of commentary on the *Bhikkhuvibhaṅga* within the *Vimativinodanī*, the sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules (Bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 1.
The Section on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa)
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Crossing Over Above the Knees (Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika-sikkhāpada) 656.
In the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, the phrase "of Migāramātā" means of Visākhā, the mother of Migāra.

In the Pāḷi, the definition "a bhikkhunī is one who has come [saying] 'Come, bhikkhunī,' or a bhikkhunī is one who is fully ordained by the three goings for refuge"—this is from the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga-pāḷi.
This was said with reference to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī— who received full ordination by accepting the eight weighty rules (aṭṭhagarudhamma) for the sake of demonstrating [the distinction]—
and the five hundred Sakyan women who went forth together with her and were ordained on one side (ekatoupasampannā) in the presence of the monks alone at the Blessed One’s command.
For it was upon the request of the Elder Ānanda that the Blessed One permitted their going forth.
They became as if they had been told, "Come, bhikkhunīs, enter into my teaching.
Because the Śākyan women were given the refuges and the precepts and then ordained through the formal ritual (kammavācā), it is said that "they were ordained by means of the three goings for refuge.
For there are no others among them who are called ordained by way of the "Come, bhikkhunī" formula and so forth. As for what is [stated] in the Therīgāthā:
Having pressed her knee to the ground and paid homage, she placed her joined palms before me;
"Come, Bhaddā," he said to me— this was my full ordination.
It is said. And in the Apadāna it is stated:
“Then, being entreated, the Leader said, ‘Come, Bhaddā.
At that moment I was ordained, and I saw a small amount of water.”

It has been stated. That too was said with reference to this meaning: that the Blessed One’s command, “Come, you, receive the going-forth and the full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the bhikkhunīs,” became the *upasampadā* because it was the cause of the *upasampadā*.
For it is likewise stated in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*: “Come, Bhaddā, go to the bhikkhunīs’ residence [and receive the going-forth] from the bhikkhunīs...”

“‘May you receive the going-forth and the full ordination in my presence,’ he commanded me; because that command of the Teacher was the cause for my full ordination, it became my full ordination. Regarding “the common pārājikas”:
these are the four [offenses] beginning with sexual intercourse. Furthermore, there are other training rules (sikkhāpada) that are common [to both genders].
Because these [rules] were formulated as common [to both orders] within the introductory narratives, settings, and so forth, which are stated in the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga;
and subsequently, when the Blessed One permitted the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhunīs, he did so by adapting them accordingly to their lack of renunciation of training, beginning with:
"Whichever bhikkhunī should intentionally engage in sexual intercourse," and so forth.
Having rearranged them and compared them with the non-common training rules, they were compiled together according to the recitation of the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.
Since the entire detailed exposition for these can be understood by the same method as that stated in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga,
it should be understood that those [common rules] have been omitted here, and only the exposition of the non-common rules is presented.

659. Since it was stated regarding the bhikkhus, "he should enter into [the act]" (*samāpajjeyya*), rather than saying "he should consent to bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggaṃ sādiyeyya*), it is said that "the bhikkhu is not to be dealt with for an offense.
By the method of "generally" (*tabbahulanayena*), this is because the originative source (*samuṭṭhāna*) consisting of action (*kriyā*) is predominant;
by this, he shows that this offense also exists as one originating from non-action (*akriyā*). Although he shows this, we, however, in this regard—
Thus we reason: "Even though there is an absence of an actual act at the moment of physical contact,
it is nevertheless an instigation of an act by virtue of the acts that occurred prior to that— such as going to a concealed place, making gestures, or showing facial expressions—
and just like the emission of semen from one who, though motionless, consents to another's effort applied to the path, even in the absence of a prior application [of one's own]."
Or, at that very moment, regarding the action consisting of the movement of one's own body produced by another's assault—

this is indeed called an "action" (kiriyā) because it arises even from a mind that consents to it, just as in the case of consenting to sexual intercourse through another's assault without exerting effort;
however, for monks, an action produced by another's assault is considered non-offensive (abbhohārika).
"Because the training rule was formulated specifically as 'one should enter into physical contact' by way of the very act being performed by oneself, there is no fault even if one consents [to it].

For otherwise, if 'action' were understood here according to the principle of its predominance, it would follow that other training rules concerning action and non-action would also have to be understood as 'action'. Therefore, having investigated—
It should be understood. "And that" refers to the fact of being originated by action. "In the same way" means one who is lustful toward bodily contact.
The commentary on the training rule concerning [touching] above the knees is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Concealer of Faults.

666. The phrase beginning with "In the second [offense], by the first," etc., is stated with reference to the fact that it was laid down [as an offense] regarding Sundarīnandā’s concealing of a fault (*vajja*).
Because it is stated as "of eight," it should be understood that even the concealing of the concealing of a fault constitutes a *pārājika*.
Because it is stated as "merely upon laying down the burden," this applies even to one who does not know the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), such as one thinking, "I will not reveal this fault."
It should be understood that at the moment of relinquishing the burden through desire, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, since that concealment occurs solely out of fear—thinking, "Knowing [my fault], the virtuous will censure me"—and since fear is associated with a mind of anger (*kodhacitta*), this is described as "painful feeling" (*dukkhavedanā*).
As for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Even though the concealment of a fault..."
"Even though it occurs through the influence of affection, nevertheless, the mind that transgresses the training rule is indeed dejected.

Thus, the concealment by means of a mind that transgresses the formal rule (paṇṇatti) has been stated as the cause for dejection; however, that is not the cause, because [the offense] can be committed even without knowing the formal rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the concealer of an offense is finished.
669. The third [section] is self-evident. 4.
Commentary on the Training Rule of Eight Bases (Aṭṭhavatthuka-sikkhāpada): 675.

Regarding the fourth [base], it refers to the intimacy (*santhava*) that friends should practice with one another, which is characterized by worldly gratification (*lokassāda*). To show this same meaning through a different formulation, it is stated: "through passion for physical contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggarāgena*).
"Three women: one should not practice sexual intercourse with those three women mentioned. "With the ignoble and the eunuchs":
the meaning is that one should not approach and practice sexual intercourse with the three types of ignoble persons and the three types of eunuchs.
And here, "ignoble" refers specifically to those with both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjanaka*). "In the organ" means in one's own...
Also in the case of the path of the anus. *Chejjaṃ* (cutting) is simply *chedo* (a cut); it is a *pārājika*.
*Vaṇṇāvaṇṇo* refers to two instances of the emission of semen. *Gamanuppādanaṃ* (instigating intercourse) is *sañcarittaṃ* (mediating marriage).

By the phrase "it is a condition because it is a preliminary stage to sexual intercourse," bodily contact is referred to as "sexual intercourse" through this metaphorical application (*kāriyopacāra*).
...is shown. "In all instances" refers to instances such as grasping the corner of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇa*).
Here, there are three factors: lustful physical contact, the presence of intent (*saussāhatā*), and the fulfillment of the eighth basis.
The commentary on the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) consisting of eight bases is concluded.
The method of commentary on the *pārājika* offenses is finished.
2. The Section on the *saṅghādisesa* Offenses.
1. Commentary on the First *Saṅghādisesa* Training Rule.

679. Regarding the phrase "he informs the companion" in the Saṅghādisesa section: here too, the meaning should be understood as "whichever of the two companions it may be, anyone informs that companion. Thus he says, "The same method applies. "Gatigata" means that which has persisted for a long time. "Āpatti" means the act of falling into an offense.

Regarding the term "nissāraṇīya," this is established in the sense of the agent; thus he says, "it causes one to be expelled. The meaning is that it separates the nun who has fallen into the offense from the Saṅgha, serving as the cause for such separation.
"Because there was no command such as 'seize him by the neck'" means because there was no such order.
"Because they did not wish them harm" refers to the perception: "Having heard my words that 'he is a thief,' some will be punished and their lives will be taken.
By this, he shows that there is no fault even if one is punished for suddenly saying "He is a thief" out of mere fear or for the purpose of seizing requisites. For [in the case] of the king's men...
The offense (*gīvā*) lies only in speaking with reference to [someone] as "this is a thief.

However, even if, based on a statement made by someone in the presence of monks or monastery attenders (*ārāmika*) such as "so-and-so has done such-and-such as a thief," the king’s men speak to those attenders and cause them to be punished, there is no offense for the monk, because he did not speak to the king’s men himself. And as for those to whom it was spoken, by them...

It should be understood as "the thief not being punished. For even if one is commanded, "Take this person's property," if he causes it to be taken by another, there is no offense for the commander because the agreement was broken.
The phrase "one who carries out his word" is stated by way of courtesy. Even for royal officers who do not carry out the command, [the rule applies] regarding the requisites taken by this person...
Even when one speaks with reference to another, saying, "Have it brought here, but do not inflict punishment upon him," or even when punishment has already been taken,

the offense does not lie solely with the one who took the punishment; for this is like the case where, after commanding someone, "Steal such-and-such goods," one feels remorse and subsequently renounces the act.
Just as there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for monks when they engage in a lawsuit for the sake of [acquiring] slaves and so forth—similar to the case of accepting them—it is said:

"An improper lawsuit (*akappiya-aḍḍa*) is not permitted. However, even if a lawsuit is brought by some monk before judges for the sake of a field or similar property, it is not improper for all [monks] to accept that field or property, provided it was previously intended for the Saṅgha.

However, as the property belongs to the Saṅgha, the offenses arise through the agency of the monks themselves. Nevertheless, it is indeed permissible for a monk who has been asked by a layperson to request protection for the sake of slaves and so forth to state that the Saṅgha possesses suitable goods, and it is also permissible for him to have a lawsuit conducted by means of monastery attendants and others.
Furthermore, it is even permissible for a monk himself to conduct a lawsuit regarding suitable items such as the site for a monastery.
"Stated for the bhikkhunīs" means that the determination regarding the request for protection—both specific and general—was stated for those bhikkhunīs who were requesting it;
it does not include the entire determination of the training rule (sikkhāpada), because that training rule is not common [to both genders].
Therefore he said, "The bhikkhunī also," and so forth. The two factors are: conducting a lawsuit against one who has not been summoned, and the conclusion of the lawsuit.
The commentary on the first Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second Saṅghādisesa training rule: 683.
Regarding the phrase "the group of Malla warriors, the group of Bhaṭiputta, etc. in the Canon: the group of Malla kings is the "Malla-group."
The *bhaṭiputtas* were certain republican rulers (*gaṇarājāno*); their group was the *bhaṭiputtagaṇa*. However, some say:
"The *mallagaṇa* was a group of merit-makers devoted to Nārāyaṇa; likewise, the group devoted to Kumāra was the *bhaṭiputtagaṇa*.
In the Teaching (*sāsana*) or in the world, a group that performs various kinds of meritorious deeds is a *dhammagaṇa*. A group that prepares perfumes is a *gandhikaseṇī*.
The group beginning with the weaver is the guild of cloth-dealers. "Having entered into what is allowable" means having attained the state of being allowable;
the meaning is that she was previously ordained. 685. In the text, "causes to go forth" means to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).

They say that for one who confers the going-forth even on one who has not entered into what is allowable, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It is called "threefold consciousness" because it must be incurred even by those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). She is a thief; knowing this, [the act is] done without authorization.
"Causing to emerge" consists of two factors.
The commentary on the second Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule.
692. Regarding "one who crosses the enclosure" in the third [offense]: this refers to one who crosses the enclosure of another village.

For it is said, "she should go to another village. Unlike the training rule on entering a village at an improper time, where it says "one who enters the precincts of an unenclosed [village]," the Pāli here uses the term "crossing over" (*atikkāmentiyā*); therefore, for one entering a village, it refers to the precincts of the house.

He says, "He steps over the area eligible for enclosure with one foot," meaning that the "crossing" of the precinct defined as the second stone-throw consists in crossing the area defined as the location of the first stone-throw, which is eligible for enclosure.

"In the middle" means in the center of the village. "Later" means at a subsequent time. By the phrase "because it is common to four villages," he states the reason why it is permissible to enter any of the four villages from the monastery.

"Crossing only to the further shore" means: not descending into the river, but either leaping from this shore or crossing through the air and so forth, she passes only to the further shore. "She returns to this very shore; there is an offense" is stated because she had descended for the purpose of going to the other side.
"In such a forest" refers to a forest characterized by being outside the boundary of the city gate (*indakhīla*).

By the words "by that very [means]" and so forth, he shows that even when the range of sight (*dassanūpacāra*) is absent, an offense occurs provided the range of hearing (*savanūpacāra*) exists. "She takes another path" means:

She takes [the robe] because she is lost on the way, not in order to leave her companion behind. Therefore, there is no offense. Regarding "being together" without an obstacle and without an emergency:
in cases such as traveling between villages, these two factors constitute "being together.
The commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 694. Regarding the phrase “of the group of those who perform [the act]” (*kārakagaṇassa*) in the fourth rule:

this refers to those by whom the formal resolution (*sanniṭṭhāna*) has been made that “this legal procedure (*kamma*) is to be performed. Some say it means “standing together at the moment of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*). Regarding the phrase “in the conduct for the sake of completion” (*netthāravatte*): it refers to the conduct that is the cause for reaching a conclusion. 698.

The Discourse on Enlightenment (Bodhikathā)
"In the Mahāvagga, 'of both Pātimokkhas' means of both Pātimokkha-vibhaṅgas. 'That which they recited as the Khandhaka' is the connection [to be understood].
A collection of sections (khandha) is a *khandhaka*; or, it is called *khandhaka* because it elucidates the sections (*khandha*).

Here, by 'sections' is intended the collection of the promulgation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning conduct and prohibitions, beginning with the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). In the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*)."

The construction is: "the meanings of those words which have been elucidated by these methods of commentary (*aṭṭhakathānaya*). Alternatively, it should be construed as "those [meanings] which are the meanings.
Here, the word *hi* (for/indeed) should be understood as serving to complete the meter.
1. "The specific cause" refers to that occasion which served as the reason for the Venerable Elder Sāriputta’s request for the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
The meaning is that the specific reason—which is like the reason stated in the passage beginning “At that time, a reflection arose”—is the reason for setting aside the locative case.
As for the phrase “of this”: what is the purpose of the exposition of the Teacher’s conduct from the time of his full enlightenment onwards in the formulation of the Vinaya?
The intention is: if there is no specific reason [for it], then what is the purpose? The purpose is the demonstration of the origin (nidāna).

The interpretation (*yojanā*). Here, by "origin" (*nidāna*), what is intended is the cause consisting of the matter, the person, and so forth, which serves as the basis for the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*);
it does not refer merely to the location where the rule was formulated. Therefore, he said, "For that which... and so on. Regarding the term *uruvelā*:
here the word *uru* signifies "great," while the word *velā* is a synonym for "bank. [It is called *Uruvelā*] because of its height and other such characteristics.
*Velā* is like *velā*. It is a vast (*uru*), great (*mahantī*) *velā*, thus it is *Uruvelā*; [the Buddha was] in that place. Therefore he said, “At Mahāvelā,” and so forth.
*Mariyādā* means the boundary of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). *Pattapuṭena* means by a leaf-bag made from the leaves of the palmyra tree and other such trees.

He said, “Having first attained full enlightenment (*paṭhamābhisambuddho*),” because this is a grammatical analysis (*niddesa*) with the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*); thus he explained it as “first enlightened (*paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho*).”
*Paṭhamaṃ* is a neuter noun used adverbially. Therefore, the construction should be understood as: "Having attained full enlightenment, he dwelt at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the very first time.
In the canonical text, regarding the phrase *atha kho*, here *atha* means "at that time," since particles have multiple meanings. *Sattāhaṃ* means "for seven days."
This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). Now, the particle *atha kho* is a fixed expression (*nipāta*) used to indicate a change of subject.
By this, he shows that having set aside the experience of the bliss of liberation, the focus is now placed upon the contemplation of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
*Paṭicca* means "having gone towards" or "having looked back at one another"; by this, the multiplicity of causes is shown.

“Together with” (*sahita*) refers to the multiplicity of causal factors. “In accordance with” (*anuloma*) is a neuter noun used adverbially. “That very same” (*so eva*) refers to that very mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*).
Or, as stated by way of the previous method, it refers to the mode of conditionality stated in the sequence beginning with “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
“In the course of occurrence” (*pavattiyaṃ*) means in the occurrence of saṃsāra.
In the Pāli, in such passages as "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is non-knowing regarding suffering and so forth.
Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions. Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is exclusively mundane resultant consciousness.

The three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) are name (*nāma*); form (*rūpa*) is divided into the primary elements and derived matter. The six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) are divided into the sensitive organs and consciousness. Contact (*phassa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are entirely of the nature of result. [And] lust (*rāga*).
Craving (*taṇhā*). Grasping (*upādāna*) consists of powerful lust and the three types of views. Existence (*bhava*), moreover, is twofold: existence as kamma and existence as rebirth.
Therein, existence as kamma is simply wholesome and unwholesome volition accompanied by taints; existence as rebirth is the aggregates that have been appropriated.

Their arising is birth (*jāti*). Their maturation is aging (*jarā*). Their dissolution is death (*maraṇa*). Based on these very things, grieving is sorrow (*soka*). Wailing is lamentation (*parideva*).
Lamentation (*parideva*). Bodily pain (*dukkha*) is physical; mental distress (*domanassa*) is mental. Excessive sorrow is despair (*upāyāsa*).

The word "arises" (*sambhavati*) should be applied individually [to each]. Therefore he said, “By this method,” and so forth. By the phrase “of the mass of suffering,” he shows that it does not belong to a sentient being (*satta*), nor to beauty, pleasure, and so on.

*Hava* means “wise” (*byatta*); it is a particle used in this sense. “The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) which accomplish the penetration of the mode of conditions in their direct order.”

In this first section, although the mode of conditions in reverse order is indeed presented through the passage beginning with “With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance alone,” it is nevertheless stated as the cause for the penetration of the mode of conditions in forward order, namely, “Since he understands the dhamma together with its cause.
And just as it is here, so too in the second section by the verse: “Since he has known the destruction of conditions.”
It should be understood that because [the Buddha] has stated [this], the passage beginning with “the destruction of conditions” and so forth was spoken.

“An ill-timed question” means it is improper and not to be answered; for having taken the non-existent self as established, one asks regarding its activity, “Who touches?”—the intention being that this is like asking, “Who touches the son of a barren woman? and so on. The sixteen doubts are: “Did I exist in the past...? and so forth.

"Was I indeed? What was I? How was I? Having been what, what was I in the past? Shall I indeed be in the future? Shall I not indeed be? What shall I be? How shall I be? Having been what, what shall I be?"
“I shall exist in the future; or indeed, shall I not exist? What shall I be? How shall I be?
From where has this being come? Where will it go?”—thus there are sixteen kinds of doubt:
five regarding the past, five regarding the future, and six regarding the present.
In this context, "What indeed? refers to doubting by depending on one or another among humans, devas, and so forth, or among kṣatriyas and so forth.
"How indeed? refers to doubting by depending on a creator such as Īśvara, or on a cause, regarding shape, form, and so forth.

“Now am I? and so forth: he now doubts whether he exists or does not exist, and [doubts] regarding his specific nature, his mode of assistance, and so on.

“The Dhamma is impure” refers to the Dhamma of wrong view. “By those with stains” refers to the six teachers, beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa. “Open up” means to disclose by way of teaching. He speaks with reference to the Noble Path as the “door.”
He chose [a place] made of solid rock. Regarding the phrase *tathūpamaṃ*, the word *tathā* here should be understood in the sense of the word *taṃ*.
Thus, the meaning is: "that which has that mountain as its simile" (*tathūpamaṃ*). Alternatively, the meaning is: "that which has a simile by way of that manner, such as a mountain.
*Dhammamayaṃ* means consisting of the supramundane Dhamma. *Uṭṭhāhi* means for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
"Arise from this seat with the body for the sake of wandering on tour, or arise with the mind through the state of being free from worldly concerns"—this is the reading.
For that very reason, he enjoined both types of application—of body and mind—with the words "wander and teach.
"O Hero," and so forth, are four vocatives by way of praise.
9. "By the Buddha-eye" means by the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*) and the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*).
These two indeed have the name "Buddha-eye. "Of good disposition" (*svākāra*): those whose dispositions (*ākāra*), such as the faculty of faith and so forth, are beautiful are "of good disposition";
they should be understood as being easy to instruct, and as having the habit of viewing the next world and blame as fearsome. Herein, there are blue lotuses...
“*Santīti uppalinī*” refers to both a creeping vine and a lotus pond; here, however, it means a lotus pond. The same applies to the others as well.
“*Udakānuggatānīti udakato anuggatāni*” means not having emerged from the water. Growing and increasing while remaining submerged within, they are called “*antonimuggaposīni*.
“*Accuggammāti udakaṃ atikkamanavasena uggantvā*” means having emerged by way of surpassing the water.
"Opened" means disclosed. "Of them" refers to sentient beings together with their supporting conditions. "Doors" refers to the doors of the Noble Path.

And this is said with reference to the manifestation of the arising of the path for those beings together with their supporting conditions by means of his own self-enlightened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*).
In the phrases beginning with "perceiving harm," the meaning should be understood as follows: "For although [the path] is well-mastered and well-functioning in myself..."
"Among humans who do not understand this sublime Dhamma, teaching it would result in harm and exhaustion of body and speech.
Thinking thus and perceiving it as harmful, I did not speak; I did not wish to speak.
But now, let those who are endowed with the necessary causes open their own vessels of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Group of Five:
10. *Āḷāra* is his name; *Kālāma* is his clan. "Knowledge arose in the Blessed One too"—did it arise only now?
Was it not the case that at the foot of the Bodhi tree all phenomena, belonging to the three times and transcending time, were seen in all their aspects? True.
Although they are seen, they are nevertheless not conceptually constructed by way of names and so forth, because omniscient knowledge is momentary, lasting for only a single thought-moment.

Indeed, it is not possible for a single consciousness to conceptually construct the infinite individual classifications of all phenomena—such as their names, classes, and so on—because contradictory conceptual constructions cannot arise simultaneously. Rather, he perceives only those phenomena that are worthy of being the objects of all such conceptual constructions.

It is possible to do so. Just as, regarding what has been seen, a conceptualization arises in whatever form one desires—as on a mental canvas by means of visual consciousness—so too here, depending upon Āḷāra, the knowledge of all modes arose immediately after the act of adverting.
And not only that; moreover, the group of five monks themselves would first understand the Dhamma, with him at their head.

Furthermore, knowledge certainly arises by depending on everything such as the fact that Āḷāra died and was reborn in the base of nothingness, and Udaka was reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

However, that [knowledge] was stated as if it were the knowledge spoken by the deity after she had observed them in succession, in order to show the rarity of the attainment of the opportune moment (khaṇasampatti). For [the Buddha’s teaching] is bound by the course of sounds.

Even that which is known by a single act of knowledge appears, when being spoken of, as if it were known sequentially; and the deities also announced to the Blessed One exactly that matter already known by him.
Therefore, it should be understood that it was said: "Knowledge arose even for the Blessed One.
Likewise, in other such instances, one should consider: "While surveying the world, he saw such-and-such; what will happen there when I have gone?"

In such passages as these, which proceed by way of demonstrating the Teacher’s desire for the welfare [of others], although a sequential order is apparent in the course of the discourse, it should be understood that the entire realization occurs through a single act of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
The statement, "The group-of-five monks were indeed very helpful to me," was spoken with reference to the fact that they had been beneficial;
however, it does not mean that those who were not beneficial were not taught the Dhamma, for he taught even those who were not helpful on account of the necessity of the Dhamma-discourse.
11. "Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree" means in the place three *gāvutas* away between Gayā and the Bodhi tree.

"The All-Conqueror" (*sabbābhibhū*) means he who stands having overcome all phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*). "Unsmeared" (*anūpalitta*) means unsmeared by the defilement of the *kilesas*.

For that very reason, he is "the Abandoner of All" (*sabbañjaha*). "Liberated through the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaye vimutta*) means [liberated] by virtue of making *nibbāna*, the destruction of craving, his object.
“Liberated. Thus, having personally known all phenomena for myself, whom else should I point to, thinking, “This one is my teacher”?

“To Kāsī’s city” means to Bārāṇasī. “I shall beat” means I will strike. Because it is proclaimed for the attainment of the Deathless, the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma is called the “Deathless Drum”; the meaning is: “I go, thinking, ‘I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.’”
"Arahasi anantajino" means that it is fitting for him to be an "Anantajina.
He is an "Anantajina" because he possesses infinite knowledge; or because he has conquered infinite defilements by means of infinite knowledge;
or because, having crushed the enemies that are the defilements, he has seized the infinite Nibbāna—which is devoid of arising and passing away—thereby being an "Anantajina."
"Hupeyyāpi" means "it might even be so"; the intention is that regarding such a jewel of a physical form, one ought to possess such knowledge.

Indeed, for him who was endowed with such a supporting cause (upanissaya), this very statement later became the condition for his encountering the Blessed One when he had fallen into suffering, for his going forth, and for his penetration of the paths and fruits. For thus it was said by the Blessed One:
For the sake of meeting him, he set out on the path on foot.

"One who is given to abundance" (*bāhullika*) means one who is devoted to an abundance of requisites. "Fallen away from exertion" (*padhānavibbhanta*) means fallen away from exertion, that is, from the practice of difficult austerities.

"The homeless life" (*anagāriyā*): there is no household life here; "the homeless" refers to the state of renunciation, which is beneficial for the home [in contrast to worldly activities] such as farming and cattle-herding.
"To that state of homelessness" means they go forth; "to that unsurpassed" means to that which is beyond compare.
"The consummation of the holy life" means the end of the holy life of the Path; the meaning is the fruit of Arhatship. For it is for the sake of that that sons of noble family go forth.
"In this very life" means in this present, manifest personal existence. "By themselves" means independently of others.
"Having realized through direct knowledge" means having made it manifest to oneself by means of one's own wisdom. "Attaining" means reaching [that state].
"In conduct" refers to the conduct that is difficult to perform. Regarding the phrase "superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and so forth:

one who is capable and able to act nobly above the human state—that is, above mundane knowledge—is an "adept noble one" (*alamariya*). "Distinction in knowledge and vision" refers to the knowledge of omniscience.
The preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) is intended. “No” means “is it not? The meaning of “this has been spoken” (*bhāsitaṃ etan*) is that this is such a variety of statement.
And they, having gained mindfulness through a single phrase—thinking, “If he had said ‘I am an Arahant’ at the time of his striving, we would have believed him, but he did not say so then;
however, now he speaks of a quality that actually exists”—[concluded]: “He is a Buddha.”
Thinking, “He has been born [as an arahant],” they felt reverence and, abandoning their address as “friend” (*āvuso*), said, “Certainly not, venerable sir.
“With a mind intent on final knowledge” means with a mind directed toward the attainment of arahantship through final knowledge.
“Ends” refers to the two parts or divisions. “Devotion to the pleasure of sense-desires among sense-objects” refers to the defiled pleasure of sense-desires regarding objective sense-objects.

Experience (*anubhava*). Alternatively, it should be understood that the "sensual pleasures" (*kāmasukhallikā*) are said to be the defilements themselves (*kilesakāma*), because they adhere to the pleasure of worldly gain (*āmisasukha*).

"Village" (*gāma*) means belonging to those who dwell in villages. "Devotion to self-mortification" (*attakilamathānuyoga*) is the pursuit of one's own mortification, such as the suffering of sleeping on thorns and so forth.
"Both extremes" (*ubho ante*) should be understood as follows: either greed or eternalism is one extreme, and either hatred or annihilationism is the other.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "cakkhukaraṇī": it is called *cakkhukaraṇī* because it makes the eye of knowledge associated with itself.

The second term is a synonym for that same thing. *Upasama* is the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Abhiññā* (direct knowledge) and *sambodha* (full awakening) are simply the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
*Nibbāna* is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). He praises the path because it leads to these goals as well. *Sammādiṭṭhi* is knowledge.
“Right intention” (*sammāsaṅkappo*) is applied thought (*vitakka*). The remainder is easy to understand from the perspective of the Dhamma itself. 14.
Having thus shown the four paths together as one, he now spoke the passage beginning with “But this, monks,” in order to show the Four Noble Truths that are to be penetrated by those paths.
Regarding the statements “Birth, too, is suffering,” and so forth: therein—
Therein, for beings being reborn in a state of existence, the very first manifestation of material and immaterial phenomena is here called "birth" (*jāti*).
And because it serves as the basis for the suffering and so forth found in those various states of existence, it is suffering;

thus, the nature of suffering should be understood in the case of aging and the rest by virtue of their serving as the basis for suffering. Furthermore, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) [are suffering] by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).
They are indeed suffering. "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavika*): "renewed existence" (*punabbhava*) is the act of making existence again;

[the term *ponobhavika*] is formed by the elision of the latter member of the compound. That which has renewed existence as its characteristic is "leading to renewed existence. "Accompanied by delight and lust" (*nandirāgasahagata*): herein, "delight" (*nandi*) is that which delights in and finds pleasure in forms and so forth;
that very delight is "lust," thus it is called "delight-and-lust. This designation emphasizes the state (*bhāva*), meaning "the state of delight-and-lust."

"Accompanied by that" means accompanied by delight and lust (*nandirāga*). "In this and that" refers to in each respective state of existence (*bhava*). Craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) is so called because it proceeds by way of the gratification of sensual desires toward the six objects of perception, beginning with visible forms.
Craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is that which proceeds together with the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) is that which proceeds together with the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). [The phrase] "the remainderless fading away and cessation," and so forth...
It is Nibbāna itself that is spoken of. In this context, *virāga* is the fading away (*virajjana*) or departure (*vigamana*). *Nirodha* is the cessation (*nirujjhana*).

By both terms, a thorough departure is expressed. That by which there is the fading away and cessation of craving without remainder is "the fading away and cessation without remainder" (*asesa-virāga-nirodha*), which is Nibbāna itself.
And because, by resorting to it, one abandons, relinquishes, and is liberated from craving and the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
They do not adhere; therefore, relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, and non-attachment are spoken of.
15. "The eye," and so forth, are merely synonyms for knowledge. 16. "As long as" means for as long a time as it takes.
"Three turnings" refers to what are known as the knowledge of the truths, the knowledge of what is to be done, and the knowledge that what was to be done has been accomplished.

Knowledge and vision with three turnings refers to knowledge and vision by way of three cycles. Herein, "this is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin of suffering"—such knowledge of the four truths as they really are is called "knowledge of the truths" (*sacca-ñāṇa*).

Within those same truths, the knowledge that discerns the duties to be performed—namely, "it is to be fully understood, it is to be abandoned, it is to be realized, it is to be developed"—is [the knowledge of the functions].
"Knowledge of what is to be done" (kiccañāṇa) means the knowledge that recognizes the completion of that task, thinking: "It has been fully understood, abandoned, realized, and developed.

"Knowledge of what has been done" (katañāṇa) means the knowledge that recognizes the state of having completed that task. "In twelve aspects" means in twelve aspects by way of three aspects for each of those same [four] truths.
"'I have fully awakened'—I acknowledged"—meaning I did not claim, "I have fully awakened, I have attained Arahantship."
"And from that time" means from the time he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Then indeed I" refers to the period following that.
"And knowledge has come to me" is said with reference to the reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "Unshakable is my liberation," and so forth, shows the mode of its occurrence.
Therein, "unshakable is my liberation" refers to the fruit of Arahantship, both in terms of its cause—which is the Path—and its object.
And its unshakability is to be understood.
"In this exposition" refers to the prose sutta (niggāthasutta). "While being recited" means while being spoken.

"The eye of Dhamma" here intends the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), because it performs the function of an eye regarding the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Whatever [it may be]," and so forth...
This was stated in order to show that even when having Nibbāna as its object, [the Wheel of Dhamma] proceeds without confusion by virtue of its function.
17. "The Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakka): it is the Dhamma of both penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and teaching knowledge (*desanā-ñāṇa*), and because it turns, it is a wheel;
thus, it is the Wheel of Dhamma. "Radiance" (*obhāsa*): it is that which arises through the power of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), produced by temperature conditioned by the mind.
A radiance stands pervading the ten-thousandfold world-system.
18. It is "one who has seen the Dhamma" (diṭṭhadhammo) because he has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths by means of this. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Because it has been attained through his own direct experience, he does not rely on another; he does not proceed here by means of another's faith, thus he is "one who does not depend on another" (aparappaccayo).
They say that as soon as the words "Come, monk" are spoken, both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) are accomplished;
for this reason, they maintain that the word "iti" there indicates the limit [of the formula].

However, some hold that the full ordination is accomplished precisely at the conclusion of the statement, "for the right ending of suffering," while the commentary [states]: "By the Blessed One’s words, 'Come, monk'..."

They say: "This statement characterized by the words 'Come, monk' is expressed by way of such phrases as 'the words "Come, monk"'—just as in the cases of [the titles] 'Musāvādavagga' and so forth. This is consistent with what is stated in the commentary on the first *pārājika*: "For the Blessed One... [omission] ...said these words: 'Come, monk;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. For as much as...

The Blessed One speaks with this restriction: all of that [training] is indeed a factor (*aṅga*). For this is said to be complete for those in training (*sekkha*) and ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*);
however, for those beyond training (*asekkha*), it should be understood as having "lead the holy life" (*cara brahmacariyaṃ*) as its conclusion, due to the perfection of the three trainings.
It is called "full admission" (*upasampadā*) because it is an attainment that has risen above and become superior to mundane attainments.

19–21. *Nīhārabhatta* means one whose meal is brought out from the village and given by the monks. *Kallaṃ nu* means "is it fitting? The passage beginning with *etaṃ mama* (this is mine) and so forth shows, in their respective order, the grasping of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*).

22–23. Regarding *tasmā ti ha*: here *ti ha* is merely a particle; the sense is "therefore. *Nibbindati* means he becomes weary [of existence] by way of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*).
*Virajjati* means he does not take delight by way of the four paths. *Vimuccati* means he is liberated by way of the fruits (*phala*).
"He is liberated. "In him who is liberated," and so forth, refers to the knowledge and vision of reviewing. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the holy life of the Path.

"What remains to be done" refers to the sixteenfold task to be performed individually regarding each of the four Truths by means of the four Paths, consisting of full understanding (*pariññā*) and the rest.
"There is nothing further beyond this state" means there is nothing further beyond this condition—the state of the sixteen tasks, or the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*).
Furthermore, he understands: "There is no further task for me regarding the cultivation of the path. Alternatively, "to this state" (*itthattāya*) means:
