"From this present state—that is, from the continuity of the aggregates currently occurring—there will be no further continuity of aggregates for me.
*Commentary on the Discourse on Going Forth* (*Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā*)
15. *Āḷambaram* means a small drum (*paṇava*). *Vikesikam* means with disheveled hair. *Vikkheḷikam* means with saliva trickling down.
"He thought it was a cemetery" connects thus: he saw his own attendants as if they were in a cemetery.
"He uttered an *udāna*" means he breathed forth a speech arising from a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). *Upassaṭṭham* means mixed with suffering; it means overwhelmed by suffering.
The meaning is: "born from the bodies of all beings. 26.
"This indeed, Yasa," the Blessed One said, referring to Nibbāna. "Graduated discourse" means discourse following a successive order.
"Disadvantage" means fault. "Lowliness" means inferiority, because it is practiced by inferior persons. "Defilement" means [the defilement] of beings by those [faults].
The meaning is "defilement" or "the object of defilement. *Kallacittaṃ* means a healthy mind.

*Sāmukkaṃsikā* refers to that which has its excellence (*ukkaṃsa*) or elevation (*ukkhipana*) by itself (*sāmaṃ*), namely, the teaching of truth. Its specific nature is shown by the words beginning with "suffering" (*dukkha*).
27. *Assadūte* means messengers mounted on horses. *Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ* means a feat of psychic power (*iddhi-kiriyā*). *Abhisaṅkharesi* means he performed.
28. *Yathādiṭṭhan* means that which was seen by means of the first path; the meaning is for one who is reviewing or seeing the plane of the Four Truths by means of the remaining three paths.
In the phrase *mātu no jīvitaṃ*, *no* is a mere particle; the meaning is "the mother’s life.
Because of his state as one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), [the Blessed One said] merely this much: "Come, bhikkhu; the Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life (*brahmacariya*)."

The Blessed One granted full ordination (*upasampadā*). For those whose taints (*āsava*) were exhausted, full ordination was permitted by this much alone, because suffering had already been completely destroyed.

"Lead the holy life" (*cara brahmacariyaṃ*) was said with reference to the fulfillment of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), which is designated as the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*), and not the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).
30. “Of the merchant and the sub-merchant families” means those families belonging to the lineages of both merchants and sub-merchants that have come down by way of tradition.
“Lowly” means inferior. 32–33. “Do not two go by one path”: do not two bhikkhus travel together on a single road. He who kills beings, whether pure or virtuous, is Māra.

He is “the Evil One” (Pāpimā) because he is intent upon evil. “From all snares” means from all the snares of the defilements. “Those divine and those human” refers to those dependent upon divine and human strands of sensual pleasure.
There are indeed snares of defilement (kilesa-pāsa) dependent upon human sensual pleasures;
he speaks with reference to all of these, specifically regarding the acceptance of honor performed by gods and humans who think, "You are a Buddha.

It binds even those possessing the five higher knowledges (pañca-abhiññā) as they move through the sky; thus it is a "sky-roaming" (antalikkhacara) snare of lust (rāga). Yet Māra imagines that even his own snares roam the sky. "Mānasa" means associated with the mind (mano-sampayutta).

He knew that [Māra] was thinking, "It is said that another son of the gods of great power is restraining him; will he perhaps turn back out of fear? When it was said, "You are slain, O Ender," Māra fled dejected, thinking, "He knows me.

34. The reflection arose: Since the desire for renunciation would arise even in those who lack the necessary support for becoming a *ehibhikkhu* (come-be-a-monk), yet Buddhas do not ordain them in that manner, he thus showed the procedure for their ordination as well.

It should be understood that he "considered" [this]. However, those who possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) approach the Blessed One and go forth by means of the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula itself.

This is to be connected with the phrase "those who are persons prohibited [from ordination]. Regarding the statement "he himself should be ordained," here, based on such expressions as "having shaved off hair and beard," what is called "going forth" (*pabbajjā*) consists of the cutting of hair, the donning of the saffron robes, and the granting of refuge; among these—
The final two [acts] must be performed by monks themselves, or caused to be performed by them.
The instruction “Ordain him” is stated with reference to all three types [of ordination]. “Having led him to a restricted boundary” means for the purpose of avoiding the disclosure of his shaving.
For it is not permissible, without informing the monks, to command another within a single boundary, saying, “Shave this man’s hair. “Having ordained him”...
The statement "having clothed himself in the saffron robes" is said specifically with reference to the cutting of the hair and so forth, because it is mentioned separately.

"He is not permitted to go forth" is said with reference to the granting of the refuges; even if the refuges are granted by the command of a monk to one who is not fully ordained, that refuge does not take effect.
"Famous" means endowed with a large retinue. "The state of being devoid of life and devoid of a sentient being": [the text continues] "hair is indeed a distinct [component] in this body..."
It includes such formulations as: “The constituent part is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid—the earth element,” and so forth;
all of this should be understood according to the method presented in the *Visuddhimagga*. “In the past” means during the arising of previous Buddhas.
“With formations crushed” is said by way of insight (*vipassanā*). “One who has developed development” is also said by way of serenity (*samatha*).
Regarding the phrase "the saffron robes should be accepted three times...":

here, one causes the robe to be received by first making a request such as, "Having taken this saffron robe for the sake of escaping all suffering," or "Having given that saffron robe, please ordain me, venerable sir, out of compassion.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Then also... refers to the acceptance [of the robe] after it has been requested three times.
This is the demonstration of the further procedure to be performed. Furthermore, "athāpi" means "even beyond that.

Some, however, say: "The words 'athāpi' are spoken for the purpose of showing the distinction in the manner of going forth without having had the robe formally accepted; and 'athāpi' has the meaning of 'atha vā' (or else).
By the phrase "what is not given is not permitted," he shows that the going forth does not take effect [in such a case].
"Having made him bow at the feet" means having caused him to incline toward the feet. For even one who bows from afar is said to "bow at the feet.
"By the preceptor (*upajjhāya*)"—here, he in whose presence one receives the *upajjha* (ordination) is the preceptor.
He whom they appoint as a teacher (*ācariya*) for the purpose of training in the *Ābhisamācārika* rules is the teacher. But if the preceptor himself...
He teaches everything himself and does not hand it over to another; thus, his preceptor (upajjhāya) also becomes his teacher (ācariya).
Just as at the time of full ordination (upasampadā), when he personally recites the formal act (kammavācā), the preceptor himself becomes the teacher of the formal act.
Having made the end [of the phrase] nasalized, he says "connected as one" (ekasambandhāni) to indicate that no interruption should be made in the middle during the time of giving.

By the phrase “he should be trained in the *ābhisamācārika* duties,” it is shown that novices must conduct themselves according to the rules of training (*sekhiya*), the *vatta* (duties), the *khaṇḍhaka-vatta* (chapter duties), and other world-transgressing precepts such as those concerning seminal emissions; one who fails to act accordingly therein is shameless and deserves disciplinary action.
The commentary on the Discussion of Going-forth is finished.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra (35):

Regarding the phrase in the text, "Attain the unsurpassed liberation," this means that they did not fall into complacency out of the fault of latent tendencies by thinking, "We have destroyed the taints;
what need have we for striving? Rather, they remained in remote lodgings for the purpose of spending their time in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
It should be understood that he exhorted him upon seeing him, both for his sake and so that others might follow his example.
The commentary on the second discourse concerning Māra is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning the Bhaddavaggiya group.
36. "This was their prior karma" refers to the prior karma for the simultaneous realization of those thirty people.

Furthermore, it should be understood that each of them individually possessed much wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) based on hearing the True Dharma, going for refuge, giving, virtue, concentration, and insight during the arising of previous Buddhas;
otherwise, their penetration [of the Truth] would have occurred on that very day.
Furthermore, the distinction of being invited as "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) and so forth would not have been achieved.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Group of Bhaddas is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Miracle at Uruvelā.
37–38. In the Pāli, *agarū* means "it should not be heavy. Regarding the phrase *ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānaṃ*, it means "when both have become aflame.
He placed [the fire] into the bowl after having subdued the power (*teja*) of that Nāga, having gladdened him with a teaching on the Dhamma, and having given him the refuges and the precepts;
then, while standing after having attended upon the Blessed One throughout the entire night, he did so for the purpose of showing it to the Jaṭilas.
It should be understood that he placed [the flower] in the bowl, not by force like a snake-charmer. "Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. 39. "Ajjaṇho" means on this one day.
"Aggisālamhi" means in the fire-hall. "Sumanamanaso" means one whose mind is similar to the minds of the Buddhas.
"Adhicitto" means one whose mind is superior through great compassion and other qualities. "Udicchare" means...
"Ullokesuṃ" means they surrounded [him]. "Anekavaṇṇā acciyo" refers to the six-colored rays of light.
The remainder of the sentence is: "I shall honor you with a regular meal.
(40) "Abhikkantāya rattiyā" means when the night has passed away; that is, at the time of midnight. "Abhikkantavaṇṇā" means...
Of beautiful complexion. *Kevalakappaṃ*: here, the word *kevala* has the sense of "without remainder," and the word *kappa* has the sense of "all around";
therefore, the meaning is "the entire forest grove on every side. *Catuddisā*: in the four directions.
*Yatra hi nāma*: that indeed, namely.

43. *Aṅgamagadhā* means the inhabitants of the provinces of Aṅga and Magadha. *Iddhipāṭihāriya* (the miracle of psychic power) is so called because it is precisely the psychic power of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-iddhi*) which, by carrying away and removing adversaries—the non-Buddhist teachers—and the faults residing in sentient beings who are to be converted, is a *pāṭihāriya*.
Alternatively, it is a *paṭihāriya* because it must be carried out or performed in dependence upon the welfare of various beings; that very thing is the *pāṭihāriya*.
The miracle itself is the marvel; thus, it is the "miracle of psychic power" (iddhipāṭihāriya).
44. "Rags from a dust heap have appeared" means that rags made of hemp, discarded after wrapping the body of the maidservant Puṇṇā and swarming with worms, have appeared as a result of his search;
these the Blessed One, while shaking the earth, took and put on.
They say that this was said with reference to the fact that he gave it later to the Elder Mahākassapa. The reflection beginning with "Where indeed...
was made for the purpose of displaying various miracles to the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila).
It is said, "having dug a lotus pond with his hand," because he removed the clay by means of his supernormal power (iddhi) as if he were digging with his hand.
46. "Let the wood be split, Kassapa," this should be understood as having been said by the Buddha when Uruvelakassapa made such a request.

The same applies to the remaining instances. 49. Regarding the phrase "during the eight nights of the winter season": here, there are four nights at the end of the month of Māgha and four at the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa;
thus, the eight nights between these two months are called the "eight-night interval" (*antaraṭṭhakā*). During those...
During the intermediate nights in the season of falling snow. "Emerging and submerging" is stated by way of performing both actions suddenly.
50. *Udakavāha* means a flood of water. *Reṇuhatāya* means covered with dust; the meaning is "not having crossed over. *Nāvāya* means by means of a raft.
"Is this you, Great Ascetic? means "Are you here? [In the original text] the letter *dha* becomes *da*, and there is an *anusvāra*.
Having said "Is this it?", it was stated as in the phrases "Once upon a time" (*ekamidāhaṃ*) and so forth. He asked, "Are you standing in this place? "This am I" means "I am standing here.
51. "For a long time" (*cirapaṭikā*) means from a long time ago. "Having washed all the requisites mixed with hair into the water"—it is also [said].

It should be joined [to the preceding]. "Khārī" refers to the requisites of an ascetic, such as the araṇi fire-drill and the water-pot; "khārikāja" refers to the carrying-pole used for transporting those items.
"Aggihutamissa" means accompanied by the implements for fire-worship. 52–3. "Upasagga" means calamity or affliction.

Regarding the phrase "four thousand five hundred miracles," this is stated excluding the fifteen miracles beginning with the taming of the Nāgas; it is said that a smaller number, being merely an excess, does not count [toward the full total].

54. *Gayāyanti*: Because it was situated not far from the river named Gayā, the village came to be known as "Gayā" by way of its feminine gender; [it means] "in that [village]. *Gayāsīse*: On the back-slab rock (piṭṭhipāsāṇa) bearing this name.

By the passage beginning, "This which arises conditioned by eye-contact... pleasure," etc., he shows the burning nature (*ādittatā*) of the remaining immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) as well, by way of the feelings of joy (*somanassa*), grief (*domanassa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) within the consciousnesses of the eye-consciousness process (*cakkhuviññāṇavīthicitta*).
This same method applies to the others as well. *Mano*: The life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*).
Because the mind-door is intended here. By "mind-consciousness," only that which has entered the cognitive process of the mind-door is included.
The commentary on the account of the miracle at Uruvelā is finished.
The commentary on the account of the meeting with Bimbisāra.
55. "Sacrifices welcome" means they say that [beings] succeed because of sacrifice. "In the acquisitions" (*upadhīsu*):

here, by way of being the basis for suffering, pleasure, and so forth, there are four acquisitions—namely, the acquisition of sense-desires (*kāma*), the acquisition of aggregates (*khandha*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesa*), and the acquisition of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
Among these, it is the acquisition of aggregates that is intended here; thus he says, "Knowing the stain in the acquisition of aggregates. "Sacrifices" (*yaññā*) means for the sake of sacrifice.
*Yiṭṭhe* means in a great sacrifice (*mahāyāga*). *Hute* refers to the daily tending of the sacrificial fire (*aggiparicaraṇa*).

*Kiṃ vakkhāmī* means "how shall I speak? 57–8. *Āsīsā* means wishes or desires. *Siṅgīsuvaṇṇanikkhenā* means by means of a heap of yellow gold (*siṅgīsuvaṇṇa*). Among types of gold, that which is fashioned through joining (*yuttikata*) is inferior;

better than that is that which is infused with mercury (*rasaviddha*); better than that is that which is produced from a mine (*ākaruppanna*); and better than even that is whatever [other superior kind].
Divine gold is the best; even among that, *cāmīkara* is the best, then *sātakumbha*, then *jambunada*, and even better than that is *siṅgīsuvaṇṇa*.
Its measure is called a *nikkha*, which is five units of gold.
They say there are many varieties, such as the eightfold gold and so forth. Regarding the "ten noble abodes":

“Here, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, is possessed of six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has shaken off individual dogmatic views, has discarded seeking, has untroubled intention, has tranquilized bodily formations, and is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
Thus it is said regarding the ten noble abodes (ariyavāsa). Therein, “having abandoned five factors” means being dissociated from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

"Endowed with the six factors": regarding the six objects of experience—desirable and so forth—the sixfold equanimity (*upekkhā*) that serves as the antidote to joy and its opposites is what is meant by the "six factors.
"Having a single guard" refers to the state of established mindfulness (*upaṭṭhita-sati*).

"Possessing four supports" (*caturāpassena*): this means one who has the four supports (*apassena*), namely, reflection (*saṅkhāya-sevanā*), endurance (*adhivāsanā*), avoidance (*parivajjanā*), and removal (*vinodanā*); by this, those supports are demonstrated. "Repelled" (*paṇunnāni*)...
He from whom the individual truths grasped separately by those who hold to views have been removed is "one who has discarded the individual truths" (*paṇunnapaccekasacca*);

by this, the abandoning of views through mundane knowledge is described. He by whom the search—consisting of the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life—has been thoroughly, completely, fully, and entirely relinquished is "one whose search has been thoroughly relinquished" (*samavayasaṭṭhesana*). By this, [the abandoning] of the three...

The absence of the [three] searches (*esanā*) has been stated. By the phrase "one whose intentions are undisturbed" (*anāvilasaṅkappo*), the state of a mind undisturbed by sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth is expressed.

By the phrase "one whose bodily formations are tranquilized" (*passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro*), the freedom from distress through union with the fourth jhāna is stated. By the phrase "one whose mind is well-liberated" (*suvimuttacitto*), the Path (*magga*) is indicated.
By the phrase "one whose wisdom is well-liberated" (*suvimuttapañño*), the knowledge of fruition (*phalañāṇa*) is stated by way of the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

For these noble ones dwell here, thus they are called "abodes of the noble ones" (*ariyavāsa*). He by whom those abodes have been dwelt in, inhabited, and accomplished is the Blessed One who has "dwelt in the abodes" (*vutthavāsa*).
"He who possesses the ten powers" (*dasabala*) means he is endowed with the ten bodily powers and the powers of knowledge. These are as follows:
"The Kāḷāvaka, the Gaṅgeyya, the Paṇḍara, and the Tambapiṅgala;..."
“Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—these are the ten elephant lineages.
Thus, these ten elephant breeds are endowed with qualities corresponding to the ten powers (*dasabala*) [of a Buddha].
Among them, the strength of the ten eldest ones, the Chaddantas, is called the “ten powers of the Blessed One’s body. And that [strength] belongs to those known as the Kālāvaka...

The strength of a thousand million ordinary female elephants, or even ten thousand million middle-sized men, is called the "Nārāyaṇa-composite strength. Furthermore, regarding those [powers] mentioned in the Pāḷi:
"In this case, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible..."

As stated in the passage beginning with “he understands things as they truly are,” these are: the power of knowledge regarding the possible and the impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of kamma (*kammavipāka-ñāṇabala*);

the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadā-ñāṇabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the world of its many and diverse elements (*anekadhātunānādhātu-loka-ñāṇabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings (*sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇabala*);

the power of knowledge regarding the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (*jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpatti-saṃkilesavodānavuṭṭhāna-ñāṇabala*); and the power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇabala*).
The power of the knowledge of the divine eye, and the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—these are the ten powers of knowledge; these are called the Blessed One’s ten powers.
"By means of the ten factors of one beyond training" refers to those ten factors associated with the fruit of Arahatship mentioned in the Canon as:
"the right view of one beyond training... [and so on] ...the right concentration of one beyond training, the right knowledge of one beyond training, and the right liberation of one beyond training."

He is endowed with the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-dhamma*). Herein, it should be understood that right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), which was mentioned in the sense of seeing, is itself also called "right knowledge" (*sammā-ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing;
furthermore, all the remaining factors associated with the consciousness of the fruit (*phala-citta*), beginning with contact (*phassa*), are what are called "right liberation" (*sammā-vimutti*).
The commentary on the account of the meeting with Bimbisāra is finished.
Commentary on the account of the going forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna:
Sāriputta was the son of the brahmin woman Sārī; Moggallāna was the son of the brahmin woman Moggalī. Regarding the wanderer Channa...
By saying "having covered his private parts with a cloth," he shows that this is not a naked wanderer (*naggaparibbājaka*).
The explanation of "known" (*upaññāta*) is "it is known" (*ñāto ceva*). The explanation of "path" (*magga*) is "and the path has been approached" (*upagato ca maggo*).

And thus, in the phrase "known as the path" (*upaññāta-magga*), the word "known" (*ñāta*) is a synonym for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). [The term *magga* is used] by means of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
The word "path" (*magga*) has already been mentioned. He shows that the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "approaching" and should also be connected with the word "path.

This is what is meant: because following closely behind is both a knowledge approached (*upagata-ñāṇa*) recognized by those seeking [the goal], and a path (*magga*) approached and practiced (*upagata-paṭipanna*) by them, therefore [he thought]: "What if I were to follow?"
“Nibbāna is known through inference” means that Nibbāna is known by means of logical reasoning (*upapatti-anumāna*).
“‘The Path’ is the explanation of this” means “seeking the path”; the sense is that one seeks it for the purpose of seeing it directly through inference.

Showing that both cessation (*nirodha*) and the means to cessation are called “cessation” by way of retaining only one term (*ekasesa*), he says “Alternatively,” and so forth. “Establishing” means concluding.

"Higher than this" means that although there was no other threefold path higher than the stream-entry (sotāpatti) attained by me from this point, nevertheless, this very thing was sought by me as the Dhamma of Nibbāna—this is the meaning.
62–3. "With that as its object" means with the liberation of the fruit of stream-entry which has Nibbāna as its object.
"Of those venerable ones" refers to those two assemblies together with their retinues; having heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma at that very moment, they [attained] Arahantship.
[The Buddha] attained [enlightenment], but the two chief disciples, due to the greatness of their own cognitive task, did so after the lapse of several days. Therefore he said, "Thus," and so forth.
The phrase "in the sense of the object" (*upayogattheva*) is stated with reference to the status of the act of envy as the object of the verb.
The commentary on the account of the going-forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is concluded.
Commentary on the Duties toward the Preceptor (Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā): 64.
"Faults and non-faults" refers to both minor and major faults. "The bowl for one who has risen" (*uttiṭṭhapatta*):
here, "one who has risen" (*uttiṭṭha*) means wandering for alms, as in such passages as "One should not be negligent when one has risen. For the purpose of rising...
The bowl that has been taken is an "uttiṭṭha-patta" (a bowl for leftovers); therefore, it is called "the bowl used for wandering for alms.

As to what fault there is in offering it [to others], he says: "For in that case," and so forth. "Therefore" means: because people perceive these very things as "leftovers" in an *uttiṭṭha-patta*, thinking "they eat from this alone";
therefore it is called *uttiṭṭha-patta* by means of the word *uttiṭṭha* itself, according to the perception of people.
"It is understood even from the word *ucchiṭṭha*. However, some say that "the word *uttiṭṭha* has the same meaning as the word *ucchiṭṭha*.
Since there is also a form with the suffix *-tvā*, namely "*uttiṭṭhā*," he said "*uṭṭhahitvā*" (having stood up).
"To take a preceptor" means to take the status of preceptor in one's mind, or the meaning is to obtain his consent through the words of request.
65. *Patissayanaṃ* means *patisso*; it is the state of behaving by relying on one who is venerable; the meaning is "whatever is respectful. *Sappatisso* means "possessing respect";
the meaning is behaving according to the instruction of another whom one has made one's elder. Therefore he said: "having established the state of being an elder.
*Sāhu* means "good" or "excellent. *Lahu* means "not heavy"; the meaning is "easy to support. *Opāyikaṃ*...
"Connected with skillful means" (upāyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ) means that such a course of action is the means for crossing over. "Appropriate" (patirūpaṃ) means proper conduct (sāmīcikammaṃ).
"With one that inspires confidence" (pāsādikenāti) means accomplish it through bodily and vocal application that brings about confidence.

"By body" (kāyena) means he makes his request by means of the body, showing hand gestures and so forth that communicate this meaning. "'Very well' (sādhū)" refers to the acceptance [of the request] by the preceptor.

Regarding the statements beginning with "sādhū" (well), the intention is that the phrase "indicates by body" and so forth was said in reference to the resident pupil’s verbal acceptance, saying "sādhū.
"By the mere act of requesting and giving" means: first, by the mere act of the resident pupil’s request, and then, by the mere act of the preceptor’s words such as "sādhū," and so on.
66. "Assa" means "of the student (saddhivihārika). "Two robes" refers to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).

"From here on" means starting from the negative particle (*na*) in the phrase "not while the preceptor (upajjhāya) is speaking"; by this, he shows that there is no offense in cases where the negative particle serves as a prohibition, such as in the rule "not too far away.
"In all cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," except in the case of emergencies, insanity, derangement, being afflicted by pain, and so forth.
Even for one who speaks without knowing the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even if he is ill;
for in times of emergency, it is permissible to speak with interruptions here and there. Thus it is with other such prohibitions involving the negative particle (*na-kāra*);
however, in other cases, even one who is ill is not exempt. In the Canon, regarding the phrase “having touched the lower seat,” this refers to the bowl or other items previously placed there.
It is stated for the purpose of avoiding contact; even after looking with the eye and knowing the absence of others, it is indeed permissible to set it down.
"Near to an offense" means precisely the act of committing an offense.
"In a village" means within the village or in a similar structure such as a pavilion. "In a house" means inside a dwelling. "In a place of retreat" means in a sitting hall.
“Dhotavālikāya” means in a place where the sand has been washed by water and is free of dust, being perfectly pure.

“Niddhūme” means in a bath-house (jantāghara) that is free from the smoke of a burning fire. A bath-house is indeed a place for sweating the body in regions where snowfall is frequent, for the purpose of warding off afflictions caused by those conditions and other diseases.
It is said that because it is concealed from darkness, many people may enter there together.

Having laid aside their robes and, in order to avoid being scorched by the heat of the fire, having smeared their faces with clay, they bathe after sweating their bodies as much as desired and rubbing them with powders and other substances.
For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: “The powder should be kneaded,” and so forth.
*Ulloka* means a place for looking upwards; the meaning is the upper part.

"Should be led elsewhere" means that from whatever place one dwells where dissatisfaction with the Teaching has arisen, one should be led elsewhere to a location endowed with the presence of virtuous friends and so forth.
"Of persons of a different character" refers to those who, whether scrupulous or unscrupulous, do not desire the teacher's progress.
However, if the teacher is unscrupulous and does not even accept advice, then those who are scrupulous are of a different character from him.
In that case, having left the preceptor, one should partake of food and other requisites only with those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*).
It should be understood here that the status of being a preceptor and so forth is not the determining factor. "Having gone to the courtyard" means having gone to the preceptor’s courtyard.

The phrase "not a cemetery" is an illustration; it should be understood that for one wishing to go outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacāra-sīma*), it is not permitted to go without having asked permission.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of the Preceptor is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of the Co-resident Student (Saddhivihārika-vatta-kathā): 67.

Regarding the phrases "should be supported" and "should be assisted" in the discussion on the duties of the co-resident student, [these are stated] with reference to [the preceptor’s] lack of respect.
For teachers and preceptors who do not sustain [their pupils] with the gift of the Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the breach of the proper conduct.
For that very reason, it is stated in the *Parivāra*: "One incurs [the offense] by making noise. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties toward a co-resident pupil is finished.
68. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Not Properly Fulfilling Duties, etc.:

"One would not fulfill the duties" means that, having recognized the time for performing duties by way of discerning the occasion, one fails to do so either through pride, indolence, and so forth, or through a lack of respect toward the preceptor and others, or through ignorance that "it is not permissible not to do it."
Or if one should not do so, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. However, there is no offense for one who does not act through lack of intention (*asañcicca*) or lack of mindfulness (*asati*), and so forth.
For all the observances (*vatta*) are indeed training rules (*sekhiya*); therefore, the entire analysis here should be understood according to the method stated among the *sekhiyas*.
"Affection based on the household" (*gehassita-pema*) means affection consisting of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"He does not know whether there has been consent or non-consent" means he does not know in this way: "If I have given my consent, there is an offense for those who do not act;
if I have refused and there was no consent, there is no offense. Because of the statement, "Among them, if one monk is endowed with proper conduct...
[and so on]... for them there is no offense," if someone says, "Your co-resident or pupil is ill..."

If he says, "I will attend upon him; I will perform everything that ought to be done, such as providing instruction and guidance," or if those students living with him and others say, "Be free from anxiety," or if they do not accept the duty of service, there is no offense for the teacher or the preceptor.
The commentary on the discussion regarding improper conduct is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Rādha (Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 69.
In the story of the Brahmin Rādha, regarding the phrase in the Pāḷi “uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto,” it means that a pale color has arisen over his entire body.
The distributive expression (*vicchāvacana*) is employed in order to show that this pale color pervades his whole body. Regarding the word *adhikāra*:
"Upakāraṃ. "Katavedino" means those who make known the benefit done to them by way of returning it.
What ought to be said regarding the formal act of full ordination (upasampadā-kamma-vācā) will be stated at the conclusion. "Parimaṇḍalehi" means with complete [robes]. 71–73.
"Paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ" means transgression of the training rules (sikkhāpada). In the Pāḷi, "piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ" refers to the strength derived from the scraps of food gathered from the ground.
Having partaken of food sought by means of morsel-by-morsel alms-gathering. "Extra gain" (*atirekalābha*) refers to a gain in excess of the food obtained through alms-round.
The classification of communal meals (*saṅghabhatta*) and so forth will be clarified in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.

"Monastery" (*vihāra*) refers to the entire monastic complex (*saṅghārāma*), including grass huts and the like, enclosed by a wall. "Half-joined house" (*aḍḍhayoga*) is a long mansion with a single hall. It is shaped like the back of an elephant or a garuḷa.
They also call it the "Long Palace" (*dīghapāsāda*). A "palace" (*pāsāda*) is a high, multi-storied building that is square in shape.
A "hammiya" is a palace that is not very high, has a flat roof, and is provided with a courtyard (*candikaṅgaṇa*). A "cave" (*guhā*) is a mountain cave. "Putimutta" refers to cow's urine.
The explanatory commentary on the account concerning the Brahmin Rādha is concluded.
**Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Toward a Teacher (Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā)** 76.
*Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno*: being exhorted by a fellow follower of the Dhamma with such training rules as, "It should be worn in this manner," and so forth.

*Vādaṃ āropetvā*: having raised an objection, [saying], "What fault is there in wearing the lower robe hanging down, etc.? If there were a fault, it would also apply to wearing the lower robe in a circular fashion, etc."

Having leveled the censure with the words, “There would be fault,” and so forth: “That very *titthāyatana*” means that the very ford (*tittha*) consisting of views is the source (*āyatana*), the place for the arising of suffering;
thus it is a “ford-source” (*titthāyatana*). “I will dwell depending on the Venerable One” means: I will live in dependence upon the Venerable One.
The commentary on the Discussion of Duties Toward the Teacher is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Sending Away and Asking for Forgiveness: 80.
It should not be understood that an offense occurs for the resident pupil merely by virtue of the characteristic previously stated.
The connection [of the words] should be understood as follows. However, in the manuscripts, having omitted the negative particle (*na*) in the phrase "not by that very characteristic," they write:
"by that very characteristic, the offense of the resident pupil is to be known. That is a scribal error.
For if the state of being an offense were accepted by that very characteristic, then it would follow for one who is released from formal dependence (*nissaya-mutta*) as well.

If it were said that there is an offense even for one who is not released, then one would incur an offense according to the characteristic thus stated. Furthermore, this would contradict the immediately preceding statement:
“Indeed, as long as a resident pupil lives under dependence upon a teacher, he must perform all the duties toward the teacher.
And in the *Visuddhimagga* as well—

“It is said: ‘The teacher who provides dependence (nissayācariya), the teacher who provides recitation (uddesācariya), the resident pupil under dependence (nissayantevāsika), the resident pupil under recitation (uddesantevāsika), and those who have the same teacher—these must be looked after as long as their dependence and recitation are not discontinued.

Therefore, by bringing the syllable *na* that has dropped out here according to the stated method, and by the very characteristic already stated for the resident pupil, it should be understood that there is no offense for the resident pupil under dependence. Thus the meaning should be grasped.
The commentary on the discussion regarding sending away and asking for forgiveness is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence (Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 83. Regarding the discussion on the cessation of dependence, the statement, "Or,

one should receive dependence from him with whom there is common enjoyment and sharing," enjoins the taking of dependence only upon those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*), because it is prohibited in the case of those lacking a sense of shame (*alajjī*).
And here, by the word "use" (*paribhoga*), co-residence (*saṃvāsa*) such as that of a single meal is included, because the use of requisites is already covered by the word "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*).
By this, he shows that one should not engage in enjoyment or co-residence with those who are shameless (*alajjī*). "There is no exemption" means there is no exemption from an offense.
"Such a person" refers to one with whom one has previously received formal dependence (*nissaya*), or one with whom there is shared enjoyment and use of requisites.
"Such a one. "So it was said" means that it was said, "I will return quickly. "Four or five days" is merely an illustration;
if the resemblance is recognized within one or two days, it should be accepted as the day it is known.
Even if it is not recognized after four or five days, one must wait for however many days it takes for it to be recognized.
However, one should not entertain even the slightest thought, "I shall look for someone who belongs to my own group.

Regarding the phrase "while the young novices are listening," an exemption is indeed possible if there is the perception that she will come even without having heard the summons, or that she is delayed due to some obstacle. Therefore it was said: "If he sends her with the message, 'I shall stay right here,' there is no exemption.

The statement "there is no exemption even for a single day" refers to one who lacks the resolve to go; however, for one who possesses such resolve, there is no fault even if several days have passed due to duties such as returning the lodgings.
"In that very place one must dwell" means that one must dwell having received dependence (nissaya) in that very same common location.
By the statement, "It is permissible to dwell in that same monastery...," the cessation of dependence (nissayapaṭippassaddhi) is stated only when the preceptor (upajjhāya) continues to provide care;
however, if he does not provide care due to anger or indifference toward the group, the dependence previously received from others [remains in force].
This shows that [the dependence] does not cease.

Regarding the cessation of dependence on a teacher, the method stated as "some teacher," etc., should be applied to the cases of the preceptor departing and so forth, and having been explained there, it should also be applied here and joined accordingly.
"Living in another monastery after having crossed two stone-throw distances" means living in another monastery outside the boundary of the precinct.
They dwell beyond two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of a stone’s throw) from the residence of their pupils.

By this, it is shown that even outside the precinct (*upacāra*), if one dwells within two *leḍḍupāta* from the residence of the pupils and others—that is, in a nearby location—the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not suspended.
However, within the boundary of the precinct (*antoupacārasīmā*), having passed beyond two *leḍḍupāta*—
For one who continues to live [under dependence], the dependence is not suspended at all.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the suspension of dependence is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Things to be Ordained.

84. In the discussion on the characteristics of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), "a novice should not be attended to" means that one should not, having become a preceptor, grant the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). "Of the one beyond training" (*asekkha*) means belonging to the one beyond training; it refers to the mundane and supramundane aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
"By way of grasping at extremes" means by way of grasping at the positions of eternalism and annihilationism.
"The last two" refers to these two factors: "he has little learning" and "he is lacking in wisdom. "The last three" refers to [the cases where] he is not capable of dealing with arisen remorse...
There are these three: not knowing the offense, and not knowing the emergence from the offense.
For the inability to dispel remorse by means of the Dhamma—consisting of the texts, the commentaries, and the methods—is indeed a lack of proficiency;
thus, that too is stated as a factor of the offense itself.

"Abhisamācāra" means excellent and supreme conduct, that is, the morality of duties and sub-duties (*vatta-paṭivatta-sīla*). The training rules (*sikkhā*) prescribed with reference to that, known as the *khandhaka* training rules, are "abhisamācārika.
Indeed, even a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is called "training" (*sikkhā*) because it must be practiced through study and so forth by those who desire to fulfill it therein.
It is the beginning of the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).

The training that constitutes the beginning of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka*) refers to the rules of training included within the two Vibhaṅgas. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:

"The rules of training included within the two Vibhaṅgas are those pertaining to the beginning of the holy life; those included in the Khandhakas and the Vatta are those pertaining to higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*).
Therefore, regarding the phrase "in the designation for trainees" (*sekkhapaṇṇattiyaṃ*), they are called "trainees" (*sekkhā*) because they are still to be trained.

It is called *paṇṇatti* because it was laid down by the Blessed One. It should be understood that all the rules of training (*sikkhāpada*) included in the two Vibhaṅgas are referred to as "the training-rule designation" (*sekkhapaṇṇatti*).

Regarding the "delimitation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpapariccheda*), here [is meant] the fourfold aggregate of feeling and so forth, as described under the "wholesome triad" and other categories, through the distinctions of genus, plane, person, association, basis, object, karma, door, characteristic, function, and so on.
"Name" refers to nibbāna; "form" refers to the classification of the primary elements and the derived matter.

The wisdom that knows these by way of such analysis is called *nāmarūpapariccheda*, and the treatise that elucidates this is also named *nāmarūpapariccheda*. By this, he shows that one must become skilled in the meaning of the Abhidhamma.
"To cause to train" means to cause to learn.
The commentary on the discussion of the five things not to be ordained is finished.
Commentary on the account concerning those who were formerly members of other sects (Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathā):

In the discussion regarding the probation for former members of other sects (*titthiyaparivāsa*), among the phrases such as “of an Ājīvaka,” etc., one who maintains the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*) is called an Ājīvaka; whereas those who maintain the doctrine of action (*kiriyavāda*)...
However, the Nigaṇṭhas and other naked heretics are also included under the term *acelaka*. The probation for heretics (*titthiyaparivāsa*) is prescribed for one who is entirely naked.
And that applies to one who comes into the presence of the monks in that very state of nakedness, not to one who has come having covered himself;
this is shown by the statement beginning with "If he too... In this context, "he too" refers to the Ājīvaka.
The "bestowing of trifling material gifts" means the giving away of even a small amount of things worthy of being given.

"Those who live off their own beauty" means those who subsist by relying solely on their own physical form. "One whose resort is prostitutes" means one for whom prostitutes are the frequent place of activity;
this same method applies everywhere. "Past youth" refers to an unmarried girl who has reached the state of being an old maid (*thullakumārī*).
Thus it was said. "Of taking" means of grasping or seizing.
The commentary on the account concerning the former member of another sect is finished.
The commentary on the account concerning the five diseases begins.
88–9. Regarding the five grounds for non-offense (*pañcābādhādivatthu*), the phrase "I am healthy, I shall disrobe" (*somhi arogo, vibbhamissāmīti*) means: "Being healthy, I shall disrobe.

"Measuring the surface of a fingernail" (*nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ*): the surface of the fingernail of the little finger is intended here. Because it is stated, "In a concealed place, [an area] measuring the surface of a fingernail, even if situated on the side not subject to growth, is permissible," this refers to a non-concealed place.
Even such [a case] is not permitted; it is established that even in a concealed place, it is not permitted if it is on the side of being enlarged.

However, regarding the statement "but in the mouth," etc., which was said to prohibit those who might take [it], it means that even in a visible place, that which is smaller than the size of a fingernail's surface and is not intended for enlargement is permitted.
“Even the size of a jujube stone” means even the measure of a jujube kernel.

By the word “even” (*pi*) in the phrase “even if it remains in an unswollen state, it is not permitted,” he shows that a boil smaller than the size of a jujube stone is also not permitted. Therefore he said, “having made it smooth-skinned” (*sacchaviṃ kāretvā*);
the meaning is, having removed the existing skin. Alternatively, the reading is “smooth-skinned” (*sañchavin*); the meaning is, having produced a new layer of skin.
The meaning [is as follows]: even when abscesses and the like have subsided, there may be discoloration on the abscesses; that is permissible.

"Having the color of lotus and white lily petals" means having the color of the petals of red and white lotus flowers. "In the same manner as stated regarding leprosy" refers to the method already explained:
it is permissible for it not to spread in a concealed place, but in other places, nothing whatsoever is permissible.

It shows [this]. Sosabyādhi is a wasting disease. Yakkhummāro is a disease that is like a demon (yakkha) which occasionally comes, throws one down on the ground, and rubs parts of the body such as the hands and face against the ground.
The commentary on the discussion of the five bases for affliction is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the King’s Servant (Rājabhaṭavatthu): 90.
“I am no longer the king’s servant,” he says when taking leave; this is said with reference to one who has been assigned to a specific post by the king himself.
However, as for one who is appointed by royal officials such as ministers and so forth, or who is the servant of those very ministers and others, by him [that...]
It is appropriate to ask even his ministers and others for permission.
The commentary on the account of the king’s servant is finished.
The commentary on the account of the thief.
91. Therefore, because the Blessed One himself is the Master of the Dhamma, he ordained Aṅgulimāla by means of the "Come, monk" formula;
the intention is that when he was laying down the training rules for the monks, he spoke thus.
"Knowing this" means they know him as one who has become virtuous.
92. *Uparamanti* means they cease; *viramanti* means they desist. *Bhinditvā* means having broken the leather thong.
*Chinditvā* means having cut the chain. *Muñcitvā* means having released the rope bond. *Vivaritvā* means having opened the village gates and so forth among the village enclosures.
*Apassamānānaṃ* means while the guards protecting the men were not looking on.
95. "In the same manner as before" means in the very same way as stated in the passage: "One who has been struck with a whip and undergone punishment.
The commentary on the story of the thief is finished.
The commentary on the story of the debtor begins.
96. "Even if he has fled" means that having learned of the arrival of his creditors, he has fled out of fear.

"He becomes liable for the debt" means that, having been recognized as being in the position of a debtor, he was admitted into the state of a monk with disregard for the debt still owed. "Little by little" means in small increments.
"It must certainly be paid" means that whether the creditor accepts the money or not, one must remain resolute in the act of giving.
This shows that other monks, saying "Do not abandon your burden," should act as his companions;
for by abandoning the burden, he might be made to pay compensation equal to the value of the goods.
The commentary on the account concerning the debtor is finished.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Bases for Slavery (Dāsavatthukathāvaṇṇanā): 97. By the phrase “purchased after being subjected to the conduct of a slave,” he excludes one who was bought for the purpose of liberating him from slavery.
For even one purchased with wealth is not a slave in that sense. In the expression “according to the conduct in various places,” it means according to the customs in this or that particular country.

By means of burning the leaf-pledge (*paṇṇajjhāpana*) and so forth, according to the rule for making one no longer a slave. At consecrations (*abhiseka*) and other such occasions, they cause all bonds to be released;
with reference to this, it is said, "by that which is common to all.

They themselves offer the leaf-pledge [to become slaves], thinking, "It is not right [for us to remain free]," and thus those women who were formerly free (*bhuñjissitthiyo*) say, "Let us too become beauty-slaves (*vaṇṇadāsiyo*)."
For the sake of their own protection, they themselves cause their names to be written on the slave registers of kings; their sons also become royal slaves.

Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain them. "They must not be ordained if they have not been given by those [owners]" means that however many owners there may be, they must not be ordained even if they have not been given by one among them.

Regarding the statement, "It is permissible to ordain them after making them free," this means that in whichever monastery those monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) were assigned, it is permissible to ordain them after making them free by informing the Saṅgha of that monastery and providing wealth through labor.
Regarding the phrase, "They become like clarified butter poured upon the head": in certain regions, when people make mirrors, they pour clarified butter upon their heads.
They pour [water] on him; it is said that by this they become his slaves. Thus, the intention is that even this is a gift given through the words of a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).
Likewise, even when given in such a way, because he is "the monastery attendant's slave" of the Saṅgha, it is stated: "He must not be ordained.
Because of the statement "what is called temporary," everything given—whether with a fixed time limit or with the desire to take him back later—is included.

It should be understood that this applies only for the duration of his life. One called a "masterless slave" is one whose family of masters has perished through death without kin, and who has no heir;

such a person may be ordained only after being made free by those of his own caste, or by the inhabitants of the village where he lives, or by local lords. Temple slaves (*devadāsa*) are also indeed slaves; for in certain regions...
They are royal slaves, or in some cases, monastery slaves; therefore, it is not permissible to grant them the going-forth.

Even if one has granted the going-forth to a slave and then, upon seeing the owner, moves him away for the purpose of concealment, he is to be charged with an offense of taking what is not given according to the number of steps taken.
However, there is no offense for the slave who flees.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Grounds for Slavery is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Blacksmith’s Head, etc.: 98.

In the discourse beginning with the inquiry regarding the blacksmith’s head (*kammārabhaṇḍu*), "blacksmith’s head" refers to one whose head is shaven because of being young and not yet bound with a turban.
He is called a smith’s son. Regarding the term *tulādhāramuṇḍaka*: here, *tulādhārā* refers to smiths who hold a scale (*tulā*) for gold, copper, and so forth in their hands;
among them, one with a shaven head and a young body is meant.
Therefore it says, "Pañcasikha, a young boy. He is called *pañcasikha* because he has bound his single crest (*sikhā*) into five braids.
He is called Pañcasikha because he has five tufts (*sikhā*); they shaved his tufts and ordained him without informing any monk.
Therefore, the permission for shaving (*bhaṇḍukamma*) was granted. "Included within the boundary" means that when a formal boundary (*baddhasīmā*) exists, it is included within that;
when one does not exist, it means included within the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*). And here, although it is said: "I allow you, monks..."
Only this much was stated: "to seek permission from the Saṅgha for the shaving of hair (*bhaṇḍukamma*). No offense was mentioned for one who does not seek permission;

nevertheless, because it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "there is no offense even for one who ordains [others] while perceiving, 'We have asked permission from everyone'...," it should be understood that for one who intentionally shaves hair without having asked permission, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Since even the shaving of hair receives the designation of "going forth as a recluse," he said, "this making of him a recluse," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "wearing a single tuft of hair":
here, they say that a tuft made with a single hair is a "single-tuft" (*ekasikhā*); however, it should be understood that even a small amount of hair is what is meant by this term.
Furthermore, it is not permitted to cut even a single hair without having asked permission.
100. "With the left hand" is said because one eats with the right hand.
103–4. Regarding the release from dependence (*nissaya-muccanaka*), among the sets of five and six duties (*vatta*), the passage beginning "Both his Pātimokkhas...
[and so on]... according to the phrasing" includes this entire classification; once the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* is known, it becomes known.
“‘He knows what is an offense; he knows what is not an offense’”—this should not be understood as referring only to offenses and so forth within the matters known by himself.
The commentary on the discussion of the smith’s tools, clothing, and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Story of Rāhula 105.
*Pokkharavassa* (The Lotus Rain): This refers to the rain that falls from the bodies of those wishing to get wet, just as [water] falls upon a lotus grove (*pokkhara*).
It is said that when this rain falls, only those who wish to get wet are drenched, while others are not. Having said, "Take alms,"...
Thinking, "There is no one called 'Gata' (the Departed); he will enjoy all the property belonging to his own kingdom for himself," King Suddhodana did not even invite him out of respect.
However, having gone home, he spent the entire night preparing a great almsgiving and arranging the seats and decorations for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
"No one... nor did anyone take a bowl," said the Blessed One; [he spoke thus] because no one took [anything], thinking that he would go only to his father's residence.

"In the family city" means in the city where his own kinsmen lived. "The practice of wandering for alms" refers to the practice of going on an uninterrupted alms-round even in his own relatives' village.
"Bhikkhācāra" means one whose movement or wandering consists of seeking alms; [it is like] a khattiya.
"Uttiṭṭha" means having risen and standing at the door of others' houses, one should take the alms-food intended for oneself.
"Nappamajjeyya" means that after refusing exquisite food obtained through invitations and the like, one should not be negligent in going for alms in that manner.
"Dhammaṃ" refers to that very practice of wandering for alms while abandoning improper means of livelihood and proceeding from house to house in regular order.
"One should practice good conduct. "He sleeps happily" means he dwells happily in the four postures.

In the second verse, "one should not practice misconduct" means one should not practice that aforementioned Dhamma as misconduct by wandering in improper resorts such as among prostitutes and the like.
The rest is exactly as previously explained. "Having heard this verse," [refers to] in one's dwelling.
Having heard this second verse spoken by the Blessed One while seated at a gathering of his kinsmen— based on his own experience of wandering for alms—
he [the King] attained parinibbāna. Furthermore, in such works as the *Dhammapāla-jātaka*, the King’s history is recounted even in subsequent periods until his final passing away.
These were spoken as a matter of context. Therefore he said, "Having realized the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having gone to the lying-in chamber":
it should be understood that if the Blessed One had not gone there on that very day and seen her, she would have died of a broken heart; thus he went.
"On that very day" means on the very day he saw Rāhula’s mother. However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"Having gone to Kapilavatthu, the Teacher ordained Nanda on the third day.

"The loosening of the hair" refers to the untying of the topknot or braid tied during childhood for the purpose of binding the royal turban; it is said that they performed this as an auspicious ceremony.
They perform [these rites]. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: “*Kesavissajjanaṃ* means the shaving of hair according to family custom.

“*Paṭṭabandho*” refers to the binding of a golden fillet upon the forehead [with the words] “Such-and-such king. The auspicious ceremony for entering a newly built palace is the “house-auspiciousness” (*gharamaṅgala*).

The auspicious ceremony for raising the royal parasol is the “parasol-auspiciousness” (*chattamaṅgala*). “The beauty of the land” (*janapadakalyāṇī*) refers to one who is the most beautiful in the country.
She is called "Kalyāṇī" because she was endowed with five auspicious qualities and other such uncommon virtues. "Tuvaṭaṃ" means quickly.

"Anicchantaṃ" means not consenting in her mind; however, when the Blessed One said, "Nandā, you shall go forth," she was unable to refuse out of respect, so she said, "Yes. And by this pretext, the Blessed One ordained her.

"Brahma-form color" means having a form identical to the form of Brahmā. "Tyassa" means "of him. "He was not able to turn back" means he was unable because the Blessed One had said, "Do not turn him back.

The sevenfold noble wealth is as follows: "The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and wisdom indeed is the seventh wealth."

Thus has been described the sevenfold noble wealth (*ariyadhana*). "In Rāhula, to an exceeding degree" means that when Rāhula went forth, there was suffering even greater than the suffering that had arisen from the going-forth of Nanda.

"After this" refers to the days following the arising of sorrow mentioned here, because for those who are non-returners (*anāgāmī*), there is no arising of a mind characterized by attachment to kinsmen or aversion. In the Canon, it says "affection for a son," and so forth.
This was said by the King to demonstrate the intensity of his affection for his son. For the affection for a son is described as "pervading the skin...
and reaching even to the marrow," because it arises from a surge of joy co-nascent with oneself and proceeds by agitating the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) throughout the entire body.
"Dearer than himself" refers to the Blessed One; "son" refers to Rāhula.
"By one who believes" means by one who has no doubt because of his words; if there is doubt, it is indeed an offense.
The commentary on the narrative concerning the case of Rāhula is finished.
The commentary on the narrative concerning the disciplinary procedure for the training rule.
106. Regarding the *sāmaṇera-sikkhāpada* and other rules, in the Canon (*pāḷi*) the term "training rules" (*sikkhāpada*) refers to sections of training.
Alternatively, they are the means for attaining the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). "Living being" (*pāṇa*) is, in the ultimate sense, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

The "taking of life" (*pāṇātipāta*) is the act of depriving it of its continuity by not allowing it to proceed, and thus striking it down with a weapon or similar means, overcoming it. This is the "killing of a living being" (*pāṇavadha*).

This is the meaning. As for its essential nature (*atthato*), it is simply the volition (*cetanā*) of a killer that originates from an action intended to sever the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of a living being while perceiving them as such.

Therefore, *pāṇātipātā veramaṇī* means: because it is the cause of the enemy [of suffering], it "removes" (*maṇati*) or "expels" (*nīharati*) the evil states such as killing, which are reckoned as enemies;
thus it is called "veramaṇī. Alternatively, it is called "viramaṇī" in the sense that "one abstains by means of this."

According to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*), "abstention" (*veramaṇī*) refers to the renunciation resulting from formal undertaking. This same principle applies to the remaining [precepts] as well.
Taking what is not given is "theft" (*adinnādāna*); it is simply the volition of stealing. Unchastity (*abrahmacariya*) is ignoble conduct;
it is the volition of sexual intercourse arising from the practice of one path by means of another path. Falsehood (*musā*) is an unreal matter; its speaking is the state of being unreal.

Intention to inform, knowing the facts as they truly are, is lying. "Surā-meraya" refers both to the fermented liquor produced from flour, rice, and so forth, and to the distilled spirits classified as *pupphāsava* and the like.
That very same substance is "majja" in the sense of being intoxicating, and it is a "pamādaṭṭhāna" (basis for negligence) in the sense of being a cause of heedlessness;
this is a designation for the volition by which one drinks it.
From the rising of the dawn until midday is what is called the time for food for the Noble Ones;
any other time is "unseasonable" (*vikāla*). In the sense of being something to be eaten, "food" (*bhojana*) here refers to everything that is "timely" (*yāvakālika*);

its swallowing is intended here by the term "food," through the elision of the latter member of the compound. Eating at an unseasonable time—that is, the swallowing [of food] at an unseasonable time—is "unseasonable eating" (*vikālabhojana*).

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "the swallowing of food that is to be consumed only during the proper time (yāvakālika) at an improper time (vikāla)," which in substance is simply the volition of swallowing food that is to be consumed during the proper time at an improper time.

"Frivolous sight" (visūkadassana) refers to seeing what is contrary to the Teaching (sāsana), being a distraction and an obstacle; this includes both the seeing and hearing of dancing, singing, and so forth.

It is also the name for all games, such as cock-fighting, wrestling, and dice-playing. Furthermore, in this context, since all five types of consciousness have the nature of "beholding" (ālocana) their respective objects, they are included under the term "seeing" (dassana);
thus, hearing is also included. It should be understood that by the words "dancing, singing, and instrumental music," one's own dancing, singing, and so forth are also included.
A garland (*mālā*) is that which, whether bound or unbound—even if made of thread and so forth—is worn for the sake of ornamentation;
it is called simply "garland. Fragrance (*gandha*) refers to any kind of fragrant substance other than scented powders and such used for anointing.

Anointment (*vilepana*) refers to a fragrant substance that has been ground and taken up, serving both to color the skin and to provide fragrance. Wearing (*dhāraṇa*) means adorning oneself with these.
"Adorning" (maṇḍana) means filling out a deficient place. "Ornamenting" (vibhūsana) means taking pleasure in [the body] by way of perfumes and by way of the coloring of the skin.
Alternatively, wearing garlands and so forth should be applied respectively [to these terms].
The basis or cause for those acts of wearing and so forth is the volition of transgression.
*Uccā* is a particle with the same meaning as the word *ucca* (high). *Uccāsayana* refers to a seat such as a throne (*āsanda*) that exceeds the proper measure.
*Mahāsayana* is a bed spread with improper coverings and one with a canopy containing blood-red elements.

For among these, the words *uccāsayana* and *mahāsayana* include both the seat (*āsana*) and the bed (*sayana*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound. *Jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇā* means the acceptance of gold and silver.
In this context, by the word "silver" (*rajata*), all forms of precious metal such as wooden coins and so forth are included;

it should be understood that pearls, gems, and the like, as well as grain, fields, and lands, are also included here. By the word "acceptance" (*paṭiggahaṇa*), both causing another to accept and taking [the gift] oneself are included.
"Grounds for expulsion" (*nāsanavatthu*) refers to the cause for the loss of one's status as a monastic member due to the state of having committed an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
107. In the Pāli, "making an obstruction for the entire *saṅghārāma*" means they create an obstruction to entry into all the *saṅghārāmas*.
Regarding the phrase "the *saṅghārāma* should be made an obstruction," the meaning is that the *saṅghārāma* should be obstructed, or an obstruction should be made within the *saṅghārāma*.
For this very reason, it is stated in the locative case as "to make an obstruction there."
The same method applies to such expressions as “food is an obstruction,” and so forth.
By the phrase “where he dwells,” the fixed dwelling-place obtained through the novice’s seniority or belonging to his own personal property is meant.
By the phrase “where he goes back to,” the residence of the preceptor or teacher is meant. Therefore he said, “his own,” and so forth. For “his own” means himself.
The meaning is "of the teacher (ācariya) or the preceptor (upajjhāya). It is called *daṇḍa* because by means of it they punish (*daṇḍenti*) or discipline (*vinenti*).

Since that very thing must be performed, it is called *kamma*; thus, it is *daṇḍakamma*, such as confinement (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. "Or cause to enter water" means to cause them to enter the water of a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*) and the like.
The commentary on the account of the basis for the disciplinary action regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada-daṇḍakamma-vatthu-kathā-vaṇṇanā*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Matter of Obstructing Without Asking Permission (Anāpucchāvaraṇavatthu): 108.
The phrase "for the co-residents and pupils as well" refers to those who have received full ordination.

For even in their case, if they disregard their teachers—the preceptor and the instructor—and if the teachers do not exercise restraint over them, then other monks must indeed carry out disciplinary measures such as obstructing them.
“They win over” means: thinking, “I will win them over by breaking away from their group,” they win them over by way of coaxing with the four bases of sympathy, such as giving and so forth.
Whether the group breaks apart or not, there is an offense in the very act of winning them over.
“It is not permitted to win them over by breaking [the group] apart” means that it is not permitted even to break [the group] apart, nor is it permitted to win them over; this is the meaning.
However, it is permissible to state the danger (ādīnava). It is permissible to speak out of reverence for the Teaching or out of compassion for others, but not out of a desire for social company.
By the phrase, "The taking of lodgings (senāsanaggāha) ceases," he indicates the interruption of the rains residence (vassaccheda).

And because even for those who are fully ordained (upasampanna), the taking of lodgings ceases upon the occurrence of a defeat (pārājika), as their status as a novice (sāmaṇera)—beginning with the going for refuge—is also destroyed.
It subsides; it should be understood that they do not even receive a share of the Saṅgha’s acquisitions.
By stating "the refuges were taken again during the first [rainy season]," this indicates that his entry into the rains residence occurred on that very same day along with the taking of the refuges.
The phrase "the rains-residence gift for the later [period]" is merely an illustration of receiving the gains of the rains residence; [it applies] both before and after that.

Furthermore, a novice whose virtue is unimpaired certainly receives the *vassāvāsika* robe-cloth that has arisen for the Saṅgha during the months [of the rainy season], as well as the timely robe-cloth (*kālacīvara*) if he enters [the rains retreat] during the first period.
If it is said, "if they were taken during the later period," this indicates both the entering of the later rains retreat and the state of having interrupted the rains residence;
for such a person does not receive a share of the timely robe-cloth. Therefore, "having obtained permission... [and so forth].
It is said, "The gain should be given.

Regarding the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gain, however, if the owners of the lodgings who are the donors say that the *vassāvāsika* must be given even to one who has entered during the later period (*pacchimikā*) for the sake of guarding the lodging and is staying in his own lodging after having performed the duties (*vatta*), [then it should be so].
It must indeed be given even without having obtained permission. As for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

“One receives the *vassāvāsika* [robe] during the later period because one has entered the rains residence again during the later period”—if this was said with reference to the intention of the donors regarding the *vassāvāsika*, it is excellent.
However, if it was said with reference to the property of the Saṅgha or the *kālacīvara*, [it is not so].
It should be understood that this is not tenable.

"Not without knowing" means that one who drinks without knowing it is "liquor" does not incur a breach of any of the precepts, such as abstaining from taking life, nor does he incur a breach of the refuges;
however, there is unwholesomeness, and there is a breach of the precept of abstaining from drinking liquor, just as in the case of wearing garlands and so forth.
It should be understood thus. "The others" refers to the abstention from eating at improper times and so forth.
For even those are indeed broken for one who intentionally transgresses them; however, they do not constitute factors of destruction when there is no mutual breaking [of the precepts].
For this very reason, the expression "when these are broken" was stated using the term "breaking."

"He should be made to confess his transgression" means that after he has been made to confess in the midst of the Saṅgha by saying, "Venerable Sir, a transgression has overcome me," and so forth, the refuge and the precepts should be given;
this is the intention because they have committed a *pārājika* offense. Therefore it is said: "He should be expelled by the removal of his marks.

For it is this very expulsion that is intended here; thus, [the text] refers to the disparagement and so forth resulting from the acts of killing living beings and the rest, which are the causes for the removal of his marks.
It was stated [in that way] because they fell together.
But surely the novice Kaṇṭaka was also one of wrong view, and for him, only the suspension by means of a formal act of punishment (*daṇḍakamma*) was mentioned below;
whereas here, the removal of the religious marks (*liṅganāsanā*) is stated for one of wrong view—what, then, is the difference between these two? This is the objection.
Keeping this in mind, he says: "For one who holds either of the two views, namely eternalism or annihilationism. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:

whoever speaks while firmly grasping any view of eternalism or annihilationism conceived by the heretics—such as "the self is the Lord, permanent, and stable," or "the self will be annihilated and destroyed"—for him...
That constitutes a ground for defeat (pārājika), and he must be expelled by the removal of his religious marks (liṅganāsanā).

However, in the case of one who has not adopted such a view but remains a follower of the Teaching, and who merely misunderstands the intent of the Buddha’s word—speaking thus even when being exhorted by the monks and refusing to relinquish that position—that view of his does not constitute a defeat; rather, he is to be expelled solely by the removal of thorns (kaṇṭakanāsanā).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the matter of not asking for permission regarding the prohibition [of ordination] is finished. 109.

Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Matter of the Eunuch (Paṇḍaka): In the matter of the eunuch, the three types—the *āsitta*, the *usūya*, and the *pakkha*—possess the physical characteristics and marks of masculinity, yet they have a rootless (*ahetuka*) rebirth-linking.
And because they resemble eunuchs (*napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*) due to the strength of their obsession with the defilements (*kilesa-pariyuṭṭhāna*), they are called "paṇḍakas.

Among them, for the two types—the *āsitta* and the *ussūya* paṇḍakas—it is possible to prevent the obsession with defilements from transgressing by means of proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and so forth;
therefore, it is stated that these may be ordained. However, as for the *pakkha-paṇḍaka*, during the dark fortnights...
The fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*) approaches like madness; it persists until one reaches transgression (*vītikkama*), at which point it turns back.
Therefore, it is said that such a person should not be admitted into the Order. To demonstrate this distinction, it was stated:
"He who [causes] others... and so forth. In that context, *āsittassa* means having poured [impurity] into the mouth, by means of discharging one's own filth.
The fever subsides. Regarding "when envy has arisen": when, through the influence of envy, a lust for one's own desire to indulge [another] has arisen, the fever of impure discharge subsides.
Because it is stated, "the seeds have been removed," a paṇḍaka does not cease to be one even when the mere signs are removed while the seeds remain.
For a bhikkhunī as well, if she removes it for reasons other than illness, there is likewise a thullaccaya offense; however, this does not constitute being a paṇḍaka.

When the seeds have been removed, even the sexual organ is no longer functional through lust, the male state disappears, the male characteristics such as facial hair also vanish, and even the full ordination (upasampadā) is lost;
furthermore, the fever of the defilements becomes difficult to restrain and leads to transgression in the case of a napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka.
Therefore, they say that even one who has been fully ordained (upasampanna) of such a kind must be expelled.

If this is so, why was the offense of defeat (pārājika) not prescribed for the uprooting of seeds? Regarding this, some say: "This was indeed already prescribed by the Blessed One, because it was stated:
'Monks, one who is a paṇḍaka (eunuch) who is not yet ordained should not be ordained; one who is already ordained should be expelled.'"
However, some say: "Because one who is a *paṇḍaka* is not such at the moment of extracting the seed, a *pārājika* offense was not prescribed for that specific moment.

But because that monk, after the seed has been extracted, later becomes a *paṇḍaka* in the manner described, he becomes one who lacks [the faculty], he is no longer a basis for full ordination (*upasampadā*), and for that very reason his full ordination ceases."

Therefore, from the time he commits the offense of being a paṇḍaka, having classified him as a *napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka* by birth, it is said that he is "incapable" (*abhabba*)—meaning he must be expelled once ordained—and not prior to that.

And although this [paṇḍaka] possesses causes [for enlightenment], because his state is like one who lacks the causes due to the destruction of his faculties, even the Path does not arise for him; so they say. Others, however, say:
The statement, "It was said that one who has become a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) through self-inflicted means prior to going forth must be expelled even after he has received full ordination (*upasampadā*);
however, for one who becomes so after being fully ordained, even by self-inflicted means, the full ordination does not cease," is not correct.
For to the same extent that one is incapable [of the religious life] due to self-inflicted means prior to going forth, to that same extent one remains so afterwards as well.
It should be understood after investigating whether it is so.
