"Abhāvaka" means one for whom there is no existence (bhāva) such as femininity and so forth. Regarding the phrase "renunciation is not forbidden," by the mention of renunciation (*pabbajjā*) alone, full admission (*upasampadā*) is also included.
Therefore he said: "And for whom renunciation is forbidden here," and so forth. In that very same faction of his...

Regarding the phrase "going forth is forbidden": here, even in the case of one who is not a *paṇḍaka*, he receives only the mere going forth (*pabbajjā*); however, full ordination (*upasampadā*) is not permitted even then.
But when one who is a *paṇḍaka* arrives, it should be understood that he is to be expelled by the removal of his religious marks (*liṅganāsanā*).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the *paṇḍaka* is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Matter of Living in Communion by Theft (Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthu): 110.
Regarding the matter of living in communion by theft: "Kolaññā" means born in the same family, or known, recognized, and well-known therein;
or those who know him [as such] are called "kolaññā," which is a name for relatives. Here, even the mere assumption of the outward signs through theft constitutes "living in communion."

Thus he said: "There are three who live in communion through theft. "Not accepting veneration according to seniority" means that he does not accept veneration from monks or novices [as if he were senior].
"Veneration according to seniority" refers to veneration from monks based on the number of years since ordination that he has falsely displayed by means of lying.

He consents; however, a young novice who consents to the veneration of senior novices, and a junior bhikkhu who consents to the veneration of seniors, do not become *theyyasaṃvāsaka*s (one living in communion through theft).
In this context, the meaning is "in the sense of communal living" (*saṃvāsatthena*).
The phrase "bhikkhu-vassāni" (bhikkhu-years) is stated according to the reading given in the section on the sense of communal living; however, having gone forth by oneself...
Even one who merely counts the years of a novice (sāmaṇera) is likewise a "one who dwells in both [orders]. And not only a man, but a woman also behaves in this way toward the bhikkhunīs;
she too is indeed a "one who dwells in communion by theft" (theyyasaṃvāsikā). Furthermore, even an initial offender (ādikammika) is not exempt here.
For an initial offender is spoken of in reference to an offense prescribed specifically for those who are fully ordained (upasampanna); therefore, even an initial offender is not exempt in this case.

“Rāja... pe... by fear”: here the word *bhaya* (fear) should be applied to each [term]. Up to the point where he is said to be “of pure mind,” this means that because of the absence of an impure mind—such as thinking, “I will deceive these monks with this mark and live among them”—he is one whose mind is pure.
Therefore, even if he were to take up the mark with an impure mind, whether he subsequently lives together with the monks or not, he is a “mark-seeker.”
Even though he lives together with them later on, he lives having become incapable [of the training].
Therefore, it should be understood that one who is incapable in both senses is included within the sense of "one who possesses the marks" (liṅgatthenaka) alone.

However, one who, out of fear of kings and the like, takes up the marks while his mind is still pure, but later gives rise to an impure thought, thinking, "I will live by counting my years as a bhikkhu," is [incapable] by the mere arising of that thought.
One who lives in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) does not exist [in this case], because he has taken the outward signs with a pure mind.

However, if he goes into the presence of the bhikkhus and performs the calculation of the novice’s age and so forth, then it should be understood that he is one who lives in communion by theft, or one who lives in communion by both means.
As for what is stated further on, along with the laying down of the burden: "This too is one who lives in communion by theft," etc.
This was said with reference to the relinquishing of responsibility by monks through associating and living together with him. Therefore, it is said:
"As long as he does not consent to living in communion. Here, the connection should be understood as: "For that long, he is not called a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who lives in communion by theft).
And in this context, even without fear of thieves and so forth, one might take the signs [of a monk] for the purpose of sport, [and yet remain] among the monks...

It should be understood that even one who, having pointed out the dwelling where he was ordained, does not consent to acts such as prostration, yet accepts [the robes] with a pure mind, thinking, "Does this mark of renunciation look good on me?", is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft).
Regarding the phrase "food for all sectarians," this refers to food prepared by setting it aside as common property for all members of various religious orders (*sāmayika*). And this...
It is said that "common food" (sabbasādhāraṇabhatta) is intended so that even co-residence might occur when monks take their designated portions of almsfood.

However, one who does not consent to such co-residence—even if he eats the monastery meals and so forth in a monastery or similar place where no other monks reside—is certainly not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who lives in communion by theft).
"By performing work" means by doing labor such as plowing and so forth. "Bowl and robe" (*pattacīvara*).
"Having taken [it]" means having maintained it in the body by way of the appearance of a bhikkhu's characteristics.
The statement, "He who goes forth in this manner is called one who dwells in communion through theft," is merely an illustration;

for even one who does not know the name "one who dwells in communion through theft" understands that "it is not permissible to act in this way" or that "one who acts in this way is no longer a recluse."
Or, thinking, "If I tell them, they will cast me out," or knowing, "I cannot succeed in the going-forth by any means whatsoever," one becomes a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft).
However, one who initially perceives, "The going-forth was thus received by me," but does not speak because he is ashamed to reveal his own improper conduct—
such as wearing white garments— in the interim, is also a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.

"He is not [a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*]. Regarding the phrase "only at the time when he was not yet ordained," the restriction here indicates that even if one knows the characteristics of a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and does not disclose it out of deception, one is still not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.

Because he has taken the outward signs with a pure mind, he is not a "one who takes the signs" (*liṅgatthenaka*); and because he has obtained full ordination, he possesses a mode of association consistent with that very status.

Because he has accepted [the status], he is not one who shares the community even in the sense of common residence (*saṃvāsa*). However, one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) is one who shares the community in the sense of the outward sign (*liṅga*), because he has taken the outward sign of one who is eligible for common residence;
thus, by the mere act of accepting common residence, he becomes one who shares the community.

"Abiding in the same sign" means abiding in the state of having the same sign. He is not a "one who shares the community through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) because [he has not taken] the sign bestowed by the monks.

Because he has not renounced his [lay] characteristics, he is not one who lacks the characteristics; because he has not renounced his claim to be a bhikkhu, he is not one who lacks the status of co-residence.

As for the reason stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*—that "he is not one who lacks the status of co-residence because he has accepted co-residence in accordance with the characteristics"—that too was stated with reference to this very same reason. Otherwise, even for a novice (*sāmaṇera*), [there would be no issue] regarding the counting of the number of years as a bhikkhu and so forth.

"Living together in accordance with the [monastic] mark" means that it has begun; thus, one who has taken up the mark [of a monk] would not be considered "one who has taken up co-residence" by monks, because the mark given to both [the monk and the novice] is common to both.

And just as it is here for a monk, so too a novice who has committed a *pārājika* offense is to be understood as not being "one who has taken up co-residence," because he has not renounced his status as a novice. "Accepting" means "having agreed."

"Having cast off the yoke of wearing the saffron robe and accepted the state of a householder"—this was said with reference to anyone who has gone forth at an advanced age, specifically referring to a novice (sāmaṇera). "In the great alms-bowls and so forth" refers to particular vessels for food placed at the doors of houses made of bamboo and other materials;
by this, he shows that in a monastery, one does not perform the counting of the rainy season retreat and other such duties together with the monks.
The commentary on the discussion concerning those who live in communion by theft is finished.
Commentary on the discussion concerning those who have gone over to other sects:

In the discussions beginning with "those who have gone over to other sects," [the phrase] "merely having taken their marks" refers to one who, without the intention of investigating and so forth, [says], "I am a member of another sect."
"…I shall become [one of them]"—by this resolve, as soon as one has physically taken up the outward mark.
"By oneself" means that without going into the presence of the heretics (titthiya), one puts on the grass-cloth garments (kusacīra) and so forth even within a monastic monastery (saṅghārāma).
"I shall become an Ājīvaka... he goes"—he goes into the presence of the Ājīvakas with the intention "I shall become an Ājīvaka," according to their procedure for going forth (pabbajjā).

For although a formal determination regarding his entry into the state of a sectarian exists, because he merely intended, "I shall go and become one," only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated for each step taken.

Although "dukkaṭa" is not explicitly mentioned in the Canon, it is stated here by analogy with the *dukkaṭa* for preliminary efforts previously described in the case of sexual intercourse and so forth.
And by this, when the characteristic marks have been accepted through the act of formal determination—

A *pārājika* offense occurs; therefore, it must be understood that in the prior attempt (*purimapayoga*), a *thullaccaya* must indeed be declared, and even one who turns back at the moment of the *thullaccaya* is freed only after being made to confess the offense.

And just as it is here, so too in the case of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*) or shedding blood (*lohituppāda*), the boundary for monks’ freedom from offenses—whether they be *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, or *pārājika*—due to prior attempts and so forth, should be understood.
Because they are contrary to the Teaching (*sāsana*), it is not stated here that there is no offense even for those who are first offenders (*ādikammika*).

However, it should be understood that these, as well as others, are mentioned here among the "incapable" (*abhabba*)— rather than being shown separately under individual training rules (*sikkhāpada*) as *pārājika* and so forth in the *Pārājika-khaṇḍa*— for the purpose of demonstrating their incapacity even for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"Taking that view" is said with reference specifically to grasping at the state of being superior while in the guise of a sectarian (tīrthika).
For even if one adopts the eternalist or other views of those sectarians, one does not become a sectarian renegade (tīrthikapakkantaka) unless the sectarian insignia (liṅga) is accepted;
conversely, even without adopting that view, if one accepts the insignia thinking, "How beautiful is their ascetic practice," one becomes a sectarian renegade.
It is indeed so. "By the absence of such a conviction" means by the absence of the conviction that one might enter the state of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) due to attachment to the status of a monk;
by this, he shows that even for one who wears grass-cloths or similar items in times of distress, there is no offense, as if he were naked.

Regarding the phrase "spoken by an ordained monk," it should be understood that although even a schismatic (saṅghabhedaka) is spoken of here as being "by an ordained monk," those such as matricides and the like may be spoken of even by one who is not ordained.
The commentary on the Discussion of Those Who Have Gone Over to the Sectarians is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Animal Basis (Tiracchānavatthu): 111.
It should be connected as "the body of a nāga that moves about in water and feeds on frogs. "Out of fear of [losing] its memory" means...

Having seen the body of the nāga, [the Buddha spoke] out of fear that the bhikkhu might cry out. Since the body of a nāga does not arise among monkeys, sloths, and so forth, he said "released," etc., in order to show the boundary for its arising.
The commentary on the discussion of the animal basis (tiracchānavatthu) is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Matricide, etc.

112. *Apavāhana* means cleansing. Because even loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] are sharp and intense toward the children of those born as humans—just as they are toward the supramundane qualities—compared to those of non-human species such as animals, it is said: “The mother who has become a human woman.”
“...mother. Just as the occurrence of wholesome states among human beings is sharp and intense, so too is the occurrence of unwholesome states;

thus he said, “He too, being of human birth,” and so forth. Regarding the term *ānantariya*: here, the fruit of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in hell immediately after death is called “immediate” (*anantara*);
that which is connected to this immediate state by way of being its producer is *ānantariya*, and [the deed] is performed by means of that. “The son of a courtesan” means:
This is merely an illustration; even the son of an unchaste woman, if he kills his own father without knowing him to be his father, becomes a patricide.
114. "The remainder" refers to those such as non-returners (anāgāmin) and so forth. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the *Manussaviggaha-pārājika*. 115.
"This is a schismatic of the Saṅgha" is said with reference to a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu. [He becomes a schismatic] even before [the formal act] constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Whether he has entered into meditative attainment (samāpanna) or his full ordination (upasampadā) is impaired by defects such as those regarding the robes, even if he causes a schism in the Saṅgha, he does not incur an immediate offense (ānantariya).
However, it should be understood that the Saṅgha indeed becomes split, and his going-forth (pabbajjā) is not thereby prevented.
The phrase "with a malevolent mind" clarifies the meaning already stated by the words "with a murderous mind. He sheds blood...
Because the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible, it is impossible for anyone by force to cut his skin or other tissues and cause blood to flow externally.
However, when struck by weapons or the like, the blood moves from its place and, becoming agitated, accumulates in one spot;
yet, even by this much, the striker is called a "shedder of blood," as was Devadatta.
However, for one who destroys a shrine (*cetiya*), a Bodhi tree, or an image and so forth, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*);
rather, it is a grave offense similar to an immediate retribution. Furthermore, branches that suck the sap from the Bodhi tree and those that obstruct a shrine containing relics should be cut down;
in this case, only merit arises.
The commentary on the account of the matricide and others is finished.
Commentary on the account of the hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka): 116.
A female hermaphrodite is one endowed with the female faculty (*itthindriya*); the other, however, is endowed with the male faculty (*purisindriya*). Of these two...
For two [sexual] states do not arise together, because this is rejected in the *Yamaka*.
However, the second sexual characteristic arises devoid of the state [of masculinity or femininity] along with an unwholesome consciousness accompanied by kamma.

For ordinary women and men as well, kamma alone is the cause of the physical characteristics and gender marks, not the state itself, because its status as a condition for anything has not been stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*. Merely...

In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), for the purpose of showing the occurrence of the physical marks (*byañjana*) and gender characteristics (*liṅga*) only when accompanied by the [corresponding] faculties (*bhāva*), the faculty is stated as the cause of the physical marks in such passages as, "dependent on the female faculty, the female marks, etc.
However, here it is stated that even without the faculty, the physical mark arises through the power of unwholesome kamma. And this applies to both types of hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*).
When lust arises in a woman, at that time the male characteristic is manifest and the other is concealed;
when lust arises in a man, at that time the female characteristic is manifest and the other is concealed.
In this context, the sequence of investigation refers to that which clarifies the manifestation of the female and male signs even at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
The sequence for investigating the meaning is intended to clarify the inconsistency in the *Kurundi* commentary. For in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is stated:
"Furthermore, the feminine gender and so forth arise having originated in dependence upon the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*) during its occurrence," and so on.

The construction is: "He has no going-forth (*pabbajjā*). And he who, having recognized both the incapable person for whom going-forth is prohibited and the capable person, grants him the going-forth and the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Or [if it is done] unknowingly, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It should be understood that there is no offense in all cases for one who does not know.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those with both sexual characteristics (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those without a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*), etc.

117. Regarding the cases of those without a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*) and so forth, the statement that "the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) has not been laid down" refers specifically to the training rule being promulgated right here:

"Monks, one who does not have a preceptor must not be ordained. As for the phrase "but the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated," this means that even in the absence of a preceptor, [the ordination proceeds] with the formula: "He seeks ordination from such-and-such a person; by such-and-such a person..."

"By means of the preceptor": this is stated because the proclamation of a preceptor has been performed in all instances by mentioning the name of a deceased preceptor, one who has disrobed, an old preceptor, or anyone else—even if they are no longer present.
For if one were not to perform the proclamation of the preceptor, it would indeed constitute a failure of the ritual (kammavipatti), as it is said: "one does not designate the person."
It may be so. For that very reason, it is stated in the *Pāḷi* as "without a preceptor" (*anupajjhāyaka*).
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, instead of saying "without mentioning a preceptor," the meaning is stated as: "not having had a preceptor accepted, entirely devoid of a preceptor.
In the *Pāḷi*, regarding the phrase "with the Saṅgha as preceptor": "This person named so-and-so desires ordination from the Saṅgha; [this person named so-and-so...]"

The meaning is: by formally announcing the Saṅgha itself as the preceptor through the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*), saying, "He requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with the Saṅgha as his preceptor.
In the same way, regarding the phrase "with a group as preceptor," the construction should be understood as: "This person named so-and-so desires full ordination from a group," and so forth.
Even when stated in this manner, the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated, because it has been stated that there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Otherwise...
"One should say that such a person is not ordained. Therefore he said, "by the Saṅgha," and so forth.

In this regard, it should be understood that when formal acts (kamma) are being performed with eunuchs or others as preceptors, if the quorum of five or more members is fulfilled even without the eunuch or others present, the act is not invalidated; otherwise, it is invalidated.
The commentary on the section concerning those without a preceptor, etc., is finished.
Commentary on the section concerning the bowl and robe, etc.: 118.
Regarding the matters of the bowl and robe, even in the absence of a bowl and robe, [the Buddha said], "For one whose bowl and robe are complete..."
Because the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has been completed, the offense is stated as *dukkaṭa* alone, without mentioning a disturbance of the formal act (*kammakopa*).
Otherwise, due to the omission of the proclamation, there would indeed be a disturbance of the formal act. However, some say:

"Just as those who were ordained by the previously authorized formal proclamation, even now those who are ordained by the formal proclamation—even without saying 'the bowl and robes are complete'—are indeed well-ordained."

They say that [this is] not appropriate. For from the time it was permitted onward, non-handing-over is indeed a failure of the proclamation, just like the failure of omitting the phrase, “So-and-so requests ordination from the Saṅgha.
That too was permitted later; yet, by not making the request with such words as, “Venerable Sirs, we request ordination from the Saṅgha,” even that [is a failure].

When conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*), if one performs the formal act (*kammavācā*) only after having stated, "This person named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha," the act is indeed well-performed;
otherwise, it is defective. For it is not permitted to omit anything whatsoever from the authorized formal act at the very last moment;
such omission constitutes a failure in the proclamation (*sāvanā*). The phrase "or other monks may wish to give [the ordination]" is the syntactical connection.
"Almsfood not selected" means almsfood that has not been taken from among the alms received by the bhikkhus. Regarding the phrase "equal to the portion of a novice":

although there is no separate "portion for novices" because they are given an equal share of material requisites, they are nevertheless similar to novices insofar as their going-forth is dependent solely upon the preparation of their bowl and robes.
It should be understood that this was said for the purpose of showing that these are like withered leaves.
Furthermore, this portion is assigned specifically to one who is destined for and close to renunciation; for that very reason, it is said, "until the bowl is cooked," and so forth.

The term "share of material goods" (*āmisa-bhāga*) refers to the communal meal given to the Saṅgha at the monastery and the offerings produced thereon; it does not refer to what is being given by donors in their own homes.
For that very reason, [the Buddha] rejected such things as *salākā-bhatta* (tickets for meals), because the donors would feel regret.
By the words "medicine" (*bhesajja*) and so forth, however, he shows that there is no fault here in providing medicine and other such items for householders.
The commentary on the discussion of the cases concerning those who have not yet received [the full precepts] is concluded.
Commentary on the Account of the Cases Concerning Those with Severed Hands, etc. (119).
Regarding the cases of those with severed hands and so forth: "At the base of the ear" (*kaṇṇamūle*) is said with reference to the cutting off of the entire ear.

"From the ear-flap" (*kaṇṇasakkhalikāya*) means from the lobe of the ear. "For one whose ear has been pierced" (*yassa pana kaṇṇāviddhe*) refers to the hole made below for the insertion of earrings and the like.

This was said with intentional reference [to a specific type of bone]. For that [bone] is capable of being joined together. "At the elephant's foot" (*ajapadake*) means at the tip of the nasal bone shaped like an elephant's foot;
for it does not extend further upward than that. It is said with reference to a shape that is not unsightly, as it is possible to join it;
however, an unsightly shape leads to the state of being offensive to the assembly.
*Khujjasarīro* means one with a crooked body. *Brahmujjugatto* refers to the Blessed One, whose body and limbs are as straight as those of Brahmā.
*Parivaṭumo* means one whose body is rounded all over; by this, he shows that such types of dwarfs are not permitted. *Kūṭakūṭasīso*:
the repetition (*āmeḍita*) is used to indicate the presence of fleshy protuberances on many parts of the head. Therefore, he said, "resembling a cluster of palm fruits."
The cluster of palm fruits is called *piṇḍi*. "With a head that gradually tapers" means with a head that becomes progressively thinner like a stupa-dome (*cetiyathūpikā*).
"With a thick bamboo-stem-like head" refers to one who possesses a head that is uniformly thick from beginning to end and is tall;
such a person is called *nāḷisīsa*. "Split-head" (*kappasīsa*) refers to one whose head is split in two like the top of an elephant's head.

The explanation of “with hair on the ears” is given by the words beginning with “by insects. With reference to the fact that hair grows even on the forehead of a monkey, he says “with the hair of the head,” and so forth.
“A monkey’s face” means a face whose eyebrows are not distinguished from the hair of the forehead. “By the wheels of the eyes” means by the black pupils.
*Ke-karoti* means one who looks askance. *Udakataraka* refers to the reflection of the sky in water for those looking down; some say it refers to a bubble on the water.
*Akkhitaraka* refers to the reflection [of the sky] for those standing directly in front; they also call them "eyeballs" (*akkhigaṇḍaka*). *Atipiṅgalakkhī* means cat-like eyes.
*Madhupiṅgala* means tawny with the color of honey. Regarding *nippakhumakkhī*, here the word *pakhuma*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

"Having eyelashes grown on the eyelids" means that because of their absence, the eyes are "eyelashless. "By inflammation of the eyes" means by a disease resulting in putrefaction at the edges of the eyelids.
"Flat-nosed" means having a nose that is not prominent. "The *paṭaṅga* frog" refers to a large-mouthed frog. "Split-mouthed" means...
"Having his mouth covered at the beginning and end" means he always has his mouth open. "Crooked-mouthed" refers to one whose lower jawbone is situated off to one side.
"One with severed lips" is one who possesses lips from which the flesh has been removed by a weapon or other means, whether by birth or subsequently.
"One with a dribbling mouth" is one whose mouth constantly drips saliva.
“Split neck” means one whose neck is bent down. “Split chest” means one whose middle of the chest is deeply sunken; the same applies to one with a split back.

All this was said with reference to those described as “having itchy limbs,” and so forth. Regarding the detailed analysis here, he says “the analysis” and so on, because it has already been stated in the section on leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) and other diseases.

“One with testicular wind-disease” (*vātaṇḍika*) means one who possesses a testicle sac from which the seed has been expelled due to a wind-disease of the testicles; even when covered by his lower garment...
One who has protruding [teeth] is not to be ordained. "Deformed" (vikaṭa) means one whose feet walk sideways; when he walks, his kneecaps go outside.
"Knock-kneed" (paṇha) means one whose feet turn backward; when he walks, his kneecaps enter within.
"Thick-shanked" (mahājaṅgha) means one with thick shanks. "Large-footed" (mahāpāda) means one endowed with a large sole of the foot.
“Between the heels” (*pādavemajjhe*) means between the backs of the heels; by this, he shows that the forefoot and the heel are similar.
“With the feet contracted in the middle” is an explanation of the cause of having club-like feet (*kuṇḍapādatā*).
“With the feet contracted at the tips” is an explanation of the gait of one with club-like feet, like that of a bird’s foot. “Walking on the back of the foot” refers to the [gait of] the foot...
"By the outer edge" and "by the inner edge"—this was said with reference to walking on both edges of the sole of the foot.

"Mammaka" (stammering) refers to the utterance of improperly articulated syllables due to the absence of purity in the vocal organs (*ṭhāna*) and the points of articulation (*karaṇa*). Indeed, he is called "mammaka" because of his imitation of speech;
and even one who possesses perfect vocal organs, if he repeatedly utters a single syllable as a hiccup, he too [is so called].
It is included right here. Alternatively, one who is capable of speaking smooth words—even while suppressing a hiccup—without slurring syllables may be ordained.

One who acts while knowing that he is not freed from an offense is indeed not freed. There is no offense for one who, out of necessity such as a threat to life, gives formal consent (kāyasāmaggi) despite his own reluctance. "Not having reached rehabilitation" means he is unfit for rehabilitation.
The commentary on the account of the cases concerning those with severed hands and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the account of the cases concerning dependence on one who is shameless (120):

Regarding the cases connected with dependence (*nissaya*), "one who shares the same portion as the bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusabhāga*) means one whose portion—consisting of the factors of qualities such as view and virtue—is the same as that of the bhikkhus; the state of being such is "sharing the same portion as the bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusabhāgatā*).
The commentary on the discussion of the grounds for dependence on one who is non-virtuous (*alajji*) is concluded.
**Commentary on the Discussion of the Grounds for Dependence for Those Travelling, etc.** 121.

Regarding the phrase "one for whom the taking of dependence is a duty" (*nissayakaraṇīyo*): here, "dependence" (*nissaya*) refers to the act of taking dependence; it is that which must be performed by him, thus qualifying the subject.
The word *paranipāto* (falling back) is to be understood. Or, "resting" … [etc. … "there is no offense":
the intention is that even if one stays there because of the desire to travel, one is still a traveler; thus, in the absence of a provider of formal support (*nissaya*) there, there is no offense.

By this, it is shown that for one who stays in dependence on the excellence of lodgings and so forth in the absence of fatigue and the like, there is an offense. And that [offense] occurs day by day due to the cause of not traveling.
They say that one incurs [an offense]. Even for one sent by elders for the purpose of tasks such as dyeing robes, one must stay only until the completion of the task, and not beyond that.
It should be understood that even when elders send a well-behaved junior monk, it is only for the sake of temporary duties and not for permanent service.
This is because it is stated: "For one traveling by boat... [etc.]... there is no offense."
It should be understood that it is not permissible to enter the rains residence in a place devoid of a provider of dependence (*nissaya*) and lacking such control, except in such circumstances.
"Depending on him" means depending upon him. Regarding the phrase "in the month of Āsāḷhī... one should go there":
here, even if the day for entering the rains residence occurs while one is still waiting, thinking, "Such-and-such an elder will come here, he will come," [one may proceed].

"Let it be so; even if one does not enter the rains residence in the place where one lived, one should go—even if it is far—to wherever one can obtain formal dependence (nissaya) and enter the later rains residence.
"By family name as well" means that instead of stating the name as "the Venerable Pippali’s candidate for full ordination," one may also use the family name.
Since this is the meaning, it is established that when asked, "What is the name of your preceptor? one should reply with the name of his clan, "Venerable Kassapa.

Therefore, even if he has some other well-known name, or if a name was assigned at that moment for the sake of easy identification, the formal proclamation (*anusāvana*) must be performed by including all of those names. Just as it is with the preceptor, so too...

For one who desires full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is permissible to perform the proclamation (*anussāvana*) by means of their clan name (*gotta*) and so forth, as well as by their name at that very moment.
At that moment, those giving the name—whether "Tissa" or "Nāga"—should do so even before the formal appointment of the instructor (*anusāsaka*).
Having done so, at the times of instructing on the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dhamma*) and asking questions, [the candidate] says: "What is your name? I am, Venerable Sir..."

When making the announcement by saying, "I am Nāga; what is your preceptor's name? My preceptor, venerable sir, is named Tissa," and so forth, it must be announced in such a way that the perception "this is my name" arises in the minds of both.
However, if at that moment one speaks using one's natural name and subsequently makes the proclamation using a different name such as "Tissa," it is not permissible.
In this regard, although the name of the preceptor himself is not specifically mentioned, if a person is referred to by any name whatsoever— such as "Tissa desires ordination"—
the ritual act is indeed well-performed. This is because, as in the case of the ordination procedure for those who lack a preceptor and so forth,
the ritual succeeds provided the person is referred to within the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), even in the absence of a preceptor or when [the candidate] is incapable.
However, if for one seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*) is performed using a name other than his own proper name, the formal act (*kamma*) is invalid;

he remains unordained. One standing there [in that situation] is like any other unordained person, because the individual who is the subject (*vatthupuggala*)—who has taken that [specific] name—is absent from that place, and because that name was not included in the proclamation. Therefore, for one seeking full ordination...
One who wishes to change the original name and gradually announce it by a new name such as "Nāga" must first inform him, saying, "You are Nāga," and so forth.

Then, even at the time of asking about the obstructive factors regarding the instruction, he should announce it by the new name such as "Nāga" only after making it clear both to that person and to the Saṅgha. [This applies] when one person has many [names].
There are [several] names, and it is appropriate to take one among them.

However, whichever name was taken for the candidate for full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) and the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) in one instance, that very same name must be used in the motion (*ñatti*) and in all the proclamations (*anussāvana*).
For if another name than the one already taken is used, the phrasing is said to be "broken" (*byañjanaṃ bhinnaṃ*).
The formal act (kamma) fails. For in both meaning and phrasing, the motion (ñatti) and the proclamation (anussāvana) must be identical;

however, one may proclaim them by prefixing the word "Venerable" (āyasmanta) throughout—such as "of the Venerable Tissa"—before the name of the preceptor, or there is no fault even if it is not so prefixed.
In the Pāli, although the word "āyasmato" (of the venerable one) is stated after the phrase "of the venerable so-and-so," nevertheless,
because we see the application of the word "āyasmā" before the name in such passages as "the venerable Sāriputta was skilled in the goal" (*āyasmā sāriputto atthakusalo*),
the usage before [the name] is more appropriate. And even if it is applied in one place but not applied in another, in that one place...
Even if one joins [the name] elsewhere after having joined it at the beginning, there is no omission in the proclamation because the name has not been omitted.

For that very reason, they say that although in the Pāḷi it says “of the venerable so-and-so,” having joined it once as “of the venerable so-and-so,” the word “venerable” is not repeated in subsequent phrases such as “with so-and-so as preceptor. And although that is so, nevertheless, in every instance, by means of a single [term]...
Whether one applies [the rule] in this manner or does not apply it at all, it should be understood that the non-proclamation (*anussāvana*) is more highly praised.
The commentary on the discussion of the grounds for dependence (*nissaya*) for those intending to travel, etc., is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the grounds for the two types of candidates for full ordination (*upasampadā*), etc.

123. "Ekānussāvane kātuṃ" means those for whom the proclamation (*anussāvana*) is done together on one side at one single moment; these are the candidates for full ordination (*upasampadāpekkhā*), and they are to be made [the object] of the single proclamation.
Therefore he said, "to make [them] the object of a single proclamation. And this phrase should be understood with the elision of a case ending (*vibhattialopa*).
Or, "by one" means by a single preceptor (*ācariya*) during the proclamation by a single formal act (*kammavācā*) at one single moment for both of them.

The meaning is as follows: according to the method beginning with, "This Buddharakkhita and this Dhammarakkhita seek ordination from the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita," the procedure for the proclamation (*anusāvana*) of two persons by a single preceptor (*ācariya*) at one moment should be understood.
By this same method, the proclamation of three persons by a single preceptor at one moment should also be understood.

The phrase "to perform the proclamation together in the same way as before" means that two [candidates] may have two teachers, or three [candidates] may have three teachers, or all three may have a single teacher, performing the proclamation together;
and that must indeed be with one who has the same preceptor (*upajjhāya*). "But not if they do not have the same preceptor."

This is a prohibitive statement meaning that it is not permissible for one teacher or two or three preceptors to perform the ordination of two or three candidates for ordination simultaneously through a single proclamation (*anussāvana*) and a single formal act of announcement (*ekānussāvane*).
However, it is not the case that it is impermissible for three [candidates] to be ordained by different teachers and different preceptors through a single proclamation; thus he said: "But if..."
“...having various teachers and various preceptors... it is permissible.

Now, as for what was stated here regarding the mutual announcement of the *saddhivihārikas* by the preceptors—namely, that “Thera Tissa [announced] Thera Sumana’s *saddhivihārika*, and Thera Sumana [announced] Thera Tissa’s *saddhivihārika*”—that is merely an illustration (*upalakkhaṇamatta*). Therefore, if Thera Tissa [announces] Thera Sumana’s...
If the Elder Sumana causes the Elder Nanda’s own *saddhivihārika* to recite [the confession], and they both serve as mutual members of the quorum (*gaṇapūraka*), it is indeed permissible.
Furthermore, if the preceptor himself recites for his own *saddhivihārika*, there is nothing at all to be said against it;
the formal act (*kamma*) is perfectly accomplished. This applies even to one who is without a preceptor.

If full ordination (*upasampadā*) is attained when the proclamation (*anussāvita*) is made by anyone at all, how much more so when it is proclaimed by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) himself for one who has a preceptor?
This is how it should be understood. For that very reason, he said "But if... and so forth, in order to show the position regarding the nine standing places.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the two subjects of those seeking full ordination is finished.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Procedure for Full Ordination (Upasampadāvidhikathāvaṇṇanā) 126. Regarding "upajjhā": this indicates that the word *upajjhā* ending in the long vowel *ā* has the same meaning as the word *upajjhāya*.

Alternatively, the word *upajjhāya* itself is spoken thus as *upajjhā* by eliding the letter *y* in the accusative and nominative cases; however, in the instrumental case and others, it remains [as *upajjhāya*].
It should be understood that there is no application of the word *upajjhā* (preceptor).

In the Pāḷi, the phrase "one should elect oneself by oneself" means that the act of election must be performed toward oneself as the object (*kamma*), with oneself acting both as the agent (*kartr*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Alternatively, in the sense of identity (*paccatte*), *attanā* is in the accusative case; thus the meaning is: "by oneself, oneself should be elected. And not only this...
In this very case, as well as in other instances such as the thirteen formal acts (*sammuti*), one must indeed appoint oneself by oneself according to this same characteristic.
Furthermore, because one is oneself qualified for the ritual act, a group consisting of at least four members is required in all cases, setting aside oneself.
"The time of truth" means the time when, having abandoned the deception of thinking "I will conceal it," one desires only the truth. "The time of reality" means...

Even in the absence of deception, the time must necessarily be observed because the basis—humanity and so forth—is real; otherwise, there would be an obstacle consisting in the subversion of the *kamma*.

This is the intended meaning. "Maṅku" means with face cast down. "Uddharatu" means let him establish [the candidate] in full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the state of being unordained (*anupasampanna*); such is the sense.
For the sake of proficiency regarding the meaning in all formal acts (*kammavācā*), the meaning of the *upasampadā* (full ordination) *kammavācā* should be understood here as follows:

*Suṇātu* is the third-person singular form used in an injunction to listen. Although this refers to the Saṅgha which is being enjoined to the act of listening, and because it is present before them, one ought to have said *suṇāhi* using the second-person singular; nevertheless, [it is used in the third person].
Because grammarians have established the use of the first person only when the word "saṅgha" is present—just as in the presence of words such as "Bhagavant" or "Āyasmant," as seen in examples like:
"May the venerable Gotama consent to me; O Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to lay down a training rule for his disciples"; "Let the venerable one depart";
and "May the venerable ones listen to me"—therefore, the use of the first person is employed here.

It is done. Or rather, this is stated by way of reverence (*gārava*). For it should be understood that even when the second-person construction arises [in relation] to those who occupy the position of a teacher (*garuṭṭhānīya*), they employ the first-person construction by way of reverence, as in such cases as "May the Sugata teach the Dhamma.
Some, however, say: "The first-person construction is used here with reference to the words 'Venerable Sir' (*bhante*) and 'Friend' (*āvuso*)."

That is not appropriate, because even in such applications as "Venerable sir, be my teacher; come, friend Upāli, instruct this one who has gone forth," only the use of the second person (majjhimapurisa) is observed.
The word *me* is the genitive case used for self-reference by the one who makes the proclamation. The word *bhante* is a term of respectful address toward elders.
The word "āvuso" (friend), however, is used among novices. Both of these [terms, *bhante* and *āvuso*] are particles;

they are identical in form even when addressing many, as in "tumhe bhante" (you, venerable sir) and "tumhe āvuso" (you, friend). The term "saṅgha" (community) generally refers to an assembly of regular persons (*pakatatta*) consisting of at least four members.
However, in this context, it refers to an assembly of five or more in border regions, and ten or more in central regions.
From this point on, it should be understood that the term "the Saṅgha" is used. Herein, this is the condensed meaning: "Venerable Sir, let the Saṅgha hear my words.

This is the formula to be recited by one who is junior. However, if the proclaimer (anussāvaka) is senior to all the bhikkhus, he should say, "Let the Saṅgha, friends, hear me. If he too should say "Venerable Sir," [he is] junior.

Or, [if one says] “Friend,” there is no disturbance of the formal act (*kammakopa*). Some, however, say: “There is no fault even if one says ‘Friend’ in one instance and ‘Venerable Sir’ (*bhante*) in another, because the address is accomplished by either term.
Now, desiring to make known a certain matter, he enjoins the Saṅgha to listen with the words “May it be heard”; while making that known, he says: “This... [ayaṃ]”
He said, “So-and-so,” and so forth. Therein, “this one” (ayaṃ) indicates the state of being in close proximity within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) of the candidate for full ordination.
By this, it is established that the ordination is valid only for one standing within arm’s reach, because it cannot be said of one standing outside of arm’s reach, “this one.
For that very reason, in the authorization of the instructor (*anusāsaka*), he [is not appointed] because he stands outside of arm’s reach.

The word "this" (*ayaṃ*) was not stated [in the formal formula]. Therefore, one who seeks full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) and has not yet been ordained must be placed within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*).
Furthermore, the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) must necessarily be employed [in the phrase] "This one, named so-and-so" (*itthannāmo*).

And it should be understood that this [usage of "this"] applies only to this first employment of the name. "Named so-and-so" (*itthannāmo*) is an indefinite indication of his name. By both [of these], this...

He indicates the name beginning with "Buddharakkhita" and so forth. Regarding the term "upasampadāpekkho," it is a *bahubbīhi* compound in the sense of different grammatical relations (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), meaning "one for whom the Saṅgha has regard for full ordination. To show that he possesses the status of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) for him, it is said:
"of this venerable one [named] So-and-so. By this, [it is shown that] "this Buddharakkhita [is the candidate] of the venerable Dhammarakkhita..."
The meaning has been shown by way of such a method as "being a co-resident (saddhivihārika) and desiring full ordination," together with the application of names.
And here, even without using the word "of the Venerable One" (āyasmato), it is permissible to say, "This Buddharakkhita desires full ordination from Dhammarakkhita.
For that very reason, in the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase "with such-and-such a person as preceptor" (itthannāmena upajjhāyena)...
The word “of the venerable one” (*āyasmato*) was not stated. Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above.
But surely, in this case, the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) should also be required to stand within arm’s reach, just like the candidate for full ordination;
so why, even when identifying the preceptor in the formula, “This person named so-and-so is seeking full ordination from this person named so-and-so”?

Is it not the case that the use of the word *ima* (this) has not been made? This is not a contradiction, because even in the absence of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there is no invalidation of the formal act (*kamma*).
For, in order to accomplish the ritual act, the name of a preceptor—even one who is non-existent—is proclaimed by way of a present term;
this is done even in cases such as the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for those without a preceptor. Therefore, even when the preceptor is not present, by the mere act of referring to him—
Because its accomplishment depends on kamma, it is not appropriate to designate it as "of this person.

"Pure with respect to obstructive states" means being completely freed from those obstructive states that by their very nature prevent full ordination— namely, those such as incapacity and so forth which render one ineligible for the status of a bhikkhu,
as well as those such as the five diseases, mutilation of the hands, and so forth, which merely cause an obstruction to the attainment of higher status.
When this has been said, even for one who is not yet free from the five impediments and so forth—which merely constitute an offense—the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is valid;
it is not otherwise. "Complete bowl and robes" means that the bowl and robes of this candidate for full ordination are complete.
When this has been said, even for one who lacks the bowl and robes, the full ordination is valid; it is not otherwise. "He requests full ordination."
This was said with reference to the fact that [the candidate] has made the formal request, beginning with the words: “Venerable Sir, I request ordination from the Saṅgha.
Thus, even though the Saṅgha has not been requested by him in this manner, the legal act (*kamma*) remains valid provided that it is stated: “So-and-so requests ordination from the Saṅgha”;
otherwise it is not. “By the preceptor” means by means of the preceptor acting as the instrument, having taken so-and-so as his preceptor.
The meaning is that he requests the Saṅgha—which is the agent (kattubhūta) for bestowing and accomplishing the ordination (upasampadā), which is the object (kammabhūta).
Because the root *yāca* (to request) takes two objects, two accusative cases are stated: "the Saṅgha" and "the ordination.
Regarding the phrase *yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ*: here, "pattakālaṃ" means the time has arrived for this; it refers to the fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha, beginning with the motion (*apalokana*).
That very same word, with the addition of the suffix *-ya*, is called *pattakalla*.

Here, however, what is intended is the formal act of ordination consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-upasampadākamma*); it has become the proper time (*pattakalla*) for the Saṅgha to perform that.
The word *yadi* indicates the propriety of the act by way of seeking consent. For whoever might think it is not the proper time there, he shall speak. This very...
For it was with reference to this matter that it was stated in the formal proclamations: "Whichever venerable one approves...

[and so on]... let him speak. Furthermore, this [formal act] is comprised of five factors: the appropriateness of the time, the perfection of the subject matter, the purity of the assembly regarding obstructive states, the perfection of the boundary, and the completion of the preliminary duties.

In this context, "perfection of the basis" (vatthusampadā) means that, apart from the eleven types of persons incapable [of ordination] and those who have committed an offense involving the loss of the status of a recluse, there must be another human male who is at least twenty years of age and has not yet been ordained.

Only when such a person exists does this formal act of ordination (upasampadākamma) of the Saṅgha become fit and valid; it is not so when such a person is absent. Furthermore, if performed in the absence of such a person, the act is indeed invalid.

The "purity from obstructive conditions" (*antarāyika-dhamma*) refers to the fact that the person who constitutes the basis for the aforementioned full ordination (*upasampadā*) is free from those defective qualities—
ranging from being afflicted by the five diseases prohibited by the Blessed One to not being permitted by one's parents,
and including such physical defects as having severed hands— which are called "obstructive" because they cause obstacles such as offenses for the Sangha that performs the act.

They are so called because they are free from those obstructive qualities that are subject to fault; and it is only when this mindfulness is present that an action is said to be "timely" (*pattakalla*), not when it is absent.
However, once an action has been performed, it is indeed well-performed, with the exception of a person who is less than twenty years of age.

As for the perfection of the boundary (*sīmāsampadā*), it is established—whether formally bound or not—as being free from all defects according to the method that will be explained in the *Uposathakkhandhaka*.
It should be understood by way of two kinds of boundaries (*sīmā*). For it is only when such a boundary exists that this formal act (*kamma*) is called "timely" (*pattakalla*);
when it does not exist, it is not. And a formal act that is performed [under such conditions] fails.

As for the perfection of the assembly (*parisāsampadā*), it refers to those who, at the very least according to the limit of the procedure, are eligible for the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).
There must be ten or five monks, not fewer; they must not have committed a *pārājika* offense; they must not have been suspended; they must be of the same communion;
they must stand within arm’s reach of one another within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*); there must be the bringing of the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it;
there must be no protest from those present; and they must be free from anyone seeking ordination (*upasampadā*)—as excluded in the *Uposathakkhandhaka*.

This [formal act] is comprised of four factors: (1) the absence of laypeople and others who have not received full ordination; (2) the absence of monks who have been suspended for an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), those of a different communion (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*), and bhikkhunīs;
and (3) the absence of persons who ought to be excluded from the vicinity of the Saṅgha.

It is only when such a perfection of the assembly exists that this is called "the proper time" (*pattakalla*); it is not so when it does not exist. Among these, even if any one of the first three factors is lacking—
If the prior action is not performed, the subsequent one fails; it does not fail for the latter.
What is called "the completion of the prior duties" refers to those things stated in the Canon beginning with, "First, he should have him take a preceptor," namely:
having him take a preceptor, pointing out the bowl and robes, and then, having placed him outside arm’s reach [of the teacher]...
The formal act of appointing an instructor; the instruction by the one so appointed after having gone [to the candidate];
his returning first and informing the Saṅgha, followed by the restoration of the candidate for ordination within arm’s reach with the words “Come hither”;
his making the candidate bow at the feet of the monks and have him request ordination; and then, the formal act of appointing an interrogator regarding the obstructing conditions.

And "questioning by one who is agreed upon"—these are the eight preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*). The completion [of the formal act] occurs through the performance of all of these according to reality.
And only when this preliminary work has been completed does this formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) of the Saṅgha become "fit" (*pattakalla*);

it is not fit otherwise. However, even if these preliminary duties have not been performed, the formal act is valid provided there is the fulfillment of the aforementioned requirements regarding the subject matter (*vatthu*) and so forth.
When these are present, it is indeed unshakable. Thus, it should be understood that in this context, what is appropriate is comprised by these five factors.
By this same method, the appropriateness for all tasks—both those previously mentioned and those yet to be described—should be understood by applying them as is fitting.
“One should ordain such-and-such a person” means: by means of bringing about ordination, one should make that person a possessor of it;
this should be understood as either an expression of aspiration (*patthanā*) or a formal injunction (*vidhi*).

For just as when it is said, “One should make Devadatta happy,” the meaning is “having produced happiness for him, one should make him a possessor of happiness,” so too here, [the phrase] “ordination for him”...
The meaning is: "Having brought it to completion, he should make that person a possessor of full ordination (*upasampadā-samaṅgin*).

And this refers to the activity of the instigator (*payojaka-byāpāra*); just as someone who is the causal agent (*hetu-kattā*) is said to "make someone happy" by producing the cause of happiness for some pure agent (*suddha-kattā*) who is already experiencing happiness, so too here, the Saṅgha, acting as the causal agent, [makes] the person who is the pure agent and who is undergoing full ordination [an ordained one].

It is said that one should ordain by accomplishing the cause for ordination. By this, it is established that ordination—which is conferred upon an individual by the Saṅgha, which bestows happiness as if it were happiness itself—is called "ordination" (upasampadā) based on the ultimate Dhamma as it functions in such a way;
thus, it possesses the status of conventional truth (sammutisacca), being designated by the Noble Ones. And herein, [the formula]: "So-and-so [requests] the Saṅgha... [is used].

Because it is stated, "he requests full ordination (*upasampadā*)," and because—unlike in the case of the probationary period (*parivāsa*) and so forth—it does not say, "May [the Sangha] grant full ordination to such-and-such a person," but rather says, "May [the Sangha] ordain such-and-such a person," this formal act of ordination (*upasampadākamma*) should be understood as not being included under "giving" (*dāna*), but rather under the specific characteristic of a formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*).
By this method, "such-and-such a person... [is to be understood].
The meaning should also be understood here in the phrase, "He ordains; he has been ordained by the Saṅgha.
For the only difference there is that it refers to the present time and the past time, whereas here it refers to a time not specifically mentioned.

"This is the motion" (esā ñatti) means this is the making known (ñāpanā) stated as "the Saṅgha should be informed. And this is for the purpose of indicating the presence of the proclamations (anussāvanā) as well.
It is said. This must certainly be stated; however, it need not be stated in the case of a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) alone.
In that case, it should be understood that the formal act of motion is completed as soon as the syllable *yya* has been uttered. "It is pleasing" means it is approved.
"Full ordination" refers to the full ordination being granted and accomplished by the Saṅgha. "He for whom it is pleasing should remain silent."
The construction [is as follows]: *tuṇhī* is a particle used in the sense of "not speaking";
the meaning is "he should be one who does not speak. This connects with the standard formula: "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha that such-and-such a person receives full ordination.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Therefore, [he remains] silent. Here, the word *āsī* (was) is to be supplied. Because [it was said] three times: "He to whom it is not pleasing should speak."
Even when being addressed, the Saṅgha remained silent and noiseless; therefore, the meaning is that it is approved by the Saṅgha.
"In this way" (*evaṃ*) means by this manner. "I maintain, understand, and comprehend this state of approval of the Saṅgha precisely through its silence"—this is the meaning.

The word *iti* is used in the sense of completion, and it is not a constituent part of the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*). Therefore, by the one who makes the proclamation (*anussāvaka*), [it is concluded].
In the phrase “I maintain [it],” it should be understood that one must conclude by stating only the syllable *mi* at the end, and the word *iti* should not be employed.
In this manner, the meaning of all ritual formulas (*kammavācā*) is to be understood.
The commentary on the discussion of the procedure for full ordination (*upasampadā-vidhi*) is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Four Supports, etc. (128).
The passage beginning with "measuring one man's height" (*ekaporisā vā*) demonstrates the manner of knowing the shadow of beings' bodies by measuring it with one's feet.
For a shadow extending up to six or seven steps is called "one man's height" (*porisā*). This, as well as the description of the measure of the seasons and so forth, [is included here].
This was stated for the purpose of performing salutations and causing others to salute after having inquired together with newcomers and ascertained their seniority or juniority.
It comes and goes, thus it is the "season" (*utu*); that very thing by which the year is measured is the "measure" (*pamāṇa*), hence he said:
"The measure of the season is simply the season. "Incomplete" means incomplete by way of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth. If, in the middle of the season...
When he has been ordained, the statement of the remaining days of that season is shown as the "statement of the portion of days.
Therefore he said: "by however many days [the season] of whichever [person] is incomplete, those days.
In that context, for whichever person who has received ordination at that moment, the season connected to him—by however many days...
The construction is: "It is incomplete for you, O day.
Because everything, such as the shadow and so forth, must be gathered together and sung or recited, it is called a *saṅgīti*; thus he said, "This very [thing]," and so on.
In that regard, it should be explained by putting [the parts] together. "What do you receive? means: at the time of your full ordination (*upasampadā*), which *vassa* (rainy season) was it?
"What season do you receive? In what [season] was your full ordination (upasampadā) obtained?"—this is the meaning. "Vassa" means "the rainy season.
Furthermore, since this declaration of the year would not be understood even if stated without it, it should be understood that by this very declaration of the season, it is shown:
"In the years of the Dispensation (sāsana-vassa), or in the years of the Kali Yuga, or in the thousandth, or in the hundredth, or in such-and-such a year, I am receiving such-and-such a season."

“Shadow” (*chāyā*) is stated here with reference to the sequence found in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). However, according to the order in which it ought to be explained, [it refers to] the year, season, month, and so forth, well-known in all places during the Kali Age:

in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a dark or bright fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar day (*tithi*) joined with a specific weekday, under such-and-such a constellation (*nakkhatta*), in such-and-such a portion of the day beginning with forenoon (*pubbaṇha*), and at such-and-such a measure of shadow or measure of *nāḷika*.
"You should say, 'I have received the full ordination from [Name]'; thus it should be explained.
Having learned this well, you should act according to the seniority of newcomers.
In the text, "kissa tvam" means "what have you been doing for all this time?"
130. "Requests for full ordination" means he requests both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā). Regarding the phrase "I shall see," the word "he says" is to be supplied;

this applies to the subsequent instances as well. By the term "should be reinstated," it is shown that the previous state of being suspended does not release one even after having gone away and received the full ordination again.
And because of that, in cases such as eating together with him, there is a *pācittiya* offense for the monks.

[The text] shows this. Regarding the phrase "there is no offense if one shares in the enjoyment or lives together," it should be understood that here "living together" includes sleeping together as well.

And the intention here is this: since he has been reinstated and is therefore a regular monk (*pakatatta*), there is no offense here on account of the *pācittiya* [offense] regarding sharing in the enjoyment with one who is suspended (*ukkhepana*).
However, as for one who, because of the view that there is no offense in what is actually an offense, does not perceive the offense—
For that reason alone, one does not even perform the counter-measure (*paṭikamma*); for until this point, one is not yet called "shameless" (*alajjī*).
Indeed, it is only by transgressing after knowing the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*) that one becomes "shameless. For it is said: "One intentionally commits an offense," and so forth.

Therefore, in this case, there is no fixed determination of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) based on such things as association with the shameless. Consequently, that [offense] is included here.
It should be understood that [the offense] has not been stated. However, regarding the statement made by someone who has not perceived this underlying intention—
that "there is no offense in sharing or living together," which refers to the absence of an offense under the Pācittiya rule,

while one nevertheless incurs a Dukkaṭa offense due to the condition of sharing with one who is shameless"— this determination of offenses should be understood as being stated only when such shamelessness exists, and not when it does not.
131. Regarding the verses beginning with "In the Vinaya," the phrase "in regard to restraints" (*niggahānam*) means in regard to the acts of restraining.
"Of those with evil desires" (*pāpicche*) refers to the acts of restraining wicked persons, and "of the modest" (*lajjīnam*) refers to the acts of supporting them.

Since one is said to practice wisely (*yoniso paṭipajjati*) precisely because one acts for the benefit of others in accordance with their welfare within the great Vinaya—which brings happiness to the virtuous—therefore, this summary verse (*uddāna*) [is given].
The connection of the phrase "I shall explain" (*pavakkhāmi*) should be understood as follows. The remainder is easy to understand throughout.
The commentary on the discussion of the four supports (*nissaya*), etc., is concluded.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā.
The method of commentary on the Mahākhandhaka is finished.
2. The Uposatha Khandhaka:
Commentary on the Discussion Beginning with the Permission for Assembling.

132. In the *Uposathakkhandhaka*, a "ford" (*tittha*) is so called because people cross over or descend there; it refers to a tenet (*laddhi*). "From this" means from the tenets of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). 135. Regarding the phrase "having committed [an offense] or having emerged from it":

here, both confession (*desanā*) and announcement (*ārocana*) are included. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "An offense that has been emerged from, confessed, or announced... [omission] ...is said to be 'non-existent'.

The word "with a person" (*manujena*) refers to one who is nearby. "To others" (*pare*) refers to persons situated at a distance; the construction is: "one should not speak words even to such other individuals."
Because it is said, “For one who has disclosed [the offense], there is comfort,” some say that even a grave offense (garukāpatti) is cleared by mere disclosure;
however, that is merely their own opinion, as it contradicts the suttas prescribing probation (parivāsa) and other such measures.
This, then, is the intended meaning here: when well-behaved monks disclose themselves as they truly are, the statement beginning with “they must, though unwillingly, undergo probation” [applies].
By relying on this, even if he is unwilling, they will by means of skillful methods grant him probation and so forth, and will inevitably establish him in the state of purity;
consequently, through his freedom from remorse and other such qualities, he finds comfort. "First, the recitation of the Pātimokkha" indicates the recitation of the Nidāna (the introductory section).
"He laid down what was not previously existing. And it is not only this [that he did]; for even that which had already been laid down previously—

It should be understood that the Blessed One, having formulated the Vinaya-mātikā by way of the recitation of the Pārājikas and so forth—beginning with the words, "In this regard, these four Pārājika rules come up for recitation"—and having himself compiled all the training rules beginning with the Pārājikas together with the recitation of the origins (nidāna), he proclaimed it as the "Pātimokkha.
With reference to all of this, [the Buddha said]: "I authorize you, monks..."
"It was said: 'to recite the Pātimokkha.
136. "This is to be understood" refers to the matter of the fact that it should be done on whichever fourteenth or fifteenth day [of the lunar half-month].
The commentary on the discussion beginning with the permission for the assembly is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Acknowledgment of the Boundary (Sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 138. “In the eastern direction”—this is merely an illustration.
However, if there is no boundary marker in that direction, one should begin from wherever one exists, first saying: “In the eastern intermediate direction, in the southern direction,” and so forth.

Having designated the landmarks in all existing locations, it is permissible to designate again that which was first designated as "in the eastern intermediate direction," because a boundary may be formally established even for one shaped like a crossroads by means of three landmarks.
"Connecting the boundary circle three times" means that the holder of the Vinaya, standing himself in only one place, [should do so] solely...
The meaning is: "binding sign to sign all around the boundary circle by means of the very words describing the signs.
For it is permissible to describe [the boundary] even without going to each respective location of the signs.
Since it is difficult to circumambulate three times around a boundary of up to three *yojanas* in a single day, the holder of the Vinaya may do so even if he has not seen it himself.

It is indeed permissible for a monk to designate a sign as it was previously established by other monks—observing it according to what someone has said, such as "This is a rock, venerable sir"—by saying, "This rock is the sign," and so forth.
A "pure mound of earth" is described as something not made by anyone, but arisen naturally; the same applies to the others. "The other" refers to the pure mound of earth and so on.
"A mountain. Regarding "of the size of an elephant": here, the measurement of an elephant should be understood by the extent of its height above the ground.
"By four or three" means by those standing in four or three directions within the boundary area.
However, it is not permissible to appoint [the boundary] even by many people standing in only one direction. But it is permissible even by two people standing in two directions.
It is not permissible. Therefore—meaning because it is not permissible by one [person]—therefore.

"Having placed that outside" means that since the characteristic of what has been designated (*kittita-nimitta*) does not extend to the boundary, performing [the act] within the boundary is improper; thus he said, "If," and so forth.
The measure of thirty-two *palas* of lump-sugar should be understood according to its shape, not by way of weighing or counting, as it would be too heavy.
The measurement by weight should be taken according to the Magadhan scale; they say that this is double the size of a worldly scale.
"Even though it is very large" means even if it is many yojanas in measure, provided it does not rise above the height of an elephant from the ground but remains dense down to the ground below.
For if a peak rises above the height of an elephant from there, it is indeed reckoned as a mountain.

"Antosārānaṃ" means that although at that moment the heartwood (*sāra*) is not yet present due to their youth, it is said with reference to the heartwood that will exist through their future development.
For even a grove of about four or five such trees, each having a circumference equal to the handle of a needle, is permissible.
"Antosāramissakānaṃ" means mixed with trees that possess heartwood; by this, it is also implied that [the grove] may be mixed with heartwood trees.
This shows that a forest is suitable. The phrase "even as much as four or five trees" is said with reference to trees of solid heartwood.

Regarding the expression "building a monastery in the middle of a forest": this refers to the manner in which, by not cutting down the trees within a cluster of trees but instead defining the monastery's boundaries with fences and the like, one constructs cells, leaf-huts, and so forth in the spaces between the trees, such that even the interior of the monastery [is surrounded by them].
"It is indeed a forest; thus they construct the dwelling"—this is the meaning.

For if they were to cut down the entire tree and construct the dwelling, then because the dwelling would no longer be surrounded by a forest, that forest standing around it would have to be designated as one [separate] place.
But here, because there is forest even inside, it is said, "the forest need not be designated. For if they were to designate it, [the boundary of] the *nimitta*...
By saying, “there is a dwelling above,” one falls into the fault stated immediately before. “A portion” means a portion of the forest;
the meaning is a portion of the forest situated on one side of a dwelling built in a place devoid of trees.
“The size of a needle’s shaft” means the size of a bamboo shaft; some say it is the size of a writing-stick. In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*...
However, in the *Avebhaṅgiyavinicchaya*, because it is stated that "any bamboo even as small as an eight-finger-breadth needle-shaft...
is a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*)," one should understand that what is meant by "needle-shaft" is a bamboo shaft even thinner than that. "In bamboo or reed tubes, bowls, etc.
means: in bamboo joints, or in reed joints, or in earthenware vessels such as shallow pans and the like. "Even at that very moment" refers to when the young seedling is [still tender].
This was said with reference to those species that grow after having withered;

however, it is not appropriate to include those which, once matured, are uprooted and replanted, yet—like branches that have been cut—wither and only survive after a long time through the emergence of new roots and sprouts, or else perish entirely.
"This" refers to the emergence of new roots and branches.
"Midway" means within the four great directions of the boundary. "Corner" refers to the points where two roads meet at each of the four corners of the boundary.

Regarding the statement "it is proper to designate them on the outer side," this means that among the roads situated outside those four corners, one road is designated for one direction and another for the opposite direction; thus, all four roads [are to be designated].
The intention is that it is appropriate to praise them in the four directions. But how is it understood that their unity is lost by merely being praised in this way?
For it is said later, in the section concerning where they have gone: “They go in the four directions.
Therefore, the reason for this must be investigated here.
Regarding the phrase “for a bhikkhunī who is crossing,” this is stated because the definition of a river is provided in the Pāḷi in the context of bhikkhunīs crossing to the other side.
For bhikkhus, even merely wetting their inner robes (antaravāsaka) is permitted.

By the statement “the same principle applies to the fourfold classification of rivers,” it is indicated that once a river has been designated in one place, it is not permissible to designate it again in another location further along.
This is what he shows. For that very reason, the term "unmixed" (*asammissa*) was employed [in the verse] with the thought: "It is appropriate to praise all four rivers as being unmixed.

"At the root" means at the beginning. "Having broken through the riverbank" means just as farmers who do not desire water cannot turn back a great flood, so too having broken through the bank of the river.
*Ukkhepimaṃ* means that which is to be drawn up by means of a bucket with a long rope.
*Asammissehi* means by mountains situated in all directions, or by any other such landmarks not separated by intervening objects like rocks.
*Sammissehi* refers to even all eight [mountains] standing such that there is a mountain in one direction and a rock in another. [Regarding] "of the landmarks..."
By the phrase “even with a hundred,” it is shown that it is permissible to describe many signs in a single direction, such as:
“What is the sign in the eastern direction? A mountain, venerable sir. Again, what is the sign in the eastern direction?
A rock, venerable sir? and so forth. “Shaped like a crossroads” means triangular. “Quadrangular” means perfectly square; [it may also mean] shaped like a drum (mudiṅga).
However, they are long and square. At one corner they are contracted, while at the other they are wide. "Having established the precinct around the boundary" means:
having established a precinct sufficient for the intermediate space (sīmantarika) outside the demarcation of those monasteries, which is to be bound as a boundary in the future.
Those monasteries in which the boundary has been bound are called "bound-boundary" (baddhasīmā).

*Pāṭekkan* means individually. *Baddhasīmāsadisāni* shows that just as those standing within established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*) are permitted to perform formal acts (*kamma*) individually without regard for one another’s consent (*chanda*) and so forth, so too are those standing within village boundaries (*gāmasīmā*).
The phrase "should come" is stated merely as a matter of propriety; hence he says, "even the coming," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "going forth, full ordination, and so forth," here the mention of "going forth" refers to the inquiry regarding the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*).

The expression "twenty-one bhikkhus" is said with reference to those who are seated; this is stated so that there may be sufficient space for both those eligible for the formal act (*kammāraha*) and those performing the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
