The instruction "stones should be placed as marks" means that at a location chosen according to one's preference, trees or other such signs should be established.

It is stated [thus] because of the difficulty of increasing [the boundary], because it would cause confusion between the two fixed boundaries, and because, due to the absence of a stone marker, it would be easy to bring and place one anywhere.
The same applies to the statement that "stone markers for the boundary line (sīmantarika) should be placed.
Regarding the phrase "even those measuring four finger-breadths," this refers to how, outside the delimitation of the trunk-boundary (khandhasīmā), there are stone markers.
A space measuring four fingerbreadths all around is excluded; the remaining area remains within the boundary of the interior of the *khaṇḍa*.
Thus, it should be understood that when those stones are placed, there is an interval of four fingerbreadths between them.
"Boundary-stones" (*sīmantarika-pāsāṇā*) refers to the stones used as markers placed at the boundaries. When describing these, one should proceed clockwise.
It should be recited while walking around [the meditation hall]. How so?
Standing in the western part of the boundary facing east, one should recite all the signs there in succession, asking, "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
Then, standing in the northern direction facing south, one should ask, "What is the sign in the southern direction?"
Having recited them in succession, he likewise stands facing west in the eastern direction and recites in succession, "What is the sign in the western direction?
Having likewise stood facing north in the southern direction, he recites there in succession, "What is the sign in the northern direction? and thus enumerates all the signs therein in order.
Again, standing in the western direction facing east, one should recite the previously mentioned [boundary markers] once more in the manner described.
In this way, for many *khaṇḍasīmā* (partial boundaries) as well, the boundary-stone markers (*sīmantarika-pāsāṇa*) must each be recited individually.
"Thereafter" means subsequently. "The remaining markers" refers to the remaining markers on the outer perimeters of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). Of both...
“They do not disturb” means they do not disturb the legal procedure (*kamma*) of both parties.
“In a hut or house” means in a grass hut built on the ground. “A mortar” means a small trench resembling the pit for a mortar.
“One should not make a sign” means that one should not make that line or that mortar a sign. And this [applies] to those [cases] as previously described.

Although it is established that it is not permissible because the signs have not yet appeared, it is stated—even from a distance—for the sake of avoiding failure, in case someone might through delusion create a sign based on a perception of imperishability.
Thus, one should understand the reason for repeatedly stating a point already established even in subsequent passages such as "without scratching the wall" and so forth;
for the failure regarding boundaries is the root of all failures in formal acts (*kamma*), such as full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Regarding this, it should be stated by way of closing every door in every respect. It should be understood that the teachers have established the legal decision here only after having explained everything.
"A wall" means one made of bricks, wood, or clay. However, in the case of a stone wall, [the boundary marker is] a single stone serving as the sign (*nimitta*).
It is appropriate to consecrate each individual [stone] according to its respective direction.

It is not appropriate to consecrate an entire wall built of many stones, because it must be referred to in the singular as "this stone is the boundary-mark" (*nimitta*). Regarding the phrase "only inside the wall":

here, even within the wall, the boundary (*sīmā*) should be understood as being strictly inside the space where the boundary-marks are situated. Having placed the boundary-stones at the front entrance...
Even for the interior and the exterior, stones should be placed and designated in a location the size of the interior space of the hut.
For in this way, the boundary is square in shape both inside and outside, including even the wall situated between the interior and the exterior of the hut.
"Outside" means all around the entire hut or house.
“The boundary is both inside and outside” means that the square boundary includes the wall standing in the middle.

140. "It overflows" means it spreads across; when a boundary established on both banks of a river extends across the river, it is called a "river-overflowing boundary.
Thus he says, "overflowing the river," for the boundary does not enter into the interior of the river. Regarding the characteristics of a river:

However, since it enters [the definition] when it is absent, and at that time the river-bank boundary does not exist, he says: "The characteristic of a river is exactly as stated in the section on river-signs.
The word *assa* means "it would be. The connection is: "But it must necessarily be a permanent boat.
By the phrase "not by a boat," he shows that even without a boat the boundary is well-bound, and that the boat is for the purpose of avoiding an offense.
“Made of a collection of trees” means a bridge constructed by joining many trees together. The phrase “made by cutting down trees” is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

“Having brought the monks standing within the boundary of all signs into hand’s-reach” is said with reference to the fact that both banks constitute the domain of a single village. “Shaped like a mountain” is said because of a headland rising up on one side.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of a boundary is finished.
Commentary on the discussion regarding the Uposatha hall, etc.: 141.
“Having abolished” means having destroyed; the sense is “having removed. And this is stated for the purpose of avoiding an offense.
142. Regarding the phrase "whatever [marks] there may be": this is stated here because the specific marks for the boundary were not explicitly mentioned in the canonical text (pāḷi).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the Uposatha hall and so forth is concluded.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion concerning the authorization of the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā).
143. "Eighteen" refers even to the Andhakavinda monastery. "Of them" means among those great monasteries.
"A little" (*mana*) is an explanation of this [term]; the meaning is "slightly crossed. To show this very point, it is said:
"It was in a state of having been crossed without being reached. "Not attending to it" states the reason why he did not transcend [the boundary] by means of psychic power (*iddhi*).

144. "That" refers to the community of bhikkhunīs. "The two [of them]" refers to those who share the same communal residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and do not live apart (*avippavāsa*). "The boundary of non-separation" is said with reference to the great boundary (*mahāsīma*).

"For the most part, they do not live apart right there" means that even for those who do not know whether the great boundary exists or does not exist, or who do not know its external limits, if the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is performed while standing within the boundary, [the act is valid]. Thus it is stated.

"That boundary is considered removed" means he said, "they will be able both to remove it and to bind it. "In a place free from danger" means in a location devoid of a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
And this [fragmented boundary] is desired even when a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) exists, for the sake of making the performance of formal acts (*kamma*) easy;
therefore, it is stated that one does not bind it in places of great congregation such as the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyangaṇa*). There too, that...
It is firmly bound, just like a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

As for the statement, "But they will not be able to bind [it]," this was said with reference to the binding of a great boundary, because the fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) has not been abolished and its non-existence is not recognized.
However, they will indeed be able to bind a fragmentary boundary in a place free from conflict. Regarding the confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*):
"Having made" means: having made an overlapping and a breach of the boundary within the existing side of the broken-off boundary;

and even on the non-existing side, having created the apprehension of a breach because the apprehension of a breach was not averted. "They would make it non-monastery" means they would make it unfit for formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma).
For previously, it was possible to perform a formal act in places free from apprehension, such as the courtyard of a cetiya; but now, even that has been destroyed.
This is the intended meaning. "It should not be abolished" means it should not be abolished by those who are unaware of the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
"Both do not know" means they do not know either the delimitation of the two areas, or whether both of them exist, or whether one or the other exists;
in all such cases, there is only doubt. "Neither to abolish nor to bind..."

The phrase "they will be able" is said with reference to the fact that even though one might be able to abolish [the boundary] by standing in a place free from apprehension, one cannot establish a great boundary (*mahāsīma*). The statement "and it is not possible...
to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*)" is said with reference to the formal act for binding the boundary. Therefore—because it is not possible to bind it—therefore, not...
The meaning is "they must be removed.

However, some say: "In such monasteries, having taken five or six monks, they should stand continuously, starting from the edge of the monastery, both inside and outside the monastery enclosure, within the range of a stone's throw, in every place the size of a bed."
First, when the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) and then the common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsaka-sīmā*) have been abolished by means of a formal act of rescission (*samūhanana*),
and while those [boundaries] still exist— whether as a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍa-sīmā*) or a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*)— in that monastery,
those bhikkhus must necessarily abolish them within a single bed-space situated between them; thereafter, only the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*) would remain.

In this case, the knowledge of the boundary or its delimitation is not a requisite factor. Rather, standing within the boundary and performing the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) with the intention, "We shall abolish it," are the requisite factors here. In the Commentary, regarding the delimitation of a great boundary, it is stated:
"But those who know the broken boundary—even if they do not know [the rule on] non-separation—will certainly be able to abolish and bind it. Thus [it refers to] the great boundary.
Because it is stated that this applies even when the community is unaware [of the boundaries],

and because they say, "It is fitting to bind both kinds of boundaries there as one pleases, and to perform formal acts such as ordination (*upasampadā*), provided only the village boundary remains," this appears to be reasonable;
yet it should be accepted after careful investigation.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the authorization of the non-separation boundary is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning village boundaries, etc., [§147]:
In the Canon, by the passage beginning, "Monks, in regard to an unappointed boundary," it is the village boundary itself that constitutes the field for a formally established boundary.
It is like the forest, rivers, and so forth, in relation to the throwing of water [for boundary-marking] among living beings.
And it shows that in a place devoid of a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), that village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) itself constitutes a common community (*samānasamvāsā*).

Regarding the phrase "the village boundary of that village," here the term "of the village" refers to the entire village domain—including fields, lands, forests, mountains, and so forth—both inside and outside the defined limits of the village boundary.

It was stated [not] that it is only the interior of the house; therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: the village boundary is that which is connected to the entire village-field of that [village].

For the conventional designation "village"—which is designated by worldly people as a unity across many portions of ground such as the interior of the house and the fields—is precisely what is here called the "village boundary"; this is the intended sense.

For the village itself is indeed the village boundary. By this same method, one should understand that in those respective locations—such as the forest, the river, the ocean, and the lake—the status of being a "forest boundary" and so forth belongs to the forest and the rest precisely as they are designated by worldly convention as single entities.
However, in common usage, the designation "village boundary" and so on is appropriate only for the limits of the village and the rest; it does not [apply to the ground itself].

In all cases, such as villages, fields, and so forth; however, within the Dispensation (Sāsana), those villages and other areas are designated by the term "boundary" (*sīmā*)—namely, "the village boundary" (*gāmasīmā*), "the forest boundary" (*araññasīmā*), and so on up to "the ocean boundary" (*samuddasīmā*)—understanding that they are themselves their own limits for the purpose of excluding everything else.
Thus it should be understood.
“Of a town (nigama)” is stated in order to indicate, by way of illustration, all the various types of village boundaries.
Therefore he said, “the city is also included. “They receive tax” is stated by way of the majority;
however, regarding those portions of land recorded on royal edicts such as, “this village is of such-and-such a portion of a *karīsa*,” in whichever [portion]—
In places such as reservoirs, boundaries of fields, cremation grounds, and mountains, they do not collect taxes; these too are indeed village boundaries.
For it should be understood that every portion of land demarcated by kings and others is a village boundary, with the exception of rivers, salt-pits, and natural lakes.
Therefore he said: "Having demarcated [the land], the king gives it to someone. But if, in that case, the king...
If one joins [land] between villages, it belongs to the boundary of the village already entered;
the same principle applies even when rivers or lakes are destroyed and converted into ponds and the like, or when they are turned into fields and the like.
However, as for those villages that have been abandoned by people oppressed by fear of kings, thieves, and so forth, and remain deserted for a long time—
However, there are villages all around; these too are each a separate village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).

For in those cases, kings have the villagers from the surrounding villages plow the land, or they collect taxes after recording the area plowed by whoever [plowed it], or they bring them into union with another village.
But as for those villages that have been abandoned even by kings, and whose village fields are separated by a great wilderness—
Having become one, they reach the boundary of a forest region devoid of villages; the former village boundary is destroyed.

However, kings, having established a large village in a certain wilderness area or similar place and settled many thousands of families there, designate the surrounding inhabited areas as "property villages" for those residing therein and grant them. But [they do not change] the old name or the original delimitation.
They do not destroy [the boundary]; those too are each a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) in themselves. To this extent, they do not abandon the status of being the boundary of the previous village.
The phrase "both that and the other," etc., is an exposition of the intended meaning of the canonical passage: "belonging to the same communion, sharing a single *uposatha*.
For therein, "that" refers to the new [boundary] which has arisen after being shifted according to the king's desire, while "the other" refers to the one that was not shifted.

The natural village boundary (*pakatigāmasīmā*): just as it is permissible to perform all *saṅgha*-kamma within a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), so too this [natural boundary] is similar to a formally established boundary in its fitness for all such kamma;
the intention is that it constitutes a common residence (*samānasaṃvāsā*) and a single *uposatha* area.

When it is stated in general terms that "it is similar to a formally established boundary," some might think it refers to the boundary for not being separated from the three robes (*ticīvarāvippavāsasīmā*), which is itself a formally established boundary; therefore, by way of precluding such similarity, [the text specifies it is like a formal boundary in its fitness for all kamma].

To show that there is also a similarity [of the boundary] with the seven *satta*-intervals above, the phrase beginning with "only" (*kevalam*) is stated here as an incidental discussion regarding the method of demonstration.
In a forest similar to the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness, where there is no common designation of a village such as "this is the field of such-and-such a village,"...
And in such a forest where they neither plough nor sow—this includes even islands in the midst of the ocean that are not on the paths frequented by fishermen and are devoid of human habitation.
For whatever place is not a village-field and is bereft of rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, all that should be understood as the forest boundary (*arañña-sīmā*).
And that [forest boundary] exists by itself, even without the seven-intermediate-space boundary (*satta-bbhantara-sīmā*).
They share the same communal residence and are similar to a bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*). Just as in the case of river-boundaries and the like, all sangha-acts (*saṅghakamma*) are permitted here.

As for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, their status as boundaries is established by the fact that they are described in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as being "similar to a bound boundary by their very nature," and so forth.
But how is the forest a boundary? It is established through the functional power (*sāmatthiya*) of the Sutta permitting the seven-league boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), and other such texts.
Just as many bound boundaries (*baddhasīmā*) were permitted for the sake of avoiding *vaggakamma* (invalid acts performed by an incomplete assembly) within a village boundary,
and as the intermediate space (*sīmantarikā*) was permitted between two of them to prevent their mutual confusion, so too here in the forest there is a seven-league boundary.
And because of the capacity of the rule established in both the Canon and the Commentary regarding the intermediate space between those two, [it follows that] this applies to the forest as well.

It should be understood that the absence of a boundary there is established by its very nature—just as with rivers and the like—precisely for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly) within it, since a seven-fathom boundary has been permitted.

For it is only those standing within that very boundary who perform a *vagga-kamma* for the sake of the location of the boundary, not those standing outside the boundary in the air, as one might do for a location in space. It is by taking this functional capacity [of the boundary] in this way that [the rule is applied].

"By the statement, 'Bhikkhus, all rivers are not boundaries' (Sabbā, bhikkhave, nadī asīmā), etc., it should be understood that even for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes—which have their boundaries demarcated by prohibition—the status of being a boundary exists by their very nature; this is what is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Then, "from the place where he stands" means from the place where that bhikkhu stands. For even if a thousand bhikkhus are standing there, [the boundary is determined by his position].

The intended meaning is that, starting from the outer edge of that established space, when the expectation of a boundary arises among the monks for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (an act performed by an incomplete assembly),
the seven-intermediate-space boundary (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*) arises spontaneously along with that [expectation], and they are thus of common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsā*). However,
in the case of a small forest where there is no suspicion of a *vagga-kamma* due to being filled with many monks—
There is no requirement for a seven-abbhantara boundary; in that case, a seven-abbhantara boundary does not arise.
It is only in the case of a forest boundary (*arañña-sīmā*) that the Saṅgha may perform a formal act (*kamma*) there. The same principle applies to rivers and so forth. For it will be said:
"If a river is not too long, and the Saṅgha sits everywhere from its source down to its mouth, then the formal act of the water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) [is performed]."

"...there is not," and so forth. By this very statement, it should be understood that when there is a dependence on a boundary (*sīmā*) for the purpose of avoiding a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly), the *udakukkhepa-sattabbhantara-sīmā* (the boundary established by the throwing of water up to the distance of seven arm-spans) arises;
it does not arise in its absence. However, some maintain that "the boundary is produced only by the act of demarcating after measuring seven arm-spans all around, and not by itself."

What they say should not be accepted. For if the boundary were to arise by way of establishing an internal delimitation, there would be no such thing as an "unbound" boundary, because the accomplishment of the monks' ritual acts would be impossible.

Furthermore, since the measure of a "hand" (hattha) is of many kinds in the world—such as the carpenter’s hand and the natural hand—and since no such specific measure of a hand has been stated in the Vinaya, [the former view is untenable].
If it were measured by anything whatsoever—even by a hand permitted by the Blessed One—one might suspect a failure of the boundary, thinking, "Was it not measured?
Furthermore, since those measuring would be unable to measure without making even the slightest deficiency or excess, there would certainly be a failure.
Moreover, as this [boundary] increases by means of overflow, it either increases or decreases according to their measurement.

Furthermore, when the Saṅgha has performed the formal act (*kamma*) and departed, this boundary—which arose through the effort of the monks—either ceases to exist through their departure or it does not.
How could it be that, like a formally established boundary, it would not persist until the disappearance of the Dispensation?
And if it were to persist, how could there be no apprehension of a confusion of boundaries throughout the entire forest, as occurs in the case of ancient monasteries?
Therefore, it should be understood that [the perception of a boundary] arises precisely through the expectation of a boundary and ceases with its disappearance.
And as it is here, so it is also regarding the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) in rivers and the like;
for even there, the "middle-sized man" (*majjhimapurisa*) is not known. Likewise, the throwing with all one's strength applies in both cases.
In whatever direction there is no space for a seven-fathom [radius] or for a water-splash, how could there be measurement or throwing there?
Since it would enter non-field areas such as village fields by way of entering them, the boundary would fail;
however, in the case of a boundary arising through dependence, the seven-fathom and water-splash boundaries exist wherever there is sufficient space.
They arise spontaneously and completely full. However, where it is not possible [for them to be full], they arise there only according to the measure of their own field, and not outside of it.

As for the observation here of the size of internal seeds or the throwing of sand and so forth, that is done for the purpose of defining the location where the boundary has been established, in order to know the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) and the house precinct (*gharūpacāra*).
It is like demonstrating the method for throwing a clod-thrower; for that very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "One either designates a boundary or delimits a water-throw.
Even when this has been done, because that delimitation cannot be known exactly as it is, those who wish to know its breadth must stand inside and remain in a place free from apprehension.
Those who are performing the *añña* (invitation) outside must send [the messenger] to a place that is very far away and free from danger.
Others, however, maintain: "There is no need for a formal boundary (*sīmā*) here;

even if a single bhikkhu has entered the forest or a river, etc., for the purpose of traveling on a road or bathing, the water-boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) of seven *abbhantara*s surrounding him is automatically established."
Just as the light of a lamp arises and vanishes the very moment it enters a village field or similar area, for that very reason,

when two Saṅghas are performing separate formal acts (kamma), it is permitted here to establish the "intermediate boundary" (sīmantarikā) between the two boundaries at a distance of one *sattabbhantara*,
as well as the "water-splash" (*udakukkhepa*). For by anyone [establishing it] at the edge of the boundary...

If a monk sent by means of a formal act (*kamma*) should create a breach of the boundary (*sīmāsambheda*) by having the boundary arising all around him touch the boundary of others—lest that happen—otherwise, even a space of four finger-breadths for a boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*) must be permitted here.
Furthermore, this is established by the statement that even for one standing in the boundary-interval, the formal act is subverted in both cases. That too...
Having surrounded it, because of the boundary that has arisen of its own accord, there would be a confusion of both boundaries, or rather, of a single one;
otherwise, the statement regarding the "corruption of the formal act" (kammakopa) would not be logical. For it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Even if one stands having left the hand’s reach within the enclosure, provided one does not overstep another enclosure of the same size outside the enclosure..."

"Even while staying [there], one may commit an offense. Furthermore, for a bhikkhu staying in a forest devoid of villages who is free from the desire to perform work, the Blessed One has permitted being separated from his three robes within a space delimited by seven *abbhantara*s;

and that delimitation is a *sīmā*. Thus, [this offense] arises even without such concern. For this very reason, it is said here: "This *sīmā* also serves as a means of avoiding separation from the three robes..."

It is said, “He obtains [it]. Therefore, they argue that the simultaneous arising [of the boundary] should be understood in the manner already stated even without the desire to perform the formal act (*kamma*).

This is not correct; for just as with the light of a lamp, since each individual person possesses their own distinct boundary, when the Sangha or a group performs a formal act, the monks standing there have their own distinct boundaries arising all around them.
Because there would arise the fault of mutual confusion among many boundaries. Furthermore, by way of overflow, both an increase and a decrease of that [boundary] would be possible.
For those arriving later, there would be the arising of a new boundary within; for those who have departed, even the boundary situated all around them would be destroyed.
However, in the Canon it is said: "Seven *abbhantara*s all around—this is the common communion therein," and so forth; thus, there is only one [boundary] of seven *abbhantara*s.
The throwing of water has been permitted, yet this boundary does not arise by its own nature or through the power of a cause, like the radiance of a lamp.

Rather, it arises solely through the Blessed One’s permission; and when the Blessed One granted these permissions, he did so specifically for the sake of making it easy for the monks to perform formal acts (*kamma*) by avoiding the requirement of a quorum (*vagga-kamma*). Thus, how could [the boundary] not apply even to those who have entered for the purpose of bathing and other such duties?

Is it because there is no purpose for the simultaneous arising of those boundaries on all sides? And since there is only one single purpose, how can there be the arising of multiple boundaries according to the number of individual monks?
It has been stated: "They stand within hand’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) without leaving the single boundary.
As for the statement regarding the establishment of the intermediate space between two boundaries, that refers only to the delimitation of that specific extent.
The statement regarding the subversion of formal acts (*kamma*) for those staying there was spoken in order to avoid,
from afar, both the suspicion of the confusion of boundaries (*sīmā-sambheda*) and the suspicion of the subversion of formal acts, due to the difficulty of discerning the limits of these boundaries.
Furthermore, as for the seven-fathom limit shown by the Blessed One in the open air for the purpose of not being separated from one's robe:
Thus, this is not a *sīmā* (boundary) at all; rather, it is simply one type of delimitation here, such as the delimitation of a field or a pond.

And in that case, when many monks are standing together, the robe must be placed within a radius of seven *abbhantara*s from each individual monk’s own standing place. It is not [measured] from the edge of the assembly.

Starting from the boundary of the assembly. For if one were to take the interior starting from the boundary of the assembly, then a robe placed at the inner limit would be outside for one standing in the middle; thus, at the rising of the sun, that [robe] would become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

However, the boundary must be taken precisely as the boundary of the assembly. Furthermore, the exemption from the offense of being separated from the robe (*cīvaravippavāsa*) here applies to the delimitation of an open space (*abbhokāsa*).

It is spoken of because it exists, but not because it is obtainable as far as the boundary-delimitation extends, as is the case with the designation "non-separation" (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) in relation to the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

For even within the great boundary, a robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) in the vicinity of a village or a village-outpost (*gāmūpacāra*). Here too, for one standing in the center, [the robe] becomes subject to forfeiture at the edge of the boundary.
Therefore, these seven *abbhantara* and water-throwing boundaries (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) are to be understood solely in relation to the aforementioned boundaries.
It is our view that both the arising and the destruction [of the forest] must be understood through the removal of its constituent parts;
this should be accepted after investigation, or else another more appropriate method should be sought from this.
However, in this context, according to the text, "in the forest, within seven abbhantaras on all sides," it refers to a forest such as the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness.

"Seven *abbhantara*s on all sides": because this [boundary] is established within a seven-*abbhantara* limit even in a forest (*arañña*) where trees and such are dense, there is no fault in its connection with the trees and so forth that constitute its own supporting forest boundary;

how much more so, then, in a place devoid of a village (*agāmaka*) which relies upon a tree as its support, where there is no need for the exemption regarding the tree concerning the separation from one's robe (*cīvara-vippavāsa*).
It should be understood that "permission" is established as being equivalent to the privilege of staying in the open air (*abbhokāsa*).
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of a boundary," it is permissible for more than seven *abbhantara*s for the sake of a boundary line (*sīmantarika*);
however, less than that is certainly not permitted, because the limit of seven *abbhantara*s is difficult to discern. Therefore, even with only one person, apart from the Saṅgha...
A bhikkhu standing outside must stand at a very great distance, having crossed over another seven *satta*-intervals;
otherwise, there is the risk of the invalidation of the formal act (*kamma*). The same rule applies to the throwing of water. For this reason, he will say:

"But what is deficient is not permitted. And here, this regulation regarding the boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*) follows the sutta that authorizes the interval between two established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*).
This should be understood as established. For although the Blessed One, by way of the introductory narrative,

permitted a boundary-line (*sīmantarika*) for the purpose of avoiding the fault of mutual overlapping and confusion between two established boundaries that depend on the same village boundary or share the same commonality,
nevertheless, in accordance with that principle, [the same applies] to those who depend on a single wilderness boundary, a river boundary, and so forth, provided they share the same commonality.
Knowing that the Blessed One did not approve of the mutual overlapping and merging of two sattabbhantara boundaries or even two *udakukkhepa* (water-sprinkling) boundaries,
nor of a place situated without an intervening space— that is, without a boundary-interval (*sīmantarika*)—

the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā established the procedure for the boundary-interval here as well. For even in the case of dissimilar boundaries, there must be dependence on a single boundary and a commonality of nature.

It should be understood that when two factors are present, even in the absence of a single boundary line (*sīmantarikā*), there is an occasion for the breaking [of the boundary]; it does not occur when they are absent.

Furthermore, it should be grasped that by the very power of establishing the boundary line, the mutual connection between these trees and so forth—just as in the case of a bound boundary—is also prohibited; this too has been shown by way of logical inference.
By the phrase “by its very nature,” he shows that it is an unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), like a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).

He shows that all *saṅgha*-formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) are permitted here because they share the same communion and the same observance-day (*ekūposatha*). “By whatever means” means by any creature whatsoever, even down to a pig or similar animal.
However, when a great flood falls from a high place into a low place, the area it has carved out may be either small or large.

Or it may be like newly drawn water, endowed with the [proper] characteristics. Here too, there is no requirement for a "water-splashing" boundary (*udakukkhepa*) in the case of small bodies of water;
however, in the case of the ocean, the formal act (*kamma*) must be performed strictly within the water-splashing boundary itself, because it is difficult to purify [the assembly] otherwise.

Again, "therein" refers to these three—rivers and so forth—which are established by worldly convention as unbound boundaries (*abaddhasīmā*), and which are mentioned again here for the purpose of avoiding a *vaggakamma* (an invalid act performed by an incomplete assembly).
The intention is to show the delimitation for that which is established by the terminology of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) and for which no physical boundary has been fixed.
In the canonical text, regarding the phrases "for a man of medium height" and so forth: it is called *udakukkhepa* because water is thrown (*ukkhipati*) there;

it is the place where the water falls. Therefore, it is "by means of the throwing of water. This is the meaning here according to the connection of the words: [the boundary is defined] from the edge of the assembly.

Starting from that point, as far as the splash of water or the place where the water falls for a man of medium height on all sides—that delimited area is here the "water-splash boundary" (udakukkhepasīmā), which is another type of common-residence boundary in rivers and so forth.
"Within that" means within that area delimited by the water-splash. And it is not only within that [specific area].

Regarding the statement that it is not permissible to stand even within one *udakukkhepa* (water-splash) distance from either side, this is because there arises a suspicion of invalidating the formal act (*kamma*) due to the difficulty of discerning the boundary of the *udakukkhepa*. For this very reason, the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* states:
"Even if one stands having left the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*) within the boundary, provided one does not cross beyond another boundary of the same extent outside the boundary..."
"Even while standing [within the boundary], one commits an offense; this is the conclusion in all the Aṭṭhakathās," so it is said.

However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, after stating, "By saying 'standing outside the hand’s reach (hatthapāsa) he commits an offense,' it is meant that he does not commit an offense wherever he may stand, provided he is outside the defined limit," it further rejects even the statement from the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Much has been elaborated [by others] beginning with the statement, “It is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Aṭṭhakathā,” but that is not correct here,
because the word of the Aṭṭhakathā [in this context] is consistent with, corresponds to, and connects with the word of the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā. For indeed,
even a space of only one span and four finger-breadths between two boundaries for splashing water constitutes a *sīmantarika*.
Setting aside the eight [rods], it is said: "Another water-splash must be established as the boundary-mark; more than that is permitted, but less is not permitted.

Thus, by this statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* spoken right here, it is stated that if one establishes a boundary-mark less than the distance of a water-splash according to the measurement of the boundary-mark, there is also a violation of the ritual act (*kammakopa*) due to the overlapping of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*). To the extent that...
And when it has been stated thus, even if only a single bhikkhu enters there, because he would be within the boundary,
it is indeed said that the formal act (kamma) is subverted. Furthermore, the statement in the Commentary,
"But a deficiency is not permitted," was spoken for the purpose of avoiding the suspicion of a breach of the boundary, even by one who finds it difficult to discern the limit of the water-sprinkling.

Because of the statement prescribing the definition of the boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*) as being precisely the extent of the interval between the seven intermediate boundaries (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*), the delimitation of these [boundaries] is difficult to discern;
furthermore, for those standing therein, there arises the suspicion of a disruption of the formal act (*kammakopa*).
It should be understood that the teachers established this very place of potential kammakopa in order to avoid it from afar, stating that it constitutes a "standing point of kammakopa."
“...that boundary. By the phrase “he quickly crosses over,” it is shown that it is permissible to perform [the act] while remaining inside without crossing over;

for it is precisely for this purpose that the boundary is demarcated by sand and so forth, otherwise there would be the suspicion of a failure in the ritual (kammakopa) as to whether or not one has indeed crossed outside. “The proclamation of another” means [the proclamation] of the whole [boundary].
The proclamation for a river-boundary (*nadīsīmā*). "A tree growing within the river" means even a tree standing outside the limit defined by the splashing of the water.

For only the bank outside the river is a place where a boundary cannot be bound, because it is of a different category (*visabhāga*); the interior of the river is not so, because it is of the same category (*sabhāga*) as the support [of the monastery].
For that very reason, it is stated: "or on the bank outside the river, within the monastery boundary," and so forth, indicating that only the bank is a place where a boundary cannot be bound.
This was shown, but it is not a river. “Even when standing by a tree”—this was said with reference to the extent of the splash of water inside [the boundary].
For it is not permitted for monks to stand outside the splash of water.
“Of the tree” means of that very tree which stands within the splash of water. “Or having cleared the boundary” refers to what has been stated above.

In the case of a monastery, the boundary has been fixed; having cleared away the village boundary by means of bringing it within hand’s reach for the monks standing there and establishing a boundary outside of that, and just as those performing an act within a water-sprinkling boundary must clear the area within the water-sprinkling boundary, so too those performing an act within a fixed boundary or a village boundary must do so only after clearing the area within the water-sprinkling boundary.
By this same principle, [the same applies] to the seven-abbhantara forest boundaries as well.
By this method, the fault of connection between these [boundaries] and trees and so forth is also shown by way of inference for the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*).

By this very same method, the fault of connection between the seven-intermediate-space boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*) and both the bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*) and the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), as well as the fault of connection between these and the seven-intermediate-space boundary, should be understood.
However, all of this is [stated] in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
It can be understood according to the method already stated; therefore, only those [boundaries] that are in close proximity to one another are shown here.
In this regard, the following is the introduction to the method for grasping the principles in accordance with the Sutta:

For just as a "formal boundary" (baddhasīmā) that has been authorized within a "defective boundary" (vipattisīmā) cannot have a connection by trees and so forth with those [other boundaries], so too a "formal boundary" authorized over rivers and the like [cannot be connected].
"Even the boundary of misfortune (*vipattisīmā*) does not exist"—by this it is established that its connection with trees and so forth, even together with those [other boundaries], is not permitted.

By this method, one should understand that the connection of trees and so forth with villages, rivers, and the like in the case of the seven-intermediate-space boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), and with forests and the like in the case of the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), is not permitted; thus these were authorized by the Blessed One.

When there is a connection between trees or other objects, a boundary fixed by a seven-fathom water-throw (*sattabbhantara-udakukkhepa-sīmā*)—which is both mutual and independent of its own supporting bases (*nissaya*)—incurs the fault of confusion with the boundaries of one another's supporting bases; this must be understood as the method that accords with the Suttas.
However, at the time of establishing the three types of boundaries, such as the fixed boundary (*baddha-sīmā*), together with their respective supporting bases, such as villages and so forth...

It should be understood that since the "overflowing" (*sambhedajjhottharaṇa*) was permitted by the Blessed One, the connection with trees and so forth is likewise permitted as a corresponding practice.
If this is so, why was a boundary of separation (*sīmantarikā*) not established between the various types of boundaries, such as those defined by the throwing of water (*udakukkhepa*)?

Because they are already distinct by virtue of their difference in support (*nissaya*) and difference in nature (*sabhāva*). Only those things that share a single support and a single nature [can form one boundary].
For this very meaning has been stated: "It indeed causes destruction by means of the intermediate space.

By this alone, it is established that when the Saṅgha performs an act within a boundary fixed with a river as its mark, it is permissible for others to perform an act even within the river, provided the water-throwing boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) extends as far as it touches the village precincts.
As for those boundaries established by worldly convention—such as the boundaries of villages, forests, rivers, oceans, and lakes—[they are not subject to the same rules].
Even when these five are connected to one another through trees and so forth, they do not incur the fault of being conflated, because such worldly convention does not exist.
For people in the world do not say that villages and the like are "conflated" with other villages or with rivers and so forth merely by virtue of their connection to trees and the like.
And regarding things established by worldly convention, their conflation or non-conflation must be understood solely on the basis of worldly convention.
Not from another. For that very reason, no method for the mutual merging of these [boundaries] is shown anywhere in the Commentary;
rather, only that which is established by the terminology of the Dispensation is shown.
Herein, regarding a bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*) first: "Having made the water that supports the earth below the limit, those who have entered the boundary..."
By such passages as "it exists," etc., the delimitation of the lower portion is shown in its entirety in the Aṭṭhakathā; however, the village boundaries and so forth are not shown there.
How, then, is this to be understood? On this point, some say: "The village boundaries and so forth also stand touching the water that supports the earth, just like a bound boundary."

However, some reject that [view] and maintain: "The river, ocean, and lake boundaries, as well as the water-sprinkling boundary dependent upon them, exist only on the upper surface of the earth and in the areas where water overflows below;
they do not extend further down because there is no overflow of water beyond that point.
But if, due to a flood of water or similar causes, there is a low-lying area even a *yojana* in extent..."

It exists; it is only the river-bounds and so forth that exist, not below them. Therefore, a bhikkhu who has entered below rivers and such by way of a tunnel at the outer bank, or by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), does not disturb the formal act (*kamma*) of those standing in the river.
However, he disturbs the formal act of the bhikkhus in a nearby village. But if he is seated in the middle between both banks of the river, [he does not disturb it].

[If] there is [a village], it vitiates the formal act for both the village and the site. However, if the bank is not within the village precincts, it is simply a non-village wilderness (*agāmakārañña*).

In that case, even if there are two banks, for those performing a formal act within a mere minor wilderness boundary (*khuddakāraññasīmā*) without a seven-abbhantara boundary, the formal act is vitiated.
If they perform it within a seven-abbhantara boundary, then, if their seven-abbhantara boundary...
The delimitation of this sitting area extends one *sattabbhantara* beyond it;

within that range, there is no violation of the formal act (*kammakopa*). However, within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), even inside a hollow or a cave where it is possible to enter, or where they might dig for and take gold, gems, and so forth, or where there is the apprehension that such things can be taken—[these are included].
...so much [of the area] below is also village boundary; there, even one sitting inside by means of psychic power (*iddhi*) commits an offense.
However, where there is not even the possibility of ordinary humans entering, all that, up to the water that supports the earth, is forest boundary (*arañña-sīmā*) only, not village boundary.
The same principle applies to the forest boundary as well; for there too, in whatever extent of space—
The forest boundary extends only as far as the upper surface [of the water].
Below that, however, it is not a forest boundary, because there is no conventional designation of "forest" for that area together with the upper surface.
For people do not say of one who has entered what is below that "he has entered the forest. Therefore, one standing there does not invalidate the formal act performed in the forest area above.
It is like one standing on the lower bank of a river [seeing those] standing on the upper bank.

For in a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), with the exception of villages, rivers, oceans, and lakes, everything else—starting from the abodes of non-humans up to the worlds of the gods and the Brahmās—is indeed forest (*arañña*).
Because it is stated, “either from a village or from a forest,” even rivers, oceans, and lakes are considered forest. However, here, regarding rivers and so forth...
Because it is apprehended as a distinct boundary-state, only what remains [after excluding inhabited areas] should be understood as "forest" (*arañña*).
In that regard, whatever extent of space people commonly designate as "a forest," this constitutes a single forest-boundary. For instance, the entire city of Indapura is one forest-boundary;
likewise for the cities of the Asuras, Yakkhas, and so forth. Furthermore, the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the gods and Brahmas situated in the sky are delimited on all sides by space.

Each forest boundary (*araññasīmā*) is like a mountain island in the middle of the ocean. In all such cases, the formal act (*kamma*) must be performed either within a seven-fathom boundary or within the forest boundary itself.
Therefore, here too, since the designation "forest" does not apply to the earth below together with the upper surface of the forest, it should be understood as a separate forest boundary.
For this very reason, there is no discussion here regarding boundaries such as villages or rivers.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, they say: "The method shown for a bound boundary—where it is stated that 'a bhikkhu possessing psychic power, standing on the surface of the earth below, performs the ritual'—is not shown [for the natural boundaries].
And this demonstration of the lower limit for these village boundaries and so forth appears reasonable, as there is no contradiction with the Suttas and other texts.

It should be accepted after investigation. When it is accepted in this way, the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) authorized within the village precinct (*gāmasīmā*) covers the area above the village precinct and below the water limit, including the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*); thus, that forest boundary also becomes part of its field.
Furthermore, by the Blessed One’s statement, “Monks, all rivers are not boundaries,” and so forth, [it is shown that] rivers, oceans, and natural lakes are excluded from the established boundary.
It is described as such by virtue of its being non-arable land (*akhettabhāva*), but not because it is a forest (*arañña*).

Therefore, even a forest must be understood as "arable land" (*khettam*) within the context of a delimited boundary (*baddhasīmā*). If this is so, why is that [boundary] not fixed there? Because there is no purpose for it;

for immediately after the expectation of a [formal] boundary, a seven-fathom boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*) occurs, and because it is compatible with the overlapping and submerging of a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) that is subsequently authorized over it.

It would indeed be the very limit of misfortune. However, even if one has established a boundary by including a portion of a forest that is not a village while standing within a village precinct, and it is thus well-demarcated, it is nonetheless invalidated by the seven-abhantara boundary prescribed by the Blessed One for forest areas that are not villages.
Furthermore, there is no obstacle between those who have entered there to perform a formal act (*kamma*) and those performing it outside of that area in the open forest.
Three *sattabbhantara* intervals must be established; otherwise, there would indeed be a failure [of the boundary].
Therefore, it should be understood that establishing a boundary in a forest devoid of villages is entirely useless.
"A branch that has entered into the river" means even a branch that reaches down to touch the surface of the earth within a river, let alone one that does not.
[It applies] to that which stands without touching [the boundary]. The same principle applies to a sprout as well.

By this, it is shown that even if a branch or the like stands having touched a river-boundary of the same class (*sabhāga*), its connection with a water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) of a different class (*visabhāga*) is not permitted.

By this very [principle], it is also shown that a connection with a *māḷaka*-boundary by means of a branch or the like standing after having touched a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) or a village-boundary (*gāmasīmā*) [is likewise not permitted].
"It is to be understood that it is declared:
'it is not permissible. The inclusion of the word 'bridge' (*setu*) excludes what stands on the bank.

By this, he shows the absence of a breach even when [the bridge] is established in the river outside the boundary of the water's overflow. Therefore, he said: 'established on the outer bank,' and so forth."

For if there were to be a breach [of the boundary] even when one has settled within a river that lies beyond the splash of water, then that too would have to be rejected because it is identical in its subversion of the formal act (*kamma*);
yet it has not been so rejected. Therefore, it should be understood that in all cases there is no fault of breach with respect to the boundary of one’s own supporting base (*nissaya-sīmā*).

“By means of a barrier” (*āvaraṇena*) means by burying wood and so forth to obstruct the water. “By means of a dam” (*koṭṭakabandhanena*) means by constructing a bridge-like embankment filled with clay and the like.
By both [expressions], he demonstrates the very same obstruction. He clarifies the meaning already stated in the phrase “having destroyed the river” by saying “a bank was built below”;
the sense is that a bank was built after obstructing the river from below. “Discarded food” (*chaḍḍitamodaka*)— [End of excerpt]
Regarding "excess water": by the phrase "having overflowed the river from its flowing point," it is shown that this is not permitted in a place situated between a pond and a river.
"Having surged up" means having become extensive by way of breaking through the banks and so forth. "The monastery boundary" (*vihārasīma*) refers to a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*).
"On a path where one cannot return on the same day" means a place where it is impossible to go and return on that very day. It is reckoned as belonging solely to the forest boundary (*araññasīma*).

He speaks with reference to a boundary established by worldly convention that is distinct from a village. "There" means on the small islands that serve as pathways for fishermen in their ordinary course.

"That place" means precisely the location where pits and such have been made, not one where they have not; this is the meaning. "Loṇī" refers to a channel that flows in the form of a watercourse, sloping toward the source of the ocean's tide.
148. "Intermingling" (*sambhindanti*) means: starting from the point where four monks cannot sit, and extending even as little as a hair’s breadth within the boundary, one intermingles.
Starting from the point sufficient for four monks, and including the entire interior, it should be understood that one "overspreads. "Entwined branches" (*saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā*).
"Standing with great branches interwoven": by this, he illustrates their extreme proximity to one another.
For even branches that merely touch branch to branch might be situated at a distance;

therefore, to show that they possess the characteristic of being completely joined together, the term "interwoven" (*viṭapa*) is employed. In this way, there would not be enough space for the monks to sit.
Having established [the new boundary] within the limits of one’s own territory, one who constructs an old monastery is said to "blend the boundaries with the boundary";
it is shown that this does not extend beyond that. "It is bound" is said with reference to the ancient monastery's boundary.
"Amba" refers to a time when, due to the destruction of the old monastery's enclosures and so forth, those who do not know [the original extent]...

The meaning is: having made the mango tree—which serves as a boundary marker for the old boundary—situated within their own boundary, and having designated a rose-apple tree situated within the boundary of the old monastery, they bind [the new boundary] by including within their own boundary that space which lies between the mango and the rose-apple trees.
And here, regarding the mango tree situated in the village which serves as a boundary marker for the old boundary, [within its] interior boundary...

It should be understood that it is stated explicitly that even if branches and leaves from a *jambu* tree are intermingled with those [of another tree], there is no failure at the time of binding the boundary, nor is there a subsequent merging with the village boundary, nor a failure of the ritual (*kamma-vipatti*).

"A place" (*padesa*) means a space sufficient for the Saṅgha to sit down. By the phrase "having set aside the boundary-interval" (*sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvā*), etc., the covering over of the merging [of boundaries] is indicated.
This shows that even a boundary that has been established without mutual contact—having failed to touch one another by means of other boundaries—is indeed no boundary at all.

Therefore, an interval of even a single finger’s breadth between two boundaries is permissible. However, because such an interval is difficult to perceive, it should be understood that in the *Aṭṭhakathās* (Commentaries), an interval of four finger-breadths and so forth is prescribed.
"Of two boundaries" means of two established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*). "The marker" (*nimitta*)...
The intention is that because it is outside the boundary of the *nimitta*, there is no fault of "confusion" (*sambheda*) at the time of the formal act of binding.
Furthermore, it is not only by being the *nimitta* itself that one causes confusion; rather, even another tree standing within the boundary (*sīmantarikā*) does indeed cause it.
Therefore, trees and so forth that grow within a small boundary are not permitted.

Thus it is. And here, since the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) has been demonstrated in all cases regarding the entry into visible trunks, branches, and so forth, it is established that there is no fault even when invisible roots enter, because they belong to the category of earth.
However, if even the roots were to enter while remaining visible, there would indeed be confusion. But mountains and rocks, even though visible, belong exclusively to the category of earth.
However, if at the very time of binding [the boundary] a single large tree stands touching both boundaries, it should be understood that the area bound afterwards is not a valid boundary (*asīmā*).
"Confusion of boundaries" (*sīmāsaṅkara*) means the intermingling of boundaries. As for what was stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "He creates a confusion of boundaries..."
The statement, "It was said because the place where two boundaries meet is difficult to discern when one has entered a boundary area after expanding it," is not correct;
for it must be said that [the expansion] also causes confusion with the village boundary.
For even there, when the markers are expanded, the place where the boundary tied to the village boundary meets is indeed difficult to discern; yet, instead of saying that there, [the author] says...

Since it is stated that there is a "confusion" (*saṅkara*) only between two boundaries that have been formally established, it should be understood that what is expressed by the word "confusion" is precisely the aforementioned fault of being interconnected.
Furthermore, although the Pāḷi states— by way of the introductory narrative— that for those whose boundary was authorized later, "that act is illegal" (*adhammika*),
and thus implies that a later-authorized [boundary] lacks the status of a true boundary, this refers to the case of two village boundaries.
It should be understood that by standing [within the boundary], causing a schism or an overlapping between two Saṅghas,
and either not establishing a *sīmantarikā* (an intermediate space) or not separating the connection of tree-shoots and so forth,
the non-boundary status of even two boundaries that have been formally authorized together at a single moment— by way of completing the formal act (*kammavācā*)— is declared.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the village boundary and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the discussion regarding the breaking of the Uposatha and so forth: 149.

Regarding the phrase "they perform [the ceremony] in an illegal manner with a quorum," this refers specifically to the recitation of the Pātimokkha when four monks are present within a single boundary.

In three cases it is permitted, and in two cases there is only the Uposatha of pure confession (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*). However, because it was not performed in that manner here, it is said to be "unlawfully" (*adhammena*).
Furthermore, because consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*) come to the Saṅgha alone, and not to a group (*gaṇa*) or an individual (*puggala*), it is therefore called "in a faction" (*vagga*).
But if two Saṅghas within a single boundary, having brought their respective *chanda* (consent) to one another, perform separate Saṅgha-kamma at the same moment—how is this to be regarded?
Some say this is permissible, but that should not be accepted because it constitutes a *vagga-kamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly).
For when they perform the *kamma*, their *chanda* and *pārisuddhi* (purification) do not extend elsewhere, as there is no such statement [to the contrary]; they remain separate.
It should be understood that this is because the boundary was authorized specifically for the purpose of performing formal acts separately. However,

it should be seen that even while the Saṅgha exists within the monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā), if for some reason three or two [monks] perform the pure-uposatha (pārisuddhi-uposatha) within the khandha-sīmā,
the formal act is indeed lawful and unanimous, because they belong to a different boundary.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the breaking of the *uposatha* and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Proclaimer of the *Pātimokkha*: 150.
"Thus do I remember this. Regarding the phrase "But this has been heard by the venerable ones," here [the meaning of] "Thus do I remember this" is as follows:
Having said this, one should speak as follows: "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited; the four *pārājika* rules have been heard by you," and so forth.
This is stated in exactly the same way in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*. By the word "heard" (*sute*), it means by the term "heard.

"Fear of forest-dwellers" (*savara-bhaya*) means fear of those who roam the woods. Therefore he said, "fear of forest humans" (*aṭavi-manussa-bhaya*). [This occurs] when the recitation of the introduction (*nidāna-uddesa*) has not yet been concluded.

He said, "The Pātimokkha is not yet recited," referring to the second and subsequent recitations, and so forth. By the three methods means by way of recitation (osāraṇa), exposition (kathana), and formal debate (sarabhañña).
Herein, the recitation of a sutta with the desire to speak its meaning oneself, or with the desire to have it spoken by another, is called "recitation" (osāraṇa).
The elucidation of the meaning of that very sutta is called "exposition" (kathana). Merely...
Reciting by means of the very tone of the text is called *sarabhañña*. "Having resolved upon recitation" means having generated the thought, "I am performing recitation.
"But speaking after having recited" means one who speaks the meaning after having himself uttered the text.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the reciter of the *Pātimokkha* is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Protest against Unlawful Acts (Adhammakamma-paṭikkosanādikathāvaṇṇanā) 155.

"Ninefold" means nine types: three based on the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, and the individual (puggala); three based on the recitation of the Sutta, the declaration of purity (pārisuddhi), and the formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna);
and three based on the quorums for the fourteenth and fifteenth days. "Fourfold" refers to [protests] against unlawful acts that are incomplete in assembly (vagga), and so forth.
It is fourfold. "Twofold" means the two-fold Pātimokkha according to the Pātimokkha for monks and the Pātimokkha for nuns.
"Ninefold" means the ninefold recitation of the Pātimokkha: five for monks and four for nuns.
The explanation of the discussion on the protest against illegal legal acts (*adhammakamma*) and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Permission to Learn the Counting of Fortnights, etc.: 156.
*Katamī* should be understood as being in the feminine gender in reference to the word *tithi* (lunar day).
163. *Utuvasse yeva* means precisely during the winter and summer seasons.
164. Regarding the term "makes known" (*viññāpeti*): here, it should be understood that making known consists precisely in performing a physical gesture after having reflected with the mind.
In the Canon, the phrase "the purity to be given to another" means that it must be given again by the giver of purity in the presence of another monk.
Because it is stated, "or he declares his actual state as a novice," this refers to one who has received full ordination while being less than twenty years of age.

It should be understood that this is shown to mean that for those who have committed an offense involving defeat (*antimavatthu*), or for those who have renounced the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāta*) and so forth, the consent (*chandapārisuddhi*) brought by them remains valid as long as they maintain the profession of being a bhikkhu;
however, from the moment they profess their own status as a novice (*sāmaṇera*) or otherwise, it no longer comes. For in the Pāḷi it is said: "When the *pārisuddhi* has been given..."
Because it is stated: "One who has reached the Saṅgha disrobes... [etc. ...one who is a paṇḍaka claims to be so; one who is an animal claims to be so;

one who is a hermaphrodite claims to be so—the formal purity (pārisuddhi) is brought forth," it is established that even for those such as paṇḍakas, the arrival of *chandapārisuddhi* (consent and purity) is certainly required during the times they are living under the claim of being monks.
Therefore, he said: "This method applies everywhere. [This includes] those who are insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by pain.
However, it should be understood that even if regular members (pakatattā) on the way declare themselves to be insane or otherwise unfit,
consent and so forth from them still arrives merely by their reaching the Saṅgha.
By the phrase "within arm's reach of the bhikkhus," he shows that consent and purification do not arrive among groups or individuals.
"For it is said in the Pāḷi: ‘One who has reached the Saṅgha. Regarding "cat’s-chain purity" (*biḷālasaṅkhalikapārisuddhi*):

this means a purity that is like a chain bound around a cat’s neck; just as the chain comes forward only when the cat comes forward and not when it does not come forward—because it is dependent upon it—so too is this purity. Alternatively, just as the first ring of a chain...
The intention is that it reaches the second cycle, but not the third; this case is also like that.

Furthermore, the mention of the cat here should be understood as a mere illustration. The commentary on the discussion regarding the permission to observe the counting of fortnights and so forth is concluded.
165. Explanation of the Discourse on the Granting of Consent, etc.:
In the Pāḷi, where it should have been said, “There are duties to be performed for the Saṅgha,” the word “duty” (*karaṇīya*) is used through a grammatical inversion. 167.
Regarding the statement, “There is no requirement for him to grant consent”: this refers to a case where, according to the Pāḷi, he remembers [the matter] at that very moment.

Because it has been stated that even if one who was previously absent fails to remember [the agreement] at some point, his non-arrival does not invalidate the *vagga-kamma* (a quorum-deficient formal act), so it is said.
However, some say, "He too must be brought within arm’s reach," but that should not be accepted. 168.
The preliminary task (*pubbakaraṇa*) is to be performed prior to the assembly of the Saṅgha. That which is to be performed during the assembly of the Saṅgha is the preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*).
It must be observed. Regarding the statement in the Pāḷi, "If one does not formally resolve [the robe], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)":

here, there is no offense if it was unintentional or due to forgetfulness. And as it is here, so it is in subsequent cases as well. However, where there is an offense committed without intention, we shall explain that separately.

By the phrase "it has been laid down," even though there is no explicit prohibition such as "one who has an offense should not perform the Uposatha," it is shown that it is indeed "laid down" by the force of the aforementioned Sutta. By this same method—
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a Tathāgata should perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha with an assembly that is not pure”—

from this method of the initial sutta, it should be understood that even performing the Uposatha together with those who are shameless is indeed prohibited, because all training rules are for the purpose of restraining the shameless.
By the phrase “by means of establishing the giving of purity,” [it refers to] one who has committed an offense.
It is thus illuminated that even the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) should not be given. Regarding the phrase "both [commit] a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing)":

here, they say that for one who confesses by the name of the offense alone, without knowing its status as a shared offense (*sabhāgāpatti*), there is a *dukkaṭa* for both the one confessing and the one receiving the confession, even though it is unintentional (*acittaka*).
Just as when the Saṅgha has fallen into a shared offense, having established a motion (*ñatti*), it performs the Uposatha...

He obtains it; likewise, even for those three, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha after establishing a formal motion (*gaṇañatti*) according to the method stated in the passage beginning, "Venerable sirs, let my words be heard: these bhikkhus have fallen into a shared offense," and so forth, and then having announced [the matter] to one another by twos.
However, if a single person with an offense goes far away, he must indeed make amends; if he is unable to reach [his destination], [he must remain there].
“Having found a bhikkhu, we shall perform the atonement,” thinking thus, the Uposatha should be performed; and having performed the atonement, the Uposatha must be performed again.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the giving of consent and so forth is finished. The commentary on the discussion beginning with the fifteen cases of non-offense is finished.
172. "Having gone on some business" means having gone outside the boundary limits to either a village or a wilderness;
this establishes that they indeed established the motion (*ñatti*) as a complete assembly at the time of setting aside the Uposatha motion.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "It has been recited, well-recited," even in all the cases of the fifteen [Uposatha days]. [If] they were a divided assembly...

Regarding the phrase "perceiving them as being in concord" (*samaggasaññino*), and so forth: when the formal motion (*ñatti*) has been concluded, at the moment of saying, "What is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha?
and so on, because monks who were outside have entered the boundary (*sīmā*), the monks are at that moment in a state of division (*vaggā*).

Therefore it was said: "Because they have entered the boundary, they are in a state of division," and so forth. By this, it is also implied that at the moment of reciting the Pārājika offenses and so on, those who perceive [the assembly] as being in division...

For those who are reciting [the Pātimokkha], there is indeed an offense; however, it has already been shown that because the motion (*ñatti*) was completed previously, there is no invalidation of the formal act (*kammakopa*).
This same intention should be understood for all subsequent sections as well.
And here, because it is stated in the Canon: "When everyone has risen... [etc. ...purity (*pārisuddhi*) should be announced in their presence," [the meaning follows].

They say that it is permissible for anyone in an assembly that has gone outside the boundary (bahisīmā) to announce their purity (pārisuddhi) in the presence of anyone [within that assembly], provided they have not made a formal resolution (anadhiṭṭhita).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the fifteen non-offenses (anāpatti-pannarasaka), etc., is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion concerning the demonstration of gender (liṅga), etc.

179. "Unknown" (aññātaka) means one who has not been seen before; thus he says, "belonging to others. "Of others" refers to those whom one has not previously seen. "The state of being of a different affiliation" (nānāsaṃvāsakabhāva) means the state of having a different doctrinal position (laddhi).
180. In the text, "they determine" (abhivitaranti) means they ascertain the absence of common affiliation (samānasaṃvāsakābhāva).

181. "Those performing the Uposatha" refers to those performing the Uposatha for the Saṅgha. For this very reason, it is said, "except by the Saṅgha. [This refers to] from the place where the Saṅgha performs the Uposatha...
Indeed, one who is going [to perform the Uposatha] must go with himself as the fourth;

however, for one going from the place where three monks are seated, it is permissible to go even together with a single monk. In the Pāḷi, the phrase "an āvāsa without monks" is merely an illustration;
for even an āvāsa that has monks—whether a *gaṇa* or an individual—is not [considered such] in relation to the place where the Saṅgha performs the Uposatha.
They say that one must go [to another place] because it is stated, "except with the Saṅgha. "They perform the Uposatha" means either the Saṅgha Uposatha or the Gaṇa Uposatha.
The phrase "in his presence" is said with reference to one going from the location of a Gaṇa Uposatha;
otherwise, it would contradict the statement, "at the very least, with oneself as the fourth."
"By one who dwells in the forest" means by one who wanders alone. "An obstacle to the Uposatha" means an obstacle to one's own Uposatha.

In the text, in phrases such as "in the assembly where a bhikkhunī is seated," the word "bhikkhunī" and so forth are used in the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇatthe*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding the demonstration of gender and so forth is concluded.
The method of commentary on the Uposathakkhandhaka is finished.
3. The Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka: Commentary on the Discussion Beginning with the Permission for Entering the Rains Retreat.
184. "On another day" (*aparasmiṃ divase*) means on the second day, the first of the fortnight (*pāṭipada*). 185.

"Or by causing the dawn to rise elsewhere" means either by going away while having some unfinished business, or by causing the dawn to rise elsewhere after having gone. "Decline" (*parihāni*) refers to the decline of virtuous qualities (*guṇa*). 187.
"A seven-day period of staying together must be observed" (*sattāhaṃ sannivatto kātabbo*) means that one must not spend the entire seven days outside [the monastery].

The time of sunrise, which marks the conclusion of the seven-day period, must again be spent within the monastery for seven days in continuous connection with the monastery. For here, the word "seven days" refers to the time that concludes the seven-day period;
and in relation to that, the term "returning" (*sannivatta*) is expressed in the masculine gender.
"Three things are deficient" refers to the latrines and other such facilities for the bhikkhunīs.
They have been lost because they were rejected.
"It does not perish" means that because others lack proficiency [in them], and because of my own death, they will not be destroyed.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the permission for entering the rains retreat is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Being Sent by Oneself (Pahiteva-anujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 199.
“A man living together with the bhikkhus” indicates one who has no other destination.
“Should go” means that one should go even if not sent for the sake of a business of the Saṅgha. And here, if non-devotees who wish to know the state of the Dispensation send [someone], to them...
It should be understood that even for those who perceive an increase in faith, it is permissible to go on account of a matter requiring seven days.

"The determination regarding the breaking of the night" refers to the determination concerning the breaking of the night—defined as the rising of the dawn outside [the monastery]—after having gone on account of a matter requiring seven days.
"It is permissible to go" means that while still remaining within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), for the purpose of a matter requiring seven days...
Having observed [the boundary] and having gone by means of this sign, it is permissible to go after forming the intention: "I will return within seven days.
Even if one had formed the intention at the previous moment but forgot it at the moment of departure, there is no fault, because it is said: "One who has business departs.
However, they say that for one who goes without forming the intention in any way whatsoever, there is a breach of the rains residence (*vassaccheda*).

However, if one has gone away having made the mental resolve, "I will return within seven days," even though there is no actual business to be done during those seven days, and he returns within the seven-day period, there is indeed an offense for him;
they say that there is no breach of the rains-residence because of his return within the seven days.
