This should be investigated further. "Bhaṇḍaka" means robe-material. To reach [the destination].
"He is not able; it is permissible" means that because he has made an effort to return on that very day, there is neither a breach of the rains-retreat nor an offense;

this is the intended meaning. "The teacher" refers to both the dependence-teacher (*nissayācariya*) and the Dhamma-teacher (*dhammācariya*), let alone the ordination-teacher (*upasampadācariya*) and the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
"He speaks; it is permissible" is said with reference to the absence of an offense after the lapse of seven days, but a breach of the rains-retreat certainly does occur.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the permission for those who have already set out is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Obstacles and Non-offenses Concerning the Interruption of the Rains Retreat (Vassaccheda): 200.
In the text, *gaṇhiṃsu* means they took [it] and ate it. *Paripātiṃsu* means they drove away; the meaning is that they pursued [them].

201. Regarding the rule that "the dawn must be caused to rise on the seventh day": the intended meaning here is that after spending six days outside [the monastery], one should enter within the boundary of the precinct (*upacāra-sīmā*) on the seventh day before sunrise, cause the dawn to rise, and then, having made a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for another seven days, depart on the following day.
However, some say: "Having returned on the seventh day, without causing the dawn to rise..."
If they say, "It is proper to go even during the day on that very same day," that should not be accepted, because it is stated that "the dawn must be made to rise.
For it is with reference specifically to making the dawn rise there on the seventh day that the text says, "A seven-day stay must be observed.
One who goes without making the dawn rise, having not re-entered within but remaining outside, [is considered to have left].
For one who spends seven days [outside], the rains-residence will indeed be interrupted because dawn has been caused to rise outside [the monastery].

Otherwise, the statement "dawn must be caused to rise" would be meaningless, as it would have to be said that "one may depart even without causing dawn to rise after entering the interior of the monastery during the seven-day period. Furthermore, in other instances, it is precisely the causing of dawn to rise [that is required].
It will be stated in the Cīvarakkhandhaka: "While dwelling in one monastery, he causes dawn to rise on the seventh day by means of the other [monastery].
Furthermore, they might say: "On the seventh day, whenever one has entered [the monastery], that very day's dawn—having passed—is what constitutes the past dawn."
Regarding the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, "It is called 'caused to rise' (uṭṭhāpito) with reference to this meaning," that does not even accord with the course of linguistic usage.
For one who enters [the monastery] after the sun has already risen cannot properly be considered its "causer of rising" (*uṭṭhāpaka*).
If it were so, then for one who has entered the rains residence (*vassa*) but has not caused the sun to rise on that day, [should he depart] on that very day for some seven-day business...

Regarding the phrase "even for one who has departed": here, it would contradict the statement "without having caused the dawn to rise," because by that [departure], the dawn belonging to that very day has already been caused to rise.

For even a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who, at the time of evening, goes to a suitable forest location and returns at that very moment, might have caused the dawn to rise and purified his ascetic practice (dhutaṅga); yet this is not so.
This is appropriate because it is stated that the dawn must be caused to rise at the very time of sunrise. For it is said:

"Having set out early, one should cause the dawn to rise at a place where there are those requiring medical treatment. If their affliction increases at the time of the dawn's rising, one should perform their service;
one must not be intent on the purification of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). The same applies to those on probation (pārivāsika) and others.
For those who lay down the formal act (*vatta*) without having caused the dawn to rise, a break in the night is prescribed. For it is said: "It should be laid down when the dawn has risen.

Also, in the training rule regarding sleeping together (*sahaseyyasikkhāpada*), the phrase "having gone out before the dawn" and so forth was stated for the purpose of avoiding the state of having slept together with those not fully ordained.
Thus, in all cases such as being separated from one's robe (*cīvaravippavāsa*), [the limit is] at the end of the night.
The appearance of dawn is shown by way of the *āgāmi-aruṇa* (the dawn yet to come), not by way of the *atīta-aruṇa* (the dawn already passed).
Therefore, the appearance of dawn here should be understood according to the method already stated, for otherwise there would be a breach of the rains residence (*vassa*).
As for the statement regarding one who has entered the rains residence departing on that very day because of some business without having caused the dawn to appear— [End of excerpt]
From the time of entering that rainy season residence, it is appropriate to go at any time provided there is a valid reason, as going is permitted whenever such a cause exists;
however, for one who has gone on a seven-day visit, departing on that very day without waiting for dawn is not proper, precisely because it is stated that "dawn must be awaited.
Or, as it is said: "If there is business to be done before the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has arrived after seven days..."
"Whether he departs, or whether that monk, O monks, should return to that residence, or should not return"— thus,
although it is permitted for him not to return during the final week, it is not allowed during other weeks. Likewise,
although it is permitted to depart without waiting for dawn during the first week, if he returns after that, he must wait for dawn [before departing again].
It must be concluded here that traveling [for this purpose] is not permitted. "Brought here" means brought to a place outside the monastery.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the absence of an offense due to obstacles and the interruption of the rains-residence is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion regarding entering the rains-residence in places such as Vaja.

203. "It is not permissible to enter" means that it is not permissible to enter by making a verbal declaration such as, "I enter the rains residence here," in the absence of a hut or similar structure.
204. In the text, *pisācillikā* refers to young *pisāca* spirits. "Having fitted a door for entry" means having made a door with a bolt.
"Having cut down a tree" means having cut off the upper portion of the hollow space. "At the top of the stump" (*khāṇumatthake*)...
At the top of a hollowed-out tree trunk, a "stilt bed" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*) is made by boring holes in the long legs of a bed and inserting cross-pieces;
even when arranged one above the other, it remains similar to the previous type. They place such a bed in cemeteries and at shrines for deities.
A house built by spreading stone slabs over four stones is also called a "stilt bed."
The commentary on the account of the approaching of Vajjī and others is finished.
Commentary on the Account of Unrighteous Agreements, etc. (205):

"In the Mahāvibhaṅga" refers to the commentary on the fourth Pārājika. Furthermore, an unrighteous agreement regarding conduct (*adhammika-katikavatta*) will indeed be revealed later in the Senāsanakkhandhaka.

207. Because for one who enters the rains residence in two dwellings within different boundaries, the first taking of a lodging ceases the very moment he steps out from the precincts with the thought, "I will stay in the second," it is therefore with reference to this first taking of a lodging that the text says:
"For that monk, monks, neither the earlier period is recognized... and so forth.

This has been stated. However, regarding the second distribution of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*), the first period (*purimikā*) is indeed recognized; one who dwells there for three months is considered to have completed the first rains-residence (*purimavassa*).
But it should be understood that if, from the second day onwards, one exceeds the precincts with the intention, "I will dwell in the first lodging," even the first period is no longer recognized.

208. Since it is stated in the Pāḷi, “If he departs on some business seven days before the Pavāraṇā,” it should be understood that even on the day of the Pavāraṇā itself, it is not permissible to go without a seven-day purpose.
Regarding the phrase *komudiyā cātumāsiniyā*: this refers to the full moon of the latter Kattika month.
It is called *komudī* because of the presence of water lilies (*kumuda*) at that time; it is so named also because it marks the conclusion of the four months of the rainy season.
And it is called the "four-monthly" [observance].
The commentary on the discussion concerning illegal agreements and so forth is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Chapter on the Entrance for the Rains Retreat is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Invitation (Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka):
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Uncomfortable Dwellings, etc. 209.
In the Pāḷi of the Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka, regarding the phrase "he should return from alms," it means that having wandered for alms, he should return.
*Avakkārapāti*: a single bowl for setting aside extra alms-food. *Avisayha*: incapable of being lifted up.
*Vilaṅghana* is lifting up; that itself is *vilaṅghaka*. "By one who lifts with the hands" (*hatthavilaṅghaka*) means by one who lifts with the hands;
thus he said, "by one who lifts with the hands. Alternatively, it may also mean "by the hand that is a lifter, that is, a *vilaṅghaka*."
The meaning is that their hands are interlaced with one another; this is what is meant by "with hands intertwined.
213. "But if he is senior" means that the monk offering the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is senior.
For it is said, "In this way, he has invited on his behalf"; here, even though he himself has not invited, [the act is valid] simply by virtue of his having reached the Saṅgha.

It should be understood that the formal act of the Saṅgha’s invitation (*saṅghapavāraṇākamma*) is indeed a formal act performed by a complete assembly (*samaggakamma*). And "by that bhikkhu" refers to the bhikkhu who is the giver of the invitation.

234. "Even many [bhikkhus] of the same seniority may invite together": the meaning is that all those who have attained full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the same year—that is, those of equal seniority—may invite together.

237. In the Canon, "wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) refers to views proceeding by way of such statements as "there is no gift," and so forth. "Extreme views" (*antaggāhikā*) refers to [views] consisting of eternalism and annihilationism.

"Grasping at the internal. In passages such as "That which you... and so forth, one should supply the word *taṃ* (that) and connect it thus: "The invitation (*pavāraṇā*) that you suspended, you suspended on account of what was seen.
239. "Exposing the basis": this refers merely to the factual matter (*vatthu*) which serves as the cause for the arising of suspicion regarding a person.
This was said with a specific intention. However, as for the basis with which he said, "A person is discerned, but not the basis," this was not said with reference to that.

For if, in the dwelling place of that bhikkhu, one were to see the catching of fish from a lotus pond and so forth, then it would have to be said, "Both the basis and the person are discerned. Therefore, he said: "In the same manner as before..."

“Throw it away,” and so forth. It should be understood that this was said because, upon seeing both the scent of garlands and the scent of decay in the body of a bhikkhu, one perceives both the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the person (*puggala*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding the lack of comfort in dwelling is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Basis for Causing Quarrels (240).
"There are two fourteenth-day [uposatha days]" means that in the third fortnight, there are two fourteenth-day observances together with the fourteenth day itself.
[The thought arises: "These quarrelsome ones will perform the invitation ceremony on the fifteenth day, even though it is the thirteenth or fourteenth."
This shows that the designations "fourteenth" and "fifteenth" for monks are used starting from their respective days of observing the Uposatha,
and not according to the lunar phases established by the movement of the moon. Nevertheless, even though it is said here, "Monks,
I allow you to follow the kings," those who follow the worldly lunar dates may also [follow them] for themselves.
One must follow the sequence of the Uposatha by performing it on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, or on the fifteenth or the fourteenth day;
however, one must not perform the Uposatha day on the sixteenth or the thirteenth day. For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi:
"Two or three Uposathas may be performed on the fourteenth day. Otherwise, [they would have to be performed] on the twelfth or the thirteenth day.

It should be understood that because it must be said, "The Uposatha is to be performed," the statement beginning with "Once in the fortnight, on the fourteenth or the fifteenth" is also spoken according to the sequence of observance (*upavuttha*), and not according to the sequence of lunar dates (*tithi*).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the basis for creating strife is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Invitation-Retention (Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathāvaṇṇanā) 241.

By the statement, "But having performed the invitation ceremony, they may set out on a journey even in the interim," it is shown that when the invitation has been retained, those who wish to depart in the interim may have the Saṅgha convened and perform the invitation ceremony.
The commentary on the discussion of the invitation-retention is finished.
The method of commentary on the *Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka* is finished.
5. The *Camma-kkhandhaka*:
Commentary on the Discourse concerning Soṇa Koḷivisa and others.
242. Regarding the section on hides (*cammakkhandhaka*): "A woolen cloak" (*uṇṇapāvāraṇa*) refers to a woolen cloak made by having the hair removed from both sides;
there is also a *vīta-pāvāra* (woven cloak) made by having cotton-wool removed from both sides, and it is called "woolen cloak" specifically to exclude that.

"In the half-moon stone" (*aḍḍhacandapāsāṇe*) refers to a stone placed at the base of a staircase with half of it inserted inside. In the text, "in the shadow of the monastery" (*vihārapacchāyāya*) means in the shade at the edge of the monastery; some also say it means "while the shadow of the monastery is lengthening."
243. *Bhogā* is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. *Accāyatā* means excessively long, [meaning] played with a harsh touch.
*Saravatī* means endowed with a sweet tone. *Atisithilā* means played with a slack touch. *Vīriyasamathaṃ* means serenity associated with energy.
And regarding the instruction "take the sign therein," when that state of balance exists, one should take the sign just as one takes the reflection of a face in a mirror.

"A sign arises; take up and produce that sign of serenity, the sign of insight, the sign of the path, and the sign of the fruit"—thus was the meditation subject explained to him, culminating in Arahantship.
(244) "Six points" means six reasons. "Inclined" means established after having penetrated [the truth]. "Inclined toward renunciation," and so forth.
All this is stated with reference to Arahantship. For Arahantship is called "renunciation" (nekkhamma) because it has emerged from all defilements;
it is "seclusion" (paviveka) because it is secluded from those very same things; it is "non-affliction" (abyāpajja) because of the absence of affliction;

it is the "destruction of clinging" (upādānakkhaya) because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging; it is the "destruction of craving" (taṇhakkhaya) because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving; and it is called "non-delusion" (asammoha) because of the absence of delusion.
"Merely faith alone" means merely faith that is unmixed with the wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*).

"Accumulation" means increase through repeated performance. "Because of being free from lust" means that, precisely because lust has departed through the penetration of the Path, he stands having penetrated and realized the state of worthiness (*arahatta*) known as renunciation (*nekkhamma*). The same applies to the remaining phrases.
This is the method. "Devoted to seclusion" (*pavivekādhimutta*) means that he declares his attainment of *arahantship* by saying, "I am devoted to seclusion.

"Adherence to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) refers merely to the grasping of what has been seized through the adherence to precepts and vows. "Returning [to it] as the essence" (*sārato paccāgacchanto*) means knowing it as having the nature of the essence. "Devoted to non-affliction" (*abyāpajjādhimutta*) means he declares his attainment of *arahantship*, which is non-affliction.

"Unmixed" (*amissīkata*) means unmixed. For the defilements (*kilesa*) mix the mind with its object; because of their absence, it is unmixed. "A violent wind and rain" (*bhusā vātavuṭṭhī*) means a powerful mass of wind.

"And of the destruction of clinging": here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Having seen the arising of the sense-bases" means having seen both the arising and the passing away of the sense-bases, such as the eye and so forth.
"The mind is liberated": by means of this practice of insight, the mind is liberated through the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
The commentary on the story of Soṇa Koḷivisa is concluded.
**Commentary on the Discussion Prohibiting Shoes with Double Layers, etc.** 245.

*Sakaṭavāhe*: This refers to a transport [of goods] delimited by two carts. Regarding the word “vāhe” (carts), although it is a plural form, it is rendered in the singular as “hiraññaṃ” (gold) because it is being looked toward as a general term, even though it qualifies a specific kind of gold.
246. *Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā*: This means having the color of a fresh ariṭṭha fruit; some also say it has the color of a wet crow’s wing.
“Dyed” is said with reference to colors such as blue and so forth that have been applied [as a stain]. Therefore he said, “having wiped it with a cloth.

For when it has been wiped in that manner, that [stain] disappears. However, as for the color—black, red, and so forth—that arises because the hide was dyed with black, red, and other dyes for the purpose of removing its foul odor, that cannot be removed by cloths and the like; it remains inherent to the hide itself.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is permissible.
"A heel-cover" refers to the leather covering for the entire heel; it is permissible merely to attach and fasten it over the upper part of the heel so as not to slip off.
"Variegated" refers to variegated cloths in terms of their shape, not in terms of color, among those things which must be entirely removed.
Because they enter into holes and such places, and because their faces resemble those of cats, great owls are called "bird-cats" (*pakkhibiḷālā*);
their skin is indeed nothing other than the feathers of birds.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the prohibition of sandals with double layers and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Sandals within the Monastery (Ajjhārāme upāhana-paṭikkhepa-kathā-vaṇṇanā):
251. "Sandals made of wool" (*uṇṇāhi katapādukā*): here, sandals made from woolen blankets (*uṇṇāmaya-kambala*) are included.

253. "At the festival of the Ganges" (*gaṅgā-maha-kīḷikāya*): [this means] at the festival of the Ganges (*gaṅgā-maha*), during the festivities. For there, men and women engage in water-sports in vehicles.
They go. A *pīṭhaka-sivika* is a sedan-chair made of wood planks and the like. A *paṭapotalika* is a swing-cot.
All such vehicles are permitted for one who is ill and unable to travel even on foot with sandals.
254. "Forms of beasts" refers to artificial representations of beasts. "Exceeding four finger-breadths" refers to those [furs] with hair on both sides or hair on one side.
This refers to the specific distinction [of size]. For it is said that items smaller than four finger-breadths are permitted for things such as *uddalomi* (wool with the nap upward) and so forth.

A "variegated woolen rug" (*vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo*) is a patterned woolen spread woven from multicolored woolen threads by means of techniques such as wall-cutting (*bhitticcheda*). A "dense flower-pattern" (*ghanapupphako*) is one with thick dye.
A "natural cotton mattress" (*pakatitūlikā*) is a cushion filled with cotton (*tūla*). A "variation" (*vikati*) refers to those variegated by weaving in the forms of lions and so forth.
It is taken up. Regarding *uddalomi*: it is stated in the *Dīgha-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā* that this is "a woolen spread with designs on both sides.
Regarding *koseyyakaṭṭissamaya*: this is woven by inserting golden threads between silk threads.
Indeed, the golden thread is called *kaṭṭissa* or *kasaṭa*. For this very reason, it is described as "made of silk and *kasaṭa*."
They say it was spoken by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. "Inlaid with jewels" means coated with gold.
"Pure silk" means devoid of such jewel inlay.
Because the skins of the *ajina* deer are exceedingly fine, they are sewn together after making double layers; thus it is called "the *ajina* seam."
"By a red canopy" means by a canopy that is entirely red. However, that which is multicolored, whether it be a woven painting (*vānacitta*) or a plaster painting (*lepacitta*), is permissible.
The same principle applies to "red footstools on both sides.

As for the phrase "or variegated," this is stated because it is allowable in every respect, and not because it is unallowable in the case of footstools with two supports; for the word "red" does not apply to what is variegated.
It is permissible [to use a canopy], because by the very inclusion of the "curtain" (*paṭaliggahaṇa*), it follows that even a painted rug is included among those things to be accepted;
however, the yellow robe (*kāsāva*) does not receive the designation "red. Therefore, it is permissible even for a canopy or for a pillow with two pads.
The phrase "if it is of the proper measure," etc., is stated for the purpose of showing that a bolster exceeding other measures is prohibited, but it is not...
This is because it was not stated in that manner for the purpose of showing the nature of high and luxurious beds. However, that pillow is permitted for laypeople observing the Uposatha.
For at that time, only high and luxurious beds were forbidden to them. Although in the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* and other texts it is said:
"With the exception of the cotton-down mattress, all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka*, even if sewn with jewels, are permitted," and so forth...
It has been stated that only the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary on the Vinaya) is to be accepted as the authority regarding what is permissible and what is impermissible.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the prohibition of sandals within a monastery is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion concerning the permission for householders' requisites and so forth.
256. *Abhinissāya* means relying upon. *Visukāyika-vipphanditānaṃ* means of the fluctuations of views and mind that have become adversaries; this is the meaning. 257.
*Yatindriyaṃ* means having the faculties restrained by way of the mind-faculty (*manindriya*). 258.
In the Canon, the *Aṭṭhakavagga* refers to the sixteen discourses (*sutta*) constituting the Aṭṭhakavagga within the Sutta Nipāta. Thus...
"‘He practiced for a long time’ means: for what reason did he dwell in the midst of the household life for so long a period without entering the going-forth?
It is said that he went forth in middle age; therefore the Blessed One spoke thus. ‘Having understood this matter’ means:
having understood in every aspect this matter—that people, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, nevertheless leap forward toward the household life even after delaying for a long time."

"In the world" means in the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*); "danger" refers to the danger of impermanence and so forth. "Without substrate" (*nirupadhi*) means Nibbāna. Regarding the statement, "The Noble One does not delight in evil," he states the reason for it: "The pure one does not delight in evil. In this context, "pure" (*sucī*) refers to a person who is purified.

259. "Kāḷasīha" is a species of black-faced monkey. "The hide is not permitted" means it is not permitted to use it as a sitting mat or a rug; however, its use as bedding, such as a floor-covering, is indeed permitted. The commentary on the discussion concerning the permission for householders' goods and so forth is concluded.
The method of commentary on the Camma-kkhandhaka is finished.
6. The Bhesajja-kkhandhaka: Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Medicines, etc.

260. In the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, "bile has entered the interior of the stomach" means that the unbound bile (*abaddhapitta*), which had remained pervading the exterior of the body, has entered the interior of the stomach; the intention is that by this, the bile becomes agitated. 261–2.
In the text, "not pleasing" means not producing a relish for it. "Susukā" is a species of fish in the ocean; they also call it a *kumbhila*. "Mixed together" means strained.

263. *Piṭṭhehi* means with flour. *Kasāvehi* means with the dregs obtained by heating hides and other materials in water. *Ubbhidaṃ* means made of saline soil. *Loṇabilaṃ* is a specific kind of salt. 264–5. *Chakaṇaṃ* means cow dung.
*Pākatika-cuṇṇaṃ* means uncooked powder of astringent substances; however, scented powder is not permitted.
In the text, *cuṇṇacālini* refers to a sieve for straining the powder ground in a mortar. *Suvaṇṇageruka* means golden ochre.
Gold, tin, and so forth. In the Pāḷi, "ointment for rubbing" (*añjanūpapisana*) refers to the medicinal substance that must be ground in order to apply it as an ointment. 267–9.

"Pills" (*kabaḷikā*) refers to medicinal substances used for fumigation (*upanāha*). A "disease caused by what was given by the housewife" (*gharadinnakābādha*) is a disease arising from a subjugating medicine (*vasīkaraṇa-bhesajja*) administered by the housewife.
"Alkali-water trickling from those ashes" refers to water in which wood-ash has been placed in a strainer and then poured into water.
Then, after the consecration, there was alkaline water that had dripped down from beneath the ashes. In the text, "unprepared bean soup" (*akaṭayūsa*) refers to unsynthesized bean soup.
Regarding "boiled-down" (*kaṭākaṭa*), they say it is bean soup made by boiling beans and straining them without stirring.
The commentary on the discussion of the five medicines and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Story of the Permission for Sugar (Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 272–4. “Making sugar” means a sugarcane plantation. “Without confidence” means with apprehension. 276.

“They refuse even when [only] a little is offered” means that they reject it because there would be an imposition upon the donors if even a small amount were given. “Even after reflecting” means that they reject it even after considering, “One can subsist with just this much; let the remainder belong to others.”

279. *Vatthipīḷana* (pressing the bladder) means massaging the bladder with the hand so that oil or other substances contained within it rise up into the body. Since surgical procedures and bladder-treatment (*vatthikamma*) are specifically prohibited for the narrow [rectal] passage, cauterization (*dahanakamma*) is indeed permitted there.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the allowance of sugar and other such items is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion regarding rice-gruel, honey-syrup, and balls of food.
282–3. In the original text (*pāḷi*), "ten grounds for this recipient" means that there are ten grounds or reasons for him according to the Dhamma.
"He bestows upon" means he gives. The connection is "he dispels the wind," which means he makes it favorable.
"The heavens have been won by you" means that the celestial worlds have been attained by you.
The commentary on the story of the rice-gruel, honey-syrup, and other offerings is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Site of Pāṭaligāma: 286.
"They were building a city at Pāṭaligāma" means that near Pāṭaligāma, on a large tract of land belonging to the domain of that very village...
"In a certain forest region they are building a city named Pāṭaliputta. "As far as the noble domain" means as far as the place where noble persons resort.
"As far as the marketplace" means as far as the place where merchants sell their goods or where they reside;
the meaning is that this will become the preeminent city for all of them. "Puṭabhedana" means...
It is a place where bundles of goods brought from various regions by carts and other means are unloaded for the purpose of sale. The term *sara* also applies to ponds and the like;
to exclude those, it is stated: "here, by *sara*, a river is intended," because it is derived from the sense of "flowing" (*sarati*) or "streaming.
"They have crossed without even a raft" means they have reached the further shore without touching even a small amount of water and without using a raft.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Foundation of Pāṭaligāma is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths at Koṭigāma: 287.
In the text, "wandered through" (*sandhāvita*) means that wandering was performed by way of taking rebirth-linking from one existence to another.

"Saṃsarita" is a synonym for that very same thing. "Mamañceva tumhākañca" means "by me and by you," or the meaning should be understood as "there was a running about belonging to both me and you," using the possessive sense. "Saṃsarita" means "wandered.
Because craving for existence itself leads from one existence to another existence, it is called "bhavanetti" (the guide to existence).
289. To explain the meaning already stated as "they were blue," it was said, "blue-colored," and so forth.
"Blue-colored" means having blue ointment. This same method applies everywhere. "Paṭivaṭṭesi" means she struck. "Ambakāya" means "to the woman";
for this is a term of address, meaning "to the female. "Upasaṃharatha" means "bring them," or "imagine that such-and-such are the Tāvatiṃsa gods."
This is the meaning. And this was spoken for the purpose of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the bhikkhus, not for the purpose of grasping after signs (*nimittaggāha*).
For all the Licchavi kings will before long meet their destruction at the hands of Ajātasattu.
The commentary on the Discourse on Truth at Koṭigāma is finished.
Commentary on the Story of Sīhasenāpati, etc., [Section] 290.
"In the council hall" (*sandhāgāre*) means in the great assembly (*mahāsabhā*) constructed for the purpose of deliberating matters of state by making it free from gaps.

"The volitional formation of going" (*gamikābhisaṅkhāro*) means the exertion (*vāyāma*) involved in departing. "And the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammassa ca anudhamman*) refers to the reason stated by you.
"Anukāraṇaṃ" means that it is exactly in accordance with the meaning stated by you; this is the intended sense.
"Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo" means that your argument, being supported by reasons, is either your own statement or a subsequent rejoinder to what has been said by others.
"Not even the slightest point comes to a ground for censure" means: is there no ground for censure in your argument? This is what is being asked.
293. "Anuviccakāraṃ" means having understood the true nature [of the Triple Gem]. One performs such acts as going for refuge to the Triple Gem.
The meaning is: "Do not act impulsively and later come to regret it.
"They should carry a banner" means they wander about proclaiming in the city, "Such a person has become our disciple who has gone for refuge," while raising a victory banner.
294. "Of the action based on a sign" means of the action of taking life that has arisen by means of the sign of eating meat.
The commentary on the story beginning with the account of the General Siha is finished.
Commentary on the discourse authorizing the use of a kitchen (kappiyabhūmi).
"Anuppage eva" means "at dawn. "Oravasaddaṃ" means a loud sound. By the word "api" (even), he permits that statement even without mentioning it [specifically].
"In the Aṭṭhakathās" refers to the remaining commentaries excluding the Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā.
"Common characteristic" means common to all the commentaries together with the Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā.
They exceed the limit for the height of the foundation. "From which point" means from which starting point, such as the bricks, they intend to erect the wall;

this is the meaning. By the statement, "But pillars may rise upwards, therefore they are permissible," it is shown that even if bricks or stones are laid down below, if [the structure] exceeds by even a single finger's breadth from the layering or from the ground...
It is established that they stand tall and turn around.
"Garden" (*ārāma*) refers to the entire monastery as delimited by the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"Dwellings" (*senāsanāni*) refers to the residences of the Saṅgha within the monastery, such as grass huts and so forth. "Vihāra-gonisādikā" means "dwellings-gonisādikā. For the dwellings—
Even those that are surrounded are called "cow-pen-like" (*gonisādika*) because they lack a formal enclosure for the monastery.

By the phrase "even half-surrounded," it is shown that what is surrounded by less than that—namely, that which is mostly unenclosed—falls under the category of "unenclosed"; therefore, it is reckoned as such.
"In this case" refers to that which is half-surrounded and so forth. It is permissible to obtain a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a storehouse for allowable goods).
The meaning is that, in the absence of a *goṇisādiya* (a place for storing fodder), any one of the three remaining types of *kappiyakuṭi* (permissible huts) may be constructed.
Regarding the phrase "their houses," it should be understood that even if a house has been built for the residence of monks, it remains the property of those [laypeople] until they hand it over.
"Excluding the vihāra" means excluding a house built for the residence of those who are fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
The meaning is as follows: "House" (*geha*) refers to a dwelling-house; however, all other places such as an Uposatha hall and so forth are non-dwelling-houses.
The fifth type of allowable place (*kappiya-bhūmi*), excluding the four types of allowable grounds, is [the house].

For even in such a house belonging to the Sangha, provided it is well-enclosed and of a size suitable for a grove, there is no fault of being "dwelt within" (*antovuttha*) and so forth, just as in an open space (*abbhokāsa*). It must be covered by some means and enclosed, and capable of accommodating a shared bed.
The fault of living indoors applies to the dwelling place of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, not elsewhere. Therefore he said, "But whatever," and so forth.
In that context, although the phrase "whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual" is stated generally for bhikkhunīs, it should be understood as follows:
for bhikkhus, there is what belongs to the Saṅgha and what belongs to an individual; for bhikkhunīs, there is likewise what belongs to the Saṅgha and what belongs to an individual.
It should be understood that it stands in a place belonging to householders for the monks.

"In the vicinity of the mouth" means that because the fault lies in what is stored inside, one incurs an offense for the purpose of putting it into the mouth, and not otherwise; therefore, it is called "in the vicinity of the mouth.
"They become broken here and there" means they are broken into pieces larger than half. "When the entire roof has perished" [is the condition].
When the roof-covering consisting of grass, leaves, and so forth—which protects against rain—is destroyed;

even though the rafters remain fixed upon poles bound with creepers above them, they are indeed deprived of their foundation. "The circle of wing-ends" refers to the covering of grass, leaves, and so forth situated above three rafters on one side.

By the statement, "It should be given to one who is not fully ordained," and so forth, it is shown that even if [food] has been kept in an unallowable storehouse (*akappiyakuṭi*), it becomes allowable when given to one who is not fully ordained; furthermore, it shows that in this case, giving with expectation is permitted, as it does not constitute [the offense of] receiving.
299. In the Canon, "he encountered [it] in the wilderness" means he arrived at a wilderness where food was scarce.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the allowable place (*kappiyabhūmi*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Story of the Hair-Wearer Keṇiya (Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā):
300. "Jaṭila" means a brahmin who wears artificially made matted hair, assumes the guise of an ascetic, is engaged in sacrifices, and is honored by the world.
"Reciters" (pavattāro) means those who speak according to their own scriptures; the meaning is "those to whom this belongs" or "by whom this was sung."
"Gītaṃ," "pavuttaṃ," and "samihitaṃ" are synonyms for one another; the meaning is that it has been "spoken.
"Tadanugāyantī" means they sing along with that which was previously sung by them. The same applies to the remaining terms.
"Yāvakālikapakkānaṃ" is said with reference to cooked food; however, raw [food] may be crushed in cold water by those who are not ordained.

A drink given after having been strained is indeed permissible even after the meal. And because this point was not stated explicitly in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, he said, "But in the *Kuruṇḍī*," and so forth.

"Sugar-cane juice that is free from sediment"—this was stated in the discussion on what may be consumed during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) by virtue of its general nature as something to be drunk;
however, it should be understood that this [specific case] is actually something to be kept for seven days (*sattāhakālika*). These are the four juices.
There are four [types of] fruit, leaf, flower, and juice.

In the Pāḷi, "the fire-sacrifice is the mouth" means it is preceded by the offering of fire. "Chandas" refers to the Veda. "The Sāvittī is the mouth, to be recited first"—this is the meaning. "Tapatam" means of those that are shining.
The commentary on the story concerning the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Foundation of Roja Malla and Others (301).
"Having shown great respect for the Buddha" means having performed acts of high esteem toward the Buddha.

The remainder of the sentence is: "I, venerable Ānanda, was indeed driven by the fear of punishment from my kinsmen. For this being the case, the word "I" is mentioned again in the phrase "thus I [spoke]."
It is appropriate. "He opened" means he opened by the mere thought, "Let it open," not by rising and opening it with his hand.
303. "A certain one" refers to Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age. "Two boys" refers to two sons who were established on the level of novice monks (sāmaṇera).
"With a nāḷi-measure and a bag" means with both a nāḷi-measure and a carrying-bag. "Gather the rice and so forth with these vessels."
"Saṅkaḍḍhatha" means "gather together. "Bhusāgāre" means in a house made of straw; it refers to a house constructed by gathering straw from within a heap of straw—this is the meaning.
The commentary on the account concerning the case of Rojamalla and others is finished.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā) 305. "Rubbing" means examining. The two cloths are mentioned by way of their names; this is a phrase intended to show their actual form, not a phrase for the purpose of excluding others, since even cotton cloth is mentioned by way of its name.

"Tumba" means vessels. A "fruit-tumba" refers to things such as gourds. An "udaka-tumba" is a water-jar. A "kilañja-umbrella" is an umbrella made by weaving bamboo and reeds. "Mixed flavor" means a flavor that has become blended together.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is finished.
7. The Chapter on the Kathina.

Commentary on the Discourse Authorizing the Kathina (Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 306. In the Kathina Khandhaka, "by way of the head" means by way of the primary [benefit]. "Kathina" means firm because it is capable of encompassing the five benefits;
thus, since "it will belong to them" is appropriate, he says "it is theirs" rather than saying "it is yours."
The statement is appropriate. "Those for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread" means not only you, but also others for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread;

the meaning is that it will belong to them. Alternatively, "to you" (*vo*) is said by combining all the monks together—both those present and those absent or yet to arrive—at that time; thus, the meaning is "to you. "It shall be theirs" (*so nesam*).

In this context, it should be connected with the words "these [privileges] belong to them. Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, these five [privileges] shall be allowable for you who have performed the kaṭhina ceremony. "The robe of one who has died" means the robe belonging to one who is dead.

Regarding the phrase "by way of having completed the rains," he said, "Having entered the earlier rains residence and having performed the first invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā), they receive [it]," because this applies in common even to those who have completed the later rains residence.
The phrase "or having arrived, they do not obtain [it]" is stated with reference even to one who has completed the rains-residence during the later period (*pacchimikā*).

"A garment smeared with grain-parchment" is stated with reference to unwashed cloth. By the words "it is not permitted not to do so," it is indicated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when there is disrespect.
"Having informed" is an instruction on the procedure to be performed by those who wish to give [the robe] without first giving it to other monks who have completed the rains-residence.
If it is asked, "In that case, has the gift not been stated by the formal act (kammavācā) itself? he says, "But the formal act... and so forth.
The intention is that, unlike the kathina robe, it is not permitted to give [the robe] by means of a formal act;
rather, it should be given after having obtained permission (apaloketvā). 308. "Mahābhūmika" means having a great range; because it possesses twenty-four modes, it is said to be "of great extension."
It exists. "Fivefold" means consisting of five pieces. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
"The first *cimilika*" refers to one's own original *cimilika* (lining) other than the cloth for the Kathina ceremony.

Regarding the phrase "merely by sewing after making a *kucchicimilika*," they say this is a designation for sewing together old and worn-out *cimilikas*. This is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*.

"Spoken word" refers to the vision [of the Dhamma]; they say it was composed for the purpose of showing that there is a distinction only in the phrasing (*byañjana*), and not in the meaning (*attha*).
"By the mere application of the wind along the back" means by the mere application of the wind along its length.
"By the mere application of the wind into the belly" means by the mere application of the wind across its width. "By what is relinquished at night" means by what has exceeded the night.
309. *Hatavatthakasāṭaka* means an extremely worn-out cloth. Regarding the phrase "not by that" (*na hi tena*) and so forth:

the intention is that by not bringing here and reciting that passage which was included in the *Parivāra*, nothing is omitted among the things to be known concerning the formal act of spreading the Kathina;
for all of that has been stated right here.

310. In the phrase *mātā viyā*, the suffix *-ka* should be understood in the sense of "like" (*iva*). Demonstrating the meaning thus established, he says: "*Mātikā* means 'mothers' (*mātaro*)" and so forth.

Regarding the word *assā*: it refers to this *mātikā*. For it is precisely the suspension of the *kaṭhina* robe (*kathinubbhāra*) at the end of the journey that arises of its own accord; thus, by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedūpacāra*), it is called "*mātikā*" as a designation for that very suspension.

Because it arises at the moment of departing (*pakkamanta*), and because there is no matrix (*mātikā*) apart from that [moment], it is appropriate to call even the text that elucidates it a "matrix" (*mātikā*). For that too is called "departing-matrix" (*pakkamanantikā*) by way of elucidating the burden of departing.
This same method applies to the remaining burdens as well. And here, "departing" should be understood as the crossing of the boundary of the vicinity (*upacārasīmā*).
The commentary on the discourse concerning the authorization of the *kathina* robe is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Things Concerning Taking Up [the Robe]: 311.
“He will not return again”—this is a demonstration of the reason for severing the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*). For among the five...

If they do not intend to return at any time during the robe season, the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) is severed by the mental act of crossing the boundary of the precinct (*upacāra-sīmā*).
However, if they intend to return, but have gone outside the precinct and do not intend to return no matter where they may be, it is severed as soon as the thought arises.
First, the impediment of the robes (*cīvara-palibodha*) is severed; [this occurs] from the point of departing with the thought, "I will not return."
It was stated [earlier] precisely because the robe had already been finished; for it was said, "having taken the robe that has been made.

For a monk who has performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, as long as there is an expectation of obtaining a robe—thinking, "I shall obtain a robe from the Saṅgha or from a donor family"—or until he obtains the requisite conditions such as the assistance of companions and, having acquired the cloth, intends, "I shall cut and make it into the form of an outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth," [the *kaṭhina* remains extended].
As long as the desire to make [robes] continues, the impediment of robes (*cīvara-palibodha*) remains unsevered. However, when the desire to make ceases—
either because one fails to obtain robes at all from the place where they were expected, or because the hope for robes has vanished through their being made and finished,
or because they have been lost or destroyed, or through a lack of concern for robes— then the impediment of robes is severed.
And here, this [first obstacle] is made manifest by the expression, "having taken the robe that has been finished.
Thus, in all subsequent instances, it should be understood that their cessation is stated first and then later, based on the sequence of the Pāli text.
Furthermore, the suspension of the Kathina is effected only by the cessation of both these obstacles, not of just one. And as for these two, in their respective order—
It should be understood that these eight headings (mātikā) are established in order to demonstrate the simultaneous cessation [of the acquisitions].

The phrase "within the boundary" (*antosaṃāya*) is stated because [the robe] was cut off at the very moment the robe was finished. The phrase "they will not have this robe made" demonstrates the cessation of the impediment of making (*karaṇa-palibodha*), because the expectation regarding the robe has vanished.
However, as for one who, out of fewness of desires (*appicchatā*) or lack of need...

Or, if one does not accept the robe-cloth in any way whatsoever, then because the obstacle of the robe-cloth has ceased for him who has gone outside the boundary—even by the mere act of his resolve that "they shall not return"—the suspension of the *kaṭhina* should be understood as ending with that resolve.
Furthermore, "that" refers to the severance of obstacles. This, however, refers to the suspension of the *kaṭhina* due to the cessation of hope, which is explained separately in detail.
The connection is: "it is not said here.

"He obtains it without expectation" means that in a family where the expectation, "We shall obtain a robe," has never previously arisen, he obtains it there—meaning he obtains it anywhere at all in a place where no expectation for a robe has arisen.
"He does not obtain it through expectation" means in a place where [an expectation] was desired.
The meaning is "he does not obtain it. "Not mentioned here" means it was not mentioned immediately following the section on "hearing" (savanantika).

"Therein" refers to that [section] concerning the transgression of the boundary (*sīmātikkantika*). One is called "transgressing the boundary" because it arises from crossing the boundary defined as the final day of the robe-season.
Some think that "transgression of the boundary" refers to the lapse of time when one is outside the boundary; for them...

If it were the case that the suspension of the *kaṭhina* could be considered "not authorized" even when there is a transgression of the robe-period within the precincts (*antoupacāra*), that would not be logical.
Therefore, it should be understood that in any instance, a transgression of the time constitutes a transgression of the boundary (*sīmātikkama*).

Furthermore, in this context, the phrase "one who has finished making robes" in the Canon is merely an illustration; even for one who has not finished making robes, there is a transgression of the boundary through the transgression of the time, and two [other types of transgressions].

[The phrase] "there is no offense" refers to either not knowing that water had been set aside, or having discarded what was set aside, or having forgotten it.

Since there is also the possibility of being in the category of non-offense when one goes unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness, the Vinaya-master, having adopted the view of non-offense in that case, spoke thus.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Other monks held the view of non-offense regarding his offense.
Because the view of non-offense had arisen even among the assembly, the plural form "others" (aññe) was employed.
“The view that there was no offense” arose because the Elder of the Suttanta school lacked expertise in the Vinaya; thus, he accepted the mere word of the Vinaya-holder.
However, for him, it was indeed an offense, because he set it aside after knowing that only a small amount of water remained.

For the training rules (*sekhiya*) are *sacittaka* (involving intention) only with respect to the knowledge of the physical basis (*vatthu*), not with respect to the knowledge of the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*). Therefore, in the Pāḷi it says: “Of that... [etc.]”
Regarding the statement, "There is the view that there is no offense in what is an offense," it is stated in all cases that this is indeed an offense.
As for the phrase "one who commits an offense," the Vinayadhara Thera, recollecting the words spoken by the Suttantika Thera when he was asked, "Was this water set aside by you?
and replied, "Yes, friend," concluded—due to his lack of skill in the formal rules—that he had committed the act intentionally, and thus held the view that it was an offense.
Having offered the sacrifice, he spoke. For that very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "The other bhikkhus held the view that she had committed an offense.
(453) "It is not yet split" means that the Saṅgha is not called "split" merely by the act of suspension (*ukkhepana*) and its subsequent following;
rather, it is when, depending on that [act], both factions seek out their own sides and, through mutual anger, [fall into division].
This was said with reference to the fact that [the offense] occurs precisely through the increase of quarreling by body and speech. Therefore he said: "And that, moreover, by way of quarreling.
"By way of urgency" means by way of haste. 454. Regarding the passage beginning with "In an improper cause," etc.:
even without accusing [the person], it is appropriate to release one from an offense out of a desire for their welfare by means of a skillful method in a situation where such is fitting.

This was stated with reference to the fact that [an act] was committed for the purpose of harming under the influence of a mind of anger, and not with reference to the absence of a constituent factor of the kamma.
For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: "This, monks, is an offense; this is not a non-offense...
[etc. ...this monk is suspended," and so forth.
455. “Sitting on the side of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma”: this is merely an illustration;

for even one who sits on the side of those who speak according to the Dhamma but adopts the views of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, remains a member of a different community (nānāsaṃvāsaka) from those who speak according to the Dhamma.
“He invalidates the formal act” (kammaṃ kopeti): this is said with reference to a faction that fails to complete the quorum of the Saṅgha. Or, wherever...
The meaning is: he sides with either those who speak according to the Dhamma or those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
"He takes them as 'these are speakers of the Dhamma'" means that he takes the monks belonging to each respective side—whether correctly or incorrectly—as "these are speakers of the Dhamma";
this makes himself a fellow resident (samānasaṃvāsaka) with those belonging to each respective side.
456. "Upadaṃsentī" means they cause [the mind] to proceed. In the text, "ettāvatā" (to this extent) implies that one should sit at a distance after reflecting:
"Having left this much space, even when a thought of anger arises, we will not be able to engage in any mutually discordant bodily action or the like.
Therefore he said, "having left the vicinity."

457. Regarding the phrases "engaged in quarreling" (*bhaṇḍanajātā*) and so forth in the Pāli: the preliminary stage of a quarrel is called *bhaṇḍana*. The physical contact of hands and so forth is called *kalaha*. Contradictory speech is called *vivāda*. 458.

Regarding the phrase "with full treasuries and granaries" (*paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāra*): here, a *kosa* (treasury) refers to the inner chamber containing valuable goods such as gold, gems, and so forth.
A *koṭṭha* is said to be a place for storing grain; a house that serves as a storehouse is a *koṭṭhāgāra*, which is a place for collecting grain.
"Abbhuyyāsī" means he went forth facing toward battle; "ekasaṅghātam-pi" means even a single combat.
"Dhovanaṃ" means washing water.
"Pariyādinnarūpā" means having a nature grasped by a mind of anger.

464. "They do not know that" means they do not know that quarrel. "Those who harbor resentment" means they bind the aforementioned mode of anger within their minds. "Manifest dangers" refers to lions and the like; "concealed dangers" refers to lust and the like.

"There is no companionship with a fool"—this is not found in the text—means that by relying on a fool, there is no companionship consisting of virtues such as morality, nor can it be obtained; this is the meaning.
466. *Attakāmarūpā* means those whose nature is desiring their own welfare.
*Anuruddhā* is an address to all three sons of good family by way of the "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*); for that reason, the plural number is employed.
"Is it endurable? Is life sustained?"—he asks this to inquire: "Are you able to maintain your bodies and sustain your lives? *Taggha*... [etc.]
*Ekaṃsaṭṭhe nipāto*: the meaning is "certainly," as in "we are certain, Bhante. Regarding *yathā kathaṃ*: here *yathā* is merely a particle;
or alternatively, *yathā-kathaṃ* is a single compound particle used for the purpose of asking about a reason, meaning "in what manner? And regarding *ekaṃ ca pana maññe cittaṃ*:
because the mental states of the others proceed by way of one person’s mind, [it is said] "our minds are, as it were, one."

The meaning [of the passage] is as follows: regarding the phrase "Kacci pana vo, Anuruddhā," here *vo* is either a mere particle or a word in the nominative plural; thus, the meaning is "I hope it is well with you.
In the phrase "Amhākaṃ," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa); the meaning is "among us three, whoever returns first.
The commentary on the Kosambakavivāda-kathā is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Journey to Pālileyyaka: 467.

*Yena pālileyyakan* is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is that he arrived at the place where the village of Pālileyyaka was located. *Daharapotakehi* means by the young young ones of the bhṛṅgarāja birds. There is also a reading *ogāhin*, which means a bathing lotus pond. In the verse of the Udāna, however, it says:
"The mind of this elephant, the Nāga whose tusks are like chariot-rims, is inclined toward seclusion."
The elephant [of the simile] corresponds to the Buddha-elephant whose mind is inclined toward seclusion. Why? Because he alone delights in the forest;
therefore, the construction [of the verse] should be understood in this way.
The commentary on the account of the journey to Pārileyyaka is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Eighteen Bases (Aṭṭhārasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā):

468. “Stand as the Dhamma stands”: this means stand in the same way that the Dhamma and the Vinaya are established; the sense is that you should stand on the side of those who speak according to the Dhamma.
473. “Whoever should oppose [this], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)”: this refers to one who does not cause a schism in the harmony of the Saṅgha.

It has been stated. However, it is appropriate to ward off those who cause schism, who are contentious, and who are shameless, because there is a statement regarding the destruction even of lodgings belonging to them.

Furthermore, since it is said, "Having made it secluded, it should be given," this should be understood to mean that one should not give the best lodging according to seniority, but rather, even for the unrestrained elders, it should be given after making it secluded from the restrained.
475. Regarding the phrase "having reinstated him by means of the formal act" (*kammavācā*):

it should be understood that since the fact that the suspended monk had committed an offense was admitted, and because the intention to reinstate him had already arisen among those who had suspended him due to his proper conduct, the followers of the suspension reinstated him of their own accord by means of the formal act for the settling of the matter (*paṭippassambhana-kammavācā*).
476. "Devoid of meaning" means lacking the sense of concord; "empty of phrasing" is the meaning. 477.

"Unconcealed conduct" refers to conduct that is beautiful and does not need to be hidden. "Not departed" means not separated from the cause. Regarding "having taken up," because it is to be accepted and grasped, the "teaching of the teacher" is what is spoken of;

thus he said, "having taken up his own teacher's teaching. "By the eight factors of a messenger" means: "he is a listener and a proclaimer, a receiver and a retainer, one who understands and one who makes others understand."
And being skilled and knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate, yet not being a maker of quarrels—by these eight qualities of a messenger.
The rest here, as well as everything below, is easy to understand.
The commentary on the account of the eighteen grounds is finished.
The method of commentary on the Kosambaka Khandhaka is finished.
Thus ends the method of commentary on the Mahāvagga within the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the Vinaya-ṭṭhakathā known as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Minor Section (Cūḷavagga) 1.
The Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka)
Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Rebuke (Tajjanīyakamma-kathāvaṇṇanā): 1.
First, in the first section on formal acts (kammakkhandhaka) of the Cūḷavagga, the phrase "balavābalava" consists of a single word.
Although it should be said as "balavabalava," the vowel *ā* has been inserted, thus it is stated as "balavābalava. This is similar to how "dukkhadukkha" and other such terms are formed.
It functions in the sense of "excessively," thus he said, “Respond very strongly.
The meaning is: “Give your reply making it exceedingly strong.
2. Regarding the phrase in the Canon, “The offense should be charged,” although [in the context of] “Venerable sirs, do not let him defeat you,” and so forth...
There is no offense prescribed for speech that gives rise to quarrels and the like, because such speech is not included within [the categories of] lying or slander;
nevertheless, when a monk is addressed by other monks—either individually or in the midst of the Saṅgha—with words not yet formally prescribed, saying:
"Friend, do not engage in mutual incitement to quarrels and the like; this does not conduce to fewness of wishes and so forth," [then an offense occurs].

The meaning should be understood as follows: whatever offense a bhikkhu incurs through disrespect, or on account of causing displeasure, or on account of engaging in speaking otherwise or harassment, that offense must be formally charged against him, just as in the case of one who has fallen away from right view.
Furthermore, even for one who has committed a light offense without this verbal statement, provided it was incurred through body or speech, that offense must likewise be charged.

However, the inclusion of the word *attanā* (by oneself) in the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) as "one who is himself a maker of strife," and the statement beginning with "and those other monks who are makers of strife...
having approached them," are taken [as examples] by way of the specific case (*vatthu*).
But as for one who is himself a maker of strife, yet having approached other makers of strife, says: "Do not..."

Even if he does not speak the words beginning with "You yourselves [should do this]," this formal act (*kamma*) must indeed be performed for him. And those performing it should recite the *kammavācā* precisely as follows:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so is a maker of strife... [and so on] ...a maker of legal disputes in the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha... Furthermore, regarding any other monks who engage in quarreling—

If she encourages others [to do so], it is likewise permissible for her to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*) in that same manner, because encouraging others also falls under the category of being a "creator of strife.

Even when one intends to perform the formal act after stating the manner in which others were encouraged, one must grasp the very meaning of the words spoken by them and compose the formula accordingly;
it should not be done merely by including everyone simply because they have come here.

Because speech is impossible here simply by virtue of having arrived [at that state]. For it should be understood that only what has been done with respect to a factual basis is unimpaired, and nothing else.
This same method applies to the acts of censure (niyassakamma) and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Twelvefold Unlawful Act (Adhammakamma-dvādasaka-kathā-vaṇṇanā):
"Done without consent" means performed without having obtained the admission of either the matter (*vatthu*) or the offense (*āpatti*).
However, if one has committed a transgression of the matter while everyone was looking on, and subsequently, out of fear of the formal act being carried out, says "I did not do it," which is a lie—
When he speaks, his very admission in the presence of the bhikkhus is the act of transgression.

It is permitted to make an admission solely for the purpose of knowing the truth as it is. However, where there is doubt, it should be understood that the matter must be carried out only after having obtained the consent [of the accused].
“Or for an offense involving defeat (pārājika)” is stated because a formal act (kamma) for defeat is performed for the purpose of removing the characteristic marks [of a monk].
“Or for an offense involving formal meeting (saṅghādisesa)” is stated, however, because there exists a distinct formal act for its removal, such as probation (parivāsa) and so forth.
As for that which follows: “He has failed in higher virtue... [etc. ...a censure formal act (tajjanīyakamma)...”

When it was said, “one should make [an act of atonement],” that was stated with reference to a light offense caused by disrespect and so forth incurred by one who is being exhorted, “Stand firm in future restraint and perform the act of atonement.

For one who has committed a light offense rooted in a failure of virtue is here described as “failed in higher virtue” through a metaphorical identification (abhedūpacāra), just as in the expression “failed in view due to excessive views.”
And just as for one who speaks after having adopted a view,

an act performed without saying "desist from this view" is called an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) because it was done solely due to a failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*) and not due to an offense; likewise, a procedure such as censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) performed against one who has fallen into a failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*),
who has descended from the quality of shame, but who— having emerged in accordance with the Dhamma— is desirous of remaining established in restraint.
An act performed solely because of a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) that does not require confession is called an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*).

For this very reason, even in the case of the act of subordination (*niyassakamma*), it is stated in the context of restraint that "the monks, being themselves subject to censure, grant probation," and so forth;

thus, the very impossibility [of such a procedure] is stated as the mark of its illegitimacy. Indeed, acts such as the act of condemnation (*tajjanīyakamma*) were authorized solely for the purpose of taming one who is untamed.
However, some say: "The phrase 'not removable by confession' is stated specifically with reference to a *pārājika* offense, not a *saṅghādisesa*.
This contradicts the statement: "It is done with regard to an offense that is removable by confession," which refers to the bright fortnight (the light side).
Furthermore, if the term "removable by confession" were applied to a *saṅghādisesa* in a figurative sense, then [the rule] "it is done with regard to an offense" would [apply].
There would be no distinction between this section and the previously stated section; nor has any distinction been shown here even in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated.

6. "All of them" refers to the three: the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), the act of demotion (*niyassa-kamma*), and the act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*). "On account of the basis for another legal act" means...
The intention is that there is no fault whatsoever in performing another formal act (kamma) by means of the basis for a different formal act than that which would result in censure (tajjanīya).
He states the reason with the words beginning "Why? (kasmā).
8. *Pannaloma* means those whose hair of pride has fallen away.
The commentary on the discussion of the set of twelve on illegitimate legal acts (*adhammakamma*) is finished. Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Subordination (*niyassakamma*): 11.
Regarding the act of subordination, in the Canon the phrase *apissu* is a combination of particles used in the sense of *api ca* (moreover/furthermore). *Nissāya te*... [text continues]

Regarding the phrase "he must live [under supervision]," some say this was stated with reference to being dependent on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), while others say it refers specifically to taking formal dependence (*nissaya*).
It should be understood that by either of these two cases, it is indicated that he is not permitted to live according to his own will. 21.

Regarding the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*): the statement "the act of banishment shall be suspended" is said with reference to those who conduct themselves properly without having departed or otherwise failed in their duties.
33. Regarding the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation), it is said that this is neither by the word of a monk nor by the word of a layperson.

Here, even figuratively, monks do not speak words of reproach toward others; however, while householders are capable of reviling [others] in their own direct manner, they do not speak such things without cause even toward those who have been helpful to them.
The intended meaning is: "You have fallen away from the qualities of a householder as well."

39. By the phrase “the possession of factors is unlike those mentioned previously,” it is indicated that this [act] is not permitted merely by the reasons stated for the *tajjanīyakamma* (reproval) and so forth.

However, it should be understood that because of the factor mentioned here—namely, striving to prevent householders from gaining profit and so on—it is permissible to perform even those [other formal acts].
And herein, [it refers to] a donor who is faithful, confident, a benefactor, and a doer...

Because it is stated, “He reviles one who attends upon the Saṅgha with low [speech],” the offense is subject to formal legal action (kamma) only through those factors connected to householders, such as reviling, when directed at such laypeople;
it is not so through reviling and the like directed at monastery attendants (ārāmika), servants (ceṭaka), and so forth.

Even in that case, once the donors and others have been asked for forgiveness, there is no longer liability to formal legal action, and the confession of the offense may be made anywhere. However, if someone, even after being asked for forgiveness three times...
It is not permissible; even if the formal act has not been performed, the offense must be confessed within the range of sight.

If he has died, or has gone to another region, or the direction he went is unknown, or if there is a threat to his life on the way, they say that whether the formal act has been performed or not, one should confess the offense after having made a truthful declaration and asked for forgiveness in the midst of the Saṅgha. This concerns a legitimate undertaking.

However, regarding the act of making amends, one should inform them of the sequence of words for seeking forgiveness by going into their presence and saying, "I did not verify [the matter] before making a formal promise; I have now made it true. Please forgive me," and so forth. 41.
In the Pāḷi, it is stated that he was overcome with shame and was unable to ask Citta the householder for forgiveness, so he traveled back again along the thirty-yojana road.
Having gone there, because of his stubbornness in pride, he failed to reveal his fault as it truly was and refused to accept the other's apology;
saying, "I do not forgive," he rejected him. Feeling humiliated, he was unable to ask for forgiveness.

Upon returning again to Sāvatthī, he was sent by the Teacher once more for the very purpose of subduing his pride, yet being unable to obtain forgiveness in the same manner as before, he returned yet again.

It should be understood that the Blessed One, having taught the Dhamma to him with the words, “One might wish for the cultivation of what is non-existent,” and so forth, crushed his pride and permitted the gift of the *anudūta* (messenger). 42. Since it is stated, “If he does not forgive... [etc.

...he must be made to confess the offense,” it should be understood that if a householder forgives beforehand, there is no requirement to confess the offense within the range of vision (*dassanūpacāra*).
46. Regarding the three *ukkhepanīyakamma* (acts of suspension), "having charged him with an offense" means:

either having separately charged him in the midst of the Saṅgha with a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) on account of not relinquishing a pernicious view, or having charged him with a *pācittiya* (offense requiring confession) at the conclusion of the formal admonition.
Here too, the phrase beginning with "Thus have I [been instructed] by the Blessed One" is stated by way of the specific case (*vatthu*).
The formal proclamation (kammavācā) should be performed by joining together the various ways in which those holding wrong views have expressed themselves.
However, even without including the manner of their grasping [the view], it should be stated: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
a wicked state of views has arisen in the bhikkhu named so-and-so; he does not relinquish that view. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha..."
Thus, it is also permissible to perform the formal act (kammavācā) based on this general principle.

65. By the phrase, "Whatever view one relies upon to engage in quarrels and so forth," it is shown that here only those quarrels and so forth arising in reliance upon a view are intended, not quarrels and so forth in their mere occurrence. Furthermore, regarding the performance of quarrels and so forth—
If one, holding the view that "there is no fault," engages in quarreling and so forth, that too is indeed a [wrong] view;
it is therefore appropriate to carry out a formal act against him for his failure to relinquish that view.
The commentary on the discussion of the act of subordination (niyassakamma) is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Kammakkhandhaka is finished.
2. The Pārivāsikakkhandhaka: Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of One Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikavatta).

75. In the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*, the phrase “even those such as those deserving to be sent back to the beginning” includes, by the word “etc.,” those deserving the *mānatta* penance, those undergoing the *mānatta* penance, and those deserving rehabilitation.
For these [categories] stand in the place of those on probation (*pārivāsika*), and those on probation stand in the place of regular monks (*pakatatta*).
“A foot-washing stand” refers to a piece of wood, a plank, or similar object upon which one stands while washing one’s feet.

“Striking with the feet” means with pebbles, gravel, and so forth. Since it is stated merely that “one performs the duties,” it is not permitted for the student (saddhivihārika) and others to perform such acts as prostrating.

The phrase “when the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* is being performed” is said with reference even to the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* performed by those who have not joined the Saṅgha for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) or those whose rains-residence (*vassa*) has been interrupted, when the Saṅgha is performing the invitation ceremony on days such as the *pavāraṇā*. “In one’s own text” means in front of the junior monks.

“*Pārivāsikassevā*” (only for one under probation): this was stated with reference to all those subject to heavy penalties at the conclusion of their rehabilitation (*abbhāna*). Since it has been permitted for each of them to receive food separately, the rest—the regular monks (*pakatatta*)—do not receive it.

“*Catussālabhattan*” means food being given in succession in a dining hall (*bhojanasālā*). “*Standing within arm’s reach*” (*hatthapāse ṭhitena*) means standing within the donor’s arm’s reach, that is, in a place suitable for receiving [the gift];
this is the intended meaning. “*In the case of the great bowl-food*” (*mahāpeḷabhattepi*) refers to large...
[This applies] even to food being given after having been placed in vessels such as rice-pots and the like. 76.

"The most grave offense" refers to an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), stated here by way of its maximum degree. However, excluding the offenses of formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*) such as acting as a go-between, these are indeed worldly offenses (*loka-vajja*) such as the emission of semen; even among those, offenses such as causing a schism in the Sangha are the most grave.
By the phrase "the act (*kamma*) is the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) of one undergoing probation," the meaning of the word *kammavācā* is also shown to be "speech that constitutes a formal act."
It should be understood as "accomplished. Regarding the term *savacanīya*, here it expresses the meaning of "one who possesses anger.
The meaning should be seen here as "an action that proceeds according to one's own word";
the intention is that one must not perform an action that proceeds by one's own command, such as saying, "Do not depart," or "Come into the presence of the masters of the Vinaya."
For when someone has spoken thus, it is not permissible to pass by with disregard; the command of the Buddha and the Saṅgha would then be transgressed.

"A ground covered with dust" is a qualification of the leaf-hut. "Requisites" refers to the robe for the rainy-season residence. "Does not obtain a lodging" means he does not obtain one by means of the distribution according to the length of the rains-residence.

The "unfailing practice" (apaṇṇakapaṭipadā) is the practice that is not contradicted. Regarding the phrase "even if one makes an effort," this includes even one who does not make an effort after having realized that [the goal] is outside the scope of possibility.

81. "In general" means by way of the commonality of those who are on probation (pārivāsika) and those who have been suspended (ukkhitaka). "In places covered with five-colored canopies" means in places covered by canopies of five kinds.
"Attached" (obaddha) means bound to activities such as rising and so forth; the meaning is "afflicted. Regarding the phrase "on a bed or a chair": here...
The word *vā* has the sense of inclusion; by this it is indicated that it is not permissible to sit even on long seats such as mats or pieces of hide.

"There is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the duties" shows that there is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the duties even when one knows that the person is more senior. "Having had the duties relinquished" is said with reference specifically to those undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties of one undergoing probation is finished.
The method of commentary on the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka is finished.
3. The Samuccayakkhandhaka:
Commentary on the Discussion of the Emission of Semen.
