97. In the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*, "I make known" (*vedayāmaham*) means "I inform" (*ārocemi*); they also explain its meaning as "I experience.

However, they praise the former [reading] because it is a statement of formal assignment (*āropana*). "Having informed, it should be laid down" is said for the purpose of being released from the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Some, however, [say that one may do so] on that very day after again undertaking the observance (*vatta*) until dawn...
They say this is also for the purpose of avoiding the interruption of the night for one who wishes to rise [for the recitation].

Because it is stated, "monks of similar standing reside," it should be understood that in a dwelling place where monks of a different status reside, it is permissible to perform the duties outside [the boundary] without undertaking them there.
Regarding the phrase, "having passed beyond two throws of a clod": this refers to the monastery.
This was said for the purpose of avoiding the vicinity where the sound of the monks' recitation and so forth could be heard.

"Having descended from the main road" was said for the purpose of passing beyond the vicinity of the monks who were traveling along the road. "Or by a thicket," and so forth, was for the purpose of avoiding the vicinity of sight.
By the statement, "He too goes before dawn on some business," [it is shown that] when the announcement has been made, even among all [the monks...]

When the bhikkhus have gone to their dwellings, if the group is incomplete, there is no fault regarding conduct or no fault regarding separation, because it has been announced that they are living together;
this is what he shows by saying, "And this," and so forth. "It is not permissible to perform the rehabilitation" means that even if it were performed, it would be as if it had not been done at all.
The commentary on the discussion of the emission of semen is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of probation for one who has concealed [the offense]:
"Of one who is pure" means of one who has not committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense of the same class, or of one who has emerged from such an offense. "In another" means...
Regarding the emergence from an offense other than that which occurs through the purification of the period of probation (*suddhantaparivāsa*):
in the Canon, the passage “The monk Udāyī was sent back by the Saṅgha for one offense... [etc.

...this is a sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*)” should be construed as “he was sent back by means of a sending back to the beginning,” having modified it according to its function (*karaṇa*). Alternatively, “sending back to the beginning... [is to be understood].
It is also permissible to connect [the phrase] "The Saṅgha consents" with the subsequent line by means of the distributive sense (*paccattavaseva*).
Regarding the passage: "Having sent the monk Udāyī back to the beginning for one offense... having sent him back to the beginning," this means:
having sent the monk Udāyī back to the beginning—having drawn him back to the day of the root offense—on account of that one offense which served as the cause, [for] that...
The construction is: "Let him grant a *samodhānaparivāsa* for an intermediate offense.

"Having had it revealed, he should be released" means that once the incurability of his condition has been made known to the Saṅgha by that very person, he should be released by way of separating him from the group of modest monks.
"A hundred offenses" refers to a hundred offenses committed on a single day by way of bodily contact and so forth. "One thousand" [refers to] ten hundreds.

There are one thousand offenses. This should be construed with the phrase "having concealed for a hundred nights. "At the conclusion of all the formal acts (kammavācā) for parivāsa" means at the end of the formal acts for all these types of parivāsa:
the two kinds of *suddhanta-parivāsa* shown below, and the three kinds of *samodhāna-parivāsa*.
"In the same manner as before" means by the method described in the section on *paṭicchanna-parivāsa*.

"Even from the vicinity of a monastery" means even from the vicinity of the monasteries of the bhikkhus outside the village. "Two throws of a clod must be crossed"—this refers to the bhikkhus' range of hearing being exceeded.
"Of the village" is not stated [in the rule]; therefore, it is not said that it is permissible to leave the vicinity of the village.
Consequently, even if one is standing within the vicinity of the village, if one is within the range of sight or hearing there—
This indicates that monks and nuns who remain standing after [the boundary] has been crossed do not effect the breaking of the night.
"In the same manner as for monks who have not laid down their formal duties" refers to the breaking of the night with respect to those who have entered the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"In that village" means in the village where the nuns reside. "Having shown himself" means as follows:

It is possible to announce [the offense] by demonstrating it in that manner. By the phrase "having been formally authorized, it should be given," it is shown that even during co-residence with one who has been so authorized, there is no interruption of the night [count].

"Of one who has been sent back to the beginning" (*mūlāyapaṭikassita*) means: of one who, having been sent back to the beginning, has again completed the probationary period (*parivāsa*). "Of three" refers to two intermediate offenses together with the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
108. If it is said, "If concealed," this refers to an offense committed after the observance of the *vatta* (duties) has been suspended.

In the *Pāḷi*, within the section on concealment for five days (*pañcāhappaṭicchanna*) during the discussion on intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*), the statement, "And thus, monks, the *mānatta* penance of six nights should be given," is not intended to be given immediately following the formal act of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanākamma*). For one who has been sent back to the beginning...

However, this was said with reference to the granting of *mānatta* for an unconfessed third intermediate offense committed during the period of practicing *mānatta* after having already completed five days of probation and having requested it.
And when *mānatta* has been granted in this manner, by means of a single six-day period, the *mānatta* for all four offenses—
including the three offenses for which *mānatta* had previously been granted— is indeed fulfilled.

This is so. However, by this same method, one should understand the procedure regarding an intermediate offense committed at the time of being eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*), as well as regarding the intermediate offenses in the section on concealment for a fortnight (*pakkhappaṭicchanna*).

Regarding the phrase "five [cases] by way of concealment for one day and so forth," this refers to treating each of the four cases—concealment for one day and so forth—as consisting of a single period of probation (*parivāsa*), a single act of penance (*mānatta*), and a single rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).

It has been stated: "There are four by way of intermediate offenses. This too was stated by treating the granting of *mānatta* and rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) as a single unit in relation to each respective sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya-paṭikassana*).
The commentary on the discussion of the probation for concealed offenses is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Simultaneous Parivāsa (Samodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā) 125.
“Because the intervening offense was concealed”— this is the statement of the reason for granting the simultaneous parivāsa,
and not for the fact that the days already spent undergoing parivāsa would be tainted by the non-concealment of the intervening offense.
Because even when a *mūlāya-paṭikassana* (sending back to the beginning) has been performed, it is possible for those days to be considered "smeared" (*makkhita*).
Therefore, immediately after the statement, “All days—both those practiced by conceit and those already spent—are indeed smeared,” the connection should be made here as follows:
“And a *samodhāna-parivāsa* (combined probation) must be granted to him. For this reason, he said, “By that very [reason],” and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of probation by combining [periods] is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of probation by combining values: 134.
By the phrase "based on one offense," the method beginning with "one offense concealed for one day, one offense concealed for two days" is indicated.

It shows. To show the state of being unconcealed: even for an offense concealed through ignorance and so forth, it shows the state of being unconcealed by means of the statement that one is "worthy of the *mānatta* [probation].
For it is said: "Friends, for one month a bhikkhu is worthy of *mānatta*.
Herein, for one month of concealment through ignorance, one does not become worthy of *parivāsa*; it is solely because of the unconcealed nature of the offense that he is worthy of *mānatta*.
The intention is that he becomes one deserving of the *mānatta* (probation). In the Canon, "the nature of malice" (*makkhadhamma*) means the desire to crush [others].

Furthermore, it should be understood that this is called the *Samuccayakkhandhaka* because it is a compendium of all the legal determinations regarding the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, such as the granting of the *parivāsa* (probation).
The commentary on the discussion of the probation involving the combination of values is finished.
The method of commentary on the Samuccayakkhandhaka is finished.
4. The Samathakkhandhaka: Commentary on the Discussion of the Settlement by Way of Mindfulness, etc.

195. In the *Samathakkhandhaka*, *sativinaya* (settlement by mindfulness) is the means of discipline for those who are unfit for formal accusation and so forth; it is to be granted to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), based upon his vast mindfulness.

196. Regarding the phrase "one who has undergone a reversal of mind" (*cittavipariyāsakato*): this refers to one who has experienced a transformation of the mind. In the passage concerning the monk Gagga... [they] accuse him.
Here, however, "this madness" (*ummattaka*) refers to what was practiced while he was insane; that very act is performed through a reversal of mind.

It means "one who has undergone a perversion of mind. The meaning should be understood as follows: they accuse the bhikkhu Gagga of an offense incurred through an improper practice (anācāra) committed by that madman who had undergone a perversion of mind.
The *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who was insane) is the discipline to be granted to one who was first deluded and later attained a state of non-delusion.

202. To show that this word is a term ending in the suffix *ika* accompanied by the augment *sa*, meaning "an action that brings about the state of being a majority for those who speak according to the Dhamma" (*yebhuyyasikā*), he said, "Of which," and so forth.
Therein, "of which action" refers to the action of the person distributing the voting sticks (*salākā*) by means of the secret method, the open method, and so on.
"The action of settling (*samatha*) dependent upon the state of being a majority is *yebhuyyasikā*"; thus it is explained.
The meaning of the term *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority) must be understood in this way; for it is only thus that this becomes what is called a "settling of legal issues" (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).

For when, through the aforementioned drawing of lots, the majority status of those who speak according to the Dhamma is established, the settlement of the legal issue subsequently occurs precisely on the basis of that majority status, and not merely by the act of proving the greater number of those who speak according to the Dhamma.

207. “The same method applies here as was stated for the *tajjanīya* (reproval) and other [formal acts]”—by this it is shown that, just like the seven formal acts beginning with the *tajjanīya*, this *tassapāpiyasika* (act of further penalty) is also a distinct act of restraint (*niggahakamma*) to be performed against one who is possessed of faults such as impurity of character and who does not abide by the judgment of the Saṅgha. For when this act of restraint has been performed, that person...

When one enters the midst of the Saṅgha for the purpose of establishing one’s own purity by saying, "I am pure," the Saṅgha is not permitted to give a formal decision (vinicchaya) regarding him, and that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is settled by the mere performance of the formal act (kamma).
How, then, does this formal act subside? Some here say: "Having been thus restrained, he remains restrained..."
Some say: "He exists [in the Saṅgha], yet he does not obtain reinstatement (*osāraṇā*). For that very reason, reinstatement is not mentioned in the Canon.

Others, however, maintain: "Because the proper conduct (*sammāvatta*) has been described in the Canon by such statements as 'he should not be ordained,' etc., reinstatement—though not explicitly stated for one who, having practiced proper conduct, falls into a state of shamelessness—is to be effected by applying the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*) through inference, just as it is done in the case of the *tajjanīyakamma* and other such acts."
"It must indeed be performed," they say; this is logical. For that very reason, the Commentary will say:
"If he is virtuous, having fulfilled the duty, he will obtain relief; if not, he will remain exactly as he was expelled.
*Tassapāpiyasikākammaṃ* is a compound formed by non-elision (*aluttasamāsa*). Therefore, he says "For this... and so forth.
The commentary on the *Sativinaya-kathā* is finished.
Commentary on the *Adhikaraṇa-kathā*: 215.

Because it transforms into a state of deformity, the mind ripens as suffering; thus he said, "The conventional expression is for the sake of mental suffering," and so forth. *Upavadanā* means accusation. *Tattheva* means in the case of reproach (*anuvadanā*).

The construction is as follows: "Because it has been understood from the beginning" means that the exposition will follow by way of commentary starting from the very beginning of the Kamma-vagga (Chapter on Kamma) as it appears in detail; "because it has been understood from the beginning" refers to its being understood through the mode of explanation starting from the outset of that section.

216. In the text, *ajjhattaṃ vā* means either within oneself or within one's own assembly; *bahiddhā vā* means either outside oneself or within another's assembly; *anavassavāya* means for the sake of non-arising.

220. “Is the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?”—this is the question. “The legal issue of dispute may be wholesome,” and so forth, is the answer. This same method applies to the remaining [legal issues] as well.

222. Even though an offense (*āpatti*) is by its very nature conventional (*sammuti-sabhāva*), when it is spoken of as being unwholesome or indeterminate through a metaphorical application of the cause [to the effect], then because a wholesome state can also be a cause for an offense, one would have to say, through that metaphorical application, “the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be wholesome.”

Having stated that, it was said, "In this context, the meaning should be understood by way of what was spoken with a specific intention (*sandhāya-bhāsita*)," in order to show the reason for the statement, "There is no unwholesome legal issue arising from an offense. And here, the intended meaning is as follows:

for if what is called an "offense" were an entity possessing the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of a phenomenon in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), then the statement, "A legal issue arising from an offense might be unwholesome," and so forth, [would not be necessary].

It would be appropriate [to say this]. Since it is shown in the commentaries on the training rules concerning corrupted faults (*duṭṭhadosasikkhāpada*) and elsewhere that it is not fitting for a conventional nature (*sammutisabhāva*) to enter into an ultimate nature (*paramatthasabhāva*)—for such a thing is exclusively of a conventional nature—it cannot, from the standpoint of the direct method (*nippariyāyato*), be said that "it may be unwholesome or it may be indeterminate.
However, if one were to do so by taking into account merely the fact of its being originated by unwholesome or indeterminate states...
It is stated by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyato*) that "it may be unwholesome (*akusala*) or it may be indeterminate (*abyākata*).

In that case, even by taking into account its being established upon wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), it would also have to be said, by way of a figurative method, that "an adjudication concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be wholesome.
Since this statement [indicates] that there exists a separate reason for the offense to be designated as unwholesome or indeterminate, rather than being fit for designation as wholesome;
This was spoken with a specific intention; therefore, the meaning here should be understood precisely according to that particular reason with which it was spoken.

Now, however, one might take it to mean that the unwholesome nature of an offense was stated only with reference to a mind capable of fulfilling the constituent factors (*aṅga*), and not with reference to any other specific cause.
To show the fault in such an interpretation, he says: "For in whatever... and so forth.

In this context, "such as digging the earth" refers to the signs of digging the earth and so forth that are exempt from formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*). Regarding the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), a wholesome state of mind (*kusala-citta*) is a factor;

for when one does not know the formal rule and, with a wholesome mind, disturbs the earth element or destroys vegetation by clearing the ground on a shrine courtyard (*cetiya-aṅgaṇa*) and so forth, the wholesome mind is the cause. "When that exists" means when that legal issue of an offense exists.
The intended meaning is: "when an offense exists that is worthy of being designated as 'wholesome' (kusala) because it has arisen from a wholesome state of consciousness.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the meaning of the phrase "when that exists" (*tasmiṃ sati*) is stated as "when that [state] is apprehended as an offense within that wholesome consciousness";
this is not tenable, because the legal issue of the offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is precisely what is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*yasmiṃ*) in the word "in which" (*yasmiṃ*).
“In that” means because it is to be clung to.

It is not possible to say [that there is no such thing]: if, even in the case of an offense that is merely conventional (sammuti-sabhāva), the designation “unwholesome” and so forth is applied because it originates from unwholesome states and the like, then the designation “wholesome” would also have to be applied;
therefore, it is not possible to say, “There is no legal issue (āpattādhikaraṇa) that is wholesome.”
The intention is that otherwise, even his status as unwholesome (*akusala*) and so forth would have to be rejected.

Therefore—since, although the three types [of consciousness], such as the wholesome (*kusala*), are equal in their capacity to constitute a factor for an offense, only the designation "wholesome" is excluded from being an offense, and not the designations "unwholesome" and so forth—this was not stated with reference to a consciousness possessing the full factors [of an offense]. Thus, "the legal issue of an offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇaṃ*).
The statement, "It may be unwholesome (akusala), it may be indeterminate (abyākata);

there is no wholesome (kusala) legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa)," was not spoken with reference to a mere state of mind that serves as a cause sufficient to fulfill the factors for originating an offense. Otherwise, one would have to say, "A legal issue arising from an offense may also be wholesome.
This implies that even the status of an offense as being unwholesome and so forth [is not absolute].
This shows that [the term] is stated merely by way of a characteristic mark (*nimitta*) and a figurative expression (*pariyāya*), and not in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). As it is said:
"That which one commits with a wholesome mind is wholesome; with the others, it is otherwise.

However, regarding the passage beginning with "But this," etc., the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) is as follows: "A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be unwholesome (*akusala*) or it may be indeterminate (*abyākata*)."
For this statement was not made with reference to some indefinite cause that might occasionally or somewhere exist;
rather, it was said with reference to that very cause which is capable of being the cause for an offense in all training rules (sikkhāpada).
For unwholesome action is the cause of every offense for one who transgresses after having learned the formal designation (paṇṇatti).
However, it is also a cause for an offense involving a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*) even for one who does not know the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).

Regarding offenses involving a formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), unwholesome states (*akusala*) do not occur solely at the moment when wholesome or indeterminate (*abyākata*) consciousness arises; at other times, they arise spontaneously.

As for the indeterminate bodily and vocal [formations], they cease at the moment of the arising of wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, as well as for one who has attained cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*).

Regarding "the offense of sleeping together": it is merely a factor (*aṅga*) of every offense, because among the six origins of offenses (*āpatti-samudāna*), there is an absence of anything devoid of bodily or verbal factors.
Therefore, this unwholesome and indeterminate nature of the offense is stated with reference specifically to the fact that all offenses are rooted in these unwholesome and indeterminate states.
However, in cases such as digging the earth, even a wholesome state can be a cause for an offense.

Even in that case, it is inappropriate to apply the designation "wholesome" to an offense by way of its proximity, because the designation of identity between what is blameworthy and what is blameless is contradictory.
To the same extent that they are mutually contradictory, to that same extent the designation of cause and effect is also inappropriate for them.
Therefore, even if wholesome [kamma] exists there, it is not subject to such designation; rather, the doors of body and speech alone are the distinct causes.

In that context, it is said to be "exclusively unwholesome" because it arises from an unwholesome mind; this is stated by way of figurative designation (*kāraṇūpacāra*). Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it refers to what is forbidden in the world.
"There is no alternative" (*vikappo natthi*) indicates that the word *siyā* has the sense of providing an alternative.

"It becomes unwholesome" means that it becomes unwholesome through figurative designation, as it is originated by the unwholesome; this is because one incurs [the offense] by means of sleeping together and so forth.

"It is indeterminate" (*abyākataṃ hoti*): because it must be incurred by way of the bodily door (*kāyadvāra*)—which is reckoned as material form (*rūpa*) and is indeterminate (*abyākata*)—consisting of the act of stretching out the back together with women and so forth, the offense (*āpatti*) is "indeterminate" by way of a metaphorical application of the cause (*kāraṇūpacārena*). "Therein" (*tattha*): in that legal issue concerning an offense consisting of a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).

"By way of intentional and unintentional" (*sañciccāsañciccavasena*): this state of alternative options refers to the manner of incurring [the offense] through knowing the formal rule and through not knowing it.
This statement was spoken with reference to this aforementioned nature of conceptualization, which is characterized as being either unwholesome (*akusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*).

If that is so, since one may incur [an offense] even through what is wholesome on the side of unintentional incurrence, this [next] statement was also spoken with reference to that conceptualization: "The legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*)."
To the question, "Why was it not said that [it] might be wholesome? he says, "But if... and so forth.
To clarify by way of origination the very meaning already stated as "of those without consciousness," he says, "even of those originating from the rubbing of sheep's wool with the foot, etc.

Regarding those originating without consciousness, the term "wholesome" (kusala)—which is inherently blameless—is applied even to the cause of a fault (āpatti) which is itself blameworthy, by means of the metaphorical usage of the word "wholesome" for its cause, namely, "one would enter upon a wholesome mind."

He shows that it is improper [to speak thus]. By the words “And not therein,” etc., having rejected the idea that it is improper to describe even the existing state of wholesome [kamma] as a cause for an offense, he shows that only the indeterminate (abyākata) states—consisting of body and speech—are the causes.
In that context, “of those that have moved and proceeded” means of those that have moved and of those that have proceeded. For the body has moved, and [speech] has proceeded.

By speech. And here, either body or speech alone is the factor (*aṅga*). And that... [as before] ...is indeterminate (*abyākata*), because it is stated precisely as such by way of being the cause of an offense for an indeterminate [action].

Thus, it is established that the statement, "The legal issue of an offense may be unwholesome (*akusala*) or it may be indeterminate," is spoken figuratively by way of a metaphorical application of the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*), and not in its primary sense (*nippariyāya*).
As for the extensive elaboration in the *Sāratthadīpanī* intended to establish that an offense possesses an unwholesome nature and so forth in a non-figurative sense,
that should not be accepted as essential, because it has already been rejected in the commentary on the *Dutthadosa-sikkhāpada*. For this very reason, here too—
in the passage beginning “the mind which is a factor of the offense”— it is shown that even an unwholesome mind serves as the cause of an offense.
The state of being distinct has thus been shown. As for what ought to be said here, that has already been demonstrated below, so we have not elaborated upon it here.

Regarding the phrase "the transgression that comes from transgressing," in this context, for one who transgresses with an unwholesome mind after having recognized [the offense], the "transgression of the offense" is said to arise from the bodily and verbal transgressions.
This same method applies to the section on the indeterminate (abyākata) as well.
The commentary on the discussion of legal issues (*adhikaraṇakathā*) is finished.

Commentary on the discussion of the principles for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇavūpasamanasamathakathā*) and so forth: In the Canon, the question begins with "A dispute as a legal issue (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), without having recourse to one method of settling... and so forth. The answer begins with "It may be... and so forth.
“*Siyātissavacanīyan*” means that it should be said, “there might be a settlement by this very [means]”; such is the meaning.

In the phrase “in the case of *sammukhāvinaya*,” it should be understood as a description emphasizing the state (*bhāvappadhāna*), namely, “because of being *sammukhāvinaya*. This applies to all sections in the same way.

“The one who acts [to reopen a settled case] reopens it”—this is merely an illustration; for whoever reopens [a settled case], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone. Regarding the committee (*ubbāhikā*).
An offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) for a matter that should be confessed (*khīyanaka*) is not mentioned there, because in that case there is no giving of consent (*chandadāna*).
235. “Having made marks of praise and dispraise” means having applied signs of small and large [size]. Therefore he said, “having fixed a perception of the sign. 242.

Regarding the phrase “the legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) ... is settled”: here the meaning should be understood as follows—that through the presence of the assembly (*sammukhāvinaya*), formal acts such as seeking permission (*apalokanā*) and so forth are successfully accomplished.
The commentary on the section concerning the settling of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇavūpasamana*) is finished.
The method of the commentary on the *Samathakkhandhaka* is completed.
5. The *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*.
Commentary on the Discussion of Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 243.
Regarding the section on minor matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka): "in the manner of eight squares" means in the form of eight compartments on a gambling board.
"In the shape of the base of a spittoon" means in the shape of the base of a spittoon for spittle. This refers to a circular support.
It is said that this is a designation for a bowl made by turning [a piece of wood] after thorns have been removed from it.

244. *Puthupāṇika*: this refers to a back-massage performed with the palms of the hands opened wide rather than being clenched into fists. It is with reference to this very thing that it is called "hand-massage" (*hatthaparikamma*).

245. Regarding "necklaces and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as earrings are included. "Hanging thread" (*palambakasutta*) refers to the form of the sacrificial threads and other ornaments worn by brahmins. "Bracelets" (*valaya*) refers to bracelets for the hands and feet.
246. "Dvaṅgule" is a plural form used for the sake of clarity; the meaning is that it is not permitted to exceed the measure of two finger-breadths.

And here they say that even for one who does not know whether two months or two finger-breadths have been exceeded, there are offenses without conscious intent (acittaka) by way of counting the hair and beard.
*With a bundle* (*kocchena*) means with a bundle made by binding together *usīra* grass and so forth, having cut them evenly. *With mud* (*cikkalena*) means with oil mixed with slime.

*Even for those whose heads are covered in dust and heated by the sun* means even for those whose heads are covered in dust and distressed by the heat. *With a wet hand* (*addahatthena*) means with a moist hand. 248–9.
*Well-sung song* (*sādhugītaṃ*) means a song associated with [themes such as] impermanence and so forth. *By a fourfold conduct* (*caturassena vattanā*) means by a complete [conduct].
By way of the mode of pronunciation. To show the common characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) of all [these], such as the wave-mode and so forth, it is said:

"of all... the characteristic. The meaning is that speaking by adding more syllables than those by which a word is complete is called "speaking with modification" (*vikārakathana*); speaking without doing so is the characteristic. "Having external hair" (*bāhiraloma*).
This is an explanation of the neuter gender: the meaning is that for one who wears [it] in such a way that external hairs are visible, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
250. In the text, "only a young mango" refers to a young mango fruit in which the seed has not yet developed.

"Having caused it to be made to fall" means having caused it to be cut down. The phrase "censured by others" is stated because of a desire for the welfare of the Dispensation; it is not [meant to imply]...
"Pariyāpuṇiṃsu" means they did not learn [it]. 251.
"The four royal families of snakes" is said because all species of snakes are subsumed within these four alone. "To make a protection for oneself" means to make a safeguard for oneself.
"May there be loving-kindness (mettā) toward the Virūpakkhas" means: may there be a state of friendship between me and the nāgas belonging to the Virūpakkha lineage; may there be *mettā*.
"May they be" is the meaning; the intention is: "May they be happy, free from suffering, and without enmity. For it is in this way that the pervasion with loving-kindness (*mettā*) occurs.
The same method applies to the others as well. "By those without feet" shows the pervasion of loving-kindness toward all beings without exception, including the families of snakes.
"May no footless creature harm me" shows the establishment of self-protection through that loving-kindness.

“*Sabbe sattā*,” etc., shows the all-encompassing radiation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward all beings by taking oneself as the analogy. In that context, “may no evil come to anyone” means: may no being—no matter how base—encounter anything that causes suffering, and may suffering not come upon them.
Having thus shown the protection of oneself through loving-kindness, the words beginning with “immeasurable” (*appamāṇo*) are now spoken to show it by way of recollecting the Triple Gem.
In this regard, unwholesome states are the factors that create limits, and their results are likewise limited; their opposites, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, are immeasurable.
The qualities and their results—the mundane and supramundane fruits—are immeasurable; because he possesses these, he is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇo*).

Alternatively, he is "immeasurable" because he possesses immeasurable, boundless qualities. "Limited" (*pamāṇavantāni*) means endowed with the aforementioned characteristics that constitute limitation.
"Snakes and scorpions" is a specific enumeration of reptiles. "Spiders" refers to a hairy-bellied monkey.
*Sarabūti* means *gharagoḷikā* (a house-sparrow).
*Paṭikkamantu* means "let them go away," the sense being "let them not cause me distress. In the phrase *sohaṃ nama*, there is an ellipsis for the word "I perform" (*karomi*).
Since protection has been established by me for both you and myself through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], and since I am that very person who belongs to the Blessed One...
"I pay homage; I pay homage to the seven [Buddhas] beginning with Vipassī"—this is the construction [of the phrase], "therefore let the spirits depart.

"In another" means that it is to be severed by means of the mental attention to foulness (*asubha-manasikāra*) and so forth regarding sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "The member" refers to the male organ devoid of seed.
For they say that when the seed is cut, one who is a *opakkamika-paṇḍaka* (one who becomes impotent through artificial means) becomes incapable [of procreation]. Some [say this].
However, they say that even at the moment of cutting off the seed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

and when the male faculty and so forth have gradually ceased, one is called a paṇḍaka, being incapable [of the religious life], and at that time he must be expelled for the destruction of his characteristic marks.
Or, "causing such suffering" means causing suffering to oneself by means of blows with the fist and so forth.

252. Regarding the phrase "this bowl is yours" in the Pāli, he speaks with reference to what was said by the merchant: "Whatever is given to one who is both an Arahant and possessed of psychic power, that [is indeed given]. Having taken that bowl, he circumambulated Rājagaha three times;
here, having circumambulated the city three times in the sky above the bowl that was fastened to a succession of bamboo poles...
The phrase "having taken the bowl" is said with reference to its state of being stationary; however, the Elder did not himself take the bowl with his hand.

Some, however, say: "By the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), that bowl released itself from the succession of bamboo poles and stood following the Elder, appearing as if it had been grasped by his hand. It remained exactly in that position.
However, it was said with reference to this that he "took the bowl from the hand of Bhāradvāja.
And as for those people... [as before] ... "they followed after," meaning those people who had not seen the first miracle followed the Elder, saying, "Show us the miracle as well!
And the Elder, assuming the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth, displayed his power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*).
He displayed them, and they, filled with wonder and amazement, raised a loud clamor. Therefore he said: "What, Ānanda, is this loud clamor, this great noise?

Regarding the statement that a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) should not be displayed, it refers to one who, having abandoned his natural form, displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga... [and so on] ...or displays various military arrays.

Thus, it is the *vikubbaṇiddhi* (power of transformation) that is intended here, which proceeds by bringing about changes in one’s own body as it has arrived; therefore he said, "But the power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is not excluded.

By nature, one who is single visualizes many—whether a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand—and having visualized them, resolves through knowledge, "May I become many"; it is in this way that it is demonstrated by way of resolve.
This is called "accomplished supernatural power through resolve" (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*). "Household items" (*gihivikaṭāni*) means things belonging to householders.
253. "Not touched" in the text means they have not been contacted. "Covered with forms" (*rūpakākiṇṇāni*) means covered with female forms and so forth.
254. "Supported by the ground" refers to bracelets or rings made of ivory and the like. Because this bracelet-supporter is not high...
Regarding the statement that "the bowls placed [there] do not fall," it is said that "it is permissible to place three bowls.
This is called a "ground-support" (*bhūmi-ādhāraka*) with reference to its height.

As for "wooden supports and staff supports," these refer to supports made from a single piece of wood and supports made from many staffs; these are higher and have the nature of falling together with the bowls.
Therefore, it is said, "well-prepared. "Like the edge of a lathe" means like the edge of that lathe where one inserts the bowl-forming tool (*dhamakaraṇa*) and so forth and carves;
because such a wooden support is not wide enough, even if the bowl is placed upon it, it falls off, and thus it is called "unstable."
"Ālindaka-miḍḍhikā-dīnaṃ" means of the parapets on the front porch and so forth; the meaning is "those situated on high foundations.
"On the outer wall" means on the exterior plastering of palaces and the like. "On a thin parapet" means on a railing (*vedikā*).
In all cases, however, it is permissible to place [the bowl] within the distance of a hand's span; but on a support, it is even permissible beyond that.
In the Pāli, *oṭṭha* means the rim of the mouth. *Pattamāḷaka* refers to a railing-like structure built higher than the ground for the purpose of preventing termites from climbing up.
"Shaped like a large-mouthed bowl" means shaped like a large-mouthed vessel (*cāṭi*).
Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who hangs it [up]," they say this applies to hanging up the bowl alone, not to hanging up the bag; however, this should be investigated.
"But with another article" means with another binding strap or article.
Because it is said, "having bound it, let him hang it," it is permissible to bind it in every way so that the shoulder-strap of the bowl-bag does not slip from the place where it is fastened.
However, even after binding it, it is not permissible to place it on top; thus, "on top... [is the conclusion].

It is said that they sit down after spreading [the cloth] and break it. In that context, "it is permissible to place it there" is stated because there is no suspicion of its being used as a sitting-cloth (*nisīdana*).
"Or having tied it up" means having placed the umbrella (*chatta*) after tying it. "Whosoever" refers to one who has either food in his bowl or an empty bowl. 255.
"To carry about" means to set it out for the purpose of wandering for alms day by day. By one who does not obtain a bowl...
However, on a certain day, after wandering for alms and eating, it is permissible to discard [the remainder]. Therefore he said: "It is permissible to consume it as a temporary loan.
The same principle applies to leaf-wraps and so forth. *Abhuṃ me* means "destruction is mine"; the meaning is "ruin is mine.
In the Pāḷi text, *pisāco vata maṃ* means "alas, this is a demon to me," or rather, this is the very reading: *pisāco vatāyaṃ*. *Pisācillikā* means...

"Pisācadārakā" means children of demons. "Chavasīsassa patto" means a bowl belonging to a corpse-head; this genitive case is used here to express the relationship between the natural object and its modification.

"Cabbetvā" means having spat out. Because it is stated, "having made a receiving-vessel," it is permissible to take water with the hand that has food remnants, sprinkle it over the bowl, and wash the hand by means of rinsing and wiping; by this much alone, the bowl [is purified].
Having accepted [the food], it is said that the hand has not yet been washed. "Taking a mouthful of water" means:

either taking up water directly from there without touching the bowl and forming a mouthful with the soiled hand, or lifting the bowl with the left hand and taking a mouthful with the mouth; both are permitted. "Rinsing with water outside" means: [rinsing] with water taken from outside.
It is permissible even to take [food] outside after having scraped off a mere morsel from two fingers. Regarding the phrase "desiring to chew it":
here, one is not permitted to set aside what is fit for others to eat, even if one desires to eat it oneself.
"Having done right there" means without removing it from its original place in the bowl itself. "Having plucked it out" means having extracted that very meat from there without remainder.
256. “With flour mixed with yeast” means with flour mixed with *surā* (fermented liquor). “To smear” means to smear the needle.
“A ladder” (*nisseṇi*) refers even to a cloth-strip sewn together by making it four cubits long and square, using four sticks;
for here, having sewn the edges of the robe evenly, they stitch the robe as desired. “To be spread upon” means upon that ladder.
It should be spread over the robe for the purpose of providing support.

Regarding the phrase "by which" (*yāyā*) and so forth, he says this because the compound *kathinarajju*—meaning the rope used for binding the robe on the ladder known as the *kaṭhina*—is a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (a compound with the middle term elided).
In that context, since wrinkles (*valiyo*) arise when one of two layers becomes excessive, therefore, regarding a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*)...
Both chapters should be understood together as referring to the binding cord and the hard (kathina) cord.
In the text, "it wears out within the kathina" means that the limit of the robe bound during the kathina period wears out.
For here, the robe dependent upon the kathina is called "kathina" by way of figurative dependence (*nissaya-vohāra*), just as in expressions such as "the beds are crying out. *Anuvātaṃ*...

They border it: having sewn a border both lengthwise and crosswise using any kind of cloth strips around the edge of the robe for the sake of its durability, one should make it such that, after inserting cords and wrapping them around the poles, it can be pulled taut so as to be equal to the robe. Such [is the manner].

The meaning [of the term *anuvāta*] is as follows. Some, however, say: "The making of a border (*anuvātaparibhaṇḍa*) was permitted specifically for the sake of preventing the decay of materials such as palm-leaf mats that are classified as *kathina*. "In the middle of it" means within the period of the old *kathina*.

"According to the measure of the monk" means according to the measure of the monk’s robe. "Another ladder" means having placed another staff both in length and in width, one should fasten [the cloth].
*Bidalakanti* is a designation for a specific action known as doubling; thus he said, "doubling.
*Pavesanasalākanti* refers to a bamboo splinter or similar object used for insertion to prevent the folds from catching. In the text, *paṭiggaha* means a finger-cuff.
(257) *Pāti* is a particular type of vessel used for setting out goods. In the text, *paṭiggahathavikā* means a bag for vessels such as bowls and the like.
"To build" means to construct with bricks and so forth for the purpose of preventing the fall of the upper part of the structure.
"Supporting beam" refers to the supporting ropes, poles, and the like. "It breaks apart" means that the hard core, such as straw or reeds, collapses in the middle of the frame.
"Having raised it up" is said with reference to the pole-frame (*daṇḍakaṭhina*).
258–9. Water that is *akappiya* (unallowable) is water containing living beings. *Upanandhi* means to bind enmity. Regarding the phrase "the highway must be traversed":

here, a "highway" (*addhānamagga*) refers to a distance of one-and-a-half *yojanas*. For one desiring to traverse such a distance, there is an offense in intentionally crossing the vicinity of a monastery.

However, for one who has gone unintentionally, having stood where he remembers [the rule], if he does not formally resolve (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*) the corner of his outer robe (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇa*) or similar items—
It should be understood that there is an offense for each step taken in walking away.

"Is not approved" means it is not sufficient. 260. "With a body full of secretions" means with a body accumulated with humors such as phlegm and so forth. "In the middle of that" means in the middle of the door-bolt.
"Above" means on the upper part of the door-bolt. "The place for placing water" means a place demarcated and prepared for the purpose of holding water.

261. In the text, *udapāna* means a well. *Nīcavatthuka* refers to the banked area surrounding the well; the meaning is that it stands level with the ground. *Udakena otthariyyati* means that rainwater coming from all sides falls into the well.

262. *Vāhenti* means they draw [the water] up. An *arahataghaṭiyanta* is a wheel-shaped device consisting of many spokes, to which buckets are fastened at each spoke, and which is rotated by one or two people.

263. *Āviddhapakkhapāsakaṃ* means having side-panels (*pakkhapāsaka*) placed all around the central circle (*kaṇṇikamaṇḍala*). *Maṇḍale* refers to the central circle. *Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvā* means having placed wooden boards and so forth in a square shape all around.
264. Some say that what is called a *namataka* is like a rug (*santhatasadi*). Others, however, say it is "made of tree bark.

*Cammakhaṇḍaparihārena* means by way of the rules for bedding and seating (*sayanāsana*), without having formally determined [the object] through a ritual act (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*). *Peḷāya* refers to a box in the form of an octagon, a hexagon, and so forth.

It is a vessel-shaped box. This is a designation for a support in the shape of a vessel, such as that into which hot rice-milk and so forth are placed, and upon which a food bowl is set so that the heat of the meal does not dissipate.
For this very reason, it is called an "āsittakūpadhāna" in the Pāḷi; and its meaning is "a support for what has been poured in," namely, the rice-milk and so forth.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, people in the border regions do not know how to make this "spittoon-stand" (āsittakūpadhāna); they make it only in the Middle Country.
However, some say that "any vessel made of iron and so forth, even if used by householders, conforms to the category of the spittoon-stand";
others, however, say that "a vessel made of allowable metal conforms only to the category of the *maḷorikā*. This should be understood after careful investigation.
Previously, the support for protecting the bowl was permitted; now, the *maḷorikā* (a bowl-cover) is permitted for the purpose of eating.
"Holed" (*chidda*) means having holes; "pierced" (*viddha*) means having a hole bored through the middle; "perforated" (*āviddha*) means having holes all around.
265. Regarding the phrase "the bowl is overturned": here, the overturning occurs by way of making it impossible to consume [the food] through the formal act (*kammavācā*).
Not by turning the bowls face down. Therefore he said, “Let the Sangha impose non-association with the Sangha,” and so forth;
the meaning is that the Sangha should, by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*), impose non-association with the Sangha upon that *vaḍḍha*.
“He should overturn the bowl” means he should carry out the disciplinary act of overturning the bowl against the *vaḍḍha*. Non-association with the Sangha...
"Acting" means the act of the Saṅgha to impose non-association upon Vaḍḍha. The meaning is: acting in such a way that non-association occurs.
Regarding the passage "he was overturned... [etc. ...non-association with the Saṅgha," the meaning should be understood here as "there is non-association with the Saṅgha.
Thus, because the Blessed One has commanded this act of non-association and because the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has been recited, [the penalty is established].

And because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "no gift whatsoever should be accepted," there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who, knowing it belongs to him, accepts it when his bowl has been turned upside down; thus, it should be accepted [only under proper conditions].
"Transgression" (*accaya*) means proceeding by overstepping the practice of the method; the sense is "offense. "He has transgressed against me" (*maṃ accagamā*) means me...
"Having transgressed and proceeded [further]" means: "We accept that from you," which is to say, we forgive that offense of yours.
In such passages as "he strives for the non-acquisition of requisites for the bhikkhus," the meaning should be understood as "one who has desisted from striving for the non-acquisition of requisites.
Regarding the phrase "non-association with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," the word "done" (*kato*) is to be supplied as a missing portion of the text.
268. "As far as the last step of the staircase" refers to the first step of the staircase;
for it was said so because that [step] was subsequently covered with cloth.

When the Elder said, "The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations," he meant that there would be censure in the future due to monks stepping on a robe used as a foot-wiping cloth, and thus the laying down of the training rule.
He spoke out of compassion for the Blessed One, intending [the phrase] "by way of warding off. "One whose womb has departed" means one who has given birth to a child.

Therefore he said, "for the sake of auspiciousness. 269–270. "A fan" refers to a four-sided fan. "An umbrella made of a single leaf" refers to an umbrella made from a single leaf, such as a palm leaf.
274–5. "For the sake of protection" means for the purpose of guarding by way of taking possession. "They let it grow long" means together with their hair.

They have it shaved and then have it shaped. "Four-cornered" means having made it square so that four corners are discernible—two above at the temples and two below on the sides of the jaw—they have it trimmed.
In the text, "they have the beard-shaft shaped" means they shave the hair on the upper lip and then shape it. "Rudhi" means a small wound.
277. In the text, “a collection of metal utensils and bronze utensils” means a hoard of metal utensils and bronze utensils.
“A mere binding” refers to a binding made of iron for the purpose of preventing axes, chisels, and so forth from falling off their handles.
“Thread” refers to thread stretched out in that shape for the purpose of weaving.

278. By the statement, “Where one remembers, there it should be tied,” it is shown that there is no offense for one who has entered [the village] after failing to tie the waistband due to non-intentionality. Regarding the phrase “made by wrapping it in the shape of a drum-head”:

some say this means it was made by joining many ropes together and then weaving them with threads of various colors; others say it may even be made from a single-colored thread by fashioning it into forms such as rings or loops.
Having shown [the example], even a *muraja* (drum) that is wrapped is permissible; however, it must be wrapped continuously after being made smooth, without showing any change in its form.

For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary on the second *pārājika*: "If many ropes are joined together and wrapped continuously with one [rope], it should not be called 'made of many ropes'; it is permissible. This refers to the *muddika-kāyabandhana* (a belt for the body).
It was prepared without having been made square. The ends of the fringe (*pāmaṅgada*) are square. "In the shape of a mudiṅga drum" means in the form of the head of a *varaka* (a type of drum).
"The end" (*pāsanta*) refers to the conclusion of the fringe. 279.

In the text, regarding the phrase "the board for the knot (*gaṇṭhika*) and the board for the loops (*pāsaka*)," it is permitted to place the knots and loops upon boards made of wood, ivory, or other materials, and then set them down with the robe. "The corner is opened" means the side facing the wind is opened.

280–1. A *pāḷikāraka* is one who establishes monks in the *pāḷi* according to their seniority. It is likewise not permitted for him to wear [the robe] in that manner. In the *pāḷi*, "muṇḍavaṭṭī" refers to wrestlers and the like. 282.

"By a standard finger-breadth" means by the carpenter’s finger-breadth (*vaḍḍhakī-aṅgula*). Some, however, say "by a natural finger-breadth" (*pakati-aṅgula*), but that does not accord with the statement regarding the four-finger-breadth limit at the back.
For a measurement of four finger-breadths by a natural finger-breadth is not [the same as] the standard measure.
"He is able to chew a tooth-stick that has become stuck in his throat.

(285) Regarding the phrase "corrupting the Buddha’s word in their own dialect" (*sakāya niruttiyā*): since the Māgadhī language is easy for everyone to speak, the meaning is that even those of low birth, when learning it, corrupt [the word].
(289) "May they not trouble the monks" means: may they not distress the monks with the smell of garlic.
291. *Avalekhanapīṭha* means a specific vessel for placing the wood used for scraping. *Apidhāna* means a lid, such as a wooden cover, and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of minor items is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Khandhaka of Minor Items is completed.
6. The Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka):
Explanation of the Discussion on the Permission for Monasteries (Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 295.
In the Chapter on Lodgings, "in the cold season" (sisire) means during the time of the cold; by way of the falling of snow, and by way of the falling of rain lasting seven days or more.
And because the harsh sensation of cold that has arisen is intended here, he says "that which is touched. The word "tato" (from that) is an ablative used in the sense of the agent;
thus the meaning is that the wind and heat are warded off by means of that dwelling, as he says "it is warded off by the dwelling. 296.
"The hole for drawing [the bolt]" is where one inserts a finger or a cord, chain, and so forth, to pull the door.
"Drawing [it] along, they cause it to touch the doorpost"—this is its designation.
To show that there is nothing improper regarding the use of a lodging, it was said: "Even if with the tip of a leopard's paw," and so forth.

Or, similar to a railing on a cetiya, having fixed either a window-lattice or a net, one should, in place of wood, [construct it] with bricks and so forth, just like the cloth-stripes and other decorations on the railing of a cetiya.
Having shown the strips and so forth above and across, it was made provided with four openings.
A "pillar window" (*thambhaka-vātapāna*) is one made by not placing wooden beams across horizontally, but rather by means of beams set vertically.

To "bind a cloth foot-wiper" means to bind something like a foot-wiper out of cloth or similar material, according to the dimensions of a window, for the purpose of preventing bats and the like from entering.
The meaning is "to speak. *Miḍḍhaka* refers to a structure made of wood, clay, or other materials in the shape of a bed-platform with a railing.
297. *Caturassapīṭha* means "square-shaped. "A foot eight finger-breadths high is permissible" means that only one eight finger-breadths high is permitted.
"Even one exceeding the measure is permissible" is said with reference specifically to the square-shaped [stool]. As for the *āyatacaturassā* (rectangular ones)...
However, even those with seven or five legs are not permitted if they have high feet. A "Bhadra-seat" (bhaddapīṭha) is one made of rattan in a square or other such shape;
thus it is said, "a seat made of rattan. "Above the wooden plank" means below the wooden surface that stands in the form of a crossbar, having placed the foot upwards.
It is said "above" with reference to the time of insertion. [The same applies to] the two hind legs of a sheep.
However, because it stands in a curved shape like a goat's leg, it is called an "eḷakapādapīṭha" (goat-footed stool). "They overturn" means they turn them over together with the beds.
Having excluded trees and creepers, he says "of whatever kind of grasses" and so forth, meaning that all remaining types of grass such as *gaccha* and the like are included.
"Upadahanti" means they place [it]. "The measure of the head" refers to that space where the entire head, together with the neck, can be placed;
showing that its width is the measure of a fist, he says "in width," and so forth.
This demonstrates the measure of the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow. By means of that, [the measure] of the pillow...

The measurement of the width is determined by cutting it into either a circle or a square and sewing it together, such that from edge to edge the broadest part is one *muṭṭhi-ratana* (a fist’s breadth) wide; it should be sewn in this manner.
Anything more than this is not permitted. Furthermore, the cloth placed at the ends, reaching from edge to edge, should be doubled.
It has three corners. Among those three corners, the distance between two corners is one span and four finger-breadths;
the middle portion, from end to end, measures one fist-length (muṭṭhiratana). This is its maximum measurement.
Therefore he said, "In the three corners," and so forth.

Since it is stated in general terms that "only a woolen blanket... indeed comes under the category of a woolen mattress (*uṇṇabhisi*)," it should be understood that even an unallowable woolen covering, such as one made of *gonaka* wool, is permissible to use for sleeping provided it is placed inside a mattress.
"In a *masūraka*" refers to a leather mattress. However, a leather bolster, even if filled with cotton, is not allowed.
In the Canon, "cloth for bed requisites" (*senāsanaparikkhāradussa*) means cloth intended for making bed requisites. "Mattress" (*bhisi*).

*Onandhitun* means to bind after having placed it inside a mattress (*bhisi*). *Paribhijjati* means that when being moved from a bed or similar place, the mattress is torn as it is rubbed against the corners of chairs and so forth by those sitting down.

*Onaddhamañca* refers to a bed that has been bound with a mattress attached as one unit. In the text, "tearing off and carrying away the skin" refers to thieves [carrying away] the skin of the mattress.
"They carry it away" means they take it by thieves. "To mark it" means to apply drops of liquid as a sign after it has been carried away by thieves.
"Wall-work" means the making of decorative lines in various colors. "Hand-work" means making any kind of sign with the hand.
"Does not fall into the text" means it does not adhere to it. "Having struck" means having rubbed against it. "It does not bind" means it is not binding; the meaning is that it does not stick.

299. “One does not even get to say ‘Do it’”—because even the mere command is prohibited, it is permissible to address the gatekeeper by way of various expressions such as, “Why do you not do [it]? Regarding the *Jātakapakaraṇa*:
any form whatsoever associated with the Jātakas—whether female, male, or otherwise—is intended. Because it is stated, “to have others cause it to be made,” this includes even an image of the Buddha.
One is not permitted to do it oneself. In the text, *pañcapaṭika* refers to the fivefold ornamentation consisting of the [five] types beginning with birth.
300. "There is no space" means that there is no room for walking all around the outside of the womb.
"Having pierced a tree" means having pierced near the top of a hewn heartwood log. "Having made" means having made a hole. "Fashioned" (*kappakataṃ*).
Having struck it like a pillar made of heartwood, it was said, "This is the 'brought-in' base of the wall. To establish it firmly on the ground for the purpose of support:
having lifted the old base of the wall, which has an equal weight externally, by means of a wooden block (kappasīsa) placed upon the stump, one should establish it on the ground by its root.
For the purpose of protection: [the protection] of the place where rain falls upon a hut that has been plastered both inside and out.
"For the sake of protection. "A screen" (*kiṭika*) means a covering made of palm leaves and the like. "Tamped clay" (*madditamattika*) is mentioned for the purpose of sealing a leak caused by rain.
"Having cleared a space on both sides of the wall" means that the area is prepared so that those standing outside do not see those sitting inside directly.
Thus, by way of closing it facing the door, he describes the place made by joining the wall and the other side of the door.
"A railing all around" means having an entrance (pamukha) pierced on every side.
"Having set up a bamboo" means having dug a post into the ground to the height of a man, and having placed and fixed upon them a side-bamboo resembling a back-bamboo. One...
Having extended the pole by placing one end against the very high edge of the monastery wall and the other end on the ground at the base of a bamboo backrest.
A "wheel-fastened box" (*kiṭika*) is like a door; it is a box with a wheel-attachment for the purpose of easily opening and closing it.
In the text, it is called an "opening box" (*ugghāṭana-kiṭika*); when not needed in marketplaces and such places, it is lifted up and fastened above.
The rear entrance-porch: having raised it by means of wooden capitals or supporting pillars, there is also the rear entrance-porch.
301. “The drinking water is heated” means the water placed in the drinking-water vessels is warmed by the sun.
303. “Three enclosures” means three perimeters. “A bamboo enclosure” includes all enclosures made of wood. “A thorn hedge” refers to all enclosures made of branches.

305. "The light vanished": that great radiance which had arisen through the power of the joy inspired by the Buddha as his object—by which his path became free from darkness as if illuminated by a thousand lamps—vanished when the force of his joy subsided out of fear upon reaching the raw charnel ground outside the city, which was crowded with corpses, foul-smelling, and loathsome.

In the verse beginning with "A hundred elephants," the meaning should be understood by joining each instance with the word "thousand," as in "a hundred thousand elephants. Regarding "the movement of a single step":
this refers to the movement of even a single step taken by one who goes for the sake of the Triple Gem, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Buddha";
the meaning is that it is the fruit of the wholesome karma conditioned by that [act]. Its sixteenth part—*kalaṃ*.
All those previously mentioned elephants and so forth are not worth even a sixteenth part of that [merit]; they do not equal it. This is merely an illustration;
they are not worth even a hundred-thousandth part.

"The darkness vanished" means it disappeared when light arose through powerful joy. "Attachments" refers to cravings (*taṇhā*). "Building work" refers to the construction work for the sake of the objects to be given.

309. *Dadeyya* means he should grant authority over the monastery in order to undertake new construction (*navakamma*). *Dinno* means the monastery has been granted for the purpose of performing new construction; or, the meaning is that new construction has been assigned to the monastery.

313–4. *Santhāgāre* means in an assembly hall. *Okāse* means in a dwelling place. *Uddissa kataṃ* means built specifically for the Saṅgha. *Gihivikaṭaṃ* means made or prepared by laypeople; the meaning is "belonging to laypeople.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of monasteries is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Taking Lodgings (Senāsanaggāhakathāvaṇṇanā) 318. “Every month, every month”: this is a demonstration of the time limit for the giving of requisites twice;
the same applies to the subsequent instances. He states the reason for the statement “it should not be taken” with the words “for by means of that very requisite,” and so forth.
The intention is that, having relied upon those very conditions and lived there, they will provide maintenance.
*Ubbhaṇḍikā* means they will have their belongings removed. *Dīghasālā* is the walking-hall (*caṅkamanasālā*).
*Maṇḍalamāḷo* is the assembly hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*). *Anudahati* means it oppresses. By the phrase "it is not permitted not to give," [the text indicates] for one who intentionally does not give.
It is explained that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for entering after having been turned back.
To clarify the meaning of what was stated as "the village of alms-resort must not be disturbed," it was said: "people there must not be told [this]," and so forth.
"Having cut off the thought" means: "seeing him going in this manner, they will stop him and provide the requisites."
"Without giving rise to such a thought. "A covering for goods" means a covering for articles; the meaning is a robe for covering the body.
The statement, "It is blameless precisely because of the purity of the mind," was said with reference to the explanation of the reason at the moment the question was asked;
it is not [the case] that there is no fault even for one with an impure mind when answering a question that has been asked. This being so:
It should be understood that this was said with reference to not going under the impression that they would question me.
"They should be looked after" means they should be maintained by repairing what is broken or dilapidated, sweeping, and so forth.
"On the muddavedikā" refers to the square platform above the jar-shaped *hammiya* platform of the cetiya. "Why should it be asked? and so forth.
This is because one obtains it by way of its natural state (*pakati*).
Furthermore, this was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the reason for the inquiry. "Having stepped back" means having moved away from the monastery. Showing that meaning, he said:
"It is at a distance of one or two *yojanas*. "Having set aside a deposit" means having set aside coins such as *kahāpaṇa*s for interest, or having designated fields and so forth.

"Thus, 'given through faith' (saddhādeyya)" means: in the sense of what is to be given out of faith, as explained by the method stated above, regarding the object of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gains.
"But the property" (*vatthu*) refers to the money (*rūpiya*) that has arisen from the local source (*tatruppāda*);

and because it has arisen from such things as fields given [with the instruction], "Enjoy the four requisites from this," it is [placed] in the hands of the managers of allowable goods (*kappiyakāraka*) with the words, "Enjoy allowable articles."
“It becomes like an object given by donors,” thus he said, “by means of the kappiyakārakas,” and so forth.

“For the well-being of the Saṅgha” means for the benefit of the Saṅgha. “By way of individuals” means by way of the apprehension of individuals, such as “the bhikkhus are distressed for lack of robes,” and not by way of the apprehension of the Saṅgha, such as “the Saṅgha is distressed.
To clarify the meaning already stated in general terms as “by way of allowable goods,” he says: “specifically by way of robes, rice, and so forth.”
And so it is said. Here, the letter *ca* should be understood as functioning in the sense of the particle *pana*, and not in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
To show the manner of seeking permission (*apalokana*) both by way of the person and by way of the allowable article (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*), it is said:
"But that should be done thus," and so forth.

"Having observed the requisite of robes" means having delimited the quantity of the requisite known as robes—obtained during that rains-residence by way of gifts of faith, small offerings, and so forth—as being "only this much. "Of the lodging" refers to the assigning of lodgings.
"A junior [assigns] for an elder, and an elder for a junior"—this refers to the assignment of lodgings by oneself for oneself.
It is said that "taking hold" (*gahaṇa*) is inappropriate; the intention is that two [people] should take hold of one another.
It is permissible to appoint eight or even sixteen people; thus, it is permissible to appoint all of them together with a single formal act of motion (*kammavācā*).
For the Saṅgha does not perform an act of censure against itself. Therefore, in the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka, regarding the appointment for a committee of inquiry (*ubbāhika-kamma-sammuti*):
"Eight people are authorized together.

"Image house" means a shrine room for statues. "Road" refers to a hall built on a road leading toward a village that lies within the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīma). The same applies to lotus ponds, the foot of trees, and so forth.
"They receive" means that the monks residing there receive [the offerings]. "Having disentangled" means [having divided] into portions sufficient for each individual.
"Having separated them. "Having assigned them to the dwellings" means having conveyed by word of mouth: "Let those living in such-and-such and such-and-such dwellings receive what arises from here.
"It should be entered" means that the gain should be received while staying in the large-lot pariveṇa;
this is the intended meaning.

"Even this" refers here to the one who is a refuse-rag wearer (*paṃsukūlika*) who relinquishes the requisite. The construction is: "This requisite for robes is also [included] as that which has been relinquished by him.
"Placing it at the base of his feet and giving a cloth" means the donors of the requisite give it.

By this, he shows that even what is given by householders after being placed at the base of the feet is permissible for refuse-rag wearers. Then, they say, "We give the *vassāvāsika* (the rainy-season gift)."
In this context, the phrase "it is not permitted for those who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūlika)" must be supplied and connected [to the following].
"Of monks who have completed the rains residence" refers to monks other than those who wear rag-robes.

"Having made a binding agreement, it should be caused to be taken" means that after staying here among the trees and so forth, one should cause them to take the robe by making a formal agreement, saying, "Take the robe."
The phrase "from the dawn of the first day of the waxing moon," and so forth, is stated with reference to the day of entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*).

However, it is permissible to receive [the robes] even after passing over the first day of the waxing moon if one has been released from the interval. "Having established a fixed routine" means having made an agreement regarding duties to be performed continuously, such as recitation and mental attention (*manasikāra*).
"Plastering with alkaline substances" refers to the preparation of the ground using solutions of alkaline liquids.

"Threefold" means threefold by way of the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*paṭivedha*). "Having purified" means having examined [the practitioner] regarding their conduct and so forth.
"The duty of wandering alone" refers to the work of meditation (*bhāvanākamma*); for it is so called because one must act as a wanderer alone, having abandoned association with a group.
The "discourse on the ten bases" refers to the discourse on fewness of desires, contentment, seclusion, non-association, and so forth.
The ten are: the undertaking of energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

The "rule regarding the use of tooth-sticks" refers to the practice stated in the discourse on stealing and the discourse on mouth-washing, concerning tooth-sticks placed in a tooth-stick shed, such as: "Only one tooth-stick should be taken each day," and so forth.
"Or a bowl... and so forth, up to "should not be spoken of," is stated for the purpose of protecting the bowl. "Improper talk" refers to frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

"The conduct of the Khandhaka" refers to the conduct remaining after the conduct for alms-gathering, as that has been taken separately under the heading of "conduct for wandering for alms" within the Khandhaka on Conduct.
Now, in order to show the procedure for dealing with the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) given by donors to those who have completed their final year of residence, it is begun with the words:
"But on the day of the final entry into the rains. If an incoming monk (*āgantuka*) arrives after the robes have been distributed, he is the incoming monk.

"At the place where [the robe] was obtained" means at the place where it was obtained according to seniority (*vassagga*). "Those who entered the rains first" refers to those who entered the rains earlier.
They had already entered the rains residence for the later period even before the arrival of the newcomer.
"What has been obtained, what has been obtained" means the robes that have come from the donors one after another.
"Neither the owner of the rains-residence robe" is said because his rains residence was interrupted. This is because the agreement had already been made at the very beginning.
"It is said, 'they do not get it without having taken [it]'; the intention is that those who prevent it from being given incur a debt.
'It should be given to them alone' means it should be given only to certain individuals among those who have entered the rains residence but have not received the *vassāvāsa* (rains-bathing) gift.
'Obtained by performing labor' means obtained by performing labor such as serving at the water station and so forth. But as for 'belonging to the Sangha,' etc., this refers to some [cases]."
The viewing for debate. In that regard, it was taken after performing an act of formal announcement (*apalokanakamma*);

thus, by performing an announcement in the manner described immediately above—“It is pleasing to give both the *vassāvāsika* [robe] of those whose rains-residence is broken and the *vassāvāsika* now arising to these”—it was taken because it was given by the Saṅgha;
therefore, even one who has gone forth (*vibbhanta*) receives it, let alone one whose rains-residence is broken. By way of the requisite conditions...

However, some teachers say that even one who has entered the rains residence for three months does not receive [the robe]—even if he has settled his wages, even if his rains residence is cut short, or even if he has left the order—because he himself has consented to take it and because the donors have also consented. And this [rule] is authoritative because it was stated later.
For that very reason, regarding a monk who has accepted the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence robe) given by the donors on the very day of the entry into the rains residence:
It was only the dwelling itself that was prescribed below [in the rule] without making a formal termination of the rains; it was not the duty of providing water, etc., or the performance of services.

For if that [duty] were indeed fixed [as part of the assignment], then only the performance of services would have been prescribed. Therefore, it should be understood that those who have broken the rains-retreat and others do not receive what has been assigned by means of the *vassa*-assignment.

By the phrase “it belongs to the Saṅgha,” it is shown that even for those who have completed the rains residence, their share of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence gift) has not been released from the status of being the Saṅgha’s property;
thus, through their departure (*vibbhama*), it becomes the property of the Saṅgha. Regarding the word “obtains”:
it is said that by merely causing the donors to accept [the gift] with the words, “Give this person my allotted share,” it is separated from the status of being the Saṅgha’s property.

"An excellent portion for the novice" is said because he is the first to receive a share; because the Elder had already taken the first portion previously; and because what is being taken now constitutes the second portion.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the allocation of lodgings is finished.
The commentary on the story of Upananda follows.

319. In the Pāli, the term *paribāhiro* (one who is excluded) is stated in both instances because, in sequence, one has been excluded from both; it does not mean being excluded from both in every respect. Therefore he said: “In the latter... [it] remains. 320. *Yaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pahoti*:
that seat, excluding beds and chairs, which is capable of comfortably accommodating three people—this is the "longer seat for the last.
Here, even those who do not share a common seat (*asamānāsanika*) may sit among the three who are free from beds and chairs.

They receive [two seats]. However, regarding beds and chairs, there are two. On long benches or on beds and chairs, only those who share the same seat may sit together in twos, because it has been permitted only for groups of two.
A "Hatthinakha" is a palace; it is called a "Hatthinakha" because it has what is called a "nakha" (claw) on its lower part. This is the name for the palace.
The lower part [of the palace] resembles a toenail; it stands adorned with many elephant forms in all directions.
Because the palace built upon it appears as if resting on an elephant’s forehead (kumbha), he says, "resting on an elephant’s forehead.
The phrase "variegated with gold, silver, and so forth" is said with reference to monastic lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha. As for private [lodgings]...
However, it is not even permissible for a monk to accept gold and other such diverse items, because it has been stated:

"In no way whatsoever should gold or silver be accepted. For this very reason, it is not mentioned in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) here as being in either a communal monastery (*saṅghika-vihāra*) or a private dwelling (*puggalika-vihāra*);
rather, it is stated regarding unallowable goods (*akappiya-bhaṇḍa*) such as woolen blankets (*gonaka*) and so forth, even in the case of a single monk.
