Because there is no fault in taking them up. "In the manner of a householder's offering" means by an offering made by householders;
the meaning is: by the method given after householders have spread out what belongs to themselves. "They may be used" means they may be sat upon.
The commentary on the story of Upananda is finished.

Commentary on the Discussion of Non-Distributable Articles (Avissajjiyavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 321. *Arañjara*: a large trough that holds much water; it is called an *arañjara* because it is capable of holding water.
Regarding the five categories beginning with "stable" (*thāvara*) and "unstable" (*a-thāvara*), the first two are stable, while the latter three are unstable.

It should be understood as "heavy goods. Regarding the phrase "he gives at the same time": here it should be seen that even if one gives less, it is permissible to take the monastery grounds from its vicinity and assign them to a more distant place that is difficult to guard.
For he will say: "If [the gift] for the monks is of greater value... it is permissible to accept it. "Having made it known" means having made it known to the Saṅgha of monks.

“Having obtained permission” is the meaning. As for the statement, “Should it not rather be said that you have more trees?”—this was said because there is an offense of theft (*avahāra*) when one takes something with a thieving mind after learning its high value, whereas the owners were giving it away without knowing the value of their own property.

“An exchange of monasteries” means [exchanging] a monastery together with its site for another monastery, whether it be a palace or other structures built on the ground of others, or one without a site.

Or, that which has a fixed base should be exchanged for something with a fixed base; however, that which lacks a fixed base should be exchanged for something that likewise lacks a fixed base, solely because it is inferior to the ground of the palace.
Thus, even among immovable things, one should exchange them only after understanding their classification as immovable.
By the phrase "suitable beds may be accepted," an unsuitable bed—such as one adorned with gold and other [precious materials]—is [excluded], [even if it is said to be] "for the Saṅgha."

This shows that even when it is said [to give], it is not permissible to accept it. When it is said, "We give it to the monastery," it is permissible for the Saṅgha, but not for an individual, just as with fields and so forth;

this is how it should be understood. "Among these" refers to beds and so forth. "The permissible and the impermissible is according to the same method already stated" means it is according to the method stated in the determinations concerning chairs, mattresses, and so on. "Or what is impermissible" refers to chairs and the like that exceed the prescribed measurements.
And [this includes] pillows and so forth. "Valuable and allowable" means that which is adorned with gold and so on, given under an allowable designation (*kappiya-vohāra*).
Because it is stated, "Black iron... [etc. ...should be distributed," even a vessel made of brass or tin—whether belonging to an individual or not—is permissible to accept and to keep;
for it must be distributed precisely because it is something to be kept by an individual.

They say this. However, that contradicts the statement from the *Mahāpaccarī* cited above: "A vessel made of round iron or bronze, whether it be an item for the use of the Saṅgha or a household utensil, is permissible. For this contradicts the statement from the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* which says:
"Whatever is made of round iron or bronze, even if it was acquired by taking it as a foot-fee (*pādaggaṇhanaka*) in the island of Sīhaḷa, should be distributed."
The statement from the *Mahāpaccarī* was shown later for the purpose of refutation.

Therefore, anything made of round copper or white copper—even a small vessel used for holding water at the feet—is strictly not to be accepted. Even when offered by householders, it is not permissible for an individual monk to accept it.
It is not permissible as a personal possession (*pārihāriya*), meaning that, unlike requisites such as a bowl, one must not keep it for oneself.

It is not permissible to consume [food] after having stored it away. However, if the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others, as if it were their own property, guard it themselves and then bring it back at the time of distribution to hand it over, it is permissible to consume it. It is also permissible to say, "Store this away and give it to the monks.
Regarding the term *paṇṇasūci*, they say it means a pen. By the phrase "even those obtained by oneself," etc., there is no fault in receiving them.

This shows that using [an object] after having set it aside constitutes an offense. And as it is here, so it is with regard to items such as a non-vessel or a wooden staff, even when they belong to oneself.
"Even if unpermitted" means that even all those things made of gold and so forth, it is permissible to use them after having touched them.
"Upakkhare" means implements. "A measure of half an arm-span" means just the size of half an arm-span; some also say it is the measure of half a fathom (byāma). "Yottāni" means leather thongs.

“Even a mere needle-handle eight finger-breadths long” means even a slender handle in the shape of a needle, such as those for weaving silk cloth (*tāsara*). “An empty book” means a book that has not been written upon.
This is mentioned here by way of the discussion on leaves. Regarding the phrase “the rubbing-board and the rubbing-mallet”:
having wrapped the dyed robe around a smooth mallet, placed it upon a smooth board, and turned it over with another smooth board on top, [one rubs it].
"One person stands having stepped onto the top. "Two people grasp the plank at its two ends and pull it back and forth"—this is what is meant by that.
However, striking with the hand after having placed it in the hand should be done when the dyed robe is still wet; this, however, is the striking with the plank-mallets.
It should be understood that [the purpose] is for the sake of releasing the state of rigidity during the dry season.
*Ambaṇa* is a pond-like structure made from the planks of a single-hulled boat; some also call it a water vessel.
A *rajanadoṇī* is a dye-vessel made from a single piece of wood. An *udakadoṇī* is also a water-vessel made from a single piece of wood.
The statement "it is permissible to make a ground-covering" refers to an unallowable skin. In that context, it is indeed permissible even to lie down using the ground-covering as a mere mat.
By the phrase "included under the category of bedspreads," it is shown that a large skin to be spread over beds and such is called a sheepskin.
"Chattamuṭṭhipaṇṇaṃ" refers to a palm leaf. "Pattakaṭāhaṃ" means a pan for cooking bowls.
The commentary on the discussion regarding items that must not be given away is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the assignment of new building work begins.

323. Regarding the phrases "by merely placing a lump [of clay]" and so forth in the Pāḷi: "placing a lump of clay" (*piṇḍanikkhepana*) means the setting down of a lump of clay at a place that is broken or dilapidated.
"New work" (*navakamma*) refers to formal authorization for new construction (*navakammasammuti*). "Door-latch post" (*aggaḷavaṭṭi*) means the door-socket or the frame of the door.
"Covering" (*chādana*) means the roofing of a house with grass and such materials. "Binding" (*bandhana*) means specifically the binding of the roof with bamboo, creepers, and so forth.
"In four cubits" is stated by way of its width measurement. However, as for its height, because it consists of many stories, even twenty cubits may be reached by a carpenter's hand;
furthermore, it is variegated with various shapes. Therefore, "four years' new work" (*navakamma*) is said of it. The same applies to the others.
In the Pāḷi, "in all the monasteries" (*sabbesu vihāresu*) is the plural accusative used in the locative sense. [It means] that one person performs the new work in all the monasteries.

The meaning is "it gives. "Warding off at all times" means that the *navakammika* (work-assigner), instead of assigning the superior bed they have received according to seniority to those who arrive, wards it off even during the [appropriate] season.
"If that dwelling decays," etc., is a decision (*vinicchaya*) outside the canonical text (*pāḷi*). "Having given a place for a couch" means a place for a couch...

"Having given it as personal property. "A third part" means one-third. Thus, even this distribution falls only within the scope of exchanging durable goods for durable goods, and not otherwise, because all the lodgings would otherwise perish.
"If he wishes to give to his co-residents" means if he [wishes to give] to the place where the requisites of the Saṅgha are kept, or to the dwelling places of other bhikkhus.

If he does not wish to give it away, but desires to give it only to his own *saddhivihārika*s, [the intention is that] for such a person you should look after it as his private property (*puggalika*); thus, not everything should be given to him.

In that context, showing the procedure to be followed, he says "The work," and so forth. For in this way, in the phrase beginning with "Evañhi," [it means] according to age, in the third part or in the half-part.
The meaning is that he is entitled to give that portion when it has been taken.
"By whom" means by whichever of those two monks. "He is the owner" means that he alone is the owner regarding the construction of a dwelling on that site;
the intention is that the other should not build there after having excluded him, for he was the one who took possession first. "In an unoccupied place" means...

In a place where no previous accumulation has been made. "Either an accumulation or a front porch" means having built an accumulation outside of a communal dwelling (saṅghika-senāsana), or a single dwelling. "Outside the wall" means outside the wall; the meaning is: in a place built by oneself.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the assignment of new building work is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Using [Furniture] Elsewhere (Aññatraparibhogapaṭikkhepādikathāvaṇṇanā) 324.
"For the purpose of maintenance work" means for the sake of beds, chairs, and so forth, which must be made or produced in such a way that they do not deteriorate from their original value.

"Circular" means made in the shape of a wheel for the purpose of wiping the feet. "Ground smoothed with plaster" means ground made smooth by being colored black or otherwise. "Or a dwelling place" means a bed, chair, and so forth.

By the phrase “It is proper to use it in that same way,” it is shown that an offense is prescribed specifically for one who intentionally uses a place for washing feet and so forth with unwashed feet when the resident monks have already washed theirs.

Because the phrase “The door as well” and so forth is stated in general terms, doors, windows, and the like—even if they are not plastered or finished—must not be leaned against. For one who leans against them without knowing [the rule], there is an offense here according to the counting of body hairs (*lomagaṇanā*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding the prohibition of using [a dwelling] for other purposes and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Allowance of Community Food, etc. (325).

Regarding the phrase "they have come to be designated by such terms as *uddesabhatta* and *nimantana*": here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with"; thus, the meaning is that they have come to be designated by such terms as *uddesabhatta*, *nimantana*, and so forth. "That too" (*tampī*) refers to community food (*saṅghabhatta*) as well.
The commentary on the discussion of the allowance of community food, etc., is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion of Designated Alms-food (*Uddesabhattakathāvaṇṇanā*):

"In the dining hall" (*bhojanasālāya*) is said with reference to the place where designated alms-food is distributed. "To be used by one person at a time" (*ekavaḷañjaṃ*) means it should be entered through a single door. "In various residences" (*nānānivesanesu*) means in the dwellings belonging to various families in their respective precincts.

"Even though he is sitting or even though he is sleeping" (*nisinnassapi niddāyantassapi*): this is a term of address used without respect; the meaning is that when an elder is sleeping, what is received from a junior is well-received.

“An envoy of confidence” (*vissaṭṭhadūta*) means an envoy who is free from apprehension because he is permitted to speak according to his own inclination. “In accordance with the nature of the inquiry” (*pucchāsabhāgena*) means in conformity with the words of the inquiry. To clarify the meaning already stated—that it is called “one standing on a peak” (*kūṭaṭṭhitikā*)—it is said, “or for the king,” and so forth.

“Everything belongs to the owner of the bowl” means that even everything such as robes and other requisites belongs only to the owner of the bowl; the meaning is that it is not permissible to take [the food] after saying, “I spoke only with reference to the meal, not to the robes and other items.
“The portion not yet made” (*akatabhāga*) means the guest’s portion; the meaning is a portion not previously assigned.

"Without saying 'What is being brought? means without asking the donor, "Which meal is being brought by you? "By one established in the ordinary [practice]" means by one established in the practice of designated meals (*uddesabhatta*).
The commentary on the discussion of designated meals is concluded.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of invited meals (*nimantanabhatta*).
"Having cut off" means without saying the words, "Take the meal. For this very reason it says, "by one who does not say, 'The meal.
"By way of morsels" means by way of each individual lump; and in this way, a vessel is not permitted for *uddesabhatta* (designated food).

For there, it must be distributed in a quantity sufficient for only one person. "Only those who have ascended the list; eight bhikkhus from the Saṅgha"—here, those who have ascended the list are the eight bhikkhus.

It should be applied as follows. Regarding the lists of communal meals (*saṅghika-bhatta*) such as designated meals (*uddesa-bhatta*) and invited meals (*nimantanā-bhatta*), when one has ascended according to the procedure established for the list of invited meals, one should go after having either designated [the meal] from the Saṅgha through a meal-designator (*bhattuddesaka*) or having had it designated by oneself;
the intention is that one should not take what is merely pleasing to oneself. "Having entered into the list" means by saying, "I take from the Saṅgha," and so forth.
The meaning is: "having informed the donor of the classification of the recited *mātikā*.
"But from the time of being bound [to a residence]" means from the time of fixing one's dwelling right there.
The commentary on the discussion regarding meals by invitation is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Ticket-Rice: "Having tied it up" means having written it down.

"Even by way of village" means even by way of a village where, for the most part, there is an equal distribution of gains. "Many ticket-rices" refers to thirty or forty meals. The phrase "if they exist" should be supplied and connected [to the sentence].
"Having observed" means having observed those meals by way of their quantity. "Giving with restraint" means [giving] so as not to go too far.
"Having made him accept by means of a reprimand against one who was unwilling, and having given it. Regarding the phrase "having returned again to the monastery":
even if he does not return to the monastery immediately, but takes the meal and afterwards brings it to his own place within the monastery to eat, that is permissible.
"By way of a single house" means even on a street, by way of the wall of a house on one side. "Even by designating" means saying, "In such-and-such a family, the *salāka*-meals shall reach you."
*Vāragāme* means a village that must be visited on alternate days because it is too far away.

*From sixty or fifty [leagues]* is said with reference to a water-jar for the purpose of carrying out disciplinary duties (*daṇḍakamma*). *Vihāravāro* (the monastery turn) refers to the turn for guarding the monastery when all the monks have gone out begging.

*Tesam* means of those who are on the monastery turn. *Phātikammameva* means merely the performance of the task of guarding the monastery. *Ekasseva pāpuṇantī* means they are assigned to each individual monk day by day; this is the meaning.

“Sugarcane-juice ladle” means a ladle for sugarcane juice. As for the statement, “Because it is taken by means of a ladle, it should not be accepted,” this was said on account of its unsuitability, not because it constitutes a breach of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga).
For it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: “A ladle of non-material things from the Saṅgha... it is indeed permissible.
“The measure of the first alms-food” means the measure of a single spoonful of alms-food. Or, having received...

"Or, even if you have not received it today, you should take it tomorrow"—this was said regarding heedfulness even when one has already received [the requisites]. Therefore he said: "As long as he receives enough... [etc.]... if he does not receive it, he should be told, 'You should take it tomorrow.
"Therein" means in that direction. "Taking that" means taking that voting-ticket (salāka) for himself from the village of the opposing party. "By him"—meaning by that person.

"From one who has gone to another region" means: for anyone staying within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*), it must be made available by means of the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) period.
Thus, when these [monks] have not arrived, it is permissible for monks in the nearby monastery to eat;
otherwise, it is considered "belonging to the Saṅgha."
"In our own alms-village" refers to the village of those who provide the tickets for meals.
"The ticket-meal in the monastery for the Elder" means that in the monastery, the ticket-meal is obtained by each individual junior elder through the allocation of all the tickets to himself.
The commentary on the discussion of the ticket-meal is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Fortnightly Meal, etc.:

Regarding the phrase “tomorrow is the fortnight,” this means that what is for the fortnight today should not be sent [to the monastery]; it should be eaten on the eighth day, and it should not be sent for the purpose of eating on the seventh day;
the meaning is that it should be sent only on the day specifically designated by the donors. Therefore he said, “But if,” and so forth.
“Tomorrow is coarse” means that because auspicious ceremonies such as weddings are being performed today, very fine food is being prepared;
[the thought is: “It will not be so tomorrow; I shall feed the bhikkhus this very day.

By saying “having undertaken the factors of the Uposatha,” etc., he shows the distinction between the Uposatha meal and the fortnightly meal (*pakkhika-bhatta*). “Caused to be bound” means restricted by the instruction: “Let the guests eat in such-and-such a monastery.”

“Even food for a traveler (*gamika-bhatta*) for a newcomer (*āgantuka*”) is said with reference to one who, having come from another village and stayed while his intention to travel had not yet subsided, is then departing elsewhere. However, for a resident (*āvāsika*) who wishes to go, only food for a traveler is obtained.
Because it is stated, “having set up an obstacle,” [this applies] even in the absence of a formal obstacle, until the impediment to going has vanished.
It should be understood that it was announced: "It is permissible to eat [only] that much. They send rice and so forth...
"It is permissible" means it is permissible because it has been brought as alms-food (*bhikkhā*). "Because it was accepted in that manner" means because it was accepted under the name of alms-food.

"Unshared property belonging to the Saṅgha" is a demonstration of the mode of the arising of remorse (*kukkucca*). Having thus felt remorse, there is no need for a formal inquiry; the intention is that it should be given away without having been formally inquired about.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the fortnightly meal and so forth is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka is finished.
7. The Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Ordination of Chasakya, etc. 330.
In the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka*, the phrase "named Anupiya" means "Anupiyā by name.

"Below the palace" (*heṭṭhā pāsāda*) means the lower floor beneath the palace; there is also a reading, "the lower palace" (*heṭṭhāpāsāda*). "Should be led forth" refers to [the seed] in the sown fields.
It should be sown. “It should be led away” means it should be removed from there. “It should be cleared” means weeds and other plants that damage the crops should be pulled out.
“It should be made straight” means it should be made into a heap; or this is simply another reading for the same term. 332.

“By what is given by others” means subsisting on requisites provided by others. “With a mind become like a deer” means with a mind that has become like a deer’s through its lack of attachment to any single place.
333. Regarding the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*): this refers to the Brahma-body produced by means of jhāna.

It should be understood that at that moment Devadatta did not suffer a loss of jhāna because the initial thought—"What if I were to inspire confidence [in someone], so that through their confidence great gain and honor might arise for me?"—was only a weak obsession; the loss occurred only later. Therefore he said:
“Simultaneous with the arising of the thought,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “two or three Magadhan village-fields”:
here, in the kingdom of Magadha, a small village-field is only one *gāvuta* in extent; a medium one is one and a half *gāvutas*;
and a large one may even be many *yojanas*. Among these, [the distance] is two medium village-fields, or three small village-fields.
"His body" means his personal existence (*attabhāva*) is three *gāvuta* in measure;
this is what is being said. "Leaders" (*satthāro*) means leaders of a group. "Nāssassa" means it would not belong to him. "Taṃ" refers to the leader. "Tenā" means by that which is unpleasant.
"Sammannati" means he shows us honor with robes and so forth, or else [the thought arises]: "This leader is honored by others."
The meaning is "he is honored. 335.
"They might break the bile in the nose" means they might pour ox-bile or fish-bile into the nostrils.
"A mule" (assatarī) is one born from a mare's womb by a donkey; for when she has conceived and is unable to bring forth [the fetus],...
Having split open the belly, they take out the fetus. Therefore it is said: "She conceives a womb for her own destruction.
(339) *Potthanikā* means a small knife; it is also called *khara*.
(342) "O elephant, do not approach the Nāga"—O elephant, do not approach the Buddha-Nāga with a murderous mind.
“Suffering” (*dukkha*) means suffering because it is the cause of suffering. “From this” (*ito*) means from this birth. “Because” (*yato*) means since, or for which reason; or it means “while going.
“And do not be intoxicated” (*mā ca mado*) means you must not become intoxicated by that.
343. “Food for three” (*tikabhojana*) means food that is to be eaten by three; having accepted more than that together as one [portion].
"To eat" means food that is the opposite of *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group); it does not mean a bowl.
"Kokālika" and so forth are the names of the leaders of Devadatta’s assembly. "An aeon" (*kappa*) refers to an aeon of life in the Great Hell;
some say this is an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), while others say it is an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
The commentary on the Discourse on the Ordination of Chasakya is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Schism in the Saṅgha: 345.
Speaking after having known another’s mind is the miracle of direct address (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*). Pure teaching of the Dhamma is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
Both of these are called a "Dhamma talk. By means of that, the Elder exhorted him. The supernormal power is called a "miracle of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).
The instruction accompanied by that is itself the Dhamma talk. By means of that, the Elder exhorted him:
"Confess the grave offense (*thullaccaya*). This refers to the grave offense incurred in performing the Uposatha and other ceremonies with the intent to cause schism.
It is stated [in the Uposathakkhandhaka and other sections] because it was laid down at the very beginning; otherwise, since these were the first offenders, there would have been no offense at all.

346. *Sarasī* means a lake. *Mahiṃ vikubbato* means of one who scratches the earth with his tusks; this is a description of the natural characteristic of elephants. *Nadīsu* means in lakes. The construction is: "of one eating lotus roots (*bhisaṃ ghasamānassa*).
*Jaggaṭo* means of one protecting a herd. 347. *Dūteyyaṃ gantuṃ* means to undertake the business of a messenger; the meaning is to perform the work of a messenger. *Sahitāsahitassa* means...
He is skilled in what is appropriate and inappropriate to say and to do; that is, he is skilled regarding what should be spoken and what should be performed.
Alternatively, he is skilled in speech intended and unintended: the meaning is that he does not dwell on mere words, but proclaims only the intended sense.
350. In the verses, *jātu* means "certainly. *Mā udapajjatha* means "may it not arise" or "let it not be. *Pāpicchānaṃ yathāgati* means "according to the destination of those with evil desires."
"Whatever is the destination and the future state of persons with evil desires—know that this is the consequence.
By this reason, he shows the manner in which Devadatta will be described later on as "wise," and so forth.

"He has indulged in negligence" means he has fallen into negligence. "In hope" refers to the accomplishment of a purpose that is certain to occur; for here it is "hope" (*āsīsā*) that is intended, not mere aspiration (*patthanā*). Grammarians maintain that the past tense may be used for such a future sense.
"He deceives, he might deceive. "With a jar of poison" means with one jar filled with poison. "He" refers to that person.
"He would not defile" means he is unable to make it mixed with poison; this is the meaning. "Terrifying" means terrifying due to its vast and deep nature.
By this, too, he shows that it cannot be defiled. "By speech" means by the speaking of faults. "He harms" means he oppresses.
The commentary on the discussion of schism in the Saṅgha is finished.
Commentary on the Questions of Upāli 351.
However, the Saṅgha is not split by this much alone; for a schism in the Saṅgha is not produced merely by the taking of voting tickets.
It has been stated. For it is only when a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) such as the *uposatha* has been performed that the Saṅgha is split.

In this regard, it should be understood that the schism of the Saṅgha is accomplished by the conclusion of the motion (*ñatti*) in the cases of the *uposatha* and the *pavāraṇā*, and by the conclusion of the formal act—such as the announcement (*apalokana*)—in the remaining formal acts.
As for the phrase “incapacity was not stated,” this refers to the passage beginning: “Monks, Devadatta has accumulated his first deed of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*). etc.

When the Blessed One spoke of the state of being an *ānantarika* (one who commits an immediate offense), he did not prescribe for him the status of a *pārājika*, which is defined as incapacity (*abhabbatā*).
By this, it is shown that incapacity, like the offense itself, is prescribed immediately [after the act] and not prior to it.
However, since it is stated here that there is no non-offense even for a first-time offender, it should be understood that Devadatta and others were not exempted either.

In passages such as "There are three foundations of mindfulness," it is precisely the denial of one foundation of mindfulness—namely, that there are no more than three—that constitutes the non-Dhamma here;
however, the prescription of the three foundations of mindfulness is not non-Dhamma, because it is indeed the Dhamma.

The same applies to the other sections concerning diminution. Regarding the increases, however, in the passage "There are six faculties," even the single [faculty] that is not a faculty [is included].
The very misrepresentation of the faculties is non-Dhamma; so it is with the rest as well.
Not only these, but any presentation anywhere that is contrary to fact—such as "there are four aggregates" or "there are thirteen bases," and so forth—is entirely non-Dhamma.
And every presentation according to reality should be understood as Dhamma. Here, "presentation" refers to that which originates the appropriate application of body and speech.

Only the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) are intended here; thus, among phenomena (dhamma) that are manifest in their own form— namely, those such as the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) in the sense of being blameless (anavajja), and those such as the unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) in the sense of being blameworthy (sāvajja)—
as well as among other indeterminate (abyākata) categories, the manifestation of any given portion according to the order established by the Blessed One is what is called "Dhamma."
And it should be understood that the exposition of what is contrary [to the truth] is shown as "non-Dhamma" (adhamma). Although, in this context,
even the Vinaya and so forth enter into the categories of Dhamma and non-Dhamma by way of being expounded according to reality or not according to reality,

it should nevertheless be understood that because they are specifically distinguished and taken separately under the names of "Vinaya" and so on, everything remaining falls into the categories of Dhamma and non-Dhamma.

The statement, "We shall treat this non-Dhamma as Dhamma," and so forth, is said for the purpose of showing that a schism in the Saṅgha occurs only for one who, having understood both Dhamma and non-Dhamma according to their true nature, proclaims them erroneously out of reliance on evil desires; it does not occur, however, for one who proclaims them while perceiving them correctly.
This same method applies to such expressions as "proclaiming what is not Vinaya as Vinaya. In that context, "leading to liberation" means...
"Ukkaṭṭhaṃ" means "excellent. By the phrase "tathaiva" (just so), he draws back the meaning stated by the passage beginning with "Thus is our teacher's lineage," and so forth.

"Restraint, abandonment, and reflection" refers to what is called the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*), the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*), and the discipline of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-vinaya*).
Therefore, he says, "This is the discipline. The dyad "prescribed and not prescribed" [is explained] by the dyad "spoken and not spoken."

In meaning they are exactly the same, as are the *duṭṭhulla-duka* and the *garuka-duka*. For that very reason, a similar exposition was made for them, beginning with: "The four foundations of mindfulness...
this is what is called 'not laid down'. *Sāvasesāpattiṃ*: an offense accompanied by a remainder of virtue. *Anavasesāpatti*:
an offense for which there is no remainder of virtue left once it has been committed.
354. In the Pāli, *samaggānañca anuggaho* means that there is assistance such that the concord of those who are united does not break; it is the granting of support and reinforcement.
355. *Siyā nu kho* means "might it possibly happen? *Tasmiṃ adhammadiṭṭhī* refers to an improper view regarding one's own proclamation that "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma.

*Bhede adhammadiṭṭhī* refers to the view that "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma" after having proclaimed it, by means of causing the proclamation to be made, the distribution of voting sticks, and so forth.

The meaning is: having abandoned oneself, while the Saṅgha consisting of a quorum of four or more is standing within the same boundary, one separates that Saṅgha of four or more from itself and—by way of performing formal acts (*kamma*) and so forth—becomes one who holds a view contrary to the Dhamma (*adhamma-diṭṭhika*) in the act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha.
"Having misapplied the view" means: whatever wrong view arises in oneself when explaining that which is non-Dhamma as being Dhamma in regard to that [schism].
The meaning is: having set that aside and concealed it, one proclaims it erroneously, thinking, "This is indeed the Dhamma.
The meaning is to be understood in this way throughout all instances.

Regarding "the view of Dhamma in schism" (*bhede dhammadiṭṭhi*): it refers to one who holds the opinion that there is no fault in causing a schism in the Saṅgha according to the method already described. This...

However, by proclaiming "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma," one becomes a holder of the view of non-Dhamma; yet, by setting aside that view while performing the act [of schism], one becomes a schismatic who is incurable.
Likewise, in the case of "one who is doubtful about the schism," there is also the setting aside of the view that is doubtful regarding the schism.
The rest is the same. In that schism characterized by the view of Dhamma, [the phrase] "one who holds the view of non-Dhamma" refers to this:
However, because he acted while misrepresenting his view as "un-Dhamma is Dhamma" during a schism, he became a schismatic of the Saṅgha who is incurable.

On the other hand, in the case of the "white side," because he acted without misrepresenting his view—either in the illumination of "un-Dhamma is Dhamma" and so forth, or in a schism where there was a view of "Dhamma"—even a schismatic of the Saṅgha becomes curable. Therefore, regarding the illumination of "un-Dhamma is Dhamma" and so forth...
Whether one holds a wrong view regarding the schism in the Saṅgha, or is in doubt regarding both,

if they set aside that view and that doubt and proclaim it as "Dhamma," and then cause a schism in the Saṅgha in the manner described, it should be understood that there is an immediate offense (ānantariya).
The commentary on the discussion of Upāli’s questions is finished.
The method of commentary on the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka is finished. 8.
The Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka):
Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties for Newcomers (Āgantukavattakathā).

357. Regarding “it should be spread out” in the section on the duties of incoming monks (*āgantuka-vatta*): it should be spread out in the sun. In the text, regarding “he should be made to pay homage”: because the junior monk pays homage of his own accord by asking about the rains-retreat (*vassa*) for the purpose of showing respect, this is what is stated. Regarding “he should be looked at”: he should be gazed upon.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties of incoming monks is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the discussion of the duties of resident monks (*āvāsika-vatta*).

359. Regarding the phrase "according to their respective places," this shows that even the act of giving—after not overstepping the designated area, shaking out the beds and chairs, spreading them out, and placing a coverlet on top—is indeed the preparation of lodgings. Thus he said:
"But it is certainly permissible to shake them out and spread them."
The commentary on the discussion of the duties of a resident monk (*āvāsika-vatta*) is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the duties of one who expresses appreciation (*anumodana-vatta*). 362.

Regarding the phrase "when seated in the fifth [position]": it means when seated for the purpose of expressing appreciation. "It is not a burden for the Great Elder" refers to the one who expresses appreciation.
"It is no burden to come. The meaning is that when one is requested by the monks themselves, one should sit while offering an expression of appreciation (*anumodana*).
The commentary on the discussion of the procedure for the expression of appreciation is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Duties Concerning the Alms-food Hall (Bhattagga-vatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 364.
"The place where people serve meals" means a location, even within the monastery, where people together with their wives and children reside and, having invited the bhikkhus, feed them.
"When seats are present" means when there are places for sitting. "Venerable sir, this is the seat."
This is said with reference to a seat that is higher than the Elder’s seat, yet situated on level ground close by;
however, it is not permitted to sit on a seat even slightly higher than the Elder’s seat without having asked for permission.

If that seat is lower, even if it is close by, it is permitted to sit there without asking for permission. "It is an offense for the Great Elder alone" refers to the offense of obstructing [another] from a seat.
*Āpatti*. "Having spread out" means having spread out the *saṅghāṭi* robe that has been put on; the meaning is "having not thrown it aside.
In the *Pāḷi*, the statement "The rice is to be received with both hands... [etc.]...

is said for the purpose of preventing the bowl from falling when one is receiving rice after placing the bowl upon the palm of the hand or upon a support such as the back of a tray or a cloth; however, when [the support] is well-prepared...
Having placed the bowl on a base and touched it with one hand, it is indeed permissible to receive the boiled rice.
The same principle applies here as well regarding the rule that "water should be received with both hands.
"Water for washing the hands" refers to the water at the conclusion of the meal; therefore he said, "having drunk the drinking water, the hands should be washed."

By this, it is shown that washing at the very end is prohibited; however, it is permissible to wash one's hands by means of drinking water or similar methods during the course of a meal and then eat again.

In some manuscripts, however, it is written that "after drinking water, the hands must not be washed," but this does not accord with the preceding statement, as [the prohibition] refers specifically to water at the conclusion [of the meal].

Because it is stated as "water for washing the hands. If people say, "Venerable sir, wash [your hands]," and so forth, this is said with reference to an elder who has finished his meal and is seated. "At the entrance" means near the door.
The commentary on the discussion of the rules regarding the refectory is concluded.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Duties of the Alms-gatherer (Piṇḍacārikavattakathādivaṇṇanā): 366.
Regarding the phrase “he makes [the monk] stand” in the Canon: they say, “Stand, venerable sir. 367.
Regarding the phrase “there are, venerable sir, lunar mansions”: there are known objects pertaining to the lunar mansions, such as the Assayuja and other constellations.
The intention is: "Do you know? Therefore he said, "We do not know, friend. The same method applies here to the phrase, "There is, venerable sir, a certain direction.
"With what is the moon joined today, venerable sir? means "With which lunar mansion (nakkhatta) is the moon joined?
369. "In the courtyard" means in the open air. "One should proceed in this very manner" shows that one should request permission for giving the recitation and so forth.

374. “For the purpose of going back and forth” means for the purpose of one’s own continuous movement. Regarding the word “ūhaditā,” since the root *hṛd* here has the sense of discharging excrement, it is said: “smeared with excrement on the outside.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the conduct of the alms-round is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Khandhaka on Conduct is completed.
9. The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha:
Explanation of the Discussion on Requesting the Recitation of the Pātimokkha 383.
In the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka, the term *nandimukhiyā* in the canonical text means "with a joyful face," due to her facing the white quarter [the east].

Although he said, "The dawn has risen," the request for the recitation of the Pātimokkha—"Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One recite"—should be understood as having been made by the Elder, because no training rule prohibiting the performance of the Uposatha on a day other than the Uposatha day had yet been promulgated.
But why did the Blessed One pass the entire three watches of the night in silence? Because [the assembly] was not pure.
It was in order to make it clear to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus that it is blameworthy to maintain communal residence (saṃvāsa) with another in such matters as the Uposatha,
and furthermore, to inform them of the training rule (sikkhāpada) so that bhikkhus might act accordingly in the future.
However, some here [hold that] the Blessed One, out of great compassion, was unable to say "you are impure" to an impure person in their very presence.

They state that "he sat down" is the reason [for his not entering the assembly]. That is not the reason, because it could not have been said even later, and because it would follow as an absurdity that the Elder Mahāmoggallāna should not have taken him by the arm and led him outside. Therefore, the reason here is exactly as previously stated.
For this very reason, [the Buddha said]: "Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a Tathāgata should [enter the assembly] with an impure..."

Having said, "One should perform the Uposatha with the assembly and recite the Pātimokkha," [the Buddha] showed the procedure to be followed by an assembly that includes one who has committed an offense, beginning with:
"And, monks, the Pātimokkha must not be heard by one who has an offense. Regarding "one of suspicious conduct" (*saṅkassarasamācāra*):
having seen some unseemly act, others [think], "This must have been done by him."
It is conduct that should be observed out of fear for the Saṅgha, or conduct that should be observed out of the fear that "these people know me to be of improper conduct.

Even one who does not explicitly profess, "I am a samaṇa," while making a living by wearing the guise of a samaṇa and by taking a share of the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha, is in effect as if he were giving such a profession; thus it is called "the profession of a samaṇa, the profession of a brahmacārī."
It has been said. "Lustful" (*avassuta*) means soaked by the oozing of defilements.

It is "corrupt" (*kasambujāta*) because it has become like refuse due to the arising of immorality, or because it has become like worthless rubbish due to its lack of essence. "Having made them go out from outside the gatehouse" means having caused them to exit from the hall at the gateway.
384. "Delighting in the great ocean" means they find delight in the great ocean through frequent seeing, entering, and so forth.
"Not as if falling down a precipice" means that it does not slope from the very beginning, like a great waterfall from a severed cliff; this is the meaning.
"Of a stable nature" means having a fixed intrinsic character (*avaṭṭhita-sabhāva*). "Fullness" means the state of being complete (*puṇṇatta*). "Nāgas" refers to the species of serpents.
The commentary on the discourse regarding the request for the recitation of the Pātimokkha is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Those Eligible to Hear the Pātimokkha (386):
"Should be recited" means that even if the meaning has been stated in any language whatsoever without using the actual Pāli text, it is still considered "recited.
"Either before or after" means either prior to the commencement of the motion (*ñatti*) or subsequent to the conclusion of the motion.
387. "Having taken both what has been done and what has not been done" means: for one who has both what has been done and what has not been done, having taken both of those.

"A lawful act of concord" (dhammikaṃ sāmaggim) means a lawful united formal act (samaggakamma). "Reopens" (paccādiyati) means he takes it up again with the intention of reopening it to perform it once more.
388. "The designations 'mode' (ākāra), etc., should be understood" means it should be understood that these are stated as synonyms for mode, characteristic (liṅga), sign (nimitta), and name (nāma).
The commentary on the discussion regarding those worthy of hearing the Pātimokkha is finished.
398. Commentary on the Discussion of the Factors of Formal Acceptance (*attādāna*).
Furthermore, in order to explain it, he said: "The *attādāna* is the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that one must formally accept and take up for oneself," [referring to] "the teaching..."

“Desiring to purify,” and so forth. “The rainy season” (*vassāratta*) refers to the period of the rains. For that too is indeed an improper time—just like a time of famine and the like—because it is difficult for a modest assembly to bring [the offender] from afar for the sake of settling the legal matter, and because it is difficult for those who have arrived to engage in their proper conduct, such as wandering for alms.
“Causing recollection” means that which produces recollection, because it generates joy and gladness at every moment of being recollected or not yet recollected.

"Free from defilements... leads to..."—here, the intention is that just as the moon and sun possess splendor when free from defilements such as clouds and mist, so too this accuser possesses splendor through the removal of the defilement of being a wicked person. 399.
"A mind of loving-kindness has been attained" refers to the jhāna of loving-kindness that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
Regarding the phrase “with a mind free from ill will” (*adosantaro*): here the word *antara* is a synonym for “mind,” which is why he says, “not having a mind that is corrupted.

Regarding “compassion” (*kāruñña*): this is simply *karuṇā*, which is why he says, “the state of compassion is the quality of *karuṇā*. He speaks of *karuṇā* as having reached absorption (*appanā*). The same applies to *mettā*.
The commentary on the section concerning the factors of taking up the self is finished.
The method of commentary on the Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is finished.
10. The Chapter on the Bhikkhunīs:
An Exposition of the Discourse on the Case of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
403. In the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*, the phrase “because women have gone forth” is a demonstration of the reason why the True Dhamma will not continue to exist beyond five hundred years.

The statement that it lasts for a thousand years by way of those who are dry-insight practitioners (*sukkhavipassaka*) and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), etc., is stated according to the opinion of the reciters of the Khandhakas.
However, in the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, [it says]: “By those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāppatta*)...”

"It stood for a thousand years; it stood for a thousand years with those possessing the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiñña); for a thousand years with those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijja);
for a thousand years with those practicing dry insight (sukkha-vipassaka); and for a thousand years it stood with those [reciting] the Pātimokkha. Thus it was said.

In the commentaries on the Aṅguttara and Saṃyutta Nikāyas, however, it is stated differently; although all these versions are mutually contradictory, they were written down in the Sinhalese commentaries according to the opinions of various reciters (bhāṇakas).

Having accepted the very method [of interpretation] that has been introduced, it was written by the Teacher because, in such a contradiction of narrative accounts (*kathā*), there is no loss to the Dispensation (*sāsana*) and no means for its correction.
Indeed, only a contradiction regarding the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) is to be corrected by means of the Suttas and other methods, not a contradiction in the path of narrative.
The commentary on the account concerning Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Permission for the Full Ordination of Bhikkhunīs (Bhikkhunīupasampadānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 404–8.
In the Pāḷi, *yadaggena* means "on which day"; *tadā* means "on that very same day. *Vimānetvā* means "having treated with contempt" or "having shown disrespect.
410–1. *Āpattigāminiyo* means "those who have fallen into an offense. *Kammavibhaṅge* refers to the *Kammavibhaṅga* in the *Parivāra*.
413–5. “Two or three bhikkhunīs” means by two or three bhikkhunīs. “They do not inform” means they do not inform the one who recites the Pātimokkha. 416.
“A fringe of cloth” means a fringe made by joining together many strips of cloth.
417. “An ornament” means a specific decorative coloration such as patterns on a bowl. “They sell” means they trade. “A binding for bending” means a binding for bending the bones of the buttocks.
422–5. *Saṃvelliyanti*: they wrap [the garment] around by tying the waistband. "Three supports" is said because the lodging at the foot of a tree is not available to them.

426–8. "Eight bhikkhunīs ward off according to seniority": the meaning is that eight bhikkhunīs, taking [their places] strictly according to the order of seniority, ward off those who have arrived later than their turn; no others do so. "Establishing a dispute" means asserting authority.
"They set it in motion" means they state the purpose.
430. "By means of a monk as a messenger" means by a monk acting as a messenger. "By means of a trainee (sikkhamānā) as a messenger" means by a female trainee acting as a messenger.

431. "It is not approved" means it is not sufficient. "Building work" refers to the granting of space on land belonging to the Saṅgha after having requested permission with the words, "Let him dwell there after performing building work."
"432–6. *Sannisinnagabbhā* means those whose pregnancy is difficult to discern. *Mahilātitthe* means at a public bathing place for women.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the authorization of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for bhikkhunīs is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka is finished."
11. The Chapter on the Five Hundred:
Commentary on the Discussion of the Minor and Lesser Training Rules. 437.
In the Pāḷi of the Chapter on the Five Hundred, regarding the statement, "Friend, do you know our Teacher?", this was said by the Elder.
Although he himself knew that the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he asked this question solely for the purpose of informing the assembly of monks who were with him,
and also to make the monks understand the opposing words of Subhadda, an old man who had gone forth late in life.
For Subhadda was addressing the assembly of householders, such as the khattiyas, who were deeply devoted to the Blessed One in Kusinārā.
Having heard of the Blessed One’s final nibbāna in the midst [of the assembly], even though he is overjoyed, he will not be able to manifest the appearance of joy through his speech out of fear;
however, having heard it here in this secluded region, he will express his own evil views according to his own inclination.
Then, using that very circumstance as a pretext, he will incite the bhikkhus and cause the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
It should be understood that he questioned him while knowing: "Having caused the frustration of the wishes of this evil bhikkhu and others like him, I shall ensure the stability of the Dispensation.
For this very reason, the Elder, by showing Subhadda’s words alone through the passage beginning, "Once, friend, at one time," had the Dhamma and Vinaya recited.
*Nānābhāvo* means the state of being in different locations with the body.

"Separation" (vippavāsa) means being apart. "Parting" (vinābhāva) means being separated by death. "Alteration" (aññathābhāva) means the attainment of another form through passing into another state of existence. 441. Regarding the statement, "If he so desires...

he might abolish [it]," because the Blessed One said "if he so desires," the monks who compiled the Dhamma—seeing that not even a single training rule need be abolished and seeing no fault in its abolition—said: "It was not laid down..."
It should be understood that [the Blessed One] spoke with the underlying intention: "We shall not lay down new rules, nor shall we abolish those already laid down," and so forth;
furthermore, "having announced them through an unshakeable formal act (*kammavācā*) similar to a formal proclamation (*paññatti*), and having undertaken them, they will continue to practice;
thus, until the disappearance of the Dispensation, these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) shall remain irrevocable. For this very reason, the Great Elders (*mahātherā*) also said: [and so on].
They practiced accordingly.

"Gone among householders" means gone among those who are householders; the meaning is that they were known by householders such as the great Khattiya donors. "Dhūmakālika" means that for this [fire], the time of smoke is the limit of its own occurrence.
443. "Even when a coarse sign is being made" refers to the passage: "If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon..."

"Or for the remainder of the eon"—thus, when an act is being performed as a sign of granting permission, which serves as the cause for the request, "May the Blessed One remain, O Lord, for an eon," [it is said] regarding a more serious offense.
"With a mind obsessed by Māra" means with a mind possessed by Māra.

445. "Ujjavanikāya" means going against the current. A "kulava" is a contemptible cutting off, destruction, or ruin; it is a useless squandering. They do not go toward that, thus they "do not bring about a kulava."
The commentary on the discussion of the minor and lesser training rules is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Chapter of the Five Hundred is finished. 12.
The Chapter of the Seven Hundred.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Bases (Dasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 446. In the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka*, "by the number of monks" (*bhikkhaggena*) means by the calculation of monks. "The earth" (*mahī*) refers to snow. 447.
"Enveloped by ignorance" (*avijjānivutā*) means covered or concealed by the hindrance of ignorance. "Ignorant" (*aviddasū*) means lacking knowledge. "Corruptions" (*upakkilesā*).

"Vuttā" means these [acts] such as drinking liquor and so forth were stated to be the defilements of those recluses and brahmins. "Sanettikā" means accompanied by craving (*taṇhā*), which is the "net.
450–1. "Ahogaṅga" is the name of that mountain. "Paṭikacceva gaccheyyaṃ" means:
I would go there first, to the place where the monks will assemble to settle that legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*). "Sambhāvesuṃ" means they arrived.
452. *Aloṇikaṃ* means food or curry that is devoid of salt. *Āsutā* means prepared with all the necessary ingredients;

alternatively, the reading is *asuttā*. 453. *Ujjaviṃsu* means they went against the current by boat. *Pācīnakā* refers to the Vajjiputtakas because they were born in the eastern region. *Pāveyyakā* means inhabitants of the Pāveyya country. 454. "Friend, are you not old? means:
"Are you not an elder who is released from formal dependence (*nissaya*); why then did the elder expel you?"

They speak of "speaking of division. The intention is: "We shall take formal dependence (nissaya) on a teacher"—that is, even though we are free from dependence, we shall live only after having taken one worthy and venerable person as our support. 455.
"Those who give the root" means those who first provide the ten bases (dasavatthu); the meaning is "resident monks. "The senior of the Saṅgha on earth" refers to...

At that time, he was senior among all the bhikkhus in the world by virtue of his full ordination (*upasampadā*). "By means of dwelling in emptiness" (*suññatāvihārena*) refers to the attainment of the fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) reached through the gateway of emptiness.

Regarding the phrase "in the Suttavibhaṅga," it refers to the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*). Furthermore, because this [rule]—"Whatever bhikkhu should eat fresh or cooked food that has been stored"—in the Sutta deals specifically with what is to be consumed during the day (*yāvakālika*), it does not apply to rock salt (*siṅgīloṇa*), which is permitted for life (*yāvajīvika*).
It is stated that for the consumption of stored food together with non-stored food, the offense of *pācittiya* is established by the very method of the *Vibhaṅga*;
however, in order to prove that this *pācittiya* is indeed found in the *Vibhaṅga*, it was said, "How [is it] in the Suttavibhaṅga?
and so forth. For in that context—regarding the consumption of food mixed with salt—it is said: "In this case, the salt is what is stored, not the solid or soft food."

The Vajjiputtakas held the perception that it was blameless (*anavajja*). It should be understood that the Sutta-vibhaṅga passage, "perceiving it as not stored when it is stored" (*sannidhikāre asannidhikārasaññī*), is cited here for the purpose of showing the offense (*āpatti*) even for those who hold such a perception.

"Together with that" means together with the salt previously received. Here, there must be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [this refers to] "with what is to be used at the proper time" (*yāvakālikena*).

The intention is that since it was not stated, "Bhikkhus, [this] has been received for life," but rather by the force of the statement, "[this] has been received on that very day," it is established that food received prior [to that day], even if it is for life, is not permitted at the proper time when its flavor has become mixed with what is to be consumed only during the proper time;
therefore, there must be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in that case. [However,] it is also the case that there need not be an offense of wrong-doing.

For if you consider that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the condition of storing, then since there is no fault of storing in the case of lifetime salt, there should not be an offense of wrong-doing;
on the other hand, do not consider that there is an offense of wrong-doing because, being mixed with food, it falls under the category of food (*āmisa*).
For in that case, there must be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) precisely because it has reached the state of food—this is the intended meaning.
For here, even by the phrase "as long as life lasts" and so forth, the absence of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is not established.
In the Pāḷi, in all instances such as "in Rājagaha, in the Sutta-vibhaṅga," the meaning to be understood is "both in the Sutta and in the Vibhaṅga.
Since each specific act, such as eating at the improper time, is prohibited in both the Sutta and the Vibhaṅga, there is an "overstepping" (*atisaraṇa*), that is, a transgression of the Vinaya.
*Vinayātisāra*: "A sitting mat (*nisīdana*) is said to be 'with a border' (*sadasa*)," this was stated for the purpose of showing what has come down in the *Vibhaṅga*.
"For one making it to that measure" means for one making it to the measure of three spans (*vidatthi*) according to the Sugata-span;
however, two spans are made for the border. The intention is that even a sitting mat without a border is permissible.
All that has been said here below is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Ten Bases is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka is completed.
Thus ends the method of exposition on the Cūḷavagga within the *Vimativinodanī*, the commentary on the Vinaya, known as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Parivāra:
Commentary on the Section on the Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) concerning the Rules of Discipline (Paññattivāra).

1. Regarding the Blessed One, whose body consists of the aggregates of Dhamma beginning with the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and who possesses a pure retinue (*visuddhaparivāra*), within the teaching of the Vinaya-piṭaka, immediately after the *Khandhakas*, there is the *Parivāra*.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Now we shall provide an exposition of the meanings not yet explained (*anuttānattha*) of that Vinaya which has been included in the compilation.

By means of the "all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*), that is, by the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); and by the "extremely purified fleshly eye" (*ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā*), day and night all around...
Because one sees even extremely subtle forms within the measure of a *yojana*, it is by means of the exceedingly pure eye of sensitivity (*pasādacakkhu*).
Regarding the passage beginning with “Is there a designation there?,” the meaning should be understood as “Is there indeed a designation there? and so forth;
thus he says: “The question ‘Is there a designation there?... and ‘By whom was it brought?’.”
2. *Pucchāvissajjanā*: in the answering of a question. *Vinītakathā*: a discourse on cases that have been settled; or this is the reading itself.
"By one origin consisting of two factors" means by one [origin] which is a collection of two factors.
Even though there is no origin entirely free from the two factors, it is for the purpose of showing that this offense does not occur without even one of those factors.
“It is by a single origination,” it is said. Now, in order to show the primary factor among those two factors, he says:

“For here, the mind is the factor,” and so forth. However, since bodily intimation—which consists of proceeding on the path or not proceeding on the path—can only arise through the very mind that intends the practice, this formal designation of an offense was established by the Blessed One with reference to those two factors.
It exists, it does not cease. Therefore, that consciousness is the limb (factor) and the cause of the body—which is designated as "bodily intimation"—but not the cause of the offense.
However, for that [offense], the body originated from that [consciousness] alone is the immediate cause;
the intention is that consciousness, on the other hand, is the cause of the cause. This same intention applies everywhere above regarding all origins associated with consciousness as a factor.

It should be understood that the ultimate nature (*paramattha-sabhāva*) of an offense—such as its being unwholesome (*akusala*) and so forth—is stated only figuratively (*pariyāyato*) in the canonical texts and commentaries by means of the supplementary statements such as "it originates from a single origination" (*ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti*). It is established that offenses are merely conventional natures (*sammuti-sabhāva*), because the distinction between those offenses that have originated and their respective origins is proven.
It is with reference to this meaning that [it is said]: "Of the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) committed by some... and so on.
This refers to the meaning defined as the impossibility of bringing about a state of non-offense through means of tranquility (*samatha*).

"By the ancient Great Elders" refers to the Great Elders who, resplendent with qualities such as the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), compiled the texts after the three previous councils; for this compilation by means of recording in books is equivalent to the fourth council.

188. "In the Mahāvibhaṅga" means in the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga. "Sixteen sections have been shown" refers to those sections by which—being characterized as the initial ones—the entire Parivāra is designated as the "Sixteen-Section Parivāra.
The commentary on the section on the formulation of rules (*paññattivāra*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section on origins (*samuṭṭhāna*).
257. Regarding the statement in the Pāḷi, "Nibbāna and designations (paññatti)":

herein, since a designation such as "person" (puggala), which is a conventional truth (sammutisacca) designated in dependence upon conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma), does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha), it is improper to say that it is possessed of the two characteristics of impermanence and suffering—which are restricted to those phenomena that possess the properties of arising and passing away.
This is because [such a designation] is merely conceptualized in the form of an agent, an experiencer, and so forth.
Because it is devoid of an intrinsic nature of its own, it is rightly called "non-self" (anattā).

Therefore, this designation (paññatti) is also stated to be "decidedly non-self" together with Nibbāna, which is its actual basis, on account of their commonality of being unconditioned (asaṅkhata). For even though a conventional designation does not exist [in an ultimate sense], it is indeed unconditioned because it is not produced by any cause.
Both "Buddha-moon" and "Buddha-sun" were stated in order to show the Blessed One’s coolness through compassion and his brilliance through wisdom.
"Hāni" means that by which one diminishes; "dukkhahāni" is the diminution of suffering, meaning the cause for the removal of all suffering.
"He taught the three in the Piṭaka": since other Great Heroes, the Fully Enlightened Ones, also teach the True Dhamma...
The construction is: "Therefore, Aṅgīrasa taught the three Piṭakas. "Of great virtue" means of great benefit. "In this way the True Dhamma is led forward":
if the mastery of the Vinaya remains undiminished, then the True Dhamma of practice and realization is likewise led forward—that is, it continues to proceed and does not decline; such is the meaning.
Regarding the question of how the mastery of the Vinaya (vinayapariyatti) persists, he says: "And from both," and so forth. It should be connected thus:
it persists as it is bound together by the Parivāra. "Of that very Parivāra" means within that very Parivāra.
"The origin (samuṭṭhāna) is made determinate" means that some [offenses] are made determinate by way of their origin. In that Parivāra, certain training rules (sikkhāpada) have a determinate origin.
The meaning is that it has been explained as not shared with others. "Another [matter] regarding the breach and the cause" means:
the breach (*sambheda*) is the state of being muddled by the mutual arising of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*); the cause (*nidāna*) is the locus of the formal rule (*paññatti-ṭṭhāna*);
and "another" refers to the persons and so forth, as well as the objects and so forth. "They are seen in the Sutta above" means that they appear below [in this work].
They are found both in what has already been stated and in the Parivāra Sutta which will be explained below. Since this is so, the application here should be understood as follows:
"He trains in the Parivāra, which is the cause for the endurance of the Vinaya that supports the entire Dispensation.
Regarding the phrase "with mixed origins," this means those whose origins are shared with others. First, at the beginning, "in the former manner" refers to the very first instance.
He speaks with reference to the method presented in the *Paññattivāra* (the section on formal rules).
For in that *Paññattivāra*, the origin story (*nidāna*) is indeed seen as well, in such passages as: "Where was the first *pārājika* laid down? It was laid down at Vesālī.

However, it should be understood that the statement, "It is seen in the Suttas occurring later," refers to the fact that [the rule] occurs in the Suttas appearing in subsequent sections. "Of that" refers to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) included within the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*.
258. *Aniyatā paṭhamikā*: This means that the female gender was assumed specifically with regard to the offense; thus, it refers to the first *aniyata* training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
In the Canon, the phrase "not following after a *pavattinī*" refers to the training rule concerning not following after a *pavattinī* who has been ordained.
260. Regarding the origin story (*vatthu*) for the training rule on wool (*eḷakaloma*): "The bhikkhunīs were washing and dyeing sheep's wool..."

Because it was stated, "They neglect the recitation and the interrogation while disentangling [the hair]," he said, "In the Vibhaṅga, the training rule regarding the washing of wool (*eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpada*) is indicated by taking this term 'they neglect' (*riñcanti*)," showing that the training rule was characterized by means of this word "neglect.

"The training rule on the rainy-season robe" (*vassikasāṭikasikkhāpada*) refers to the training rule concerning the seeking of a rainy-season robe at an improper time. "The training rule on treasure" (*ratanasikkhāpada*) refers to the training rule concerning the taking back of treasure or what is considered treasure.
265. In the Pāḷi, “by Buddha-knowledge” means by the knowledge of omniscience that has been fully penetrated. 267.
By the statement, “The Tathāgatas do not teach,” he shows the prohibition against teaching the Dhamma to one who holds a sunshade in his hand.
269. “Unmade” (akata) means unmixed with anything else; the meaning is that it has a fixed origination. Alternatively, “unmade” means not previously existing; the meaning is that it is brand new.

270. Regarding "the compendium of origins" (*samuṭṭhāna-saṅkhepa*): here, it is a "compendium" (*saṅkhepa*) because similar origins are condensed and gathered therein; thus, it is the heading of the origins.
It is a "guide" (*netti*) because it leads and guides away from bodily and verbal misconduct; this refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Since that itself is the Dhamma, he says "of the Dhamma of the Vinaya Piṭaka" (*vinayapāḷidhammassa*).
The commentary on the section concerning origins is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section of questions and answers regarding intermediate cases.

271. "How many offenses?"—this question is asked by attributing unity through their genus (*jāti*) with respect to the five classes of offenses beginning with the *pārājika*, while taking into account the internal subdivisions such as sexual intercourse and theft. "How many offense-categories (*āpattikkhandha*)?"—here the distinction is only this much:

that each [class] is considered individually in the sense of a heap (*rāsa*), with respect to its internal subdivisions. "The *vinītavatthu*s (bases for training) are simply those things already trained in."
The abstentions from offenses are called "bases of training" (*vinītavatthu*) because they are the causes for states such as freedom from remorse and gladness;

in their actual meaning, these are simply blameless qualities such as abstinence. It "destroys" (*vināseti*) the unwholesome side consisting of lust and so forth—which has acquired the name "enmity" (*vera*) because it is the cause of enmity—thereby "removing" (*maṇati*) that enmity.

“He goes away, breaking up the assembly for hearing the Dhamma” means that while many people are sitting together listening to the Dhamma, he disrupts that gathering of those listening to the Dhamma and departs after rising.

“Being disrespectful” means simply not manifesting satisfaction where there is a reason for satisfaction, nor manifesting a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) where there is a reason for such urgency. “Bodily immodesty” refers to improper physical conduct occurring through haughtiness.

274. Loving bodily action is that which has arisen from loving-kindness (*mettā*). "By both" means by both the novices and the elders. "He treats with affection" means he makes that person an object of endearment; asking "of whom?", he says "of his fellow-celibates" (*sabrahmacārīnam*).
The phrase "he eats by dividing the food among persons" connects with what precedes. To show that very division among persons, it is said: "to such-and-such," and so forth.

"By making one free from slavery" means having liberated one from the slavery of craving, it means establishing one in the state of living as a master with respect to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). "It leads out" means it proceeds; the meaning is that it conduces to the complete destruction of suffering.
The commentary on the section on the questions asked is finished.
The commentary on the section on the six origins of offenses begins.

276. "By the first origin of offenses" means solely by means of the body. Because an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) arises exclusively from a conscious state (*sacittaka*), it is stated that "it should not be said [that it occurs without consciousness].

Since the five classes of offenses beginning with those involving formal meeting of the Sangha (*saṅghādisesa*) and ending with wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) can also occur without consciousness, it is stated "it may be";
the meaning is that the commission of an offense "may be" or "could be. By low and high [conditions] such as birth and so forth...
Because it was prescribed specifically for the offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*) during the act of eating, that [offense] arises exclusively from speech and mind;
thus it is said [in the second method of origination], "No," because there is no *pāṭidesanīya* offense to be entered into by speech alone.

However, in the third [method], it is said, "It may be," because a *pāṭidesanīya* offense can arise on account of a nun who is showing signs of being weary [of the meal] when one does not dismiss her with body or speech.

Although reviling (*omasana*) arises from the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*), which is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), it is shown that the offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*)—which is prescribed on account of that [reviling]—arises by way of the fifth [factor].

Therefore, in the fourth section it is said, "one should not say 'he would incur a wrong speech,'" whereas in the fifth section it is said, "'it may be' should be said. However, for one who reviles by means of a bodily gesture alone...

It should be understood that even in the case of a *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech), there is only *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) because of the absence of bodily play (*kāyakīḷā*). However, in the sixth section, although the body exists, it is not a factor for the *dubbhāsita*;
rather, it is shown that the sixth [section] is included within the fifth origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) by the negation "not indeed" (*na hi*), and not because it is entirely absent therein.

This is to show that there is no offense for what is ill-spoken. For it is not the case that an offense of ill-spoken words cannot occur for one who reviles with body or speech out of a desire for sport.
Indeed, whatever one enters upon by means of the fifth [method], one necessarily enters upon that same thing by means of the sixth as well, just like the offense of teaching the Dhamma;
this is how it should be understood. The rest is easily understood from the section on the origins (samuṭṭhāna).
The commentary on the section concerning the origin of six offenses is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Committed Offenses 277.
Now, for the sake of easily seeing the lightness [of the penalty] regarding those offenses that are to be committed by the first origin in the second [section], [it is said]:

Only the *kuṭikāra* (building a hut) and so forth have been specifically extracted [from the list of offenses], not because others do not exist, since offenses such as acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*) are also present.
The same applies to the second origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and the rest. By the phrase "perceiving it as allowable" (*kappiyasaññī*), he shows the absence of mental intention (*acittakatā*).

By the phrase "builds a hut" (*kuṭiṃ karoti*), he shows the absence of vocal application (*vacīpayoga*). By both together, he shows that there is the occurrence of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) and other offenses through the body alone.
[The text] shows this. In the same way, the subsequent [sections] should be treated accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "they originate from one origin," this is stated here with reference to those offenses specifically shown as originating from the body alone;
however, without such specification, those offenses certainly originate from other origins as well, as appropriate. The same applies to what follows.
“*And by means of the ‘covering over as with grass’”*—this is stated with reference to the four types of offenses, excluding those involving *saṅghādisesa*.
“Having made an agreement, he builds a hut”: the meaning is that he makes the agreement verbally and he himself performs the building physically.
The commentary on the section concerning the offense for one who has built is finished.
Commentary on the Verses on the Origination of Offenses (Āpattisamuṭṭhānagāthāvaṇṇanā) 283.
The third section of verses, however, was spoken in order to show that very same matter already stated in the second section by way of summary.

In this context, although it should have been said “bodily” (*kāyika*)—meaning “the body itself”—it is stated as “bodily” (*kāyikā*) due to a grammatical inversion of the word. Therefore he said: “By that...”
"Arising" means that the body is declared to be the source [of suffering].

"Seeing seclusion" refers to one whose nature is to see both the seclusion from the hindrances and Nibbāna, due to being secluded from all conditioned things and because of the cause for such seclusion.
"Skilled in the analysis" is an address to one who is proficient in both the *Vibhaṅgas*. Here...
In this way, there is no such thing as another person asking; rather, the Elder Upāli himself asked and answered in order to make the meaning clear.
Following this method, the meaning should be understood throughout all [the sections].
The commentary on the verses concerning the origin of offenses is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Conditions for Failure (Vipattipaccayavāra): 284.
In the fourth section, the "conditions for failure," the phrase "on account of failure in virtue" (*sīlavipattipaccayā*) means on account of the concealment of failure in virtue.
286. "On account of failure in view" (*diṭṭhivipattipaccayā*) means on account of not relinquishing failure in view.
287. Regarding "conditioned by failure in livelihood" (*ājīvavipattipaccaya*): here, *ājīva* means that which they live by depending upon it; it refers to the four requisites.

That very [set of requisites], because it has failed through wrong attainment, is called "failure in livelihood" (*ājīvavipatti*). The meaning is: the cause of that failure in livelihood, namely, the motive for its production and enjoyment.
The commentary on the section concerning conditions of failure is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on the Condition of the Basis (Adhikaraṇapaccayavāra-vaṇṇanā) 291.

Regarding the fifth section, the "Condition of the Basis for Formal Acts" (*kiccādhikaraṇapaccaya*): this refers to the conditions consisting of the formal acts (*kamma*) known as the motion (*apalokana*), the motion with a proposal (*ñatti*), and the motion with a proposal followed by a proclamation (*kammavācā*).
