"Five" here means that for those who perform [formal acts] after making a motion based on an illegal agreement (*adhammikakatikā*) and so forth, there is no ground for success; such is the meaning. In the fifth [section].

In the section on the *adhikaraṇa-paccaya* (the condition of legal issues), it should be understood that under the condition of a legal issue involving an act (*kicca-adhikaraṇa-paccaya*), a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs at the conclusion of the formal motion (*apalokana-vasāne*), while those who perform formal acts such as the *ñatti-kamma* with the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) and so forth are included under *thullaccaya* and other offenses.

"The remaining offenses" refers to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala-samāpatti*) and so forth. The statement "there are no other offenses" is said with reference to those blameworthy offenses that partake of the nature of failure (*vipatti*) and the like.
The commentary on the section on the conditions for legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-paccaya-vāra-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section on the synonyms for legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-pariyāya-vāra-vaṇṇanā*), concerning the classification of the methods for settling disputes (*samatha-bheda*).

293. In the sixth section, the phrase beginning with "non-greed as the precursor" and so forth is stated with reference to the dispute of one who speaks according to the Dhamma (*dhammavādin*) for the sake of the non-perverted stability of the Dispensation (*sāsanaṭṭhiti*).

The eighteen grounds for schism (*bhedakaravatthu*) are the bases for taking up and illustrating [the points] such as "un-Dhamma" regarding the Dhamma and so forth; these alone are the grounds for schism here, because they are the causes for disputes such as physical quarrels.
They are called "bases" (*ṭhānāni*) because they provide scope; "grounds" (*vatthūni*) because they serve as supports; and "planes" (*bhūmiyo*) because they are foundations.
The phrase "unexplained roots" (*abyākatahetū*) is stated with reference to the disputes of those beyond training (*asekkha*). The "twelve roots" (*dvādasa mūlāni*) are:

anger and enmity, denigration and spite, envy and avarice, deceit and fraud, evil desire and great desire, and the dogmatic adherence to one's own views, stubbornness, and the refusal to relinquish them.

By way of these six pairs, there are twelve factors—namely, the six phenomena such as greed and so forth, together with the six causes—which are the roots of a legal dispute involving contention (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). 294.
Regarding "the fourteen roots": those same twelve, together with bodily and verbal actions, constitute the fourteen roots of a legal dispute involving accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).

295. In order to show that in cases such as digging the earth—excluding those offenses defined by formal rule (paṇṇatti)—there is an offense rooted in wholesome or indeterminate consciousness, it is said:

“Non-greed is the precursor,” and so forth. The statement beginning with “The seven classes of offenses are the bases” is said because offenses arise on account of concealing the seven classes of offenses.
“On account of the legal issue of an offense, there are four types of offenses... [and so on].

For it is said: "He incurs [an offense]. The phrase "six causes" is stated because it is inappropriate to apply the conventional designation of "causes for incurring offenses" to wholesome states, and not because wholesome causes do not exist.
For it is said: "Non-greed is the precursor," and so forth; indeed, it is the very causes for incurring offenses that are spoken of by the name "precursors."

296. Regarding the passage beginning with "four kinds of legal acts (kamma) are bases," it is stated that the speech of a formal motion (apalokana-vācā) and the speeches of the motion (ñatti) and so forth are "legal acts" (kamma).

For these very [speeches], when they have reached the state of being a legal act for those who have attained unity within a single boundary (sīmā), are called "bases and grounds" (ṭhānavatthubhūmiyo) by virtue of their status as the foundation for the legal procedure (kiccādhikaraṇa)—which is of the nature of a communal function (saṅghagaṇakicca) consisting in the performance of the proclamation through the consent [of the assembly].
They are so called. "The Saṅgha is one root" is stated by way of the majority;

for in the case of a formal act consisting of a motion (*gaṇa-ñatti*), a motion with resolution (*apalokanā*), or a motion followed by a single proclamation (*ñatti-dutiya*), the group itself is the root. "From the motion" is said because the formal acts consisting of a motion, a motion followed by two proclamations, and a motion followed by four proclamations possess the form of a motion and have the motion as their precursor.
For among the two types of motions—those involving a motion and those involving a motion and proclamations—the proclamations themselves are likewise rooted in the formal act.
They are grouped together. This analysis of the motion (ñatti) will be made clear further on.
“These seven methods for settling... by way of method”—this is the statement of the question.
“It may be”—this is the answer. “And how might it be?”—this is the question again. “There are two methods for settling a legal issue arising from a dispute,” and so forth; this is the answer again.
In this context, "by way of the basis" (*vatthuvasena*) is the statement of the reason for the proposition that "the seven methods of settling (*samatha*) are the ten methods of settling.
"By way of the method" (*pariyāyena*) is the statement of the reason for the proposition that "the ten methods of settling are the seven methods of settling.
The meaning is: by way of the basis known as the fourfold legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), and by way of the method known as the sequence of the teaching.
The commentary on the section concerning the sequence of legal issues (*adhikaraṇapariyāyavāra*) is finished.
**Commentary on the Section on Commonalities, etc.** 297.

In the seventh section, the section on commonalities (*sādhāraṇavāra*), the term "common" (*sādhāraṇā*) means that they share in the function of settling a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). This applies everywhere in the same way.

298. In the eighth section, "Belonging to That" (*tabbhāgiya*), the term "belonging to that" means belonging to that side because they contribute to the settling of a legal dispute concerning a contention (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
The commentary on the sections on commonality and so forth is finished.
This concludes the commentary on the section on the commonality between the methods of settlement (*samatha*) and non-settlement.

299. In the ninth section, the Chapter on the Commonality and Non-commonality of the Settling Methods (*samatha*), it is asked: “Do all settling methods settle a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) in one way, or in various ways?
In response, it is stated: “Some settling methods are common to other settling methods; some settling methods are not common to other settling methods.

Then, enumerating the settling methods that serve as the causes for the pacification of legal issues—such as disputes (*vivāda*) and so forth—in their proper order, the text says: “Majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*),” and so on.

Since no other method of settling a dispute (*samatha*) is possible without the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of), the remaining six methods of settling are said to be common to the *sammukhāvinaya*.
However, because those six depend upon one another, they are said to be not mutually common to each other.
The same principle applies to the section on "belonging thereto" (*tabbhāgiya*).
The commentary on the section on the commonality of *samatha* and *asamatha* is finished.
Commentary on the section beginning with *samatha-sammukhāvinaya*:

In the eleventh section as well, "sammukhāvinaya" and so forth constitute the question; "yebhuyyasikā, sativinaya," and so forth constitute the answer. In this way, the division of questions and answers should be understood for the sections on the Vinaya and the Kusala, as well as those that follow.
In that context, regarding such passages as "therein, *sammukhāvinaya* may be wholesome," the wholesomeness and other qualities of *sammukhāvinaya* and so forth,

as well as the wholesomeness and other qualities of disputes and so forth, are stated by way of various metaphorical designations (*upacāra*) based on the wholesome states and so on arising in the persons appointed to those respective disciplinary acts and to the disputes themselves.
For this [procedure] called *sammukhāvinaya* consists in the presence of the Saṅgha and so forth.

Because they possess a nature free from blame (*anavajja*), even though unwholesome states (*akusala*) may exist within them, it is not appropriate to apply the designation "unwholesome" to them, just as one does not apply the designation "unwholesome" to a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that face-to-face settlement (*sammukhāvinaya*) is not unwholesome. 304.
Regarding those [other methods] following that: wherever a majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) is applicable, there face-to-face settlement is applicable, and so forth.
This was stated in order to show that *sammukhāvinaya* is invariably associated with the other methods of settlement (*samatha*), whereas there is no mutual association among the other six methods.
The commentary on the section concerning *sammukhāvinaya* as a method of settlement is concluded.
306. The commentary on the section on "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) begins with the words:
"These phenomena, namely 'legal issues' (*adhikaraṇa*) or 'principles of settlement' (*samatha*), are conjoined.

This was stated in order to show that the principles of settlement occur only within legal issues as appropriate, and to demonstrate that they have no separate existence apart from those legal issues.

"Having analyzed them, one should demonstrate their distinction": having separated them from the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the methods of settling disputes (*samatha*), and having made them distinct—that is, having established their mutual non-mixture—one asks:

"Is it possible to demonstrate their distinction, which consists in their state of existing as mutually unmixed, and to demonstrate their non-association at the very moment the legal issue is being settled?"
“*Adhikaraṇaṃ*,” and so forth, is a demonstration of censurable speech. One who says, “Do not speak thus,” should be told, “Do not speak thus.

However, since it is not possible for there to be a characteristic of settling other than through the methods of settlement (*samatha*) regarding legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), he rejects the distinction defined as abandonment and persistence.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of their characteristics, there certainly exists a distinction between the methods of settlement and legal issues.

It should be understood thus: "The methods of settling (*samatha*) are settled by means of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*)" means that all methods of settling reach their conclusion through the four types of functional legal issues—such as the *apalokana* (formal announcement) and so forth—and not by others;
it is with reference to this meaning that it was said. For this very reason, he will say:

"The *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is not settled by a legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). [The *sativinaya*]... [etc. ...is not settled by a legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*)."
"It is not settled; it is settled by means of a legal issue concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)," and so forth.
307–313. The section on settlement (*sammativāra*) begins with the question: "By how many methods of settling (*samatha*) is a legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) settled?

Immediately following that, the section on what is settled and what is not settled (*sammatinasammativāra*) is intended to demonstrate the connection and lack of connection between the methods of settling and the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).

The section on settling by means of settling (*samatha-adhikaraṇa-vāra*), beginning with "They are settled by means of settling," was stated in order to show the mutual relationship of the methods of settling (*samatha*) among themselves,
as well as the mutual relationship of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) with the methods of settling, and the way in which legal issues are pacified by means of settling.
Furthermore, the section on originating (*samuṭṭhāpeti-vāra*) was stated for the purpose of showing the manner in which legal issues arise from other legal issues.
It is said: "Which legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) does it not produce? The meaning is that by its mere own arising, it does not give rise to even a single legal issue.

To explain how, indeed, it does give rise to one, he says: "But furthermore," and so forth. In this context, "they arise" means they arise through successive conditions rather than arising immediately after [the initial cause];
this is the intended sense. By the phrase "righteousness and unrighteousness," etc., [he refers to] both...
Due to disputes among individuals, there arises a mutual destruction of security;
because of that, as they increase their quarreling by seeking out factions, the dispute reaches a state of subsidence upon encountering some large assembly led by a conscientious guide of the Saṅgha.
But when it does not subside in that way, the dispute gradually increases until it causes a schism even within the entire Saṅgha.

It gives rise [to disputes], and from those [disputes] come accusations and so forth; thus, in the absence of causes for pacification through such a successive sequence, the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) arise.
With reference to this, it is said: "The Saṅgha disputes; this is a dispute-legal-issue (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is that the dispute which occurs when the Saṅgha is disputing is a dispute-legal-issue. This same method applies to the remaining [types of legal issues] as well.
The commentary on the section on association (*saṃsaṭṭhavāra*) is finished. Regarding the commentary on the section on association (*bhajativāra*): 318.
Furthermore, in the subsequent section, the passage beginning with "the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) among the four types of legal issues" refers to the legal issues.

This was stated for the purpose of showing the state of association (*saṃsagga*), even though they possess the condition of mutual dependence (*aññamañña-paccayatā*) according to the method already explained.

In such passages as "the legal question of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) belongs to the legal question of dispute among the four legal questions," the legal question of dispute among the four legal questions belongs only to the state of being a legal question of dispute, and not to the state of being any other legal question; that is, among the four legal questions, it possesses only the nature of a legal question of dispute.

The meaning should be understood as follows: that which is dependent on a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is itself included within it and is subsumed precisely by way of being a legal issue arising from dispute.
As for the question, "To how many of the seven methods of settling does a legal issue arising from dispute belong?

and so forth, this was stated in order to show the specific method of settling (*niyata-samatha*) that applies when there is the pacification of the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). In that regard, how many methods... [text ends]
"It resorts" means: for the sake of its own pacification, how many forms of serenity (*samatha*) does it approach, and by resorting to how many forms of serenity does it attain peace?

"Included in how many forms of serenity" means: in order to pacify itself, into how many forms of serenity has it entered by way of being similar to them? "Comprehended by how many forms of serenity" means: by those which effect pacification.
By how many means of settling (samatha) is it comprised for the purpose of bringing about pacification?
The commentary on the section on "classification" (bhajati-vāra) is finished.
The section on questions concerning the Khandhakas.

Commentary on the Answers to the Questions (Pucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā) 320. The *Upasampadakkhandhaka* is the *Pabbajjākhandhaka*. "Together with the exposition" (*saniddesa*) means with its detailed explanation (*niddesa*).

Alternatively, the reading is *sanniddesa*, which has the same meaning. In the phrase "together with the introduction and the exposition," this refers to that which elucidates the setting, the persons involved, and so forth.
The introductory statement is called the "Nidāna" (Introduction). The training rules (sikkhāpada) specified in dependence upon that introduction are called the "Niddesa" (Exposition).
The meaning is: "I ask concerning the Khandhaka, which is the composite whole consisting of those [rules] as its constituent parts.
By "the highest words," the statements that define the offenses are intended. Of these... how many offenses are there?
The meaning is: how many classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) are there as designated by those words? One might ask: "Are not offenses the property of persons alone, and not of words?
Why, then, has this description been made in the manner of a possessive relation, saying 'how many offenses are there for the most excellent words'?
To this he says: "By whichever word," and so forth. In the Canon, the mention of "Uposatha" and so on refers specifically to the Uposatha Khandhaka and other such sections.
The commentary on the answers to the questions is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section on single items (*ekakavāra*) within the method of numerical progression (*ekuttarikanaya*).

321. Furthermore, in the Ekuttarikanaya, "transgressed by one who does not know" refers to transgressions such as digging the earth or sleeping on a high bed committed by one who is ignorant of the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*) or the underlying basis (*vatthu*).
Even these become obstacles for one who, having later realized they have fallen into them, fails to perform the remedial action.

This was said with reference to the *dukkaṭa* offenses for breaking the rule of conduct (*vatta*) incurred by those who have already undergone probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth after [the original offense].

Some say it refers to the intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*) that must be incurred at that very moment; however, since those prior offenses will be mentioned later by the term "intermediate offenses" itself, the former interpretation is more appropriate.
Regarding "intermediate offenses during the purification of the root" (*mūlavisuddhi*), this refers to acts such as sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*).

A *saṅghādisesa* offense consisting of an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) committed at the time of practicing the purification of the *parivāsa* and *mānatta* previously granted— without having first performed them all— is [purified] by means of purification according to value (*agghavisuddhi*). That is to say,
when one who has committed an intermediate offense is sent back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassitvā*),

and having shaken off [the offense] through the process of *odhāna* and *samodhāna*, and having combined it with the previous offense, he practices the purification of the *parivāsa* and so forth again, according to the value of that [combined] offense.
"Again, she commits an intermediate offense (antarāpatti).

"With the same persistence" means with the intention of wishing to commit that same offense once more; the intended meaning is that even if the offense has been confessed in this way, it is not cleared.
He speaks thus to demonstrate the fault that reaches its peak when one commits an offense without having laid down the burden (dhuranikkhepa).
“In the eighth case, for a bhikkhunī, it is indeed a pārājika offense. And this applies not only to a bhikkhunī;
even for bhikkhus, if they take ghee or other such items little by little through theft without relinquishing their burden, it is indeed a pārājika offense when the value reaches one *pāda*.
However, some say: “In the eighth case, for a bhikkhunī, it is only a pārājika offense.”
They say that this was stated with reference specifically to the eight grounds (aṭṭhavatthuka) because it has been so declared.
Regarding "a legitimate promise" (dhammika-paṭissava): this refers to a legitimate promise made in the presence of laypeople, such as "I will spend the rains retreat here," and so forth;
whereas an illegitimate promise (adhammika-paṭissava) would be one such as "I will strike so-and-so," and so forth.
There is no offense by means of causing one to fall from truth.

One who is thus accused is one accused contrary to the Dhamma; even if he himself does not remain in truth and in the unshakable state but conceals it, he is indeed one who has been accused contrary to the Dhamma.
Only wrong view that is certain of the five deeds of immediate retribution is called "certain of falsehood. The four...
The paths are called "fixed in rightness.
The commentary on the section on single terms is finished.
The commentary on the section on pairs begins.

322. Regarding the phrase "among the lords himself together with his retinue," he said, "of one with a supple back," and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), offenses such as cutting off the genitals or killing oneself are included.
"Or the treasurer’s paintings" means either the restoration of householders' goods or paintings depicting the likenesses of men, women, and so on.
The statement, "He incurs [an offense] by not giving robes and so forth," refers to the rule: "Monks, a student must be supported by his preceptor."

This statement—"He should be assisted... [and so on]... the bowl should be given"—was spoken with reference to the *dukkaṭa* for one who, out of disrespect, fails to provide material support, and the *pācittiya* for a nun.
The offense incurred by not giving back robes that have been forfeited (*nissaṭṭha*) and so forth is also included herein.

"Confessing in the presence of" means confessing a similar offense, as well as those that do not require confession (*adesanāgāminī*) and so forth. Regarding the mention of the origin (*nidānuddesa*), the offense—

One incurs an offense by not making it known and by not teaching. "Not accepting the exhortation" refers to one who does not accept the words spoken by the monks for the purpose of exhorting the bhikkhunīs, excluding those who are foolish, sick, or traveling.

There are also offenses in giving to another what was intended for one's own use, and in entering a village while wearing only the inner and outer robes (*santaruttara*) without having put on the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
[The offenses] are to be incurred through non-usage alone. "Measure" is the defining characteristic for the accomplishment of the immediate offense of schism in the Saṅgha.

"To a fool" refers specifically to one who is conscientious yet ignorant of the procedure for taking formal dependence (*nissaya*). "To a conscientious person" refers to one who is competent and investigating the suitability of the person providing dependence.
Regarding the statement, "Two matters are established by the Vinaya," he says that "matters found in the Vinaya are *vinayika*."

Regarding the phrase "one who has not reached expulsion" (*appatto nissāraṇaṃ*): here, the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*) is intended by the term "expulsion" because it involves being expelled from the monastery.

And since a person who does not corrupt families is said to be "one who has not reached [the grounds for] it," even if he is burdened with many offenses, he is called one who has not reached [the grounds for] expulsion. However, because even for one burdened with many offenses and so forth, if he so desires—

It is said, "The Saṅgha may perform an act of banishment"; therefore, one who has been suspended is *sunissārita* (well-suspended), whereas one who is entirely pure and free from offense should be understood as *dunnissārita* (badly suspended).

Regarding the phrases "not having attained reinstatement" (*appatta-osāraṇa*) and so forth, "reinstatement" (*osāraṇa*) here refers to the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*). The meaning is that certain individuals, such as those with severed hands, though they have not attained it because it is forbidden for them, are nevertheless "reinstated," while others, such as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), are "badly reinstated."
The commentary on the section on groups of two is finished.

Commentary on the section on groups of three (323): Regarding the "offense of shedding blood" among the groups of three, this refers to an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*). "By the address 'friend'" means by the form of address "friend" (*āvuso*).
"An offense" means an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding the phrase "the rest, both by night and by day":

here, all offenses such as the first *kathina* robe-offering, which are to be committed at the rising of the sun, should be understood as falling into the third category alone, because they are to be committed precisely within the interval between night and day.
Alternatively, because they are to be committed when the sun has risen, they are included among those offenses to be committed by day.

"Entered" (paviṭṭhā) should be understood as follows: the offenses for giving exhortation (*ovāda*) to nuns when the sun has set, as well as the offense for standing together with a man in the darkness of night, must be committed specifically during the night.
Offenses such as visiting families before the meal (*purebhattaṃ*) or eating food that is not left over (*anatiritta-bhojana*) must be committed only during the day. Some...
However, some say that the training rules (sekhiya) connected with eating, as well as [the rules regarding] eating in a group and so forth, are to be transgressed only during the day.
Therefore, it should be understood that, setting aside such offenses, the remaining ones belong to the third category.

"Not less than ten years" is stated because the training rule was prescribed specifically for a fool who is exactly ten years [of standing]. Regarding the co-resident disciples (saddhivihārika) and resident pupils (antevāsika):
Even one with ten years of seniority incurs the offense of improper conduct (*asammāvattanāpatti*) and the giving of formal support (*nissaya*) and so forth to those who are shameless (*alajjī*);

likewise, those with less than ten years of seniority incur the offense of not following a preceptor for two years while she is ordaining others, and so forth. "With an indeterminate mind" (*abyākata-citto*) is said with reference to the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅga-citta*) of one who is sleeping.
"Not inviting [the Sangha]" (*appavārento*) means not inviting out of disrespect, or not having invited due to some circumstance on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
When the Saṅgha is performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, one who fails to perform it out of disrespect commits that same offense on the dark fortnight as well;

thus, no restriction is seen to the effect that it occurs only on the bright fortnight. However, since one who has spent the rains retreat in the later period is permitted to perform Pavāraṇā only on the full moon of the later Kattika month, one who commits an offense there due to failing to perform Pavāraṇā commits it specifically on the bright fortnight.
"It must be restricted" is how it should be understood. "It is allowable during the bright fortnight"—here too, the same principle applies.

By the statement, "One incurs an offense in the winter if one has not formally relinquished [the bedding]," it is shown that for one who does not relinquish it, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) precisely because of the restrictive rule: "One should determine [the bedding] for the four months of the rains.
Departure and so forth, due to duties not to be performed upon entering the rains retreat, also [apply] during the rains.

One incurs [these offenses] only within [the monastery]. A sick person alone [incurs them] regarding medical treatments such as enemas. Stepping on [the ground] with unwashed feet and similar acts are also incurred only within.

Entering the monastery grounds without asking permission and so forth for a bhikkhunī occurs only within the boundary (sīmā). For one undergoing formal dependence (nissaya), departing without asking permission and so forth occurs only outside the boundary.

Furthermore, all illegal acts (adhamma-kamma) such as failing to reveal an existing offense during the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the formal admonition for an offense, and the ordination of one less than twenty years of age, also [occur within].

It occurs within the Saṅgha itself. Even in cases such as the *gaṇa-uposatha* performed contrary to the Dhamma, it occurs precisely in the midst of the group and so forth. Even the taking of formal dependence (*nissaya*) in the presence of one who is shameless constitutes an offense against an individual.
"The three unrighteous grants of the *amūḷhavinaya*" refers to one who, although insane at the time of the transgression, was not insane [at the time of the granting].
If one intentionally commits an offense and, when later exhorted by the monks, remembers it yet says "I do not remember," or if one speaks falsely,
saying "I remember it as if in a dream," or if one says that everything done during a state of insanity is permissible for everyone—
the three formal acts of *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) granted to these three are illegitimate.
“Apakatatta” means one who is ignorant of the Vinaya. Therefore it is said: “He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense.

Regarding the statement, “The formal act (kamma) must be performed against those who do not relinquish their view,” this refers to the fact that for one being exhorted by the bhikkhus, a dukkaṭa offense necessarily arises due to the non-relinquishing of the view; or rather, a pācittiya offense also certainly occurs.

The phrase "the distinction of making the mouth the drumhead, etc. refers to the various types such as playing the mouth-drum and so forth. "Upaghāteti" means "destroys. "By means of suppressing the seed, etc. means performing acts such as rejoicing after having suppressed the mind-seed.
The commentary on the section of threefold groups is finished.
The commentary on the section of fourfold groups.
324. In the sets of four, "this" refers to a householder’s requisite. "To give the key" means to give the opening key for the purpose of opening the door and placing requisites inside.
It is also permissible to put away [the requisites] inside oneself when they have been brought for the sake of the Saṅgha.
Therefore he said: "It is permissible to have them placed inside."
Regarding the phrase "the male gender first arises among the original founders," he says, "by way of its first arising.
In the Pāḷi, the expression "there is no offense for interrupting the rains retreat" means that there is no offense connected with the interruption of the rains retreat.
"Speaking with wisdom" (*mantabhāsā*) means speaking with *manta*, which is wisdom (*paññā*). The phrase "starting from the ninth nun" refers to [the rule] "I allow you, monks..."

This is stated because one must rise for the first eight bhikkhunīs according to seniority, and for the rest according to their agreement, as per the words: "For the remaining [bhikkhunīs], it is according to their agreement.

By saying, "Even one who says 'it is not allowable here' incurs an offense in the border regions," and so forth, he shows that for one who intentionally speaks of the allowable as unallowable, or the unallowable as allowable, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases.

"It is called 'preliminary duty' (pubbakaraṇa)," so it is stated in the commentaries; the intention here is that those [duties] have been extracted from the Parivāra. However, showing those intended here, he says "the desire for purity" (chandapārisuddhi), and so forth.
The commentary on the section on the tetrads is finished.
The commentary on the section on the pentads.
325. Regarding the phrase "having asked for permission regarding cakes, there is an absence of wandering":
since the alms-collector lacks this factor—namely, "being invited to a meal"—the intention is that, by virtue of that training rule, he is entirely without offense.

"Brought back after being taken to the charnel ground" refers specifically to the garments worn and wrapped [by the deceased] which were discarded after those who had performed the funeral rites for the peta at the charnel ground had bathed and departed.

In the Pāḷi, "in five ways" means by way of the five factors of theft (*avahāraṅga*). However, according to the objects (*vatthu*), there are offenses categorized as *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa* based on the distinction between grave and light.
That which is caused by the manifestation of defilements (*kilesa-samudācāra-hetuka*) through the union of male and female and so forth is called "representative artistry" (*paṭibhāna-cittakamma*).
"He asked ten thousand questions" means that he swept away ten thousand questions concerning the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
He questioned the junior monk. The other junior monk, because he had traveled along that same path himself, answered everything;

through this, the elder was inspired with confidence. "He completed his duty" means he brought his task to its conclusion. It should be understood that the elder, being one whose taints were destroyed, spoke these words beginning with "What is it, friend?
in order to make the benefits of sweeping manifest to everyone.

The phrase “standing on his knees at the footstool for the feet” (*padacetiya*) is an elliptical addition to the text. “I shall cause him to be reproved” means: “I shall cause the Blessed One to reprove himself; I shall cause him to restrain himself.
“This much is sufficient as a basis for taking up” means: this much speech is to be taken up for the purpose of settling the legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*);
the construction is: “restraining [him] so that, having heard it, he is able to understand. And here, “without restraining the limit of his own speech... [is the context].

There are five factors to be understood by combining one [factor] from the phrase "without grasping the limit of another's speech," one from "he acts contrary to the Dhamma," and one from "without consent," together with the two preceding ones. "The matter" (*vatthu*) refers to the transgression of sexual misconduct and so forth.
One does not know the matter by way of determining the connection of the discussion and the sequence of the narrative; that is, by either the accuser or the accused.

Or, speaking in accordance with the sequence of the discourse already stated and in conformity with their questions and answers, one is said not to know the subject matter by way of the sequence of the discourse;

and likewise, when speaking in accordance with the legal decision (vinicchaya) known as the "basis of the training" (vinītavatthu) within the Sutta-vibhaṅga, one is said not to know the subject matter by way of the sequence of that legal decision. "It is a formal act consisting of a motion" (ñattikammaṃ) means it is a formal act [performed] by a motion.
The connection is: "he does not know that it is called 'concluded'. Regarding the phrase "one who has reached the point of the formal act through the motion" (*ñattiyā kammappatto*):

even when the motion is concluded, he remains one who has merely reached the point of the formal act. The meaning is: because the formal act is concluded only at the stage of the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the motion itself is what is called "concluded";
thus, he does not know that this is the cause for the motion.

In the Pāḷi, the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha is stated as "the five purifications" because it is the cause of purification from offenses and because it is to be performed by those who are purified.
The commentary on the section of fivefold groups is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the section of sixfold groups, etc.

326. Regarding the sixfold sets and so forth, in the Pāḷi it says "six kinds of disrespect": there are six kinds of disrespect toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, heedfulness, and hospitality;
and it should be understood that there are likewise six kinds of respect toward those same things.
The phrase "it may be worn for a maximum of six years" is a presentation of the maximum limit as it appears in the Vibhaṅga.
328. "By the seven [precepts] included in the Pāli" means by the seven precepts on false speech included in the training rule on lying, beginning with:

"First, he thinks: 'I will speak a falsehood. 329. "'How could that be found here?'"—he dispels resentment by thinking: "How, for what reason, could that non-engagement in harmful action be found *here*, in this person, or in this world-dwelling?
330. "By way of [the views] such as 'The world is eternal,' etc. refers to: "The world is eternal; the world is not eternal. The world is finite; the world is infinite."
The world. Or: "The soul and the body are the same," or "The soul is one thing and the body another.

"A Tathāgata exists after death," "A Tathāgata does not exist after death," "A Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—thus come these ten views that grasp at extremes.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Wrong view and so forth" refers to the ten states of perversion (*micchatta*):
the eight beginning with wrong view and wrong intention, together with wrong knowledge and wrong liberation. Among these, wrong knowledge is delusion (*moha*) associated with wrong view.
Wrong liberation is the perception of being liberated in one who is not actually liberated.

"Perverted" refers to the ten factors beginning with right view and ending with right knowledge and right liberation. In this context, right liberation is the fruit of arhatship; however, it should be understood that "right knowledge" refers either to the knowledge associated with that [liberation] or to the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
The method of single-increment is concluded.
[Now follows] the commentary on the questions and answers concerning the Uposatha and other observances.

332. Regarding the "Invitation Verses" (*pavāraṇagāthā*) in the inquiries concerning the *Uposatha* and other observances, the act of inviting (*pavāraṇā-vācā*) itself is performed through three points: what has been seen, heard, and suspected. Furthermore, the verses spoken in this manner are classified according to their specific meters (*jāti*) as defined by the characteristics of prosody (*chandovicitilakkhaṇa*).
The commentary on the sections of six, etc., is concluded.
The method of commentary for the *Mahāvagga* is finished.
The Section on Designations:
First Grouping of Verses;
An Exposition of the Training Rules Enacted in Seven Cities.
335. "Three hundred and fifty" means three hundred plus fifty. By the term *viggaha* (conflict), the conflict involving human beings is expressed.

"Exceeding" refers to the first *kaṭhina* [period]. "Black" means pure black. "Occurred" refers to the announcement that it has occurred. "And abuse toward nuns" refers to the training rule stated as: "Whosoever nun should abuse a monk.
"Both schisms" refers to the two training rules concerning schism in the Saṅgha. "By the name of the inner robe" refers to [the robe] for an unrelated nun.
"Receiving a robe from the hand" has been stated. "Thread" means having requested thread and having it woven.
"At the wrong time" means eating at the wrong time. "Wandering" means wandering before the meal or after the meal. "Bathing" means bathing within half a month.
"Having given a robe" means criticizing [the monks] after a robe has been given by a complete Saṅgha. "Mountain-top" means dancing and singing.

“Wandering” means undertaking a journey during the rainy season. “Right there” refers to the training rule prescribed in reliance upon residing in that very place without departing on a journey after having completed the rains residence.
“By the giving of consent” means by the giving of consent by one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*).

“The four *pārājikas*” are those not shared with the bhikkhunīs. “The sixteen” refers to the first five training rules, the sixth being the corruption of families; these six, along with the ten *nissaggiyas* not shared with the bhikkhunīs, [make up the sixteen].
"Thirty-four" refers to the thirty-two rules in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga— excluding the first *kathina* rule, the acceptance of black robes, the use of money for robes,
having robes woven, mixing silk with wool, and having wool washed— and the twelve rules not shared with the nuns, making thirty-four in total.
"One hundred and fifty-six" refers to the remaining one hundred and fifty-six rules, excluding the thirty-two training rules prescribed at Vesālī and other locations.
The ten *garayha* rules are the remaining ten *pāṭidesanīya* rules, excluding the two training rules concerning meat that has been specifically prepared for oneself.

The seventy-two *sekhiya* rules are the remaining *sekhiya* rules, excluding the three: making a slurping sound while eating, taking food with the hand, receiving a water-pot, and rinsing the bowl with rice grains still in it.

“Lying down” refers to the training rule concerning lying down with one who is not fully ordained. “Digging” refers to digging the earth. “Go away, O deity” refers to the training rule concerning living plants.

“Pouring water containing living beings” refers to pouring water that contains living beings. “A large monastery” refers to a spacious monastery. “Something else” refers to speaking otherwise than what was said.

“The door” refers to the installation of the bolt as far as the door-socket. “In accordance with the Dhamma” refers to one who is being addressed in accordance with the Dhamma. “Drinking milk” refers to the training rule concerning making a slurping sound.
"Goat's wool" refers to the washing of goat's wool. "And a bowl" refers to a second bowl.

"Exhortation" refers to the exhortation after approaching the dwelling place of the bhikkhunīs. "Medicine" refers to the training rule concerning the invitation for requisites for four months. "Forest-dweller" refers to the fourth *pāṭidesanīya*.
"Exhortation" refers to not going either for the exhortation or for the communal living.

337. Having stated the answer to the question, “And those who [commit offenses] up to the third time,” as “These indeed are those who [commit offenses] up to the third time,” it would have been appropriate to state the answers to the subsequent questions beginning with “Common” and “Uncommon.

However, since that was not stated, and instead eight questions beginning with “How many are the offenses involving cutting” were answered in the interim, immediately following those, [the text states]: “Two hundred and twenty... [etc.]”
The questions concerning what is common and so forth were answered in that very sequence, beginning with “Of the bhikkhus… forty-six matters for bhikkhus not shared with bhikkhunīs.
Therefore, he said, “But because this question, ‘And those which are up to the third time,’ etc.,” in order to show the reason for answering them in that sequence.

338. The verses beginning with “Washing and receiving” (*dhovanañ ca paṭiggaṇho*) are indeed the verses of the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā. “The sitting mat for six years” (*chabbassāni nisīdanaṃ*) refers to two training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
“Two kinds of wool” (*dve loma*) refers to two training rules concerning sheep’s wool, in terms of washing and transporting it beyond three *yojanas*.

“The rainy-season robe and by one living in the forest” (*vassikā āraññakena ca*) refers to the training rule regarding the seeking of a rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) together with the rule regarding dwelling in forest dwellings.
"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) refers to requesting exquisite food. "Deficient" (*ūna*) refers to the ordination of one who is less than twenty years of age.
"Together with a woman" refers to going after having made an appointment. "Whatever training" (*yā sikkhā*) refers to whichever training rule.

"And whatever training regarding the sitting mat" (*nisīdane ca yā sikkhā*) refers to the training rule concerning having a sitting mat made that exceeds the prescribed measure. The same applies here to "the rain-cloth and the bathing cloth."
In the Pāḷi, it says: "These one hundred and seventy are the rules not common to both.
This means that there are forty-six training rules not common to monks (bhikkhus) with nuns (bhikkhunīs), and one hundred and thirty not common to nuns with monks;
thus, there are one hundred and seventy training rules not common to both. One hundred and seventy.
“Forty” refers to the count of the training rules common to both [monks and nuns]; the meaning is that there are one hundred and seventy-four training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
By “classifications” (*vibhattiyo*), both the classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) and the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth are intended.

For these are classified according to the divisions of Pārājika and so on, and according to the divisions of the monks’ Uposatha and so forth. Thus he said, “the classifications,” and so on. “Of these” refers to the eight.

Of the *pārājika* offenses and so forth. "By two" and so on is a demonstration of the settling of legal issues such as those arising from disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) by means of the methods of settlement (*samatha*).
The commentary on the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed in the seven cities is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the offenses of *pārājika* and so forth.
339. This refers to the statement beginning with "Regarding this, 'an offense entailing expulsion' (pārājika) is what was said," and so forth.
For although this was not included among the questions previously raised under the heading "heavy or light" and so on, it is mentioned here in the passage:
"Explain all of these as well; come, let us hear your words. Thus, it refers to other [points] as they were stated: "Explain all of these as well..."
"Come now, let us hear the words"—this shows that it was indeed accepted in this way. Therefore, it was said: "Of that which is included by this word of entreaty," and so forth.
*Ativassati* means it rains upon; the meaning is that the rainwater enters. *Dhammānaṃ*: just as that which maintains the four requisites is called a *dhamma*, [it refers] to those.
Hence he said: "of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhammānaṃ*)". *Gāthāsaṅgaṇikaṃ* means the collection of verses (*gāthāsaṅgaha*).
The *Gāthāsaṅgaṇika* is so called because those various matters are collected, counted, and explained therein by means of verses.
The commentary on the offenses such as the *Pārājikas* is finished.
The method of the commentary on the first *Gāthāsaṅgaṇika* is completed.
341. Explanation of the Discussion on the Splitting of the Legal Case by Reopening, etc.:
“Enough, friend,” having thus persuaded those who were his adversaries—that it was enough to engage in quarreling and the like for the sake of robes, bowls, and so forth—means: “Enough.”
The intention is that they settle their dispute by being made to see the fault in their quarreling and so forth, and by asking one another for forgiveness;
it is not, however, by means of each other seeing whether an offense has been committed or not. Therefore he said, "solely by means of a decision outside the Pāḷi.

He spoke the passage beginning with "One who [relies] on uneven things," etc., showing that a monk who relies on uneven bodily actions and so forth is called "one who relies on the uneven," one who relies on wrong view is "one who relies on the crooked," and one who relies on powerful persons is "one who relies on the powerful."
The commentary on the discussion concerning suborning and causing schism is finished.
342. Regarding the commentary on the origin and other factors of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*):
"By way of offenses arising dependent upon an offense" refers to those who conceal the offenses of others as well as their own.
This was stated with reference specifically to offenses such as *pārājika* for those who conceal a fault (*vajjapaṭicchādī*),

and not to all offenses. Regarding "duties arising in dependence on duties," this refers to the duties of a nun who follows [the formal act] by way of the duties arising in dependence on formal acts such as suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and not by way of all duties.
344. In the Pāḷi, to the question “By how many kinds of legal issues (adhikaraṇa)?”, it is stated: “By one kind of legal issue, namely, a legal issue concerning business (kiccādhikaraṇa).
To the question “In how many places?”, it is stated: “In three places: in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group (gaṇa), and in the presence of an individual.
To the question “By how many means of settlement (samatha)?”, it is stated: “By three means of settlement. By these three as well...
By these [questions], it should be understood that one single mode of settling has been both asked about and answered.

Regarding the statements "A legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) is a legal issue arising from an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa)," and so forth: the question is whether a legal issue arising from a dispute is also a legal issue arising from an accusation and so on;
the answer is that a legal issue arising from a dispute is indeed a legal issue arising from a dispute itself, but it is not a legal issue arising from an accusation or the others.
The commentary on the origins of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-nidāna*) is concluded.

**Commentary on the Sevenfold Diversity of Calming (*samatha*) and Other Topics, §354:** In the response to the question regarding legal issues, the term "discourse" (*vohāra*) in the text refers to verbal discourse of body and speech that results in diverse ripening—that is, the mutual production of suffering due to its varied maturation. "Strife" (*medhaga*) refers to a quarrel that has reached a state of full development.
*Anusampavaṅkatā* (bending along) is the state of being inclined by way of repeatedly associating with the accusation of failure.
*Abbhussahanatā* (excessive exertion) is the state of having become overly zealous. *Anubalappadānaṃ* (providing support) is the act of giving encouragement even to those who are accusing.

*Kammasaṅgahābhāvena* (by way of the absence of inclusion in formal acts) means that because it lacks the inclusion in the duties to be performed by the Saṅgha and others, it consists merely of being in the presence of the Saṅgha and so forth, which is the basis for *sammukhāvinaya*.
The commentary on the sevenfold diversity of tranquility is concluded.
The method for the commentary on the classification of legal issues is concluded.
The second collection of verses.
Commentary on the Questions and Answers Regarding Exhortation, etc., [Section] 359:
In the second collection of verses, the Elder Upāli posed the questions beginning with, “What is the purpose of exhortation?
The Blessed One gave the answers beginning with, “Exhortation is for the purpose of reminding. Thus, the Elder Upāli himself asked the questions and—
They also say that he gave a response.
"The grasping of the *manta*" means the grasping of their deliberations; the meaning is the grasping of the intended purport (*adhippāya*) of both the Suttantika Theras and the Vinayadhara Theras.
"For the purpose of establishing a separate determination" means for each of them individually.
The intention is that, having understood their purpose and having also adopted the method initiated by them, [the Elder spoke] for the sake of reaching a final decision.
By saying, "Do not speak in haste," and so forth, the Elder spoke on the duties of an investigator (*anuvijjaka*), as if advising some investigator standing before him.

"The duty of inquiry" (*anuyuñjanavatta*) refers to the sequence of inquiry; furthermore, since that [duty] applies even to the domain of transgressions against all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*),...
It must be performed in accordance with each respective training rule (sikkhāpada); therefore, it is called "in accordance with the training rules.
It destroys one's own course means it ruins one's progress toward a happy destination (sugati).

Since the word *anusandhi* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), he said: "‘In accordance with the connection’ means in accordance with the sequence of the discourse (*kathānusandhi*). [The phrase] "by way of the connection of the discourse" (*vattānusandhitenā*)...
The same principle applies here as well. "Connected with conduct" (*vattānusandhita*) means connected with behavior;
the sense is: "of one whose admission is consistent with her conduct. Therefore he said: "That which [is established] by her conduct," and so forth.
In the text, the passage beginning with "an intentional offense" (*sañcicca āpattiṃ*) and so on is stated by way of the characteristics of the shameless and the modest among monks and nuns.

This is because the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) pertain to them in every respect. However, for novices (*sāmaṇera*) and others as well, the characteristics of being shameless (*alajji*) or modest (*lajji*) should be understood by way of their commonality, namely, the intentional transgression of their respective training rules and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "speech connected to the context of the discussion": he does not understand the speech connected to the context of the discussion between the one who has been accused and the investigator.
When they have stated one reason, [the respondent], not having himself perceived that, speaks only what he personally prefers;

this is the meaning of "unconnected to the matter. And "words consistent with the decision" means words that are in accordance with the determination of whether there is an offense or no offense made by the investigator (anuvijjaka).
The commentary on the response to the questions beginning with "Codanā" is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the duties of the investigator (*anuvijjaka*) in the *Codanākaṇḍa*.

360. In the text, regarding the passage beginning with "Yaṃ kho tvaṃ," the meaning is: "Friend, as for this monk whom you are accusing, on what fault do you accuse him? On which failure do you accuse him? This applies in all such instances. 361.
"Suspected of impurity" means suspected by a suspicion that has arisen in an improper place regarding impurity. Therefore, it says, "suspected of being groundless. 364.
In the text, "The Uposatha is for the sake of concord" means that it is not for pure monks to remain independent of one another.
Having assembled at the place for the Uposatha, by means of mutually inquiring into and declaring purity through such statements as, "Venerable sirs, announce your purity;
are the venerable ones pure here? I am pure, friends," one avoids those who are unsuitable and, with those who are suitable, acts for the sake of achieving harmony of body and mind.

"Invitation for the sake of purification" means for the purpose of establishing mutual purity by having one another speak regarding what has been seen, heard, and so forth. "Both these" refers to both of these: material gifts and reliance on a person.
The commentary on the duties of the investigator is finished.
*Cūḷasaṅgāma*.
The Description of the Conduct of the Investigator (Anuvijjaka) 365.

*Tatra hi*: in that assembly. *Attapaccatthikā*: persons who are enemies to oneself—that is, hostile persons who desire one's harm and seek to find fault with a person who reproves others out of a sense of shame and goodness.
*Sāsanapaccatthikā*: those who are enemies to the Dispensation—persons who [propound] the word of the Buddha in a manner inconsistent with their own improper conduct.

He explains [the two types]: those who follow the course of craving and those who follow the course of views. "Having plunged into" means having entered into the midst of the Saṅgha by way of overcoming the shameless.
"That one who dwells in the battle" refers to that accuser as being called "one who dwells in the battle.

Regarding the phrase "even what has been seen, heard, or sensed, such as talk about kings, etc.": it should be connected thus: by not speaking even of talk about kings, thieves, and so forth through the medium of what was seen or heard, nor of talk about food and so forth through the medium of what was sensed.

In the passage beginning with "dependent on what is allowable and what is unallowable," etc., by the phrase "the distinction between the material and the immaterial," he shows its nature as the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

By the phrase "connected with the practice of serenity (samatha), etc.," he shows its nature as the entire Sutta Piṭaka. Therein, "the practice of serenity" refers to the sequence for the cultivation of serenity;
likewise for "the practice of insight" (vipassanā). "Dependent on standing, sitting, duties, etc. refers to [conduct] within the midst of the Saṅgha and so forth.
Having established a respectful attitude, [the teaching] is based on rising from one's seat and so forth, as well as on the practice of the fourteen great observances (*mahāvatta*) and others;
by the word "and others," the meaning is that it is also based on fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so on. "When a question has arisen" means when someone has asked a question.
This is merely an illustration; the intended sense is: "Speak on whatever Dhamma has presented itself."
“Family lineage” (*kulapadeso*) refers to a specific family, such as the royal family of Kāsī, even among the various castes beginning with the Khattiyas.
This is precisely what is meant by the statement: “Family lineage is to be understood by way of the Khattiya family and so forth. “In the midst of the assembly” (*sannipātamaṇḍale*) means:

having stood up for the purpose of informing the Saṅgha of the manner in which one is found to be deficient oneself, one looks here and there at the faces of others in the middle of the assembled Saṅgha.
One should not act [with agitation]. The meaning is that one should speak in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya while remaining seated, in such a way that everyone hears it.

In the Pāḷi, "without ferocity" (*acaṇḍikatenā*) means by not adopting a state of ferocity; the meaning is "without harshness. By the phrase "being compassionate for their welfare" (*hitānukampinā*),...
The preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) has been explained. By the phrase "one should be compassionate," compassion that has reached absorption (*appanā*) is indicated.

By the phrase "one who seeks the welfare [of others]," the preliminary stage of compassion is indicated. Therefore he said: "Both compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion should be established;
this is the intended meaning in both cases. *Lajjiyā* means one who possesses a sense of shame (*lajjinī*).
"Having had him recite the duties of application (*anuyogavatta*)" means the duties stated as "I shall speak at the proper time," and so forth.

The "duties of application" refer to the practice of application according to the sequence of conduct for application; having had him recite them means having had him apply himself in that very same sequence—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "with straightforwardness and gentleness" (*ujumaddavena*), he shows the word to be supplied: "he should behave toward. [This applies] both to teachings and to persons.

Regarding the phrase "and," this should be connected with the standard expression "one should be equanimous"; thus he says, "One should be understood as equanimous toward both phenomena (dhammas) and persons (puggalas)...
pe ... equanimous. For one who oversteps what ought to be done in any given instance is not called "equanimous.
Respect (gārava) is to be exercised toward phenomena, whereas toward persons, it is through the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā).
There is respect for partiality. Therefore, it should be understood that one who has not transgressed this rule is neutral toward them. 366.

"For the purpose of comparison" means the intention is that it was stated for the sake of making a decision after comparing [the views] when doubt has arisen as to whether it is an offense or not an offense.
"For the purpose of showing the meaning" means for the sake of the meaning to be established—the subject of comparison such as the offense—and for the accuser and the accused.
It is for the purpose of clarifying the nature [of the offense] by means of the accuser's own admission.

"For the purpose of making known the matter" means that the matter thus clarified is for the purpose of informing, causing reflection upon, and securing the acceptance of it by both the accuser and the accused, as well as by the Saṅgha.
"For the purpose of establishing the person" means [establishing] the accuser and the accused in the offense by means of their own admission.
It is for the purpose of establishing [the person] in non-offense. "For the purpose of reminding" means for the purpose of reminding one who has forgotten.
"For the purpose of making them compliant" means for the purpose of making one compliant when, even after the fault has been pointed out, they accept it but fail to perform the remedy.
"They should not be disparaged" is the demonstration of the intended meaning. In that regard, they should remain only in a position of being non-deceptive.
It should be understood that she is to be sent away, and not the others.
"For the sake of parinibbāna without remainder" means for the sake of parinibbāna which is the cause for there being no rebirth-linking in the future.

For what is called "parinibbāna" refers to the aggregates—consisting of the final death-consciousness and the kamma-born materiality—of those whose taints are exhausted; and these [aggregates] are, in every respect...
Because the underlying tendencies have been utterly severed, they no longer serve as proximate or other conditions for renewed existence, being devoid of other conditions such as craving.
Therefore, it is called "unconditioned parinibbāna. "That" refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For this very reason, he said "in that. "The Vinaya manual" means the adjudication of the Vinaya. "Attentive listening" means the application of the ear.
The meaning is "hearing. Therefore he said, "the knowledge that arises.

Because liberation itself is the primary factor through the aforementioned succession of causes beginning with restraint by the Vinaya, he said, "liberation consisting of the fruit of arahantship," specifying it as the liberation of the mind.
Alternatively, it is the liberation of the mind by way of final nibbāna, having not grasped at any phenomenon whatsoever.

The liberation (*vimokkha*) and release (*vimuccana*) from the continuity of consciousness (*cittasantati*) and the continuity of materiality born of karma bound to that consciousness is their disappearance by way of non-rearising;
"for this purpose" means for the sake of this disappearance—thus the meaning should be understood here by way of conclusion.
(367) In the verses on the duties of inquiry, "by the skillful one, the wise one" refers to the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "Done" (*kata*) means produced or brought into being.

The meaning is "it has been made known. Regarding the phrase "by that very [fact]," etc., the meaning is that by not knowing what was done and what was left undone, one does not know the sequence of events before and after;
furthermore, one does not know whatever has been done or left undone by another bhikkhu as well.
"To one who is similar to oneself" means to one who is similar to oneself by virtue of being possessed of the aforementioned faults.
The explanation of the investigator’s conduct is finished.
The explanation of what must be known, etc., by one who declares the "Great Battle."
368–374. In the *Mahāsaṅgāma*, the phrase "one who frequents the battlefield" (*saṅgāmāvacara*) is stated with reference to an investigator (*anuvijjaka*).
"The matter" (*vatthu*) refers to transgressions such as sexual misconduct. "The source" (*nidāna*) refers to the place of promulgation, such as Vesālī.
Regarding the statement "the person who is not the perpetrator must be known," it should be understood here that the "person" is one who acts as a leader within the Saṅgha or a group.

375. Regarding the training rule on emission (*vissaṭṭhisikkhāpada*): this refers to the training rule on seminal emission (*sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpada*), which is stated by way of the discharge of semen that has ten colors, beginning with blue.
For that [semen] is described as "colored and colorless" (*vaṇṇāvaṇṇa*) by way of its having a faint color such as oil and so forth, or an abundant color such as blue and so forth.
Here, the syllable *a* in the word *avaṇṇa* is used in the sense of abundance.

379. Regarding the statement "up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmās, they are twofold": here it should be understood that among the Suddhāvāsa deities such as the Avihā and others, those who are noble ones (ariya) belong exclusively to the faction of the proponents of the Dhamma, whereas the others belong to both factions.
The commentary on what must be known by one who engages in conventional discourse is finished. [Now begins] the section on the division of the Kathina.
Commentary on the Kathina and Related Matters (Kathināthatādivaṇṇanā) 404.
"By way of what has not yet arrived regarding the kathina" means that when the preliminary application such as fetching water has arisen, the subsequent primary action such as washing arises;

thus, by way of that preliminary application not yet having arrived, it serves as an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*). And its status as a condition belongs to that which has become the effect.

Since the conditions (paccaya) arise depending upon the state of being produced, and not without that [state], it was stated by way of that method, but not in terms of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) in all cases. Therefore he said, "Of the application," and so forth. Therein, the connection is:
"The sevenfold preliminary action (pubbakaraṇa) is a condition for the application. He states the reason with the words, "Since," and so forth. "For the sake of the preliminary action" means:
For the purpose of accomplishing the preliminary preparation (*pubbakaraṇa*). "In the case of the pre-arising condition" (*purejātapaccaye*) means within the domain of the pre-arising condition.
"This" refers to the application (*payoga*). Among the phenomena such as washing and so forth, it does not obtain even a single phenomenon that serves as its own pre-arising condition;
the meaning is that there is no preliminary preparation existing prior to its own arising. "It obtains" [refers to] the post-arising condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*).
It receives the "prior operation" (*pubbakaraṇa*); the meaning is that it becomes a postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*).

In the canonical text, regarding the statement "fifteen states are a condition by way of co-nascence condition" (*sahajātapaccayena paccayo*), since neither "of the prior operation" nor "of the application" (*payoga*)—nor anything else arising as a result of conditions—is mentioned, the fifteen states themselves [act] as a mutual co-nascence condition.
The meaning of "condition" (paccaya) should be understood in this way, because there is no other [dhamma] arising together with them. This applies everywhere in what follows.

Therefore he said, "But as for the conascence condition," and so forth. In the phrase "the matrixes and the impediments," it should be understood that by the word "and" (ca), the five benefits are included.
The same should be understood in the phrase "of the matrixes and the impediments."

The meaning of these [terms] also arises immediately following [the explanation of] the *mātikā* and so forth. For that very reason it is said: "Fifteen states are related by way of co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
"Hope" (*āsā*) refers to hope for robes. "Basis" (*vatthu*) refers to the unobtained robe that serves as the objective basis for that hope.
For, depending upon a robe promised by donors with the words "We shall give" or "We shall make," there subsequently arises—
The expectation regarding robes (*cīvarāsā*) is stated by way of being a condition such as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
"Of expectations and non-expectations" means both the expectation that arises regarding a robe that is obtainable and the non-expectation that arises regarding a robe that is not obtainable;

the meaning is "of those expectations and their cessation. The plural form "expectations" (*āsānaṃ*) is used with reference to the distinction of their arising moment by moment. [This applies] to the expectation and the non-expectation.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said, "hope and lack of hope.
The commentary on the section concerning the stiffening of the robe and so forth is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the classification of the preliminary duties, the introduction, and so forth.
406–7. "Six kinds of robes" is said with reference to any one among the six, such as linen (*khoma*) and so forth.
However, the plural form "robes" (*cīvarāni*) is used in an inclusive sense.

In this context, within the Pāḷi passage beginning with "the material, hope, and lack of hope," the robe that arises through expectation based on the benefits of the *kathina* being spread is called "the material. This refers to the *kathina* robe.
It should be understood that this is stated by means of the terms "cause" (hetu) and "condition" (paccaya).

408. The passage beginning with "by three things... relinquishment" (paccuddhāro tīhi dhammehi) is stated for the purpose of showing that it is not permissible to relinquish something other than the triple robe—such as a rain-season garment (vassikasāṭikā)—for the sake of spreading the kathina, nor is it permissible to spread it after having performed the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). [The phrase] "by verbal expression" (vacībhedena) [is used].
By this, it is shown that the formal act of spreading the *kaṭhina* does not succeed with the body alone.
The commentary on the analysis of the preliminary acts, the causes, and so forth is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the analysis of what is to be known regarding the *kaṭhina* and other matters.

412. "In regard to those phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so forth" means in regard to those phenomena, both material and immaterial, such as: "Bhikkhus who have spent the preceding rains-retreat," "a Saṅgha not deficient by even five members," "the robe-month," and "robes acquired in accordance with the Dhamma and justice. "Existence" (satī) means while they exist.

"State of being mixed" (missībhāva) means the state of conjunction, which is a mere designation for a collection. Therefore he said: "In the ultimate sense, there is no single phenomenon that exists [as a composite]."
416. "They arise together" means that they become *ārahā* (those for whom it is appropriate) simultaneously with the suspension of the *kathina*.
For from the time of the spreading of the *kathina* onwards, all suspensions of the *kathina* arise depending on various respective causes; therefore, they are said to be of simultaneous origin.
Among those, only two—the intermediate suspension and the suspension by reason—are like a monastery where the *kathina* has not been spread.
When performing [the ceremony] together with the entire *kathina*-spreading, they cease along with it and reach the state of being lifted (*uddhāra*).

However, the remaining [cases], where one performs the respective individual *kathina*-spreading for each person by way of severing the two obstacles (*palibodha*), reach the state of being lifted themselves, but not through the entire *kathina*-spreading. And regarding the various ways of lifting the *kathina*:

“Cessation” (nirodha) means the occurrence of the state of being lifted (uddhāra-bhāva) by depending on this or that cause; and thus, “arising” (uppatti) refers precisely to the lifting of the Kathina.

Therefore he said: “All [the factors] arise together with the purpose,” and so forth. Therein, “the first two” refers to the two types of lifting—the interim lifting and the common lifting—which were mentioned first in the Pāḷi as “having a single arising and a single cessation. Regarding those...

Regarding "in cases such as departure" (*pakkamānantikādisu*): "having reached the state of being suspended" (*uddhārabhāvaṃ pattesu*) means having reached the cessation known as the state of suspension;

this is the meaning. "The Kathina-extension remains" (*atthāro tiṭṭhatīti*): setting aside the person who has departed taking the robe already made, the Kathina-extension remains for the rest because of the presence of obstacles (*palibodha*).
The commentary on the section concerning what is to be known regarding the Kathina robe and other matters is finished.
The method of the commentary on the Paññatti-vagga (Chapter on Formal Rules) is finished. The Saṅgaha-vagga (Chapter on Compendium).
The Commentary on the Section on Non-Settling: The Five Cases of Upāli, 421.
"To be performed by a unanimous assembly" means that after having previously been divided regarding legal disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), they subsequently achieve unanimity.

[These are] things that should be done by those who have approached [the assembly]. But why would those possessing a sense of shame (*lajjino*) enter into formal unity (*sāmaggi*) with an assembly mixed with the unrestrained?
To this he says: "In the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth," and so on. Therein, "while they are present" means while the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies are not being performed.
"No support should be given" means that for the sake of preventing them from proceeding further and further, one should say, "We too shall not perform the Uposatha," and so forth.
No support for the quarrel should be given; rather, having established concord through the Dhamma and the Vinaya, the unrestrained monks themselves must be disciplined—this is the intended meaning.
Therefore he said, "If the Saṅgha, having caused [the monk] to confess his transgression," and so forth.
"It does not please the monk" means that he is dissatisfied due to seeing even a slight fault in certain individuals. This is also the disclosure of a view (*diṭṭhāvikamma*).
"Having made [it known]" means having disclosed one's own view to a fellow monk, saying, "This is not acceptable to me.

"Should approach" means that, since there is no loss to the Dispensation, one should give physical communion without disturbing the concord; in such a situation, partaking with those who are shameless does not constitute an offense and is indeed permissible.
However, it is not appropriate to associate with those who are practicing for the destruction of the Dispensation.
There is indeed an offense and the destruction of the Dispensation. Therefore he said, "But where it is contrary to the Dhamma," and so forth.
By the phrase "the manifestation of one's view is not permitted," he shows that there is an offense even for the disclosure of a wrong view.
422. "Black speech" means speech defiled by lust, hatred, and so on; it is an illustration and an exposition of speech that is harmful.

*Assā* means indicating what is harmful. *Mānaṃ nissāya* means: even though the Saṅgha has not assigned the burden of making a formal decision to you, you rely on pride, thinking, "I alone am worthy to pronounce judgment in this matter.

*Yathādiṭṭhiyā* means according to one's own corresponding view. The meaning is that one does not declare [the matter] after having grasped whatever view is appropriate to that specific point. *Assa attano*...
He speaks with reference to the meaning of non-Dhamma and so forth, not to the person;

the meaning is that it is the view corresponding to his own essential nature, which is designated as "non-Dhamma" and so forth. "Having discarded their conviction" means having abandoned the corresponding conviction;

the meaning is "not having grasped it. Therefore he said: "having become one who holds the conviction of Dhamma and so forth regarding what is non-Dhamma and so forth. Alternatively, [regarding] oneself...
By concealing one's own tenets (*laddhi*) and answering in accordance with the disposition of the individual, one does not speak according to one's own view.

In this context, the phrase "having become one who holds the tenet of 'dhamma' regarding what is non-dhamma, etc. should be understood to mean "acting as if one were one who holds the tenet of 'dhamma' regarding what is non-dhamma, etc."
The commentary on the Nappaṭippassambhanavagga is finished.
Commentary on the Vohāravagga, etc.: 424.
*Kammañatti* means a motion that constitutes the formal act (*kamma*). It is a motion that constitutes the formal act independently of a proclamation (*anussāvana*).

The meaning is as follows. "Motion for the basis of the formal act" (*kamma-pāda-ñatti*) refers to the motion that serves as the foundation and the basis for the proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*) within formal acts such as those consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

"In nine instances" refers to the nine instances beginning with reinstatement (*osāraṇa*). "In two instances" refers to formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) and those consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*).

"In accordance with the Suttas" is said with reference to the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) which constitute the Suttas in accordance with the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*. "In accordance with the Vinaya" [is said with reference to the Great Authorities which constitute the Vinaya].

In the *Mahāpadesa* (Great Authorities), which conforms to the *Khandhaka-parivāra*, there are four points to be understood by way of method (*naya*) for the Suttantika: namely, the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), which consist of the meanings to be grasped according to the method of those discourses permitted or prohibited within the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
"Expositions of views" (*diṭṭhīnaṃ āvikammāni*) means the making manifest of the attainment of offenses; that is to say, the formal acts of confession (*desanākamma*) regarding offenses.

"In such a way that the view is made manifest by four or five" means that just as when it is made manifest, the confession of an offense is said to have been made in the presence of one person who has become unified with four or five, so too does he confess.
And while confessing in this manner, he takes three or four bhikkhus together with himself and confesses in the presence of one. Thus...
