It is not permissible to confess [the offense] in this manner. An offense confessed in such a way is not cleared, and there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of the confession itself.
However, it is permissible for two or three [monks] to confess together.
Regarding the phrase "by non-seeing": this refers to the failure to see the practice of those who uphold the Vinaya as they avoid what is improper.

The meaning should also be understood as “by not following their example. “By perceiving what is unallowable as allowable” means by perceiving silver and so forth, which are unallowable, as tin and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “he incurs [the offense] either by asking and not hearing, or by not hearing what is being said to others,” it should be applied separately as:
“either not hearing after having asked, or not hearing what is being said while being asked. “By way of exceeding one night, etc. means...
Having stayed apart from one’s robe that has been formally resolved upon, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense by exceeding one night.
By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), the inclusion of exceeding six nights and so forth is intended.
450. “Bringing harm and the teaching of the Kali age”: the meaning is that by uttering words of anger that bring about harm, or by attributing fault, one strives toward misfortune.
454. "In conventional terminology" (*vohāraniruttiyā*) means that he has not attained the knowledge that distinguishes the various words expressive of their respective meanings.

455. "Skilled in applying rounded phrasing" (*parimaṇḍalabyañjanāropane kusalo*) means that he is incapable of explaining a subject matter using rounded word-phrases or of understanding what has been said by others. 458. "By means of a proclamation" (*anussāvanena*) means by way of successive statements.
Therefore he said, "Did you not [say]... and so forth, which is what we have already stated. This, then—

The connection is with the word "revealed" (*pakāsito*). In this context, since the word "this" (*yam*) does not depend on a [specific] statement but depends solely on the meaning of the statement, the sense to be understood is: "we have stated that meaning in order to reveal, by means of that statement, the absence of any distinction.
For this very reason, the reference is made in the masculine gender as "this indeed" (*svāyam*); the meaning is: "this is its absence of distinction."

467. “Even on the legs of a bed, etc., one might strike one’s forehead”: this means that when one has spread out a piece of leather in the dark and bows down to pay homage, one’s forehead or eye strikes against the bed and so forth.

By this, he explains both the absence of an offense even for one who pays homage in such a manner, and the fact that there is no total prohibition of paying homage. Thus it is in all cases where [the action] is not prohibited by other suttas.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to pay homage to those who are naked and so forth. "Turning toward one side" (*ekato āvaṭṭo*) means having turned and entered into the faction of those who have gone to a state of fault.
Therefore he said, "standing on the side of the enemy. "Being paid homage" (*vandiyamāno*) means being paid homage by bowing down.

Among those worthy of homage, because both the preceptor for instruction (*uddesācariya*) and the preceptor for dependence (*nissayācariya*) may be junior, they are [here] referred to as "elders" (*vuḍḍhā*).
Thus they are to be understood as those who are worthy of veneration.
"As stated previously" refers to the offenses involving the prohibition against sharing a sleeping place and so forth. "The other" refers to that which involves a conscious mind.
The commentary on the section beginning with the Vohāra-vagga is finished.
The Second Group of Verses on the Enumeration:
An Explanation of Offenses Concerning the Body, etc. 474.
Having himself asked, for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya, “How many offenses are there? and so forth, the Elder Upāli—

The answer has been given. "Of the bhikkhunīs alone... and so forth... "called the eightfold basis" means that there is only one offense prescribed for bhikkhunīs which is called the eightfold basis. 475.
Regarding the phrase "the formal act and the bases of the formal act": herein, since in the case of formal acts consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), the motion itself is the formal act.

In formal acts consisting of one motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) or one motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), it stands as the basis for the motion that constitutes the formal act;
therefore, these two are called "functions of the motion" (*ñattikicca*).

Together with the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), the offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) are included; thus, in all ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*), [the offense applies] by way of one who is ordained in only one [of the two orders].
This was said with reference to the previously mentioned *dukkaṭa*. "In the first training rule" means in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the first training rule of the Chapter on Exhorting Bhikkhunīs.
Regarding "an illegal formal act": when an illegal formal act of appointment as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs occurs, two sets of nine offenses are incurred;
and when a legal formal act occurs, two [other] sets of nine offenses are incurred—thus four sets of nine are stated. For one who requests raw grain and then eats it...

In the preliminary effort of making oneself understood and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); at the act of swallowing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). It is stated that the offenses of wrong-doing are already included along with the offense of expiation.

Regarding such phrases as "departing" and "standing," when a bhikkhunī has stood having departed from hand’s reach with one foot, performed some business, and then desires to stand having departed with the other foot, at that time she [incurs the offense] in due order.
It receives this conventional designation: “she stands relinquishing,” or “having relinquished, she stands.

For otherwise, there would be no distinction between her departure from the vicinity of a village and her mere relinquishing of hand’s-reach, since both involve the act of going. Or, regarding the phrases “she sits down” or “she lies down”:
here too, according to the aforementioned intention, she sits down while relinquishing hand’s-reach by means of half a seat, or by means of the entire seat.
One should construe it thus: "she sits having relinquished [the body] with half the body; she lies down having relinquished it with the whole body.
The commentary on bodily and other offenses is concluded.
Commentary on the *Pācittiya* Rules: 476.
"All have different bases" means that there are five distinct *pācittiya* offenses based on the distinction between the five types of substances, such as ghee, fresh butter, and so forth.
This same method applies to the nine *pācittiya* rules concerning exquisite foods, and so on. By this—

This shows that although the training rules concerning medicine and choice food were laid down as individual rules, they are each like five training rules due to the diversity of their subject matter, similar to the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses for bhikkhunīs.
For this very reason, it is said: "They have different subject matters. Having accepted ghee itself, [and placed it] in many vessels...
For one who lets more than seven days pass, even though many offenses may arise according to the number of vessels,
they all share the same underlying basis (*ekavatthuka*). Likewise, it should be understood that for one who requests ghee-food in many places and then eats it—
either all at once or separately— the offenses likewise share the same underlying basis.

In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase “he should confess with a single utterance, as stated by the Kinsman of the Sun,” one should connect it by supplying the word *iti* (thus), so that it reads: “‘He should confess’—this is what was stated. The same applies to the remaining cases.
In the expression “those who follow the schism,” the word *ādi* (etcetera) is indicated as being elided. All those [offenses] occurring up to the third time are included in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*;
they are treated as one by way of the common category of *saṅghādisesa*, and as another by way of the common category of *pācittiya*. Thus, regarding the “up-to-the-third-time” offenses...
It should be understood that it is stated as "three. And here, there is indeed an *dukkaṭa* for the motion (*ñatti*), and two *thullaccayas* for each of the two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*).
These are not included in the *mātikā*. It is on account of what is included in the *mātikā* that it is stated here as "three.
By "the Saṅgha and so forth" is meant by the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual acting as the cause. "One of pure virtue" means by way of having attained a state of complete purity.
"Of newly arisen virtue. For that which has newly arisen is called "wondrous" (*abbhuṇha*); the meaning is "one whose virtue is purified.
Therefore he said, "natural.
Regarding the phrase "the benefits stated in the Kosambakakkhandhaka," this refers to [the passage] in the Kosambakakkhandhaka: "If these monks..."

Having shown the danger of not acknowledging an offense by saying, "They will suspend me for not seeing an offense; they will not perform the Uposatha together with me," and so forth, the method for confessing an offense through the faith of others is also clarified by implication.
[Furthermore, there is] performing the Uposatha together, performing the Pavāraṇā, performing Saṅgha formal acts, and sitting on a seat.

This was said with reference to eight benefits, namely: sitting while drinking gruel, sitting while eating a meal, lying down in a single shelter, and performing salutations and so forth according to seniority.
"Of four" is said with reference to those [confessions] found in the Vinaya Piṭaka. But what is that confession of transgression? It is fourfold.
"What is the meaning? [This is the sense. "Of those intent on killing" means of archers employed for the purpose of killing.
"Of the attendant" refers to one mentioned in the context of the training rule concerning sleeping together (*sahaseyya-sikkhāpada*).
"Of eight bhikkhunīs" means when another has arrived after eight bhikkhunīs starting from the senior seat.
A seat must be given to a senior bhikkhunī. However, it is permissible not to give one to a junior bhikkhunī who has arrived among eight [senior] bhikkhunīs;
she should sit in the place obtained for the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
Alternatively, a seat may be given by the other, more junior bhikkhunī to the eight senior bhikkhunīs. "Nine formal acts" refers to the nine acts themselves, beginning with reinstatement (osāraṇā).
The commentary on the *Pācittiya* rules is concluded.
**Commentary on Persons Not to be Venerated, etc.** 477.

"Ten persons" refers to ten individuals: the nine types of non-ordained persons—namely, those of a different communion (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*), a woman (*mātugāma*), and a paṇḍaka—as stated in the passage beginning, "Monks, these nine are not to be venerated," together with the five types beginning with those undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). Thus, there are ten persons.

“Twelve faults of action” means twelve actions associated with fault. “Perfections of action” means accomplished actions; that is, purified actions. “This very same” means [an assembly] that is both righteous and unanimous.
He says “the Endless Victor” (*anantajina*) because he has conquered and attained the endless *nibbāna*; thus he says “the limited,” and so forth. “He himself” refers to that very Blessed One.
By such statements as “To you who profess the Vinaya, we listen to your Vinaya,” it is shown that Upāli Thera alone was a bearer of the Vinaya.
Having asked as if to one standing face-to-face, he gave an answer as if it had been answered by him.
In that context, "of one who professes the Vinaya" means of one who professes, "I know the Vinaya. "The Vinayas" means we listen while the Vinaya is being spoken by you.
478. In the Pāḷi, the phrase "pārājika," etc., is stated by way of including what has not been included among those things mentioned in both Vibhaṅgas.
The commentary on persons who are not to be saluted, etc., is finished.
This is the verse for wiping away the sweat.
Commentary on the Questions on Non-Separation (Avippavāsapañhāvaṇṇanā) 479.

In the verses concerning the wiping of sweat, "unallowable communal use" (*akappiyasambhoga*) refers specifically to the communal association with those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), such as participating in the Uposatha ceremony and so forth.
In the phrase "my questions" (*pañhā me sa*), the letter *m* serves as a sandhi-conjunction; and [the word] *esa*...
It is stated by way of a change of gender; the meaning is "this is the question. Alternatively, the word *pañha* (question) should be understood as being of two genders.
Therefore he said, "This is the question," and so forth.
"With reference to heavy goods" means with reference to the exchange of heavy goods for heavy goods. "Ten" means ten.

"Persons not to be saluted" refers to the eleven types of persons incapable [of progress]. "Not shared with regard to the training" means that it is a training rule not shared with the monks because of the training rule permitting the carrying of a razor-case.
"I do not say above the collar-bone" refers to the *pārājika* offense even when [the act] occurs in the mouth situated above the collar-bone on the head.

I do not say so. "Below the navel" means: even excluding the passages for excrement and urine situated below the navel, how could one be defeated on account of sexual intercourse in any other part of the body? This is the meaning.
"The matter of cutting off" refers to a *pārājika* offense.
The commentary on the questions concerning non-separation is finished.
Commentary on the questions concerning the *pārājika* offenses, etc.: 480.

Regarding "a robe-shed (*dussakuṭi*) and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are included huts covered with reeds, rushes, leaves, grass, and so on, as well as those covered with grass, leaves, and the like.

He embraces [the offense]. For if one were to have a woman standing inside such a hut—after having spread cloth or other materials on the path outside—enter by that means, he would be subject to a *pārājika* offense.

It is stated with reference to a change of gender; for when the gender changes, because the formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is relinquished, it is stated with reference to the offense incurred in consuming [food] again without having formally accepted it anew.
In the Pāḷi, "there may be twenty bhikkhus assembled" means that twenty bhikkhus have come together; by this, he shows that the Saṅgha is worthy of performing all formal acts (kamma).
Regarding the verse, "clad," it means clad with the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and having donned the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) doubled over, with the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) wrapped around.
Thus, when even a mere drop of black [stain] has reached those three robes on the body of a bhikkhunī, as soon as it is washed away by water—
The meaning is that they are subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
Regarding the verse "one who kills a woman," one should not kill a woman who has been one's mother, nor should one kill a man who has been one's father.
"A non-noble" (*anariya*) means one should kill only one who is not an *arahant*; by this, he shows that even the killer of an *arahant* does not [fall under this category].
"Immediately touching" means that it touches with immediate consequence (*ānantariya*).
"Like a well-established banyan tree" is said with reference to a tree one league in extent.
"In the seventeen rules" refers to the seventeen *saṅghādisesa* offenses prescribed for bhikkhunīs.
The commentary on the questions concerning the Pārājika and other offenses is finished.
The commentary on the fifth section, the Kamma-vagga (Section on Formal Acts), is concluded.

483. Regarding the section on formal acts (*kammavagga*), it is stated that "except for the month of Kattika" because, once the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have been set aside, it is not permissible to perform an Uposatha after having performed a Pavāraṇā of concord (*sāmaggī*) in the month of Kattika.

However, if those who have performed the Great Pavāraṇā separately in different boundaries (*nānāsīmā*) achieve concord within the month of Kattika, there is an Uposatha of concord (*sāmaggī-uposatha*).
Thus it should be performed by them, but not the *pavāraṇā*. This is because a further *pavāraṇā* is not prescribed for those who have already performed the *pavāraṇā* within the same year.
"The day of concord" (*sāmaggī-divasa*) is said with reference to the act of establishing concord on a day other than the regular *uposatha* day.
However, if the Saṅgha establishes concord on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, then that is not a "day of concord *uposatha*"; it is simply the fourteenth or fifteenth-day *uposatha*.
...there is. The same method applies to the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) above as well.

"The day set aside by postponement" refers specifically to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, which was set aside because [the monks] were harassed by quarrelsome persons or because they had made an arrangement for the invitation ceremony due to some business. And "the two full-moon days."

There are two full-moon days: the full moon of the earlier Kattika and the full moon of the later Kattika. Thus, "in these four ways" refers to the combination of the two full-moon days with the *sāmaggī-pavāraṇā* (the invitation for harmony) and the *cātuddasī-pavāraṇā* (the invitation on the fourteenth day).
This is stated according to the normal course of conduct; however, when such circumstances arise, [it may be done] on both full-moon days.
The first two— the fourteenth of the dark fortnight and the fifteenth immediately following it—
are also days for the *pavāraṇā*. Thus, having set aside these seven types of *pavāraṇā* days,
it is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* on any other day.

484. "Having performed the formal proclamation (*anussāvanakamma*)" means: having first made the proclamation, and immediately after that proclamation, having stated the entire motion (*ñatti*) with the words "This is the motion," and finally having said "This is the motion"—this is the intended meaning.
485. "That which is this" refers to the classification of phonemes (*byañjana*). Regarding the phrase "the classification is tenfold through the cognition of phonemes," it should be construed as:
"the classification of phonemes is tenfold, that is, of ten kinds. To the question "By what is this classification [made]? he says: "Through the cognition of phonemes."
The "phoneme-consciousness" (*byañjanabuddhi*) is the intelligence that generates the phonemes (*akkhara*), which are designated as "phonemes" because they manifest the intended meaning and wording.

By means of that phoneme-consciousness—the sense being that it occurs precisely through the specific types of consciousness that originate the phonemes—or alternatively, when [a preceding vowel] is followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), this [consonant] is also heavy; such is the construction.
In this context, among the terms beginning with "āyasmato," those consonants that are contiguous, such as *s*, *k*, *m*, and so forth, are called a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
That which has such a conjunction following it—such as the vowel *a*—is termed "followed by a conjunction" (*saṃyogapara*).

"Short" (*rassa*) refers to a vowel devoid of consonants such as *a*. "Not followed by a conjunction" (*asaṃyogapara*) refers to a vowel accompanied by consonants such as *y* or *n*, as in the examples "yassa" and "nakkhamati."

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Even one who says "suṇāṭu me" and so forth—without changing the letter *ta* to *tha*, but instead making it merely lax within the same class of consonants (*vagga*)—commits a phonetic error (*durutta*), provided that the appropriate substitution (*ādesa*) is not applied.
For instance, when it should have been said "saccikatthaparamatthena," it is said "saccikaṭṭhaparamaṭṭhena"; and when it should have been said "atthakathā," it is said "aṭṭhakathā."

In various places it is so stated; it is appropriate to use such forms as seen in the application of the Pāḷi and its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), and to speak in accordance with them, but nothing other than that is permitted.
Therefore he said: "Without breaking the tradition (*paveṇi*) that has come down in succession," and so forth.

Regarding cases where a long vowel should be used but a short one is employed—such as when "bhikkhūnaṃ" should be said but "bhikkhunaṃ" is used, or "bahūsu" [is used instead of "bahūsuṃ"]—it is likewise acceptable.
In cases where one should say "bahūsu," one may say "nakkhamati"; where one should say "na khamati," one may say "na khamatī";
or where one should say "upasampadāpekkho," one may say "upasampadāpekho"—in such corresponding instances, it is permissible to transpose long vowels for short ones and short vowels for long ones.
However, one must not say "nago" when "nāgo" should be said, nor "sagho" when "saṅgho" should be said.
Or, one may speak in such inappropriate places as saying "tiso" when "tisso" should be said, or "yācantī" when "yācati" should be said.
However, it should be understood that connection (*sambandha*) and delimitation (*vavatthāna*) are permissible in every respect.
"In the remaining boundaries as well" means in all ten [types], beginning with the "excessively large" (*atimahatī*).
488. Regarding "to be performed by a quorum of four" (*catuvaggakaraṇa*): it refers to those matters that must be carried out by a Saṅgha consisting of four members.

"Not excluded" (*anissārita*) means not cast out from the community, either by the suspension of the Uposatha and so forth, or by being of a different communion through a difference of doctrine. For in the Commentary it is said:

"'Of one who has been dealt with' (*apakatatta*) means of one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), or of one for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā have been suspended"; thus, a monk for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā have been suspended [is meant].
"It must be understood as 'one who is not yet fully integrated' (apakatatta). By 'those of pure virtue,' those who have not committed a *pārājika* offense are intended.
However, in the case of formal acts such as probation (*parivāsa*), even those who have committed a grave offense must be understood as 'not yet fully integrated. The statement 'the rest...

are indeed entitled to give their consent' refers to those standing at a distance from the Saṅgha beyond arm's reach; for those standing without having left that distance, they are not entitled to give consent."
Even those [who are] more than four members of the Saṅgha become eligible for the consent (*chanda*) only after they have stepped outside the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*).
Therefore, the consent or the purity (*pārisuddhi*) must be given by one who remains standing outside the reach of the hand from the Saṅgha.
The commentary on the section on formal acts (*kammavagga*) is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Notification (Apalokanakamma):

496. Even nowadays, in cases such as "if [one says] 'he is a novice monk' and so forth," even speaking dispraise of the Buddha and others, or explaining what is unallowable as allowable and so forth, falls precisely within the failure of view (diṭṭhivipatti). For this very reason, he will say: "He should be made to relinquish that adherence."
The same method applies to the bhikkhus as well. "One of wrong view" means one who grasps the intention of the Buddha’s word in a distorted way;

he is also described as being "endowed with an extreme view. Some, however, say that it is "one endowed with either an eternalist or a nihilist view," but that is not correct, because [the text] speaks of the grasping at eternalism and annihilation specifically regarding novices.

Because it was stated in the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) below that [the penalty] serves as the cause for the removal of status (*liṅganāsanā*), and because here the intention refers specifically to the removal of status through disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma-nāsanā*).

It should also be given to him: even if he possesses qualities such as being talkative (*mukhara*), etc., it must be given to one who does not desist from censuring others and so forth—even without having been questioned, without having been made to admit it, and without having been charged with an offense—regardless of whether an offense has already been confessed. To one who desists...
However, it should not be granted to one who is seeking forgiveness.
"Granting the Brahma-punishment" means granting a harsh punishment, a severe punishment.

For when formal acts such as *tajjanīya* (reproof) have been performed, there is no refusal to provide instruction and admonition. But when the Brahma-punishment has been granted, in that case—along with...

It is not permissible to perform even that which has been refused by those who have undergone a formal act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and so forth, because by the phrase "not even to be spoken to" and so on, even mere conversation and dialogue are prohibited by the word "no.
For upon seeing him, the monks do not even turn their heads to look at him;
thus it must be avoided, since that punishment was authorized precisely for the purpose of making him humble (*nimmadana*). For that very reason...
The Elder Channa, though he had been subjected to acts such as *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension), did not fear;
yet when the *brahmadaṇḍa* was imposed upon him, he fell down in a swoon, thinking, "I have been utterly abandoned by the Saṅgha.

It should be understood that for one who, knowing of another who has received the *brahmadaṇḍa*, continues to associate with them without being excluded, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); otherwise, the prescription of the *brahmadaṇḍa* would be meaningless.
Because it would follow that [the act] is rendered meaningless. "By that" means by means of the Brahmadaṇḍa.
Just as with those who have undergone acts such as the *tajjanīya-kamma*, one must likewise conduct oneself correctly toward the Saṅgha, even more so than before.

And that has been shown in its own form in the passage beginning, "Gentle and humble in conduct. Therefore, he said: "The Brahmadaṇḍa should be lifted for one who, having conducted himself correctly, asks for forgiveness."
The connection is: "That which was authorized by the Blessed One as an act not to be saluted.

Having shown the general manner in which it was authorized by saying, "To perform a disciplinary act against that bhikkhu," one should understand that the Pāḷi beginning with "Then indeed" was extracted to show the specific manner in which it was authorized.
"This is the occasion for this *apalokana*-kamma (act of seeking permission)."
It is the locus for the occurrence of the general category of *apalokana-kamma*.
Although it does not exist through a distinction from its particulars, it is expressed as if dependent on a qualification in order to show its non-occurrence elsewhere.
By the statement "the action itself is the characteristic," all remaining types—such as *osāraṇā* and so forth—are included by way of the general characteristic of *apalokana-kamma*.
Because it is grasped [by the mind], action itself is its characteristic; thus he shows the etymological derivation as "the characteristic of action" (*kammalakkhaṇa*).

This should be understood as the place of completion for the remaining actions mentioned, just as the aggregates, bases, and elements are the place of completion for the remaining aggregates and bases not explicitly mentioned.
For this very reason, he will say: "But here is also a determination of the characteristic of action that is outside the canonical text," and so forth.
It should be understood that just as it is here, so too the characteristic of the formal act (*kamma*) is stated in the subsequent sections concerning the *ñattikamma* and others.
"Its performance" refers to the procedure for performing an act that is not to be saluted.

It should be seen that by the words "is not to be saluted," it is shown that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who salutes [such a person]. For indeed, just like trampling upon a formal agreement (*katika*) made by the Sangha, there is an offense for one who transgresses the authorization of the Sangha with disrespect.
Since this [definition] is taken merely as an illustration of an act that is not to be performed by the Saṅgha, the characteristic of an act applies to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha as well.
The place for distributing voting tickets is called the *salākagga*. The places for serving rice and gruel are called the *yāgagga* and *bhattagga*.
For in these places too, the entire Saṅgha has assembled just as at the Uposatha, and the act is a *vaggakamma* (an act performed by a faction).
There is no such thing as later criticizing [the act], saying, "We did not know this.

However, they do criticize when it is performed within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (an incomplete boundary). For when seeking permission to give requisites belonging to the Saṅgha—such as robes that have not been cut—to those staying within the *upacārasīmā*, it must be done only after obtaining the consent of everyone present.
As for a person of a different class who performs a legitimate (*dhammika*) formal motion...
If he prevents it, it is permissible to do so by means of a stratagem, either by having him go outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) or by entering a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).

Regarding that which is indicated in general terms as "performing an act of consultation" (*apalokanakamma*), he speaks of "one whose robe is not cut off," etc., in order to show that specific act of consultation in its particular form.
If the robe must indeed be given only after consulting, then what [is the point]?
Regarding the "authorization for dispensing small quantities," he said, "But by one who dispenses small quantities," and so forth.
"A nāḷi or half a nāḷi" is a demonstration of the measure of what should be given after seeking permission day by day.

By this, he shows that only the amount necessary for subsistence should be requested, and nothing more. "On a single day only," and so forth, refers to [the period of] ten or twenty days within one [day].

This shows the demonstration of the limit for what must be given on a day-by-day basis; by this, it is shown that it is not permissible to request [permission] in such a way as "as long as I live" or "until I recover from my illness.
Regarding "the obstacle of debt" (*iṇapalibodha*), the connection is: "it is permissible to give the substance of the debt.
And that [debt] must be only a moderate amount for one who is hindered by creditors, who is modest and virtuous, and who is a benefactor of the Teaching.
Having determined that it is allowable property and having obtained permission, it should be given; however, it must not be a large debt such as a thousand or a hundred thousand.
For such a thing should be sought out and given to such a bhikkhu by all bhikkhus through the practice of alms-gathering.
"From a deposit" means from goods placed with a money-changer for the purpose of maintaining a shrine after they have been invested at interest.
"Even with what belongs to the Saṅgha" means not only from the source of that [income], but also with goods given to the Saṅgha by donors for the sake of the four requisites; this is the meaning.

"It is not permissible to provide a meal for the Saṅgha" implies that it is not permissible to have one prepared even when it is being done by those giving a great almsgiving, as if it were a meal for the Saṅgha.
Because it is said, "It is pleasing to enjoy it as one likes," one may take either a small or a large amount sufficient for one's own consumption;
however, one is not permitted to take more than that. "On the Uposatha day" is merely an illustration;
on whatever day it is performed, it is indeed well-performed. While performing it, [one should think]: "Whatever [is within] this monastery, inside the boundary..."
The agreement should be made thus: "It is my wish that what belongs to the Saṅgha... [etc. ...be used as one pleases.
Likewise, for two or three [monks], the only difference here is the statement: "It is pleasing to the Venerable Ones. "Of those too" means of the trees.
"That same agreement" means that no separate agreement need be made.

"Tesam" means "of the trees. "The Saṅgha is the owner" is the connection [between the two]. "In the former monastery" refers to a monastery where a formal agreement (*katika*) had been made for use as one pleases in the past.

"Having built monastic courtyards (*pariveṇa*), they maintain them" was said with reference to a place where, if left unprotected, fruits and flowers would perish and the trees would decay; in such a case, there is no formal agreement for the Saṅgha.

The meaning is "circulation. However, those trees which were planted by sowing seeds and tended from the very beginning must also be enjoyed by the planters themselves after they have given a tenth part [to the monastery].

"By them" means by the caretakers. "Therein" means in that monastery. "At the root" means at the beginning; the sense is "formerly. "A long-standing agreement" means one for an indefinite period of time.
The agreement is for the purpose of enjoying [the food] as one pleases. "Without remorse" means without feeling remorse, thinking, "This has not been distributed.
"It is merely for the sake of complaining" means that there is no fault for those who eat much because of that complaining, since they have taken only what is sufficient for their own consumption;
the intention is that even while complaining, one should take and eat only what is enough for oneself.

It is said that one should not say, "Take it," because if this were said, they might imagine it was given by that very monk himself, and through that, the possibility of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) arises.
Therefore he said, "having deliberated," and so forth. "A half-portion" means a half-portion from the share of a single monk.
And when giving, [he should think], "The Saṅgha has permitted me to give this much. Thus he refers to himself.
Having released it, one should give it after speaking in such a way that they develop confidence in the Saṅgha itself.

"Without expecting anything in return" means that even when giving one's own property to persons who have been authorized—such as those who are ill, those traveling, or those in authority—it must be given without expecting anything in return;
however, for persons who have not been authorized, one must not give even without expecting anything in return.
"It is allowable" means that what belongs to the Saṅgha itself must be given [to him] as it has been prepared.

Even if it is his own property, if the providers of requisites and others take it themselves out of trust, he should not prevent them; since what has been obtained is permissible, he should remain silent.
"As was said before" refers to the reason for remaining silent, which was already stated previously in the passage beginning, "For if he were angry, he might even cut down the trees," and so forth.
Even though no harm has been done by them, it is appropriate to remain silent out of compassion; however, it is not appropriate to say things such as, "Take [it].

Because it is a heavy object... [the phrase] "it should not be given" is stated because living trees are like a monastery (*ārāma*), and because the timber has not yet reached the state of being a house-building material;
thus, it is not permitted to give it by saying, "You may take everything yourself. Or, "having made it an unoccupied dwelling" means that which did not previously exist there.
When the time for maintaining the lodgings had arrived and the fruit season had come.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the formal act of seeking permission is finished.
Commentary on the section beginning with "The Benefits" (Atthavasavagga), etc.
498. Regarding the phrase "enmity pertaining to the future life, which consists of the suffering of karmic ripening":

here, because [the unwholesome states] are produced by enmity such as killing living beings and so forth, and because they are the cause for the attainment of enmity, they are called "feelings of suffering as karmic ripening.

Furthermore, the phrase "of the various ten courses of unwholesome action" is stated again in order to include together with the enmities those unwholesome states that are free from the five specific enmities of killing living beings and so forth.
499–500. "That action" refers specifically to the formal acts such as the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*); the connection is that "the seven classes of offenses are what is called 'prescribed'.
Regarding the phrase "in the interval when no training rule had been prescribed by anyone":

this refers to the period from the beginning of this eon up until the full enlightenment of our Blessed One, during which time—excluding Kakusandha and the others—no training rule had been prescribed by anyone.
The meaning is "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*). Regarding the discussion on what has been "resolved" (*vinīta*): the "training rules" are simply the bases for resolution.

For these are called "training rules" because they clarify the respective sections of training, and they are called "subsequent ordinances" (*anupaññatti*) because they establish further rules concerning offenses and non-offenses.
The commentary on the section on the Benefits and so forth is concluded.
The method of commentary on the Saṅgahavagga is finished.
Thus, it should be understood that the Parivāra is adorned by these three great sections: the Mahāvagga, the Paññattivagga, and the Saṅgahavagga.
Thus ends [the section] from the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya, titled Vimativinodanī.
The method of commentary on the Parivāra is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the concluding discourse:
in the final verses, there is a formal acknowledgment of the analysis (*vibhāga-paṭidesanā*), because [the text] has been analyzed by means of the Ubhatovibhaṅga, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra.
The construction is as follows: "In which Vinaya Piṭaka" refers to that which teaches the analysis of the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra.
"Of that" means of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"The Teacher’s Great Bodhi" is said with reference to the southern branch [of the Bodhi tree]. That which is called the Pariveṇa named Padhānaghara—
In that regard, it should be connected thus: "He dwelt in that palace belonging to the lord of the great town, which was built and enclosed with beautiful ramparts. The construction is as follows:

"The commentary on the Vinaya—which is successful and perfected through its complete analysis—was undertaken by way of, or in reliance upon, the glory of the Buddha; or else, depending on his (the Buddha’s) exhortation."
“Of Sirinivāsa” means of the king named Siripāla, who was the abode of glory (*siri*).
“In the year of victory” means in a year endowed with victory. It was stated again, “This was begun in the year of victory,” for the purpose of showing the time it commenced.
“Raining in due season” means having the habit of raining at the appropriate time. “Deva” means a cloud.
The commentary on the concluding discourse is finished.
And to this extent, that which was undertaken as the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā [is completed].
The commentary is not overly extensive, yet it provides a complete analysis.
Measured by the extent of the text consisting of fifty recitation sections,
this *Vimativinodanī* has reached its ultimate completion.
This [teaching] has been completed without obstruction;
it has reached its conclusion. May all living beings attain that very conclusion which is their heart's desire.
By means of the Elders who are knowers of the Vinaya and whose conduct is pure and austere—
By whatever merit I have gained through thus composing this commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya— which was sought after by those who are distrustful, overly diffuse,
or fearful of the textual knots— may I, having attained supreme enlightenment, [lead others to it].
Having elucidated the meaning of the Vinaya, that which provides the characteristics along with the method,
which bestows the eye of knowledge that cuts through doubt, and which avoids the loss of the text through omissions, inversions, or excessive prolixity;
"I shall lead sentient beings to purity from the suffering of saṃsāra.
May all people, together with all worldly enjoyments and virtues,
be devoted to the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One."
The Commentary Dispelling Doubt is completed.
